The Twenty-One Rig-Shakhas

Patanjali, in the Paspashahnika section of his Mahabhashya, writes:

एकविंशतिधा बाह्वृच्यम् ।

एकविंशतिधा बाह्वृच्यम् ekaviṃśatidhā bāhvṛcyam

"The Bahvricha [Rigveda tradition] exists in twenty-one forms [i.e., has 21 shakhas]."

That is: the Rigveda has 21 shakhas — a claim already supported, as noted in Chapter 2, by other evidence. A further citation from the same source lists several by name, along with the shakha-counts of the other Vedas:

बाह्वृच्यमेकविंशतिधा । अथर्ववेदो नवधा । ... बाह्वृचस्य—ऐतरेय-बाष्कल-कौषीतक-जानन्ती-बाह्वि-गौतम-शाकल्य-बाभ्रव्य-शैंग्य-मुद्गल-शौनकशाखाः ।

(approximate reading, given scan condition) "The Bahvricha [tradition] is twenty-one-fold; the Atharvaveda nine-fold... Among the shakhas of the Bahvricha [Rigveda]: Aitareya, Bashkala, Kaushitaka, Jananti, Bahvi, Gautama, Shakalya, Bhabhravya, Shaingya, Mudgala, and Shaunaka."

That is: the Rigveda has 21 shakhas, the Atharvaveda 9; among the Rigveda's shakhas, those named here are Aitareya, Bashkala, Kaushitaki, Jananti, Bahvi, Gautama, Shakalya, Bhabhravya, Shaingya, Mudgala, and Shaunaka (eleven of the full twenty-one are named explicitly in this passage).

A further, more granular breakdown of Rigveda sub-branches appears in a citation the text gives just after the "21 shakhas" passage above:

सर्वे ते बह्वृचाः पुष्पिशिखो भूत्वा पञ्चविंशतिधा भिन्नाः । तद्यथा शाकलाः । बाष्कलाः । माण्डव्या इति । तत्र दश शाकलाः । अष्टौ बाष्कलाः । सप्त माण्डव्या इत्ययं ब्राह्मणबद्ध्यचानां शाखा पुष्पिशिखो भूत्वा पञ्चविंशतिधा भिन्नाः ।

सर्वे ते बह्वृचाः पुष्पिशिखो भूत्वा पञ्चविंशतिधा भिन्नाः । तद्यथा शाकलाः । बाष्कलाः । माण्डव्या इति । तत्र दश शाकलाः । अष्टौ बाष्कलाः । सप्त माण्डव्या इत्य् अयं ब्राह्मण-बद्ध्यचानां शाखा पुष्पिशिखो भूत्वा पञ्चविंशतिधा भिन्नाः । sarve te bahvṛcāḥ puṣpiśikho bhūtvā pañcaviṃśatidhā bhinnāḥ | tadyathā śākalāḥ | bāṣkalāḥ | māṇḍavyā iti | tatra daśa śākalāḥ | aṣṭau bāṣkalāḥ | sapta māṇḍavyā ity ayaṃ brāhmaṇa-baddhyacānāṃ śākhā puṣpiśikho bhūtvā pañcaviṃśatidhā bhinnāḥ |

"All these Bahvrichas, having become 'Pushpishikha,' are divided into twenty-five kinds — namely, the Shakalas, the Bashkalas, and the Mandavyas. Of these: ten are Shakala, eight are Bashkala, and seven are Mandavya. This [Brahmana-linked] shakha grouping, having become Pushpishikha, is thus divided into twenty-five kinds."

(10 + 8 + 7 = 25, confirming the reading "pañcaviṃśatidhā," twenty-five-fold, throughout this passage.)

original p. 50

The Rigveda's shakhas fall into three broad groups — Shakala, Bashkala, and Mandavya — with the Shakala group having 5 sub-divisions, Bashkala 8, and Mandavya a further number, adding up across all groups.

The author Achalanka (of the Rajavartika) mentions Vedic shakha names at two points in his work, though the printed text contains errors that prevent a fully accurate reading here. One such citation lists a long series of names — Shakalya, Bashkala, Kauthumi, Satyamugri, Jabalayana, Kalasha, Madhyandina, Mauda, Vaishvalayana, Badarayana, and others — totaling 67 shakha-founders across all four Vedas, of which only the first two (Shakala and Bashkala) belong specifically to the Rigveda.

The Charanavyuha, among the Atharvaveda's Parishishtas, states:

तत्र ऋग्वेदस्य सप्त शाखा भवन्ति । तद्यथा आश्वलायनाः । शांखायनाः । साध्यायनाः । शाकलाः । बाष्कलाः । ऐदुम्बराः माण्डूकाश्चेति ।

"Of these, the Rigveda has seven shakhas, namely: Ashvalayana, Sankhyayana, Sadhyayana, Shakala, Bashkala, Aidumbara, and Mandukya."

— though who exactly "Sadhyayana" and "Aidumbara" refer to is difficult to establish. A citation from the Skanda Purana (via the Anubhashya, 1.1.1) describes Vyasa's successive divisions of the text — fourfold, then twenty-four-fold, then hundred-fold and thousand-fold, and finally, with an eye to conveying its meaning, twelve-fold, at which point he composed the Brahma-sutras. In short, this source holds that the Rigveda had twenty-four shakhas.

original p. 51

The Five Main Groupings of the Rigveda's Shakhas

Among the Rigveda's 21 shakhas, the significant ones can be grouped into five:

एतेषां शाखाः पञ्चविधा भवन्ति । शाकलाः । बाष्कलाः । अश्वलायनाः । शांबायनाः । माण्डूकेयाश्चेति ।

"Of these, the shakhas are of five kinds: Shakala, Bashkala, Ashvalayana, Shambayana, and Mandukeya."

That is, the full 21 are distributed across these five groupings. Max Müller, however, wrote of this differently, noting in his own English scholarship:

"We miss the names of several old Sakhas such as the Aitareyins, Saisiras, Kaushitakins, Paingins."

— that is, we lack the names of several old shakhas such as the Aitareyins, Saisiras, Kaushitakins, and Paingins. But regarding the Saisira specifically, he adds in a note:

"The Saisira sakha, however, may perhaps be considered as a subdivision of the Sakala sakha."

— which finds support in the Puranas, as we shall see. Hariprasad, too, holds that "Shakala" must have been an actual sage, citing his own Veda-sarvasva: "It is understood that the person who first made the divisions of this Samhita's suktas and Mandalas known to everyone was a sage named Shakala" (p. 35), and elsewhere: "The Rik Samhita's expositor was Shakala, who was very ancient; and the compiler of the [ordered] Sat-samhita was Shakalya, who came later than Shakala." Some deficiency appears in Max Müller's fivefold grouping, however, and Hariprasad's claim — that Shakala predates Shakalya — appears to be a significant error, as the following evidence shows.

Section 8 — The Shakala Shakhas

Much confusion surrounds the name "Shakala" — whether it refers to a founding sage or to his disciple Shakalya, and which came first. A few illustrative parallels help: the disciples of the Vajasaneya lineage are collectively called "Vajasaneya," their shared Samhita named after that same source; disciples of Yajnavalkya called "Charaka" likewise gave their name to the Charaka shakhas; and Kalapi's disciples became known as "Kalapa." In just this way, Shakalya's disciples came to be called "Shakala," and the Samhita they propagated became traditionally known as the "Shakala Samhita." In support, two verses from the Vayu Purana:

देवमित्रस्तु शाकल्यो महात्मा द्विजसत्तमः । चकार संहिताः पञ्च बुद्धिमान् पदवित्तमः ॥ तच्छिष्या अभवन् पञ्च मुद्गलो गोलकस्तथा । खालीयश्च तथा वत्स्यः शोकरीयस्तथा पञ्चमः ॥ (Anandashrama edition, Vayu Purana)

"Devamitra Shakalya, the great-souled, foremost of the twice-born, wise, and most learned in the [Vedic] words, composed five Samhitas. His five disciples were: Mudgala, Golaka, Khaliya, Vatsya, and Shokariya."

A parallel passage in the Brahmanda Purana (ch. 35) gives nearly the same account with the father's name as "Vedamitra" and slightly different disciple names — Mudgala, Goshala, Khiliyan, Vatsya, and Shaishireya — the last name here matching Max Müller's "Saisira."

original p. 53

Further support appears in the Vishnu Purana (ch. 3.4):

देवमित्रस्तु शाकल्यः संहितां तामधीतवान् । चकार संहिताः पञ्च शिष्येभ्यः प्रददौ च ताः । तस्य शिष्यास्तु ये पञ्च तेषां नामानि मे शृणु ॥ मुद्गलो गोशलश्चैव वात्स्यः शालीय एव च । शिशिरः पञ्चमश्चात्र श्यैत्रेयः स महामुनिः ॥

"Devamitra's [son] Shakalya studied that Samhita, composed five Samhitas, and gave them to his disciples. Hear their five names: Mudgala, Goshala, Vatsya, and Shaleya; and Shishira as the fifth, the great sage also called Shyaitreya."

The author notes that printed Puranic editions show considerable corruption in these founder-names, but by comparing several manuscript copies held at Dayananda College — including two unusually clean copies of the Vishnu Purana (nos. 1230 and 4375) against a Brahmanda Purana manuscript (no. 3190) — a corrected reading emerges:

वेदमित्रस्तु शाकल्यो महात्मा द्विजसत्तमः । चकार संहिताः पञ्च बुद्धिमान् पदवित्तमः ॥ तच्छिष्या अभवन् पञ्च मुद्गलो गालवस्तथा । शालीयश्च तथा वात्स्यः शैशिरीयस्तु पञ्चमः ॥

"Vedamitra's [son] Shakalya... composed five Samhitas. His five disciples were: Mudgala, Galava, Shaleya, Vatsya, and Shaishiriya as the fifth."

A further, related tradition appears at the start of the Shaishira Shiksha text (a manuscript of which is held in the Madras Government Oriental Manuscripts Library):

मुद्गलो गालवो गार्ग्यः शाकल्यश्चैशिरिस्तथा । पञ्च शौनकशिष्यास्ते शाखाभेदप्रवर्तकाः । शैशिरस्य तु शिष्यस्य शाकटायन एव च ॥

"Mudgala, Galava, Gargya, Shakalya, and likewise Shaishiri — these five were disciples of Shaunaka, and were the founders of the shakha-divisions. And Shakatayana was a disciple of Shaishiri."

That is: Mudgala, Galava, Gargya, Shakalya, and Shaishiri were the five disciples of the sage Shaunaka, and it was they who founded the various shakha-divisions.

original p. 54

The considerable variation among these textual traditions shouldn't surprise us — the author suggests the names should likely be harmonized as: "Gargya" read as "Vatsya"; "Shakalya" (where it appears as a disciple-name) read as "Shaleeya"; and "Shaunaka" read as "Shakalya." A further citation, from Gangadhara's commentary on the Vikritavalli, quotes two similar (but even more corrupted) verses, which the author sets aside as unreliable and at odds with the accepted tradition.

Conclusion: there are five Shakala shakhas: (1) Mudgala, (2) Galava, (3) Shaleeya, (4) Vatsya, and (5) Shaishiri. Let us examine each.

1. The Mudgala Shakha

No Samhita text survives for this shakha, and no clearly identifiable family or sutra-tradition currently claims descent from it. Taking one Rigveda-related passage as a starting point: the name "Mudgala" occurs twice in genealogical portions of the Brihaddevata, each time in close association with Shakapurni (a known Rigveda shakha-founder) and the teacher Shakatayani, suggesting Mudgala was himself either a teacher, a shakha-founder, or at least a contemporary scholar of standing. From this the author concludes that this Mudgala was likely a disciple of Shakalya, and that his father was named Bhrigvashva — a name also found in the Nirukta (9.3).

original p. 55

A further anecdote recounts Bhrigvashva's son Mudgala the sage winning a battle fought alongside two companions, Vrishabha and Dridhana. Separately, the Rigveda's Mandala 10, Sukta 102 is attributed to a rishi called Bharmyashva-Mudgala — though whether this is the same Mudgala is genuinely uncertain, resting more on inference and traditional anecdote (as related by Yaska) than solid evidence; the name "Mudgala" may equally have been carried by other, later individuals within the same textual lineage, including possibly disciples of Jaimini. The author cautions that tracing this identity is largely speculative and should be treated with appropriate scholarly caution.

For a fuller genealogy, the author draws on the Western Indologist F. E. Pargiter's Chronology of Ancient India, which traces a lineage: Bhrigvashva (Mudgala) → Vadhryashva → Divodasa (per the Vayu Purana). The author questions whether this sequence is truly compatible with Mudgala having been a disciple of Shakalya, given the number of generations that would have to separate Vyasa's era from Shakalya's — and notes that another scholar, Professor Sitanath Pradhan, connects Divodasa (Vadhryashva's son) to specific Rigveda mantras, along with a possibly related figure named Sujata...

original p. 56

...raising the further question of whether Divodasa and a contemporary called Saijavana (or similar) are one figure or two — a genuine puzzle the author flags rather than resolves. Mahabharata and Puranic tradition generally place Mudgala in the Angirasa lineage; the Vana-parva (ch. 96) tells of a Mudgala's renowned charity, praised by Yudhishthira, and local Bihar tradition associates him with the town of Monghyr (Munger) on the Ganga — though none of this is firmly evidenced. The author concludes that "Mudgala" was clearly borne by several different sages across different eras — the Bhrigvashva-lineage Mudgala should not be casually equated with the Rigveda shakha-founder Mudgala — and cross-references a Nirukta passage naming Shatabalaksha as this Mudgala's son and Vadhryashva as his brother, and two Ayurvedic Charaka Samhita sages named "Maudgalya," contemporaries of the Mahabharata era. Fuller detail, the author notes, belongs properly at the opening of the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra (1.1).

2. The Galava Shakha

Likewise textless today, this shakha's founder Galava is identified as "Panchala" (of the Panchala country) and alternatively "Babhravya" — credited in the Rik-Pratishakhya, Nirukta, Brihaddevata, and Ashtadhyayi-commentary tradition with establishing the Rigveda's sequential textual order, earning him a prominent place among Vedic scholars. Panini's grammar and Patanjali's Mahabhashya cite a rule (roughly 4.1.104 / 6.1.77) associating Galava's name with a grammatical designation tied to the Panchala region, reinforcing this geographic identification.

original p. 57

The Aitareya Aranyaka (3.2) records an actual point of ritual disagreement between two shakha-founding teachers:

नेदमेकस्मिन्नहनि समासयीत इति ह स्माह जातूकर्ण्यः । समासयीत इति गालवः ।

"'This [rite] should not be compressed into a single day' — so said Jatukarnya. 'It should be so compressed' — said Galava."

— confirming Galava as a genuine shakha-founding teacher of the Shakala tradition. The Charaka Samhita's opening section, describing sages gathered in the Himalayas (itself compiled in the Mahabharata era, when Vedic shakhas and Brahmana texts were actively circulating), names a Galava the author identifies with this same Rigveda teacher; and the Mahabharata's Sabha-parva (ch. 4) lists a Galava among the sages present in Yudhishthira's magical assembly hall, strengthening the identification.

original p. 58

Babhravya = Galava: A Historical Tangle

The Skanda Purana's Nagara-khanda describes a Galava serving as minister to a Kaurava king, comparable to Vidura; the Matsya Purana (ch. 48.20) names a "Babhravya" as minister to Subalaka, king of southern Panchala, credited there with devising the Rigveda's sequential ordering — likely the same tradition, differently named, and the author suggests "Subalaka" may simply have been conflated with "Galava" in transmission. Untangling exactly which Galava/Babhravya is which — sage, minister, or a descendant/lineage bearing the name — remains genuinely unresolved; the author notes a similar historical tangle exists around a King Hiranyanabha Kaushalya in a Samaveda-related account, and that even Pargiter's scholarship (pp. 92–93) could not fully resolve this class of problem.

3. The Shaleeya Shakha

Also textless today, attested only by scattered grammatical citations — e.g., the Kashika-vritti lists "Shaleeya" alongside Ashvalayana, Aitikayana, Aupagana, and Aupamanyava in one place (1.1.1), and alongside Gargiya and Vatsiya in another (4.2.105).

original p. 59

4. The Vatsya Shakha

Its relationship to the Shaleeya shakha is unclear. Patanjali's Mahabhashya (4.2.104), illustrating a grammatical rule for naming schools (gotra-charana), lists example forms including "Vatsyakam," confirming Vatsya as a recognized shakha name. Manuscript variants of the Sankhyayana Aranyaka and Aitareya Aranyaka waver between the readings "Vatsya" and "Baadhva" at a few points (Sayanacharya's commentary follows "Baadhva"), though the author argues "Vatsya" is likely the correct original reading. A possible further connection to a "Vatsa" or "Kaundinya" shakha within the Shukla Yajurveda tradition cannot be confirmed without better manuscript evidence.

5. The Shaishiri Shakha

Likewise without a surviving Samhita or living tradition, but well attested by citation. The Anuvakanukramani opens:

ऋग्वेदे शैशिरीयायां संहितायां यथाक्रमम् । प्रमाणानुवाकानां सूक्त्यैः शृणुत शाकलाः ॥

"O Shakalas, hear now, in due order, the number of suktas in each Anuvaka of the Shaishiriya Samhita of the Rigveda."

And the Rik-Pratishakhya opens with a similar reference to expounding its subject "in the Shaishiriya [tradition]." A manuscript of the Rik-Sarvanukramani (Calcutta Asiatic Society) similarly

original p. 60

references "Shakalya, in the Shaishiriya [tradition]" in its closing portion. The Vikrtavalli notes that the sage Vyadi described, within this same Shaishiriya-Samamnaya tradition, the eight types of textual modification (vikriti) beginning with the Jata-patha.

Extent of the Shaishiriya shakha: 84 Anuvakas, 1,017 Suktas, 2,004 Vargas, 10,471 mantras — broadly matching the Anuvakanukramani and Rik-Pratishakhya figures cited earlier, though nothing further about this shakha's specific Samhita is known. Notably, Sayanacharya's own commentary belongs to this Shaishiriya shakha tradition — a detail worth keeping in mind, since it is this very commentary that the present translation follows throughout. A Brahmanda Purana account (part 3, ch. 2) also describes a sage named Shishira, born a Kshatriya (son of Ashvasena, in the lunar/Chandravamsha lineage of Shunahshotra) who became a Brahmin — plausibly an ancestor within this shakha's lineage.

The Shakalya Samhita

The five Shakala sub-shakhas discussed above all trace to a common root text — called the Shakalya, Shakalaka, or Shakaleeya Samhita — held in especially high regard within Vedic tradition. The Vyakarana-Mahabhashya states:

शाकल्यस्य संहितामनुस्रावयन्ति ... शाकल्येन सृष्टां संहितामनुनिशाम्य देवः प्रांशावर्णः ॥

"They continuously recite Shakalya's Samhita... having heard the Samhita composed by Shakalya, the gods [approved/were pleased]."

That is: once Shakalya completed his Samhita, the gods heard it and gave their approval. Tradition holds that Katyayana's Rik-Sarvanukramani was itself composed following this Samhita, which opens: "atha ṛgvedāmnāye śākalake..." ("Now, in the traditionally transmitted Rigveda, in the Shakala [recension]...").

original p. 61

The Vedartha-dipika states plainly: śākalyoccāraṇaṃ śākalakam — "what Shakalya recited is called 'Shakalaka.'" This confirms the Sarvanukramani describes all Samhitas belonging to the Shakala tradition collectively. The author notes one specific scholarly disagreement: McDonell's claim that the "Sanjnana-sukta" mentioned at the Sarvanukramani's close belongs to the Shakala Samhita appears doubtful, since better evidence suggests it is actually a Khila-sukta belonging to the Bashkala Samhita instead.

The Anuvakanukramani gives the Shakalya Samhita's word-count:

शाकल्यदृष्टे पदलक्ष्मेकं सार्धं च वेदे त्रिसहस्रयुक्तम् । शतानि चाष्टौ दशकद्वयं च सदानि षट् चेति हि चर्चितानि ॥

शाकल्य-दृष्टे पदलक्ष्मेकं सार्धं च वेदे त्रिसहस्रयुक्तम् । शतानि चाष्टौ दशकद्वयं च सदानि षट् चेति हि चर्चितानि ॥ śākalya-dṛṣṭe padalakṣmekaṃ sārdhaṃ ca vede trisahasrayuktam | śatāni cāṣṭau daśakadvayaṃ ca sadāni ṣaṭ ceti hi carcitāni ||

— summarized as: the Shakalya Samhita contains, in total, 1,53,826 words.

Sayanacharya's own Aitareya Aranyaka commentary likewise references the Shakalya Samhita by name, confirming its continued use as the standard reference text; later manuscripts (e.g., Asiatic Society ms. no. 231) refer to it simply as "Shakala."

Section 9 — The Bashkala Shakhas

Establishing who "Bashkala" was requires some care, since a similarly-named figure appears in the Mahabharata's Adiparva unrelated to any shakha-founder — the author explicitly warns not to confuse the two. The Brahmanda Purana gives the actual shakha-founder's lineage:

चतस्रः संहिताः कृता बाष्कलेन द्विजसत्तमः । शिष्यानध्यापयामास शुश्रूषाभिरतान् हितान् ॥ बोध्यं तु प्रथमां शाखां द्वितीयामग्निमातरम् । पाराशरीं तृतीयां तु याज्ञवल्क्यां चतुर्थकम् ॥

"Bashkala, foremost of the twice-born, composed four Samhitas and taught them to his devoted disciples: the first shakha Baudhya, the second Agnimatara, the third Parasharya, and the fourth Yajnavalkya."

original p. 62

A parallel Brahmanda Purana verse gives the same four names with only minor spelling variants (Baudhya, Agnimahara, Parashara, Yajnavalkya). But a separate genealogical passage in the same Purana, and the parallel reading in the Vishnu Purana, replace the fourth name "Yajnavalkya" with "Jatukarnya" instead — and the author, weighing the manuscript evidence (and noting that the Bhagavata Purana's twelfth canto independently names Jatukarnya, not Yajnavalkya, as a Rigveda teacher), concludes that "Jatukarnya" is the correct reading here, not "Yajnavalkya." The four Bashkala sub-shakhas are therefore: Baudhya, Agnimathara, Parashara, and Jatukarnya.

1. The Baudhya Shakha

Baudhya belongs to the Angirasa gotra. Panini's grammar states: kapi bodhād āṅgirase (4.1.102) — "the suffix 'kapi' applies to 'Bodha' within the Angirasa [lineage]," forming "Baudhya." That is: those of the Angirasa gotra descended from Bodha's son are called Baudhya (or, alternately, "Baudhi").

original p. 63

Baudhya's name also appears in a Brihaddevata verse, though textual corruption is significant here — McDonell's and Rajendralal Mitra's editions diverge substantially, and McDonell himself flags the passage as corrupt in his footnotes. Working through the manuscript variants, the author reconstructs the sense as identifying a teacher named Baudhya, and suggests the adjacent name "matara" in the same verse should be read as "Agnimatara" — the two shakha-founders apparently named together. Separately, the Mahabharata's Adiparva mentions a "Bodhi" serving as Adhvaryu priest at King Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice (Sarpa-yaga); Baudhya the shakha-founder is said to have had a son, Yatati, whose own grandson's story appears at the start of the Shantiparva — though no Samhita or Brahmana text for this shakha survives.

2. The Agnimatara Shakha: known only from the single Brihaddevata verse just discussed — nothing further about this shakha is known.

3. The Parashara Shakha: no Parasharya Samhita has been located elsewhere, though a related figure, "Aruna Parashara" (a Brahmin), is mentioned in a separate lineage text (title: "On the Kalpa-form nature of the Aruna-Parashara-shakha-Brahmana," Brahmanda Purana edition, p. 13) — whether this is the same Parashara shakha is left an open question. The Kashika-vritti grammar commentary (on sutra ~7.2.104) separately names an "Arunaparasharya," again of uncertain connection. Patanjali's Mahabhashya (4.3.110) cites the example "sārasharakalpaḥ," which the author takes as confirming a Kalpa-sutra text once existed for this Rigveda Parashara-shakha specifically.

original p. 64

4. The Jatukarnya Shakha

The Sankhyayana Shrautasutra names a teacher Jatukarnya at four points, once as "Jalapaja Jatukarnya," described as family priest (purohita) to the kings of Kashi, Videha, and Kosala, with a son named Purnindhana (also called Shreetavika). He also appears in the Sankhyayana-Grihyasutra and the Shambavya-Grihyasutra's genealogical section, strengthening his identification as the Rigveda shakha-founder; further mentions occur in the Kaushitaki-Brahmana tradition and at the opening of the Charaka Samhita, though the author cautions that these scattered references cannot be confirmed with certainty as all referring to one and the same person. Variant name-forms (Jatukarnya, Jatukarna, Jatukarni) appear as cited authorities in Dharmasutra literature as well.

The Bashkala Samhita

Just as the Shakalya line has its root Samhita, the Bashkala line should likewise trace to a common Bashkala Samhita (or at least an independent Bashkala Brahmana), though no copy survives directly — its extent is inferred instead from references within the Shukla Yajurveda's Pratijna-sutra...

original p. 65

The Bashkala Samhita, continued

The Pratijna-sutra's commentary states that the Bashkala-related Brahmana texts share a single, distinctive accentual quality, and goes on to distinguish the Shakalya and Bashkala traditions specifically by their opening and closing verses. Citing the Ashvalayana Grihyasutra and commentaries by Devasvamin, Haradatta, and Narayana, the author establishes that the Shakala Samhita opens with "samānī va ākūtiḥ" and closes with a verse ending in "iṣe"; the Bashkala Samhita closes instead with "tac chaṃyor āvṛṇīmahe" — which is itself the closing mantra of the "Sanjnana-sukta." This implies the Sanjnana-sukta serves as the Bashkala Samhita's concluding hymn, a position the Sankhyayana-Grihyasutra (5.9) shares — suggesting the Sankhyayana Samhita likewise ends with this same hymn. On this point, the Western scholar Bühler wrote, in his introduction to the Sankhyayana Grihyasutra:

"It is well known that [tacchamyoravrisheemahe] is the last verse in the Bashkala Sakha which was adopted by the Sankhyayana school."

The author pushes back on this characterization: the Sankhyayana tradition has its own distinct Samhita rather than simply "adopting" Bashkala's, even though the two traditions do happen to share this same closing hymn — a coincidence of shared ending rather than evidence that one was absorbed into the other.

original p. 66

Comparing the Shakala and Bashkala Sukta-Sequences

The Anuvakanukramanike states:

गौतमादौशिज कुत्सक परुच्च्वैशादृष्णेः सरः । कुत्साद्दीर्घतमा इष्केष तु बाष्कलक क्रमः ॥ २० ॥

gautamād auśija kutsaka parucchvaiśādṛṣṇeḥ saraḥ | kutsād dīrghatamā iṣkeṣa tu bāṣkalaka kramaḥ || [a few words in this particular verse remain uncertain even at higher resolution]

This much difference exists between the Shakalya krama and the Bashkala krama in the first Mandala. Following the Bashkala krama's own order: Mandala/sukta numerals in this specific table carry some residual uncertainty at this resolution and are given as best legible.

Opening words Rishi / Suktas
उप प्रयन्तः (upa prayantaḥ) Gotama's suktas, ~43–49
नासत्याभ्यां (nāsatyābhyāṃ) Kakshivan Dairghatamasa Aushija, suktas ~116, 126
अग्निं होतारं (agniṃ hotāraṃ) Paruchchhepa, suktas ~132, 134
इमं स्तोमं (imaṃ stomaṃ) Kutsa, suktas ~94–115
वेदिषदे (vediṣade) Dirghatama, suktas ~140–164

This is the Bashkala krama. In the Shakala krama, Kutsa's suktas come immediately after Gotama's suktas — described in detail in the Brihaddevata (2.83).

The Sankhyayana Shrauta-bhashya (2.3) records a verse on the total mantra-count difference between traditions:

एकं सहस्रं दश सप्त चैवाष्टावतश्च बाष्कलक्षेऽधिकानि । तान्स्वारणे शाकले शैशिरीये वदन्ति शिष्टा न शिलेषु विप्राः ॥ २३ ॥

एकं सहस्रं दश सप्त चैवाष्टाव् अतश् च बाष्कलक्षेऽधिकानि । तान् स्वारणे शाकले शैशिरीये वदन्ति शिष्टा न शिलेषु विप्राः ॥ ekaṃ sahasraṃ daśa sapta caivāṣṭāv ataś ca bāṣkalakṣe'dhikāni | tān svāraṇe śākale śaiśirīye vadanti śiṣṭā na śileṣu viprāḥ ||

"One thousand and seventeen, and eight more besides — these [additional mantras] belong to the Bashkala [tradition]; learned Brahmins declare them absent in the Shakala/Shaishiriya svarana [reading], not [merely] omitted by chance."

The Bashkala shakha's text has eight more suktas than the Shakala shakha's text.

original p. 67

This concludes the discussion of the Bashkala shakha. A reference work, Kavindracharya's manuscript catalogue (entry ~218), lists a text titled "Bashkalashakheeya-Samhita and Brahmana," and a short Upanishad called the Bashkala-mantropanishad also exists.

Section 10 — The Ashvalayana Shakhas

The Ancient Ashvalayana

Tradition traces a teacher called Kaushalya Ashvalayana (so named for hailing from Koshala) to a lineage recorded in the Brihadaranyaka/Kaushitaki-Upanishad genealogies: King Janaka's Hotr priest was named Ashvala, and his son came to be called "Ashvalayana" — plausibly the same figure carried forward in Rigveda tradition, since the Hotr's role is specifically tied to Rigveda recitation. This Ashvala is described as belonging to a Kuru- or Panchala-region Brahmana family; the Prashna-Upanishad instead places Ashvalayana in Kosala — neighboring regions, so no real contradiction. The Charaka Samhita's opening (1.1) independently names an "Ashvalayana" among the sages gathered at the Himalayas, and the Mahabharata's Anushasana-parva (~v. 85) states that Ashvalayana was a grandson of Vishvamitra.

The Ashvalayana of the Buddha's Time

Interestingly, a different Ashvalayana appears centuries later: the Majjhima Nikaya's Assalayana Sutta (a Buddhist text) describes a young Brahmin named Ashvalayana encountered by Gautama Buddha during his teaching career, already accomplished in Kalpa, Shiksha, the three Vedas, and history among other disciplines (per Rahul Sankrityayan's translation, p. 108) — evidently a much later individual bearing the same name and professional title, not the Vedic shakha-founder himself.

original p. 68

The Buddha-Era Ashvalayana Was Not the Shakha-Founder

Some Bengali writers mistakenly conflated the Buddha-era Ashvalayana with the author of the Ashvalayana-Grihyasutra. The author rejects this: since Ashvalayana the shakha-founder belongs to the Vyasa-disciple lineage, his era must predate the Buddha by many centuries at least — the Buddha-era figure of the same name and Vedic learning was simply a different, much later person, and a distinct "Ashvalayana" tradition/family name persists in many parts of the country even today independent of this confusion.

Turning to the shakha itself: the Puranas offer no genealogical account of an "Ashvalayana" shakha-founder comparable to what exists for the other shakhas, and it remains genuinely uncertain whether an independent "Ashvalayana Samhita" (distinct from the standard Shakala text) ever existed, despite the shakha's fame today resting on the well-known Ashvalayana Shrauta- and Grihyasutras. The author gathers several pieces of manuscript evidence bearing on this question: a Kavindracharya catalogue entry titled "Ashvalayana-Samhita or Brahmana"; a note that the commentator Mahidasa gives a different word-count for the Ashvalayana text than other authorities; and a Bikaner manuscript (catalogue no. 3, l. 63) explicitly labeled as belonging to the Ashvalayana shakha, ending with the phrase "iti aśvamāske aśvano'dhyāyaḥ" ("thus the Ashva-related chapter") — though the author notes this label may not be entirely accurate.

original p. 69

Further evidence: a Punjab University (Lahore) manuscript titled "Rik-Samhita's Ashvamashaka" opens by naming itself the "Ashvalayana-Samhita," and its final varga (100th) — containing five specific mantras culminating in "tac chaṃyor āvṛṇīmahe" — closely parallels the Bashkala Samhita's own concluding Sanjnana-sukta, though with a small but notable difference (two additional mantras present in one tradition but not the other, one of which is actually from the Atharvaveda), leading the author to treat this material as a Parishishta (supplement) specific to this manuscript rather than confirming a wholly separate Ashvalayana Samhita. A Dayananda College library manuscript (catalogue no. 4818) similarly ends with "Thus concludes the Ashvalayana-sutra," though without enough context to confirm which shakha's text it actually represents. Raghunandana's Smriti-tattva also quotes a passage explicitly attributed to an "Ashvalayana-Brahmana"

original p. 70

— though this passage is traceable to the Aitareya Brahmana itself, and old Bengali and Mithila scholarly custom evidently referred to Aitareya Brahmana citations under the name "Ashvalayana Brahmana" as a matter of convention, rather than indicating a genuinely separate text. An Asiatic Society catalogue entry (no. 944) confirms this identity explicitly.

The Basis of the Ashvalayana Kalpa-sutra

Since Kalpa-sutras are normally composed as authoritative supports for one specific shakha (treating that shakha's own mantras as primary and others' as secondary), the question becomes whether the Ashvalayana-sutra follows this same pattern or draws more broadly. Citing four separate ancient commentators on the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra, the author builds a clear case that it does not confine itself to one shakha:

Devasvamin, the earliest commentator, writes in his opening remarks that the text's intended "samamnaya" (traditional recension) could be read as Shakala, Bashkala, "or indeed all the Rigveda's shakhas" collectively.

Devatrata similarly holds that whichever shakha's mantras are traditionally received and Vedic in character are equally treated as valid scriptural authority for this Sutra's purposes — the underlying unity of "the Rigveda" across its shakhas is what actually matters, not adherence to one specific recension.

original p. 71

Gargya Narayana (son of Narasimha) concludes that the Ashvalayana-sutra is "a single sutra common and equal to both the Shakala and Bashkala shakhas," drawing on Nivid, Puronuvakya, and Valakhilya material from both traditions alongside the Aitareya Brahmana.

Shadguru-shishya, in his introduction to his Sarvanukramani commentary, states the matter most directly:

शाकलस्य संहितैका बाष्कलस्य तथापर । द्वे संहिते समाश्रित्य ब्राह्मणान्येकविंशतिः ॥ ऐतरेयकमाश्रित्य तदेवान्यः प्रपूरयन् । कल्पसूत्रं चकाराश्व महर्षिर्गणपूजितः ॥

"There is one Samhita of Shakala, and another of Bashkala. Relying on both these Samhitas, together with the twenty-one Brahmanas [and] the Aitareya [Brahmana] to complete it, the great sage Ashva[layana], honored by the assembly, composed the Kalpa-sutra."

All four commentators thus converge on the same essential point: the Ashvalayana Kalpa-sutra was never tied to a single Samhita — Devasvamin and Devatrata frame its scope as the whole Rigveda, while Gargya Narayana and Shadguru-shishya specify its dual grounding in both the Shakala and Bashkala traditions together. The author next turns to testing Devasvamin's broader claim against a specific citation within the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra itself (3.10)...

original p. 72

Testing this against a specific citation (three mantras beginning "kṣiprim vātaram," found only in the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra and nowhere else in the standard textual tradition), the author finds a genuine complication: the Brihaddevata's own traditional sukta-list includes a "Brahmajnanam" sukta found across all variants of the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra (~5.6) but in no other manuscript tradition — proving that some material genuinely unique to the Ashvalayana Sutra exists outside any single known shakha. The conclusion: no Shrautasutra text can be shown to belong exclusively to one single Rigveda shakha, and whether a single root-text ultimately underlies both Shakala and Bashkala, or whether an independent Ashvalayana Samhita once existed in its own right, remains genuinely unresolved — reasonable scholars differ, and the question stays open.

Section 11 — The Sankhyayana Shakhas

Sankhyayana is listed as the fourth division in the Charanavyuha. Its Brahmana and Aranyaka texts survive, but the Puranas offer no account connecting it to a specific Samhita — leaving the same kind of open question already seen with Ashvalayana.

The Sankhyayana Samhita

  1. A Rigveda manuscript in the Alwar state library is labeled as belonging to the Sankhyayana shakha, though the author has not personally examined it.
  2. Kavindracharya's catalogue (no. 84) records a Sankhyayana Samhita and Brahmana.
  3. The Sankhyayana Shrautasutra cites several unusual mantras absent from the Shakala tradition (noted in Hillebrandt's edition, ~p. 108) — for instance, sutras 8–9 cite the mantras "venastāt... śaṃca" and "ayaṃ venaḥ" by their opening words only, implying they once had a place within a Sankhyayana Samhita. A commentator's claim that these arose independently within this shakha's tradition doesn't hold up, in the author's view — it's unlikely a Samhita reading would be freshly invented at the time a Sutra was being composed. Similar citations-by-opening-word occur for the Sanjnana-sukta and other mantras throughout the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra and Pratishakhya, and several mantras in the Sankhyayana Aranyaka have no counterpart at all in the Shakala reading.

Conclusion: a genuinely independent Sankhyayana Samhita, somewhat different from the Shakala text, most likely did once exist.

The Four Sub-Divisions of Sankhyayana

These are: (1) Sankhyayana proper, (2) Kaushitaki, (3) Mahakaushitaki, and (4) Shambavya.

1. The Sankhyayana Shakha

Its Brahmana survives in the Anandashrama (Poona) and Lindner editions; its Aranyaka, Shrauta-, and Grihya-sutras survive as well, though these editions contain some errors not worth correcting here.

original p. 74

An Editorial Error in the Sankhyayana Material

The Aranyaka portion in particular has been printed with a significant conflation: Sankhyayana and Kaushitaki — a related but genuinely distinct sub-branch — have been mixed together where they should have been published as two separate texts. Supporting evidence: Lindner's own edition acknowledges overlapping portions between the two Brahmanas but cannot always distinguish genuine shared text from mere shakha-variant readings, especially given how much his Malayalam-script source manuscript diverges from Devanagari-script copies. Structurally, the Sankhyayana Aranyaka's first two chapters cover the Mahavrata rite, after which the Kaushitaki Upanishad begins from chapter three onward — meaning the Kaushitaki Upanishad is really just one portion within the Sankhyayana Aranyaka as printed, though manuscript evidence (including a Madras Government collection copy) shows real wording differences between the "Kaushitaki" and "Sankhyayana" readings of the same passages (e.g., Kaushitaki Upanishad 2.1's "sa iha ketau vā" against Sankhyayana's variant, or "pratibhānti" vs. "prati yanti") — differences of wording, not of substance, but real nonetheless. Grihyasutra manuscripts show similar variation.

Conclusion: Sankhyayana and Kaushitaki are two distinct shakhas, and should be edited and printed separately rather than conflated as they have been.

An Unnamed Author in the Sankhyayana Tradition

An old introductory verse (peetika) prefacing the printed Sankhyayana Sutra names no author directly — he is identified only as "descendant of" someone, without further detail, leaving his identity unclear to this day.

His Name Was Acharya Brahmadatta

Vasudeva, author of the Sankhyayana-Grihya-Sangraha, writes at the opening of his own work...

original p. 75

...on behalf of this teacher, composing a commentary named for Brahmadatta. In his supplementary explanation, he further specifies details of the seven disciples' rishi, deity, and meter as explained by "Acharya Brihaddatta."

A manuscript in the Tanjore royal library, titled Sankhyayana-Shrautasutra-siddhi, is attributed to an author named Narayana, who states in his opening verse that he composed his clear exposition ("Saddrishti") having learned Brihaddatta's doctrine according to proper tradition. Together, these sources indicate that Acharya Agnisvami, Brahmadatta, and others wrote commentaries on the Sankhyayana Shrauta- and Grihyasutras, with Agnisvami apparently preceding "Varadatta's son" chronologically. The author further identifies this "Varadatta's son" as Brahmadatta himself — supported by the commentary's own mangala-shloka naming Brahmadatta and repeated internal references — plausibly hailing from the "Artiya" region, and notes it is not at all improbable that this is one and the same person referenced under slightly different names across these sources.

Shambu and Sankhyayana

The name "Shambu" is borne by several figures. A Kaushitaki-Samhita passage names a "Kaushika Shambu" in dialogue with a figure called Shakayanya.

original p. 76

A Mahabharata passage (Anushasana-parva) tells of King Brahmadatta of Panchala granting a treasure to the sage Shambu and thereby attaining liberation — likely a different, later Shambu than the Vedic-era figure. Separately, the Mahabharata (Adiparva, Shantiparva) and the Skanda Purana's Nagara-khanda describe two brothers, Shambu and Likhita, sons of Devala (or, per the Nagara-khanda, of Shandilya) — accounts that differ somewhat in detail but may both refer to authors of Dharmashastra texts. The author traces a plausible lineage: a son of "Shakha" became known as "Shankhya," whose own son became "Sankhyayana" — with a "Shankhya" independently named in the Charaka Samhita's opening section (1.7).

The Sankhyayana Tradition and Teacher Suyajna

The name "Sankhyayana" recurs across the Ashvalayana-Grihya, Sankhyayana-Grihya, and related texts. The commentator on the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra repeatedly identifies the actual author/teacher (sutrakara) of this Sutra tradition as Suyajna — cited by name at several points in the commentary. At the close of the Sankhyayana Aranyaka, a figure named Gunakhya-Sankhyayana discusses Suyajna's lineage, raising the question — left open here — of what relationship, if any, connects Suyajna and Gunakhya-Sankhyayana.

2. The Kaushitaki Shakha

No independent Samhita is known for this shakha, and what differences exist from the Sankhyayana Samhita appear minor rather than substantial. Two commentaries exist on its Brahmana — one by an author named Vinayaka; the family/gotra of the second commentator remains unknown.

original p. 77

Its commentary, called Sadartha-vimarshini, survives in three copies at the Madras Government Oriental Manuscripts Library. The Kaushitaki-Shrautasutra likewise closely resembles the Sankhyayana-Shrautasutra, differing only slightly in its chapter divisions (per a Mysore catalogue note); three copies exist (Mysore, Madras, Lahore), and future editors are advised to take note of this before editing either text.

The Kaushitaki–Sankhyayana Relationship: an Adyar Library manuscript of the Sankhyayana Brahmana is titled on its cover "Sankhyayana-Brahmana, following the Kaushitaki tradition." A related manuscript of Narayana's Sankhyayana-Shrautasutra commentary (Bhandarkar Institute, Poona) closes its third chapter with a colophon describing itself as "composed following the Kaushitaki tradition." Together these confirm a real, acknowledged connection between the two traditions. A Kashi-printed edition of the Kaushitaki Grihyasutra even closes with: "Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Kaushitaki Grihyasutra of the Sankhyayana shakha — this indeed is the Kaushika-sutra" — raising the separate question of how the name "Kaushika" enters here.

The Real Name of "Kaushitaki"

Kaushitaki's father was named Kushitaka (cited in the Tandya Brahmana, 18.8.9); Grihyasutra usage elsewhere ("Kahola Kaushitaka") suggests Kushitaka's alternate name was Kahola — and a sage Kahola is independently known as the disciple and son-in-law of the great sage Uddalaka. This Kahola's son was none other than the famous Ashtavakra, per the Mahabharata's Vana-parva (ch. 132): Uddalaka gave his own learned daughter in marriage to his disciple Kahola, and in that generation, two sages stood foremost in sacred learning — Ashtavakra, son of Kahola, and Shvetaketu, son of Uddalaka — making Ashtavakra and Shvetaketu cousins through this marriage.

original p. 78

That is: Kahola was Uddalaka's son-in-law; his son Ashtavakra and Uddalaka's son Shvetaketu were thus generational cousins by marriage, both belonging to the Vedic scholarly tradition. Whether the shakha-founder "Kaushitaki" is to be identified directly with this same Kahola — father of the famous Ashtavakra — is a claim the author treats as a plausible but not fully certain conjecture, complicated further by manuscript variants distinguishing "Kaushitaki" from "Kaushitakeya" (the latter tied to the Kashyapa gotra) as arguably two different people, per Panini's grammar.

3. The Mahakaushitaka Shakha

Cited in Ashvalayana and other Grihyasutra genealogies. The commentator "Anardiya-Brahmadatta" states directly that the final three chapters of the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra (from 14.9 onward) were drawn by its author Suyajna from a distinct Mahakaushitaki source-text — implying this shakha had its own independent Brahmana. Vinayaka Bhatta's commentary on the Kaushitaki Brahmana cites this Mahakaushitaka Brahmana as an authority at seven separate points.

original p. 79

4. The Shambavya Shakha

No Samhita or Brahmana is confirmed for this shakha, but its Kalpa-sutra survives. The Jaiminiya-Shrautasutra's commentary compares its scale to Ashvalayana's: where Ashvalayana treated the entire yajna-science in 12 chapters, Shambavya covered the same ground in 24 — though it's unclear how these chapters split between Shrauta and Grihya material (by rough analogy with the Kaushitaki Grihya's six chapters, the Shambavya Shrauta portion would come to about 18). Citations of this text appear in Haradatta Mishra's commentary and in Arunagirinatha's commentary on the Raghuvamsha (4.38); the Ashvalayana Grihyasutra (3.10.3) also cites "teacher Shambavya's" view directly, though the name suffers corruption in some printed editions (appearing incorrectly as "Shambashya" in one). The Shambavya-Grihya-Karika's own opening verse pays homage to "the Kaushitaki-tradition teacher Shambavya, foremost of sutra-composers" before proceeding to comment on his Grihyasutra — though whether the underlying text truly has five chapters, and the exact nature of the Shambavya–Kaushitaki relationship, remain open questions pending further textual discovery.

The Sage Shambavya Was a Resident of the Kuru Region

The Mahabharata's Ashvamedhika-parva (ch. 90) describes a Brahmin named Shambavya (the name appearing with several spelling variants — Sambachya, Sambhavya, Shambhavya — across different printed editions, with "Shambhavya"/"Shambavya" judged most likely correct) who visited King Dhritarashtra during the king's forest-dwelling (Vanaprastha) period. This Shambavya was a Rigveda scholar skilled in statecraft (artha-shastra), hailing from the northern Kurujangala region — identifying him as a resident of the Kuru country.

Section 5 — The Mandukeya Shakhas

The fifth main division of the Rigveda's shakhas. The Puranas offer no details about its internal divisions (unlike the Shakala/Bashkala groups, where Shakapurni and Bashkali-Bharadvaja's divisions are at least named) — whether any connection exists between those named divisions and the Mandukeya group cannot be confirmed.

The Brihaddevata's Textual Tradition (Amnaya)

original p. 80

The Brihaddevata's opening verse — "having bowed to the seers of the mantras, [I shall state the deities of the suktas] in the order of the traditional recension" — establishes beyond doubt that this text was composed on the basis of some particular textual tradition (amnaya) distinct from the mainstream ones. As evidence: the Brihaddevata's tradition (10.105) includes a sukta beginning "brahma jajñānaṃ prathamaṃ purastāt..." ("Brahma, first-born, arose in the east...") — a hymn absent from both the Shakala and Bashkala shakhas' texts and from Shakala's Sarvanukramani, though some of its mantras appear across all textual variants of the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra (3.4)...

original p. 81

...confirming this. Since this "Brahma-jnanam" sukta doesn't appear in the Ashvalayana tradition, and the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra (ch. 16) cites the same sukta's mantras across all its textual variants, and no other Rigveda shakha attests it at all — the author concludes this hymn must belong specifically and solely to the Mandukeya shakha, firmly anchoring the Brihaddevata text's affiliation there. The Aitareya Brahmana (1.1) and Kaushitaki Brahmana (4.4) both cite only the opening words of this same mantra-group, explicitly noting it belongs to "other shakhas" rather than their own.

A further passage from the Brihaddevata's third chapter documents a specific sequence: ten suktas dedicated to the Ashvin deities (opening with "shashvaddhi vām"), followed by a "Saupanna-sukta" (opening "upasrayantiḥ") and five further Agni-related suktas — an ordering found in neither the Shakala nor Bashkala traditions, with the opening mantra itself absent even from the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra. While not fully certain, this specific sequence is reasonably inferred to belong to the Mandukeya tradition as well.

Mandukeya's Family and Homeland

Mandukeya was so named as "son of Manduka" — called "Shauravira" at the start of the Sankhyayana Aranyaka (2.3) and "Kauravira" in the Aitareya Aranyaka (3.1). One of Manduka's sons was named Dirgha (per Sankhyayana) or Jyeshtha (per Aitareya); the Mandukeya discussed here appears to be that son's brother. This Mandukeya's own son was named Madhyama, also attested in both Aranyakas, whose mother's name is given as Pratibodhi (or Pratiyodhi) — rendered "Pratimedhi" in the Brahmanda Purana (1.5.5). The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra's rishi-tarpana (ancestor-offering ritual) section...

original p. 82

...names her Pratibodhi (2.3.44). Madhyama's residence in Magadha is attested in the Sankhyayana Aranyaka; given some textual corruption in both Aranyakas at this point, exact names should be revisited by future editors, but it appears all three of Manduka's sons — including Madhyama — were connected to Magadha.

The Extent of the Mandukeya Tradition

If the Brihaddevata text is indeed the primary window onto the Mandukeya tradition, its scope is nonetheless limited — ancient times likely saw multiple, slightly varying Brihaddevata-type reference works across different Rigveda shakhas, which eventually merged into the single composite text now in print, making full internal consistency impossible to verify. What can be reconstructed from the current printed text is only a general outline of the Mandukeya shakha's distinctive readings — roughly 12 suktas are described in sequence, with notes on which also appear in the Shakala shakha and which are unique to Mandukeya.

Was Mandukeya the Same as "Bahvricha"?

"Bahvricha" ordinarily just means "a Rigvedin" — used generically in the Shatapatha Brahmana (~10.5.4.10) and in the Mahabhashya. Revisiting Patanjali's earlier statement that "the Bahvricha [tradition] is twenty-one-fold": the name may derive from the Rigveda's comparatively larger number of mantras relative to other Vedas, or from the fact that, apart from the Yajurveda, other Vedic material is largely in prose. The author argues that "Bahvricha" does not correspond to a separate, distinct shakha alongside Mandukeya — it's simply a general term, with the Shakala, Bashkala, and (to a slightly greater degree) Sankhyayana lines all having comparatively larger mantra-counts. The idea that "Bahvrichatva" constitutes some further sub-division specifically within the Mandukeya shakha does not hold up.

original p. 83

Is "Bahvricha" a Distinct Shakha, Separate from Shaingi and Kaushitaki?

The author argues yes — "Bahvricha" is not merely a generic synonym for "Rigveda" but names an actual distinct shakha, with evidence:

  1. The Kaushitaki Brahmana (26.5) records a dialogue in which Madhuka Garshya is asked which deity Soma has: the Bahvricha tradition holds Indra as Soma's deity, while the Kaushitaki view holds it is Indra-Agni jointly — treating "Bahvricha" as a named tradition standing alongside (not identical to) Shaingya and Kaushitaki, even though all three are, in the broad sense, "Rigvedic."

  2. The Madhyandina Shatapatha Brahmana (~11.5.1.10), discussing the Pururavas-Urvashi dialogue hymn, states that "the Bahvrichas" count this sukta as having fifteen mantras — matching the Rigveda's own count for this hymn (10.95, eighteen mantras in the standard text, with the Brahmana's count reflecting the Bahvricha reckoning specifically) — confirming the Shatapatha follows the Bahvricha shakha's own tradition here.

  3. Citations of a "Bahvricha-Brahmana" in commentary on the Apastamba Shrautasutra mostly align with known Aitareya/Kaushitaki material, but one citation (8.28.3) preserves a mantra found in no other surviving Rigveda text — strong evidence that "Bahvricha" here refers to a genuinely distinct, otherwise-lost shakha tradition.

The View of A. B. Keith

The Western Vedic scholar Keith writes, regarding this same question:

"It is perfectly certain that he meant some definite work which he may have had before him and in all probability all his quotations come from it." (Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1945, p. 496)

original p. 84

Keith continues, offering a tentative identification:

"And this fact does suggest a mere conjecture that the Brahmana used was the text of the Paingya school." (same source, p. 498)

The author rejects this specific identification — the earlier Kaushitaki Brahmana evidence (26.5) already distinguishes Bahvricha from the Shaingya (Paingya) shakha directly, so Keith's guess doesn't hold up, even though his broader instinct (that a real, specific text lies behind these citations) was correct.

Further supporting evidence for Bahvricha as a genuine, separate shakha:

  1. The Katha-Grihya's commentary (25.6) cites a "Bahvricha-Grihya" sutra on sun-viewing (Adityadarshana) not found in either the Ashvalayana or Sankhyayana Grihya texts.
  2. Devapala's commentary on the Katha-Grihya (2.6) separately cites a passage from a "Bahvricha-Brahmana."
  3. Bhattoji's Mahabhashya-tika cites one passage as being from "the Bahvricha-sutra commentary" and another, elsewhere, explicitly as being from "the Ashvalayana-sutra" — using two different names, confirming they are understood as two distinct shakhas.
  4. Medhatithi's discussion in his Manava-Grihyasutra commentary (1.7) is worth close examination on this same point.

"The Grihya of the Kathas, and the Grihya of the Bahvrichas and Ashvalayanas"

This phrase itself implies that the Kathas had two separate Grihyasutras available to them — one from the Bahvricha shakha, one from the Ashvalayana shakha. Kumarilabhatta's Tantravartika (1.3.11) confirms the general principle:

"It is observed that, like the Pratishakhya texts, Grihya-texts too follow shakha-specific variation — for instance, the Vasishtha[-Grihya-sutra] is followed only by the Bahvrichas, while the Shambali-prescribed text is accepted by the Vajasaneyins."

That is: Dharma- and Grihya-texts, like Pratishakhya texts, vary by shakha — Bahvricha-shakha followers use the Vasishtha-sutra, while the Vajasaneyins (a Yajurveda tradition) use the Shambalikhita-Dharmasutra instead. This passage from Kumarila makes it clear beyond doubt: Bahvricha is indeed a distinct, separate shakha of the Rigveda, not merely a generic synonym for "Rigvedin."

original p. 85
  1. The Vyakarana Mahabhashya (~7.4.44) discusses teaching Rigveda mantras to a young student "in the Bahvricha branch designation" — again treating it as a specific named shakha.

Turning to authorship: the Bhagavata Purana (12.6.4) describes the sage Shaunaka of Naimisharanya as himself "the Bahvricha [scholar]" (bahvṛcaḥ śaunako) — confirming Shaunaka's personal connection to this shakha, and making it plausible that his Brihaddevata was composed on the basis of the Bahvricha (or Mandukeya) tradition specifically. Separately, the teacher Shambavya (discussed earlier under the Sankhyayana section) is also identified as "a Bahvricha" — a Rigvedin — though not himself the founder of this particular branch.

The Brahmanda Purana (earlier section, ch. 63) lists several sage-authors: "Bahvricha, Bhargava, Shaila, Sankritya, and Jajali" — though most of these names are badly corrupted in the manuscripts, "Bahvricha" itself is consistently attested across copies, confirming it names an actual Rigvedin sage.

This completes the main shakha-divisions as given in the Charanavyuha. Two further divisional accounts given in the Puranas remain to be covered.

The Shakapurni Division, as Described in the Puranas

The Brahmanda Purana (earlier section, ch. 63) states:

प्रोवाच संहितास्तिस्रः शाकपूर्णे रथीतरः । निरुक्तं च पुनश्चक्रे चतुर्थं द्विजसत्तमः ॥ तस्य शिष्यास्तु चत्वारः शैल्यश्च क्रौञ्चकस्तथा । धीमान् शतबलाक्षश्च गजल्यश्चैव द्विजोत्तमः ॥

"Rathitara taught three Samhitas to Shakapurni, and this foremost of the twice-born further composed a fourth work, the Nirukta. His four disciples were: Shailya, Kraunchaka, the wise Shatabalaksha, and Gajalya, that foremost of the twice-born."

original p. 86

Summary: through this teacher-disciple succession, the shakha branching from Shakapurni split into three Samhita-traditions; Rathitara additionally composed an independent Nirukta text. Four disciples — Shailya, Ikshalaka, Shatabalaksha, and Gaja — are named as his students in printed sources, though the first two names in particular have become severely corrupted across the manuscript tradition (visible even across the Vayu, Vishnu, and Bhagavata Puranas), likely due to script changes over the centuries compounded by editors "correcting" uncertain readings according to their own judgment. Vishnu Purana copy no. 1320 क्श्रांच्यो वैतालकिः
Vishnu Purana copy no. 4375 क्श्रांच शैलाककः
Printed Bhagavata (Madras edition) शैजन्वैताल...
Bhagavata commentator Vira-Raghava शैंजवैताल...
Bhagavata commentator Vijaya शैंगिश्चैलाल...

Looking at all these variants, the author settles on three reconstructed name-pairs as most likely correct, based on the Brahmanda Purana's readings specifically:

शैंगक्ष्वो द्वालकस्था । शैंग्य बैद्वालकस्था । शैंग्यक शैलालकस्था ॥

शैङ्गक्ष्वो द्वालकस्था । शैङ्ग्य बैद्वालकस्था । शैङ्ग्यक शैलालकस्था ॥ śaiṅgakṣvo dvālakasthā | śaiṅgya baidvālakasthā | śaiṅgyaka śailālakasthā ||

(reconstructed as Shaingya-Ikshalaka, Shaingya-Baidalaka, and Shaingyaka-Shailalaka).

1. The Shaingya Shakha

A genuine Rigveda-related shakha, as already established from evidence discussed earlier. Its Brahmana and the existence of an associated Kalpa-sutra...

original p. 87

...whether this shakha has its own Samhita remains entirely unknown to this day. The Charaka Samhita's opening names a sage "Shaingi," whose son was likely "Shaingya" — a person by this name is separately listed among those present at Yudhishthira's assembly hall (Sabha-parva, 2.4). Shaingya's own son, Madhuka, is cited in the Brihaddevata (~1.75) and referenced in passing across the Shatapatha, Aitareya, and Kaushitaki Brahmanas, as well as frequently in the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra — including his view on the Agnyadhana (fire-establishment) rite, which later commentators note as differing only slightly from the Kaushitaki view; on the question of Soma's associated deity, Shaingya's view and the Kaushitaki Brahmana's statement turn out to be essentially identical. The Madhyandina Shatapatha Brahmana further records that Madhu-Shaingya received special teaching from Yajnavalkya connected with the Vajasaneya sacrifice. Evidence for a Shaingya-Grihyasutra or Dharmasutra appears in the Smritichandrika, the Maskari commentary on the Gautama-Dharmasutra, and Haradatta's writing — this branch's texts appear to have been more prevalent specifically in South India.

3. The Baidalaka Shakha

Uddalaka, of the Gautama lineage (son of Aruna, hence also called "Aruni"), was the father of the famous Shvetaketu. Uddalaka Aruni — a resident of Panchala, contemporary with King Janamejaya, and a disciple of Dhaumya-Ayoda — has his story begin in the Adiparva (1.3). Owing to his Gautama lineage, this branch is known in the world as the "Gautama-shakha," though the Vyakarana-Mahabhashya and other texts call it "Aruneya" (a separate discussion of the Aruneya-Brahmana follows elsewhere in this chapter). A teacher named Gautama appears frequently in the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra and must have been a Rigveda teacher.

original p. 88

(A separate Samaveda "Gautama-shakha" also exists and should not be confused with this Rigveda branch — details given elsewhere.)

2. The Shailalaka Shakha

Possibly an alternate reading for "Baidalaka" in the Brahmanda Purana variants — which of the two readings is original cannot be determined with certainty. This shakha's Brahmana is cited in the Ashtadhyayi (~4.1.100), and Sudarshanacharya's Bhashya-Prakashika commentary on the Shri-Bhashya quotes a lengthy passage from it (p. 173, with further references at pp. 108, 110, 195).

3. The Shatabalaksha Shakha

This name appears with several variants across the Brahmanda, Vayu, Vishnu, and Bhagavata Puranas (Shvetabalaksha, Shvetavalaka, Balaka, Babalaka, Vyalika), with "Shatabalaksha" the most commonly used form today. The Nirukta (~11.18) names a Shatabalaksha, son of Vyaghrapada, who was himself son of Mudgala (the same Mudgala-shakha discussed earlier) — and per this same Nirukta passage, Shatabalaksha himself became an author of Nirukta material. If this Shatabalaksha was indeed a disciple of Shakapurni, the likelihood strengthens that he is one and the same as this Nirukta-author.

Shakapurni's Fourth Disciple

Beyond the three disciples who became shakha-founders, Shakapurni had a fourth disciple named (with variant readings) Gaja, Gaingama, Niruktakrit, Niruktakrut, or Viraja — the authentic form cannot be determined with confidence. One associated Kalpa-sutra text is called "Hrasvika." The Shabara-bhashya on the Mimamsa-sutra (~1.1.31) lists examples of Kalpa-sutra texts: "Vashaka, Hastika, Kaundinyaka," and similarly named works — raising the natural question, if "Gaja" is indeed the correct disciple-name, of what connection might exist between him and this "Hastika-Kalpa" text.

original p. 89

The Final Puranic Divisions of Shakha-Founders

Bashkali Bharadvaja

Distinct from the earlier-discussed Bashkala lineage. The Skanda Purana's Nagara-khanda (ch. 68) mentions a "Danavendra Bashkalya," a disciple of Vyasa — not himself a shakha-founder. Shankaracharya's Vedanta-sutra commentary (1.3.33) separately mentions "Bashkali questioned by Baadhya" — plausibly referring to the actual shakha-founder. The Brahmanda Purana (earlier section, ch. 63) gives his lineage:

बाष्कलस्तु भरद्वाजस्तिस्रः प्रोवाच संहिताः । त्रयस्तस्य भवन्तीष्ट्या महात्मानो गुणान्विताः ॥ धीमांश्च त्वापसीषश्च पन्नगारिश्च बुद्धिमान् । त्रीयश्चार्जुनस्येष्ट तपसा संचितव्रताः ॥ वीतरागा महात्मानः संहिताज्ञा संहारगाः । इत्येते ब्रह्मविच्छाप्रोक्ताः संहिता यैः प्रवर्तिताः ॥

"Bashkala Bharadvaja taught three Samhitas; through devotion, his three [disciples] became great, virtuous souls: the wise Apasisha and wise Pannagari, and a third, dear to Arjuna, whose vows accumulated through austerity — passionless, great-souled, learned in the Samhitas, declared knowers of Brahman, by whom these Samhitas were propagated."

That is: Bashkali Bharadvaja had three disciples.

Disciple 1 — "Apanishena": variant readings include Apanasha, Nandayaniya, Kaalaayani, and Baalaayani; the first two may share a common root, but nothing can be said with certainty.

Disciple 2 — "Pannagari": variants include Pannagaani, Gaargya, and Bhajya across different Puranic manuscripts — none of which fits comfortably. A possible connection to "Bhujyu Lahyaayani" (named in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 3.3.1) is considered, though this identification has its own complications given the Brihadaranyaka-Kaushitaki tradition's own account...

original p. 90

...leaving the third disciple's identity (whether a mere messenger or a genuine shakha-founder) unresolved from the Bhagavata account. Per the Ashtadhyayi, "Parnagaru" is associated with the Prana country. The Brahmanda Purana instead names this third disciple "Arjuna," with further variants:

आर्व्व । कथाजन । तथाजन । कासार ।

आर्व्व । कथाजन । तथाजन । कासार । ārvva | kathājana | tathājana | kāsāra |

— again, no confident determination among these is possible.

Tally: across these Puranic accounts, the author counts eighteen total Rigveda Samhita-founding teachers — five of the Shakala group, four of the Bashkala group, three of Shakapurni's disciples, and three of Bashkali Bharadvaja's disciples (plus related figures). One commentator, in his own gloss, restates Patanjali's line on the number of Bahvricha shakhas:

एकविंशतिधा बाह्वृच्यम् । सप्तदशधा इत्येके ।

एकविंशतिधा बाह्वृच्यम् । सप्तदशधा इत्य् एके । ekaviṃśatidhā bāhvṛcyam | saptadaśadhā ity eke |

"The Bahvricha [tradition] is twenty-one-fold; some say seventeen-fold."

— reflecting a genuine, acknowledged difference of scholarly opinion inherited from his own teachers, rather than a settled figure.

Other Rigveda Shakhas Not Clearly Connected to Those Already Described

1. The Aitareya Shakha

The existence of the well-known Aitareya Brahmana itself confirms a corresponding "Aitareya" shakha. The Ashvalayana Shrautasutra (1.1) and the Nidana-sutra (5.4) both use the terms "Aitareyin" and "Aitareyakam" for it; the commentator Gargya Narayana likewise treats "Aitareyin" as a specific shakha-type, as does Varadatta's son in his Sankhyayana-Shrauta commentary ("Aitareyikam," ~1.1.7). Medhatithi's commentary on the Manu-sutra (~3.6) states directly:

"The twenty-one Bahvricha [shakhas], distinguished into the Ashvalayana, Aitareya, and other such divisions."

That is: among the Rigveda's 21 shakhas, Ashvalayana, Aitareya, and others are counted — confirming Aitareya's place as one of the recognized 21.

original p. 91

The Aitareya-Grihya: though this shakha's Brahmana and Aranyaka are well known, its Grihyasutra is only inferred. Haradatta's commentary on the Ashvalayana Grihyasutra notes: "And the Aitareyins' statement — [the mantra beginning] 'bhava,' etc., is common everywhere" — suggesting a shared marriage-rite recitation, plausibly drawn from an actual (if now-obscure) Aitareya Grihyasutra.

The Aitareya Shakhas and the Nine-Shraddha Question: Devanabhatta's Smriti-chandrika and a related citation (attributed to Shivaswami) preserve variant readings of a verse on how many types of Nava-shraddha (ancestral rites) different shakhas recognize:

नवश्राद्धानि षडाहुराश्वलायनशाखिनः । आपस्तम्बाश्च दित्याहुः पञ्चभिः षड्भिरैतरेयिणः ॥

"Ashvalayana-shakha followers say the nine shraddhas number six; the Apastamba followers likewise say six; the Aitareyins reckon them, with some flexibility, as five or six."

Since this distinctly Aitareya view doesn't appear in known Ashvalayana texts, the author raises — without resolving — the question of what independent Aitareya text this view might originally have come from.

2. The Vashishtha Shakha

Bühler edited and published the Vasishtha-Dharmasutra as Rigveda-related, though which specific shakha it belongs to remains unclear. Kumarilabhatta's Tantravartika (1.3.11) — cited earlier regarding the Bahvricha shakha's use of this same text — is revisited here in more detail...

original p. 92

गृह्येन वै परिगृह्येते । वासिष्ठं बह्वृचैरेव । कम्बिलिशकोक्तं वै वाजसनेयिभिः । आपस्तम्बोधायनीये कृत्तिरीयैरेव प्रतिश्यसे इत्येवम् ॥

"...are each adopted through their own Grihya[-text]. The Vashishtha [text] is used only by the Bahvrichas; the Kambilishaka-prescribed [text] by the Vajasaneyins; the Apastamba and Baudhayana [texts] only by the Taittiriyas..."

That is: just as Pratishakhyas differ by shakha, so do Grihyasutras — Samaveda followers use the Gautama and Gobhila sutras; Bahvricha-shakha followers (i.e., Rigvedins) use the Vashishtha-sutra; Vajasaneyins use the Kambilishaka material; and Taittiriya-shakha followers use the Apastamba and Baudhayana sutras. If Kumarila is right that the Bahvricha shakha is genuinely distinct, this confirms the Vashishtha tradition's specific association with it — though the Vasishtha Shrauta- and Grihyasutras themselves still merit closer investigation.

The Charanavyuha texts preserve a numerical accounting distinguishing the Vasishtha material from other portions by word-count, and Mahidasa's variant reading similarly distinguishes a specific chapter/varga ("Indrotibhih," with a word-count of 79) as absent from the Vasishtha gotra's own portion — confirming that the Vasishtha shakha was indeed treated as a genuinely distinct branch.

3. The Sulabha Shakha

Attested in the Vyakarana-Mahabhashya (~4.1.104/4.3.104) via a grammatical rule for rishi-derived names, giving forms like "Sulabhaishcheya," "Sulabha," and "Maitreya" — connected to a Rigveda-linked Brahmin lineage, though whether this corresponds to a specific "Shaulabha-Brahmana" text remains a matter for further investigation.

4. The Shaunaka Shakha

The sage Shaunaka, though a Brahmarshi renowned for conducting many long sacrificial sessions, was not himself primarily devoted to the path of ritual action. One of his disciples was Ashvalayana. Tradition places him in connection with the Mahabharata's account of King Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice (Sarpa-yaga), during which the terrible story [of the Mahabharata itself] was first recounted.

original p. 93

Shaunaka himself is not counted as a Rigveda shakha-founder as such, but rather as a broader teaching authority — Ashvalayana being his disciple, and himself citing a Rigveda-shakha sutra as his own guru's work. Beyond establishing this much, no further questions about this particular shakha can be resolved here.

Summary — All the Rigveda Shakhas Discussed in This Chapter

  1. Mudgala Shakha

  2. Galava Shakha

  3. Shaleeya Shakha

  4. Vatsya Shakha

  5. Shaishiri Shakha     — these five are the Shakala shakhas

  6. Baudhya Shakha

  7. Agnimatara Shakha

  8. Parashara Shakha

  9. Jatukarnya Shakha     — these four are the Bashkala shakhas

  10. Ashvalayana Shakha

  11. Sankhyayana Shakha

  12. Kaushitaki Shakha

  13. Mahakaushitaki Shakha

  14. Shambavya Shakha     — these four are the Sankhyayana-group shakhas

  15. Mandukeya Shakha

  16. Bahvricha Shakha

  17. Shaingya Shakha

  18. Uddalaka = Gautama = Aruna Shakha

  19. Shatabalaksha Shakha

  20. Gaja = Hastika Shakha 21–23. The three Bashkali-Bharadvaja shakhas (Apanishena, Pannagari, Arjuna)

  21. Aitareya Shakha

  22. Vashishtha Shakha

  23. Sulabha Shakha

  24. Shaunaka Shakha

original p. 94

The Vyakarana-Mahabhashya states the Rigveda has 21 shakhas, yet the list just compiled runs to roughly 26–27 names. The author reconciles this by suggesting that some of the additionally-identified names should properly be understood as sub-divisions nested within the main twenty, rather than fully independent branches — though confirming exactly which ones is not straightforward given the limited evidence currently available. The Anubhashya's citation from the Skanda Purana, and a separate account in the Anandasamhita, both repeat the same "21" figure — suggesting either that a few names in the present list are duplicates/overlaps counted separately, or that all these sources made their count on a broadly similar (if not perfectly reconcilable) basis. Neither possibility, the author notes, would be especially surprising.

Footnote: The Brahmanda Purana's earlier section (chapters 63–64) treats the division of the Veda, the names of Vedic shakhas, and the shakha-founders connected to the Shukla Yajurveda and Vajasaneya-Samhita at much greater length than could be included here — what appears in this chapter is only a focused extract, gathered and gone into in detail specifically where it bears on Rigveda shakha-founders. This Brahmanda Purana has itself been published, with a detailed introduction, as part of the "Sri Jayachamarajendra Grantharatnamala" series (see the list of Books published by Palace Authorities, Mysore) — the very same royal publication series backing the Rigveda Samhita volume being translated here. Chapters 63–64 referenced throughout this chapter belong to that Purvabhaga (earlier section) of the Purana.

— Chapter Five (The Branches of the Rigveda) concludes here. —
