Chapter Nine — The Brahmanas and Aranyakas of the Rigveda

original p. 168

Explaining the Meaning of the Word "Brahmana"

Although "Brahmana" is grammatically a masculine-form word, it is used, when referring to this class of text, in the neuter gender. A "Brahmana" text consists of the sentences within the Samhita tradition that explain context, ritual application (viniyoga), and precedent/history (purva-itihasa) — matters necessary for understanding the Samhita's mantras — composed after those mantras themselves were already established and known. This neuter usage is consistent across the Taittiriya Samhita, Brahmana, Sutra, and Nirukta literature; the Taittiriya Brahmana (2.5.1) offers a clear example. The lexicon Medini distinguishes the word's senses directly:

ब्राह्मणं ब्रह्मसंघाते वेदभागे नपुंसकम् ॥

"'Brahmanam,' in the sense of 'an assembly of Brahmins' or 'a portion of the Veda,' is neuter."

The Vishnudharmottara Purana (part 3, ch. 72) offers a related but more ambiguous usage:

मन्त्राः सब्राह्मणाः प्रोक्ताः स्वार्थं ब्राह्मणं स्मृतम् । कल्पना च तथा कल्प्यः कल्प्यं ब्राह्मणस्तथा ॥

"The mantras together with the Brahmana are declared; the Brahmana is remembered for its own [distinct] purpose. Likewise, prescribed/ordained material (kalpana) is also [called] Brahmana."

The final occurrence of "Brahmana" in this verse is genuinely ambiguous — reading it as referring to the Brahmin caste doesn't fit well either, leaving open whether this is a rare masculine usage or simply a corrupted reading. The Mahabharata's Udyoga-parva (ch. 42) provides a clearer case of masculine usage:

य इमे ब्राह्मणाः प्रोक्ता मन्त्रा वै प्रोक्षणे गवाम् । एषे प्रमाणं भवत उताहो नेति वासव ॥

"These Brahmanas that are declared, and the mantras for the sprinkling of cows — is this authoritative for you, or not, O Vasava [Indra]?"

Here "Brahmana" is unambiguously masculine; some scholars simply treat such instances as "Arsha" (archaic, sage-sanctioned irregular forms) without further debate. Turning to the subjects of knowledge contained within the Brahmana texts, the Atharvaveda states...

original p. 169

इतिहासश्च पुराणं च गाथाश्च नाराशंसीश्चानुव्यचलन् । (Atharvaveda 15.6.11)

"And Itihasa (legend), Purana, Gathas (ballads), and Narashamsi (praise-verses of men) followed along."

That is: a collection of Itihasa, Purana, Gatha, and Narashamsi material is found within the Brahmana texts.

The Word "Brahmana" and Its Meaning

Grammarians, commentators, glossators, and lexicographers all explain "Brahmana" somewhat differently. Sayanacharya, in the foundational introduction to his Rigveda commentary, writes:

मन्त्रस्य अविनक्तार्थस्य तु विनियोगबोधनाय ब्राह्मणवाक्यमुपयुक्तम् ॥

"The Brahmana statement serves the purpose of explaining the ritual application (viniyoga) of a mantra whose meaning is not directly stated."

That is: Brahmana-statements help clarify both Vedic meaning and a mantra's ritual application. Grammatically, whatever a mantra states in relation to Brahman (sacred knowledge) constitutes what "Brahmana" refers to — supported by the Shruti statements "brahma vai mantraḥ" and "vedo hi brahma," and by the further authority: "the Brahmanas are the explanatory expositions of the Vedas." In this sense, "Brahmana" takes on the meaning of statements that clarify Vedic mantras.

"Brahmana" is also explained in relation to yajna-duties — where the Brahmana texts explain ritual acts connected with a yajna, that explanation itself is what "Brahmana" means. As an example:

दूरोहणं रोहति तस्म्योक्तं ब्राह्मणम् ॥ (Aitareya Brahmana 3.24)

"'He ascends the Durohana [rite]' — this is the Brahmana stated for it."

This "Durohana Brahmana" is explained as follows:

दूरोहणं रोहति । स्वर्गो वै लोको दूरोहणम् । स्वर्गमेव तं लोकं रोहति य एवं वेद । यदेन दूरोहणां स असौ वै दूरोहो योऽसौ तपति । कश्चिद्वा अत्र गच्छति । स यद्दुरोहणं रोहत्येतस्मैव तद्रोहति । हंसनत्वा रोहति । हंसः शुचिषद्विश्व वै हंसः शुचिषक् ॥ इत्यादि ॥

"He ascends the Durohana. Heaven indeed is the world called Durohana ['difficult to ascend']. He who knows this thus indeed ascends to that heavenly world. Since it is difficult [to ascend], that indeed is 'Duroha' — that [sun] which burns/shines. Does anyone go there? When he ascends the Durohana, he ascends for that very [heaven]. He ascends by means of the swan (hamsa) — 'the swan dwelling in purity...' and so on."

From this, it's clear that the "Durohana-Brahmana" explains the meaning of the word "Durohana" itself. Another example...

original p. 170

यद्गौरिवीतं तस्म्योक्तं ब्राह्मणम् ॥ (Aitareya Brahmana 4.2)

"'That which is Gaurivita' — the Brahmana stated for it."

Explained as:

गौरिवीतं षोडशि साम कुर्वीत तेजस्कामो ब्रह्मवर्चस्कामस्त्येजो वै ब्रह्मवर्चसं गौरिवीतम् । तेजस्वी ब्रह्मवर्चसी भवति य एवं विद्वान् गौरिवीतं षोडशि साम कुरुते । नानदं षोडशि साम कर्तव्यमित्याहुः ॥

"One desiring vitality (tejas) and Brahmic radiance (brahmavarcas) should perform the Gaurivita Shodashi chant — tejas is indeed Brahmavarcas, [and this is] Gaurivita. He who, knowing this, performs the Gaurivita Shodashi chant becomes vital and radiant. It is said the Shodashi chant should not be performed without proper accompaniment."

This Gaurivita-Brahmana explains the word "Gaurivita" itself. Similarly, for "Chaidumbari":

अथास्य चैदुम्बरीमासन्दीं संभरन्ति । तस्य उक्तं ब्राह्मणम् (Aitareya Brahmana 8.12)

"'Now they gather for him a Chaidumbari seat.' Its Brahmana is stated:"

चैदुम्बरीं समन्यारभन्त इषमूर्जमन्वारभ इत्युद्गार्व अन्नाद्यमुदुम्बरो यद्वै तद्देवा इषमूर्जं व्यभजन्त तत उदुम्बरः समभवत्स्याश्च त्रिः संवत्सरस्य पच्यते ॥ (8.14)

"They take hold of the Chaidumbari together with vigor and nourishing strength — the Udumbara (fig tree) is food itself. Since the gods once divided vigor and nourishing strength between them, from that the Udumbara came into being, and it ripens three times a year."

From these examples, statements in the Brahmanas that explain a word's meaning were evidently themselves understood as expositions "of Brahman" — hence such explanations came to be called "Brahmanas."

Across the Shrauta-, Grihya-, Shulba-, and Dharma-sutras, and in the Nirukta and Nidana texts, it is customary, when citing a Brahmana passage as authority, to close with "iti vijnayate" or "iti ha vijnayate" ("thus it is known"). Why exactly this phrasing is used isn't entirely clear; Durgacharya's Nirukta commentary (2.11, 3.14) glosses it as "thus it becomes known even upon examining the Brahmana passage itself."

Two Kinds of Brahmanas

Bhatta Bhaskara's introduction to his Taittiriya Samhita commentary (1.4.1) states:

द्विविधं ब्राह्मणम् । कर्मब्राह्मणं कल्पब्राह्मणं चेति ॥

"Brahmana is of two kinds: Karma-Brahmana and Kalpa-Brahmana."

That is: the Karma-Brahmana explains the procedure for rites and the ritual application of mantras, without praising or criticizing the rites themselves; the Kalpa-Brahmana contains only the mantra-text itself, without stating its application.

original p. 171

"Anubrahmana"

Commentators generally gloss this as "brahmana-sadrsham anubrahmanam" — "that which resembles a Brahmana is called Anubrahmana" — i.e., not a Brahmana proper, but a text resembling one. Some apply the term to small individual Brahmana-portions within the Samaveda; the sage Satyavrata and others apply it to smaller Brahmana texts other than the Tandya-Brahmana. The Nidana-sutra cites several such passages under this name. Bhatta Bhaskara's Taittiriya-Samhita commentary (1.4.1, on the Brahmana portion 1.5.11.1) glosses a passage:

अश्वा वेतानि हविर्गोंशि भवन्ति ॥

अश्वा वेतानि हविर्-गोम्शि भवन्ति aśvā vetāni havir-gomśi bhavanti

"These become the horse-related oblation materials..."

as "anubrāhmaṇaṃ ca bhavanti" — "and these become Anubrahmana." Madhava's Taittiriya Brahmana commentary (1.4.1) similarly opens a passage:

अथ राजसूयस्यानुब्राह्मणम् ॥

अथ राजसूयस्यानुब्राह्मणम् atha rājasūyasyānubrāhmaṇam

"Now, the Anubrahmana of the Rajasuya [rite]..."

Together these confirm that certain internal sub-portions of a Brahmana are specifically termed "Anubrahmana."

The Brahmanas of the Rigveda

1. The Aitareya Brahmana

The Rigveda has two Brahmanas: the Aitareya and the Kaushitaki (also called the Sankhyayana-Brahmana). The Aitareya Brahmana consists of five Panchikas (groups), each with five chapters (adhyayas) — 40 chapters in total. Its subject matter runs roughly as follows: Given the density of precise chapter/section cross-references in the original for this table, the ranges above are given at the level the source presents them, with normal care but without claiming pinpoint certainty on every individual sub-reference.

  • Chapters 1–2: the rules governing Soma-yagas such as the Jyotishtoma, and the sacrifice's overall sequence.
  • Chapter 3: the Agnishtoma yaga and related matters.
  • Panchika 3, chapters 4–5: the Ukthya, Shodashi, and Atiratra yagas.
  • Panchika 3 (ch. 5) through Panchika 4 (ch. 1): the Gavamayana rite.
  • Panchika 4 (chs. 4–5): the Adityanamayana and Angirasamayana rites.
  • Panchikas 4–5 (further chapters): the Dvadashaha (twelve-day rite).
  • A later chapter: the Yajamana's required duties — Prayashchitta (atonement) rites, the timing of the Agnishtoma, and the duties of the Brahma-priest.
original p. 172
  • Chapters 6–30: descriptions of the duties of other Ritvij priests.
  • Chapters 31–40: the yajnas a Kshatriya must perform, and the royal coronation (Rajyabhisheka) ceremony.

Why is it called "Aitareya"? Sayanacharya's own commentary preserves the story: a certain sage had several wives, one named Itara, unloved by the rest. Her son was accordingly called "Itareya" (son of Itara) by others, though his given name was Mahidasa. When the father performed yajnas, he favored his other sons over Itara's son. In her distress at this neglect, Itara prayed to the goddess Bhumidevi (Earth), who — pleased with her devotion — granted the boy a throne surpassing heaven itself and blessed him with mastery of the Rigveda's Brahmana, Aranyaka, and Upanishad. Because Mahidasa, son of Itara, composed these very texts, they became known as the Aitareya Brahmana, Aitareya Aranyaka, and Aitareya Upanishad.

Where the Aitareya Brahmana Circulated

The Charanavyuha (third Kandika) quotes a verse from the Mahanarnava:

तुंगा कृष्णा तथा गोदा सह्याद्रिशिखरावधि । आ आंध्रदेशपर्यंतं बह्वृचाश्चैवशालायनी ॥

तुङ्गा कृष्णा तथा गोदा सह्याद्रि-शिखरावधि, आ आन्ध्र-देश-पर्यन्तं बह्वृचाश् चैव-शालायनी tuṅgā kṛṣṇā tathā godā sahyādri-śikharāvadhi, ā āndhra-deśa-paryantaṃ bahvṛcāś caiva-śālāyanī

"From the Tunga, Krishna, and Godavari [rivers], up to the peaks of the Sahyadri mountains, extending as far as the Andhra region — there the Bahvricha [tradition], via the Ashvalayana line, [is established]."

That is: the Aitareya Brahmana (belonging to the Bahvricha/Ashvalayana shakhas) circulated along the Tungabhadra, Krishna, and Godavari river regions, and across the country from the Sahyadri range to Andhra — the Rigveda-shakha Brahmins of these regions study the Aitareya Brahmana specifically.

2. The Kaushitaki Brahmana

The Brahmana of the Sankhyayana shakha is called the Kaushitaki-Brahmana (some instead call it the Sankhyayana-Brahmana). A manuscript held at the Bodleian confirms this dual naming, closing with: "kauṣītakī-matānusāre śāṅkhāyana-brāhmaṇam" ("the Sankhyayana-Brahmana, following the Kaushitaki tradition"). A commentator named Mahisabana, glossing the Charanavyuha's second Kandika, cites a further verse locating the tradition geographically:

उत्तरे गुर्जरे देशे वेदो ब्रह्म च ईरितः । कौषीतकब्राह्मणं च शाखा शांखायनी स्थिता ॥

उत्तरे गुर्जरे देशे वेदो ब्रह्म च ईरितः, कौषीतक-ब्राह्मणं च शाखा शाङ्खायनी स्थिता uttare gurjare deśe vedo brahma ca īritaḥ, kauṣītaka-brāhmaṇaṃ ca śākhā śāṅkhāyanī sthitā

"In the northern Gujarat region, the Veda and Brahman are proclaimed; there, the Kaushitaki-Brahmana and the Sankhyayana shakha are established."

original p. 173

According to this verse, the Brahmana belonging to the Sankhyayana shakha shares its name with the "Kaushitaki-Brahmana." Shankaracharya's Vedanta-sutra commentary (~1.3.33 and 3.3.10) and Panini's sutra (~4.1.79) both cite this Brahmana's name.

The text's actual author cannot be determined with certainty, but calling it either "Kaushitaki" or "Sankhyayana" is equally acceptable — the Sankhyayana Aranyaka itself records that Uddalaka gave his teaching to Kahola-Kaushitaki, who was in turn Sankhyayana's own teacher; hence either name applies to this Brahmana.

The text runs to 30 chapters. Most of its subject matter matches the Aitareya Brahmana, though a few topics — notably the description of the Somayaga — are treated in greater detail here. Broadly: the Aitareya Brahmana follows the Rigveda's Shakala (or Bashkala) shakha, while the Kaushitaki-Brahmana follows the Sankhyayana shakha.

The Aitareya Aranyaka

Certain texts are meant specifically for Brahmins, called Aranyakas, generally regarded as belonging to the concluding portion of the Brahmanas, treating subject matter similar to the Brahmanas themselves — but since they were prescribed to be studied only in the forest, they came to be called "Aranyakas." Sayanacharya's Taittiriya Aranyaka commentary states:

अरण्याध्ययनादेतदारण्यकमितीर्यते । अरण्ये तदधीयानः शैश्वं वाक्यं सृज्यते ॥

अरण्याध्ययनाद् एतद् आरण्यकम् इतीर्यते । अरण्ये तद् अधीयानः शैश्वं वाक्यं सृज्यते ॥ araṇyādhyayanād etad āraṇyakam itīryate | araṇye tad adhīyānaḥ śaiśvaṃ vākyaṃ sṛjyate ||

"Because it is studied in the forest, this is called 'Aranyaka' — so it is said. [One who studies it in the forest...]" (the second line's precise sense remains somewhat uncertain even at this resolution)

That is: because subjects useful to forest-dwelling Vanaprasthas and to knowledge-seeking sannyasis are explained within these Aranyakas and Upanishads, it was prescribed that they be studied only in the forest, with a calm mind — hence the name "Aranyaka."

Among these, the Aitareya Aranyaka belongs to the Aitareya Brahmana, and the Kaushitaki Aranyaka to the Kaushitaki Brahmana. The Aitareya Aranyaka has five parts (each itself called an "Aranyaka"): the first with 5 chapters, the second with 7, the third with 2, the fourth with 1, and the fifth with 3 — 18 chapters in total.

The first Aranyaka describes the Mahavrata rite — itself one portion of the Gavamayana described in the Aitareya Brahmana (ch. 4, section 1). This is a rite performed within a single day, and this section details the day's required observances: the morning pressing (Pratah-savana), midday pressing (Madhyandina-savana), evening pressing (Sayam-savana), and related matters.

original p. 174

The second Aranyaka has two parts: chapters 1–3 explain ritual meaning, while chapters 4–5 contain the well-known Aitareya Upanishad. The third Aranyaka describes the distinctions of accent (svara), articulation (sparsha), and breath (ushma) connected with the Samhita, Pada, and Krama recitation-methods, naming many sages. The fourth Aranyaka collects mantras connected with the Mahanamni verses, also found in the Samaveda's Naigeya shakha. The fifth Aranyaka describes the "Nishkevalya Shastra," recited on the midday-pressing day of the Mahavrata.

Compilation

Tradition holds that Mahidasa (promulgator of the Aitareya Brahmana) composed the first two Aranyakas; Ashvalayana composed the third; and Shaunaka composed the remaining portion. The Rikvarnanukramanike records the following account of the many texts in this lineage:

शौनकीया दश ग्रन्थास्ते ऋग्वेदगुप्स्रये । अष्टानुक्रमणीत्याद्या छन्दस्सी दैवती तथा ॥ अनुवाकानुक्रमणे सूक्तानुक्रमणे तथा । ऋक्सादयोर्विद्वांश्च बार्हद्दैवतमेव च ॥ प्रातिशाख्यं शौनकीयं स्वार्थं दशमनुच्यते ।

शौनकीया दश ग्रन्थास् ते ऋग्वेद-गुप्स्रये । अष्टानुक्रमणीत्याद्या छन्दस्सी दैवती तथा ॥ अनुवाकानुक्रमणे सूक्तानुक्रमणे तथा । ऋक्सादयोर् विद्वांश् च बार्हद्दैवतम् एव च ॥ प्रातिशाख्यं शौनकीयं स्वार्थं दशम् अनुच्यते । śaunakīyā daśa granthās te ṛgveda-gupsraye | aṣṭānukramaṇītyādyā chandassī daivatī tathā || anuvākānukramaṇe sūktānukramaṇe tathā | ṛksādayor vidvāṃś ca bārhaddaivatam eva ca || prātiśākhyaṃ śaunakīyaṃ svārthaṃ daśam anucyate |

"These are Shaunaka's ten texts for the protection of the Rigveda: the Ashtaka-anukramani and similar works, the Chandas[-anukramani], and likewise the Daivata[-anukramani]; the Anuvaka-anukramani, and likewise the Sukta-anukramani; [a work] on the words of the Rik and related matters, and the Brihaddaivata itself; and the Pratishakhya composed by Shaunaka is called the tenth, for its own purpose."

And further:

शौनकीयं च दशकं तच्छिष्यस्य त्रिकं तथा । द्वादशाध्यायकं सूक्तं चतुःसद्गृह्यमेव च ॥ चतुर्थारण्यकं चेति ह्याश्वलायनसूत्रकम् ॥

शौनकीयं च दशकं तच्-छिष्यस्य त्रिकं तथा । द्वादशाध्यायकं सूक्तं चतुः-सद्-गृह्यम् एव च ॥ चतुर्थारण्यकं चेति ह्य् आश्वलायन-सूत्रकम् ॥ śaunakīyaṃ ca daśakaṃ tac-chiṣyasya trikaṃ tathā | dvādaśādhyāyakaṃ sūktaṃ catuḥ-sad-gṛhyam eva ca || caturthāraṇyakaṃ ceti hy āśvalāyana-sūtrakam ||

"Thus Shaunaka's ten [texts]; and likewise his disciple's [Ashvalayana's] three: the twelve-chapter Sukta[-related Shrautasutra], the four-part Grihyasutra, and the fourth being the Aranyaka — these together constitute the Ashvalayana-sutra corpus."

That is: Shaunaka wrote ten Rigveda-related texts — (1) Arshanukramani, (2) Chandonukramani, (3) Devatanukramani, (4) Anuvakanukramani, (5) Suktanukramani, (6) Rigvidhana, (7) Padavidhana, (8) Brihaddaivata, (9) Pratishakhya, and (10) Shaunaka-smriti. His disciple Ashvalayana composed the twelve-chapter Shrautasutra, the four-chapter Grihyasutra, and the fourth Aranyaka within the Aitareya Aranyaka. Shaunaka himself compiled the fifth Aranyaka. Sayana's Aitareya Aranyaka commentary states:

आत एव पञ्चमे शौनकेनोदाहृताः । (१-५-१) ताश्च पञ्चमे शौनकेन शाखान्तरसात्म्या पठिताः । (१-५-१)

आत एव पञ्चमे शौनकेनोदाहृताः । āta eva pañcame śaunakenodāhṛtāḥ | (1.5.1) ताश् च पञ्चमे शौनकेन शाखान्तर-सात्म्या पठिताः । tāś ca pañcame śaunakena śākhāntara-sātmyā paṭhitāḥ | (1.5.1)

"These indeed have been cited by Shaunaka in the fifth [Aranyaka]... and these were recited by Shaunaka in the fifth, drawn appropriately from other shakhas." (the exact sense of a couple of words here remains somewhat uncertain)

Therefore, in Sayana's own view, it was Shaunaka himself who composed the fifth Aranyaka.

original p. 175

On the Aitareya Aranyaka, Scholar Keith Writes

"As might be expected they (the verbal coincidences between the Aitareya Brahmana and the Aranyaka) are constant and show unmistakably the connection of the two works."

That is: the Aitareya Brahmana and Aranyaka show extensive similarity in both language and word-usage, confirming the two texts' close mutual connection.

2. The Sankhyayana (or Kaushitaki) Aranyaka

The Sankhyayana Aranyaka has 15 chapters in total, divided into sections (khandas) as follows: A handful of individual khanda-counts in this table are given as best legible at this resolution.

Adhyaya Khanda Adhyaya Khanda Adhyaya Khanda
1 8 6 20 11 8
2 18 7 25 12 8
3 7 8 11 13 1
4 18 9 8 14 3
5 8 10 8 15 1

This Aranyaka resembles the Aitareya Aranyaka in every respect — its description of the Mahavrata and related rites matches closely. Chapters 1–2 cover material corresponding to the Aitareya Aranyaka's 1st and 5th Aranyakas; chapters 3–6 correspond to its 2nd Aranyaka. Chapters 7 onward constitute the well-known Kaushitaki Upanishad — since some manuscript copies lack these Upanishad chapters entirely, there is reasonable suspicion that this portion may have been appended to the Aranyaka at some later date.

At the end of this Aranyaka appears a closing statement:

गुणाख्याश्चांबायनादस्माभिरधीतम् ॥

गुणाख्याश् चाम्बायनाद् अस्माभिर् अधीतम् ॥ guṇākhyāś cāmbāyanād asmābhir adhītam ||

"This has been learned by us from Gunakhya-Sankhyayana."

The word "asmābhiḥ" ("by us") here may refer to the many disciples of Gunakhya-Sankhyayana; alternatively, Sankhyayana himself may have compiled the first four chapters, with his disciples compiling the final one.

Chapter Ten — The Rishis of the Rigveda

original p. 176

Before reciting a sukta's mantra, one must first state that sukta's rishi, meter (chandas), and deity — a tradition inherited from ancient times. It is said that reciting a mantra without knowing these three yields no benefit and constitutes a wrongdoing. Sayanacharya states, in the introduction to his commentary:

अविदित्वा ऋषिं छन्दो दैवतं योगमेव च । योऽध्यापयेज्जपेद्वापि पापीयाज्जायते तु सः ॥

अविदित्वा ऋषिं छन्दो दैवतं योगम् एव च । योऽध्यापयेज् जपेद् वापि पापीयाज् जायते तु सः ॥ aviditvā ṛṣiṃ chando daivataṃ yogam eva ca | yo'dhyāpayej japed vāpi pāpīyāj jāyate tu saḥ ||

"Without knowing the rishi, the meter, the deity, and the [ritual] application, whoever teaches or recites [a mantra] becomes, indeed, a greater sinner."

What exactly are this "rishi," "deity," and "meter"? Katyayana, in the Sarvanukramani, defines them:

यस्य वाक्यं स ऋषिः । या तेनोक्ता सा देवता । यदक्षरपरिमाणं तच्छन्दः । अक्षैस्स ऋषयो देवताश्छन्दोभिरसाधारणम् ॥

यस्य वाक्यं स ऋषिः । या तेनोक्ता सा देवता । यद्-अक्षर-परिमाणं तच्-छन्दः । अक्षैस् स ऋषयो देवताश् छन्दोभिर् असाधारणम् ॥ yasya vākyaṃ sa ṛṣiḥ | yā tenoktā sā devatā | yad-akṣara-parimāṇaṃ tac-chandaḥ | akṣais sa ṛṣayo devatāś chandobhir asādhāraṇam ||

"He whose utterance it is — he is the rishi. She who is addressed by it — she is the deity. Whatever the syllable-count is — that is its meter. [The correspondence of] rishis, deities, and meters, [determined] through syllables, is specific to each [mantra]."

That is: the mantra's composer is its rishi; the deity the mantra addresses is its deity; and the systematic arrangement of syllables is called meter. Rishis, seeking prosperity, pleased the deities through these metrically-structured utterances.

Saying the rishis "composed" the mantras is not, strictly, Vedic doctrine — rather, they are the mantras' "seers" (drashtaras): the mantras became manifest to them. As Sayana's commentary puts it:

अतीन्द्रियस्य वेदस्य परमेश्वरानुग्रहेण प्रथमतो दर्शनात् ऋषित्वम् ।

अतीन्द्रियस्य वेदस्य परमेश्वरानुग्रहेण प्रथमतो दर्शनात् ऋषित्वम् । atīndriyasya vedasya parameśvarānugraheṇa prathamato darśanāt ṛṣitvam |

"Rishihood consists in the first perception, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, of the Veda, which transcends the senses."

Mantras are not perceivable through the ordinary senses; whoever it was to whom these mantras first became manifest, by divine grace, is a rishi — so Sayana's commentary explains.

The Rishis

"Rishi" means "one who knows" — derived from the root ṛṣ in the sense of knowledge ("ṛṣa-jñāne"). By that logic, any knowledgeable person could be called "rishi." But the word "rishi" [in the specific Vedic sense]...

original p. 177

...does not carry this generic sense of "anyone who knows anything." Only those who directly perceived the mantras themselves are counted as their rishis — this is the general view; "perceiving" here means the mantras became revealed to them. Anandatirtha's own Rig-bhashya states:

यः पश्यति स्वयं वाक्यं स ऋषिस्तस्य कीर्तितः । (ऋग्भाष्य) यथा यः स्वयमध्ययनेन विनैव यद्वाक्यं पश्यति स तस्य वाक्यस्य ऋषिः प्रकीर्तितः । (ऋग्भाष्यटीका)

यः पश्यति स्वयं वाक्यं स ऋषिस् तस्य कीर्तितः । yaḥ paśyati svayaṃ vākyaṃ sa ṛṣis tasya kīrtitaḥ | (Ṛgbhāṣya) यथा यः स्वयम् अध्ययनेन विनैव यद् वाक्यं पश्यति स तस्य वाक्यस्य ऋषिः प्रकीर्तितः । yathā yaḥ svayam adhyayanena vinaiva yad vākyaṃ paśyati sa tasya vākyasya ṛṣiḥ prakīrtitaḥ | (Ṛgbhāṣyaṭīkā)

"He who himself perceives an utterance — he is declared its rishi." (Rig-bhashya) "That is: whoever perceives a given utterance by himself, without prior study, is proclaimed the rishi of that utterance." (Rig-bhashya-tika)

Whoever, without prior study, perceives the mantras through divine grace alone is that mantra's rishi. Before reciting any Vedic mantra, we must state its rishi, deity, and meter — those named as rishis in the Anukramani and similar texts are likely those who first attained the mantras; examining the Puranic statements about the rishis makes this clear. That is: those named in the Anukramanika, or spoken of in yajnas as the mantras' "seers," were most likely the very first seers of those mantras.

अर्वाक् द्वादशाब्देस्तर्दीक्ष्याश्यृषिरीण सः । (आनन्दऋग्भाष्य) इवं यो द्वादशाब्देस्तर्वागधीक्ष्यापि प्रतिशद्ये सोऽस्य ऋषिरेव ॥ (ऋग्भाष्यटीका)

अर्वाक् द्वादशाब्देस् तर्-दीक्ष्याश् यृषिरीण सः । arvāk dvādaśābdes tar-dīkṣyāś yṛṣirīṇa saḥ | (Ānanda-ṛgbhāṣya) इवं यो द्वादशाब्देस् तर्वागधीक्ष्यापि प्रतिशद्ये सोऽस्य ऋषिर् एव ॥ ivaṃ yo dvādaśābdes tarvāgadhīkṣyāpi pratiśadye so'sya ṛṣir eva || (Ṛgbhāṣyaṭīkā)

(This particular verse pair concerns a twelve-year period of study/qualification connected to rishi-status; several individual words are difficult to render with full confidence even at this resolution, so the Sanskrit is given as transcribed, without forcing a precise English rendering of every phrase.)

original p. 178

The rishis of the first Mandala begin with Madhuchchandas and others; those who saw a hundred mantras are called "Shatarshina." The rishis of Mandalas 2–7 — Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vamadeva-Gautama, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, Pavamanya, and others — are termed "Madhyama," while the 8th Mandala's rishis are called "Kshudrasukta" and "Mahasukta." The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra confirms this:

अथ ऋषयः शतर्षिनो माध्यमा गृत्समदो विश्वामित्रो वामदेवोऽत्रिर्भरद्वाजो वसिष्ठः प्रगाथाः पावमान्याः क्षुद्रसूक्ता महासूक्ता इति ॥

अथ ऋषयः शतर्षिनो माध्यमा गृत्समदो विश्वामित्रो वामदेवोऽत्रिर् भरद्वाजो वसिष्ठः प्रगाथाः पावमान्याः क्षुद्रसूक्ता महासूक्ता इति ॥ atha ṛṣayaḥ śatarṣino mādhyamā gṛtsamado viśvāmitro vāmadevo'trir bharadvājo vasiṣṭhaḥ pragāthāḥ pāvamānyāḥ kṣudrasūktā mahāsūktā iti ||

"Now, the rishis: Shatarshina, Madhyama, Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vamadeva, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, the Pragathas, the Pavamanyas, the Kshudrasuktas, and the Mahasuktas — thus."

These Are the Rishi-Classifications

Among the rishis, there are said to be several classes — Maharshi, Rishi, Rishika, Rishiputra, and Shrutarshi. Harishchandra's commentary on the Charaka-sutra states four kinds:

मुनीनां चतुर्विधो भेदः । ऋषयः, ऋषिकाः, ऋषिपुत्राः महर्षयश्च ।

मुनीनां चतुर्विधो भेदः । ऋषयः, ऋषिकाः, ऋषिपुत्राः महर्षयश् च । munīnāṃ caturvidho bhedaḥ | ṛṣayaḥ, ṛṣikāḥ, ṛṣiputrāḥ maharṣayaś ca |

"The division among sages (munis) is fourfold: Rishis, Rishikas, Rishiputras, and Maharshis."

According to Harishchandra, excluding Shrutarshi, there are only these four divisions.

अतीतानागतानां च संबन्धाद्ह्यार्षं स्मृतम् । अतस्त्रिकालं वक्ष्यामि तद्ध्यार्षसमुद्भवम् ॥ २० ॥ इत्येता ऋषिजातीस्ता नामभिः शं च वै शृणु ॥ २१ ॥

अतीतानागतानां च संबन्धाद् ह्य् आर्षं स्मृतम् । अतस् त्रिकालं वक्ष्यामि तद् ध्य् आर्ष-समुद्भवम् ॥ इत्येता ऋषिजातीस् ता नामभिः शं च वै शृणु ॥ atītānāgatānāṃ ca saṃbandhād hy ārṣaṃ smṛtam | atas trikālaṃ vakṣyāmi tad dhy ārṣa-samudbhavam || ityetā ṛṣijātīs tā nāmabhiḥ śaṃ ca vai śṛṇu ||

(This verse concerns the "Arsha" quality's connection to past and future time and its threefold temporal origin; the precise sense of a few individual words remains uncertain even at this resolution.)

1. Maharshi = Ishvara (the Divine Ones)

भृगुर्मरीचिश्चात्रिश्च ह्यंगिराः पुलहः कृतुः । मनुर्दक्षो वसिष्ठश्च पुलस्त्यश्चेति ते दश ॥ ७९ ॥ ब्रह्मणो मानसाः सृष्टा उद्गाथाः स्वयमुच्चराः । सप्तैवर्षयो यस्मात् सृतास् स्यान्महर्षयः ॥ ८० ॥

भृगुर् मरीचिश् चात्रिश् च ह्य् अङ्गिराः पुलहः क्रतुः । मनुर् दक्षो वसिष्ठश् च पुलस्त्यश् चेति ते दश ॥ ब्रह्मणो मानसाः सृष्टा उद्गाथाः स्वयम् उच्चराः । सप्तैव ऋषयो यस्मात् सृतास् स्यान् महर्षयः ॥ bhṛgur marīciś cātriś ca hy aṅgirāḥ pulahaḥ kratuḥ | manur dakṣo vasiṣṭhaś ca pulastyaś ceti te daśa || brahmaṇo mānasāḥ sṛṣṭā udgāthāḥ svayam uccarāḥ | saptaiva ṛṣayo yasmāt sṛtās syān maharṣayaḥ ||

"Bhrigu, Marichi, and Atri, and likewise Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Daksha, Vasishtha, and Pulastya — these are the ten. Created from Brahma's mind, self-proclaiming... From whom the seven [great] rishis arose — these are the Maharshis."

Among the rishis, the first rank belongs to the Maharshis. Bhrigu, Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Daksha, Vasishtha, and Pulastya — these ten are the mind-born sons of Brahma, called "Ishvara" (divine lords). Being the foremost among all rishis, they are given the designation "Maharshi."

original p. 179

2. Rishi

ईश्वराणां सुता ह्येते ऋषयस्स्वान्निबोधत । काव्यो बृहस्पतिश्चैव कश्यपश्च्यवनस्थ ॥ ९३ ॥ उतथ्यो वामदेवश्च अगस्त्यश्चैषिजस्थ । कर्दमो विश्रवाश्च शक्त्या वाल्मीक्यस्थावर्तकः ॥ ९४ ॥ इत्येते ऋषयः प्रोक्तास्सपसा चर्षितां गताः ।

īśvarāṇāṃ sutā hy ete ṛṣayas svān nibodhata | kāvyo bṛhaspatiś caiva kaśyapaś cyavanasya ॥ utathyo vāmadevaś ca agastyaś caiṣijasya | kardamo viśravāś ca śaktyā vālmīkyas tāvartakaḥ ॥ ityete ṛṣayaḥ proktās sapasā carṣitāṃ gatāḥ |

"Know these to be the sons of the Ishvaras [Maharshis] — the rishis: Kavya (Ushanas), and likewise Brihaspati, Kashyapa, and Chyavana; Utathya, Vamadeva, and Agastya... Kardama, Vishravas, and, by his power, Valmiki... — these are declared rishis, who attained excellence through toil/austerity."

That is: Ushana-Kavya, Brihaspati, Kashyapa, Chyavana, Utathya, Vamadeva, Agastya, Ushik, Kardama, Vishravas, Shakti, Valmika, and Arvata form the second class of rishis — sons of the Maharshis (Bhrigu and others), who attained the rank of "rishi" through austerity (tapas).

3. Rishiputra — Rishika

ऋषिपुत्रास्त्वृषीकांस्तु गर्भोत्पन्नान्निबोधत ॥ १०० ॥ वत्सरो नग्नहश्चैव भरद्वाजश्चैव च । ऋषिदीर्घतमाश्चैव बृहदुक्थः शरद्वते ॥ १०१ ॥ वाजश्रवा सुविप्रश्च वश्याश्च पराशरः । दधीच शंशपाश्चैव रांका वैश्रवणस्थ ॥ १०२ ॥ इत्येते ऋषिकाः प्रोक्तास्स्वे सत्या ऋषितां गताः ।

ṛṣiputrās tv ṛṣīkāṃs tu garbhotpannān nibodhata ॥ vatsaro nagnahaś caiva bharadvājaś caiva ca | ṛṣi-dīrghatamāś caiva bṛhaduktaḥ śaradvate ॥ vājaśravā suvipraś ca vaśyāś ca parāśaraḥ | dadhīca śaṃśapāś caiva rāṅkā vaiśravaṇasya ॥ ityete ṛṣikāḥ proktās sve satyā ṛṣitāṃ gatāḥ |

"Know that the Rishiputras, or Rishikas, are born of [ordinary] lineage. Vatsara, and likewise Nagnaha, and Bharadvaja; Rishi-Dirghatama, and likewise Brihaduktha, Sharadvata; Vajashrava, Suvipra, Vashya, and Parashara; Dadhicha, and likewise Shamshapa, Ranka, Vaishravana — these are declared the Rishikas, who, true to their own nature, attained rishihood."

That is: Vatsara, Nagnaha, Bharadvaja, Dirghatama, Brihaduktha, Sharadvata, Vajashrava, Suvipra, Parashara, Dadhicha, Shamshapa, Ranka, and Vaishravana are called "Rishika" — the legitimate (aurasa) sons of the [second-class] rishis.

A disputed point: where rishis are elsewhere classed into "five kinds," Rishiputra and Rishika are treated as distinct categories, whereas here they are counted as one and the same — such differences of opinion recur across the Puranas, and a description of the remaining two categories has not yet been located.

The Rishis of the Bhrigu Lineage — 1

The Puranas state there are 14 rishis of the Bhrigu lineage, named as follows: Given the density of proper names in this passage, the transliteration above is given as faithfully as legible, without forcing a full grammatical translation of what is essentially a name-list.

वित्ते मन्त्रकृतः सर्वे कृत्स्नशास्त्रान्निबोधत । भृगुः काव्यः प्रचेताश्च दधीचो ह्यास्स्वानसः ॥ १०४ ॥ चैवर्षिश्चथ जमदग्निश्च विदः सारस्वतस्थ । आश्मर्षीश्च्यवनश्च वीतहव्यः सुमेधसः ॥ १०५ ॥ वैन्यः पृथुर्दिवोदासो वाध्र्यश्वो गृत्सशौनकाः । विकोनविंशतिश्चैते भृगवो मन्त्रवादिनः ॥ १०६ ॥

vitte mantrakṛtaḥ sarve kṛtsna-śāstrān nibodhata | bhṛguḥ kāvyaḥ pracetāś ca dadhīco hy āsvānasaḥ ॥ caivarṣiś catha jamadagniś ca vidaḥ sārasvatasya | āśmarṣīś cyavanaś ca vītahavyaḥ sumedhasaḥ ॥ vainyaḥ pṛthur divodāso vādhryaśvo gṛtsaśaunakāḥ | vikonaviṃśatiś caite bhṛgavo mantravādinaḥ ||

(A list of the Bhrigu-lineage rishi-composers: Bhrigu, Kavya, Pracheta, Dadhicha, [and others including] Jamadagni, Chyavana, Vitahavya, Sumedhas, Pṛthu Vainya, Divodasa, Vadhryashva, and Gritsa-Shaunaka — nineteen in total, all reciters of mantras.)

original p. 180

The mantra-seeing rishis of the Bhrigu lineage, numbered in the verse above:

# Name # Name # Name
1 Bhrigu 7 Jamadagni 13 Sumedhas
2 Kavya (Ushanas=Shukra) 8 Vida 14 Vainya Prithu
3 Pracheta 9 Sarasvata 15 Divodasa
4 Dadhyaj (Atharvana) 10 Ashmarshena 16 Vadhryashva
5 Ashvavan 11 Chyavana 17 Gritsa(mada)
6 Chaiva (Rishika) 12 Vitahavya 18 Shaunaka

The verse states "vikonaviṃśati" (nineteen), but this list gives only eighteen names — perhaps because "Vaidya" and "Vrighu" were meant to be counted separately, though Vedic texts treat "Vena's son Vrighu" as a single figure, "Vaidya Vrighu." Some one name has evidently dropped out of this particular list.

The genealogical tree of these rishis varies across different Puranas. The Mahabharata's Adiparva (60–70) gives it thus:

Bhrigu - Kavi (Shukra, teacher of the Daityas) - Chyavana - Aurva - Rishika - Jamadagni

The Mahabharata treats this lineage only this briefly before moving to other rishi-lineages. Other Puranas add that Chyavana had two sons by his wife Sukanya — Apnavan and Dadhyarcha; Apnavan's son Aurva lived in the Madhyadesha and held a rivalry with Kartavirya-Arjuna over territorial matters. Vitahavya was originally a Kshatriya who became a Brahmin through the teaching of a Bhrigu-lineage rishi; Gritsamada and Shaunaka were both born within his lineage.

The Close Connection Between the Bhrigu Lineage and the Atharvaveda

Among the Atharvaveda's many names is "Bhrigvangiro-veda" (the Veda of Bhrigu and Angiras) — reflecting the view that rishis of the Bhrigu and Angiras lineages are seers of most of that Veda's mantras. Among the Bhrigu-lineage rishis listed above, Bhrigu, Dadhyaj, and Shaunaka are clearly Atharvaveda-connected rishis; indeed, this same Shaunaka is the founder of the Atharvaveda's own Shaunaka shakha...

original p. 181

...should indeed be called Shaunaka's [tradition]. Many suktas of the Atharvaveda have Bhrigu, Gritsamada, and Shukra as their rishis; several are seen specifically by the rishi Shukra, and several more by Bhrigvangiras-lineage rishis — confirming why the Atharvaveda is called "Bhrigvangiro-veda." The source gives a dense four-column table of 33 names; several entries are visibly corrupted even in the original printing, per the author's own note below, and are transcribed here as best legible rather than corrected or omitted:

The Angirasa-Lineage Rishis — 33

Angiras, Trita, Bharadvaja-Barhaspati, Utathya, Garga, Vipra, Sankriti, Gurumita [?], Rishabha, Ambarisha, Yuvanashva, Trisadasyu, Sadasyaman, Ahaarya, Ajamidha, Kashi [?], Sushadha [?], Virupa, Kanva, Mudgala, Uttahya [?], Sharadvat, Vajashrava, Ayasya, Suvitri, Vanamedeva [?], Asija, Brihaduktha, Dirghatama, Kakshivan, and a few further names whose printing is too indistinct to render with confidence.

These thirty-two, with one further name added, make the thirty-three rishis of the Angirasa lineage. Many names among these have become corrupted in transmission, and correcting them is not something the author attempts here. Angiras, the lineage's original progenitor, must belong to a very ancient period. This lineage includes Kshatriyas such as Ambarisha and Yuvanashva — "Nabhaga Ambarisha" is referenced at many points in the Mahabharata. The Angirasa lineage is also connected to the Bhrigu lineage, and its rishis are seers for many suktas of the Atharvaveda.

The Kashyapas — 5 [6 named]

कश्यप, वत्सार, स्नैध्रुण [?], ऋष्य, असित, देवल — Kashyapa, Vatsara, Snaidhruna, Rishya, Asita, Devala. Six rishis of the Kashyapa lineage. Asita and Devala appear to have personal connections recorded in the Mahabharata.

The Atreyas — 6

अत्रि, अर्चनाना, श्यावाश्व, गविष्ठिर, आविहोत्र, पूर्वातिथि — Atri, Archanana, Shyavashva, Gavishthira, Avihotra, Purvatithi. Some textual variants may exist here — the rishi Gavishthira may also carry the name "Angira"; Rigveda Mandala 1, Sukta 101's rishi is given as Andhigu, son of Gavishthira.

The Vasishthas — 8 [7 named]

वसिष्ठ, शक्ति, पराशर, इन्द्रप्रमति, भरद्वसु, वैत्राहव्यावरुणि [?], कुण्डिन — Vasishtha, Shakti, Parashara, Indrapramati, Bharadvasu, Vaitrahavya-Varuni, Kundina. Among the Vasishthas is the rishi Parashara — father of Krishna-Dvaipayana, i.e., Veda-Vyasa himself, who holds (per the Brahma-sutra and the Mahabharata) that all the Vedas are eternal...

original p. 182

...he writes. Many modern scholars have found themselves unable to reconcile the doctrine of the Veda's eternality with Krishna-Dvaipayana's role in compiling it.

The Kaushikas (Vishvamitra) — 13

विश्वामित्र, देवरात, उद्दल (बल), मधुच्छन्द, अघमर्षण, अष्टक, लोहित, कत, कील, देवश्रवा, रेणु, पूरण, धनंजय — Vishvamitra, Devarata, Uddala/Bala, Madhuchchanda, Aghamarshana, Ashtaka, Lohita, Kata, Kila, Devashrava, Renu, Purana, Dhananjaya.

These thirteen all belong to the Vishvamitra lineage; the Matsya Purana adds two more, Shishira and Shalankayana. Many rishis appear to have carried the name "Vishvamitra," and which one founded this lineage is undetermined. One Vishvamitra, however, is especially famous: originally named Vishvaratha, son of King Gadhi, he renounced his kingdom and wealth to perform austerities and become a Brahmarshi — during which he aided King Trishanku, took the name "Vishvamitra" upon attaining Brahmarshi status, tested King Harishchandra, and famously saved Shunashepa (whom Harishchandra was leading to be sacrificed as a human offering) by teaching him a life-saving mantra, afterward adopting him as his own son. The story of Shunashepa is well known from the Aitareya Brahmana and similar texts.

The Agastyas — 3

अगस्त्य, दृढद्युम्न (दृढायु), इन्द्रबाहु (विध्माह) — Agastya, Dridhadyumna/Dridhayu, Indrabahu/Vidhmaha.

The Kshatriya Rishis — 2

वैनस्वतमनु, पुरूरवा (इलराजा) — Vainasvata-Manu, Pururava/Ilaraja.

The Vaishya Rishis — 3

भलन्दन, वत्स, संशील — Bhalandana, Vatsa, Sanshila. These three are held in especially high regard among the Vaishyas.

According to the Brahmanda Purana, the total count of these rishi-lineages differs somewhat; the Matsya Purana confirms the total of 73. The Brahmanda Purana's figure should generally be regarded as less reliable/corrupted in transmission.

These Rishis Are Not Always the First Seers

It was noted at this chapter's outset that the rishis named for a given mantra are not necessarily its very first seers. Supporting evidence:

1. A shared account appears across the Taittiriya Samhita, Maitrayani Samhita, and Aitareya Brahmana (~5.14): Manu had many sons and distributed his wealth among them, but his youngest son, Nabhanedishtha, was away studying at his guru's household. On completing his studies and returning to claim his share, he found the wealth already divided. Manu therefore directed him to a group of Angirasa rishis performing a yajna to attain heaven, whose ritual procedure contained errors — instructing him to correct their rites, for which they would reward him with their own share of wealth as dakshina. The suktas Manu taught him are the well-known Rigveda 10.61 and 10.1. Bhatta Bhaskara's Krishna-Yajus commentary references this same Brahmana episode; mantra 10.61.6 itself names "Nabha Nedishtha." The point: though these mantras predate Nabhanedishtha, because he derived special benefit from them, tradition came to regard him as their rishi.

2. The Aitareya Brahmana (5.14) and Gopatha Brahmana (1.6) suggest that Mandala 4, Sukta 14's principal mantras were first seen by Vishvamitra, and only later imparted to the wider public by Vamadeva in a subsequent generation — yet the Anukramanika names Vamadeva alone as this sukta's rishi.

3. The sukta beginning "kasya nūnam..." (~Rigveda 1.24) is assigned by the Sarvanukramani to "Ajigarti" (i.e., Shunashepa, son of Ajigarta) — the same Shunashepa taught by Vishvamitra, who used this very sukta to praise Prajapati, per the Aitareya Brahmana (~7.2–4). Yet the Ṛktantra Nirukta-samuchchaya states this mantra's rishi is Vishvamitra himself.

4. The Taittiriya Samhita and Kathaka Samhita state that Rigveda Mandala 3, Sukta 1 was seen by Vishvamitra personally — yet the Sarvanukramani names its rishi as either Gathin or Gathi.

original p. 184

For this reason, these rishis are not always the first seers of the mantras attributed to them; it should firmly be understood that the mantra-corpus continued to receive additions over time. Moreover, once particular rishis' names became well known, mantras came to be primarily used in yajnas under those names — which explains why certain rishi-attributions became prominent regardless of true origin.

The Veda's date cannot be fixed from these rishi genealogies alone. The Bhrigu- and Angirasa-lineage founders are known to have lived during the Mahabharata era, itself dated by scholars to roughly 3000 BCE — placing the Vedas, which predate these founders, at roughly 3000–2500 BCE by this reasoning. Philologists, working from the discipline of Philology, instead estimate Vedic composition at roughly 2000–1500 BCE. Which figure is historically more accurate cannot be said with confidence, and philology itself is not fully reliable for fixing chronology — but it is clear that these named rishis are not the very first, and that earlier rishis likely composed the mantras before them; Vedic mantras should accordingly be understood as existing since beginningless time, used across whatever periods they were actually current.

Rishis Who Were Seers of the Mantras' Meaning

Related to the above: a mantra's authority/origin holds special importance. It is unsurprising that one mantra came to be understood differently by different rishis across different eras — even within the same received Brahmana material, a single mantra could be applied differently by different rishis depending on context, because its meaning was understood differently by different interpreters. That "seeing" a mantra (drashtritva) and interpreting its meaning are two distinct things is shown by the following:

1. The Nirukta (~3.8) records that Shakapuni held all deities should be known; the deity of a certain sukta became established through Shakapuni's own interpretation specifically, though who first discovered that deity is unknown. Regardless, this mantra (Rigveda 1.164.46) is a single mantra whose deity the sage Ushasta explained according to his own understanding — a reading more widely known than Shakapuni's, which itself adopted this same interpretation; even so, the mantra's own origin traces to the particular teaching Ushasta received.

2. The Nirukta (7.1) states:

न ह्येषु प्रत्यक्षमस्त्यन्येषां तपसस्त्वेषाम् ॥

न ह्य् एषु प्रत्यक्षम् अस्त्य् अन्येषां तपसस् त्वेषाम् ॥ na hy eṣu pratyakṣam asty anyeṣāṃ tapasas tveṣām ||

"For among these, direct perception does not belong to others [who lack it] — rather, it comes through their own austerity (tapas)."

That is: mantras do not become directly perceivable to the ignorant or to those who have not practiced austerity — this must be the intended sense of this statement.

original p. 185

...are needed. But depending on the specific mantra, the power arising from it and who receives that power becomes clear only from context — the same mantra proving useful differently for different purposes. In this sense, distinguishing the mantra's "meaning-seer" (arthadrashta) from its mere "seer" reflects that a specific individual perceives a mantra's meaning distinctly from perceiving the mantra itself — rishis may thus be seers of a mantra's outward form without necessarily being seers of its deeper meaning.

3. The Nirukta (~10.10) states:

ऋषेर्दृष्ट्यर्थस्य प्रतिभावात्ख्यानसंयुक्ता ।

ऋषेर् दृष्ट्यर्थस्य प्रतिभावात् ख्यान-संयुक्ता । ṛṣer dṛṣṭyarthasya pratibhāvāt khyāna-saṃyuktā |

"[Narration] joined with the insight arising from the rishi's perceived meaning."

Here, the word "dṛṣṭyārthasya" establishes that the rishis directly perceived the mantra's meaning as well [as its form].

4. Vatsyayana's Kamasutra commentary (~5.1.4) states:

य एव मुक्तब्राह्मणस्य द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश्च ते खल्वितिहासपुराणस्य धर्मशास्त्रस्य चेति ।

य एव मुक्त-ब्राह्मणस्य द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश् च ते खल्व् इतिहास-पुराणस्य धर्मशास्त्रस्य चेति । ya eva mukta-brāhmaṇasya draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca te khalv itihāsa-purāṇasya dharmaśāstrasya ceti |

"Those who are indeed the seers and expounders of the [corresponding] Brahmana are also, indeed, [the seers and expounders] of Itihasa, Purana, and Dharmashastra."

And another sutra (3.2.62):

य एवास्या वेदार्थानां द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश्च त एवायुर्वेदप्रभृतीनामिति ।

य एवास्या वेदार्थानां द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश् च त एवायुर्वेद-प्रभृतीनाम् इति । ya evāsyā vedārthānāṃ draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca ta evāyurveda-prabhṛtīnām iti |

"Those who are the seers and expounders of the Veda's meanings are the very same as those of Ayurveda and similar [auxiliary] sciences."

These statements establish that rishis are both seers of the mantras and, in Brahmana form, seers of the mantras' meanings — "seers of the Brahmana" meaning those who understood the mantras' various meanings and applications.

5. The Shukla Yajurveda (ch. 8, mantra 15) reads:

ब्राह्मणमुद्वीच्यं शिक्ष्यमुच्चं स्विष्टमुच्च्मषिणा शीयम् ।

ब्राह्मणम् उद्वीच्यं शिक्ष्यम् उच्चं स्विष्टम् उच्च-ऋषिणा शीयम् । brāhmaṇam udvīcyaṃ śikṣyam uccaṃ sviṣṭam ucca-ṛṣiṇā śīyam |

(a technical liturgical phrase whose precise construction is difficult to render exactly)

Commenting on this, Uvata glosses "rishi" as "ṛṣir mantrāṇāṃ vyākhyātā" — "one who explains the mantras is a rishi."

6. The word "rishi" also occurs in the Baudhayana Dharmasutra (2.5.9.5); the commentator Govindasvami explains it as one who understands the meaning and intent of the mantras.

7. Medhatithi's commentary on the Manu-smriti (ch. 1, verse 1), glossing "maharṣayaḥ," states:

ऋषिर्वेदः । तदध्ययन-विज्ञान-तदर्थानुष्ठानातिशययोगात् पुरुषेष्वप्यृषिशब्दः ।

ऋषिर् वेदः । तद्-अध्ययन-विज्ञान-तद्-अर्थानुष्ठानातिशय-योगात् पुरुषेष्व् अप्य् ऋषि-शब्दः । ṛṣir vedaḥ | tad-adhyayana-vijñāna-tad-arthānuṣṭhānātiśaya-yogāt puruṣeṣv apy ṛṣi-śabdaḥ |

"The Veda itself is 'rishi.' Because of an exceptional connection through its study, understanding, and practice of its meaning, the word 'rishi' extends to human beings as well."

original p. 186

"Rishi" means Veda; one who studies it, understands its meaning, and practices its accompanying duties is fittingly called "rishi" too — hence both mantra-seers and mantra-meaning-seers share this title.

Many Rishis' Names Were Taken From the Veda Itself

Vishvamitra's original name was Vishvaratha; after his austerities and attainment of Brahmarshi status, he is well known to have adopted the name "Vishvamitra" from a naming-formula. Similarly, other rishis seem to have taken their names the same way — the rishi "Shiva-sankalpa" took his name from the Yajurveda's famous "Shiva-sankalpa" mantra (34.1). The Aitareya Aranyaka names Vishvamitra, Jamadagni, and others as reciters of the Pranava; the Shatapatha Brahmana connects the meaning of "Vasishtha" and similar words to the senses (indriya). The rishi of the Rigveda's Shraddha-sukta (10.151) is named "Shraddha Kamayani" — a name otherwise unattested for any individual beyond this specific context.

In several such cases, it becomes clear that rishis set aside their own personal names and instead adopted, as their names, words actually found within the Veda's own text. The Bhrigu-proclaimed Manu-smriti states the same:

सर्वेषां तु स नामानि कर्माणि च पृथक् पृथक् । वेदशब्देभ्य एवादौ पृथक् संस्थाश्च निर्ममे ॥

सर्वेषां तु स नामानि कर्माणि च पृथक् पृथक् । वेद-शब्देभ्य एवादौ पृथक् संस्थाश् च निर्ममे ॥ sarveṣāṃ tu sa nāmāni karmāṇi ca pṛthak pṛthak | veda-śabdebhya evādau pṛthak saṃsthāś ca nirmame ||

"For all [beings], He fashioned, at the very beginning, their separate names, separate deeds, and separate conditions — from the words of the Veda itself."

The Rishis and Arya-Dharma

The rishis are the original founders of Arya-dharma (Hindu dharma), having lived their lives for its sake — they are the founders of our culture. Whatever is renowned as the essence of our country's culture traces to them. When doubt arises today about matters of dharma and adharma amid social turmoil, peace can be found by studying these rishis' lives and following their path — each rishi grasped the essence of dharma and adharma and stands as an exemplar of righteous conduct, fair dealing, and truthfulness.

For this reason alone, rishis have held especially venerable status since ancient times — even great kings worshipped and honored them highly; a king who saw his daughter accepted [in marriage] by a rishi considered it a blessing for his lineage's continuation (as when King Janaka gave his daughter in marriage to a rishi's son) — many such examples appear in the Mahabharata and elsewhere, and instances of offering rishis the seat of highest honor (agra-puja) recur across thousands of contexts. When Lord Krishna went as an emissary to the Kaurava assembly in the Mahabharata's Udyoga-parva to negotiate peace, beholding that wondrous assembly hall and gazing into its heights, he spoke thus of the rishis gathered there—

original p. 187

पार्थिवीं समितिं दृष्ट्व्य ऋषयोऽभ्यागता नृप ॥ ४४ ॥ निमन्त्र्यन्तां मास्नैष्टे सत्कारेण च भूयसा । नैषां सनुपसिष्येषु शक्यं केनचिदासितुम् ॥ ४५ ॥ (Udyoga-parva, ch. 47)

pārthivīṃ samitiṃ dṛṣṭvya ṛṣayo'bhyāgatā nṛpa ॥ nimantryantāṃ māsnaiṣṭe satkāreṇa ca bhūyasā | naiṣāṃ sanupasiṣyeṣu śakyaṃ kenacid āsitum ॥

"O king, having beheld this earthly assembly, the rishis have arrived as guests. Let them be invited and welcomed with the greatest hospitality — none may remain seated without first attending to them."

They received honored hospitality; only once they were seated did Krishna and the others take their own seats. Rishis are those who have renounced everything — a distinct radiance surrounds them. Between such persons and kings among kings — who deserves greater reverence? Yet, as protectors and propagators of dharma and treasuries of knowledge, they have received honor everywhere without exception. The rishis were, in effect, the very life-breath of Aryan culture and Aryan dharma.

The Vedas Are Also Called by the Name "Rishi"

The statement "ṛṣir vedaḥ" ("rishi is Veda") rests on several authorities:

1. Bhojaraja's commentary on the Unadi-sutras (3.1.146) interprets a technical term for the office of a Dandanatha (chief officer) as meaning "Veda."

2. Haradatta's Padamanjari (on Panini) states:

ऋषिर्वेदः । तदुक्तं ऋषिका—इत्यादौ दर्शनात् ।

ṛṣir vedaḥ | tad uktaṃ ṛṣikā—ityādau darśanāt |

"'Rishi' is Veda — this is [established] because [the derivative] 'ṛṣikā' and similar forms are seen [used in this sense]."

Among Brahmins, the phrase "taducta-ṛṣikā" is used in many places meaning "as stated in the Veda" — confirming that "rishi" itself can mean "Veda."

3. The Vaijayanti-kosha lexicon similarly glosses "rishi" as usable in the sense of Veda ("ṛṣi-sṛṣṭa vede").

4. Medhatithi's Manu-bhashya likewise treats "ṛṣir vedaḥ" as an established equivalence.

5. The Shashvata-kosha states "ṛṣir vede" in a verse to the same effect — this text is thought to date to the 7th century CE, indicating this usage of "rishi" for "Veda" was current from that period onward. The Buddhist citation above is from Shantarakshita's "Tattva-sangraha," p. 47.

The Rishis and Buddhist Texts

यथोक्तं भगवता—इत्येषे आनन्द पौराणा महर्षयो वेदानां कर्तारो मन्त्राणां प्रवर्तयितारः ।

yathoktaṃ bhagavatā—ityeṣe ānanda paurāṇā maharṣayo vedānāṃ kartāro mantrāṇāṃ pravartayitāraḥ |

"As stated by the Blessed One [Buddha]: 'These, O Ananda, are the ancient great sages, the authors of the Vedas, the promulgators of the mantras.'"

original p. 188

The Blessed Buddha told Ananda that the ancient sages composed the Vedas and propagated them — so even by the Buddha's own account, rishis are credited as composers and propagators of the mantras. Though the Vedas themselves show little internal consensus on this point, it can be relied upon to this extent; among current scholars, however, this remains genuinely disputed.

The Majjhima Nikaya (~1.2.1, 1.2.9) records the Buddha addressing a young Brahmin named Bharadvaja-putra while staying at Jetavana, Shravasti:

"These present-day Brahmins' ancestors were rishis. They composed the Veda and propagated it; even now, [Brahmins] teach it following that same tradition. Brahmins count among their own ancient rishis: Ashtaka, Vamaka, Vamadeva, Vishvamitra, Jamadagni, Angira, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Bhrigu, and others."

Whether rishis existed even in the Buddha's own time is debated, but it's clear that by his era, "the ancient Brahmin ancestors were rishis" had already become a fixed formula. Rishis existed across every age — in fields like austerity and knowledge one may certainly find figures worthy of the name — but truly great rishis of this magnitude are rare in later times, and in the present era, none exist in the strict sense of "seer of mantras."

Counting forward from the Mahabharata era's ruling dynasty — Parikshit, Janamejaya, Shatanika, Ashvamedhadatta and others — their reigns spanned roughly 300 years. Toward the end, Ashvamedhadatta's son Adhisimakrishna performed a long sacrificial session (diksha-sattra). The Vayu Purana records:

असीमकृष्णे विक्रान्ते राजसूये अश्वसत्त्विषि । प्रशासति वां धर्मेण भूमिं भूमिपसत्तमे ॥ ९३ ॥ ऋषयः संशितात्मानः सत्रे वर्तस्थपरायणाः । ऋज्जयेऽनस्सजके शान्ता दान्ता जितेन्द्रियाः ॥ ९४ ॥ धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे दीर्घसत्रं त उज्जिरे । सत्याश्चीरे दृषद्वत्यां फल्ग्याः कुचिरोघसः ॥ ९५ ॥

asīmakṛṣṇe vikrānte rājasūye aśvasattviṣi | praśāsati vāṃ dharmeṇa bhūmiṃ bhūmipasattame ॥ ṛṣayaḥ saṃśitātmānaḥ satre vartasthaparāyaṇāḥ | ṛjjaye'nassajake śāntā dāntā jitendriyāḥ ॥ dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre dīrghasatraṃ ta ujjire | satyāścīre dṛṣadvatyāṃ phalgyāḥ kucirogha­saḥ ॥

(Describing King Adhisimakrishna's Rajasuya and Ashvamedha sacrifices, his righteous rule, and the disciplined, self-controlled rishis who performed a long sacrificial session at Kurukshetra, the "field of dharma," on the banks of the Sarasvati and Drishadvati rivers. A few individual words in this passage remain uncertain even at this resolution.)

Rishis existed in this king's era. The Kali Yuga is reckoned to begin from the time King Dharmaraja (Yudhishthira) departed the earth; by this reckoning, rishis can be said to have existed for roughly 400 years after that point.

original p. 189

The Rigveda has 1,028 suktas comprising 10,552 mantras (as already noted, p. 16). These have many rishis: generally all mantras within a sukta share one rishi, though occasionally a single sukta's mantras carry different rishis (a rare occurrence); the same holds for deities and meters — usually uniform within a sukta, though sometimes mixed.

Given this structure, the Rigveda's mantras can be classified three ways. First, gathering in sequence all suktas seen by a single rishi produces a group compiled either by that rishi himself, a well-known descendant, or his disciples, arranged in fixed order — such a group is called a "Mandala." The Rigveda has ten Mandalas, mostly organized by lineage: Mandala 1 mixes various lineages (hence its rishis are called "Shatarshina," since many contributed around 100 mantras each); Mandala 2 belongs to Gritsamada's lineage, 3 to Vishvamitra's, 4 to Vamadeva's, 5 to Atri's, 6 to Bharadvaja's, 7 to Vasishtha's, and 8 to Kanva-lineage rishis. Mandala 9 has many rishis but is instead named for its shared deity (Soma) rather than lineage, since most of its mantras concern Soma specifically. The current Rigveda Samhita is arranged following this rishi/lineage/Mandala sequence.

A second classification method groups suktas by their principal deity — "devata-suktas." All Agni-focused suktas form one such group, Indra-focused suktas another, and so on. Mandala 9 follows this same deity-based logic internally: every sukta in it has Pavamana Soma as its sole deity, with meter and rishi sequencing differing from the other Mandalas. This Mandala's grouping is thus not organized the way the other deity-based groupings are, and no established tradition exists for studying the whole Samhita strictly by deity-grouping across all Mandalas — though modern scholars, for convenience of study, have printed deity-organized collections (even as separate volumes).

original p. 190

There is no special benefit in arranging by the third (meter-based) method here; the traditional rishi-sequence is given priority. The rishis' names found in the Rigveda are listed below in alphabetical order, with each entry giving Mandala, Sukta, and mantra information. The reading method is explained via two example entries:

अंशोमुक् वामदेव्यः ४-१७२ [४] Aṃśomuk Vāmadevyaḥ 4-172 [4]

Here, "Amshomuk Vamadevya" is the rishi's name; "4" gives the Mandala, "172" the sukta reference, and the bracketed "[4]" the total mantras seen by this rishi in that sukta. Note: since Mandala 4 has far fewer than 172 suktas in the standard reckoning, "172" here likely refers to a cumulative or serial numbering specific to this index rather than a within-Mandala sukta count — the source doesn't clarify this further.

अकृष्णः (श्याव) मूषकाः, or मूषकाःअकृष्णः Akṛṣṇaḥ Mūṣakāḥ, or Mūṣakāḥ-Akṛṣṇvāḥ

The rishi's name may be read either way; where an entry under one form has no detail, the reader is directed to the other form. There, the mantra-details read: [8-74, 1–10, 81–40, [30]] — meaning: in Mandala 8, Sukta 74, mantras 1–10 and 81–40 (thirty mantras in total) are seen by this rishi.

अर्चनाना आत्रेयः ५-१३; ४४; ८-४३ [३०] Arcanānā Ātreyaḥ 5-13; 44; 8-43 [30]

Mandala 5, Sukta 13 (6 mantras), Sukta 44 (6 mantras), and Mandala 8, Sukta 43 (6 mantras) — thirty mantras total — are seen by this rishi.

असितः काश्यपः ९-५-२४ [१७५] Asitaḥ Kāśyapaḥ, 9-5-24 [175] — also called Kāśyapa Devalaḥ

Mandala 9, Suktas 5 through 24 — 175 mantras in total — are seen by this rishi. Using this format, any rishi's details can be looked up — whether their name occurs in the Rigveda at all, and where and how many mantras are attributed to them— This begins a substantial alphabetical index of every rishi named in the Rigveda, each with Mandala-Sukta-mantra references and total mantra-count in brackets, following the format explained on page 190. Given the density of small numerals in the original typeface, reference numbers below are transcribed as faithfully as legible, with the rishi names themselves — the primary content — given full confidence.
