Chapter Eleven — The Deities of the Rigveda

original p. 205

Among the mantras, whatever subject a given mantra primarily describes is spoken of as that mantra's deity — as already noted earlier in this chapter via the citation "yā tenoktā sā devatā" ("she who is addressed by it is the deity"). If a mantra's essential subject is Agni, its deity is Agni; deities may likewise be Indra, the Ashvin-deities, the Maruts, Savitr, Surya, Rudra, Vishnu, Vayu, and others.

A sukta of one or several mantras may share a single deity throughout; or different mantras within one sukta may carry different deities; or even a single mantra's first and second halves may address different deities, or describe multiple deities together. Generally, though, one sukta (or one mantra) having a single deity is the norm.

Agni, Indra, Varuna, the Ashvins, the Maruts, Vayu, Aditya, Ushas, Ratri, Mitra, Vishnu, Rudra, Soma, Aka [Akasha?], and others are the principal deities — Agni and Indra having by far the most suktas, with other deities considerably fewer. Within each Mandala's sukta-sequence, Agni-deity suktas generally come first, followed by Indra-deity suktas, then other deities in turn — a pattern generally followed across all Mandalas. Mandala 9 alone is an exception: every sukta there shares Pavamana Soma as its sole deity, with no other deities appearing; only the rishis and meters vary within it.

original p. 206

Among the principal deities named above, depending on context, rivers, mountains, knowledge, weapons, the thunderbolt, the sacrificial altar, the pestle and mortar, grinding-stones, and similar objects also appear as deities in certain places. In the Danastuti hymns praising a king or patron's generosity, dialogues between two speakers are likewise treated as deities in several suktas. Mandala 1 in particular contains many such minor deities.

Rishis are observed to have composed hymns of praise following certain fixed groupings: the Ashvin-deities are always praised jointly; likewise Mitra-Varuna, Soma-Surya, Indra-Varuna, Indra-Vayu, Indra-Vishnu, and Indra-Soma are frequently praised together, while other deities are praised individually.

In Rigvedic times, people worshipped these deities at home much as is still done today, and prayed to and worshipped them specifically during yajnas. Not everyone performed every ritual act described in the Rigveda — only the wealthy did. Undertaking a ritual required resources, a proper household, necessary supplies, and several assisting priests; the poor could only pray in words acknowledging their inability to perform such rites for lack of means, and a purohita who spoke modestly rather than demandingly was preferred as one's priest.

The Rigveda is filled, cover to cover, with hopeful aspiration — famously oriented toward experiencing whatever happiness life offers. The primary intent behind praying to the deities is this: freedom from worldly bondage and attainment of heaven and its higher joys are asked for, alongside longevity, prosperity, valor, and progeny — direct, worldly joys. Victory over enemies, health, freedom from want, food, and clothing appear to be life's primary aims here: These are given in the source as Kannada renderings of the mantras with their Rigveda references, rather than the Sanskrit text itself at this point.

"Agni, give strength and prosperity to me, my leader." — useful to many. (VII.5.9)

"O Indra, provide for what we lack. Give our leader the sustenance he needs, abundant valor and offspring; act mercifully; by that strength may we live long." (VII.24.6)

"May we live a hundred years." (VII.66.16)

The rishis appear motivated by experiencing life's fullness rather than any attitude of renunciation (vairagya) toward it — one searches the Rigveda largely in vain for a mantra expressing detachment from the body, life's impermanence, or similar renunciate sentiment.

original p. 207

ददात नो अमृतस्य प्रजायै (VII.57.6)

ददात नो अमृतस्य प्रजायै dadāta no amṛtasya prajāyai

"Grant us, for our progeny, [a share] of amrita (immortality)."

The precise meaning of "amrita" here is unclear, and scholars differ: the Western scholar Roth held it means "the deathless"; Grassmann took it as "long life"; Sayanacharya himself glosses it as "water." In VII.76.4–5, the rishis describe their ancestors behaving as equals alongside the deities; in VII.59, one mantra explicitly requests immortality. Only in a few such instances are matters of the hereafter (amushmika) raised at all — nowhere does a path of renunciation (viraktimarga) appear to be taught. On the whole, the Rigveda seems to hold that safeguarding worldly happiness is itself life's proper aim.

Even though Rigveda mantras are said to serve ritual purposes, they are not, like Yajurveda mantras, entirely subordinated to ritual action — they show real simplicity and poetic craft, with hymns arising from genuine feeling rather than appearing contrived.

As already noted, deities were understood to accept devotees' prayers and come to their aid — raising the question of whether these deities have a form like ours, and if so, what kind. Generally, every Rigvedic deity represents some aspect of nature that has taken on form and become an individual deity. Dawn (Ushas) was itself a source of wonder to the Vedic rishis, worthy of worship — natural phenomena of this kind came to be conceived as deities.

Even long after deity-worship began, these natural phenomena continued to inspire wonder, awe, and reverence in the rishis — who were not mere ritual technicians; worshipping embodied deities never made them forget the underlying natural phenomena. Forgetting simply wasn't in their nature.

Even Indra, Varuna, Agni, and other deities given clear form in the Vedas — and indeed all the other deities too — never became fully and completely personified beings. Reading about these deities, one can readily recognize their natural origin: which aspect of nature took this particular form. This may be called "arrested personification" — attributing form and personality only partially to what is inherently formless. To appreciate that this personification remains incomplete, comparison with other traditions helps: the Greeks similarly conceived natural forces as deities, but over time these became entirely human in behavior. Their chief deity, Zeus — the original cause of everything, foundation of all that is praiseworthy — is nonetheless also described (under the name "Jove") as fickle by nature, possessing the very flaws an ordinary person might have — complete humanization, in other words. The Vedic deities, by contrast, remain half in human-like form while the other half stays rooted in their original, foundational natural essence.

original p. 208

The qualities described for these deities generally recur across the Vedic pantheon as a whole. But some retain only lifeless/material aspects in their personification — a pillar, a chariot, and similar things — never becoming fully animated; this occurs only in limited contexts.

One further point deserves attention: Henotheism. When a particular deity is being praised, that deity alone is proclaimed supreme for the occasion — whichever deity is invoked in context receives this "foremost" treatment, shifting from deity to deity without disrespecting any other:

"The God in question, alone, is present to the mind of the singer; with him, for the time being, is associated everything that can be said of a divine being; he is the highest, the only God, before whom all others disappear, there being in this, however, no offence or depreciation of any other God." (Kaegi, p. 33)

This kind of description appears only occasionally; since every deity receives every kind of attributed quality, determining relative rank becomes difficult — though some individual, distinguishing characteristics can still be identified for each.

Deities can be grouped three ways, per Yaska: according to Nirukta-shastra, scholars declare deities to belong to earth (Agni), the mid-region/atmosphere (Vayu or Indra), and the celestial region (Surya) — other deity-names within the Veda are simply variant designations for these same three deities' functions, or else all other deity-names ultimately belong to one of these three, since each name corresponds to a specific mantra context. Yaska proceeds from here to discuss these deities' embodied forms. atha ākāra-cintanaṃ devānām

"अथ आकारचिन्तनं देवानाम्" — "Now, the Contemplation of the Deities' Forms"

Three views exist on this: (1) deities have human-like form; (2) they have no form; (3) they take shape in some particular manner not equivalent to conventional embodiment. This last, ambiguous possibility is closest to the "arrested personification" concept discussed earlier.

Before examining each deity's individual characteristics, one point should be fixed first: considerable variation exists between the Rigveda's deities and those of the much later Puranic texts — variation that developed gradually. The regard accorded certain deities in ancient Indian thought differs markedly from what later tradition gives their counterparts: some deities holding especially important places in the Vedas have no place at all in the Puranas, or, where they do retain a place, have undergone great transformation.

original p. 209

In this way, deities holding a lesser place in the Vedas gained far greater prominence in the Puranas. Among the Rigveda's principal deities — Indra, Agni, and others — their standing in the Puranas diminished considerably, with Brahma, Vishnu, and Maheshvara (Shiva) becoming foremost instead. Vishnu, given real prominence in only a few Rigveda suktas, gained far greater honor in the Puranas. Newer deities like Lakshmi, Parvati, and Kubera came to prominence in the Puranas; meanwhile, famous Vedic names — Aryama, Bhaga, Parjanya, Ushnik, and others — appear nowhere at all in the Puranas, while Savitr, Pushan, Mitra, Surya, and similar deities came to be merged and identified as one.

Among the Rigveda's deity-groups, the two most important from the outset are Agni and Indra. Indra is the enemy-slayer (Vritrahan), of limitless power and strength; Agni has somewhat fewer suktas than Indra. The name "Agni" itself recurs, with small variations, across related languages: Latin ignis, Lithuanian ugnis, Slavic (Old Church Slavonic) ognis — all meaning fire. This Agni, in the Veda, is described as a shared phenomenon spanning deity, human, and nature — among the five elements (earth, water, light/energy, air, and space), he is described in manifold forms as a kind of energy (tejas).

This Agni takes three forms: on earth, as fire; in the mid-region, as lightning; and in the celestial sphere, as the sun. Earthly fire is produced by friction, using two small sticks (called "tāyī" — VII.1.1, VII.3.9) rubbed together. Between the clouds, Indra produces Agni [as lightning], or brings it about through water. This Agni, though continuously present in offering-fires, never diminishes — though the Veda doesn't dwell on this inexhaustibility specifically, discussing instead only Agni's forms relevant to yajna and domestic use.

यो अप्स्वा स्वग्ने तपसि मदन्ती प्राच्छकार स्वतवः शचीभिः ॥ (VII.6.4)

यो अप्स्वा स्वाग्ने तपसि मदन्ती प्राच्छकार स्वतवः शचीभिः ॥ yo apsvā svāgne tapasi madantī prācchakāra svatavaḥ śacībhiḥ ||

(a technically dense verse whose precise construction is difficult to render with full confidence)

As soon as day breaks, one should perform the fire-rite to Agni and begin the day's duties — the day itself begins with fire. He is the eldest among all priests. The instant ghee is offered into the fire, Agni rises up in flame; his "teeth" (the arrangement of flames) are bright and pure, his head a form of radiant energy. He is the master (yajamana) of all — the master of the household. Shuchitanu, Tapurmurdha, Vishruti, Grihapati — he alone is the family's own priest (kula-purohita), performing every priestly function himself; he is not merely a priest, but a sage (jnani) too. the word "Kavi": VII.15.2

original p. 210

Agni acts as a mediating messenger (duta) between gods and humans, performing this duty in yajnas — one prays to Agni to summon the other deities (viśvasya devam ityakaḥ, VII.16.1).

In yajnas, Agni assists by driving away wicked influences, purifying even what is base (VII.6.3). Tradition holds that Angiras and other rishis first brought Agni down from heaven to earth, and that the deity Matarishvan first brought Agni to humankind — a story reflecting how lightning striking down from the sky gave rise to fire on earth, natural phenomena woven into human life and told in narrative/historical form.

In this way, Agni performs his role in three forms — lightning, sacrificial fire, and celestial fire — retaining individuality in each without ever becoming fully personified as human; his natural, inherent character is never forgotten entirely.

Agni's connection with water has its own legend. Building on this, the Mahabharata's Vana-parva (~ch. 224) and Shalya-parva (~ch. 48) tell a striking story: the gods, fearing danger, took Agni's ritual duty away and gave it to another; feeling insulted, Agni went and hid himself submerged in the ocean. Unable to conduct rituals without him, the gods searched and eventually discovered him hiding there; propitiating him, they persuaded him to resume his duties (X.51–52). The Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita (~2.6.3) recounts this with slight variation.

Following Agni, the next chief deity is Indra — with even more hymns dedicated to him than Agni; no other deity approaches these two in this respect. Indra pervades every aspect of nature even more thoroughly than Agni. In the Zend Avesta, Indra's name appears as "Andra," though there his status is much diminished, reduced to a demon (pishacha); yet his chief epithet, "Vritra-slayer," survives there too, as "Verethraghna."

In the Veda, Indra lacks no admirable quality. Summarized briefly: Indra was born from heaven, or from earth (VII.20.5); as soon as born, he drank Soma (VII.98.3); he is the most ancient of deities, yet ever-youthful; generous, courageous, destroyer of enemies, of infinite strength; supporter of the falling heavens; golden-armed (hiraṇyabāhuḥ, VII.34.4); his horses are yoked...

original p. 211

...his golden-horsed chariot; his weapon is the thunderbolt (vajra); none equals him in Soma-drinking, through which he becomes intoxicated and destroys the rakshasas (VII.22.1,2 & VII.29.1) — on one occasion drinking Soma poured from thirty vessels (VII.77.4), among other feats.

With Vishnu's aid, Indra defeated the demons Vritra, Ahi, Shushna, Namuchi, and Shambara — who had obstructed the waters — releasing what they had blocked (VII.99.4–5) and destroying the Asuras along with their cities. Indra is a great hero and warrior; his arms alone reduce enemies to trembling submission. He watches over humankind as a father would, forgiving human transgressions with a generous heart, punishing adharma within his purview, and destroying the Dasyus, demons, and sinners.

Three qualities stand out among Indra's attributes. First: he presides over strength and power, holding supreme authority even over Brahminical power, with essentially no restraint placed on his conduct — regarding this exalted character:

"Indra embodies so completely the human qualities of brag and bluster, gluttony, drunkenness and lust, as to make him the peg upon which to hang scepticism." (Bloomfield, Vedic Religion)

These traits — ordinary human pride, gluttony, drunken indulgence, obstinacy, and susceptibility to desire — are indeed found in his portrayal, which could give rise to skepticism regarding deities generally.

Second: Indra is the ideal of martial valor, regarded as a leader in battle; those going to war pray to him and rely on his help in destroying enemies — even foes otherwise difficult to overcome are expected to fall before his aid.

Third: the slaying of Vritrasura. A few examples on this point:

इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचं यानि चकार प्रथमानि वज्री । अहन्नहिमन्वपस्ततर्द प्र वक्षणा अभिनत्पर्वतानाम् ॥ (1.32.1)

इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचं यानि चकार प्रथमानि वज्री । अहन्न् अहिम् अन्व् अपस् ततर्द प्र वक्षणा अभिनत् पर्वतानाम् ॥ indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocaṃ yāni cakāra prathamāni vajrī | ahann ahim anv apas tatarda pra vakṣaṇā abhinat parvatānām ||

"Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, which the thunderbolt-wielder performed first: he slew the serpent (Ahi), released the flowing waters, and split open the flanks of the mountains."

Indra's heroic feats are numerous — the sukta opens by promising to relate the principal ones. A demon named Ahi had obstructed the rivers flowing from the mountains and the waters descending from the atmosphere; Indra killed him with his thunderbolt and released the waters to flow again — the same episode is retold with variation across other mantras.

original p. 212

अयोद्देव दुर्मद आ हि जज्ञे महावीरं तुविबाधस्य जीषम् । नातारीदस्य समृतिं वधानां सं रुजानः पिपिष इन्द्रशत्रुः ॥ अहास्यपृष्ठे अस्थात्स इन्द्रस्य वज्रुं धिषणौ जघान । वृष्णो वधिः प्रतिमानं बुभूषन् पुरुत्रा वृत्रो अशयद्व्यस्तः ॥ (1.32.6 & 7)

अयोध् देव दुर्मद आ हि जज्ञे महावीरं तुविबाधस्य जीषम् । नातारीद् अस्य समृतिं वधानां सं रुजानः पिपिष इन्द्रशत्रुः ॥ अहास्य पृष्ठे अस्थात् स इन्द्रस्य वज्रुं धिषणौ जघान । वृष्णो वध्रिः प्रतिमानं बुभूषन् पुरुत्रा वृत्रो अशयद् व्यस्तः ॥ ayodh deva durmada ā hi jajñe mahāvīraṃ tuvibādhasya jīṣam | nātārīd asya samṛtiṃ vadhānāṃ saṃ rujānaḥ pipiṣa indraśatruḥ || ahāsya pṛṣṭhe asthāt sa indrasya vajruṃ dhiṣaṇau jaghāna | vṛṣṇo vadhriḥ pratimānaṃ bubhūṣan purutrā vṛtro aśayad vyastaḥ ||

(Describing how the arrogant Vritra, born as a challenger to the great hero Indra, could not withstand the onslaught of his blows; broken and crushed, he continued fighting even so, but — struck down by Indra's thunderbolt while trying to match the "bull" [Indra] — lay shattered and scattered in many places. A few individual words remain uncertain at this resolution.)

The demon, proud that none could confront him, was a great hero yet consumed by arrogance, and challenged Indra to battle; unable to withstand Indra's blows, he began afflicting the weak and helpless. Indra's blows destroyed Vritra's limbs one by one, yet he kept fighting even so, until finally struck down and felled in many places.

Who is this Vritrasura? What water did he obstruct, and what water did Indra release? Such questions arise naturally, and scholars have offered many differing answers — even the Nirukta itself gives more than one interpretation.

First: the "Storm Theory" (what Westerners call the Chandamaruta-vada). Here, Vritra is a malevolent deity withholding water within the clouds; Indra, lord of the clouds or rain-deity, pierces the clouds through the storm's power, releasing rain. Accepting this requires reading "parvata" (mountain) as meaning "cloud" — attested elsewhere in the text:

य एम्बयन्ति पर्वतान् तिरः समुद्रमर्णवम् (I.19.7)

य एम्बयन्ति पर्वतान् तिरः समुद्रम् अर्णवम् ya embayanti parvatān tiraḥ samudram arṇavam

"[The waters] which flow past the mountains, through the vast, surging ocean..."

Here "parvata" is glossed precisely as "cloud" — the interpretation followed by many Western scholars. But the Vritra-episode involves further elements the theory must also explain: after slaying the demon, Indra releases the waters, creates the sun, and frees the cows — three elements a full interpretation must account for together, which the Storm Theory alone does not fully cover.

Second: the "Dawn Theory." Here, Indra himself is the Sun, destroying darkness and spreading light across the world — "go" (cow) also meaning "ray [of light]." This theory is reasonably consistent, though it leaves unclear whether the darkness destroyed is night's darkness or darkness caused by clouds.

Both theories leave room for objections. If Indra is the rain-deity, what role remains for the deity Parjanya? — this question naturally arises.

original p. 213

A third theory also exists — that of the Western scholar Hillebrandt, sometimes called the "Ice/Frost" theory. Here, Vritra is a demon who freezes and obstructs the waters during winter; Indra, acting like the sun, melts them and sets them flowing again. This theory has not gained wide acceptance either.

यः शम्बरं पर्वतेषु क्षियन्तं चत्वारिंश्यां शरद्यन्वविन्दत् । ओजायमानं यो अहिं जघान दानुं शयानं स जनास इन्द्रः ॥ (II.12.11)

यः शम्बरं पर्वतेषु क्षियन्तं चत्वारिंश्यां शरद्य् अन्वविन्दत् । ओजायमानं यो अहिं जघान दानुं शयानं स जनास इन्द्रः ॥ yaḥ śambaraṃ parvateṣu kṣiyantaṃ catvāriṃśyāṃ śarady anvavindat | ojāyamānaṃ yo ahiṃ jaghāna dānuṃ śayānaṃ sa janāsa indraḥ ||

"He who found Shambara, dwelling in the mountains, in the fortieth autumn; who slew the mighty serpent Ahi, lying prostrate along with Danu — he, O people, is Indra."

This suggests Indra found and killed a demon hidden in the mountains in "the fortieth year" — a specific timeframe raising the question: fortieth year from when? A Puranic story explains: Indra, having completed the required 100 Ashvamedha sacrifices, attained the office of Indra; around this time, the mountains still had wings, flying about at will, landing, and causing damage, until Indra cut off their wings with his thunderbolt — an event occurring shortly after he assumed his position, to which this "fortieth year" refers.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his Arctic Home in the Vedas, offers a different reading: this Indra-demon war reflects a struggle between darkness and light. In polar regions, darkness (and twilight) persists far longer than elsewhere. The "water" in this mantra, per Tilak, isn't rainfall or river-water but the vast water believed to envelop the entire world — the Puranas describe the earth as surrounded by a sphere of water, itself surrounded by air, itself surrounded by space; light and darkness arise from the sun's movement through this system, and, per Tilak, the sun and moon's movements are linked to the movement of this cosmic water-mass. The demon's obstruction of this water-mass's movement caused damage to the world beyond imagining — so Indra's slaying of the demon and restoring the water's motion was an act of tremendous benefit to the world, which is precisely why this feat is regarded as the foremost among all his heroic deeds.

Soma

Apart from Agni and Indra, Soma is the Rigveda's most celebrated deity — the entire ninth Mandala is devoted to his praise, and references to Soma recur even while praising other deities elsewhere. When inviting Indra and Agni to a rite, the poet specifically prays they come for Soma-drinking. Tradition variously describes the Soma-vine as originally existing in heaven before coming to earth; on earth, its...

original p. 214

...abode was atop mountain peaks. The Soma-creeper was pressed by stones (gravana) to extract its juice, described as sweet, honey-like in taste — its drinking bringing mental joy, bodily strength, and vigor, extensively praised by the poets. This Soma-juice itself is described as being like ambrosia (amrita).

In the Avesta, the deity "Hoama" corresponds to Soma. The Rigveda describes Soma as growing on mountains, white in color, with hard stalks — called king of the herbs/forest-plants, its juice extracted with stones, warding off disease, granting immortality, and ruling among the deities; this description recurs consistently across the text. Because Soma connects to so many different yajnas, its original, precise significance is difficult to pin down.

In a few Mandala-9 suktas, and in the Krishna Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, "Soma-nadi" is described with a consort identified with the Moon (Chandra); later Puranic tradition famously identifies Soma's consort as Uma (Parvati), and its lunar association became firmly established.

Given how much remains to be said about Soma, only a brief account is given here — a fuller discussion follows in the introduction to Mandala 9.

Having considered Agni, Indra, and Soma together, let us turn to Varuna.

Varuna

Varuna and Indra differ greatly, each holding an almost opposite disposition: where Indra presides over strength and worldly prosperity, Varuna is lord of righteous life (dharmic existence).

वृत्राण्यस्कु समिधेषु जिष्णुते वृत्रस्यस्क्ये अभि रक्षते सदा । (VII.83.9)

वृत्राण्य् अस्कु समिधेषु जिष्णुते वृत्रस्यस्क्ये अभि रक्षते सदा । vṛtrāṇy asku samidheṣu jiṣṇute vṛtrasyaskye abhi rakṣate sadā |

(A technically difficult verse contrasting Indra's and Varuna's respective roles — precise construction uncertain at this resolution.)

This mantra, addressing both deities, shows their distinction: "Indra performs the task of slaying, while Varuna performs the task of protection." Ethical integrity and truthfulness are Varuna's chief qualities; omniscience and imperviousness to deception are his as well. Because of these qualities, it is Varuna's duty to examine all sin committed in the world and punish sinners — he alone chastises those who transgress the path of dharma, the corrupt, and the wicked. (VII.65.3)

सत्यानृते अवपश्यन् जनानाम् (VII.49.3)

सत्यानृते अवपश्यन् जनानाम् satyānṛte avapaśyan janānām

"Watching over the truth and falsehood of people."

He observes people's honesty and dishonesty; his laws cannot be transgressed with impunity. Wrongdoers approach him with great humility, seeking forgiveness or compassion...

original p. 215

...offering prayers. Varuna's relationship with his devotee is compared to that of father and son — people who have sinned through ignorance beg his forgiveness as a child calls out to its father.

Many further characteristics are attributed to Varuna: he is perceptible only in the devotee's mind (VII.88.2); he possesses great power and mental steadfastness; his vision reaches far; his eye is the sun; nothing in the world escapes him; he holds Asura-like (mighty/lordly) power and māyā — a distinctive power especially associated with Kshatriyas (VII.28.4); his knowledge and awareness are without limit.

Rita (ऋत)

The word describing the ethical, righteous order Varuna presides over is "Ṛta." This word carries three distinct senses in the Rigveda.

First, it means the law of nature (prakriti-niyama) — natural phenomena proceeding in fixed, unbroken order: sunrise and sunset, day and night, occurring in unvarying sequence because of Rta. Even the deities are said to be "born of Rta" — the word carries considerable weight in compounds like ṛta-jāta, ṛta-jña, ṛta-yoni, ṛta-vayana, and others. Every daily phenomenon in the world follows this law of Rta.

Second, by the same natural principle, deity-worship, yajnas, and similar rites also follow this rule — the governing order of a properly performed yajna is likewise called "Rta." Because a yajna's many ritual acts must proceed in fixed sequence, and offerings (havis) must be properly presented to the deities, a yajna too is described as proceeding "by Rta."

Finally, by extension, the ordered regulation of each person's own daily life is also called "Rta" — the very scripture of a truthful person's existence, which everyone must follow. Whether or not one observes this is precisely where Varuna's role comes in: "Rta" means dharma, truth, and the like; its opposite means adharma, falsehood, and the like.

Varuna created heaven and earth and is the cause of their stability; he alone causes the sun to shine and the rivers to flow, and holds authority over the ocean, the wind, and similar domains (VII.86.1, VII.87.5, VII.87.6).

Some Rigveda mantras connect Varuna with the deity Mitra — and since Mitra is associated with the sun, the question arises of what Varuna's own connection is (VII.87.1). Sayanacharya's commentary on this mantra states:

अस्तं गर्भ सूर्य इव वरुण इत्यच्ये । स हि स्वगमनेन रात्रीर्जनयति ।

अस्तं गर्भ सूर्य इव वरुण इत्य् उच्यते । स हि स्वगमनेन रात्रीर् जनयति । astaṃ garbha sūrya iva varuṇa ity ucyate | sa hi svagamanena rātrīr janayati |

"'[He goes] home, like the sun — thus Varuna is spoken of.' For he, by his own setting, brings the nights into being."

original p. 216

The setting sun is itself called "Varuna" — withdrawing and thereby creating the night. For this reason, Prof. Oldenberg holds that Mitra is identified with the sun and Varuna with the moon.

Ultimately, Varuna and Mitra together receive a joint designation — "Sindhupati" (lord of rivers/waters) — a name for this jointly-presiding water-deity found in the Puranas and in Sayanacharya's own work.

In the Zoroastrian tradition (Ahura Mazda, or Ormazd), "Ahura" describes a deity whose qualities and functions match the Rigveda's Varuna closely — the Veda itself calls Varuna "Asura" (most powerful), making comparison between the two instructive.

The Greek deity Ouranos also resembles Varuna — regarded as the sky covering the earth. If "Varuna" is derived from the root vṛ ("to cover"), this fits — hence Varuna is also called by the name "Akasha" (sky/space).

Combining these two aspects, Puranic tradition came to describe Varuna as ruling the infinite, while certain earthly suktas are held to treat him as presiding specifically over the mass of waters.

The Ashvin Deities

Mandala 7's suktas 67–74 are devoted entirely to the Ashvin deities, with many further suktas praising them scattered across other Mandalas. Famous as physicians (vaidyas), and known by the name "Sarasvya" [swift-moving?], they are especially fond of Soma-drinking. They are said to arrive in a golden chariot yoked with birds, aid the suffering, and cure disease — ever ready to help directly in difficult situations. Because they are almost always praised as a joint pair, their individual distinguishing qualities receive relatively little separate attention. In the Nirukta, when asked who the Ashvins are, Yaska answers: "Some say heaven and earth; some say day and night; and some say the sun and moon" — leaving the matter genuinely open.

Many stories are told of these deities: they restored youth and long life to the rishi Chyavana, granting him worldly happiness (I.116.10); they rescued Bhujyu, son of Tugra, helplessly drowning in the ocean's depths after he prayed to them, finding him abandoned in a hopeless situation and safely bringing him to shore (I.116.5); they restored the severed leg of the rishi named Vishpala (or Rebha, per differing accounts), thrown into the water for ten days — believed connected to a sacrificial affair (satra); they gave eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, making the crooked upright. (I.116.24; I.112.8)

original p. 217

...the rishi Atrishpravadhya, thrown into a burning pit by demons, was rescued by the Ashvins, who protect such devotees (I.116.8; VI.50.10). They restored a quail's severed limb after a wolf attacked it, and restrained the quail's father from a curse; the quail then prayed to the Ashvins, who took compassion and restored its eyes (I.116.16; I.117.17). Vishpala, whose leg was severed in battle, received an iron leg from them (I.116.15); a crow whose wings were cut had them regrown by these deities (I.116.22). Many further such stories exist.

Surya (The Sun)

At night's darkest hour, moonlight fades, and at that moment the sun's approach becomes bright and powerful; rising from the depths of the vast ocean each morning, he illuminates every direction as he ascends. The youthful, beautiful-eyed imagery in the Ashvin stories above is, in some views, appropriately connected to solar characteristics.

This deity holds a very important place in the Veda, though his standing diminished considerably in later Puranic tradition, where he becomes merely the gods' physician with relatively few devotees.

Savitr, Surya, Mitra, Pushan, and Vishnu can, in a sense, be treated as a single deity under different names — though because the sun performs varied functions, each function came to be regarded as its own distinct deity.

The root of "Savitr" means: that which generates all things, gives consciousness (chaitanya) to the world, and dispels darkness. In the period just before sunrise — when darkness is dissipating but full daylight hasn't yet come — the sun is called "Savitr." Per Sayanacharya, "Savitr" names the sun specifically in this pre-dawn phase; Yaska similarly holds that when the sun has not yet risen but has become visible, it is called "Savitr."

Many suktas are devoted to Savitr, who — seated in a golden chariot — destroys people's sins and grants their desires, and who stirs and inspires the human mind. Among all Vedic mantras addressed to Savitr, the most important and significant is the Gayatri — renowned as the "mother of the Vedas."

This Gayatri is the tenth mantra of its sukta in Mandala 3, and recurs in the Samaveda (~1.2.1.9), the Shukla Yajurveda's Vajasaneyi Samhita (3.35; 22.9; 30.2 and similar places), the Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita (1.5.6.4; 4.1.11.1), and the Taittiriya Aranyaka (1.11.2). No other mantra in the Rigveda receives as much praise as the Gayatri, and it is highly praised within the Yajurveda as well.

original p. 218

Surya, wholly luminous, has Dyauh (Heaven) as father and Aditi as mother; Ushas is his sister. Golden-hued horses draw his chariot; he is steadfast and worldly, giving light to the whole world and strength to all living beings. In later Puranic texts, this deity retains only a small, ordinary place, considered subordinate to the world's greater regulating powers. Mantras dedicated specifically to Surya are relatively few in the Rigveda (III.59).

Mitra

One entire sukta is devoted to Mitra (III.59); elsewhere he is praised jointly with Varuna, without particular individual emphasis on his own glory.

Pushan

This deity knows all paths and guards travelers from dangers — thieves, wild animals, and the like. He is guardian of cattle, reuniting lost animals with their owners, and watches over all beings. He drives a goat-drawn chariot; toothless, he eats crushed food; and alone among the deities has the ability to find what is lost or hidden.

Vishnu

Relatively few mantras are dedicated to Vishnu alone — he is generally praised jointly with Indra or Agni ("Indra-Vishnu," "Agni-Vishnu"). In later Puranic tradition, Vishnu attains the highest position, some texts even granting him supreme overlordship — but in the Vedas, he holds only an ordinary place.

Vishnu is described as measuring the world in three steps — understood as measuring the earth, the atmosphere, and the sun's orb in the sky with these three forms; some read the three steps as sunrise, midday, and sunset. Later Puranic tradition elaborated this into the full story of the three worlds (heaven, earth, netherworld) oppressed by an Asura king, whereupon Vishnu, in the guise of Vamana (the dwarf), requested three paces of land from the demon-king Bali, then assumed his true form to measure the three worlds, thereby reclaiming the kingdom through this charitable pretext and subduing the Asura. Vishnu is also celebrated for aiding Indra in the Vritrasura-slaying episode; Surya, Agni, Ushas, and others are likewise associated with these events.

Vishnu carries a further name, "Shipivishta," bearing two possible senses — "improperly clothed/covered," or "possessing intense brightness." On this (VII.100.6), Tilak's Arctic Home states:

"The poet, therefore, asks Vishnu not to be ashamed of this epithet, because says he, the form indicated by the bad name is only temporarily assumed as a dark armour for the purpose of fighting the Asuras, and as it was no longer needed, Vishnu is invoked to reveal his true form to the worshipper."

original p. 219

This unfavorable form was assumed only temporarily, for defeating demons; once that task was accomplished, the form became unnecessary, hence worshippers pray for Vishnu to reveal his true form.

Sayanacharya generally explains Vishnu's name via "pervasion" (vyapti) — the root viś meaning "to enter/pervade." Another proposed etymology has been offered by Western scholarship as well. In support, the Samaveda (2.1024) states: "yasyoru viṣṇur vicakrame pṛthivyām adhi śānave" — "Vishnu, who strode across the earth."

Vishnu is credited with creating heaven and earth, and his qualities across past, present, and future are impossible to fully determine — his capability knows no limit; he pervades everything.

Ushas (Dawn)

No other deity receives mantras as sweetly and beautifully composed as those for Ushas — roughly 20 suktas across the Rigveda are dedicated to her, with Mandala 7's suktas 75–81 devoted to her entirely. "This radiant deity, granting a full life through her own light, spreads across all directions" (III.61.4).

Ushas is daughter of Dyauh (Sky) and sister of Ratri (Night); Surya is her beloved. She is mistress of the world, bringing things into being and taking form again and again, moving swiftly to dispel darkness and awaken everyone to their tasks. She wakens sleepers and, having banished darkness, brings joy to all. Born anew each time, she is called ever-youthful (yuvati), yet is also eternal — all living beings' lives depend on her. Vedic-era poets described dawn this way while never neglecting the practical vessels and implements of yajna; Ushas is prayed to, from a yajna's very outset, as protector and giver of wealth, valor, and progeny.

Per Tilak's reading, some passages describe Dawn as a daily, routine event, while others describe her as unending or continuous — evoking the dawns of polar regions, where sunrise is preceded by dawn-light persisting for many days running. Elsewhere, the following verse conveys this same idea:

तानीदहानि बहुलान्यासन् या प्राचीनमुदिता सूर्यस्य । यतः परि जार इवाचरन्त्युषो ददृश्रे न पुनर्यतीव ॥ (VII.76.3)

तानीद् अहानि बहुलान्य् आसन् या प्राचीनम् उदिता सूर्यस्य । यतः परि जार इवाचरन्त्युषो ददृश्रे न पुनर्यतीव ॥ tānīd ahāni bahulāny āsan yā prācīnam uditā sūryasya | yataḥ pari jāra ivācarantyuṣo dadṛśre na punaryatīva ||

"Those were indeed many days that passed before the sun's rising, during which Dawn was seen moving about like a lover [going to her beloved], as though she would never return again."

In this "sunrise-becoming" period, many days passed, during which Ushas moved like an infatuated young woman heading to meet her beloved — implying both a many-day gap between the horizon's reddening and actual sunrise, and that all those days were counted as belonging to a single extended "Dawn." For the words "ahāni bahulāni" ("many days") here, Sayanacharya and other scholars offer differing interpretations.

original p. 220

The philosophical tradition found in the Rigveda connects to India's much broader philosophical heritage. Our country is renowned as a land of philosophy — from ancient times, people here have fearlessly questioned life's uncertainties and pursued answers relentlessly. From royal sages like Janaka and Ajatashatru, to Yajnavalkya, Nachiketa, and other Brahmin thinkers, to Shankaracharya, Kumarila Bhatta, and various social reformers, our country has deeply engaged with the world's philosophical foundations — so it is only natural that the seeds of this enduring philosophical tendency should already appear in the Rigveda itself.

The subject of philosophy is nowhere stated with full clarity in the hymns, nor addressed directly by ordinary devotional suktas — yet, in a manner anticipating the Upanishads, philosophical inquiry does begin to surface within the Samhita, if less prominently than later. Generally, in the Rigveda, natural forces have each become distinct deities — but a single, deep divine power manifesting in many forms is also glimpsed:

एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥ (I.164.46)

एकं सद् विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्य् अग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानम् आहुः ॥ ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||

"That which is One, the wise call by many names: they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan."

That is: the wise refer to one single reality by various names — Agni, Yama, Matarishvan — implying that all deities are different forms of a single underlying deity. This sukta (1.164) more broadly touches on the five elements, historical matters, and psychological subjects too — heaven and earth, days, months and years, human birth and life-rites, the origin of life, and the workings of the world are all treated within it.

While performing yajnas and similar rites, rishis began attending closely to their practical benefits and planning accordingly — but ritual technique alone didn't satisfy their minds; curiosity about the true origin of things led them into genuine inquiry and debate. In this process, simple faith in deities embodied in human-like form began to waver, giving way to the understanding that nature and its many aspects are manifestations of one divine power taking different forms.

Questions like "Who am I? Where did I come from? How did this varied universe come into being?" seem to have persistently occupied the rishis' minds. Though the things prayed for in the Veda are largely worldly — wealth, cattle, land, progeny, and similar earthly goods — questions of life, death, and what follows death clearly occupied their thoughts as well. Because the rishis held a strong desire to continue living, they came to believe that life in the world of the deities, after death, would be eternal — giving this the name "amritatva" (deathlessness).

original p. 221

Many speculative accounts exist regarding this world's origin and beginning. In (X.121), Hiranyagarbha is named as the cause of creation; in the Purusha-sukta (X.90), the cosmic Virat-Purusha is described as the world's root cause; in another sukta, everything is said to arise from water alone.

In Mandala 10's famous Nasadiya-sukta ("nāsad āsīt..."), the pre-creation state of the universe is described as an indescribable, wondrous condition — its treatment of creation aligns remarkably with modern scientific causal reasoning, and contains philosophical perspectives fresh even by later standards.

Whatever the case, the hopeful spirit (asha) so characteristic of the Veda is uniquely its own, renowned among ancient scriptures generally.

Note: The subject of the deities has been treated only very briefly in this chapter. Going forward, wherever a specific deity's suktas come up for explanation, that deity's subject matter will be discussed as extensively and thoroughly as possible.

Chapter Twelve — Meters (Chandas)

Page 221 (continued)

Across every language, the most celebrated, elevated texts are composed in meter (chandobaddha). In Sanskrit, the Puranas, Dharmashastras, and Kavyas are all metrical works; the Vedas follow this same pattern, falling under metrical composition. Several reasons likely explain why verse became the norm from the very beginning. First: feelings naturally take the form of rhythm or meter (chandas) more readily than plain prose — meter meaning the patterned arrangement of high and low, long and short sounds. Even ordinary speech, when moved to express devotion toward the deities, took on rhythmic structure. It's well known that ancient kings composed rhythmic, clear-minded verse for the delight it brought; scholars across fields likewise preserved the ancient Vedic tradition over long periods by writing in meter and adhering to established conventions. Since metrical texts are far easier to memorize and retain than prose — a matter of common experience — the Vedas came to be composed in verse.

The Shiksha texts, discussing the defining characteristics of meter, state—

original p. 222

"छन्दः पादौ तु वेदस्य" ("Chandas is the Veda's feet")

Just as legs are necessary for a person to stand, meter (chandas) is equally necessary for the Vedas to endure, unaltered, across time.

The word "Chandas" derives from the root chad ("to please, delight" — chadi āhlādane). As already noted, the Veda's chief purpose is to please the deities and bring joy to those attending yajnas — over time, "Chandas" itself came to mean "Veda."

Because Vedic Sanskrit's grammar and meters are, from a modern standpoint, less strictly regularized than classical Sanskrit, the term "Bhāndasa" (i.e., "Chandas-style," archaic Vedic usage) came to cover all Vedic linguistic forms generally — and in more recent usage, "Bhandasa" has come to mean, simply, "irregular."

Chandas is one of the six Vedangas. Among works on the subject, Pingala's treatise is by far the most celebrated, covering not only Vedic meters but classical Sanskrit meters as well.

Vedic meters show no particularly rigid internal pattern — no fixed rule governs the placement of short or long vowels, or heavy/light syllables (guru-laghu). Only the total syllable-count distinguishes one meter from another.

The Rigveda's many suktas each contain several mantras; each mantra has two or more feet (pada) — generally three or four — and each pada carries a fixed syllable-count. Below is given the Rigveda's principal meters, their sub-varieties, and details of pada-count, syllable-count, defining rule (sutra), an example mantra, and its location:
