As already noted, apart from total syllable-count, no other rule governs these meters — but even this rule doesn't hold perfectly everywhere. Where a pada should carry a certain syllable-count, occasional variance appears — 11 where 10 is expected, or vice versa. In the verse given earlier as an example of the Pankti meter, the fourth pada in fact has only seven syllables rather than the expected eight:

रथं हिरण्ययं दर्भ (this pada) मंहिष्ठः सूरिरभूत् (this pada) वर्षिष्ठ मुक्रथश्रवः (this pada)

Whether this variance arose from carelessness on the part of the Vedic poets themselves, or from some discrepancy that crept into the text as it has come down to us, cannot be said with certainty.

original p. 230

Two opinions exist on this subject. Some hold that the Vedas, being non-human in origin (apaurusheya), faultless, and sacred, make it inappropriate to imagine any discrepancy in the received text — such readers take it upon themselves to somehow reconcile any apparent metrical irregularity wherever it appears. Others hold that acknowledging discrepancies in the received text is acceptable. Neither view should be adopted unconditionally in full; a middle path between the two is more appropriate. Deciding that every apparent metrical discrepancy must be corrected would be presumptuous; but refusing, as a blanket policy, to ever acknowledge a metrical deficiency across all mantras is, in wise persons' view, equally improper.

Scholars have agreed on the following legitimate methods for reconciling apparent metrical deficiencies:

(1) When two vowels that would ordinarily combine by sandhi occur — the preceding vowel eliding into the following — they should instead be read separately, avoiding the combination. This generally applies when i, ī, u, ū combine with a or ā, producing elision; in such cases, the elided vowel should be restored and read separately.

श्रेष्ठे अग्ग्ये दीदिहि पुरो नो (2.1.4)

श्रेष्ठे अग्ग्ये दीदिहि पुरो नो śreṣṭhe aggye dīdihi puro no

This is in the Trishtubh meter, which should carry 11 syllables per pada — but as printed, only ten appear. Therefore "śreṣṭhe" should be read (restored) as "pra iṣṭhe":

श्रेष्ठे अग्ग्ये दीदिहि पुरो नोऽजस्रया सूम्याऽयविष्ट ।

श्रेष्ठे अग्ग्ये दीदिहि पुरो नोऽजस्रया सूम्याऽयविष्ट । śreṣṭhe aggye dīdihi puro no'jasrayā sūmyā'yaviṣṭa |

Here, instead of "sūryyaḥ," it may be read (restored) as "su ūrmi ā."

(2) Where an "-aḥ" ending or an elided "-e" ending has been lost, it should be restored and read as its own separate syllable.

अग्ग्ययोऽग्ग्यिभ्यो (restored: अग्ग्ये अयो अग्ग्यिभ्यो) (2.1.4) वनस्स्त्व अव (restored: वनस्पते अव) (2.3.10)

(3) In several words, the semi-vowels "y" and "v" (where historically derived from vowels via sandhi) should be restored to their original vowel form as separate syllables.

प्रजावतीषु दुर्य्याय दुर्य (1.1.9)

restored: प्रजावतीषु दुरि आय दुर्य

(4) In some words, a long vowel, or the letters "e" and "o," should be read as two separate short vowel-sounds. Given the technical density of these sandhi-restoration examples and the resolution of the scan, a few individual syllables in the "restored" forms above carry some residual uncertainty, though the overall method and rule being illustrated in each case is clear.

ययोरसुर्य ग मक्षितं ज्येष्ठं (2.42.1)

restored: ययोरसुर्य ग मक्षितं ज्यविष्ठं

वृष्टिं परिज्ञा वातो ददातु । (2.40.9)

restored: वृष्टिं परिज्ञा वा अतो ददातु

original p. 231

(5) Some words are commonly abbreviated in recitation — for example, "śāvaka" is read as "pavaka," and "sunānaḥ" should be read as if written "svānaḥ." Many such words exist.

Not everyone accepts that these meters' defining characteristic lies in total syllable-count alone; scholars in our own country have not focused closely on this question, and opinions here vary. Western scholars, however, have pursued the matter further — examining whether any deeper rhythmic system underlies the syllable-arrangement of these mantras. It would be wrong to think the poets composed with mechanical, rule-bound precision; yet careful examination shows no single fixed method either — one context favors one meter, another avoids it, for reasons that vary. What is clear is that meaning was never subordinated to meter in these compositions — meter had to remain secondary to meaning. From this balance of meaning and rhythmic structure together, it can be said with confidence that this poetry was composed with real craft.

Prof. Arnold wrote a book titled Vedic Metre, in which he identifies four stages in the development of Vedic meter:

(1) Spontaneous composition, done in a spirit of competition with one another. Mantras from this period show considerable variation in their parts, both external and internal. Mandala 6 and the final Mandala belong mostly to this period.

(2) Free composition gradually becomes systematized and takes on fixed structure — the Gayatri and Trishtubh meters predominate here. Mandalas 3, 4, and part of Mandala 5 belong to this group.

(3) Trishtubh and Jagati meters increasingly predominate. A large portion of Mandala 1 and a small portion of Mandala 10 belong to this — the "middle period."

(4) Beyond this, the meters already mentioned continued in free use — most of Mandala 10 belongs to this final period.

Vedic poets were master craftsmen in the art of poetry — later poets do not compare to them in syllabic arrangement and rhythm. Per Prof. Arnold's own view, this developmental history explains why modern scholars have not attached great importance to the systematic use of meter [in assessing the Veda's antiquity/authorship].

Chapter Thirteen — Commentators on the Rigveda

original p. 232

Many commentators have written Rigveda commentaries (bhashya) since ancient times. Even now, modern scholars attempt to explain Vedic meaning specifically through Western-language scholarship, sometimes critiquing interpretations given in traditional-language commentaries. Ancient scholars' Sanskrit-language interpretations, along with brief biographical accounts, will be presented here as relevant.

Providing either an extremely ancient interpretation of the Vedas, or one tracing back to their very origin, has always mattered greatly to Brahmins. Over time, as Brahmins themselves grew somewhat removed from full understanding of the Vedas, and as the Veda's true meaning came to encompass ever more varied subject matter, it no longer seemed fitting that Brahmins alone should carry the honor of the commentarial tradition.

Setting Brahmins aside, the first to undertake explaining the Veda's meaning were the Niruktakaras — Yaska, author of the Nirukta. Yaska is reasonably well known even among those most familiar with ancient commentators, and subsequent commentators drew extensively on his work — though his own original text does not survive to us intact. Even so, his standing as the first commentator rests on the fact that his views and interpretations survive in fragments, drawn upon within many later commentaries. Having explained the meaning of a number of mantras in an ordered, systematic fashion, and having his own opinions preserved in this well-arranged way, calling him a Veda-commentator fits naturally — no other Vedanga author wrote so systematically. For this reason, Yaska's subject is presented in this chapter alongside the careful, ordered life-histories of the commentators who followed.

Among these commentators, those who completed a full commentary specifically on the Rigveda are rare. Sayanacharya alone produced a complete commentary — and his commentaries on all four Vedas have, to at least some degree, been made accessible to everyone; no one else has written so thoroughly. For this reason, Sayana's commentary deserves particular emphasis. Approximate period: 630 CE

1. Skandasvami

As far as currently known, the earliest Rigveda commentator is Skandasvami. Well-known later commentators drew on statements from his commentary. In the eighth Ashtaka's opening section, a verse about him occurs; the same verse recurs at the end of the fourth Ashtaka.

original p. 233

वल्लभी विनिवास्ये तावृग्गर्थागमसंश्रुतिं । भर्तृध्रुवसुतश्चैव स्कंदस्वामी यथाश्रुति ॥

वल्लभी विनिवास्ये तावृग्-गर्थागम-संश्रुतिं । भर्तृध्रुव-सुतश् चैव स्कन्दस्वामी यथाश्रुति ॥ vallabhī vinivāsye tāvṛg-garthāgama-saṃśrutiṃ | bhartṛdhruva-sutaś caiva skandasvāmī yathāśruti ||

"Residing at Vallabhi, having thoroughly learned the meaning and tradition of the Rik — the son of Bhartridhruva, Skandasvami, as tradition relates."

Skandasvami was from the Vallabhi region; his father was Bhartridhruva. His period is dated to around 630 CE, on the strength of some supporting evidence, allowing the confident statement that he composed his Rigveda commentary around that date.

Harisvami, who composed a commentary on the Shatapatha Brahmana, records in his own text:

नागस्वामी तत्र ... श्रीगुहस्वामिनन्दनः । तत्र याजी प्रमाणज्ञ आढ्यो अल्काकृतः समेधितः ॥ तन्नन्दनो हरिस्वामी प्रस्फुरद्वेदवेदिनिर्जः । त्रियावाख्यानाध्श्रीयोऽद्गीतंत्क्रो गुरोर्मुखात् ॥ युक सम्राट् कृतवान् सप्तसोमुसंस्का स्तथक्कृतिं । व्याख्यां कृत्वाध्यापयन् श्री स्कंदस्वाम्यस्ति सेवे गुरुः ॥

(A genealogical verse, difficult to render with full grammatical precision at this resolution, tracing a teacher-lineage: Nagasvami, son of Shri Guhasvami; his own accomplished son Harisvami, renowned in Vedic knowledge, who received exposition directly from his teacher's own mouth and composed further ritual texts; concluding: "Having composed and taught a commentary, I serve Shri Skandasvami as my teacher.")

That is: Harisvami was the grandson of Guhasvami, son of Nagasvami, and a disciple of Skandasvami, the Rigveda commentator. Elsewhere in the same text, Harisvami states his own date:

युदाब्दानां कलेर्जग्न्य सप्तत्रिंशच्छतानि वै । चत्वारिंशच्च मासाश्चाष्ट स्यात् तदा भाष्यमिदं कृतम् ॥

युदाब्दानां कलेर् जग्न्य सप्तत्रिंशच्-छतानि वै । चत्वारिंशच् च मासाश् चाष्ट स्यात् तदा भाष्यम् इदं कृतम् ॥ yudābdānāṃ kaler jagnya saptatriṃśac-chatāni vai | catvāriṃśac ca māsāś cāṣṭa syāt tadā bhāṣyam idaṃ kṛtam ||

"When 3,700 years of the Kali era had elapsed, along with 40 [more], and 8 months — then this commentary was composed."

That is: Harisvami composed his Shatapatha Brahmana commentary in the 3,740th year of the Kali era. By one reckoning, the Kali era began in 3102 BCE, placing this commentary's composition around 638 CE. Since Skandasvami's own commentary predates this, his period can be dated to approximately 630 CE.

Skandasvami did not write a commentary on the entire Rigveda. Among surviving manuscripts, a complete commentary exists only for the first Ashtaka; only partial commentary survives for the second through fifth Ashtakas. One manuscript notes Skandasvami's commentary concluding at the end of the fourth Ashtaka's first chapter; another notes it ending at 1.24.4. These manuscripts are held in the Trivandrum, Adyar, and Madras Government libraries, and this commentary has recently been printed in Travancore.

Skandasvami holds that the Vedas are primarily meant for use in yajnas; at the start of every sukta, he provides a verse or gloss identifying that sukta's rishi and deities. In his view, knowledge of meter (chandas) is unnecessary for understanding the Veda's meaning.

original p. 234

न छन्दः । अनुशयाज्यमानवजनत्वादिति ।

(a technical grammatical remark on why meter need not be treated as authoritative in a particular case; precise construction uncertain at this resolution)

Skandasvami cites many authorities from the Nighantu, Nirukta, and Brihaddevata, using phrases like "smaranam," "smṛti," "smaranti," "kecit" ("some say"). In the fourth Ashtaka, commenting on mantra 1.33.4's words "viśvaṃ jagat," he writes:

केचित्तु—विश्व कशब्द क स्थावरवचनक जगदित्येतेन समुच्चेयं ते स्थावरं जंगमं च बुध्यतामिति—एवं व्याचक्षते

(Explaining that some commentators take "viśva" to denote the stationary and "jagat" the moving, together comprehending both — precise wording uncertain in places.)

This makes clear that Vedic commentators existed even before Skandasvami himself.

2. Narayana

Venkata Madhava writes in his own commentary:

स्कंदस्वामी नारायण उद्गीथ इति श्री क्रमात् । चक्रुः सप्तैकवग्वाख्यं पदवाक्यार्थगोचरं ॥

(Stating that Skandasvami, Narayana, and Udgitha composed a commentary together, in due succession, covering the meaning of words and sentences.)

That is: Skandasvami, Narayana, and Udgitha together composed one Rigveda commentary. Narayana's own portion has not yet been located; a manuscript in the possession of Sham. Sambashiva Shastri contains only small portions of the fifth and seventh Ashtakas.

It is conjectured that the Samaveda commentator Madhavabhatta was Narayana's son. Madhavabhatta gives a brief self-introduction:

स्कंदस्वामिसच्चनारायणपण्डितस्य सुतश्चेति संभाव्य माधवपण्डितस्य कृतौ सामवेदव्याख्यायां...

(Identifying himself as son of the Pandit Narayana, associate of Skandasvami, in his own Samaveda commentary.)

And:

पंचाग्निना माधवेन श्रीनारायणसूनुना सनितुः परां भक्तिमालंब्य तत्प्रसादात् भाष्यं कृतम् ।

(By Madhava, maintainer of the five sacred fires, son of Shri Narayana, having relied on supreme devotion to Savitr [the Sun], through whose grace this commentary was composed.)

Madhava Pandita opens his own commentary with this invocation:

ॐ श्रीगणपतये नमः । ॐ नमः सानुवेदाय । रक्षे जुषे जन्यसत्यव्रत्ये स्थितौ प्रजानां प्रलये तमःस्पृशे । अजाय सर्गस्थितिनाशहेतवे त्रियामयाय त्रिगुणात्मने नमः ॥

(An invocation to the unborn, threefold, three-gunas-embodying deity, cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.)

This same auspicious verse also appears in Banabhatta's Kadambari. Since it's implausible that the Samaveda-commentator Madhava Pandita borrowed this verse from Bana, Madhava Pandita must predate Bana, who lived in the first half of the 7th century CE. It follows that Narayana — Skandasvami's associate and Madhava's father — lived around 600 CE, placing Skandasvami himself in this same period, as already established.

original p. 235

3. Udgitha

Skandasvami's second associate. Both Sayanacharya and Atmananda cite Udgitha's statements in their own commentaries. A manuscript of this commentary, covering Rigveda 10.3.1 through 10.43.3, is held by Bhagavaddatta of Lahore, author of Vaidika Vangmaya kā Itihāsa (History of Vedic Literature). Udgitha identifies himself at the end of each chapter with this formula:

वनवासी विनिर्गताचार्यस्य उद्गीथस्य कृतौ ऋग्वेदभाष्ये चतुष्पंचाशोऽध्यायः समाप्तः ।

वनवासी विनिर्गताचार्यस्य उद्गीथस्य कृतौ ऋग्वेदभाष्ये चतुष्पञ्चाशोऽध्यायः समाप्तः । vanavāsī vinirgatācāryasya udgīthasya kṛtau ṛgvedabhāṣye catuṣpañcāśo'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ |

"In the work of the teacher Udgitha, who came from Vanavasi [or Vallabhi], in this Rigveda commentary, the fifty-fourth chapter is concluded."

"Vanavasi" here may originally have read "Vallabhi-vinivasi" — if "vinirgata" means "having come from elsewhere and settled," this would identify Udgitha as a resident of the Vallabhi region [the same region as Skandasvami]. Like Skandasvami, Udgitha holds that the Veda serves yajna purposes, though he does not record each sukta's rishi and deity — likely expecting readers to consult the Arshanukramani directly for that. Approximate period: 800 CE

4. Hastamalaka

Hastamalaka was one of Shankaracharya's four famous disciples. The Veda-commentary attributed to this name is understood to have actually been written by a later person sharing the name — no copy of it has been found, nor has substantial supporting evidence. Approximate period: 1100–1200 CE

5. Venkata Madhava

Sayanacharya's own commentary on the rishi of 1.79.3 states that Madhavabhatta holds the mantra beginning "vi hi sotoḥ" to be Indrani's own statement — a view found in Venkata Madhava's commentary. This confirms Venkata Madhava predates Sayanacharya.

The Nighantu-commentator Devarajayajva (1450 CE) also predates Sayanacharya. In the introduction to his own Nighantu-commentary, he writes:

श्रीवेंकटाचार्यतनयस्य माधवस्य भाष्यकृतौ नानानुक्रमण्याः...सरालोचनात्...स्कंदस्वामि–भवस्वामि–गुहदेव–श्रीनिवास–माधवदेव–उवट–भट्टभास्करमिश्र–भरतस्वाम्यादि विरचितानि वेदभाष्या...निरीक्ष्य क्रियते ॥

(Devarajayajva states that his own work draws on the various Anukramanis and on the Veda-commentaries composed by Skandasvami, Bhavasvami, Guhadeva, Shrinivasa, Madhavadeva, Uvata, Bhatta Bhaskaramishra, Bharatasvami, and others, in the commentarial tradition of Madhava, son of Shri Venkatacharya.)

original p. 236

...Venkata Madhava's son Madhava, in his own Anukramani commentary, states he examined other Acharyas' commentaries before composing his own — confirming Venkata Madhava predates Devarajayajva.

Keshavasvami's Nānārthārṇavasaṃkṣepa (~1200 CE) gives an etymology of "gaulabba" based on Venkata Madhava's own authority:

दृयोःस्त्व्ये तथा ह्याड स्कंदस्वाम्यश्च भूरिशः । माधवाचार्यसूरिश्च कोऽद्येत्कृच्च भाषके ॥

(A verse invoking Skandasvami and Madhava Acharya as authorities among commentators; precise construction difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)

Venkata Madhava himself, at the end of the 8th Ashtaka's 3rd chapter, indicates his own era:

विकोनषष्ट मध्यायं व्याकरोदितिमाधवः । जगतावेकवीरस्य विषये निवसत्सुखम् ॥

विकोनषष्ट मध्यायं व्याकरोद् इतिमाधवः । जगताव् एकवीरस्य विषये निवसत् सुखम् ॥ vikonaṣaṣṭa madhyāyaṃ vyākarod itimādhavaḥ | jagatāv ekavīrasya viṣaye nivasat sukham ||

"Madhava composed this — the fifty-ninth chapter — dwelling happily in the domain of [King] Ekavira in the world."

That is: he resided in the kingdom of a king named Ekavira. Among Chola-dynasty kings, several bore the name "Vira," ruling in these periods: Regnal dates transcribed as legible; some individual digits carry residual uncertainty at this resolution.

King Reign (CE)
Virarajendra 1063–1070
Vira Chola I 1078–1079
Vira Chola II 1183–1189
Vira Chola III 1178–1201
Virarajendra (later) 1202–1233

The most recent of these, Virarajendra, ruled up to about 1233 CE — placing Venkata Madhava's own period at approximately 1200 CE.

In his Rigveda commentary, Venkata Madhava includes a few autobiographical verses identifying himself as son of Venkatacharya, a resident of a village called Gomarcha in the Chola country, contemporary with King Ekavira.

Devaraja, in his own Nighantu-commentary (at 1.14.1), cites Venkata Madhava's commentary, concluding:

इत्युक्तं (वेंकट)माधवस्य प्रथमभाष्यम् (1.14.1)

"Thus stated in (Venkata) Madhava's first commentary."

Devaraja cites Venkata Madhava's commentary at many further points in his own text — but many of these cited statements are not found in the Venkata Madhava commentary currently available. It's possible Venkata Madhava composed two separate commentaries.

original p. 237

Manuscript Copies of Venkata Madhava's First Commentary

  1. Travancore Government Library — the first Adhyaya of the first Ashtaka.
  2. Copies held by individual pundits.
  3. Madras Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (Devanagari script) — lacks the fourth Ashtaka; corrupted in places.
  4. Travancore Government Library (second copy) — only the last four Ashtakas.
  5. Mysore Government Library — from the middle of the first Ashtaka's third chapter to the end of the first Ashtaka.
  6. Travancore Government Library (third copy) — only the first and second Ashtakas.
  7. Punjab University Library, Lahore — mostly complete.
  8. Dayananda College Library, Lahore — mostly complete.
  9. Dr. Malayalamkar's private collection — of his two copies, the first contains only the eighth Ashtaka's commentary.

The Lahore-held manuscripts, though slightly incomplete, are the most complete overall. Drawing on these along with other supporting texts, Dr. Suroopa published this Venkata Madhava commentary in four parts; a copy of this edition is held at the Mysore Government Oriental Library.

The Special Features of Venkata Madhava's First Commentary

(1) This commentary generally follows the yajna-oriented tradition. Like Skandasvami's and others', it is not lengthy — quite concise, in fact. The mantra's own text is woven directly into the commentary's wording; word-derivation (padasiddhi) is not extensively explained wherever it occurs. On his own brevity, Venkata Madhava writes:

वर्जयन् शब्दविस्तरम् । शब्दैकगतिसंय्यैरिति

"Avoiding elaboration of words... by a single, direct course of expression."

That is: he states there is no wordy elaboration in this commentary, though he claims to have attempted explaining every meaning, even if only briefly.

(2) Venkata Madhava made an unusually thorough study of the Brahmana texts, evident throughout his commentary. In his own view, mere familiarity with the Brahmana texts is not, by itself, sufficient for understanding the Veda's meaning.

original p. 238

Venkata Madhava's own verse on his methodology:

अस्याभिस्त्यै मंत्राणामर्थः प्रत्येकमुच्यते । येऽज्ञाता ये च संदिग्धास्तेषां वृद्धेषु निर्णयः ॥ संहितायास्तु रीयांशं विज्ञानं तद्गुणा तनाक । निरुक्तव्याकरणयोरास्येद्वेषां परिश्रमः ॥ अथ ये ब्राह्मणार्थानां विनेकाः कृतकल्पनाः । शब्दरीतिं विजानंति ते सर्वं कथयंत्यपि ॥ ताण्डके शाट्यायनके श्रुमः शतपथ्येऽपि च । कौषीतके काठके च स्याद्यस्यैव स पंडितः ॥ ऐतरेयकनस्याकं सैप्प्रलादमथर्वणं । तृतीयं तित्तिरिप्रोक्तं जानन् वृद्ध इहोच्यते ॥ न भाळविकमस्याभिस्था वैत्रायणेयकं । ब्राह्मणं चरकाजातं च क्रतं मंक्योसबंधनम् ॥

(Explaining that mantra-meanings should be settled, where uncertain, by consulting the elders/tradition; that mastery of Nirukta and grammar alone yields only partial understanding of the Samhita; and that true scholarship requires knowledge of the Brahmana texts across many shakhas — the Tandya, Shatyayana, Shatapatha, Kaushitaka, Kathaka, Aitareya, Saipralada/Atharvana, and Taittiriya Brahmanas — while confessing no access to the Bhallavi, Vaitrayaniya, and Charaka Brahmanas.)

That is: in this commentary, each mantra's meaning is explained individually; where a meaning is unknown or doubtful, it is determined by those versed in the Brahmana texts. Among modern scholars, those skilled only in Nirukta and grammar can grasp merely a quarter of the Rik Samhita's meaning — full understanding requires mastery of the Brahmana portions and the ritual procedures (karmangas) they describe. Those versed in the Tandya, Shatyayana, Shatapatha, Kaushitaka, and Kathaka Brahmanas are called true scholars (panditas); those who further know the Aitareya, the Atharvana-Saipralada, and the Taittiriya Brahmanas are called "elders" (true authorities). Venkata Madhava admits he had no access to the Brahmana portions explaining the mantras of the Bhallavi, Vaitrayaniya, and Charaka traditions.

This confirms Venkata Madhava studied the Aitareya, Kaushitaka, Shatapatha, Taittiriya, Katha, Tandya, Shatyayana, and Saipralada Brahmanas — but not the Bhallavi, Vaitrayaniya, or Charaka Brahmanas. Beyond all these, the Shatyayana Brahmana is cited most extensively in this first commentary — worth noting that its readings closely resemble those of the Jaiminiya Brahmana.

(3) Venkata Madhava's commentary also extensively cites the Katyayana Sarvanukramani, the Nidana-sutra, the Nighantu, the Nirukta, Shaunaka, and the Brihaddevata as supporting examples. At many points he references "Nirukta" or "Yaska" generically without naming a specific passage — and generally cites the shorter/abridged recension of the Nirukta.

original p. 239

Venkata Madhava also cites the Brihaddevata extensively, generally aligning with McDonell's manuscript "A" — and at some points, his readings appear superior to McDonell's own manuscript.

(4) Venkata Madhava's treatment of Ashtaka, Adhyaya, Varga, Mandala, Sukta, and mantra divisions is not reliable enough to follow closely, and is therefore not reproduced here. His alignment of Ashtaka/Adhyaya/Varga divisions with the earlier Samhitas' rishi-positions is uncertain, and differing readings can be found within the Brahmana texts themselves. Some count the total mantras at roughly 10,000, including dvipada (two-footed) verses; counted separately, the dvipada verses number around 1,050. The Anuvakanukramani and Charanavyuha's stated totals for a shakha's full extent are, in various places, disregarded by Venkata Madhava.

(5) On matters of Yajus, Nirukta, and the root-index of the Nighantu, Venkata Madhava holds that certain material attributed to Yaska is in fact a later interpolation (prakshipta). Approximate period: 1100 CE

6. Lakshmana

Bhāvaprakāśana is a work on poetics (Alankara), authored by Sharadatanaya (~1150 CE). His father, named Lakshmana, composed a Rigveda commentary — not available to us directly, but Sharadatanaya's own text confirms his father composed a Veda-commentary:

आर्यावर्ताख्यदेशे स्थितो जनपदो महान् । मेरूत्तर इति ख्यातस्स्य दक्षिणभागतः ॥ ३ ॥ ग्रामो मातरपूज्याख्यो द्विजसाहस्रसंमितः । तत्र लक्ष्मणनावासीद्द्विजः काश्यपवंशजः ॥ ४ ॥

आर्यावर्ताख्य-देशे स्थितो जनपदो महान् । मेरूत्तर इति ख्यातस् स्य दक्षिणभागतः ॥ ग्रामो मातरपूज्याख्यो द्विजसाहस्रसंमितः । तत्र लक्ष्मणनावासीद् द्विजः काश्यपवंशजः ॥ āryāvartākhya-deśe sthito janapado mahān | merūttara iti khyātas sya dakṣiṇabhāgataḥ || grāmo mātarapūjyākhyo dvijasāhasrasaṃmitaḥ | tatra lakṣmaṇanāvāsīd dvijaḥ kāśyapavaṃśajaḥ ||

"In the land called Aryavarta lay a great region known as Meruttara, to the south of which was a village called Matarapujya, home to a thousand Brahmins. There resided Lakshmana, a Brahmin of the Kashyapa lineage."

original p. 240

त्रिंशता क्रतुभिर्विष्णुं कोशयावास वेदवित् । वेदानां भाष्यमकरोन्न्याव्या यो वेदभूषणम् ॥

त्रिंशता क्रतुभिर् विष्णुं कोशयावास वेदवित् । वेदानां भाष्यम् अकरोन् न्याव्या यो वेदभूषणम् ॥ triṃśatā kratubhir viṣṇuṃ kośayāvāsa vedavit | vedānāṃ bhāṣyam akaron nyāvyā yo vedabhūṣaṇam ||

"Through thirty sacrifices, this Veda-knower propitiated Vishnu; he, an ornament of the Veda, composed a commentary on the Vedas with proper method."

That is: in the village of Matarapujya, south of Meruttara, the eminent Brahmin Lakshmana, of the Kashyapa lineage, performed thirty yajnas, pleased Vishnu, and composed a Veda-commentary titled "Vedabhushana" ("Ornament of the Veda"). Since Sharadatanaya lived around 1150 CE, his ancestor Lakshmana can be placed some generations earlier. Approximate period: 12th century CE

7. Dhanushyajva

त्रिवेदीभाष्यकारेण धानुष्कयज्वा तु चरणशब्दस्स्वदर्शनाभिधायीति देवता विशेषस्स्वदर्शनमिति स्पष्टं व्याख्यातम् । यद्वा—महस्सत् अरवत् खवं धन्ययज्ज्ञा व्याख्यातम् । त्रयीनिष्ट विद्गेन धानुष्कयज्ज्ञा त्रिष्टि वेदभाष्येषु सप्रमाणमुपसस्त् ।

(A technical passage identifying Dhanushyajva as commentator on all three Vedas; precise construction difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)

From these statements in the Veda-acharya's Sudarshana-mimamsa, it is understood that a scholar named Dhanushyajva composed commentaries on all three Vedas and belonged to the Vaishnava tradition — though these commentaries have not been located anywhere to date. Period: 1198–1278 CE

8. Anandatirtha

Renowned as the Acharya who established the Dvaita philosophical doctrine, known by many names — Anandatirtha-Bhagavatpadacharya, Purnaprajna, Madhva. He states his own date in his own work, the Mahabharata-Tatparya-Nirnaya:

चतुस्सहस्रे त्रिशकोत्करे गते संवत्सराणां तु कलौ स्फुटिन्याम् । जातः पुनर्विप्रतनुः स भीमो दैत्यैर्निगूढं परितत्त्वमाह ॥

चतुस्सहस्रे त्रिशकोत्करे गते संवत्सराणां तु कलौ स्फुटिन्याम् । जातः पुनर् विप्रतनुः स भीमो दैत्यैर् निगूढं परितत्त्वम् आह ॥ catussahasre triśakotkare gate saṃvatsarāṇāṃ tu kalau sphuṭinyām | jātaḥ punar vipratanuḥ sa bhīmo daityair nigūḍhaṃ paritattvam āha ||

"When four thousand and some [thirty-odd] years of the Kali era had passed, in this manifest age, he — Bhima [reborn] — took form again as a Brahmin, and declared the truth that had been concealed by demons."

That is: Madhvacharya was born after 4,300 years of the Kali era had elapsed — corresponding to 1198 CE. Tradition holds he lived for 80 years within the Madhva tradition.

His commentary: composed in verse (shloka) form, covering only the Rigveda's first 40 suktas — that is, the first two chapters and a small portion of the third. Shri Raghavendra Yati, a disciple in his lineage, states in his own Mantrartha-manjari—

original p. 241

ऋक्याभागकैकोत्रसहस्रसूक्तमध्ये कानिचिच्चत्वारिंशत् सूक्तानि भगवत्पादैः...व्याख्यातानि

"Among the [1,028] suktas of the Rigveda portion, some forty suktas were explained by the Bhagavatpada [Anandatirtha]."

Every manuscript of the Madhva commentary reads "ṛgbhāṣyaṃ sampūrṇam" ("the Rig-commentary is complete") right after the 40th sukta — confirming he composed commentary for exactly 40 suktas. A devoted worshipper of Vishnu, Madhva maintains throughout his works that Vishnu alone is supreme; his commentary opens accordingly:

स पूर्णत्वप्रमाण्नं पौरुषे सूक्त ईरितः । स एवाखिलवेदार्थः सर्वशास्त्रार्थ एव च ॥

स पूर्णत्व-प्रमाण्नं पौरुषे सूक्त ईरितः । स एवाखिल-वेदार्थः सर्व-शास्त्रार्थ एव च ॥ sa pūrṇatva-pramāṇnaṃ pauruṣe sūkta īritaḥ | sa evākhila-vedārthaḥ sarva-śāstrārtha eva ca ||

"He, established by proof of his own completeness, is declared in the Purusha-sukta. He alone is the meaning of the entire Veda, and indeed the meaning of all scripture."

That is: Narayana is complete/perfect, named "Purusha" in the Purusha-sukta; that same Vishnu is expounded by every Veda, and all scriptures take him alone as their true subject.

Jayatirtha, who wrote commentarial glosses on several of Anandatirtha's texts, affirms this same view in his own Sambandha-dipika:

अतस्तेषां भगवत्पक्षप्रकारप्रदर्शनार्थं कासांचिदृचां भाष्यं करिष्यन्...प्रयोजनं च दर्शयति ।

"Therefore, in order to demonstrate the manner of the divine [Vishnu-centered] interpretation, [Madhva], about to comment on certain verses, ... also shows his purpose."

For this very reason, Madhva interprets the word "Agni" itself as meaning "Lord" Vishnu:

आह तं स्तौत्यशेषस्य पूर्वमेव हि तं प्रभुम् । ऋगर्थश्च त्रिविधो भवति । विशस्तावत्तृषिद्धाग्न्यादिरूपः । अहस्तदन्तर्गतेश्वरलक्षणः । अन्योऽध्यात्मरूपः । तत्रितयसंगृहेदं भाष्यम् ।

"He speaks of that Lord, praising him first of all. And the meaning of a Rik-verse is threefold: first, as already established in the form of Agni and other deities; second, characterized by the Ishvara [Lord] dwelling within that same form; and third, in adhyatmic [inner/spiritual] form. This commentary encompasses all three together."

That is: this teacher interprets the Veda in three ways — first, addressing deities beginning with Agni; second, describing the nature of the Supreme Self residing within Agni and the others; and third, in a purely spiritual (adhyatmic) sense. But primarily, per Anandatirtha, the Veda's ultimate subject is Vishnu.

Some special features of his commentary:

अग्रेणेत्वं यदग्निष्ट्वमित्यग्रे नाम शक्ष्णेशः । एवमेवाह भगवान् निरुक्तं बादरायणः ॥

(Explaining the word "Agni" as "the foremost, most excellent one"; this reading, he notes, is stated by Bhagavan Badarayana [Vyasa] himself in the Nirukta.)

(1) In his commentary on the very first mantra, since the very first word is "Agni," he interprets it as "the most excellent, the foremost" — a reading he attributes to Badarayana [Vyasa] himself.

original p. 242

ऋक्संहितायां स्वाध्याये निरुक्ते व्यासनिर्मिते ।

"In the Rik Samhita, in [its] recitation-study, and in the Nirukta, composed by Vyasa..."

Since Madhva repeatedly writes "this is Vyasa's own view" at various points, he must have had access to some Vyasa-authored text as a source.

(2) His works cite many "shrutis" as authorities — Paingi-shruti, Barka-shruti, Tura-shruti, Ananda-shruti, Shaushkalya-shruti, and others — though what exactly these texts are is not clearly known today.

(3) On the division of the Vedas, he records Vyasa's own view, following Puranic authority:

अनन्ताः श्च वेदानां शाखाः कर्मानुसारतः । संक्षेपं कृतवान् व्यास शिष्यश्च तदनुज्ञया ॥ अष्टकाध्यायवर्गादिभेदं च कृतवान् प्रभुः । स्वाध्यायविश्रमार्थाय तस्मात्कृत्वा विपर्ययः ॥

"The Vedas' shakhas are limitless, following [various] ritual practices; Vyasa made an abridgment, as did his disciples with his permission. The Lord [Vyasa] also created the division into Ashtaka, Adhyaya, and Varga, for the sake of providing rest-points during study."

That is: both the Veda's shakha-divisions and its Ashtaka-based divisions were made by the Divine [through Vyasa] — the abridgment following usefulness in yajnas, the Ashtaka-divisions for convenience of study. This same view appears in Venkata Madhava's commentary too:

अष्टकाध्यायविच्छेदः पुराणैर्ऋषिभिः कृतः । उद्ग्राहार्थं श्रद्धेशानामिति मन्यामहे वयम् ॥ वर्गाणामपि विच्छेद आर्ष एवेति निश्चयः । अध्ययनाय शिष्याणां विभागो वर्गशः कृतः ॥

"The division into Ashtaka and Adhyaya was made by the ancient rishis — we hold this was for aiding the faithful's retention. The Varga-division too is certainly of rishi-origin, made for students' convenience in study."

This also helps confirm Venkata Madhava's chronology relative to Anandatirtha.

Anandatirtha wrote 37 works in total, including the Mahabharata-Tatparya-Nirnaya, Bhagavata-Tatparya-Nirnaya, Gita-Tatparya-Nirnaya, Gita-Bhashya, Rig-Bhashya, and various Upanishad-Bhashyas. Scholars of the Madhva tradition collectively call these works "Sarvamula" — the foundational basis of Madhva doctrine. Later disciples and their own disciples wrote commentarial glosses (tika) and notes (tippani) on these foundational texts.

Jayatirtha's Gloss on the Madhva-Bhashya

Jayatirtha wrote glosses on Madhvacharya's Rig-Bhashya, Gita-Bhashya, and other works — earning him the renowned title "Tikacharya" (Master of Commentarial Glosses). He lived roughly 30–40 years after Madhvacharya, likely beginning to write his own works around 1303 CE.

original p. 243

On Rigveda 8.9.10's word "Vajinivati," Jayatirtha notes Madhva used it without specifying gender explicitly. On this, Narasimha's own Vivriti (explanatory sub-commentary on Jayatirtha) states:

विशेषान्नमन्नवत् क्रिया वा वाजिनीति माधवव्याख्या प्रत्युक्ता ।

"Whether 'special food,' 'food-like,' or an action called 'Vajini' — Madhava's interpretation here has been countered."

This shows that, per Narasimha, Jayatirtha is critiquing Madhava's own interpretation. On this same word, Venkata Madhava's and Sayana's readings run:

वाजिनीवति अन्नवत्त्रयाती ।

In Venkata Madhava's first commentary, this word is glossed simply as "annavatī" (possessing food) — what his interpretation says in a possible second commentary cannot be determined. If Jayatirtha's critique targets both Sayana and Madhava here, his own date would need to be placed somewhat later than otherwise assumed. Regardless, Jayatirtha's explanatory work stands as solid evidence of his own scholarly caliber.

Narasimha's Explanatory Commentary on Jayatirtha's Gloss

Narasimha's Vivriti closes noting the specific Shaka-era year in which he composed it. He is evidently a fine scholar of Vedic literature, referencing the Kashika, Nirukta, Ekaksharanamamala, Dhatuvritti, Jaiminiya Mimamsa, Nighantu, Anukramani, Anukramanikabhashya, Unadi, Unadi-vritti (Panchapadi), Amarakosha, Dhananjaya, Vishva, Vararuchi, Brahmana, Kaiyata, Abhidhana, Bhagavad Gita, Chandogya-bhashya, Nyayasudha, Ujjvaladatta (Dashapadi-vritti), and the Mahabhashya — citing the Nighantu and Unadi texts especially extensively. At one point in his text:

कर्णाटकभाषया वाड्वीति तथा महाराष्ट्रभाषया वासलेति उच्यते ।

"In the Karnataka language it is called 'vāḍvī'; likewise, in the Maharashtra language, it is called 'vāsale.'"

This suggests Narasimha resided in the border region between Karnataka and Maharashtra.

Raghavendra Yati's Mantrartha-Manjari

Raghavendra Yati is another celebrated author of the Madhva tradition, well known for his Upanishad commentaries. He also composed an independent commentary on Anandatirtha's Rig-Bhashya. In his second auspicious verse:

संग्रहिष्यामि ऋग्भाष्यश्लोकार्थान्सुगमां स्फुटम् ।

"I shall compile the meanings of the Rig-Bhashya's verses, clearly and accessibly."

In his own commentary, he cites the Shabara-bhashya, Chandrika, Aitareya-bhashya, Sutrakarantara, the Gita, Kanva-shruti, and similar works — the Mantrartha-manjari itself standing as good testimony to Raghavendra Yati's scholarly caliber and erudition.

original p. 244

Narayana's Explanatory Commentary on the Jayatirtha Gloss

Like Narasimha, another scholar named Narayana also wrote an explanatory commentary on Jayatirtha's gloss, titled Bhāvaratna-prakāśikā; a copy is held at the Baroda Library. He is recorded as a disciple of Raghavendra. Approximate period: 1300–1400 CE

9. Atmananda

For an introduction to Atmananda, commentator on the "Asya Vamasya" sukta (RV 1.164.1) embedded within the Rigveda, Max Müller offers a brief note (name only) on page 137 of his History of Ancient Sanskrit Literature. Müller's own view is that since Atmananda cites Skanda, Bhaskara, and others but never cites Sayana, Atmananda likely lived somewhat before Sayana.

Texts and Authors Cited by Atmananda

An extraordinary bibliography for a single sukta's commentary: Skandabhashya, Udgitha, Bhaskara, Shaunaka, Vedamitra, the Brihaddevata-author, the Anukramanika-author, Vishnudharmottara, Nirukta, Pushtaroktakalpa, the Bhagavad Gita, the Mahabharata, Puranas, Smritis, Padakara, Keshavacharya (a Vedanta author), Shankaracharya, Vedanki, the Upanishads, the Vishnu Purana, the Nighantu, a Sampradayajna authority, Yoga-Yajnavalkya, Vriddha-Shaunaka, a Yoga text, Shakapuni, the Pancharatra, Prashamsa, Vriddha-Manu, the author Lakshmidharacharya (Atmananda's own elder brother), Shankha, the author of the Chandrika (an Apastamba-related text), Vijnaneshvara, Atmajnana, the Yama-smriti, the Harivamsha, Sarvajna, Gadadhara, a Bhattacharya (possibly Kumarila), the Nrisimha-mantra-kalpa, the Maha-Bhagavata, Shvetashvatara, Shivadharmottara, the Yajnavalkya-smriti, the Prokta-Upanishad-parishishta, the Vasishtha-Ramayana, the Skanda Purana's Kalika-khanda, the Taittiriya texts, the Brahma-Gita, an unnamed commentator, Shaingi-shastra, the Ekaksharanighantu, the Bharadvaja-sutra, Bhoja, a Vartika-author, Dravidasvami (a disciple of Shankaracharya), the Vivarana, Vachaspati, the Mahayogashastra, the Bappruchi-Aranyaka, the Vasishtha-Vedanta-karika, the Ratnaprashna, the Bhoja-nighantu, and the Naradiya Purana — all cited within this single commentary.

Atmananda's Era

Among these names, Bhoja, Vijnaneshvara, and the Chandrika-author are especially worth examining. The Chandrika-author is Devanabhatta himself, who also composed the Apastambakanda. Per Pandit Pandurang Vaman Kane, Vijnaneshvara's era runs from roughly 1050 to 1100 CE; the Smriti-chandrika's era begins in the early 13th century.

Who exactly Atmananda's elder brother Lakshmidharacharya was cannot be determined with certainty — he is not the same Lakshmidharacharya who composed the Kalpataru (in 1153 CE)...

original p. 245

...whose father is named Bhattojaddyada, whereas Atmananda's own father is stated as Vishnu Prakashakara — confirming these are two distinct individuals. Among Vedic commentators, Atmananda cites Skanda, Udgitha, Bhaskara, and others, but never cites Sayana's examples — suggesting Atmananda lived somewhat before Sayana, most likely in the 14th century, though firmer evidence is scarce.

Manuscript Copies of Atmananda's Commentary

Only three copies have been located: one at Baroda, one at Punjab University (Lahore), and one at the India Office, London. The Baroda copy carries no date. One Lahore copy closes with:

शके १३६३ दुन्दुभिनाम संवत्सरे मासे श्रावण शुद्ध ४ भृगुवासरे ।

"In Shaka year 1363, the year named Dundubhi, month of Shravana, 4th day of the bright fortnight, on Friday."

That is, this manuscript was copied in Vikrama Shaka 1363 (~1441 CE). The India Office manuscript likewise carries no date, but per Eggeling (who catalogued the India Office texts), it was likely copied around 1600 CE.

Style

Atmananda opens his commentary:

अधियज्ञ विषयं स्कन्दादिभाष्यम् । निरुक्तमधिदैवतविषयम् । इदं तु भाष्यमध्यात्मविषयमिति । न च भिन्नविषयाणां विरोधः । अस्य भाष्यस्य मूलं विष्णुधर्मोत्तरम् ।

"Skanda's and similar commentaries treat the adhiyajna (ritual) subject; the Nirukta treats the adhidaivata (deity) subject; this present commentary treats the adhyatma (inner-self/spiritual) subject. There is no contradiction among these differing subjects. The root source of this commentary is the Vishnudharmottara."

That is: Skanda's commentary and similar works address the ritual dimension, the Nirukta the deity-dimension, and Atmananda's own commentary the spiritual dimension — with the Vishnudharmottara as its foundational source.

Atmananda was an Advaitin, following Shankara's philosophy, and the spirit of Advaita surfaces throughout his commentary. His treatment of one famous Rigveda mantra illustrates this well:

इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुरथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् । एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥ (RV 1.164.46)

इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणम् अग्निम् आहुर् अथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् । एकं सद् विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्य् अग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानम् आहुः ॥ indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān | ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||

"They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; and also that divine, well-winged Garutman. That which is One, the wise call by many names — they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan."

original p. 246

That all the Vedas' meaning rests in the Supreme Self alone is what this mantra's commentary conveys; when glossing individual words like "Agni," Atmananda selects only those senses through which knowledge of the Supreme Self arises.

Beyond this, whichever Kalpa-text Atmananda cites at the close of each mantra-commentary likewise clearly states this same spiritual meaning — a text some centuries older than Atmananda himself, identifiable as the "Pushtaroktakalpa." Though not found within the printed Vishnudharmottara, it may well be a portion of that same work. Its relevant statement:

इन्द्रादिशब्दो गुणयोगतो वा वृत्त्युक्तिगो वापि परेशमाहुः । विप्रास्स्यदेकं बहुधा वदन्ति प्राज्ञास्त्व नानापि सदेकमाहुः ॥

"The words beginning with 'Indra,' whether through connection with qualities or through their etymological function, refer to the Supreme Lord. The learned speak of this One in many ways; the truly wise, though speaking of many, declare it to be one single reality."

This confirms Atmananda's commentary is not without foundation — this same spiritual reading of the Veda was clearly current well before his time.

Authorities Drawn from Shakapurni

Atmananda's citations from Shakapurni are worth examining. On RV 1.164.14:

चक्रं जगच्चक्रं भ्रमतीति वा चरतीति वा करोतीति वा चक्रं इति शाकपूणिः ॥

"'Chakra' [wheel] — the world's wheel — [meaning] 'that which revolves,' 'that which moves,' or 'that which acts' — is 'chakra' — thus Shakapurni."

And on mantra 40:

उदकं—इति सुखनामेति शाकपूणिः ।

"'Udaka' [water] means 'happiness/well-being' — thus Shakapurni."

The first is drawn from Shakapurni's Nirukti, the second from a Nighantu — confirming Atmananda had read Shakapurni's Nirukta directly. His scholarship shines through his commentary throughout. Period: 1315–1387 CE

10. Sayana

Among Vedic commentators, Sayanacharya holds an especially venerable position. His vast study, exceptional familiarity with the Vedas, and scholarship across many disciplines are all evident from his Vedic literary output — his Veda-commentary stands as the clearest testament to his extraordinary caliber.

His commentaries on the Vedas' Samhitas and Brahmanas are not only exceptionally excellent and clear but also correctly reveal the subtle truths hidden within the vast body of Vedic material...

original p. 247

...clarifying the subtle truths concealed in Vedic material in a fully accessible way — an immense service. Even accounting for all the earlier commentators, their works aren't fully available to us today, with only some names known; where Vedic commentaries do survive, they typically cover only a small, abridged portion. Among all who received honor for composing Veda-commentaries, Sayana's own achievement stands foremost. His own celebrated fellow-commentators were his brothers — ministers to the Vijayanagara kings, who protected the Vedic commentarial tradition and composed many excellent texts, achieving leading positions in scholarship. Owing to circumstance, this great man's biography has not come down to us in full detail — even so, we present here, with what help is available, a summary of the main points of his life.

Sayana was born into a well-known Brahmin family in South India, of the Bharadvaja gotra. His father was named Mayana, his mother Shrimati. His family specialized in interpreting the Krishna Yajurveda — hence Sayana first wrote a commentary on the Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita before turning to the Rigveda. He had an elder brother, Madhavacharya, and a younger brother, Bhoganatha.

Madhavacharya served as minister to the Vijayanagara kings, and was a great authority in Dharmashastra, Purva-Mimamsa philosophy, and many other disciplines. Harihara and Bukka, founders of the Vijayanagara kingdom, relied on these ministers in matters of state. The city of Vijayanagara was renowned for its beautiful architecture, trade-derived wealth, and prosperity — celebrated among leading historians as especially famous for these qualities during this period.

Madhavacharya is credited with many works, though not all attributions are fully certain; several, however, are well-established:

(1) Parashara-smriti-vyakhya — known as Parashara-Madhava, a very large text. (2) Kalanirnaya (or Kalamadhava). (3) Jaimini-nyayamala — an authoritative commentary on the sage Jaimini's Purva-Mimamsa philosophy. (4) Jivanmukti-viveka — a Vedanta text discussing liberation-while-living. (5) Sarvadarshanasangraha — a famous Advaita-Vedanta text. (6) Vaiyasika-nyayamala — a commentary explaining the Vedanta-sutras.

original p. 248

...composed with the aid of his teacher's own brother, Bharati-tirtha.

Whether this Madhavacharya and the famed monk Vidyaranya were one and the same person, or two distinct individuals, remains genuinely debated. Some scholars firmly hold they are identical; others find this doubtful without offering a strong counter-case. Most of the works discussed here are attributed to Madhavacharya, and it is well-established that Madhavacharya, minister to Vijayanagara's founding kings, holds the central historical role — a question examined in detail by Sriman Hastavakal Krishnamachari's article in Indian Historical Quarterly (Vol. VI, pp. 701–717), which weighs the evidence on whether "Madhavacharya" and "Vidyaranya" name one figure or two across his ministerial and later monastic careers.

Inscriptions describe him as "Upaniṣan-mārga-pravartanācārya" (the teacher who established the path of the Upanishads) and as a great hero who drove Muslim settlers out of a place called Kokai and administered the Goa and Banavasi regions.

Per Kane's History of Dharmasastra (p. 374), Vidyaranya was an extraordinary scholar and statesman who served as a pillar of support during Vijayanagara's founding days, before embracing sannyasa in old age, renouncing all worldly ties, and spending his remaining years in meditation — a guide across many spheres of life whose biography still inspires many today.

The third brother, Bhoganatha, though less famous than the other two, was every bit their worthy sibling. He served as a close companion-minister (narma-sachiva) to Sangama II, son of Kampana — confirmed by that king's Bitragunta inscription:

इति भोगनाथसुधियो संगमभूपालनर्मसचिवेन । श्रीशंकपुरसम्मद्ब्ये शासनपत्रेषु विलिखितं श्लोकाः ॥ (Epigraphia Indica, Vol. III, p. 23)

"These verses were composed by the learned Bhoganatha, companion-minister to King Sangama, and inscribed upon the charters at Shri Shankapura."

While Sayana and Madhava excelled in the Veda, Vedanta, Mimamsa, and Dharmashastra, Bhoganatha was a poet of the first rank — attested by the many works Sayanacharya cites from him in his own Alankara-sudhanidhi, and by the verse-form Bitragunta inscription itself. Sayana cites from six of Bhoganatha's works in total.

original p. 249

Bhoganatha's Six Works

  1. Ramollasa — a poetic work in praise of the Ramayana.
  2. Tripuravijaya — describing Shiva's destruction of Tripura.
  3. Udaharanamala — a collection of example verses for Sanskrit poetics (alankara) texts, all praised even by Sayanacharya himself.
  4. Mahaganapatistava — a hymn to Ganapati.
  5. Shringaramanjari — on the erotic/romantic sentiment (shringara).
  6. Gaurinathashtaka — an eight-verse hymn to Gaurinatha (Shiva).

Sayanacharya held these works in special regard, once writing that examples of poetic ornamentation should be drawn directly from them:

तेषामुदाहरणानि भोगनाथकाव्येषु दृश्यानि ।

"Their examples are to be found in Bhoganatha's own poetic works."

As evidence of his exceptional poetic skill, here are verses he composed praising his patron, Lord Sangama:

यस्य दृष्ट्य विमुद्ध युद्ध यांरसा वार्थ् नामभिमतानुबन्धिनि । हन्त नूनमनुयान्ति सस्यं कर्णिळ्ळ तरुकामधेनः ॥ ८ ॥ युद्य शिप्रसरणेन भू यसाप्प दने युष्टिपरं जगत्रयी । अश्व शे विफलतां न चन्द्रमाः केवलं कुमुदिनीविकासनात् ॥

(Verses in praise of King Sangama; the dense poetic compounds are difficult to render with full grammatical precision at this resolution, but their overall register is clearly one of elaborate courtly praise.)

Based on texts and inscriptions, it becomes clear that Sayanacharya was connected to four successive Vijayanagara kings — Kampana, Sangama II, Bukka I, and Harihara II — the brothers holding the position of minister and serving the empire throughout all four reigns.

Kampana was the second son of Sangama I — younger brother of Harihara, the empire's founder — and ruled the kingdom's eastern provinces, likely corresponding to today's Nellore and Kadapa districts. For Kampana's son Sangama II, the brothers governed efficiently during his childhood and ensured his excellent education; once he came of age, they handed him the kingdom and moved to serve at the court of his uncle Bukka I (1350–1379), continuing as ministers into the reign of his son Harihara II (1379–1399), assisting each king in turn.

That a scholar who composed commentaries on all four Vedas possessed extraordinary learning is only natural — but that this same man was also an exceptional warrior, wielding a sword in battle with real valor, is genuinely astonishing to consider. These were not merely deeply immersed Mimamsakas skilled at explaining difficult Vedic mantras — they were capable administrators of a great kingdom, and mighty warriors who themselves entered the battlefield. Immense scholarship combined with worldly shrewdness and sound judgment...

original p. 250

...mental strength, divine grace, scholarship, and heroism all combined in them. Alongside his lord Sangama, Sayana personally led an army to capture the Chola kingdom's Kampana region and the fortress town of the Kondavidu chief (Indian Antiquary, 1916, p. 23). The Alankara-sudhanidhi describes his valor:

जगद्गीर्यस्य जागर्ति कृपाणः सायणप्रभोः । किमित्येते वृथाटोपा गर्जन्ति परिसंस्थिनः ॥

"The sword of Lord Sayana, of world-renowned fame, stays ever vigilant — why then do these surrounding forces roar with such empty bluster?"

He showed extraordinary administrative skill as well. When Kampana died, his son Sangama was still an infant, so the full weight of governance fell on Sayana — reflected in this verse describing the prosperity that followed under his stewardship:

सत्यं मुखं भवति शासति सायणार्ये संस्प्राप्तभोगसुखिने सकलाश्च लोकाः ।

"It is truly said: when the noble Sayana governs, all peoples come to enjoy prosperity and happiness."

His domestic life was equally blessed — he had three sons: Kampana (a lover and practitioner of music), Mayana (a skilled poet in both Sanskrit verse and prose — R. Narasimhacharya, Ind. Ant. 1916, p. 20, identifies him with the "Madhava" who compiled the Sarvadarshana-sangraha, which if true implies deep knowledge of every theistic and atheistic school of Vedanta), and Singana (expert in the Veda, especially its Krama and Jata recitation methods, embodying all the qualities of a true Brahmin that Sayanacharya himself describes at the close of his Shatapatha Brahmana commentary).

According to Some Scholars (Dr. Aufrecht's Catalogus Catalogorum, p. 711)

Sayana passed away in 1387 CE, during Harihara II's reign — placing him at the height of his career in the second half of the 14th century.

Sayanacharya's Works

Among his works, the commentaries on the Vedic Samhitas and Brahmanas are by far the most important — sufficient testimony alone to his scholarly depth. But Sayana wrote more than these commentaries; many further texts are attributed to him, or appear scattered across reference catalogues. Many of these attributions cannot be accepted as genuine — on grounds of style and treatment of subject matter, it's clear that ordinary scholars composed some of these and their works simply became attached to Sayana's famous name by reputation. The texts listed below, however, can confidently be called genuinely his on every count, and their own internal colophons support this same conclusion.

original p. 251

As statesmen occupied with political affairs, the brothers must have composed their works on Dharmashastra, grammar, and poetics only in their spare time — and having enjoyed Vijayanagara royal patronage, they produced several important and scholarly works across disciplines. Below, so far as it can be determined, is the list of these texts in their likely order of composition.

1. Subhashitasudhanidhi — a compilation of wise verses (subhashitas) drawn from many texts; apparently his first work, composed while serving as minister to King Kampana, per the closing colophon:

इति पूर्वपक्ष्विन समुद्याश्वीश्वरारिराय विशाल श्री कंपश्राज महाप्रधान—भेरद्वाजंवशमुक्तक—मायणकरत्नाकर सुधाकर—माधवाळ्वतरुसहोदर—श्री सायणाचार्य विरचिते सुभाषितसुधानिधौ—

(A dense colophon-style compound describing Sayanacharya as chief minister to the illustrious King Kampana, an ornament of the Bharadvaja lineage, and brother of the eminent Madhava; precise word-by-word parsing is difficult at this resolution given the density of the compound.)

2. Prayashchittasudhanidhi (also called Karmavipaka) — a text on atonement rites (prayashchitta), a major branch of Dharmashastra.

3. Dhatuvritti — known as the Madhaviya Dhatuvritti, an authoritative treatment of every Sanskrit verb root (dhatu) found in Panini's Dhatupatha; named in tribute to his elder brother Madhavacharya, to whom Sayana expresses deep devotion in the text.

4. Alankarasudhanidhi — a Sanskrit poetics text distinguished by an unusual feature: rather than drawing its illustrative verses (udaharana-shlokas) from generic subject matter — typically devotional or panegyric — as is customary, Sayana draws his examples from events in his own and his brothers' lives, making this text a valuable biographical source in its own right.

The next three texts — Prayashchittasudhanidhi, Dhatuvritti, and Alankarasudhanidhi — are confirmed, by their own closing verses, to have been composed during the reign of Sangama II:

At the opening of the Prayashchittasudhanidhi:

तस्य (सङ्गमस्य) मन्त्रिशिरोरत्नमस्ति मायणसायणः ।

"His (Sangama's) crown-jewel among ministers is Sayana, son of Mayana."

original p. 252

श्रेण मायणपुत्रेण सायणेन मुनीषिणा । ग्रन्थः कर्मविपाकाख्यः क्रियते करुणावता ॥

"By the eminent, wise Sayana, son of Mayana, compassionate as he is, this text called Karma-vipaka is composed."

In the Dhatuvritti:

अस्ति श्रीसंगमक्ष्मापः स्पृद्धीतलपुरन्दरः । तस्य मन्त्रिशिरोरत्नमस्ति मायणसायणः ॥

"There is King Sangama, Indra himself upon earth. His crown-jewel among ministers is Sayana, son of Mayana."

At the end of the Alankarasudhanidhi:

इति...श्रीमत्संगमराजसकलराज्यधुरन्धरस्य सकलविद्यानिदानभूतस्य भोगनाथाग्रजस्य श्रीमत्सायणाचार्यस्य कृतावलंकारसुधानिधौ ॥

"Thus [ends] the Alankarasudhanidhi composed by the illustrious Sayanacharya — elder brother of Bhoganatha, foundation of all learning, and bearer of the entire administrative burden of King Sangama's realm."

5. Purushartha-sudhanidhi — a text of Puranic verses on the four aims of human life (purushartha), composed at the command of his new patron King Bukka, after Sayana handed the kingdom over to Sangama and moved to Bukka's court — likely the first work he composed there, before beginning the Veda-commentaries.

6. The Veda-Bhashyas — discussed further below.

7. Ayurveda-sudhanidhi — an Ayurvedic text, also referenced in the Alankarasudhanidhi:

आयुर्वेदसुधानिधिव्यसनिभिः श्रीसायणार्योदितं भैषज्यम् ।

"The medicinal remedy stated by Shri Sayanacharya, devoted to the Ayurveda-sudhanidhi."

8. Yajnatantrasudhanidhi — a text on yajnas and related rites. These last two texts were composed during the reign of Harihara II, Bukka's son, a king with great personal faith in Vedic ritual practice who gave it considerable encouragement, as their opening verses attest.

The Veda-Commentaries

These commentaries showcase Sayanacharya's unparalleled scholarship — his genius shines through here more than in any of his other works, earning them a permanent place in Sanskrit literature and standing as the foremost of everything he wrote. The opening verses of the Taittiriya Samhita commentary reveal something remarkable: King Bukka first asked his own guru, Madhavacharya, to compose the Veda-commentaries. But Madhavacharya, weighed down by his responsibilities, did not personally undertake the task — instead directing his own younger brother Sayanacharya to compose them, while himself remaining a guide and source of encouragement throughout rather than stepping away entirely. In gratitude for his elder brother's guidance, Sayana named the commentaries "Madhaviya" (of/belonging to Madhava).

original p. 253

Sayanacharya wrote commentaries for these Samhitas:

  1. Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya-shakha Samhita
  2. Rigveda Samhita
  3. Samaveda Samhita
  4. Shukla Yajurveda's Kanva Samhita
  5. Atharvaveda Samhita

He also commented on the Brahmana and Aranyaka texts belonging to these Samhitas — though his Shatapatha Brahmana commentary appears more hurriedly composed than the rest, having been written, as its own opening states, at the very end of his life.

A. Krishna Yajurveda 1. Taittiriya Brahmana 2. Taittiriya Aranyaka and Upanishads

B. Rigveda 1. Aitareya Brahmana 2. Aitareya Aranyaka

C. Samaveda 1. Tandya (Panchavimsha) Brahmana 2. Shadvimsha Brahmana 3. Samavidhana Brahmana 4. Arsheya Brahmana 5. Devatadhyaya Brahmana 6. Upanishad Brahmana 7. Samhitopanishad Brahmana 8. Vamsha Brahmana

D. Shukla Yajurveda 1. Shatapatha Brahmana

Per this list, Sayanacharya composed his Krishna Yajurveda commentary first, before turning to the other Vedas. Yet the Rigveda is established, on many grounds, as foremost among the four Vedas — the root source of Sanskrit itself and the most ancient of the four. If one asks why Sayana did not begin with the Rigveda commentary instead, he answers this himself at the opening of his Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika (introduction): the Vedas' primary use is in yajnas, and whatever yajna is performed, its central officiant is the Adhvaryu priest — who, taking up a given form of the sacrifice, enacts/describes it (this is the sense of "yajñasya mātrāṃ vimimīte," "he measures out the yajna's form"). What he must follow is the Yajus [Yajurveda]...

original p. 254

...the Veda he must know first is the Yajurveda — so Sayana composed that commentary first, taking up the Rigveda only afterward. His own family tradition was Yajurvedic besides, making this a natural order for him as well.

The Introductions (Bhumikas) to the Veda-Commentaries

Sayanacharya wrote a separate introduction for each Veda-commentary — themselves significant works, discussing many important topics connected to the Veda.

The Taittiriya-bhashya's introduction covers the Veda's defining characteristics, its authority, and briefly its status as a valid means of knowledge; the two branches of Veda-commentary (connected to the four purusharthas, and connected to the origin of Brahma-knowledge); and the divisions of yajnas — explaining what elements every yajna requires and what elements are specific to particular rites.

The Rigveda-bhashya's introduction is the most useful of all — tracing the interpretive tradition from its very beginning and establishing his own doctrine, addressing objections raised about studying the Vedangas point by point with full reasoning, and drawing on Jaimini's Purva-Mimamsa logic wherever relevant to offer systematic, well-argued resolutions. It covers the Veda's defining characteristics, its self-authenticating nature (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) independent of human authorship, the Vedanga tradition, and the divisions of Veda and Brahmana — explaining the Veda's purpose and showing how each Vedanga discipline illuminates its meaning.

The Samaveda-bhashya's introduction discusses Veda-characteristics along with Sama-chanting (samagana) and its manner of performance in detail, again drawing on Purva-Mimamsa material to settle the main questions surrounding Sama-singing.

The Kanva-Samhita (Shukla Yajurveda) bhashya's introduction briefly discusses that Veda's own portions, explains the intended meaning of the injunction "svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ" ("one's own Vedic recitation should be studied"), and gathers together the main subjects of the Shukla Yajurveda's chapters.

The Atharvaveda-bhashya's introduction covers, on Puranic authority, the Atharvaveda's exceptional usefulness and necessity for kings' priests (rajapurohitas) and Brahmins alike; studying the Veda grants knowledge of mantra-meaning, and the introduction also covers the Veda's own authority (pramanya) and the determination of word-meanings.

original p. 255

Across all these introductions, the topics fall into two broad groups: elements common to all the Vedas, and elements specific to a single Veda.

Common elements include: mantra and Brahmana together defining the Veda (whatever is not mantra is Brahmana); the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheyatva) and eternality (nitya-vada), with refutation of opposing views; that the Veda carries genuine meaning rather than being mere sound to recite; the distinctions among Rik, Yajus, and Sama; and the Veda's own two-fold division — one Kanda describing ritual action (karma), the other describing the path to Brahma-knowledge and its attainment — meaning that dharma and Brahman together constitute the Veda's subject matter, and knowledge of these its ultimate purpose.

Veda-specific elements include, for instance: discussion of the completeness of the philosophical schools, praise for the effort of Vedic exegesis, an introduction to the Vedangas, and (for the Shukla Yajurveda) a brief survey of its 40 chapters.

The Commentator Sayanacharya

The Vedas are extremely ancient texts, and even the commentaries that survive to us show considerable variation. Garbled statements, ambiguous usages, and words without fixed convention are woven throughout the Veda from the start — so anyone wishing to understand it correctly must, above all, be thoroughly grounded in the traditional Vedic scholarly disciplines, embodied in the six Vedangas: Shiksha, Vyakarana, Chandas, Nirukta, Jyotisha, and Kalpa.

  • Shiksha — explains the correct method of Vedic recitation and pronunciation.
  • Vyakarana (grammar) — based on word-formation, aids in understanding even subtle usages.
  • Chandas (meter) — identifies the meters of the mantras.
  • Nirukta — clearly explains distinctly Vedic-specific usages.
  • Jyotisha (astronomy/astrology) — helps determine the correct timing for yajnas.
  • Kalpa — explains the procedure for performing yajnas and related rites.

Beyond these six, the Purana, Itihasa, Dharmashastra, and the Anukramani texts are called Upangas (subsidiary limbs) of the Veda, and are likewise essential. For determining the precise meaning of mantras, the Mimamsa-shastra is absolutely indispensable — thorough study of all these is required before undertaking Vedic commentary. Mimamsa itself divides into Purva- and Uttara-Mimamsa, both ultimately serving the same goal: properly explaining the Veda's meaning.

original p. 256

"पूर्वोत्तरमीमांसयोर्वेदार्थोपयोगे गौतिस्स्व एव"

(A heading affirming that both Purva- and Uttara-Mimamsa serve the purpose of determining the Veda's meaning.)

As evidence of Mimamsa's usefulness, the introductions establish the Veda's defining characteristics, its non-human origin, its self-authenticating validity, and the principle that injunctive statements carry genuine meaning (not mere recitation) — all through the Mimamsa-sutras directly.

Sayanacharya himself mastered all these disciplines thoroughly before undertaking his commentary, and with the express intention that anyone seeking to understand the Veda should first grasp these same foundations, he discusses each of them extensively in his introductions.

Sayanacharya and Modern Scholars

Sayanacharya's commentaries prove immensely useful not only to those studying the Veda traditionally, but to modern scholars as well. Those comparing Philology and Mythology to uncover Vedic meaning also find valuable material in his commentary. Sayanacharya determined word-meanings following Nirukta and grammatical principles wherever possible, and relied on his own independent judgment wherever those disciplines fell short — material of genuine interest to anyone pursuing deeper philosophical truth. Even in matters of accent and pronunciation, he made full use of grammatical science, and his treatment of the deities likewise contains much of value.

Moreover, it can fairly be said that no other commentary comprehensively explains the Vedic mantras the way Sayana's does. Others may have composed Vedic commentaries before him — some still survive — but no one else appears to have undertaken commentary on all four Vedas together with their associated Brahmanas and Aranyakas.

For modern scholars researching the special elements hidden within the vast body of Vedic material, understanding the traditionally received meaning remains essential — the very foundation-stone for their work. No other text presents this traditional interpretation as clearly and completely as Sayana's commentary. However far modern scholarship advances, it must remain grateful to Sayana — no building stands without a foundation, and Sayana's commentaries occupy exactly that place. It is impossible to imagine what state Vedic scholarship would be in today without them. The Western scholar Prof. Wilson, who translated the Veda into English, expressed this same view, writing as follows—

original p. 257

"He (Sayana) undoubtedly had a knowledge of his text far beyond the pretensions of any European Scholar, and must have been in possession, either through his own learning, or that of his assistants, of all the interpretations which had been perpetuated by traditional teaching from the early times."

This concludes the discussion of Sayanacharya's biography; the remaining commentators follow. Approximate period: 1500 CE

11. Ravana

Known to have written commentaries for both the Rigveda and Yajurveda (edited in part by Edward Hall); only a small portion of the Rigveda commentary has been published. His sectarian affiliation is unknown, but the work belongs to the Vedanta tradition, written in a simple, clear style — Atmananda's commentary resembles it somewhat, and cites it in a few places.

Dating: Suryapandita, author of the Paramarthaprabha commentary on the Gitavali (called the Lilavati-tikeya), quotes the Ravana Rigveda commentary; Suryapandita's own work is dated to roughly 1450 CE, per its own colophon — suggesting Ravana's Bahvrichaka commentary was composed roughly 400 years before that.

Some scholars hold that "Ravana" is simply another name for Sayanacharya himself, not a distinct person — this is incorrect, as becomes clear from a direct comparison of the two texts' own stated aims:

सायणभाष्यकार्य राध्यै विशाखाप्रायेण बाह्य संग्रानुविषयो दर्शितः । रावणभाष्ये तु अध्यात्म्यीत्याभ्यंतरसंग्रानुविषयो दर्शितः उपटीपाख्ये तोभयनुस...

(Distinguishing Sayana's commentary, which shows the exoteric/ritual meaning, from Ravana's commentary, which shows the inner/spiritual (adhyatmic) meaning, with a related sub-commentary combining both; precise construction difficult at this resolution.)

His other texts:

Yajurveda-bhashya — not available. Rigveda-padapatha — not found complete; only its first Ashtaka survives, held at the Dayananda Mahavidyalaya library, Lahore. This text differs in small ways from Shakalya's own Padapatha. Approximate period: 1515–1543 CE

12. Mudgala

Nothing is reliably known of his background — no solid evidence exists, and he never mentions his own circumstances anywhere in his text. In one copy of his commentary, held at the India Office...

original p. 258

...one manuscript is held at the India Office, another at the Bodleian; neither is complete — one Bodleian copy has only the first Ashtaka, while another (in London) has four or five Ashtakas. A note connects this to a printed edition attributed to a "Lakshminarayana," though no solid basis for this has been established; based on the manuscript evidence, however, this copy can be placed roughly within the same century as Sayana.

Mudgala uses grammatical terminology extensively throughout, generally conducting his own analysis within that framework, though his commentary appears to cover only the essential, summarized portions rather than full detail:

आरोच्च पूर्वभाष्यं च बध्चिचस्य समन्ततः । गहनं मन्यमानेन सुबोधेन समुद्धृतम् ॥ नवशीतं युग्णाश्चीरात् शिककायाश्चांजनम् । तथा समुद्धृतं सारं प्राशिनां बोधसिद्धये ॥ मौद्गल्यगोत्रेण च मुद्गलेन प्राक्तनभूतेन सुसंस्कृतेन । युथार्थभूतेन सुसाधकेन समुद्धृतं सारमिदं वरिष्ठम् ॥

(Mudgala, of the Maudgalya gotra, describes having examined the earlier [Sayana] commentary in full, found it profound and dense, and extracted its essence in accessible form for students' understanding — precise word-by-word construction is difficult at this resolution, but the overall claim is clear.)

An example of his commentary style, on the opening mantra (RV 1.1.1):

हे अग्ने ! त्वां देवं दीप्यमानं हविष्पंको होमद्रव्यसमेत मर्तासो मर्त्य ईळते । अहं च जातनेदसं जातं वेदो धनं यस्मासौ जातवेदा तमेविधं त्वां त्वां मन्ये सौमि । स त्वं हेड्य हप्यवाकसाधनानि हवींषि आनुषक् निरन्तरतयानुसक्रं यथा तथा वक्षि वहसि ॥

(A worked example of Mudgala's commentary style on the Rigveda's opening mantra, glossing "jātavedasam" as "one whose wealth is knowledge" and explaining the offering-bearing role of Agni; precise phrase-by-phrase construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)

His commentary can fairly be called a summary of Sayana's, closely following it — though a discernible method governs his condensation, as this example on a single mantra shows. This page opens mid-passage with a lengthy worked commentary example — likely continuing the discussion of a commentator introduced on the preceding, untranscribed portion — followed by two dense Sanskrit citation blocks whose precise phrase-by-phrase construction is difficult to render with confidence at this resolution, discussing matters of ritual purpose, deities, and heroic/kingly imagery in a technical exegetical register. The discussion then turns to the following named commentators:

original p. 259

14. Devasvami

His commentary itself is not available, but its existence is well confirmed through citations. He also composed commentaries on the Ashvalayana Grihyasutra and Shrautasutra — a separate Rigveda commentary from him seems less certain.

In Vimalabodha's commentary on the Mahabharata:

मया भोजजन्ये जराचार्य शेवस्वामिवेदनिष्टु—विप्राडनुवाकार्थस युर्च लोचनेनायमार्गः कृतः ।

(Citing Devasvami's Vedic Nighantu as a source; precise construction uncertain at this resolution.)

That Devasvami composed an introduction to the Mahabharata has not otherwise been recorded — so the text Vimalabodha references here must be his Rigveda commentary instead.

His period is not definitively known. General sources record that Acharya Devasvami composed an abridged Mimamsa-commentary, apparently based on the Shabara-bhashya. If this is the same Devasvami as the Rigveda commentator, he would predate the Vikrama era.

15. Bhattabhaskara

His commentary has not been located anywhere, though he is known to have composed a commentary on the Taittiriya Brahmana; he is also said to have written a Rigveda commentary.

16. Uvata

One manuscript, in a context explaining an obscure word's meaning, cites "Uvata" as its authority — on this basis, it can be conjectured that Uvata too composed a Rigveda commentary. (Dr. Raj's article, read at the Fifth Oriental Conference, p. 261)

original p. 260

But since this same citation also occurs in a Yajurveda commentary, whether Uvata composed a genuine Rigveda commentary remains genuinely ambiguous.

Katyayana's Sarvanukramani also has its own commentary (author unspecified), reasonably substantial in scope — and though formally a commentary on the Anukramani rather than the Rigveda text itself, it explains matters connected to Rigveda interpretation so extensively that it may fairly be counted as a Rigveda commentary in its own right.

17. Haradatta

Composed a commentary on the Ashvalayana-mantra-shiksha text (manuscripts survive at Mysore, Madras, and Trivandrum); Devarajayajva's own Nighantu-bhashya cites Haradatta's commentary at several points. He also composed:

  1. Rikagni-kanda-vyakhya
  2. Apastamba-Grihyasutra-vyakhya — titled Anakula
  3. Apastamba-Dharmasutra-vyakhya — titled Ujjvala
  4. Ashvalayana-Grihyasutra-vyakhya — titled Anavila
  5. Gautama-Dharmasutra-vyakhya — titled Mitakshara

The commentators discussed above are the principal ones. It is understood that many further commentators existed beyond these, but since their commentaries and related works cannot be located, their details are not covered here. Modern vernacular-language attempts at Vedic interpretation — such as those written in Hindi and other regional languages by scholars like Dayananda Sarasvati — have not gained full recognition among Vedic scholars, and given their comparatively lesser standing, there is no felt need to detail them here.
