"This mantra, the Atharvaveda's opening verse, is stated according to the Pippalada [recension]. Its deity is Varuna, its meter Gayatri. Here, where [other recensions] read 'śaṃ no bhavantu' ('may they be auspicious to us'), this one instead reads 'āpo bhavantu' ('may the waters be...')."

Besides this Chandogya-mantra commentary, this author also composed a Mantrabrahmana-bhashya and a Paraskara-Grihya-bhashya. Period: 1315–1387 CE

Chapter Fourteen — Commentators on the Atharvaveda

1. Sayana

The Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda all have many surviving commentaries — but Atharvaveda commentaries are exceedingly rare. Only Sayana's commentary survives today, and even that covers only the first four sections (khandas), preserved in a very fragile manuscript, published with great effort by Pandit Pandurangashastri.

वाच्याय वेदत्रितयमामुष्मिकफलप्रदम् । ऐहिकामुष्मिकफलं चतुर्थं व्याचिकीर्षति ॥

वाच्याय वेद-त्रितयम् आमुष्मिक-फल-प्रदम् । ऐहिकामुष्मिक-फलं चतुर्थं व्याचिकीर्षति ॥ vācyāya veda-tritayam āmuṣmika-phala-pradam | aihikāmuṣmika-phalaṃ caturthaṃ vyācikīrṣati ||

"Having expounded the three Vedas that grant results in the hereafter, he now intends to expound the fourth, which grants results both in this world and the next."

That is: having composed commentaries on the three Vedas granting other-worldly fruits, Sayana now turns to the Atharvaveda, which grants both worldly and other-worldly results.

अत एकर्चादीनामृषीणां विंशतिसंख्यकत्वात् वेदोऽयं विंशतिकाण्डात्मक संस्थः ।

"Since the rishis, beginning with those of the single-verse [hymns], number twenty, this Veda is accordingly structured into twenty Kandas."

That is: because this Veda has twenty rishis (starting with the one-verse hymn's rishi), it is divided into twenty Kandas.

The commentary's introduction covers many Atharva-specific topics:

अथर्ववेदस्य नवभेदा भवन्ति । तद्यथा पैप्पलादास्तौदाः शौनकीया जाजला जलदा ब्रह्मवदा देवदर्शाश्चारणवैद्याश्चेति ॥

"The Atharvaveda has nine divisions: Paippalada, Tauda, Shaunakiya, Jajala, Jalada, Brahmavada, Devadarsha, and Charanavaidya."

That is: the Atharvaveda's nine branches are the Paippaladas, Taudas, Maudas, Shaunakiyas, Jajalas, Jaladas, Brahmavadas, Devadarshas, and Charanavaidyas. Connected to the Atharvaveda are five Kalpa-texts: Nakshatrakalpa, Vaitanakalpa, Samhitakalpa, Angirasa, and Shantikalpa — of which the Kaushika and Vaitana Kalpas served as the main sources for this commentary.

This commentary is understood to survive in complete form at Gwalior. The chapter number on this page is not fully legible at this resolution — likely "fifteen," continuing the sequence after Chapter 14 on Atharvaveda commentators — but is noted here with appropriate caution rather than asserted with false confidence.

Chapter Fifteen — Authors of the Padapatha

original p. 285

Having now discussed the subtle particulars of many Veda-commentators, let us turn to introducing the authors of the Padapatha — the word-by-word (as opposed to continuously euphonically-combined) recitation text of the Vedic Samhitas.

The Padapatha of the Vedic Samhitas is extremely ancient. Whether the Padapatha predates the Samhita, or the Samhita itself is the original form from which the Padapatha was derived, remains genuinely disputed among scholars — but it is undisputed that knowledge of the Padapatha is immensely helpful to any commentator. Among Sanskrit-literary circles, scholars characteristically incline toward their own preferred interpretation, or follow established convention, when explaining a word's components — offering varying explanations for a single word's multiple meanings, and for compound words (samasa) and their meanings, in differing ways, as a long-established custom. Because many rishis' differing opinions on word-meanings, and the Veda's own special/varying senses, have caused genuine doubt since ancient times, rishis in many early periods composed word-division (padavibhaga) texts for the Veda. Commentators on Vedic words must accordingly feel free to attempt various interpretations according to their own capacity — this need not be a source of hesitation. For this reason, even among the Samhitas' extremely ancient Padapathas, whatever variation exists is understood to have arisen from the very beginning in this same way. The rishis held that variation in pronunciation or accent (svara) — whether in the Vedangas or in matters of intonation — is a serious matter, and accordingly composed the Veda's own Padapatha, following each shakha's specific method, as an integral practice woven into many shakhas and their sub-branches — alongside each Veda's Shiksha-texts (phonetic manuals) and Pratishakhyas. With the help of these texts, the tradition of Vedic study has remained firmly established, variations in Padapatha included.

Padapathas exist only for the Samhitas — the Brahmana, Aranyaka, and other Vedic portions have none, since no tradition of studying their Padapatha specifically developed. Commentaries themselves differ only slightly from the Padapathas — from a commentary, a mantra's intended meaning becomes known, but understanding that meaning requires word-division (padaccheda) first; and knowing a word's grammatical nature, its suffixes, and its compound-formations likewise requires the Padapatha. Padapathas are thus extremely ancient relative to the Vedas and extremely important — practically an integral part of the Veda itself — and of immense help to commentators.

original p. 286

Anyone wishing to understand the Vedas must study all the Padapathas. In contexts where a single word carries different meanings, differing methods of word-division, shakha-specific variant forms, or meaning-based distinctions all prove useful — all understood through the Padapathas. While one established order governs the sequence of word-division and accent-arrangement, applying these according to one's own intellectual capacity for one's own purposes need not surprise Vedic researchers.

Modern linguistic scholars, however, argue that the Padapathas contain many faults — an argument that, on closer examination, traces mostly to some scholars raising unnecessary criticism without having grasped certain finer points. Linguistics is, after all, a relatively young discipline, whereas the Padapatha-authors were traditional scholars well versed across grammar, meter, Kalpa, and related disciplines. Understanding these Padapathas therefore remains extremely necessary for every Vedic scholar.

1. Authors of the Rigveda Padapatha

1. Shakalya

The Brahmanda Purana (earlier section, ch. 63) gives these verses:

शाकल्यः प्रथमस्तेषां तस्मादन्यो रथीतरः । बाष्कलश्च भरद्वाज इति शाखाप्रवर्तकाः ॥ देवमित्रस्तु शाकल्यो ज्ञानाहंकारगर्वितः । जनकस्य स यज्ञे वै विनाशमगमद्द्विजः ॥

"Shakalya was the first among them; besides him, Rathitara; and Bashkala and Bharadvaja — these were the shakha-founders. Devamitra's [son] Shakalya, proud with the arrogance of his knowledge, met his downfall at King Janaka's yajna, this twice-born one."

And elsewhere:

देवमित्रश्च शाकल्यो महात्मा द्विजपुङ्गवः । चकार संहिताः पञ्च बुद्धिमान् वेदवित्तमः ॥

"Devamitra's Shakalya, the great-souled, foremost of the twice-born, wise, and most learned in the Veda, composed five Samhitas."

(The Vayu Purana's parallel verse, ch. 60.86, reads "padavittamaḥ" — "most learned in words" — in place of "vedavittamaḥ.") Shakalya, Rathitara, Bashkali, and Bharadvaja were shakha-founders; among them, tradition holds that Devamitra Shakalya, arrogant with the pride of his knowledge, engaged Yajnavalkya in debate at King Janaka's assembly-hall and, having been defeated, suffered public disgrace.

Devamitra Shakalya was deeply learned in the Vedas and founded five Samhitas (or shakhas). He is also known by three further names: Vidagdha Shakalya, Devamitra Shakalya, and Sthavira Shakalya.

original p. 287

This Shakalya is mentioned in both the Nirukta and the Brihaddevata. Keith and other Western scholars hold that Shakalya lived roughly 600–700 years [before a given reference point] — an opinion without solid basis. Taking the Puranic accounts above as the basis instead places his era within the Mahabharata period, roughly 3000 BCE.

The Rigveda's Padapatha was printed in Bombay in 1861 CE, and Max Müller and other scholars generally follow it — though not perfectly; a few places show differences between the Nirukta's own Shakalya-Padapatha and this printed edition. Whose authorship the currently available Sarvanukramani-sukta's Padapatha belongs to cannot presently be determined.

2. Ravana

Ravana composed both a Rigveda commentary and a separate Padapatha — though Shakalya's Padapatha remains far more ancient and authoritative. Ravana's Padapatha closes with a detailed date:

इति सप्तमाष्टकेत्पनोध्यायः ॥ इति रावणकृतपदसप्तमाष्टकः समाप्तिमगात् । सप्तमाष्टकस्य वर्ग अष्टचत्वारिंशदुत्तरं शतद्वयं (248) परिधाव्यब्दे (1524) दुर्मति शके (1644) वर्षे आषाढे मासि कृष्णसप्तम्योदश्यां भृगुवासरे आर्द्रानक्षत्रे दर्शनयोगे शर्वार्यां महापीणे भास्करक्ष्यात्मजरिणा लिखितं कर्कस्थयो रविबुधयोः सिंहस्थे केतौ च मिथुनस्थे शुक्रे विस्वानस्थे मन्दे कुम्भस्थयो राहु-मंगलयोर्मिथुनस्थे चन्द्रमसि ॥

(A detailed colophon giving the completion date of Ravana's seventh Ashtaka Padapatha — Shaka/Vikrama year references, the month of Ashadha, a specific lunar day, weekday, and nakshatra, along with the precise planetary positions at the time of writing. Individual numerals and a few technical terms carry some uncertainty at this resolution, but the overall nature of the colophon — a full astronomical dating — is clear.)

This manuscript copy is roughly 400 years old. Differences exist here and there between Shakalya's and Ravana's Padapathas — for instance, in RV 10.144.1's "kuhakasya," Shakalya's reading divides it into two words ("kuha kasya"), while Ravana's treats it as a single word. Ravana's Padapatha has not gained any particular prominence.

2. Authors of the Yajurveda Padapatha

The name of the Madhyandina Samhita's Padapatha-author is not yet known.

Page 296 (concluding the Padapatha chapter)

नावगृष्ठम् । यथा शाकल्येन अधिवासं इति नावगृहीतम् । आत्रेयेण तु अध्यवासं इत्यवगृहीतम् । तस्मादवग्रहोऽनवग्रह इति ॥ (Skandasvami's Nirukta-bhashya, 3.13)

Padapatha-authors' opinions vary widely — on prefixes (upasargas) as much as on avagraha marking. Shakalya does not mark "adhivāsam" with avagraha; Atreya marks the corresponding word as "adhyavāsam." Such disagreements recur throughout the Padapatha tradition.

Chapter Seventeen — Ancient Efforts in Investigating the Meaning of the Veda

In this chapter, we examine what kinds of efforts the ancients made toward understanding the Veda's meaning, and what texts from these efforts survive today.

The Brahmanas, themselves a portion of the Veda, already engage in explaining meaning — the very first such attempt. Their primary aim, however, was not to explain mantra-meaning as such, but to describe the significance of yajna-related rites, establishing the special connection between mantras and their corresponding ritual actions. They sometimes explain a mantra's meaning in general terms, or occasionally gloss specific words. Collected together, such incidental explanations would form a substantial body of material — yet even so, a great many words and sentences remain without any explained meaning.

Though the well-known Sarvanukramani is available to us today, proper interpretation of the Veda depends primarily on Yaska's Nirukta — no other surviving text has been found to serve this purpose as thoroughly, though even the Nirukta does not fully resolve every difficulty in understanding the Veda's meaning.

The single most important text aimed specifically at explaining the Veda's meaning is Yaska's Nirukta. No earlier text serving this same purpose has been found to have survived; but this text too, in relation to the Vedas...

original p. 297

...bears no relation to chronology at all. Yaska sometimes glosses words in a specifically Vedic sense, and sometimes in the sense of Sanskrit as then commonly spoken — and occasionally applies both senses to the very same word. For example:

इवेति भाषायां च अन्वध्यायं च । अग्निरिवेन्द्र, इनेति । नेति प्रतिषेधार्थीयो भाषायाम् । उभयमन्वध्यायम् ।

"'Iva' [like] is used both in ordinary Bhasha and in the Vedic recitation (Anvadhyaya) — as in 'Agnir iva Indra.' 'Na' carries a negating sense in Bhasha; both senses [negation and comparison] occur in the Anvadhyaya."

That is: "iva" carries the same sense in ordinary Bhasha (the term used for the Sanskrit of Kavyas and similar literature) as in the Veda — "agnir iva" means "like Agni." But "na," which negates in ordinary Bhasha, carries both negation and comparison in the Veda: in "na vindhe asya suṣṭutam," it negates; in "dyaur ṇa pratinākavaḥ," "dyaur ṇa" means "like the sky." Citing both senses side by side this way confirms that, in Yaska's own time, both forms of Sanskrit were current.

In the Nirukta's introduction, Yaska also addresses an objection concerning Vedic interpretation itself: that if the Vedas have no coherent meaning, composing commentary on them serves no purpose. The objection cites substandard sentences, mutually contradictory statements, needless repetition of already-known meanings, and words with no discernible meaning — concluding that Vedic mantras are meaningless and any commentary on them futile. Yaska addresses each such objection with examples and a reasoned answer in his traditional introduction — not necessary to detail further here.

This argument settles one important point: even in Yaska's own time, the Veda was not in common circulation among ordinary people, and its language was not easily understood generally.

Two further considerations from the Nirukta confirm this. If the Veda were already understood by people, what need would there be for a lexicon (shabdakosha) at all? And why would the Nirukta repeatedly perform etymological derivation (rūpa-vṛkṣa-vṛtti — tracing which root a word-form derives from and how) on words, citing other commentators' interpretations before arguing for his own? If the words were already familiar, such effort to establish their meaning would be unnecessary. Yaska appears to lean on grammar as his main aid in proposing meanings — inherited tradition does not seem to have helped him much, suggesting that tradition itself was already fading by his time. A considerable gap must therefore separate the Veda's own era from Yaska's.

original p. 298

...even having examined all these elements, Yaska never claims his own interpretation is definitively correct — nor should one assume the Nirukta's help alone suffices for grasping the Veda's true meaning.

At one point, the Nirukta reveals just how far earlier interpreters had gone on a given question — for instance, regarding the word "Vritra" (what creature is it? what color?):

ततक्यो वृत्रः । मेघो इति स्थैराक्याः । त्वाष्ट्रोऽसुर इत्यैत्याहासिकाः ।...अपां च ज्योतिषश्च मिश्रभावकर्मणो वर्ष कर्म जायते । तत्र उपमार्थेन युद्धवर्ण भवन्ति । अहिनवत्तु खलु मन्त्रवर्ण ब्राह्मणवादाश्च । विवृद्धशरीरस्य स्रोतांसि निवारयांचकार । तस्मिन् हके प्रसस्संदिरे आपः ।

(Recounting multiple rival views on Vritra's identity — cloud, the demon son of Tvashtri, or a serpent of the Vedas/Brahmanas — and the rain-producing mixture of waters and light behind the "battle" imagery; precise phrase-level construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)

That is: the Niruktakara school holds Vritra to be a cloud; Puranic writers hold him to be Tvashtri's demon son; still others call him a serpent of the Vedas and Brahmanas — Yaska records all these competing views. This shows that the Nirukta doesn't determine word-meanings from grammar alone, but from historical/traditional considerations too. Toward the text's end, answering what qualifies someone as a rishi, Yaska states that whoever reaches a conclusion through sound reasoning is equal to a rishi — praising a logically well-established statement as carrying the same value as a rishi's own utterance.

In the Vedic era, everything proceeded on the strength of faith — one might even call it unquestioning faith — and mantras were accepted as authoritative on that basis alone. But by Yaska's own time, faith and belief alone no longer sufficed to convince people; full conviction required a well-reasoned, logically sound case. This is precisely why Yaska found it necessary to support his own claims with grammar and with the corroborating statements of earlier scholars.

Panini's grammar is generally concerned with classical Bhasha (contemporary speech) rather than the Veda — whatever Vedic word-forms it does describe are recorded merely as exceptions to Bhasha's general forms, limiting its usefulness for understanding Vedic meaning directly.

Shankaracharya generally wrote commentaries on the Upanishads — but even there, only on the major ones — with no proper commentary on the Samhita itself; his Upanishad commentaries occasionally touch on individual mantras in passing.

Even though the Purva-Mimamsa-shastra's stated purpose is to establish the Veda's meaning, examining the text from beginning to end reveals not specific Vedic meanings but rather the method by which the Veda should be interpreted — laying out many interpretive rules rather than glossing mantras directly...

original p. 299

श्रुतिलिङ्ग वाक्यप्रकरणस्थानसमाख्यानां समवाये पारदौर्बल्यमर्थविप्रकर्षादिति ॥

"Among Shruti (direct statement), Linga (indicator), Vakya (syntax), Prakarana (context), Sthana (order), and Samakhya (name/definition) — where these conflict, each successive source is weaker than the one before it, owing to its greater remove from direct meaning."

That is: among mutually conflicting sources of evidence bearing on a single mantra, whichever comes earlier in this list — Shruti, Linga, Vakya, Prakarana, Sthana, Samakhya — takes priority over what follows; the complete statement (full Vakya) holds authority. Purva-Mimamsa thus explains the method of meaning-determination rather than specific meanings themselves.

The most important text written directly for explaining the Veda's meaning is Sayanacharya's own Vedartha-prakashika — an exhaustive, comprehensive Rigveda commentary from beginning to end, accompanied by a substantial, invaluable introduction.

Near a bend of the Tungabhadra river in Bellary District, at the now-ruined site called Vijayanagara, the Karnataka empire was founded in the mid-14th century CE by Bukkaraya. Sayanacharya served as this king's guru; he and his brother Madhavacharya both did exceptional work in founding Vijayanagara and in the world of letters. Madhavacharya later became known as Vidyaranya, the name he remains famous under today — and it is this same Madhavacharya who wrote the Sarvadarshanasangraha, compiling the core tenets of the established Vedanta schools, as well as the verse-form Advaita-Vedanta text Panchadashi. Beyond his Rig-Yajus-Sama Veda commentaries, Sayanacharya also commented on the Aitareya Brahmana, its Aranyakas, and similar texts.

In the Vedartha-prakashika, Sayanacharya explains, for every Rigveda mantra: the meaning of each word, the etymological breakdown of difficult terms, relevant grammatical points, and — at the head of each mantra — which yajna it belongs to and how it should be used there.

Modern scholars find many shortcomings in Sayanacharya's commentary by their own lights — most importantly, that Sayana never examines the mantras from a critical or historical perspective. For him, the Veda is a body of sacred text in which every statement carries authoritative validity; attempting to critically examine it would itself be a mistake. Since mantras exist for use in yajnas, with each mantra devoted to a specific deity, it is precisely this ritual-application perspective that governs his entire commentary.

original p. 300

This reverential attitude leads Sayana, upon examination, to offer differing explanations for the same word across different contexts without hesitation. Where a meaning is unclear, he gathers earlier commentators' views and sometimes offers his own determination — but often without clarifying why one particular sense was chosen from a word's several possible meanings, or why his own interpretation was preferred. Though it's well established that words sharing a root can carry multiple senses, he doesn't consistently draw on this systematically; readers must work out for themselves why a given meaning was chosen in a given context, since he rarely states this explicitly in advance.

The Nirukta, by contrast, generally settles a word's meaning based on its inherent grammatical derivation. It also draws together material scattered across the Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Sarvanukramani, and Brihaddevata — Puranic stories tied to history, and biographical material underlying the Veda's own composition — material not found gathered together anywhere in Sayanacharya's own text.

It is not the case that the Veda's interpretation remained entirely unsettled until Sayana's time — one example illustrates this well. In Mandala 1's ninth section, the well-known "Hiranyagarbha" sukta, with its refrain of "Ka" ("Who?"), poses a famous interpretive puzzle from the very start: should "kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema" ("to which god should we make offering?") be read with "ka" as an ordinary interrogative pronoun, or does "Ka" itself become the name of the deity — the very creator-god whose name pervades the whole hymn?

अत्र कं शब्दोऽनिर्दिष्टस्वरूपत्वात् प्रजापतौ वर्तते ।

"Here, the word 'ka' ('who'), owing to its indefinite/unstated referent, applies to Prajapati."

That is: since "kasmai" ("to whom") applies to one without a fixed, determinate form, it comes to apply to Prajapati himself — Ka thus becoming, in effect, a name for the Creator.

original p. 301

युद्वा सृष्ट्यर्थं कानुयते इति कः । कवेर्डप्रत्ययः ।

"Or: 'he who desires creation' — hence 'ka,' from the root ku with the suffix ḍa."

Or: because he possesses the desire to create, he is denoted by "ka."

युद्वा कं सुखं तद्ग्रहत्वात् इत्युच्यते ।

"Or: 'ka' means happiness — because he embodies that happiness, he is so called."

A further explanation comes as a story:

अथवा इन्द्रेण सृष्ट्वा प्रजापतिर्दिव्यं महत्त्वं तुभ्यं प्रदाय अहं कः ईदृशः स्यामित्युक्त्वा । स इन्द्रः प्रत्युचे यदीदं ब्रवीषि अहं कः स्यां तदेव त्वं भवेति । अतः करणात् इति प्रजापतिराख्यायते ।

"Or: having created [the world], Prajapati granted his own divine greatness to Indra, saying 'I too should become such as this — what (ka) am I?' Indra replied: 'Since you ask what (ka) you should become — become exactly that.' For this reason, Prajapati came to be named 'Ka.'"

That is: when Indra prayed to become as venerable as Prajapati, Prajapati granted him that greatness and asked, "What (ka) should I become now?" Indra answered, "Become exactly that — 'Ka.'" This is why Brahma came to be named "Kaḥ."

In this way, something that could be explained simply and naturally instead receives an effortful, ill-fitting interpretation forced by some external rule — traditional understanding giving way to freshly invented meanings. So much for the faults found in Sayana's approach; now for its usefulness.

One side of the picture has been given above; the other cannot be ignored. Considering it fairly reveals the true value of Sayanacharya's contribution. Had Sayanacharya never written his commentary, what state would Vedic scholarship be in today? It is hard even to imagine. Objecting to his work is easy — but even those who object must acknowledge their own debt to it. Max Müller himself, while editing this very text, wrote:

"........Those who recollect the history of Vedic scholarship........know best that with all its faults and weaknesses Sayana's Commentary has a Sine qua non for a scholarlike study of the Rigveda. I do not wonder that others who have more recently entered on that study are inclined to speak disparagingly of the scholastic interpretations of Sayana. They hardly know how much we all owe to his guidance in effecting our first entrance into this..."

original p. 302

"...fortress of Vedic language and Vedic religion, and how much even they, without being aware of it, are indebted to that Indian Eustathius.....Who does not know how much assistance may be derived from a first translation, even though it is imperfect, nay, how often the very mistakes of our predecessors help us in finding the right track? If we can now see further than he could, let us not forget that we are standing on his shoulders."

Anyone examining Vedic scholarship will see that Sayanacharya's commentary, faults and all, has not been surpassed. Even its critics must acknowledge its special mastery.

This field was not empty before Sayana, nor did he claim to be its first pioneer — as already discussed, earlier commentaries offered real help, but Sayana's own text has one quality theirs lack: ease of understanding without excessive effort. Sayanacharya himself, in composing his commentary, drew on and names many predecessors: Bhattabhaskara, Skandasvami, Atmananda, the Nirukta-authors, Bashkala, Kashyapa, the Aitihasikas (traditional historians), the Naidanas (Nidana-sutra experts), grammarians (Vyakaranikas), tradition-bearers (Sampradaya-vids), self-knowers (Atmavids), elder-teachers (Vriddhashasanas), and earlier commentary-authors such as Devasvami — among others.

Other lesser-known Rigveda commentaries are also mentioned in passing: the Ravana-bhashya, Kaushika-bhashya, Gaudartha-vritti, and works by scholars in the lineage of Bhavasvami, Sthanaka, and Madhavadeva. None of these approach the completeness of Sayanacharya's own commentary, and none survive to us today.

original p. 303

Mahidhara's and Uvata's Yajurveda-commentaries, though well-known, offer no help for the Rigveda — only the commentaries already discussed serve that purpose.

Vedic scholars' efforts to preserve the Veda over the centuries deserve real praise, but must be acknowledged as offering little direct help in determining the Veda's meaning. The ancients did not rely on written texts alone in investigating Vedic meaning — in that early era, texts hadn't gained much traction, so a guru would teach the Veda orally, mouth to ear, imparting correct pronunciation directly, generation after generation. The guru pronounced each word distinctly and in order; the disciple listened and repeated it back, as many times as needed; mispronunciations were corrected on the spot. Because sustained accurate recitation of lengthy metrical passages required long practice from childhood, words were taught divided into two or three portions at a time, with a sukta, a full chapter, or occasionally two or three chapters assigned according to the student's capacity.

Study paused on Paurnamasa, Ashtami, Chaturdashi, Purnima, and eclipse days. Each morning, after his own rituals, the guru assigned the day's or week's new lesson in fixed sequence; students practiced the previous lesson before receiving the new one. In this way, students worked through the entire Samhita along with its corresponding Brahmana, Aranyaka, and Upanishads — alongside the Vedangas (Shiksha, etc.), Kalpasutra, Dharmashastra, Puranas, and Itihasa — pausing during the Ashadha rainy season. This full course was reckoned to take roughly twelve years.

Beginning Vedic study required prior upanayana (the sacred-thread initiation with the Gayatri mantra) — without it, one had no standing to study the Veda at all. Throughout the period of study, the student had to reside in the guru's own household, serving him and his elders with reverence. These regulations appear in the Grihyasutra texts...

original p. 304

...After completing Vedic study, following personal capacity and available time, further shastras (or other Vedas) could be studied; the disciple would then take leave of the guru with a satisfying dakshina and return home, studies complete. This is the ancient tradition.

The Method of Vedic Study

Rishis established various graduated recitation-sequences to aid retention of the Veda once fully taught. These sequences are extremely ancient, and wherever Vedic study survives today, Padapatha and its related sequences are still learned directly from the guru's mouth in this same order:

जटा माला शिखा रेखा ध्वजो दण्डो रथो घनः । अष्टौ विकृतयः प्रोक्ताः क्रमपूर्वा महर्षिभिः ॥

"Jata, Mala, Shikha, Rekha, Dhvaja, Danda, Ratha, Ghana — these eight Vikritis (modified recitation-forms), built upon Krama, are declared by the great rishis."

Not all eight remain in practice today — only Samhitapatha, Padapatha, Kramapatha, Jatapatha, and Ghanapatha survive in current use in this country. Below, these are briefly illustrated for a single mantra; the same method extends to every mantra in the Rigveda.

1. Samhitapatha (Continuous Recitation)

Definition: "paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃhitā" — "the closest proximity [of sounds] is Samhita" (Panini's Ashtadhyayi, 1.4.109); or, "the extreme closeness of phonemes is termed Samhita." The source shows this verse marked with Vedic accent notation — udatta/anudatta/svarita marks above and below syllables — which cannot be reproduced in plain text here, but the verse itself is given in full.

ओषधयः सं वदन्ते सोमेन सह राज्ञा । यस्मै कृणोति ब्राह्मणस्तं राजन्पारयामसि ॥ (RV 10.97.22)

ओषधयः सं वदन्ते सोमेन सह राज्ञा । यस्मै कृणोति ब्राह्मणस् तं राजन् पारयामसि ॥ oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante somena saha rājñā | yasmai kṛṇoti brāhmaṇas taṃ rājan pārayāmasi ||

"The herbs converse together with King Soma: 'Whomever the Brahmin acts for, O King, him we carry safely across.'"

2. Padapatha (Word-by-Word Recitation)

Definition: "pada-vicchedo'saṃhitaḥ" — "word-division without [phonetic] combination" (Katyayana's Pratishakhya-sutra).

The same verse, divided into its twelve individual words:

१ओषधयः २सं ३वदन्ते ४सोमेन ५सह ६राज्ञा । ७यस्मै ८कृणोति ९ब्राह्मणः १०तं ११राजन् १२पारयामसि ॥

original p. 305

This mantra has 12 words in total. When performing word-division, the Samhita's euphonic accent-changes are not indicated in the Pratishakhya texts, so they are not detailed here either.

3. Kramapatha (Step Recitation)

Definition: "krameṇa padadvayasya pāṭhaḥ" — reciting pairs of words in sequence; Krama-patha is also called "Yogarudha Samhita." "Krama serves the purpose of memorization" (Pratishakhya-sutra 5.8, Katyayana).

१ओषधयः २सं । २सं ३वदन्ते । ३वदन्ते ४सोमेन । ४सोमेन ५सह । ५सह ६राज्ञा । ६राज्ञेति ६राज्ञा ॥ ७यस्मै ८कृणोति । ८कृणोति ९ब्राह्मणः । ९ब्राह्मणः १०तम् । १०तं ११राजन् । ११राजन् १२पारयामसि । १२पारयामसि १२पारयामसि ॥

That is: each word is paired with the next and recited together, following the Samhita's phonetic-junction rules — first words 1+2, then dropping word 1 and pairing 2+3, and so on to the sentence's end, where the final word is repeated twice, observing the clause's proper concluding form (e.g., "rājñeti rājñā"). Compound (samasa) words use avagraha marking similarly — e.g., "purohitam iti puraḥkṛtam," "ṛtaṃ dhāta iti ṛtabhṛtam." Kramapatha builds accent-proficiency and helps in correctly word-dividing any Vedic mantra.

4. Jatapatha (Braided Recitation)

Definition:

अनुलोमविलोमाभ्यां त्रिवारं हि पठेत्क्रमम् । विलोमे पदवत्संधिरनुलोमे यथाक्रमम् ॥

"One should recite the Krama three times — forward and reverse. In the reverse order, phonetic combination follows the word-form; in the forward order, it follows the regular sequence."

Example: Anuloma (forward) 1+2; Viloma (reverse) 2+1; Anuloma (forward) 1+2. A note clarifies that the numerals preceding each word throughout these examples indicate that word's position — 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. — in the original mantra.

original p. 306

Second definition of Jata:

क्रमे युग्मोऽग्ये पदजातमेन द्विरभ्यसेदुत्तरमेन पूर्वं । अभ्यस्य पूर्वं च तथोत्तरे सदे वसानमेवं हि जटाभिधीयते ॥

"In the Krama pair, one should twice repeat the latter word with the former; having done so, then repeat the former with the next following pair likewise — proceeding continuously in this way, this is called 'Jata.'"

Example: Krama = 1+2; Vikrama (reverse) = 2+1; Sankrama = 1+2.

That is, Jatapatha requires this word-joining pattern: 1+2+2+1+1+2, then (dropping word 1) 2+3+3+2+2+3, then 3+4+4+3+3+4, then 4+5+5+4+4+5, then 5+6+6+5+5+6, and so on.

Example: oṣadhayaḥ saṃ samoṣadhyaya oṣadhayaḥ saṃ | saṃ vadante vadante saṃ saṃ vadante — and so forth.

Within Jatapatha, five distinct patterns of word-combination occur, named Krama, Utkrama, Vikrama, Abhikrama, and Sankrama — each is explained by example below:

(1) Krama — one word joined with the next (1+2). Example: oṣadhayaḥ sam || sam vadante || vadante somena || etc.

(2) Utkrama — a single word repeated twice in a row (1+1, 2+2). Example: oṣadhaya oṣadhayaḥ || sam sam || vadante vadante || etc.

original p. 307

(3) Vikrama — a word joined with the preceding one (2+1, 3+2). Example: samoṣadhayaḥ | vadante sam | somena vadante etc.

(4) Abhikrama — following Utkrama, the first word repeated twice again in succession (1+1). Example: oṣadhaya oṣadhayaḥ etc.

(5) Sankrama — repeating the original Krama pairing once more (1+2). Example: oṣadhayaḥ sam etc.

Krama Utkrama Vikrama Abhikrama Sankrama
1+2 2+2 2+1 1+1 1+2

Full Jatapatha example (first half of the mantra):

ओषधयः सं समोषधय ओषधयः सं । सं वदन्ते वदन्ते सं सं वदन्ते । वदन्ते सोमेन सोमेन वदन्ते वदन्ते सोमेन । सोमेन सह सह सोमेन सोमेन सह । सह राज्ञा राज्ञा सह सह राज्ञा । राज्ञेति राज्ञा ॥

The second half of the mantra is recited following this same pattern.

5. Ghanapatha (The "Dense" Recitation)

Definition:

शिखां (जटां) मुक्त्वा विपर्यस्य तत्त्वदासि पुनः पठेत् । अयं घन इति प्रोक्तो वेदविद्भिर्महर्षिभिः ॥

"Having completed the Shikha (Jata) pattern and reversed it, one should recite it once more from the start in that same form — this is declared 'Ghana' by the Veda-knowing great rishis."

That is: first the Jatapatha recitation of words 1, 2, 3; then their reversal (viloma); then a repeated recitation of the same words again — this method is called Ghanapatha.

original p. 308

Ghanapatha's full combination formula:

1+2+2+1+1+2+3+3+2+1+1+2+3, 2+3+3+2+2+3+4+4+3+2+2+3+4, and so on.

Shikha (Jata) recitation Reversal Repeated recitation
1+2+2+1+ 2+1+1+ 1+2+3
2+3+3+2+ 3+2+2+ 2+3+4, etc.

Full Ghanapatha example (first portion):

ओषधयः सं समोषधय ओषधयः सं वदन्ते वदन्ते समोषधय ओषधयः सं वदन्ते । सं वदन्ते वदन्ते सं सं वदन्ते सोमेन सोमेन वदन्ते सं सं वदन्ते सोमेन । सोमेन सह सह सोमेन सोमेन सह राज्ञा राज्ञा सह सोमेन सोमेन सह राज्ञा । सह राज्ञा राज्ञा सह सह राज्ञा । राज्ञेति राज्ञा ॥

The second half of the mantra is recited following this same pattern.

The Varaha Purana states on this matter:

पदक्रमविशेषज्ज्ञो वर्णक्रमविज्ज्ञणः । स्वरमात्राविशेषज्ज्ञो गच्छेदाचार्यसंसदम् ॥ संहितापाठकः पुण्यं द्विगुणं पदपाठकः । त्रिगुणं क्रमपाठेन जटापाठेन षड्गुणम् ॥

"One who knows the specifics of word-sequence, the order of letters, and the fine points of accent and duration may enter the assembly of teachers. A Samhita-reciter earns merit; a Pada-reciter, double; a Krama-reciter, triple; a Jata-reciter, sixfold."

That is: mastery of Samhita, Padapatha, Kramapatha, correct pronunciation, accent, and duration qualifies one as a skilled acharya. Complete study of the Samhita alone brings merit; Padapatha study doubles it; Kramapatha triples it; Jatapatha brings sixfold merit — so states the Varaha Purana. Chapter number as legible; sequence continues from the previous chapter.

Chapter Eighteen — Modern Efforts in Vedic Study

original p. 309

Having clarified in earlier chapters what the Veda and Vedangas are, and explained the Rigveda in specific detail, we now turn to examining the proper method of Vedic study, reviewing both modern and ancient efforts made toward it.

As Western scholars came to our country, many took up the study of our literature. Even as some of our own scholars neglected our ancient culture, foreigners embraced these texts, writing extensively in books and articles — editing, republishing, critically examining, dating texts, studying ancient coins, and publishing old palm-leaf manuscripts. Western effort in this regard deserves particular mention, extending beyond the Vedas themselves to the Vedangas as well. Among Western scholars, German scholars in particular have excelled — owed to German's own recorded historical-linguistic connection to Sanskrit, a connection no other Western language shares to the same degree. Western scholars find it natural to critically examine texts this way; our own readers, working from more traditional viewpoints, have found a purely academic approach less immediately comfortable to adopt. It must be acknowledged, though, that Western scholarship has shown one imprudent tendency: treating certain received Vedic traditions as unnecessary to accept at face value — though this isn't every Western scholar's stated position. Since this discipline is comparatively recent, it's unsurprising that not everything in their work is fully correct — but this doesn't diminish its overall value; these texts remain extremely useful for understanding the Vedas.

Let us now briefly examine the modern efforts made toward Vedic study.

original p. 310

In the mid-18th century, the French writer Voltaire spoke highly of Brahmins' wisdom, and a text called "Ezour-Vedam" (a spurious "Veda") became known at Oxford in translation. William Jones translated Kalidasa's Shakuntala into English. Colebrooke later wrote an influential essay on the Vedas.

Colebrooke's essay deserves special mention for candidly describing the Veda's linguistic difficulty, advising that no one seeking full understanding of the Veda should neglect this challenge. His observations held for a long time, though later, deeper Sanskrit scholarship moved past some of his specific conclusions — even so, his pioneering effort, undertaken before Sanskrit studies had matured, deserves real credit.

Following him, the French scholar Eugène Burnouf edited and published the Rigveda Samhita from many gathered manuscripts, building on Colebrooke's work — though he could complete only part of it before his death.

The German scholar Rudolph Roth, in the St. Petersburg Sanskrit-German Lexicon (8 volumes), traced Vedic-era word usage across all its varying senses with example sentences for each — a work whose usefulness Vedic scholars still rely on today.

The German scholar A. Weber wrote Indische Studien, covering the Vedas, Vedanta, grammar, Nirukta, and lexicography comprehensively, as well as the well-known History of Sanskrit Literature.

The German scholar Franz Bopp studied Sanskrit primarily for comparative linguistics rather than Vedic interpretation specifically — his writings are more introductory in nature, focused on language comparison across the broader Indo-European family rather than Sanskrit alone. Even so, his contribution to Sanskrit scholarship generally was substantial...

original p. 311

...whether Bopp's stated neutrality actually held up in practice is a separate question — writers sharing his broad perspective generally accept traditional textual views as authoritative up to a point, but depart from tradition once critical examination begins, giving priority to the subject itself over inherited convention. Truly impartial scholars on Hindu-shastra topics remain genuinely rare.

Remarkably, the first printed edition of the sacred, ancient Rigveda Samhita was not published in India at all — a German scholar, Max Müller, edited it together with Sayana's commentary and published it in England. This edition became the foundation of modern Vedic study; before it, study proceeded solely through oral instruction. Max Müller also wrote Ancient Sanskrit Literature, extensively covering Vedic literature and publishing much previously unavailable material alongside Vedic citations — a work whose usefulness for correctly understanding Vedic meaning remains undiminished even today.

Among later scholarship, Muir's The Original Sanskrit Texts stands out as especially important — arranging citations from many texts in order to reach reasoned conclusions. In Muir's own words:

"In treating the several topics....I propose in each case, to adduce, first any texts bearing upon it, which may be found in the hymns of the Rigveda; next, those in the Brahmanas and their appendages, and lastly, those occurring in any of the different classes of works coming under the designation of Smriti."

That is: for each topic, he first cites relevant Rigveda material, then the Brahmanas and their appendages, and finally the various Smriti-class texts — covering the Vedangas, Shrautasutras, Grihyasutras, Manu and other Dharmashastras, and the Puranas. From this, our own ancient writers' opinions on various matters, and how these opinions shifted across eras, become clear. Topics covered include the caste order, Brahmin-Kshatriya relations, connections between Hindus and other peoples (Greeks, Romans), the linguistic evidence for the Vedas' origin and authority, Hindu history, and life in Vedic-era society. This book is immensely useful for any serious student of the Rigveda.

original p. 312

Dr. Haug published a Brahmana text with an attractive, detail-rich introduction.

Wilson produced a complete English translation of the Rigveda (and also translated the Vishnu Purana and wrote Hindoo Theatre). His Rigveda translation closely follows Vedic-language meaning, especially in its early volumes — by his own account, he avoided speculative interpretation where meaning was unclear, preferring to follow Sayana's own commentary over divergent Western annotations wherever the two differed. In a place or two his own era's assumptions surface, but this doesn't diminish the work's overall value.

Ludwig and Grassmann, German scholars, each produced independent German translations with markedly different prose approaches from one another — and both differed sharply from Wilson in places, rejecting the idea that the Veda's meaning can be fully recovered through tradition alone, instead pursuing critical/historical determinations that sometimes yield divergent conclusions.

Grassmann also produced a small but valuable Sanskrit-German dictionary specifically for the Rigveda, tracing roughly a thousand word-usages by root and giving context-appropriate meanings for each.

Kaegi wrote a critical German-language study of the Rigveda's subject matter (later translated into English) — cited repeatedly throughout the present work.

Geldner and Pischel, two German scholars, jointly produced a Vedic-studies volume clarifying how the Veda's meaning should properly be approached. They re-examined obscure or seemingly contradictory Vedic words, tracing them to their proper forms and offering fresh, previously unclear interpretations; several suktas were re-translated into German with word-by-word glosses, etymological notes, and commentary surveying all prior interpretive attempts...

original p. 313

...their conclusions blend ancient and modern viewpoints, neither fully accepting tradition nor entirely rejecting it without reason — a genuinely balanced approach.

Whitney's grammar is a highly valued text, generally more connected to modern Sanskrit scholarship than other current grammars — but it also makes a deliberate effort to show Vedic and classical grammatical forms side by side wherever they diverge (e.g., devaḥ, devasya, devebhiḥ, devaiḥ, with Vedic variants noted alongside). Its treatment of pronunciation is likewise extremely useful.

Prof. Oldenberg's introduction to his own translation greatly assists Vedic students — discussing meter, grammar, etymology, and related matters for individual mantras and Brahmanas, and citing interpretations found across German, French, and English scholarship on each point, giving readers a comprehensive single-source overview of the field's major interpretive positions.

These works, published through journals of the German Oriental Society, The American Oriental Society, and The Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland among others, are not lacking in scholarly rigor.

Bloomfield's Concordance to Rigveda, and Prof. Macdonald and Dr. Keith's Vedic Index of Names and Subjects, represent enormous European scholarly labor. Related works worth mentioning include Prof. Lenman's Noun Inflection in the Veda, Dr. Arnold's Vedic Metre, and Bloomfield's American Lectures on the Religion of the Veda.

Among Indian scholars, S. P. Pandit began translating the Rigveda into both English and Marathi, writing clear, concise annotations on difficult passages under the title Vedartha-yatna — unfortunately, he passed away having completed only through the third Mandala.

original p. 314

Tilak wrote two independent works, The Orion and The Arctic Home in the Vedas — both concerning Vedic chronology and astronomy: the first proposing a dating for the Vedic period based on astronomical calculation (not fully accepted by later scholars), the second arguing for an Arctic/polar original homeland for the Aryans.

Efforts continue as well to spread understanding of the Veda more broadly among ordinary readers, in English and in regional languages — useful work in its own way, even where methods remain debated.

Vedic-subject scholarship and critique continue to be published even now, with a good deal of further work still unpublished and ongoing. Chapter number as legible; sequence continues from the previous chapter.

Chapter Nineteen — The Method of Studying the Veda

Having now surveyed the work of ancient and modern scholars toward Vedic study, let us examine how the Veda itself should be studied to grasp its meaning — what attitude a student should bring, and what the aim of such study should be.

Every student, in their school years, reads many textbooks across subjects, generally aiming to pass examinations. But should the goal be merely passing exams, or genuinely acquiring the knowledge those books contain? Should the goal belong to the teacher, the student, or both? There should be no aimlessness at all — the goal should be set appropriately to the student's stage of education, age, chosen field, and station in life...

original p. 315

...applying one's own intellectual capacity in any context, and determining how to benefit oneself and others — or grasping the underlying principle of any new subject encountered through experience — is, at minimum, what education should achieve.

For a student, the primary goal of Vedic study should be genuine knowledge-seeking: gathering material, examining it broadly, comparing traditional and other viewpoints on difficult points, and reaching one's own reasoned determination — this is the mark of a true student. Since some mantras and words carry genuinely uncertain meaning, Vedic study demands real seriousness; conclusions should be earned through effort and held with confidence, not settled prematurely or left in confusion.

Astikas (orthodox believers holding the Veda to be non-human and self-authenticating in origin) treat the Veda as wholly divine, its authority beyond question, valuing Vedic study chiefly for its own merit rather than critical instruction. Sayanacharya, working from this same standpoint and his own expertise in ritual matters, treats yajna-related explanation as primary throughout his commentary — applying no critical or historical lens to the Veda, and never doubting its unified authority, even where the Rigveda itself shows no single unified textual foundation or subject.

As already discussed, Sayanacharya's traditionalist approach accepts received opinion; where interpretations genuinely conflict, he doesn't insist on a single fixed meaning, nor does he require every determined meaning to rest on demonstrable proof — settling on an ungrounded meaning didn't trouble him the way it does modern critical scholarship.

Western scholars, by contrast, approached Vedic study critically from the outset. Some, in critiquing fellow Westerners, argue that Sayanacharya should still be given priority in establishing the Veda's meaning...

original p. 316

...say the Acharyas [should be given final authority] — arguing Sayana's commentary shows the correct path. But Roth, without altering Vedic study's core principles, adopted a modern critical approach from the outset — using inductive reasoning and cross-contextual comparison as his main tools, examining the Rigveda historically, gathering every occurrence of a word, comparing its usage alongside related terms, and tracking its meaning's evolution over time. Where Roth and like-minded scholars erred was in discarding the ancient scholarly tradition entirely — a fault of his own making, leading his explanations astray at many points.

Going forward, Vedic study needs a genuine middle path between these two extremes: following tradition where it proves reliable, while applying sound method to examine genuinely problematic points, determining meaning contextually case by case.

Worked example — the words "Ari" and "Arya": Both occur throughout the Samhita with varying senses depending on context. "Ari" generally carries the senses "wealthy person," "fierce rival," and "enemy": These citations illustrate "ari" shifting between senses across contexts — precise phrase-level translation is difficult to render exactly at this resolution, but the semantic range they collectively demonstrate is clear.

विश्वो ह्यन्यो अरिराजगाम — (10.27.1) विश्वगूर्को अरिष्टुतः — (8.1.33) आ विश्वगूर्कः स्थिरमत्क्रे — (1.41.9) उतानेः सुभगां अरिर्वोचेयुः — (1.5.6)

Across these examples, "ari" sometimes means "wealthy person" (dhanika) and elsewhere carries the other senses noted — illustrating how a word's usage must be judged case by case. "Ari" can even mean "king" or "Indra" in some contexts. Over time, the sense naturally extended from "one who rivals prosperity" to "an obstacle to progress," to "a competitor," and finally settled into simply "enemy" (shatru) as its established later usage.

The word "Arya" shows a similar range of meaning: Further citations illustrating "arya"'s range of meaning across contexts — precise phrase-level translation is difficult at this resolution.

इना विश्वास्यार्य आ द्युम्नानि मानुषाणाम् — (4.30.18)

original p. 317

मंहिष्ठो अर्यः सख्ये — (8.1.33) वक्ष्वेऽटयो रन्थ्विरस्त्वे — (6.31.3) विश्वां अर्य उपगतातिं वज्रन् — (6.48.2) तिरो अर्यो हवनागि कृतं नः — (6.41.3)

In current Sanskrit usage, "ari" has settled into the fixed meaning "enemy," while "aryaḥ" has fallen out of use — "Arya" itself may derive from this same root.

In this way, every sentence containing such words must be examined and its meaning determined by context — and where a meaning has genuinely shifted over time, that shift must be justified with sound reasoning. Chapter number as legible; sequence continues.

Chapter Twenty-One — Subjects Expounded in the Veda: Differing Opinions on This Point

The Traditional (Vedic/Astika) View

Astikas, who accept the Veda's authority, hold that the Vedas are beginningless (anādi) and eternal (nitya) — never originating at any point in time, having existed since beginningless time. Whatever needs to be known in this vast universe is held to be contained, in compressed form, within the Veda — the ultimate authority. The Shatapatha Brahmana states: "Prajapati, wishing to create, needed to know the complete range of eternal ritual-forms and materials needed for creation. He then considered these three: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda — known to contain everything." All meters, revealed texts (shrutis), life-force, and deities are said to be contained within it. This is eternal, beginningless, and alone called "Sat" (Being) from time without beginning — the Veda encompassing everything, with no question of it deriving from anything prior. This same subject is discussed in the Purusha-sukta...

original p. 318

तस्माद्यज्ञात्सर्वहुत ऋचः सामानि जज्ञिरे । छन्दांसि जज्ञिरे तस्माद्यजुस्तस्मादजायत ॥ (Purusha Sukta, RV 10.90.9)

"From that all-offering yajna, the Riks and Samans were born; the meters were born from it, and the Yajus arose from it."

That is: from that yajna (the Supreme Being), the Riks, Samans, and Yajus all came into being — the same view of the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheya) found across the texts cited above.

But the Samhita portion is chiefly concerned with ritual action (karma) — pleasing the deities through worship and yajna to accumulate merit — and many texts hold this to be a lesser pursuit than the knowledge (jnana) taught in the Upanishads as the true cause of liberation. The Bhambhoyoga Upanishad states:

सोऽहं भगवो मन्त्रविदेवास्मि नात्मवित् । श्रुतं ह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्यस्तरति शोकमात्मविदिति सोऽहं भगवः शोचामि तं मा भगवाच्छोकस्य पारं तारयत्विति । तं होवाच यद्वै किंचैतदध्यगीष्ठा नामैवैतत् । नाम वा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः...

"'I am, reverend one, a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self; yet I have heard from the likes of your reverence that one who knows the Self crosses beyond sorrow. I am full of sorrow, O reverend one — may you carry me to sorrow's far shore.' He replied: 'Whatever you have studied is merely name. Name alone is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda...'"

Many hold that the Veda-Samhitas and related shastras, however celebrated, cannot resolve the sorrow of worldly existence (samsara-duhkha) — that liberating the Self lies beyond their scope. The Gita expresses this same view:

यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके । तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः ॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2.46)

"As much use as there is in a well when floodwater surrounds it on every side, so much use do all the Vedas hold for a Brahmin who has attained true knowledge."

Put simply: the Veda describes rituals granting heaven and worldly/other-worldly pleasure — of no further use to one who has attained knowledge of Brahman.

Madhavacharya, in his Vedartha-prakasha, defines the Veda thus:

इष्टप्राप्त्यनिष्टपरिहारयोरलौकिकमुपायं यो ग्रन्थो वेदयति स वेदः । अलौकिकदेशे प्रत्यक्षानुमाने व्यावर्त्येति ।

"That text which teaches a transcendent (alaukika) means for obtaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired — that is the Veda. 'Transcendent' excludes ordinary perception and inference as the means in question."

That is: the Veda teaches a path — distinct from perception and inference — for both attaining desired ends and avoiding undesired ones.

original p. 319

Many texts discuss the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheyatva) at length, especially in Sayana-related literature — the core doctrine holding that the Veda is apaurusheya, eternal, and of ultimate/transcendent significance.

On this point, the Vedanta-paribhasha's introduction states:

न हि तावत्पुरुषेणोच्चार्यमाणत्वं पौरुषेयत्वम् । गुरुमुखेऽपि अध्यापकसंप्रदाया पौरुषेयत्वाशक्त्ये । नासि पुरुषाभीनोत्पत्तिकत्वं पौरुषेयत्वम्...किंतु सजातीयोच्चारणानेक्षोच्चारणविषयत्वम् । तथा च सर्गाद्यकाले परमेश्वरः पूर्वसर्गसिद्धवेदानुस्पूर्विसमानानुस्पूर्विकं वेदं विरचितवान् न तु तद्विजातीयं वेदमिति न सजातीयोच्चारणानेक्षोच्चारणविषयत्वं पौरुषेयत्वं वेदानाम् । भारतादीनां तु सजातीयोच्चारणमनपेक्ष्योच्चारणमिति तेषां पौरुषेयत्वम् ॥

(A technical Vedanta-paribhasha argument distinguishing mere recitation by a person from actual authorship: since the Creator, at each creation-cycle, reproduces the Veda in the exact same sequence as the prior cycle's Veda — rather than composing something new and different — the Veda does not qualify as "authored" (paurusheya) the way texts like the Mahabharata, freely composed without such fixed precedent, do. Precise phrase-level parsing is difficult at this resolution, but the overall argument is clear.)

That is: the Supreme Being, at each creation, reproduces the Vedas exactly as in the prior creation-cycle — "dhātā yathā pūrvam akalpayat" ("the Creator fashioned it just as before") — and because the Vedas continue unchanged across every successive cycle, they are called apaurusheya and eternal.

This represents the view found across various texts. But what does the Veda itself suggest, upon direct examination? Consider:

इदं ब्रह्म क्रियमाणं नवीयः (2.35.40[?]) ब्रह्म कृण्वन्तो हरिवो वसिष्ठाः (1.12.4[?]) ब्रह्मेन्द्राय वज्रिणे अकारि (6.42.6[?]) इत्यादि ।

(Citations referencing prayers/hymns being "newly composed" or "fashioned" by named rishis — e.g., "this prayer being newly made," "the Vasishthas fashioning a prayer," "a prayer was made for thunderbolt-wielding Indra" — precise mantra locations given as best legible.)

Two things become clear from such statements:

(1) The mantras were composed by rishis or knowledgeable persons. (2) There are both older and newer rishis, and correspondingly older and newer suktas.

Supporting this same view are mantras using verb-roots meaning "to take form/be born" (jāta) or "birth" (janya) in connection with the mantras themselves.

original p. 320

मन्त्रं ये वारं नर्या अतक्षन् (2.34.1) । अवस्यवो न वयुनानि तक्षुः (1.19.7) । विश्वान्यर्यो भुवना जजान (3.31.1) । इन्द्र ब्रह्माणि जनयन्त विप्राः (2.13.8) । तस्मा उक्थं जनये यज्जुजोष (2.19.1) । इन्द्राय ब्रह्म जनयन्त विप्राः (2.10.10) ।

(Citations of mantras describing themselves as "carved," "fashioned," or "generated" by rishis/inspired poets — precise locations given as best legible.)

But these contexts may simply indicate the time and rishi associated with a mantra's ritual use, rather than proving the mantra was newly created then — the "old rishi/new rishi" distinction discussed earlier isn't so easily dismissed either.

Elsewhere, statements convey the directly opposite view — that mantras became perceptible to rishis purely through divine grace, with Speech herself personified and praised as their true source:

यज्ज्ञेन वाचः पदवीयमायन् तामन्वविन्दन्नृषिषु प्रविष्टाम् । तामाभृत्या व्यदधाप्यर्भुधे तां सप्तरेभा अभि सं नवन्ते ॥ (10.71.3)

"When, through the yajna, they traced Speech's path, they found her having entered into the rishis; having received her, they distributed her further; the seven singers together celebrate her."

Rishis' own utterances are elsewhere attributed extraordinary power:

विश्वामित्रस्य रक्षति ब्रह्मेदं भारतं जनम् (3.33.11) । विनेन्न कं दाशराज्ञे सुदासं प्रावदिन्द्रो ब्रह्मणा वसिष्ठाः (7.33.3) । वसिष्ठस्य स्तुवत इन्द्रोऽश्चोदुरुं कृत्स्न्यभ्यो अकृणोदुलोकम् (7.33.5) ।

(Citing Vishvamitra's prayer protecting the Bharata people, and Indra aiding Sudas in the Battle of Ten Kings through the power of the Vasishthas' prayer — precise locations as best legible.)

Yet elsewhere still, rishis express genuine doubt about their own poetic power and admit their own insufficiency (RV 1.164.37, 6.37).

Such genuinely divergent views coexist within the Veda itself, making any single, tidy determination difficult — even as texts grounded in Vedic authority insist, without qualification, that the Vedas are apaurusheya and faultless, a claim not easily reconciled with the Veda's own varied self-descriptions.

One plausible resolution: the rishis originally lacked full confidence in their own poetic power, and so came to believe their own utterances were not truly their own composition, but something that dawned on them through divine grace — lacking the courage to consider this belief mistaken. This very belief may be the seed from which the later, firmer doctrine of Vedic apaurusheyatva grew, becoming progressively more entrenched over time.

original p. 321

Those investigating the Upanishads' philosophical principles hold that view superior to the ritualistic one; even critically-minded scholars share this preference, while Sayanacharya emphasizes the Veda's practical ritual value instead. This represents the ancient scholarly view; now consider the modern view:

"The Primitive Aryans were children easily susceptible to the influence of their surroundings, highly imaginative, simple and innocent."

That is: early Aryans were simpler than their descendants, not fully grasping natural phenomena, and thus prone to personify and imagine — believing in deities corresponding to natural causes, performing rituals out of unreasoned fear, and composing prayers and hymns from whatever satisfaction or feeling moved them, before having faced great hardship. This isn't a conclusion drawn from the mantras' content directly, but from their careful composition and thoughtfulness, it becomes clear their composers were, from early on, actually quite intellectually mature.

Another view holds that the Vedas are neither especially modern nor ancient — their true era becomes clear from careful examination of the mantras themselves: their meters, distinguishing stylistic features, and structural conventions all point to a mature compositional era.

Yet another view holds that the Rigveda is not a systematic philosophical text at all, but simply a collection of the earliest hymns — pointing to war-themed suktas and the stories of Sarama, Bhrigu, and Angiras as evidence. Drawing comparisons to Phoenician civilization and its interactions with Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, and Greece, this view holds that linguistic evidence connects ancient Aryan civilization to a broader trade network — the Ganges region once connected to the Mediterranean by water routes now lost to history, explaining why European and Hindu regions later grew disconnected. This remains one hypothesis among several.

original p. 322

The Rigveda's content can be divided several ways: mantras of ordinary/everyday concern, spiritual (adhyatmic) mantras, and practical/ritual mantras. Deity-focused mantras generally aim to please the deities, concerned with sons, progeny, cattle, and similar worldly goods. Spiritual mantras are comparatively few, including cosmological/metaphysical inquiry alongside more worldly questions — genuinely difficult territory, since even certain deity-worship can be understood in either a worldly or spiritual register, and the line between "practical" and "spiritual" mantras isn't always sharp.

Among clearly ritual/practical suktas: the marriage sukta, funeral suktas, and the gambling sukta stand out. Mandala 10's Yama-sukta (the Yama-Yami dialogue) addresses matters connected to marriage and kinship.

One striking marriage-sukta verse has the bride declare her own domestic authority:

"...having pleased my husband's mind, may I experience happiness; I have made no vow against a shared household. Aryama, Bhaga, Savitri, and Purandhi and the other deities have placed the role of household-deity upon me alone." (~10.85.46)

This closing verse of the marriage sukta reveals how sacred marriage was held to be in a woman's worldly life, and elsewhere she declares her wish for authority above all other women of the household — the mother-in-law, the daughters-in-law, and other kin — a natural desire for one's own rightful domain (~10.85.46).

The marriage sukta connects to nearly every important rule governing the institution — a rare and carefully composed sukta deserving special mention.

Genuinely historically-informative suktas, however, are few. Where they exist, they generally serve to illuminate some royal lineage's history, praising a king's generosity or Indra's favor, revealing how far kings honored the deities and giving the historical basis for the Purohita's role — the rishis maintaining their relationship with the deities through devotion and the expectation of generous gifts in return. (~7.18; 6.16 series; 1.2; 4.5, etc.)

original p. 323

Danastuti (praise-of-gift) hymns praise the donor's qualities, name the gift itself, and record the donor's lineage, the poet's own name, family, and gotra (see 5.61.5-6; 4.2.10, etc.).

A famous humorous sukta (10.108[?] — Gambler's Lament) portrays a compulsive gambler's addiction with real wit — some read it as pure humor, others more seriously, but either way it connects to the gambler's own household troubles and his wife, serving as a genuine warning against gambling's material and moral dangers.

On women, a few notable verses appear:

"A woman does not walk an easy path." (8.33.17) "There is no such thing as friendship with a woman; her heart is like a hyena's heart." (10.95.15) "Many women, on many occasions, surpass men." (5.60.6, 2)

It's also noted (10.39.14) that young women are courted for the sake of wealth.

Following the Nyaya tradition, the Atharvaveda-adjacent material includes necessary medicinal plants and remedies for physical weakness and disease:

"This is a medicine for every disease." (10.97.6)

Indra restores a skin-disease-afflicted woman to health (8.90; 10.14.1, 3); one at death's door is saved (10.18.2, 8); a woman seeking to marry a man drives off her rival and binds him to her (10.145); and a woman awaiting her lover casts all the household to sleep (4.54.5-8).

Finally, Brahmodyas are a form of riddle-hymn — describing someone's qualities rather than naming them directly. In one set of mantras (~8.4[?]), the unnamed deities are, in sequence, Indra, Rudra, Vishnu, and the Ashvins — inferable from description alone, and relatively easy riddles. Far harder Brahmodyas apply this technique to earth and sky, sun and moon, wind, cloud, and rain — Sukta 1.164 being the prime example.

Chapter Twenty-Two — The Rigveda: Its Doctrine

original p. 324

As discussed earlier, the great majority of Rigveda suktas connect to some doctrine or belief tied to the deities — determining a sukta's context, its divine connection, and its dedicated deity requires real care. Two aspects of the Rigveda's content deserve special note. First: these mantras of praise (stuti) each belonged to a specific rishi — not every rishi's mantra held equal renown, and what survives as "the Rigveda's view" is really a merger of many individual views across a long period, so any general statement about its "intent" necessarily glosses over real historical variation, capturing only shared, common qualities.

One view holds that the Vedic-era Aryans, being entirely uncivilized, were simply awestruck by natural phenomena, personifying nature and composing hymns to praise the cattle-wealth they possessed. I cannot fully accept this — the claim of extreme primitiveness, however often repeated, doesn't hold up.

Even granting limited planning, the rishis clearly composed with real worldly awareness — their careful attention to meter and structure, each mantra crafted with a specific purpose, each deity praised to secure favor for a particular yajna, mantras revised and refined over time, and appropriate mantras composed as community needs demanded within inherited compositional conventions (1.104.1; 1.63.1[?]; 3.16.7, etc.) — none of this is the work of uncivilized, primitive people. This is my counter-argument.

The Vedic doctrine's most important trait, and its practical value, lies in its embodiment of ritual action (karma) — of great use to practitioners and result-seekers alike. The Rigveda's genuine poetic spirit suggests an era where sacrificial practice was already well-established and mature...

original p. 325

...the ritual acts of yajnas — composed with a poet's rhythmic care, or sung with a warrior's rallying spirit — sought longevity, wealth, fame, sons, and cattle for the community through fire-offerings and Soma-libations (see e.g. 1.1.8; 1.1.9).

The Rigveda, being primarily connected to the Purohita class, naturally reflects their own worldview — where priestly matters took priority, devotion to the deities was steadfast, and prayer went well beyond basic subsistence. In war, kings prayed for victory through their Purohita, pleasing their chosen deity and considering it improper to abandon that deity for a rival one once devotion had been pledged. Mandala 7's suktas show Vasishtha's own royal patron relying jointly on Indra and Varuna for aid in the same battle — even while helping one side, no hesitation existed about opposing the other:

"Hear my prayer, all-knowing Indra; look upon these battle-difficulties. Many pray to you; I too pray, trusting in you." (7.18.1)

This confirms that faith in the deities, mediated through the Purohita, was believed capable of securing victory — righteousness and divine reliance together constituting the true path to success.

Purohitas performing yajnas would receive a tenth share (dakshina) of what was gained from the king, offering divine assistance in return — a mutual relationship where both sides had to remain satisfied for the arrangement to succeed. Generous praise-gifts to Purohitas are recorded as Danastutis.

In the Vedic era, deities were not enshrined in temples for worship, nor worshipped individually within households — only invoked in sequence during yajnas and pleased through Soma-offerings and similar rites. Among the deities, Agni and Indra held the highest importance; a full treatment of all the deities appears elsewhere in this book. This concludes Chapter Twenty-Two.

Chapter Twenty-Three — Social Life in the Vedic Era

original p. 326

Modern researchers, using comparative philology, have established with reasonable confidence that Indians, Persians, Greeks, Germans, and Italians all once formed a single unified group, living together in one place. The Avesta's language shows close similarity to the Rigveda's language, indicating that, in ancient times, one group split off, another remained, and both continued residing side by side for a long period. Later, the Hindus entered India specifically. It can be determined, with reasonable precision, from the names of rivers appearing in the Rigveda, which places the Aryans first settled. Following the Ganga river's route, further eastward-region rivers' names occur less frequently. The Sindhu and its own tributary rivers — the Vitasta (present-day Jhelum), Asikni (Chenab), Parushni (Ravi), Vipas (Beas), and Shutudri (Sutlej) — all appear by these names in the Rigveda. The Ganga river's name appears just once, in a single place (10.75.5). This suggests that, when much of the Rigveda was composed, the Aryans had not yet penetrated as far as the Ganga's banks. The Kubha (Kabul) and Suvastu (the Swat) river-names also occur, confirming that at the time much of the Rigveda was composed, the Aryans were settled across the region spanning Kabul to the Punjab.

Villages, forts, and cities built of brick are also mentioned, alongside forts of stone (1.104.1; 1.44.10; 7.6.5; 7.15.14; 7.18.1[?]) — though whether these were the deities' own fortresses or genuinely fortified structures used decoratively remains a debated point.

Among people's chief occupations were agriculture and animal husbandry. Every deity is prayed to, at some point, for crops, wealth, horses, and cattle — praying for cattle in particular is especially common. People valued these as their wealth. No other name for wealth appears elsewhere in the Veda quite so often — only in the Atharvaveda does "Akshaya" (imperishable wealth) occur as a term.

प्रीहिमत्रं यवमत्रमथो माषमथो तिलम् । (Atharva — 8.70[?].2)

original p. 327

Roasted grains and crushed handfuls mixed with ghee were offered to deities (2.1[?].5; 2.13.2[?]). Various domesticated animal species are named, especially oxen and horses (5.19.3; 5.83.7; 10.121[?]); ox-meat cooking is occasionally mentioned too (5.5[?].2; 8.3[?].3; 8.66.10) — though whether such practices reflect universal custom or occasional exception is hard to determine, much as with Soma consumption itself, since some later ritual texts explicitly restrict it.

Rishis of this era excelled in chariot construction, and skilled craftsmen (kushalaru) practiced this trade — chariot-building imagery recurs frequently in poetic metaphor. Weaving was likewise common, its imagery ("thread") also used metaphorically in mantra composition. Woodworking/carpentry, leatherwork, and metalwork are all mentioned as Aryan crafts.

Trade is scarcely mentioned, and seafaring activity even less so — what boat-usage appears seems oriented toward river-crossing rather than genuine sea voyages.

Marriage was arranged by the father; widow remarriage appears to have been considered acceptable. Details of husband-wife relations are scarce, but the wife held a significant position within the household — "household deity, mistress of the household" — with authority over domestic affairs; there's little evidence of exclusive husbandly authority in this domain. A house without a mistress, it's noted, could not properly function; a newly arrived young bride becomes the household's own yajamana (ritual mistress). This blessing was offered to a bride newly arriving in her husband's home:

सम्राज्ञी श्वशुरे भव सम्राज्ञी श्वश्र्वां भव । ननान्दरि सम्राज्ञी भव सम्राज्ञी अधि देवृषु ॥ (10.85.46)

"Be sovereign over your father-in-law; be sovereign over your mother-in-law. Be sovereign over your sister-in-law; be sovereign over your brothers-in-law too."

That is: may you hold authority over your in-laws — meaning, may you look after their welfare (yogakshema). Elsewhere, further—

original p. 328

"From the very beginning, before the father-in-law's time itself, this position remains fixed" — meaning her authority over mother-in-law and household affairs was established from the outset. That is: women held an honored place in domestic life, connected to maintaining household happiness (10.85).

On the wider question of women's authority, the term "kshatriya" (used elsewhere for the warrior class) and terms for "wife" appear used in overlapping ways (1.109.2[?]; 1.126.1[?]; 1.109.8; 10.86.9[?]; 6.75.19; 8.75.9[?]; 10.95.1[?]). A woman is described achieving independence by bringing an errant husband back under control (10.34.11-12[?]).

Marriage aimed at mutual companionship and establishing a lineage — prayers commonly requested sons for one's family, with the eldest son apparently holding special priority (including a special inheritance share), though whether daughters held inheritance rights is unclear. No evidence suggests anything but genuine mutual affection within Vedic-era families.

Whether monogamy or polygamy was the established norm isn't entirely clear — some Rigveda passages place no restriction on plural wives (4.5.5[?]), and specific status for co-wives appears unfixed in places (10.72.8[?]; 10.71.4[?]).

Remarriage after divorce doesn't appear to have been common practice — marriage was held to be a supremely sacred act, and mantras generally express the wish that a woman's marriage remain permanently fixed to one husband, without dissolution:

कुणस्सिद्ध्योष्णा कुण वस्त्रोऽरश्चिना कुहाभिसिक्तं करकः कुहोषतुः । को वां शयुत्रा विधवेव देवरं मर्यं न योषा कृणुते सधस्थ आ ॥ (10.40.2)

(A difficult passage concerning marital fidelity and the comparison of an abandoned woman to a widow turning to a brother-in-law; precise construction uncertain at this resolution.)

Manu (9.46.20) similarly permits a widow to marry her husband's brother (devara) under certain circumstances — but the same chapter (9.46.10) restricts such a marriage to lasting only until she bears a son.

Abandonment of marital duty and infidelity are both known to have occurred (10.34.4; 10.40.6; 3.53.1), and one mantra describes women as headstrong and fickle-minded (8.33.17).

original p. 329

Infidelity was believed to bring destruction, with the deities prayed to for the ruin of an unfaithful person's lineage (1.167.4[?]; 4.5.5; 4.5.6[?]).

People lived organized in tribal groups. Each tribe was distinct and independent, joining forces only temporarily during war; each had its own king with his own lineage, and each royal household maintained its own Purohita (2.42.1[?]; 2.11.8[?]) — kings gave a portion of earned wealth to Indra as tribute, while the Purohita's task was to pray for wealth and the destruction of enemies, receiving a share of royal gifts in return, as many Danastuti hymns attest (10.148[?]).

On deity-worship, already discussed — but whether Vedic-era practice included idol worship remains genuinely unclear. Max Müller and others hold that it did not:

"The Religion of the Veda knows of no idols. The worship of idols in India is a secondary formation, a later degradation of the more primitive worship of ideal gods."

That is: no image-worship ritual is mentioned in the Vedic era; idol-worship developed later, a corruption of an earlier, more imaginative form of worship. Dr. Bollensen opposes this view, citing passages (3.53.8; 8.83.8[?]) suggesting deities were understood to have physical bodies and hold weapons — a genuinely unresolved scholarly question.

On Caste (Varna)

The caste system is one of Hindu society's most defining, enduring features, still distinctly maintained today by inherited custom — and some scholars hold that caste distinction is not a very ancient feature at all, but a later development in our country's history.

Indeed, through Mandala 9, the Rigveda shows no established basis for caste distinctions. Only in Mandala 10's Purusha Sukta (10.90) does the fourfold varna system first appear:

ब्राह्मणोऽस्य मुखमासीद्बाहू राजन्यः कृतः । ऊरू तदस्य यद्वैश्यः पद्भ्यां शूद्रो अजायत ॥ (RV 10.90.12)

ब्राह्मणोऽस्य मुखम् आसीद् बाहू राजन्यः कृतः । ऊरू तद् अस्य यद् वैश्यः पद्भ्यां शूद्रो अजायत ॥ brāhmaṇo'sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ | ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata ||

"The Brahmin was his mouth; the Rajanya (Kshatriya) was made his arms; that which became the Vaishya was his thighs; from his feet the Shudra was born."

original p. 330

...from the Virat-Purusha's face the Brahmin was born, from his arms the king (Kshatriya), from his thigh-region the Vaishya, and from his feet the Shudra.

Some scholars hold that this sukta stands apart from the Rigveda's general flow and style, suggesting a later addition — though others dispute this. One theory holds that the body-part imagery reflects a functional division: Brahmins, born of the mouth/head, took up knowledge and learning, becoming particularly devoted to deity-worship and governance-adjacent affairs; those relying on physical strength for society's protection became Kshatriyas; trade and agriculture fell to Vaishyas; and whatever labor supported the body's basic needs and other humbler tasks fell to Shudras. This suggests occupational necessity, rather than everyone being assigned a single fixed task from birth, gave rise to these four divisions naturally. Puranic and related texts, however, state plainly that the four-varna division is fixed by birth (janmataḥ siddha).

The Gita states:

"चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः"

"The fourfold varna was created by me, according to the division of qualities (guna) and actions (karma)."

That is: the four varnas were organized according to their respective qualities and work — not fixed by birth as such. But since, over time, the qualities of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra families came to be inherited by birth in practice, some argue — based on the word "sṛṣṭam" ("created") in this very verse — that the division was intended as a birth-based lineage system from the very beginning. This concludes the chapter's discussion of the Rigveda's social world.

Chapter Twenty-Four — Special Grammatical Features in the Rigveda

original p. 331

Comparing Vedic Sanskrit with classical Sanskrit reveals considerable differences on both sides — verb-forms and noun-declensions differ significantly, though case-formation still follows one underlying method, with a more restricted range of alternate forms than classical usage typically shows (two or three variant forms for a single word being common). Verb (tiṅanta) forms differ slightly too; the Veda makes wide use of potential/subjunctive-like mood-marking, present in classical Sanskrit only in more limited, indicative-restricted form. The Veda's sandhi (euphonic combination) rules show many differences from classical practice — a few key points are examined below.
