The Culminating Conclusion

एवं सत्यध्वर्युसंबन्धि यजुर्वेदे निष्पन्नं यज्ञशरीरमुपजीव्य शेषभूता स्तोत्रशस्त्ररूपा सानगाथा इतरेण वेद...

एवं सत्य् अध्वर्यु-संबन्धि यजुर्वेदे निष्पन्नं यज्ञ-शरीरम् उपजीव्य शेष-भूता स्तोत्र-शस्त्र-रूपा सानगाथा इतरेण वेद... evaṃ saty adhvaryu-saṃbandhi yajurvede niṣpannaṃ yajña-śarīram upajīvya śeṣa-bhūtā stotra-śastra-rūpā sānagāthā itareṇa veda...

"Thus it being established that the yajna's own body is formed specifically within the Yajurveda, connected to the Adhvaryu — the remaining elements, in the form of hymn (stotra) and recitation (shastra), are supplied by the other Vedas..."

This is the pivotal conclusion of the entire discussion: since the yajna's essential body/structure resides in the Yajurveda, and the Rigveda and Samaveda merely furnish its accompanying hymn and recitation elements, the Yajurveda holds the dominant, foundational role — justifying why it was explained first. And since the Samaveda's own verses are entirely drawn from the Rigveda, between these latter two, the Rigveda rightly comes next — which is precisely the task Sayana now undertakes.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...veda with regard to the performance of sacrifices. "The [name] 'Mantras' comes from manana [thinking]; 'Chandas' from chadana [to cover]; 'Stoma' from stavana [praising] and 'Yajus' from yajati [to sacrifice]." [Ni. VII. 3, 6].

This being so, the body of the sacrifice is formed in the Yajur Veda, the Veda of the Adhvaryu priest: the hymn and lesson required by the sacrifice as parts of it are filled up by the other two Vedas. Here then the Yajur Veda is dominant, and it has been properly first explained. For the rest, since the Sama verses are all taken from the Rig Veda, of these two the Rig Veda should be explained first, and this accordingly is what we are about to do.

Chapter 4. Purva-pakṣa — Since the Veda Has No Defining Marks or Proofs, No Such Text as "the Veda" Exists

Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu illaddarinda vēdavemba granthavē illavendu pūrvapakṣavu" Printed pages 362–367 of the source.

original p. 362

द्वैयेन पूर्ग्येके इत्येव जीव्यस्य यजुर्वेदस्य प्रभुगुण व्याख्यानं युक्तम् । तत ऊध्वं साम्नामृगात्मकत्वादुभयोर्मध्ये प्रभुमके ऋग्व्याख्यानं युक्तमिति सिद्धे इदानीं व्याख्यायते ॥

(Concluding: since the yajna's essential body resides in the Yajurveda, its commentary rightly came first; and since the Samaveda is itself constituted of Riks, between the Rigveda and Samaveda, the Rigveda rightly comes next — this now being settled, the Rigveda-commentary is undertaken.)

Keeping this reasoning in mind, Yaska Maharshi clarifies the etymology showing that the Yajurveda — the Adhvaryu's own Veda — holds the power to establish the yajna's essential form: "manana" (reflection) yields "mantra"; "chādana" (covering/binding together) yields "chandas"; "praising" yields "stoma." The yajna's principal form must therefore arise from the Yajurveda, with the Rik and Sama Vedas serving a supporting, auxiliary role. This establishes that the Yajurveda holds primacy for yajna-performance — justifying its commentary being composed first. And since every Samaveda mantra is itself found within the Rigveda, between these remaining two, the Rigveda rightly comes next. Accordingly, the Rigveda-commentary now begins.

The Rigveda-Bhashya Proper Begins: A Logical Challenge to the Veda's Very Existence

लक्षणप्रमाणाभ्यां वेदस्यावधारण इति पूर्वे पक्षे—

lakṣaṇa-pramāṇābhyāṃ vedasyāvadhāraṇa iti pūrve pakṣe—

"In the objection concerning the determination of the Veda through definition and proof—"

ननु वेद एव तावन्नास्ति । कुतस्तदवान्तरभेद ऋग्वेदः ? तथा हि । कोऽयं वेदो नाम ? न हि तत्र लक्षणं प्रमाणं वास्ति । न च तदुभयमृते किंचित्सिध्यति । लक्षणप्रमाणाभ्यां हि वस्तुसिद्धिरिति न्यायविदां मतम् ॥

ननु वेद एव तावन् नास्ति । कुतस् तद्-अवान्तर-भेद ऋग्वेदः । तथा हि । कोऽयं वेदो नाम । न हि तत्र लक्षणं प्रमाणं वास्ति । न च तद्-उभयम् ऋते किंचित् सिध्यति । लक्षण-प्रमाणाभ्यां हि वस्तु-सिद्धिर् इति न्याय-विदां मतम् ॥ nanu veda eva tāvan nāsti | kutas tad-avāntara-bheda ṛgvedaḥ | tathā hi | ko'yaṃ vedo nāma | na hi tatra lakṣaṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ vāsti | na ca tad-ubhayam ṛte kiṃcit sidhyati | lakṣaṇa-pramāṇābhyāṃ hi vastu-siddhir iti nyāya-vidāṃ matam ||

"Objection: The Veda itself does not exist at all — how then can there be a subdivision of it called the Rigveda? Consider: what is this thing called 'Veda'? Neither a definition (lakṣaṇa) nor a proof (pramāṇa) of it exists. And without both of these, nothing whatsoever can be established — for it is the settled view of logicians (Naiyayikas) that the establishment of any entity requires both definition and proof."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

But may it not be said, There is no such thing as Veda, how can there be a part of it known as the Rig Veda? For what is this you call Veda? You cannot define it: you cannot prove that as defined it exists. And without such definition and proof nothing is established. Do not logicians assert that things are established by definition and proof of existence?

original p. 363

...a distinguishing mark by which something can be pointed out. "Pramana" (proof) means stating separately, "this object bears such-and-such a mark" — the means by which an object's true nature is determined through its own characteristic marks. Logicians hold that a thing's real nature becomes known only through such proofs. Since the Veda has neither a definition nor a proof, how can the entity called "Veda" be established to exist at all?

First attempted definition, and its refutation:

प्रत्यक्षानुमानागमेषु प्रमाणाविशेषेण किमो वेद इति तल्लक्षणमिति चेन्न, मनुस्मादिस्मृतिष्वातिव्याप्तेः । समयबलेन सम्यगदृष्टानुभवसाधनसमिति अस्यागमलक्षणस्य तास्स्वपि सद्भावात् ।

प्रत्यक्षानुमानागमेषु प्रमाणाविशेषेण किम् एष वेद इति तल्-लक्षणम् इति चेन् न, मन्व्-आदि-स्मृतिष्व् अतिव्याप्तेः । समय-बलेन सम्यग्-अदृष्टानुभव-साधन-समितिः अस्यागम-लक्षणस्य तास्व् अपि सद्भावात् । pratyakṣānumānāgameṣu pramāṇāviśeṣeṇa kim eṣa veda iti tal-lakṣaṇam iti cen na, manv-ādi-smṛtiṣv ativyāpteḥ | samaya-balena samyag-adṛṣṭānubhava-sādhana-samitiḥ asyāgama-lakṣaṇasya tāsv api sadbhāvāt |

"If you say that, among the three valid means of knowledge — perception, inference, and revealed word (āgama) — the Veda is defined as the last of these, we reply: no. This over-extends to the Smritis of Manu and others as well, since the accepted definition of 'āgama' — 'that which serves as the means for correctly apprehending what is unseen (adṛṣṭa)' — applies equally to those Smritis."

Second attempted definition, and its refutation:

अपौरुषेयत्वे सतीति विशेषणादोष इति चेन्न, वेदस्यापि परमेश्वरनिर्मितत्वेन पौरुषेयत्वात् ।

अपौरुषेयत्वे सतीति विशेषणाद् दोष इति चेन् न, वेदस्यापि परमेश्वर-निर्मितत्वेन पौरुषेयत्वात् । apauruṣeyatve satīti viśeṣaṇād doṣa iti cen na, vedasyāpi parameśvara-nirmitatvena pauruṣeyatvāt |

"If you say that adding the qualifier 'provided it is non-human in origin (apauruṣeya)' removes this flaw, we reply: no. For the Veda too, having been made by Parameshvara (the Supreme Person), is thereby of personal/human origin (pauruṣeya)."

Third attempted definition, and its refutation:

शरीरधारिजीवनिर्मितत्वाभावादपौरुषेयत्वमिति चेन्न, सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुष इत्यादिभिः प्रसिद्धः शरीरित्वात् । कर्मफलदानशरीरधारणाभावमात्रेणापौरुषेयत्वे, विनश्वरशरीरग्रहणवार्यादितत्त्वात् । ऋग्वेद एवास्य शरीरम् (Shatapatha Brahmana 8.4.3)

शरीर-धारि-जीव-निर्मितत्वाभावाद् अपौरुषेयत्वम् इति चेन् न, सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुष इत्य् आदिभिः प्रसिद्धः शरीरित्वात् । कर्म-फल-दान-शरीर-धारणाभाव-मात्रेणापौरुषेयत्वे, विनश्वर-शरीर-ग्रहण-वार्यादितत्त्वात् । ऋग्वेद एवास्य शरीरम् । śarīra-dhāri-jīva-nirmitatvābhāvād apauruṣeyatvam iti cen na, sahasraśīrṣā puruṣa ity ādibhiḥ prasiddhaḥ śarīritvāt | karma-phala-dāna-śarīra-dhāraṇābhāva-mātreṇāpauruṣeyatve, vinaśvara-śarīra-grahaṇa-vāryāditattvāt | ṛgveda evāsya śarīram |

"If you say that 'non-human origin' means 'not made by an embodied living being,' we reply: no. It is well established, from texts such as 'the thousand-headed Purusha,' that this same being does possess a body. And if 'non-human origin' is meant only in the sense of not taking on a body for the purpose of dispensing karmic fruits, that distinction concerns merely the taking on of a perishable body, among other such considerations — for indeed, 'the Rigveda itself is his body' (Shatapatha Brahmana 8.4.3)."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

If you attempt to define what you mean by Veda by saying that of the three kinds of evidence, perception, inference, and revealed Scripture, it is the last, that will not do. The definition is too wide, including, as it would do, the smritis of Manu and others. For by universal consent revealed Scripture is defined to be that which is an instrument of the right apprehension of things not evident to the senses. And such a definition applies to these smritis as well.

You propose to add, "provided it be not of human origin," and think in that way to make your definition faultless. No. For the Veda, too, made as it was by the Man Paramesvara, the Supreme Lord, is of human origin.

You will perhaps next say that by "not of human origin" you mean "not made by a corporeal living being." But no. Since from texts like "The Man has a thousand heads," it is clear that this Lord too, has a body.

original p. 364

Regarding the three proofs of knowledge — perception (प्रत्यक्ष pratyakṣa), inference (अनुमान anumāna), and revealed word (आगम āgama) — even if the last of these, "āgama," is proposed as the Veda's defining mark, this fails: since Manu's and other Smritis also possess this same "āgama" quality, the flaw of over-extension (अतिव्याप्ति ativyāpti) results, since they too would have to count as "Veda." A sound definition (लक्षण lakṣaṇa) must avoid three classical flaws:

  • अतिव्याप्ति (ativyāpti, over-extension): the stated mark applies to other things too (e.g., defining milk as "that which is white" also catches lime).
  • अव्याप्ति (avyāpti, under-extension): the stated mark fails to cover part of the intended thing (e.g., defining horses by "red color" excludes horses of other colors).
  • असंभव (asambhava, impossibility): stating a quality the thing doesn't actually possess at all.

Whatever definition of "Veda" one proposes free of these three flaws will, since Manu's and similar Smritis share the same "āgama" quality, still fall into ativyāpti. The characteristic of being "āgama" therefore cannot serve as the Veda's true defining mark.

Fourth attempted definition, and its refutation (regarding embodiment):

If you say the "body" in question is specifically one produced by the karmic results of a past life — and that the Veda's own author has no such body, which is what you really mean by "non-human origin" — this too fails. For the Vedas are described as produced through such beings as Agni, Vayu, and Aditya: "The Rigveda was born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya" — confirming that Parameshvara composed the Vedas at the instigation of Agni and the others.

Fifth attempted definition, and its refutation (mantra + brahmana):

You might next suggest that "Veda" simply names the collected body of mantras and brahmanas. This too fails — since no one has yet clearly established what precisely constitutes a "mantra" or a "brahmana." It is therefore clear that no adequate definition of the term "Veda" exists.

If, finally, you propose that "apauruṣeyatva" (non-human origin) itself simply is the Veda's defining mark — since the Veda is not made by any finite person — this too fails, for the Veda is itself [made by] Parameshvara...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

But, you say, the kind of body you mean is one which is the result of the works of a previous life: the author of the Veda has no such body, and that is what you mean when you say that it is "not of human origin." No again. For the Vedas were produced by such living beings as Agni, Vayu, Aditya. (p. 6) Witness such texts as "The Rig Veda was born from Agni, the Yajur Veda from Vayu, the Sama Veda from Aditya." From which it must be recognised that the Lord made the Veda at the instance of Agni and others.

Another definition you may suggest is that by Veda is meant a collection of sayings made up of mantras and brahmanas. This will not do. For no one has yet been able to say what is a mantra, and what a brahmana. It is clear then that there is no adequate definition of the term Veda.

original p. 365

...since it is made by someone, the quality of "personal origin" (pauruṣeyatva) necessarily follows — and countless texts are made by persons, so why should the Veda deserve any special regard on that basis? If the Veda is instead called apauruṣeya because no embodied living being made it — that too fails, since the Veda itself states "sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" (the thousand-headed Purusha), affirming Ishvara's own possession of a body. And if apauruṣeya means merely "not made by one embodied through karmic result," this too fails: the Veda states it was born from special beings — Agni, Vayu, Aditya — the Rigveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya — meaning Parameshvara, who impels Agni and the others, is himself the true author of the Shruti. And if "Veda" simply names the collected group of mantras and brahmanas, that too fails, since no one has ever clearly determined what precisely qualifies as a "mantra" or a "brahmana." The Veda, in short, has no valid defining characteristic whatsoever.

Turning to proof (pramana):

नापि तस्यावे प्रमाणं पश्यामः । ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमथर्वणं चतुर्थम् (छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् ७.१.२) इत्यादिवाक्यं प्रमाणमिति चेन्न, तस्यापि वाक्यस्य वेदान्तःपातित्वेनात्माश्रयत्वप्रसंगात् । न खलु निपुणोऽपि स्वस्कन्धमारोढुं प्रभवति ।

नापि तस्यावे प्रमाणं पश्यामः । ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदम् अथर्वणं चतुर्थम् इत्य् आदि-वाक्यं प्रमाणम् इति चेन् न, तस्यापि वाक्यस्य वेदान्तःपातित्वेनात्माश्रयत्व-प्रसङ्गात् । न खलु निपुणोऽपि स्वस्कन्धम् आरोढुं प्रभवति । nāpi tasyāve pramāṇaṃ paśyāmaḥ | ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam atharvaṇaṃ caturtham ity ādi-vākyaṃ pramāṇam iti cen na, tasyāpi vākyasya vedāntaḥpātitvenātmāśrayatva-prasaṅgāt | na khalu nipuṇo'pi svaskandham āroḍhuṃ prabhavati |

"Nor do we see any proof of its existence either. If you say that a statement such as 'O Lord, I study the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth, the Atharvana' (Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.2) serves as proof — we reply: no. Since that very statement, being itself contained within the Veda, falls into the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). Indeed, no one, however skilled, can climb upon his own shoulder."

वेद एव द्विजातीनां निःश्रेयसकरः पर इत्यादिस्मृतिवाक्यं प्रमाणमिति चेन्न, तस्याप्यश्रुतिमूलत्वेन निराकृतत्वात् । प्रत्यक्षादिकं शंकितुमप्ययोग्यम् । वेदविषया तु लोकप्रसिद्धिः सार्वजनीनापि नीलं नभ इत्यादिवच्च । तस्माल्लक्षणप्रमाणरहितस्य वेदस्य सद्भावे नांगीकार्यं शक्यते इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥

वेद एव द्विजातीनां निःश्रेयसकरः पर इत्य् आदि-स्मृति-वाक्यं प्रमाणम् इति चेन् न, तस्याप्य् अश्रुति-मूलत्वेन निराकृतत्वात् । प्रत्यक्षादिकं शङ्कितुम् अप्य् अयोग्यम् । वेद-विषया तु लोक-प्रसिद्धिः सार्वजनीनापि नीलं नभ इत्य् आदि-वच् च । तस्माल् लक्षण-प्रमाण-रहितस्य वेदस्य सद्भावे नाङ्गीकार्यं शक्यत इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥ veda eva dvijātīnāṃ niḥśreyasakaraḥ para ity ādi-smṛti-vākyaṃ pramāṇam iti cen na, tasyāpy aśruti-mūlatvena nirākṛtatvāt | pratyakṣādikaṃ śaṅkitum apy ayogyam | veda-viṣayā tu loka-prasiddhiḥ sārvajanīnāpi nīlaṃ nabha ity ādi-vac ca | tasmāl lakṣaṇa-pramāṇa-rahitasya vedasya sadbhāve nāṅgīkāryaṃ śakyata iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||

"If you say that a Smriti-statement such as 'the Veda alone is the supreme means of ultimate good for the twice-born' serves as proof — we reply: no. Since this too, being rooted in Shruti itself, is rejected for the same reason. Perception and similar means aren't even worth considering here. As for the Veda's popular renown among people — however universal, it is like the common expression 'the sky is blue' [mere convention, not genuine proof]. Therefore, the existence of a Veda lacking both definition and proof cannot be accepted. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

This concludes the objection (purva-paksha). Sayana's own resolution follows next.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Nor do we see any proof of the existence of such a thing. You would like perhaps to quote by way of such proof the text, "Lord, I study the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, and the fourth, the Atharva Veda." In vain. That very verse is in the Veda, and you fall into the vice of putting forward a thing to support itself. Now, no man, however clever, can mount his own shoulder.

Nor is such a smriti as, for example, "The Veda is the only means of happiness for the twiceborn," a proof of the kind we want. It must be rejected for the same reason, as being based upon the aforesaid text of the Veda.

original p. 366

...we see no proof at all that those Vedas exist. If it's argued that the statement—

ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येष्मि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमाथर्वणं चतुर्थम् । ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyeṣmi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham | (Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.2)

"O Lord, I now study the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth, the Atharvaveda"

—clearly proves the Vedas exist — that's not possible, since this very statement is itself part of the Veda (occurring within the Chandogya Upanishad), producing the fallacy of self-dependence: if the Veda's own authority is in question, how can a statement that is itself part of the Veda serve as proof? No man, however skilled, can climb up and sit upon his own shoulder.

If we cite the Yajnavalkya-Smriti's statement, "the Veda alone is the highest means of ultimate good for the twice-born," as proof that the Vedas exist — that too fails. All Smritis are rooted in Shruti — that is, they follow Shruti itself — so the very same fallacy of self-dependence arises here too. The Vedas' existence cannot be established through Smriti statements either.

In everyday affairs, no one can deny things visible to the eye — so shouldn't everyone accept perceptual proof? Should we accept the Veda's existence simply because the subject is widely renowned, and everyone visibly engages with Vedic matters? No — because many things considered "perceptually evident" in ordinary life turn out to rest on mere illusion, just as it is commonly (but falsely) held that the sky is blue-colored. Is this anything but illusion? Therefore, there is no valid basis for accepting that an entity called "Veda," lacking both definition and proof, exists. This concludes the objection (purva-paksha).

A Methodological Note: Purva-Paksha and Siddhanta

When examining any subject, pointing out its flaws and objections through careful, reasoned argument to show "this is not correct" is called the purva-paksha (prior view, or objection). Correspondingly, resolving those very flaws and objections one by one, with sound reasoning, and firmly establishing the subject's true nature, is called the siddhanta (established conclusion). To properly grasp the subjects expounded in the shastras, tradition holds that the purva-paksha should be presented first, with the siddhanta established afterward. This purva-...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The three kinds of evidence—perception, inference and Scripture, are not to be so much as thought of here: while, as for common notoriety, the common notoriety in regard to the Veda, universal as it is, may be as much an error as everybody's belief that the sky is blue.

It is then clear that since the Veda is not capable of definition or proof, it cannot be admitted that there is such a thing. This is the prima facie case.

original p. 367

...-paksha, siddhanta, and related components together form what is called an "adhikarana." Its definition:

विषयोऽविषयश्चेति पूर्वसंपक्षिस्फोत्तरं । निर्णयश्चेति संबद्धं शास्त्रेऽधिकरणं मतम् ॥

"Subject-matter and doubt, together with the objection and its answer, and the determination — this combination is considered an 'adhikarana' in the shastras."

That is: an adhikarana comprises five distinct parts — the subject-matter (vishaya), the doubt (samshaya), the objection (purva-paksha), its answer, and the final determination (siddhanta). Each is examined in turn before the siddhanta is finally established as correct. The Sanskrit continues into a dense technical discussion — concerning how "mantra" and "brahmana" are properly distinguished, and reasoning toward the meaning of "apauruṣeya" — which the source's own English translation below renders in full; given the density of this passage, the English rendering is the more reliable guide to its content at this resolution.

The Resolution (Uttara-Paksha) Begins: Determining the Veda's Definition and Proof

अत्रोच्यते । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मकत्वं तावदुष्टं लक्षणम् । अत एवापस्तम्बो यज्ञपरिभाषायामाह । मन्त्रब्राह्मणयोर्वेदनामधेयमिति (आ. प. १२) । तयोस्तु स्वरूपविवेचने...

अत्रोच्यते । मन्त्र-ब्राह्मणात्मकत्वं तावद् उष्टं लक्षणम् । अत एवापस्तम्बो यज्ञ-परिभाषायाम् आह । मन्त्र-ब्राह्मणयोर् वेद-नामधेयम् इति (आपस्तम्ब यज्ञ-परिभाषा १२) । तयोस् तु स्वरूप-विवेचने... atrocyate | mantra-brāhmaṇātmakatvaṃ tāvad uṣṭaṃ lakṣaṇam | ata evāpastambo yajña-paribhāṣāyām āha | mantra-brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam iti (Āpastamba Yajña-paribhāṣā 12) | tayos tu svarūpa-vivecane...

"To this we reply: the definition of the Veda as consisting of mantras and brahmanas is, in fact, faultless. This is precisely why Apastamba, in his Yajña-paribhāṣā, states: 'The name Veda applies to the mantras and the brahmanas' (Apastamba Yajña-paribhasha 12). As for determining the precise nature of each of these..."

We now state the resolution (samādhāna) to the objection. Calling the body of words comprising mantras and brahmanas "the Veda" is, in fact, a faultless definition. As for the objection that "mantra" and "brahmana" themselves remain undefined — the answer is that whatever the shastra-tradition designates as "mantra" is indeed mantra, and the remainder is brahmana. This is exactly why the great sage Apastamba, in his Yajna-paribhasha-sutra, states: "mantra-brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam" — the name "Veda" applies to both mantras and brahmanas together.

So also we shall make clear in what follows in what sense we take the term "not of human origin." Proofs, too, of the existence of the Veda, of the kind described, sruti, smriti, common notoriety, must be...

Chapter 5. Siddhanta — the Veda Does Have Defining Marks and Proofs; and Why a Commentary Is Needed at All

Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu iveyendu siddhāntasamarthaneyu" Printed pages 368–373 of the source.

original p. 368

This is accepted. This point will be settled further ahead. Similarly, on the question of "apauruṣeyatva," we shall clarify our stated definition later. The three types of proof — shruti (revealed word), smriti (tradition), and loka-vyavahara (common human practice) — must all be accepted together as establishing the Veda's existence.

Consider: jars and similar objects have no self-illuminating power — they depend on other light sources and cannot shine on their own. But does this mean everything luminous must depend on another's help to shine? The sun, moon, and stars shine of their own accord, without needing any external light. A pot's lack of self-illumination doesn't contradict the sun's genuine self-luminosity. Likewise: just because an ordinary human, however skilled, cannot climb onto his own shoulder, does that mean the Veda — possessing unlimited power — cannot illuminate itself the same way? No. The Veda's power is unobstructed, and it can therefore reveal and prove itself, just as it reveals everything else. The fallacy of self-dependence, then, simply does not arise for a text of such undiminished power. As those versed in ancient tradition say of the Veda's own unblunted power:

"The Veda can make clear what has been, what is, and what is to be — what is near, and what is far off."

This being so, proof drawn from Smriti (itself rooted in the Veda), as well as proof drawn from common notoriety (rooted in both Shruti and Smriti), must also be accepted. It therefore stands firmly established that the Veda, duly proven by both definition and proof, cannot be overturned by any skeptic.

A New Objection: Even If the Veda Exists, Is It Authoritative?

ननु अस्तु नाम वेदाख्यः कश्चित् पदार्थः । तथापि नासौ व्याख्यानम् अर्हति । अप्रमाणत्वेनानुपयुक्तत्वात् । न हि वेदः प्रमाणम् । प्रमाणलक्षणस्य तत्र दुःसंपादत्वात् । तथा हि । सम्यक्... nanv astu nāma vedākhyaḥ kaścit padārthaḥ | tathāpi nāsau vyākhyānam arhati | apramāṇatvenānupayuktatvāt | na hi vedaḥ pramāṇam | pramāṇa-lakṣaṇasya tatra duḥsampādatvāt | tathā hi | samyak... (the final compound's exact reading is uncertain at this resolution; the sense is confirmed by the embedded English translation below)

"Very well — we grant that the thing called 'Veda' exists. Still, it isn't worth commenting on, since it carries no authority (pramāṇya), and being without authority, it is of no real use. The Veda is of no authority. Why? Because you cannot show that the defining mark of valid proof (pramāṇa) resides in it." Some define "pramāṇa" as the instrument of right knowledge; others say it is the means of acquiring [knowledge]...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...recognized. It may be that jars and such-like things have no power to illustrate themselves. It does not follow that the sun, moon and stars have no such power. In the same way, though it be granted that a man cannot stand on his own shoulder, nevertheless may the Veda, whose power is undimmed, be able to illustrate itself, as it illustrates other things. For this very reason they who know old tradition speak thus of the unblunted power of the Veda. "The Veda can make clear what has been, what is, and what is to be, what is near and what is afar off." This being so, proof led from the smriti, which is based on the Veda, as well as proof led from common notoriety which is based on both these, must also be admitted. Therefore it stands sure that the Veda, established duly as it is by definition and proof, cannot be overthrown by any of the infidels.

You will next say, I grant that the thing called Veda exists. Still it is not worth a commentary. It is of no authority, and therefore of no use. The Veda is of no authority. Why? Because you cannot show that the characteristic of evidence resides in it. Some define evidence as the instrument of right knowledge. Others say it is the means of acquiring...

अनुभवसाधनं प्रमाणमिति केचिल्लक्षणमाहुः । अपरे तृषष्ट्यधिगतार्थगन्तृ प्रमाणमित्याचक्षते । न चैतदुभयं वेदे संभवति । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मको हि वेदः । तत्र मन्त्राः केचिदबोधकाः । अम्यक् स त इन्द्र ऋष्टिरेको मन्त्रः । (ऋ. १.१०९.३[?]) यद्रिस्मिन् धायि तमपश्यया विददृक्षः । (ऋ. ८.९३.२८[?]) सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतु (ऋ. १०.१०६.६) इत्येवंजातीयान्यन्यान्यपि अपान्तमन्युस्त्रिपलप्रभर्मिः इत्यादयः (ऋ. १०.६८.३[?]) उदाहार्याः । न ह्येतैर्मन्त्रैः किंचिज्ज्ञेयार्थोऽवगच्छते । विशेषतः संभव एव यदा नास्ति तदा तस्य ज्ञानकारणसाधनत्वं च दूरास्थितम् ॥

अनुभव-साधनं प्रमाणम् इति केचिल् लक्षणम् आहुः । अपरे तृ-षष्ट्य्-अधिगतार्थ-गन्तृ प्रमाणम् इत्य् आचक्षते । न चैतद् उभयं वेदे संभवति । मन्त्र-ब्राह्मणात्मको हि वेदः । तत्र मन्त्राः केचिद् अबोधकाः । ... न ह्य् एतैर् मन्त्रैः किंचिज् ज्ञेयार्थोऽवगच्छते । विशेषतः संभव एव यदा नास्ति तदा तस्य ज्ञान-कारण-साधनत्वं च दूरास्थितम् ॥ anubhava-sādhanaṃ pramāṇam iti kecil lakṣaṇam āhuḥ | apare tṛ-ṣaṣṭy-adhigatārtha-gantṛ pramāṇam ity ācakṣate | na caitad ubhayaṃ vede saṃbhavati | mantra-brāhmaṇātmako hi vedaḥ | tatra mantrāḥ kecid abodhakāḥ | ... na hy etair mantraiḥ kiṃcij jñeyārtho'vagacchate | viśeṣataḥ saṃbhava eva yadā nāsti tadā tasya jñāna-kāraṇa-sādhanatvaṃ ca dūrāsthitam ||

"Some define 'pramana' (valid proof) as 'the means of [right] experience.' Others say it is 'that which leads to knowledge of an object not previously known.' Neither definition applies to the Veda. For the Veda consists of mantras and Brahmanas — and among the mantras, some convey no discernible meaning at all: 'amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭir' is one such mantra; 'yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidad ṛkṣaḥ' is another; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu' another; and 'apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmiḥ' and similar besides may be cited. These mantras yield no discernible meaning whatsoever. And when there is no possibility of meaning at all, being a means or cause of knowledge is all the more remote."

We grant, then, that an entity called "Veda" exists — but what need is there to compose commentary on it? Since the Veda carries no valid authority (pramana) and yields no genuine use, commenting on it serves no purpose. The Veda cannot count as "pramana," since it lacks the defining marks proposed for valid proof: some define pramana as "the means productive of correct experience"; others define it as "that which reveals an object not previously known." Neither definition applies to the Veda. As already stated, the Veda consists of two parts — mantra and Brahmana. Taking the mantra portion first: does either definition of pramana apply there? It does not — and several mantras are cited here as examples: "amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭi," "yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidat," "sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu," and "apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmā." These mantras convey no meaning at all. And if they convey no meaning whatsoever, then their serving as a means to correct knowledge becomes, quite obviously, altogether impossible.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...knowledge not held before. Neither of these is found in the Veda. You have said that the Veda is composed of mantras and brahmanas. Now of the mantras some convey no sense at all. One mantra is "amyak sa ta indra rishtih." Another, "yadrismin dhayi tam apasyaya vidat." Another, "srinyeva jarbhari turpharitu." And others such, for example, as "apantamanyus tripalaprabharma," could be cited. These mantras yield no sense at all. But if there be no knowledge at all in these, right knowledge and the means to that, it is obvious, cannot be there.

अधः स्विदासीदुपरि स्विदासीदिति (ऋ. १०.१२९.५) मन्त्रस्य बोधकत्वेऽपि स्थाणुर्वा पुरुषो वेत्यादिवाक्यवत्संदिग्धार्थबोधकत्वान्न प्रामाण्यम् ॥

अधः स्विद् आसीद् उपरि स्विद् आसीद् इति (र्व् १०.१२९.५) मन्त्रस्य बोधकत्वेऽपि स्थाणुर् वा पुरुषो वेत्य् आदि-वाक्यवत् संदिग्धार्थ-बोधकत्वान् न प्रामाण्यम् ॥ adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīd iti (RV 10.129.5) mantrasya bodhakatve'pi sthāṇur vā puruṣo vety ādi-vākyavat saṃdigdhārtha-bodhakatvān na prāmāṇyam ||

"The mantra 'adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt' (was it below, or was it above?) (RV 10.129.5), though it conveys some meaning, conveys only a doubtful, ambiguous sense — like the statement 'is it a post, or is it a man?' — and therefore lacks authority."

Take the mantra "adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt." Even though its words convey a meaning of sorts, it leaves genuine room for doubt — much like asking whether something is a stump or a man. Since it fails to convey a settled, coherent meaning, how could such a mantra carry any authority?

ओषधे त्रायस्वैनमिति (Taittiriya Samhita 1.2.1.1) मन्त्रे दर्भविषयः । (Ashvalayana Grihyasutra 1.12.4) स्वधिते मैनं हिंसीरिति क्षुरविषयः । (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1.3) श्रुणोत ग्रावाण इति पाषाणविषयः । एतेष्वचेतनानां दर्भक्षुरपाषाणानां चेतनवत्संबोधनं श्रूयते । द्वौ चन्द्रौ चन्द्रमसाविति वाक्यवद्विसंवादिबोधकत्वात्प्रामाण्यम् ॥

ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् इति मन्त्रे दर्भ-विषयः । स्वधिते मैनं हिंसीर् इति क्षुर-विषयः । शृणोत ग्रावाण इति पाषाण-विषयः । एतेष्व् अचेतनानां दर्भ-क्षुर-पाषाणानां चेतनवत् सम्बोधनं श्रूयते । द्वौ चन्द्रौ चन्द्रमसाव् इति वाक्यवद् विसंवादि-बोधकत्वात् प्रामाण्यम् ॥ oṣadhe trāyasvainam iti mantre darbha-viṣayaḥ | svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīr iti kṣura-viṣayaḥ | śṛṇota grāvāṇa iti pāṣāṇa-viṣayaḥ | eteṣv acetanānāṃ darbha-kṣura-pāṣāṇānāṃ cetanavat sambodhanaṃ śrūyate | dvau candrau candramasāv iti vākyavad visaṃvādi-bodhakatvāt prāmāṇyam ||

"In the mantra 'oṣadhe trāyasvainam' ('O herb, protect him'), the subject is sacred grass (darbha). 'Svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīḥ' ('O razor, do not harm him') concerns a razor. 'Śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ' ('Hear, O stones') concerns stones. In these, inanimate things — grass, razor, and stones — are addressed as though sentient beings. Such statements, conveying something self-contradictory (like saying 'there are two moons'), cannot carry authority."

That is: the mantras "O herb, protect him" address grass (darbha), "O razor, do not harm him" address a razor, and "Hear, O stones" address stones — in each case treating lifeless objects as if they were conscious beings capable of understanding and acting on a command. This, the objection argues, is as absurd as claiming there are two moons — and such statements therefore cannot possibly be authoritative.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Or take the mantra, "adhah svid asid upari svid asit." This gives a sense, it is true. But it is the same kind of sense as that of such a sentence as, That is either a man or a post. The meaning it yields is a doubt, and how can that be authoritative?

The mantra, "oshadhe trayasvainam" is about grass. That other, "svadhite mainam hinsih" is about a razor, "Srinota gravanah" is about stones. Here you have in the Veda lifeless things like these addressed as if they were sentient beings. But this is as absurd as the saying that there are two moons, and such sayings therefore cannot be authoritative.

एक एव रुद्रो न द्वितीयाय तस्थे (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.6.1) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्रा अधि भूम्याम् (Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1.1) इत्येतयोस्तु मन्त्रयोर्यावच्छिवमहं मौनीति वाक्यवद्व्याघातबोधकत्वादप्रामाण्यम् ॥

एक एव रुद्रो न द्वितीयाय तस्थे (तैत्तिरीय संहिता १.८.६.१) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्रा अधि भूम्याम् (तैत्तिरीय संहिता ४.५.१.१) इत्य् एतयोस् तु मन्त्रयोर् यावच् छिवम् अहं मौनीति वाक्यवद् व्याघात-बोधकत्वाद् अप्रामाण्यम् ॥ eka eva rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.6.1) sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrā adhi bhūmyām (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1.1) ity etayos tu mantrayor yāvac chivam ahaṃ maunīti vākyavad vyāghāta-bodhakatvād aprāmāṇyam ||

"'Rudra is one alone; he does not stand as a second' (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.6.1); and 'thousands upon thousands are the Rudras upon the earth' (Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1.1) — these two mantras convey a plain self-contradiction, like a man declaring aloud, 'I am silent' — and are therefore without authority."

One mantra states that Parameshvara, as Rudra, exists alone with no equal second; another states there are thousands upon thousands of Rudras in the world. These two statements plainly contradict each other — like a man declaring, "as long as I live, I remain silent" — the very act of speaking the claim contradicts it. How can the claim of silence hold, once spoken aloud? A mantra conveying mutually contradictory meanings in this way cannot carry authority.

आप उन्दन्त्विति (Taittiriya Samhita 1.2.1.1) मन्त्रे यजमानस्य क्षौरकाले जलेन शिरसः सेचनं ब्रूते । शुभिके शिर आरोह शोभयन्ती मुखं ममेति मन्त्रे विवाहकाले मंगलाचरणार्थं पुष्पनिर्मितायाः शुभकायाः वरवध्वोः शिरस्यवस्थानं ब्रूते । तयोश्च मन्त्रयोर्लोकप्रसिद्धार्थानुवादित्वादनधिगतार्थगन्तृत्वं नास्ति । तस्मात्स्मृतिभागो न प्रमाणम् ॥

आप उन्दन्त्व् इति मन्त्रे यजमानस्य क्षौर-काले जलेन शिरसः सेचनं ब्रूते । शुभिके शिर आरोह शोभयन्ती मुखं ममेति मन्त्रे विवाह-काले मङ्गलाचरणार्थं पुष्प-निर्मितायाः शुभकायाः वर-वध्वोः शिरश्य् अवस्थानं ब्रूते । तयोश् च मन्त्रयोर् लोक-प्रसिद्धार्थानुवादित्वाद् अनधिगतार्थ-गन्तृत्वं नास्ति । तस्मात् स्मृति-भागो न प्रमाणम् ॥ āpa undantv iti mantre yajamānasya kṣaura-kāle jalena śirasaḥ secanaṃ brūte | śubhike śira āroha śobhayantī mukhaṃ mameti mantre vivāha-kāle maṅgalācaraṇārthaṃ puṣpa-nirmitāyāḥ śubhakāyāḥ vara-vadhvoḥ śiraśy avasthānaṃ brūte | tayoś ca mantrayor loka-prasiddhārthānuvāditvād anadhigatārtha-gantṛtvaṃ nāsti | tasmāt smṛti-bhāgo na pramāṇam ||

"The mantra 'āpa undantu' ('may the waters moisten him') states that water should be poured over the sacrificer's head at the time of shaving. The mantra 'śubhike śira āroha śobhayantī mukhaṃ mama' ('O beautiful one, ascend the head, adorning my face') states that a flower-garland should be placed on the bride's and groom's heads at marriage for an auspicious purpose. Since both mantras merely restate what is already commonly known, they fail to reveal anything previously unknown — and so this ritual-instruction portion too is not valid proof."

That is: these mantras merely describe customs already familiar from ordinary life — pouring water while shaving, placing a garland at a wedding — conveying nothing genuinely new. Since valid proof must reveal something not already known, even this portion of the Veda fails to qualify as pramana.

Self-contradictory sayings of this kind cannot be authoritative.

Chapter 6. The Defining Characteristics of Mantras — Examination of the Related Mimamsa Sutras — Purva-pakṣa and Siddhanta

Original title: "Mantragaḷa lakṣaṇādivicāravu — tatsambandhavāda Mīmāṃsāsūtragaḷa vimarśeyu — pūrvapakṣa mattu siddhāntagaḷu" Printed pages 374–388 of the source.

जलादिदृश्येण शिरःक्षेदनादेर्लोकसिद्ध्यैकपि तदभिमानिदेवतानुग्रहस्यअप्रसिद्धत्वाद्विषयस्यानाज्ञातार्थज्ञापकत्वम् । ततो लक्षणसद्भावात्स्वैर्मन्त्रैर्भागस्य प्रामाण्यम् ॥

जलादि-दृश्येण शिरः-क्षेदनादेर् लोक-सिद्ध्य्-ऐकपि तद्-अभिमानि-देवतानुग्रहस्याप्रसिद्धत्वाद् विषयस्यानाज्ञातार्थ-ज्ञापकत्वम् । ततो लक्षण-सद्भावात् स्वैर् मन्त्रैर् भागस्य प्रामाण्यम् ॥ jalādi-dṛśyeṇa śiraḥ-kṣedanāder loka-siddhy-aikapi tad-abhimāni-devatānugrahasyāprasiddhatvād viṣayasyānājñātārtha-jñāpakatvam | tato lakṣaṇa-sadbhāvāt svair mantrair bhāgasya prāmāṇyam ||

"Though acts such as pouring water while shaving the head are, by themselves, well known in ordinary life, the favor of the deity presiding over that act is not commonly known — so this subject matter does indeed reveal something previously unknown. Therefore, since the defining mark of valid proof is genuinely present, this mantra-portion is authoritative."

This is Sayana's own resolution to the preceding objection: while the outward act described (pouring water, placing a garland) may be common knowledge, the specific divine favor connected to performing it in the prescribed ritual manner is not — and it is precisely this previously-unknown element that the mantra reveals, satisfying the very definition of valid proof.

Turning to Jaimini's Own Mimamsa-Sutras

एकदेवाभिप्रेत्य भगवान् जैमिनिर्मन्त्राधिकरणे मन्त्राणां विवक्षितार्थत्वमसूत्रयत् (Purva Mimamsa 1.2.31-41) । तानि च सूत्राणि क्रमशः प्रवर्तयिष्यामः । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं सूत्रयति ॥

एक-देवाभिप्रेत्य भगवान् जैमिनिर् मन्त्राधिकरणे मन्त्राणां विवक्षितार्थत्वम् असूत्रयत् (पूर्व मीमांसा १.२.३१–४१) । तानि च सूत्राणि क्रमशः प्रवर्तयिष्यामः । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं सूत्रयति ॥ eka-devābhipretya bhagavān jaiminir mantrādhikaraṇe mantrāṇāṃ vivakṣitārthatvam asūtrayat (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 1.2.31–41) | tāni ca sūtrāṇi kramaśaḥ pravartayiṣyāmaḥ | tatra pūrvapakṣaṃ sūtrayati ||

"With this very idea in mind, the venerable Jaimini, in his section on mantras, formulated in sutra-form the doctrine that mantras carry an intended meaning (Purva-Mimamsa 1.2.31–41). We shall now present these sutras in their proper order — beginning with his own formulation of the objection (purva-paksha)."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Lastly, it is true that such acts as the pouring of water over the head at a particular ceremony and the like are matters of common knowledge. But the respect shown to the deity is not. And we have therefore here the act of conveying a truth not known before. For all these reasons the mantra portion of the Veda falls under the definition of what constitutes evidence, and is therefore authoritative.

It is with this in view that the holy Jaimini in his mantra chapter sets out in sutras the doctrine that the mantras recited at the sacrifice are intended to convey a meaning. I shall now cite and explain these Sutras in their order. And first Jaimini sets out the arguments for the doctrine which he intends to controvert.

original p. 375

A "sutra" is a sentence composed with the fewest possible words to convey many subjects concisely, without any loss of meaning. In ancient times, many rishis composed their treatises in this style — the Yoga, Vyakarana, and other philosophical schools (darshanas) are similarly composed, and, being terse, require commentary to unpack. We now turn to explaining several sutras from Jaimini's own Purva-Mimamsa-sutras concerning the meaning of mantras, beginning with the objection (purva-paksha) as Jaimini himself states it.

चेदर्थशास्त्रत (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.31) स विनाभिधेयो यस्य शास्त्रे ब्राह्मणवाक्ये तदर्थशास्त्रम् । तस्माच्चाविशक्तार्थो मन्त्र इत्यर्थः । इत्येवं हि । उक्तं हि (Taittiriya Samhita 1.1.1; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.1.1.4) मन्त्रेण प्रथमप्रभनमुभयीयते । पुरोडाशं प्रथयिष्येति (Taittiriya Samhita 1.1.1; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.2.1.1) ब्राह्मणेऽपि तदेवाभिप्रेत्य प्रस्तुतचोदनाय प्रवृत्तं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् प्रवृत्तम् । तथा सति मन्त्रेणाप्ययमेवार्थो बोधाय प्रवृत्तः ।

चेद् अर्थ-शास्त्रत (जैमिनि सुत्र १.२.३१) स विनाभिधेयो यस्य शास्त्रे ब्राह्मण-वाक्ये तद्-अर्थ-शास्त्रम् । तस्माच् चाविशक्तार्थो मन्त्र इत्य् अर्थः । ... ced artha-śāstrata (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.31) sa vinābhidheyo yasya śāstre brāhmaṇa-vākye tad-artha-śāstram | tasmāc cāviśaktārtho mantra ity arthaḥ | ...

"The mantras convey no [independent] meaning, since there exists an 'artha-shastra' — a separate text explaining their meaning — namely, the Brahmana [portion]. Thus a mantra's meaning is unfixed/dependent [on the Brahmana]. For instance: it is said that the first application is conveyed through the mantra, and the statement 'I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake' occurring in a Brahmana passage was made with this same intent, using the Brahmana's own sentence to direct the ongoing rite — showing that the mantra was employed to convey this very same meaning [already given by the Brahmana]."

That is: from the sutra "ced artha-shastrata" through to the sutra on "vidhi-shabda" (injunction-words), a single adhikarana (topic-section) runs, with each sutra explained in turn. The opening sutra's meaning: mantras have no independent meaning, because a separate "artha-shastra" (meaning-explaining text) — namely, the Brahmana — already exists to explain them. If a mantra genuinely had its own meaning, people would grasp it directly, with no need for an accompanying Brahmana passage. Since a Brahmana explanation is needed, this shows the mantra itself conveys no independent meaning — illustrated by the Brahmana statement "I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake," used precisely to supply the meaning the mantra alone fails to convey.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The mantras are meaningless, because there is a shastra of identical meaning.

By shastra is meant a brahmana. If the meaning which the mantra is naturally fitted to convey is the meaning of the brahmana, the brahmana may be said to be of identical meaning with the mantra. But the existence of such a brahmana goes to show that the...

original p. 376

For instance, the mantra "uru prathasva" refers to spreading out the purodāśa cake — and this same act is described in the Brahmana passage "purodāśaṃ prathayati" ("the Adhvaryu spreads the purodāśa"). Since the Brahmana merely restates what the mantra already conveys, what genuine use does such a Brahmana serve? If the mantra's meaning is already clear on its own, the Brahmana statement becomes pointless. But if instead the mantra's own meaning is what remains unclear, and the Brahmana serves to clarify its viniyoga — the procedure and context in which the mantra should be applied — then the Brahmana genuinely earns its purpose. On this view, if mere recitation of the mantra during the yajna is held to be its primary function, we must then accept that recitation serves some adṛṣṭa (unseen, imperceptible) purpose.

On this, the upholder of the doctrine to be controverted states another argument:

ननूच्चारणार्थत्वे सत्यनिष्टं प्रयोजनं परिकल्प्येत । अर्थाभिधायकत्वे तु दृष्टं लभ्यते । तस्माद् व्याख्यानस्यानुवादकत्वम् अभ्युपेत्य मन्त्रा अभिधानार्थत्वेनैवेत्य् आशङ्क्य उत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥ nanūccāraṇārthatve saty aniṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ parikalpyeta | arthābhidhāyakatve tu dṛṣṭaṃ labhyate | tasmād vyākhyānasyānuvādakatvam abhyupetya mantrā abhidhānārthatvenaivety āśaṅkya uttaraṃ sūtrayati || (the exact word-division here is uncertain at this resolution; the sense — that if mantras existed merely to be recited, an unwelcome unseen purpose would have to be posited, whereas taking them as meaning-conveying yields a directly observable purpose instead — is confirmed by the Kannada explanation and the embedded English below)

But suppose instead we say the very purpose of reciting mantras at the yajna is to convey their meaning — this would establish a dṛṣṭa (directly perceivable) purpose for the mantras. Between the two kinds of purpose, perceived and unperceived, an unperceived purpose should only be invoked when no perceived purpose can be found. If the Brahmana merely repeats the mantra's own meaning, then the meaning of mantras recited during the yajna...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...mantra is used without any reference to its meaning. For example, take the mantra "uru prathasva." It refers to the spreading out of the purodasa. But that very thing is referred to in the brahmana "purodasam prathayathi." That being so, if you say that the sense is got from the mantra, you as good as made out the brahmana to be a useless thing: whereas, if you say with me that the mantra is used with no reference to its meaning, then the brahmana becomes useful as teaching the sacrificial act referred to. Therefore at the time of the sacrifice the only use of the mantras lies in the mere recitation of them.

But here a doubt arises. To say that the use of the mantras at the sacrifice lies in their recitation only is to devise for them a spiritual use. But a non-spiritual material use lies at hand, namely, that of conveying their meaning. (Such a procedure is illegitimate.) In spite of the fact that on this view we must admit that the brahmanas merely repeat what has been said in the mantras, must we not hold that the mantras are recited at the sacrifice with one purpose and purpose only, namely, that of conveying their meaning?

The upholder of the doctrine which is to be controverted therefore states another argument.

original p. 377

...we would have to accept that mantras do convey meaning in this sense. But if we accept that a mantra has this meaning-conveying capacity, another objection immediately arises — explained in the next sutra.

"Vakya-niyamat" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.32)

अग्निर्मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (RV 8.44.16) इत्येवमेव वाक्यं पठितव्यमिति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निरित्येवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टेव भवत्येव । तस्मान्नियतपाठक्रमफलायोच्चारणमेव मन्त्रप्रयोजनम् । ननु पाठक्रमनियममात्रात्स्याद्यष्ट्वार्थज्ञेऽपि मन्त्रपाठक्रमबोधार्थं चेवेत्याशंक्य तत्र दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

अग्निर् मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (र्व् ८.४४.१६) इत्य् एवम् एव वाक्यं पठितव्यम् इति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निर् इत्य् एवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टैव भवत्य् एव । तस्मान् नियत-पाठ-क्रम-फलायोच्चारणम् एव मन्त्र-प्रयोजनम् । ... agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut (RV 8.44.16) ity evam eva vākyaṃ paṭhitavyam iti mantre niyama upalabhyate | arthapratyāyanaṃ tu mūrdhvāgnir ity evaṃ vṛttyapi sveṣṭaiva bhavaty eva | tasmān niyata-pāṭha-krama-phalāyoccāraṇam eva mantra-prayojanam | ...

"It is a settled rule that the mantra 'agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut' must be recited in exactly this word-order, and no other. Yet conveying its meaning would work equally well in a rearranged form such as 'mūrdhāgnir...' Therefore, the mantra's purpose lies solely in its recitation according to a fixed word-order — for the sake of that order's own fruit, not for conveying meaning. One might object that even granting this fixed order, its purpose could still be to teach the proper recitation-sequence to someone who already knows the mantra's meaning. Anticipating this, Jaimini now formulates a further objection identifying an additional flaw in that view."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Since the words must be recited in a particular order.

It is received doctrine that the mantra "agnir murdha divah kakut" must be recited with the words in that order, and in no other. But if we changed the order and said "murdhagnir &c.," the meaning would be the same. So the only use of the mantras lies in their being recited in such a way as to secure the full fruit of the fixed order of the text.

It may, however, be said, that side by side with the spiritual benefit obtained by reciting the mantras in the order of the text, the recitation serves also the purpose of conveying a meaning. To guard against such an argument, he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

original p. 378

"Buddha-shastrat" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.33)

अग्नीदग्नीन् विहर (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.1) इति एष मन्त्रः प्रयोगकाले पठ्यते । तच्चाग्निविहरणादिकमाग्नीध्रेणाध्ययनकाल एव स्वकर्तव्यत्वेन बुद्धम् । तस्य च बुद्धार्थस्य पुनर्मन्त्रेण शासनमनर्थकम् । न हि सोपानत्कः पादे प्रतिमुंचति । तस्मात् बुद्धस्यापि अर्थस्य स्मारणाय मन्त्रेण स्मारणमस्तीत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

अग्नीद् अग्नीन् विहर (तैत्तिरीय संहिता ६.१.१.१) इति एष मन्त्रः प्रयोग-काले पठ्यते । तच् चाग्नि-विहरणादिकम् आग्नीध्रेणाध्ययन-काल एव स्वकर्तव्यत्वेन बुद्धम् । तस्य च बुद्धार्थस्य पुनर् मन्त्रेण शासनम् अनर्थकम् । न हि सोपानत्कः पादे प्रतिमुञ्चति । ... agnīd agnīn vihara (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.1.1) iti eṣa mantraḥ prayoga-kāle paṭhyate | tac cāgni-viharaṇādikam āgnīdhreṇādhyayana-kāla eva svakartavyatvena buddham | tasya ca buddhārthasya punar mantreṇa śāsanam anarthakam | na hi sopānatkaḥ pāde pratimuñcati | ...

"'Agnīd, distribute the fires' (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.1) — this mantra is recited during the ritual performance. But distributing the fire and similar duties have already been learned by the Agnidh priest, as his own responsibility, during his period of study. Instructing him again, through a mantra, about something he already knows serves no purpose. Indeed, no one puts a second shoe on a foot that already wears one."

That is: the objection here is that mantras convey no meaning, since their sole function is recitation — not instruction, because reciting an already-known meaning serves no purpose. It was already established that mantras must follow a fixed recitation-order (per the previous sutra); now a further flaw is illustrated. "Agnīd agnīn vihara" is an injunctive mantra (vidhi-mantra), also called a "prescriptive" (preṣaṇa) mantra, recited during the yajna to direct the priest performing a task while he performs it. In every yajna, fire is kept burning in the Agnidh's own fire-pit before the ritual begins, and before the rites commence, this fire is carried from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars — this mantra commands precisely that act. But this mantra's meaning is already generally known to every priest participating in the yajna. What purpose is served by restating something everyone already knows?

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Since the command is already known.

"Agnid agnin vihara" is a directory text, which is recited at the time of sacrifice. Now the duty of distributing the fire or the like has already been learnt as part of his work by the priest when engaged in study. It is a useless proceeding to instruct him by a mantra with regard to a thing which he has already learnt. If your foot has a shoe on you do not clap another on the top of it.

original p. 379

Generally, yajnas employ sixteen priests, organized into four groups (गण gaṇa):

  • होतृगण (hotṛgaṇa, Hotr-group) — मैत्रावरुण/प्रशास्त्र (maitrāvaruṇa/praśāstra), अच्छावाक (acchāvāka), ग्रावस्तुत् (grāvastut) — priests connected to the Rigveda.
  • अध्वर्युगण (adhvaryugaṇa, Adhvaryu-group) — प्रतिप्रस्थाता (pratiprasthātā), नेष्टा (neṣṭā), उन्नेता (unnetā) — priests connected to the Yajurveda.
  • उद्गातृगण (udgātṛgaṇa, Udgatr-group) — प्रस्तोता (prastotā), प्रतिहर्ता (pratihartā), सुब्रह्मण्य (subrahmaṇya) — Samaveda priests.
  • ब्रह्मगण (brahmagaṇa, Brahma-group) — ब्राह्मणाच्छंसी (brāhmaṇācchaṃsī), आग्नीध्र (āgnīdhra), पोता (potā) — priests who must be learned across all the Vedas.

The Shatapatha Brahmana (10.4.1.7) states that a yajna should not proceed with only sixteen priests — followers of the Kaushitaki shakha therefore appoint a seventeenth priest, the सदस्य (sadasya), who oversees the entire proceeding to ensure everything runs correctly (this appointment is not customary among Ashvalayana-shakha followers).

The mantra "Agnīd agnīn vihara," discussed above, is used specifically when carrying fire from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars. But the Agnidh and other priests such as the Adhvaryu already know their duties, and the meaning and purpose of the mantras, from their period of Vedic study. Restating what is already known is therefore pointless — as pointless, the objection says, as putting a second shoe over a foot already shod.

This might be answered as follows: what the mantras state may indeed already be known — but it could be forgotten through carelessness, and the mantras then serve a genuinely useful reminding function. Very well — let us grant that mantras can serve to remind priests of forgotten matters. But some mantras assert things that are outright impossible. This is addressed in the next sutra.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

It may, however, be said that the mantra may be a useful reminder for the avoidance of a careless forgetfulness. To guard against this he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

original p. 380

"Avidyamāna-vacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.34)

चत्वारि शृंगा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य (RV 4.58.3) इति मन्त्रे आम्नायते । न खलु चतुःशृंगत्वादियुक्तं किंचिद्यज्ञसाधनं विद्यते यन्मन्त्रशाखेनास्मर्येत । ...

चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य (र्व् ४.५८.३) इति मन्त्रे आम्नायते । न खलु चतुः-शृङ्गत्वादि-युक्तं किंचिद् यज्ञ-साधनं विद्यते यन् मन्त्र-शाखेनास्मर्येत । catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya (RV 4.58.3) iti mantre āmnāyate | na khalu catuḥ-śṛṅgatvādi-yuktaṃ kiṃcid yajña-sādhanaṃ vidyate yan mantra-śākhenāsmaryeta |

"The mantra states: 'four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands has it' (RV 4.58.3). But no sacrificial implement possessing four horns and the like actually exists, which this mantra could be supposed to remind the priest of."

Even granting mantras a memory-jogging function, this fails for mantras describing things with no real-world referent at all — like this famously cryptic verse. Since no such four-horned, three-footed, two-headed, seven-handed object exists among yajna implements, this mantra cannot serve even as a reminder of anything real.

"Acetane'rtha-bandhanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.35)

ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् । श्रुणोत ग्रावाणः । इत्याद्यचेतनवचनेषु मन्त्रेषु चेतनोचितं रक्षणश्रवणादिकमर्थं बध्नाति । स च चेतनस्वापादुचितः ।

ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् । शृणोत ग्रावाणः । इत्य् आद्य् अचेतन-वचनेषु मन्त्रेषु चेतनोचितं रक्षण-श्रवणादिकम् अर्थं बध्नाति । स च चेतन-स्वभावाद् उचितः । oṣadhe trāyasvainam | śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ | ity ādy acetana-vacaneṣu mantreṣu cetanocitaṃ rakṣaṇa-śravaṇādikam arthaṃ badhnāti | sa ca cetana-svabhāvād ucitaḥ |

"In mantras such as 'O herb, protect him' and 'Hear, O stones,' meanings befitting sentient beings — protection, hearing, and the like — are attached to statements addressed to inanimate things. But such meanings are properly suited only to conscious beings."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Since the mantra mentions things that have no existance.

There is a text in the Veda, "He has four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands." Now there is no implement of the sacrifice in any way corresponding to this description, which the mantra might be supposed to put the priest in remembrance of.

It may, however, be said, that some immanent deity is referred to here. To guard against this he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

Since the mantra attaches a meaning to a thing which is not a living being.

In such mantras as "oshadhe trayasvainam" and "srinota gravanah" the words attach to lifeless things a meaning, such as protecting or hearing, which befits only sentient beings. And this is improper.

original p. 381

"Naṣṭābhimāni-vyapadeśa" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.36)

ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् इति मन्त्रे यजमानस्य त्राणं दधीति (दधिनः, वनस्पतीनां) गुम्भिगे सेरितम् । "अर्ये दर्भीये, ऐष यजमानं रक्षतु" इति इदर अर्थवु । मत्तोंदु मंत्रवु—"श्रुणोत ग्रावाणः" (Jai. Su. 1.2.36) एंदु । इदर अर्थवु—"एल्यै कल्लुगळे, नावु अरिकेमाडुवुदन्नु केळि" एंदागुवुदु ।

(Continuing the objection: mantras address inanimate darbha-grass and pressing-stones with the sentient qualities of "protecting" and "hearing" — qualities properly belonging only to conscious beings, making such address improper unless some presiding deity is understood as the true addressee.)

It might be said that, per the doctrine of the "abhimānivyapadeśa" sutra in the Vaiyasika Shastra, such clauses truly address some immanent presiding deity rather than the inanimate object itself. To guard against this resolution, a further objection follows.

"Artha-vipratiṣedhāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.37)

अदितिर्द्यौरदितिरन्तरिक्षम् (RV 1.89.10[?]) इति मन्त्र आम्नायते । यद् एव द्यौः तद् एवान्तरिक्षम् इति अपि-प्रतिṣiddham । एवं विषयं एव रुद्रः (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.6.1) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्राः (Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1.1) इत्याद्यपि अत्र किल कथम् ।

अदितिर् द्यौर् अदितिर् अन्तरिक्षम् इति मन्त्र आम्नायते । यद् एव द्यौः तद् एवान्तरिक्षम् इत्य् अपि-प्रतिषिद्धम् । एवं विषयं एव रुद्रः ... सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्राः ... इत्य् आद्यपि अत्र किल कथम् । aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam iti mantra āmnāyate | yad eva dyauḥ tad evāntarikṣam ity api-pratiṣiddham | evaṃ viṣayaṃ eva rudraḥ ... sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrāḥ ... ity ādyapi atra kila katham |

"The mantra states: 'Aditi is Dyaus (Heaven), Aditi is Antariksha (the mid-region).' But to say that what is Dyaus is the very same as Antariksha is a self-contradiction. Similarly, one might cite here 'Rudra is one only' alongside 'the Rudras in their thousands.'"

The objection: since a single mantra identifies Aditi simultaneously with two distinct cosmic regions (Heaven and the mid-air), and separate mantras contradictorily describe Rudra as both singular and countless-in-thousands, such mutually inconsistent statements cannot be meaningful or authoritative.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source: This page continues the purva-paksha's own dialectical structure: it is Jaimini himself who, within the objection, anticipates and pre-empts a possible metaphorical defense — not yet Sayana's siddhanta, which comes later.

It may, however, be said that in accordance with the doctrine laid down in the "abhimanivyapadesa" sutra of the Vaiyasika Shastra the real subject of such clauses is some immanent deity. To guard against this he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

Since the meanings are mutually contradictory.

There is a text, "Aditi is Dyaus, Aditi is Antariksha." But to say that what is Dyaus is Antariksha is a contradiction in terms. There might be cited, too, in this connection such texts as "Rudra is one only," and "The Rudras in their thousands."

original p. 382

नसु त्वैमेव माता च पिता त्वैमेवेत्यादवन्तरिक्षादिरूपश्चेनादितिः स्तूयते । एवमेकस्यापि रुद्रस्य योगसामर्थ्याद्बहुमूर्तिस्वीकारोऽस्तु । ततो नार्थविप्रतिषेध इत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

ननु त्वैम् एव माता च पिता त्वैम् एव इत्य् आदव् अन्तरिक्षादि-रूपश् चेनादितिः स्तूयते । एवम् एकस्यापि रुद्रस्य योग-सामर्थ्याद् बहु-मूर्ति-स्वीकारोऽस्तु । ततो नार्थ-विप्रतिषेध इत्य् आशङ्क्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥ nanu tvaim eva mātā ca pitā tvaim eva ity ādav antarikṣādi-rūpaś cenāditiḥ stūyate | evam ekasyāpi rudrasya yoga-sāmarthyād bahu-mūrti-svīkāro'stu | tato nārtha-vipratiṣedha ity āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||

"[One might say:] just as we say of someone, 'you alone are my mother, and you alone are my father,' Aditi is likewise praised metaphorically in the form of Antariksha and similar epithets. Similarly, let it be granted that the one Rudra, through his own yogic power, assumes many forms. Therefore, there is no genuine contradiction of meaning. Anticipating this possible defense, [Jaimini] now formulates yet a further objection, identifying a different flaw."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

It may, however, be said that in such a text Aditi is praised metaphorically under the form of Antariksha, as when we say of some one that he is our father and mother. And that Rudra, though one in himself, takes on many forms by his supernatural power. To guard against this he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

"Svādhyāyavad-vacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.39)

पूर्णिका नाम काचिद्योषिदवघातं करोति । तत्समीपे माणवकः स्वाध्यायग्रहणकालं कदाचिदवघातमन्त्रमधीते। न च तस्यार्थप्रकाशनविवक्षाऽस्ति, प्रतिमुशलप्रहारं तस्य मन्त्रस्यापश्यमानत्वात्पदग्रहणमात्रं इच्छत इव मन्त्रानभ्यस्यति। तत्र स्वाध्यायकाले पठितोऽप्यश्वं मन्त्रो यथा पूर्णिकां प्रति स्वार्थं न ब्रूते तथा कर्मकालेऽपि स्वार्थं न वक्ष्यति।

पूर्णिका नाम काचिद् योषिद् अवघातं करोति । तत्-समीपे माणवकः स्वाध्याय-ग्रहण-कालं कदाचिद् अवघात-मन्त्रम् अधीते । न च तस्यार्थ-प्रकाशन-विवक्षाऽस्ति, प्रति-मुशल-प्रहारं तस्य मन्त्रस्यापश्यमानत्वात् पद-ग्रहण-मात्रं इच्छत इव मन्त्रान् अभ्यस्यति । तत्र स्वाध्याय-काले पठितोऽप्य् एवं मन्त्रो यथा पूर्णिकां प्रति स्वार्थं न ब्रूते तथा कर्म-कालेऽपि स्वार्थं न वक्ष्यति । pūrṇikā nāma kācid yoṣid avaghātaṃ karoti | tat-samīpe māṇavakaḥ svādhyāya-grahaṇa-kālaṃ kadācid avaghāta-mantram adhīte | na ca tasyārtha-prakāśana-vivakṣā'sti, prati-muśala-prahāraṃ tasya mantrasyāpaśyamānatvāt pada-grahaṇa-mātraṃ icchata iva mantrān abhyasyati | tatra svādhyāya-kāle paṭhito'py evaṃ mantro yathā pūrṇikāṃ prati svārthaṃ na brūte tathā karma-kāle'pi svārthaṃ na vakṣyati |

"A certain woman named Purnika is pounding grain with a pestle. Nearby, a young brahmin student, engaged in his daily lesson, happens to be reciting the pestle-mantra (avaghāta-mantra). He has no intention of conveying its meaning — evident from the fact that he does not synchronize the mantra with each fall of the pestle; he seems merely intent on memorizing the words, and practices this mantra among others [without regard to Purnika's work]. Just as this mantra, though recited during study, conveys no meaning relevant to Purnika, so too it will convey no meaning even when recited during the actual ritual."

That is: just as a mantra's meaning goes unattended during rote study, so too its ritual application conveys no genuine meaning — since the objection holds that mantra-recitation and the accompanying ritual action (here, pounding grain) proceed with no real connection between them, mantras recited without understood meaning yield no fruit for the rite performed alongside them.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Because the mantras at the time of sacrifice express no meaning, any more than they do when one is learning them by heart.

Suppose that a certain woman, called Purnika, is plying the pestle. Near her a brahmin boy, engaged in learning his daily lesson, chances to be reciting the pestle mantra. He has no wish to convey the meaning of the mantra. This is evident from the fact that he does not make his mantra keep time with the fall of the pestle. He is only learning the words by heart, and in doing that repeats over and over again this among other mantras, And just...

original p. 384

Resolution to the Purnika objection: there is no intention of conveying meaning when the student recites the mantra during rote study, and Purnika herself has no capacity to grasp it. But in yajna-rites proper, the Adhvaryu priest reciting mantras does know their meaning, does intend to convey it, and those present are capable of understanding it. The claim that mantras are meaningless does not hold.

"Avijñeyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.40)

केषांचिन्मन्त्राणामर्थो विज्ञातुं न शक्यते । तद्यथा । अम्यक्स त इन्द्र ऋष्टिरस्मे (RV 1.24.8[?]) इत्येको मन्त्रः । सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतू (RV 10.106.6) इत्यपरो मन्त्रः । ननु एतस्मान्मन्त्रार्थबोधायैव निगमनिरुक्तव्याकरणानि सन्तीत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

केषाञ्चिन् मन्त्राणाम् अर्थो विज्ञातुं न शक्यते । तद् यथा । अम्यक्स त इन्द्र ऋष्टिर् अस्मे इत्य् एको मन्त्रः । सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतू इत्य् अपरो मन्त्रः । नन्व् एतस्मान् मन्त्रार्थ-बोधायैव निगम-निरुक्त-व्याकरणानि सन्तीत्य् आशङ्क्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥ keṣāñcin mantrāṇām artho vijñātuṃ na śakyate | tad yathā | amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme ity eko mantraḥ | sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū ity aparo mantraḥ | nanv etasmān mantrārtha-bodhāyaiva nigama-nirukta-vyākaraṇāni santīty āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||

"The meaning of some mantras cannot be ascertained at all. For example: 'amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme' is one such mantra; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū' is another. One might object that Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana exist precisely to illuminate such mantras' meaning — anticipating this, a further objection is formulated."

That is: since the meaning of numerous mantras cannot be properly determined at all — these two being prime examples — it follows that mantras exist merely for recitation, not meaning.

A resolution is then offered: it is precisely to explain such difficult mantras' meaning that disciplines like Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana arose; with their help, understanding mantra-meaning is readily achievable — the claim of impossibility does not hold.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...as in such a case the pestle mantra is at lesson time recited without conveying its meaning, so at the sacrifice it will not convey its meaning.

It may, however, be said, that in the case here supposed the boy has no wish to convey the meaning, while Purnika on her side (being a woman) is incapable of understanding it. It is different in the sacrifice. There the adhvaryu does wish to convey the meaning, and can understand it. To guard against this, he puts another objection in the form of a sutra.

Because some mantras are unintelligible.

The meaning of some mantras cannot be made out. Take, as one example, the text "amyak sa ta indra rishtir asme." And, as another, "srinyeva jarbhari turpharitu."

It may, however, be said that parallel vedic passages, the nirukta, and grammar are there to throw light on such mantras. To guard against this, he states another objection in the next sutra.

original p. 385

"Anitye-saṃyogān mantrānarthakyaṃ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.41)

किं ते कृण्वन्ति कीकटेषु (RV 3.53.14) इति मन्त्रे कीकटो नाम जनपद आम्नातः । तथा नैचाशाखं नाम नगरं प्रमगन्दो नाम राजेत्येतद्वा अनित्या आम्नाताः । तथा च सति स्यात्प्रमगन्दात्प्राय मन्त्रो भूतपूर्व इति गम्यते । तदेवं नित्यस्य शास्त्रादिभिर्हेतुभिर्मन्त्रार्थप्रत्यायनार्थत्वं नास्ति । किंतूच्चारणादृष्ट्यार्थ इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥

किं ते कृण्वन्ति कीकटेषु इति मन्त्रे कीकटो नाम जनपद आम्नातः । तथा नैचाशाखं नाम नगरं प्रमगन्दो नाम राजेत्य् एतद् वा अनित्या आम्नाताः । तथा च सति स्यात् प्रमगन्दात् प्राय मन्त्रो भूतपूर्व इति गम्यते । तद् एवं नित्यस्य शास्त्रादिभिर् हेतुभिर् मन्त्रार्थ-प्रत्यायनार्थत्वं नास्ति । किन्तूच्चारणाद् ऋष्ट्य्-अर्थ इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥ kiṃ te kṛṇvanti kīkaṭeṣu iti mantre kīkaṭo nāma janapada āmnātaḥ | tathā naicāśākhaṃ nāma nagaraṃ pramagando nāma rājety etad vā anityā āmnātāḥ | tathā ca sati syāt pramagandāt prāya mantro bhūtapūrva iti gamyate | tad evaṃ nityasya śāstrādibhir hetubhir mantrārtha-pratyāyanārthatvaṃ nāsti | kintūccāraṇād ṛṣṭy-artha iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||

"In the mantra 'kiṃ te kṛṇvanti kīkaṭeṣu' (RV 3.53.14), a country named Kikata is mentioned; likewise a city named Naichashakha and a king named Pramaganda — all non-eternal, transient things. This being so, it follows that the mantra must postdate King Pramaganda's era. Thus, for these reasons — along with the shastra-based arguments already given — mantras serve no purpose in conveying meaning; their purpose lies instead in the unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa) obtained through mere recitation. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

That is: since mantras mention transient, historically-bound proper names — a country, a city, a king — accepting that mantras convey meaning would force one to admit the Vedas are non-eternal, contradicting the doctrine that they are beginningless (anādi) and non-human (apauruṣeya). Therefore, only the unseen fruit of recitation itself can be the mantras' purpose — no other fruit exists.

This concludes the full nine-part objection (purva-paksha), spanning from "Buddha-shastrat" through this final sutra — nine separate arguments marshaled to establish that mantras serve recitation alone. Jaimini's own resolution follows in the next sutra.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source: The source scan repeats printed pages 384–385, already translated above; the duplicates are not translated again. The translation resumes at printed page 386.

Because they have to do with non-eternal things.

In the text "kim te krinvanti kikateshu" mention is made in the Veda of a country called Kikata, as also of a city called Naichasakha and a king called Pramaganda. From which we can infer that this text at least did not exist before king Pramaganda.

From all these reasons it must be concluded that at the sacrifice the mantras have no use as conveying a meaning. Their use is a spiritual one, and lies in their recitation only. This is the view to be controverted, and Jaimini now lays down in sutras the doctrine he establishes.

original p. 386

A Methodological Note, then Jaimini's Own Resolution Begins

In his Purva-Mimamsa sutras, before establishing that mantras do carry meaning, Jaimini himself first gathered every possible objection on the subject and presented them as the purva-paksha. Sayanacharya, rather than composing his own independent arguments, works directly through Jaimini's own sutras — though in places he interprets them along a path somewhat different from the classical commentators (Shabara, Kumarila, and others), who did not, sutra by sutra, anticipate the siddhantin's coming resolution before commenting on each subsequent sutra.

One notable divergence: Mimamsakas do not generally accept resolutions like "lifeless objects have presiding deities" or "yogis possess extraordinary powers" as doing genuine argumentative work — Shabara's own commentary instead holds that reciting mantras with meaning as the primary intention involves no fault at all. Sayanacharya, however, resolves this very objection using the sutra "abhimāninyaḥ pa-devatāḥ" ("the deities are the presiding spirits [of these objects]"). By anticipating objections this way throughout, Sayana's argument reads as complete and self-contained. We follow Sayanacharya's own interpretation of Jaimini's sutras from here onward.

There, Jaimini formulates the siddhanta (resolution):

"Api śiṣṭasya vākyārthaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.42)

तुशब्देन मन्त्राणामुद्दिष्टार्थमुच्चारणमात्रं वारयति । क्रियाकारकसंबन्धेन प्रतीयमानो वाक्यार्थो लोकवेदयोरविशिष्टः । तथा सति यथा लोकेऽर्थप्रत्यायनायैव वाक्यमुच्चार्यते तथा वैदिकयागप्रयोगेऽपि दृश्यम् । मन्त्रेण प्रकाशितस्यार्थोऽनुष्ठातुं शक्यते न...

तु-शब्देन मन्त्राणाम् उद्दिष्टार्थम् उच्चारण-मात्रं वारयति । क्रिया-कारक-सम्बन्धेन प्रतीयमानो वाक्यार्थो लोक-वेदयोर् अविशिष्टः । तथा सति यथा लोकेऽर्थ-प्रत्यायनायैव वाक्यम् उच्चार्यते तथा वैदिक-याग-प्रयोगेऽपि दृश्यम् । मन्त्रेण प्रकाशितस्यार्थोऽनुष्ठातुं शक्यते न... tu-śabdena mantrāṇām uddiṣṭārtham uccāraṇa-mātraṃ vārayati | kriyā-kāraka-sambandhena pratīyamāno vākyārtho loka-vedayor aviśiṣṭaḥ | tathā sati yathā loke'rtha-pratyāyanāyaiva vākyam uccāryate tathā vaidika-yāga-prayoge'pi dṛśyam | mantreṇa prakāśitasyārtho'nuṣṭhātuṃ śakyate na...

"The particle 'tu' (but) rules out the view that mantras exist merely for recitation with no intended meaning. The meaning of a sentence, understood through the relation between action and its agents/instruments, is the same whether in ordinary speech or in the Veda. Just as, in ordinary life, a sentence is uttered precisely to convey meaning, the same must hold in Vedic ritual application as well. What a mantra reveals can indeed be acted upon, not..."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

But the meaning of a sentence has the same relation to the words in the Veda as in any other book.

The word "but" here shows that Jaimini is about to reject the view that the use of the mantras is a spiritual one, lying only in their recitation. The meaning of a sentence is...

original p. 387

...tv aprakāśitaḥ | tasmān nityodgvrekasyocāraṇārtha-prakāśanarūpaṃ dṛṣṭam eva prayojanam | nanu bhūrasi nāri asi śrīṣṭakṛtye traiṣṭubhena chandasā dade (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.1.1[?]) iti mantre āmnātaḥ | tena tv iva mantreṇa prakīrtitaḥ punarbhryābhrimādatte taṃ caturbhir ābhriṃ ādatte (Taittiriya Samhita 3.1.1.7[?]) iti vidhīyate | tad etad viprāṣṭheṇ vaiphalyaṃ syād ādikta-śaṃkyottaram sūtrayati ॥

(This citation carries the sutra's own argument, worked through the well-known "ābhri" (digging-implement) example, comparing a mantra's descriptive content to a corresponding Brahmana injunction to test whether both can meaningfully coexist without redundancy; some phrase-level readings remain uncertain at this resolution, though the overall argument is clarified by the embedded English translation below.)

That is: mantra-meaning is established through the relation of action and its instruments, exactly as in ordinary speech — this holds equally for sacred and secular language alike. The word "tu" ("but") in this sutra rejects the earlier objection's claim that mantras serve merely recitation and not meaning; a new meaning, once revealed by a mantra, is what makes ritual action possible, and this alone is the mantra's directly observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — not some purely "spiritual"/unseen one. Just as an ordinary sentence is uttered specifically to convey its meaning, so too must a Vedic mantra be understood as functioning the same way.

A further objection is then raised: consider the sequence of mantras running from "abhrir asi nārir asi" through "traiṣṭubhena cchandasā dade" — on your view, this passage fully describes the taking-up of the "ābhri" (a ritual implement). If so, the Brahmana's separate injunction "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" ("one takes up the ābhri with four [strokes/portions]") becomes entirely redundant. Jaimini anticipates and answers this objection in the next sutra.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...arrived at by the relation of cause and effect subsisting between the words and it, and this holds good of all words whatever, sacred or profane. That being so, just as in common talk a sentence is uttered in order that it may convey its meaning, the same law must be recognized in the case of a Vedic sacrifice. For only the rite which is illustrated by a mantra can be performed, not that which is not so illustrated. Therefore the recitation of the mantras has one immediate use and one such use only, and that is not a mystical one. They are recited in order that they may convey their meaning.

But, it may be said, take the text from "abhrir asi narir asi" down to "traishtubhena tva chhandasa dade." According to your view that text tells all about the taking of the "abhri." In that view the direction to that effect contained in the brahmana "chaturbhir abhrim adatte" became perfectly useless. He anticipates and answers this objection in the next sutra.

original p. 388

The general point: acting according to a purpose already understood is the aim [of ritual action] — one must be able to say why a given act is performed, since even if the act itself succeeds mechanically, uttering words devoid of meaning cannot explain "why" it was done. The reason each individual mantra is recited must be known; without this, others simply perform the action mechanically. Since this defeats the purpose behind ritual acts, a mantra's meaning must be understood as serving a genuinely observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — precisely what its "prāptaviṣṭyaṃ prayojanam" (immediately applicable purpose) consists in, per the Shabara-bhashya. Meaning is therefore not a matter of unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose alone — it is directly observable purpose. To claim otherwise contradicts how language works in ordinary human affairs, where sentences are understood specifically to convey meaning; the same applies to Vedic sentences. The unseen fruit that arises specifically from the act of recitation itself is a separate matter — but understanding the meaning is what makes the resulting Dharmic fruit (dharma) possible, and this is what both types of purpose ultimately serve together.

If a mantra's meaning is granted, but the Brahmana's own separate injunction (e.g., regarding the fourfold use of the "abhri") becomes redundant given this — that objection was raised on the previous page. It is resolved as follows: this mantra alone does not specify by itself how many strokes constitute proper use of the "abhri" — that detail must be learned from elsewhere. Even granting the mantra's own meaning, the Brahmana statement "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" still serves an independent, non-redundant purpose, specifying the count — resolving the apparent contradiction between the objection and the resolution.

"Guṇārthena punaḥ-śrutiḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.43)

मन्त्रेण प्रतीतस्यार्थस्य ब्राह्मणे यत् पुनःश्रुतिस्तद्देशे चतुःसंख्यालक्षणगुणविधानार्थत्वेनोपयुज्यते । एकस्य विधानस्याभावे चतुर्भ्रां मन्त्राणां मध्ये येन केनाभ्रिं आदद्यीत । तन्निमित्तं वाग्भ्रतश्च (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.2.1[?]) इत्येतच्छस्त्राभिधानाद्ये । (Taittiriya Samhita 3.1.2.1) इत्येतत्र मन्त्रसामर्थ्येन प्राप्तस्य रचनादानस्य पुनर्ब्राह्मणवाक्यं विनियोजकमाम्नायते । तदेतत्तु न्यर्थमित्याशंक्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

(Jaimini's own resolution formula: where a mantra's meaning is restated in a Brahmana passage, that repetition serves the specific purpose of specifying a quantifying detail — here, the "fourfold" count — not otherwise established by the mantra alone. Precise word-level construction is difficult to render with full confidence at this resolution, though the overall doctrine is confirmed by the embedded English translation below.)

That is: where a mantra's own already-understood meaning is repeated in a Brahmana passage, that repetition is not redundant — it serves to specify a quantifying detail (here, that exactly four applications are required), a detail the mantra by itself leaves open, since without such specification, a priest might assume he had the option to use any single one of the four mantras referenced.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Either the second saying is accompanied by a circumstance.
