Chapter 7. The Definition of Pariṣaṅkhyā

Original title: "Pariṣaṅkhyālakṣaṇa" Printed pages 389–393 of the source.

original p. 389

The sutra's meaning: restating what is already said serves to indicate a distinctive point contained within it. Why repeat, in the Brahmana, what the mantra already states? Because the mantra contains a directive about the "abhri" (spade), followed by three further similar mantras — but if one simply followed the mantra alone, the act of taking up the tool could be completed using just one of the four, leaving the remaining three mantras' purpose unclear. The Brahmana resolves this by stating "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" — one must recite all four mantras before taking up the tool. Since "caturbhiḥ" ("with four") appears nowhere in the mantra itself, without the Brahmana's help, an Adhvaryu might recite only one mantra of his choosing and consider the act complete — improperly performed by shastric standards. The Brahmana's repetition thus serves specifically to supply this missing detail.

But consider the Taittiriya Samhita's mantra "imām agṛbhṇan" ("I have grasped this"), which clearly instructs taking up a rope. The Taittiriya Brahmana restates the same matter: "aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("one takes up the rope called ashva"). Here too, one might object that the mantra's application becomes redundant. Anticipating this, the sutra "parisaṅkhyā" follows.

"Pariṣaṅkhyā" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.44)

गर्दभाभिधानीं नादत्त इति निषेधः परिसंख्या । तदर्थमिदं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् ॥

गर्दभाभिधानीं नादत्त इति निषेधः परिषङ्ख्या । तदर्थम् इदं ब्राह्मण-वाक्यम् ॥ gardabhābhidhānīṃ nādatta iti niṣedhaḥ pariṣaṅkhyā | tadartham idaṃ brāhmaṇa-vākyam ||

"'One does not take up the rope called gardabha [donkey-rope]' — this implied prohibition is called pariṣaṅkhyā (exclusive specification). The Brahmana statement exists precisely for this purpose."

That is: the Brahmana's repetition here isn't redundant either — it implicitly excludes an alternative (a "donkey-rope," as opposed to the "horse-rope" specified), a specification the mantra alone cannot convey.

The sutra's meaning: "This Brahmana statement is a prohibitive injunction (niṣedha-vidhi)." Before following Sayanacharya's own argument, it helps to understand the classical Mimamsa taxonomy of injunctive statements (vidhi) — sentences prescribing that a given act be performed in a given way. Mimamsa authorities recognize three kinds:

(1) Apūrva-vidhi ("wholly new" injunction) — a sentence prescribing an act knowable by no other means. "One who desires heaven should perform yajna"; "one should sprinkle the grain [with mantra]" — these are apurva-vidhis, since no alternative path exists to fulfill the stated aim.

(2) Niyama-vidhi (restrictive injunction) — where two possible methods exist for performing some act, and a sentence specifies that only one of them should be adopted...

It must put on a meaning foreign to it, namely, that of not taking, And, thirdly, "taking the gardabha rope" a meaning which presents itself, as the word rope of itself includes both the asva and the gardabha ropes, has to be barred. Not so, we answer. On your view (that...

original p. 391

The other method isn't explicitly negated — it simply becomes moot. Take "vrīhīn avahanti" ("he husks the grain [by pounding]"): to prepare the puroḍāśa cake, grain must be cleaned, husked, and ground. Husking need not be done only by pounding — peeling is equally conceivable — and this niyama-vidhi specifically prescribes pounding. Once pounding is followed, the occasion for peeling never even arises; no explicit prohibition is needed. Niyama-vidhi sentences apply precisely in such contexts, where the alternative was never independently established.

(3) Pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi — its defining characteristic:

विधिर्द्व्यन्तमप्राप्ते नियमः स्यादुके गतिः । तत्र चान्यत्र च प्राप्ते परिसंख्येति कीर्त्यते ॥

विधिर् द्व्य्-अन्तम् अप्राप्ते नियमः स्याद् उके गतिः । तत्र चान्यत्र च प्राप्ते परिषङ्ख्येति कीर्त्यते ॥ vidhir dvy-antam aprāpte niyamaḥ syād uke gatiḥ | tatra cānyatra ca prāpte pariṣaṅkhyeti kīrtyate ||

"Where nothing else is otherwise attained, that instruction is 'vidhi'; where one of two paths is already established and the instruction directs toward one, that is 'niyama'; where both this and another alternative are equally attained, and one is exclusively specified, that is called 'pariṣaṅkhyā.'"

That is: where no path besides the stated one can accomplish a given task, it is vidhi; where either of two paths would work and only one is prescribed, it is niyama; where more than one path is simultaneously viable and one is exclusively singled out, it is pariṣaṅkhyā. Such a statement — prescribing that only one of several available options be taken, the rest set aside — may seem unnecessary, since the situation alone would suggest which path to take anyway; but it earns its purpose precisely by prohibiting the other paths.

Example: "pañca pañca-nakhā bhakṣyāḥ" ("the five five-clawed [animals] are edible") — meaning only these five specified clawed animals may be eaten; other animals may not, though there's no requirement that all five must be eaten. This is precisely why pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi differs from apūrva- and niyama-vidhi: failing to perform what is stated in the latter two counts as a defect (karma-lopa) in the rite, but this defect does not apply to pariṣaṅkhyā.

Pariṣaṅkhyā itself comes in two kinds: Shrauti (explicit, marked by words like "eva," "only") and Lakshaniki (implied, established through the sentence's own structure without such marker-words). The sentence under discussion belongs to this second, implied category — which is precisely why further discussion is needed.

The mantra "imāmu gṛbhṇan" is used in the fire-altar construction rite (agnichayana): bricks are needed for the fire-pit, horses and donkeys carry the required earth, and ropes are needed to lead them — this mantra is recited while taking hold of such a rope. Without the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("thus he takes the horse-named rope"), the mantra might be recited while taking up either the horse's or the donkey's rope; this Brahmana statement clarifies that it should specifically accompany taking up the horse's rope, not the donkey's — precisely the pariṣaṅkhyā function.

An objection arises: without this Brahmana statement, three flaws would follow if the mantra alone were held to demand taking up any rope indiscriminately — abandoning the natural meaning of "ādāna/grahaṇa" (taking/holding), assuming a foreign meaning ("not taking"), and failing to exclude the donkey's rope, which the general word "rope" would otherwise include. As stated:

श्रुतार्थस्य परित्यागः अश्रुतार्थस्य कल्पनात् । प्राप्तस्य बाधो द्वेषं परिसंख्या त्रिदोषणा ॥

श्रुतार्थस्य परित्यागः अश्रुतार्थस्य कल्पनात् । प्राप्तस्य बाधो द्वेषं परिषङ्ख्या त्रिदोषणा ॥ śrutārthasya parityāgaḥ aśrutārthasya kalpanāt | prāptasya bādho dveṣaṃ pariṣaṅkhyā tridoṣaṇā ||

"Abandoning the stated meaning, constructing an unstated one, and barring what is otherwise independently established — pariṣaṅkhyā suffers from these three flaws."

Once the mantra is established as relating to the act of taking hold, the question becomes: taking hold of what? Since the mantra itself uses the word "rashanā" (rope), it must refer to taking hold of a rope in general. Once this general sense is established...

This is a round-about way of getting the meaning, and therefore we must look to the sentence lying before us, "asvabhidhanim adatte," for the link between the mantra and the act of taking. The indication furnished by the presence of the word rope in the mantra goes no further than the general meaning and this general meaning is at once specialised by the sruti word...

Taking up the donkey's rope only becomes "attained" after several intervening steps — merely reciting the mantra doesn't make it directly applicable; only after grasping various intervening matters does the donkey-rope possibility even arise. But once the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" is understood, none of this difficulty arises: it becomes clear that the mantra must accompany taking up specifically the horse's rope. Since the donkey's rope was never genuinely "attained" as a live option, there's no room for the "barring what is established" flaw — and without that flaw, "abandoning one's own meaning" doesn't arise either. With neither flaw applicable, the sutra calls this a pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi precisely in the sense that it excludes the (never truly viable) taking of the donkey's rope.

On further reflection, however, this statement arguably isn't pariṣaṅkhyā in the strict classical sense at all — pariṣaṅkhyā's defining mark is excluding other genuinely available means to accomplish a task, but here no other means was ever truly possible. Once the Brahmana statement clearly prescribes the intended means without ambiguity, the question of grasping the unwanted donkey-rope never arises. This same point appears in the Tantravartika:

ननु एवमप्राप्तिविधिरेवायं संजात इति न वक्तव्यम् । परिसंख्येति फलेनैवं अभिधानाद्दोषः । (तन्त्रवार्तिक)

नन्व् एवम् अप्राप्ति-विधिर् एवायं संजात इति न वक्तव्यम् । परिषङ्ख्येति फलेनैवम् अभिधानाद् दोषः । nanv evam aprāpti-vidhir evāyaṃ saṃjāta iti na vaktavyam | pariṣaṅkhyeti phalenaivam abhidhānād doṣaḥ | (Tantravārtika)

"One might object: this then simply becomes an ordinary injunction (for something not otherwise attained), and the term 'pariṣaṅkhyā' should not apply. But calling it pariṣaṅkhyā on the strength of its resulting function, rather than its strict formal structure, involves no real flaw."

In sum, whether or not this statement technically counts as pariṣaṅkhyā, one point stands firmly established: there is no room whatsoever for the flaw the objector (pūrvapakṣin) alleges. The Brahmana statement conveys a genuinely new point not otherwise present in the mantra.

Sutra's meaning: since a mantra's own hidden/deeper meaning can be directly examined, mantras are not without purpose. The word "vā" (or) here signals this. Connected with "uru prathasveti prathayati" ("spread wide," he spreads) is an arthavāda: "yajñapatim eva tat prathayati" ("it spreads out the yajamāna himself"). The Adhvaryu recites this mantra while spreading the puroḍāśa cake — and just as the cake expands, so too the yajamāna gains growth in wealth and grain, per this arthavāda's own intended meaning. The Brahmana statement exists precisely to connect this arthavāda to the mantra.

On Arthavāda

According to the Mimamsakas, the Veda's overriding purpose is performing yajnas to obtain unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit — the Brahmanas prescribe the ritual acts, while the Samhita supplies the mantras recited while performing them. But Brahmana texts don't consist solely of injunctions (vidhi-vākya) — some portions fit neither prescription nor prohibition. Rather than dismiss these as meaningless (which would compromise the Veda's own defining coherence), Mimamsakas hold that such passages support the Veda's central purpose indirectly — setting aside their surface/literal sense to grasp a different, connective meaning tied to the injunctions nearby. Such statements are called arthavāda, generally either praising an enjoined act or condemning a prohibited one. Arthavāda divides into four kinds:

(1) Praśaṃsā — praise (of what is enjoined). (2) Nindā — censure (of what is prohibited).

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

From its mention in the mantra.

The adhvaryu, referring to the purodasa quotes the mantra and says, Spread it out. And because he says this we understand the act of spreading it out to be the work of the...

original p. 396

(3) Parakṛti — relating that some great person in the past performed the enjoined act. (4) Purākalpa — narrating an ancient historical account.

These statements convey that fruit accrues from performing an enjoined act, helping a person decide whether to undertake it, by clarifying its good or bad aspects — supporting the injunctions in this way.

Corresponding to the three pramanas (perception, inference, revealed word), arthavādas are likewise classified into three kinds:

(1) गुणवाद (Guṇavāda) — where the stated meaning contradicts direct perception, it is called guṇavāda (a metaphorical statement). Example:

आदित्यो यूपः । āditya yūpaḥ | "The sun is the sacrificial post"

— taken literally this is meaningless; the intended sense is that the post, like the sun, shines with brilliance — brilliance being their shared quality (guṇa).

(2) अनुवाद (Anuvāda) — restating an already-known fact. Example:

अग्निर्हिमस्य भेषजम् । agnir himasya bheṣajam | "Fire is the remedy for cold"

— common knowledge to everyone.

(3) भूतार्थवाद (Bhūtārthavāda) — matters impossible to establish through perception or inference. Example:

इन्द्रो वृत्राय वज्रम् उदयच्छत् । indro vṛtrāya vajram udayacchat | "Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vritra"

On this third category, a genuine disagreement exists between Agama-authority proponents (like Badarayana and Sayana) and the Mimamsakas. Sayanacharya holds that rejecting the literal truth of bhūtārthavāda statements would render all texts — Veda, Purana, Itihasa alike — unauthoritative. The Mimamsakas instead hold that bhūtārthavādas must be read purely as praise or censure, not literal fact. But the Mimamsaka position doesn't fully hold up: consider that the "Ratrisukta" yajna's own mantras nowhere state the rite's fruit — that fruit appears only in the associated arthavāda. Even the Mimamsakas must therefore accept that arthavāda genuinely conveys authoritative new information in such cases.

adhvaryu. As in common talk whoever says, Do this may be looked on as the real agent, so here the adhvaryu who says, Spread it out, is he who spreads it out.

As to the argument that the mantras must have a spiritual use in the sacrifice, because it is strictly enjoined that such a text as for example, "agnir murdha divah," be recited in that order of the words only, his answer to that is in the next sutra.

original p. 397

The Mimamsakas' "fruit-authority" doctrine (that every Vedic statement is authoritative only insofar as it supports yajna-performance) meets genuine resistance in the Upanishads and Gita.

In the Chandogya Upanishad:

तद्यथेह कर्मचितो लोकः क्षीयते एवमेवामुत्र पुण्यचितो लोकः क्षीयते (Chandogya Upanishad 8.1.6)

तद् यथा इह कर्म-चितो लोकः क्षीयते एवम् एवामुत्र पुण्य-चितो लोकः क्षीयते tad yathā iha karma-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate evam evāmutra puṇya-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate

"Just as here, a world built through action decays, so too, in the next world, a world built through merit likewise decays."

And in the Bhagavad Gita:

यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः । वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2.42)

याम् इमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्य् अविपश्चितः । वेद-वाद-रताः पार्थ नान्यद् अस्तीति वादिनः ॥ yām imāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadanty avipaścitaḥ | veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ ||

"That flowery speech which the unwise proclaim, O Partha, devoted to the letter of the Veda, declaring 'there is nothing else [beyond ritual fruit]'..."

That is: just as worldly fruit is transient, so too are the heavenly pleasures gained through yajna — both texts hold that those who claim yajna-fruit as the only, ultimate reward are "avipaścitaḥ," the unwise (i.e., the Mimamsakas).

Returning to resolve the earlier fixed-word-order objection: in statements like "uru prathasva," the word "prathayati" was construed as connected to an arthavāda — but then where does the actual injunction to spread the puroḍāśa come from? The sutra "mantrābhidhānāt" answers this: the Adhvaryu addresses the puroḍāśa directly — "O puroḍāśa, spread yourself out" — and by this address alone, it becomes clear that the Adhvaryu himself must perform the spreading. This mirrors ordinary experience: if one person tells another to do something, carrying it out becomes that person's own responsibility — no separate injunction is needed. Note: "mantrābhidhānāt" is not itself one of Jaimini's own sutras — it is a Shabara-bhashya sentence Sayana has interspersed while working through Jaimini's sutras, itself carrying sutra-like concision, a technique commentators occasionally employ.

Even so, since word-order must not be altered (altering it produces nonsense), this sutra answers the objection that mantras yield only unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit.

"Aviruddhaṃ param" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.47)

परं द्वितीयसूत्रोक्तं स्यात्प्रत्ययं पूपस्वाकशंसाकसं न हि अयं साकल्क्रमनियमादृष्ट्यं निवारयामः ॥ किं तर्हि ॥ मन्त्रेण जायमानमर्थप्रत्यायनं दृष्टप्रयोजनत्वान्नोपेक्षितव्यमिति ब्रूमः । ननु प्रोक्षणीरासादय (Vajasaneyi Samhita 1.33) इति मन्त्रो बुद्धमेवार्थं शास्ति । तदयुक्तम् ।

परं द्वितीय-सूत्रोक्तं स्यात् ... न हि अयं साकल-क्रम-नियमादृष्ट्यं निवारयामः ॥ किं तर्हि ॥ मन्त्रेण जायमानम् अर्थ-प्रत्यायनं दृष्ट-प्रयोजनत्वान् नोपेक्षितव्यम् इति ब्रूमः । ननु प्रोक्षणीर् आसादय इति मन्त्रो बुद्धम् एवार्थं शास्ति । तद् अयुक्तम् । paraṃ dvitīya-sūtroktaṃ syāt ... na hi ayaṃ sākala-krama-niyamādṛṣṭyaṃ nivārayāmaḥ || kiṃ tarhi || mantreṇa jāyamānam artha-pratyāyanaṃ dṛṣṭa-prayojanatvān nopekṣitavyam iti brūmaḥ | nanu prokṣaṇīr āsādaya iti mantro buddham evārthaṃ śāsti | tad ayuktam |

"What was said in the second sutra is not contradicted by us — we do not deny the unseen benefit of the fixed recitation-order. What then is our point? We say that the meaning-conveying function arising through the mantra, being a directly observable benefit, must not be overlooked. But doesn't the mantra 'prokṣaṇīr āsādaya' merely prescribe an already-known matter? That objection does not hold."

Sutra's meaning: what the second sutra states is not opposed to our view. The intent of "vākya-niyamāt" (the second sutra) was that altering the mantra's word-order yields an improper result — this we don't deny; reciting mantras does yield a fruit. But our own position is: reciting a mantra also produces knowledge of its meaning, which helps carry out yajnas properly — and this directly observable benefit (dṛṣṭa-prayojana) must not be neglected or denied. Mantras, in other words, possess both the unseen fruit the objector claims and a directly observable one.

This answers the third original objection ("buddha-shāstrāt") — recall the "agnīd agnīn vihara" example, objected to as useless repetition of already-known matter. Here, the Vajasaneyi Samhita's "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" is cited: reciting this mantra, one places the mantra-sanctified water...

"Sampreṣakarmaṇo garhānupalambhe saṃskāratvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.48)

संप्रेषकर्मणो गर्हा त्वदुक्त दोषो नोपलभ्यते । बुद्धस्यापि अर्थस्य मन्त्रेणानुसंस्करणान्नियमाद्दृष्टलक्षणस्य संस्कारस्य सद्भावात् । यच्चोक्तं चत्वारि शृंगेति मन्त्रेऽसंभवमेवार्थमभिधत्त इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

संप्रेष-कर्मणो गर्हा त्वद्-उक्त दोषो नोपलभ्यते । बुद्धस्याप्य् अर्थस्य मन्त्रेणानुसंस्करणान् नियमाद् दृष्ट-लक्षणस्य संस्कारस्य सद्भावात् । यच् चोक्तं चत्वारि शृङ्गेति मन्त्रेऽसंभवम् एवार्थम् अभिधत्त इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥ saṃpreṣa-karmaṇo garhā tvad-ukta doṣo nopalabhyate | buddhasyāpy arthasya mantreṇānusaṃskaraṇān niyamād dṛṣṭa-lakṣaṇasya saṃskārasya sadbhāvāt | yac coktaṃ catvāri śṛṅgeti mantre'saṃbhavam evārtham abhidhatta iti tasyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||

"The fault you alleged for acts commanded by 'presha' (directive) mantras is not actually found. Even for already-known matter, reciting the mantra confers a directly-observable refinement (saṃskāra) upon the act, following the established rule. As for the earlier objection that the 'four-horned' mantra states something self-evidently impossible, an answer to that follows too."

Sutra's meaning: since an injunctive statement conveys ritual refinement (saṃskāra), it escapes the objection. Mantras like "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" and "agnīd agnīn vihara" are presha-mantras — directive mantras commanding that certain acts be performed. Their stated meaning may already be known, but reciting the mantra to re-announce the act carries a special unseen fruit precisely through following this rule.

Though one learns during study what acts must be performed at their proper time, this knowledge doesn't remain constantly active in memory — it stays latent. Some means is needed to bring it to conscious attention; one could try to recall it through deliberate focus alone, but the rule requiring the act be performed specifically accompanied by this mantra rules out other means of recollection. The claim that presha-mantras are meaningless therefore does not hold.

That is: "if it remained actively in memory, recalling it via the mantra would be unnecessary. Whether "saṃskāra" is understood as conferring a special unseen fruit (imparting a new quality) or as awakening a hidden mental impression, either way mantras are established as meaningful and beneficial.

This resolves the fourth objection ("avidyamāna-vacanāt") — that mantras like "catvāri śṛṅgā" ("four horns") describe things never experienced in ordinary life.

"When a sentence states something non-existent, we recognize a secondary/metaphorical meaning, based on precedent. As follows: the four priests — Hotr, Udgatr, Adhvaryu, and Brahma — are this sacrifice's 'horns.' The morning pressing and the other two pressings are its three 'feet.' The Garhapatya and other sacred fires, together with the seven meters, are its 'hands.' It is bound threefold through the Rigveda and the other Vedas. 'It fulfills desires' — hence it is called a 'bull' (vṛṣabha); it 'roars' — that is, the hymn of praise — and, from the word 'etc.,' does so repeatedly. This same great deity (Mahādeva), this life-breath in the form of the sacrifice, has entered mortals — hence humans having two principal [organs/heads] need not be taken too literally. Metaphorical usage is seen in ordinary life too — as when we call a woman 'swan-toothed' or 'Kashi's own curly-locked one,' describing her as embodying these qualities directly. Likewise, addresses to inanimate things — 'O herb, protect him,' 'hear, O stones' — should be understood as oriented toward praise. Where the herb itself is said to protect [the wearer], need it even be said that the one who prepares and ties it also protects him? Similarly, the stones too..."

This is the celebrated allegorical reading of the "four-horned bull" mantra: rather than describing a literal impossible creature, it poetically describes the yajna itself — its four priests as horns, its three daily pressings as feet, its sacred fires and meters as hands, and its threefold Vedic foundation as its binding — resolving the fourth objection entirely.

In such mention there is a special meaning.

The four officiating priests—hotri, adhvaryu, udgatri and brahma—are the four horns of this sacrifice. The morning, noon, and evening oblations are its three feet. The sacrificer and his wife are...

original p. 401

Sutra's meaning: in a context stating a non-existent thing, that sentence carries a special, secondary meaning. Where any sentence describes non-existent things, a different, secondary meaning must be construed — setting aside the apparent literal meaning. Non-Vedic literature uses such devices too: describing a river as "चक्रवाकस्तनी" (cakravāka-stanī, having chakravaka birds as her breasts), "हंसदन्तावली" (haṃsa-dantāvalī, rows of swans as her teeth), काश (kāśa) grass as her garment, शैवल (śaivala) moss as her hair — one naturally understands a meaning beyond the literal claim. The same principle applies to the objector's cited mantra "चत्वारि शृङ्गा" (catvāri śṛṅgā) — it need not describe a literal four-horned, three-footed creature at all:

चत्वारि शृङ्गाणि (catvāri śṛṅgāṇi, Four Horns) — the four principal priests carrying out the yajna's work: होतृ (hotṛ), अध्वर्यु (adhvaryu), उद्गातृ (udgātṛ), and ब्रह्मा (brahmā).

त्रयः पादाः (trayaḥ pādāḥ, Three Feet) — the morning pressing (प्रातःसवन prātaḥ-savana), midday pressing (माध्यंदिनसवन mādhyandina-savana), and evening pressing (सायंसवन sāyaṃ-savana).

द्वे शीर्षे (dve śīrṣe, Two Heads) — the यजमान (yajamāna, patron of the sacrifice) and his wife.

सप्त हस्ताः (sapta hastāḥ, Seven Hands) — the गायत्री (gāyatrī) and the other Vedic meters (seven in number).

त्रिधा बद्धः (tridhā baddhaḥ, Threefold Bound) — bound together through the Rigveda and the other Vedas.

वृषभः (vṛṣabhaḥ, Bull) — one who "rains down" (वर्षति varṣati) desired boons, like rainfall.

रोरवीति (roravīti, "Roars") — he who repeatedly recites the mantras in the form of स्तोत्र (stotra) and शस्त्र (śastra) (hymn and recitation).

If it is said of it that it roars mightily, the meaning is that it is repeatedly the cause of sounds in the shape of the stotra and the Shastras. "This great god," that is, this god in the form of his fully-developed sacrifice, "has approached mortals," that is, men, and men only, can have part in it. A river is described as having two chakravaka birds for her breasts, white swans for her lines of teeth, the kasa plant for her garment, and the saivala plant of her hair. In the same way such texts as "oshade trayasva" and "srinota gravaeah," in which things without sense are addressed by name, must be construed as implying praise. "If in...

original p. 402

Great God (Maho Deva) — this deity in the form of the yajna itself. Entered Mortals — has taken abode within humans, meaning: the authority to perform this yajna belongs to human beings alone.

That is: this mantra's real purport is that the above elements are the principal constituents of every yajna-rite — not a description of some strange creature. Recognizing the secondary meaning elsewhere too shows the claim that mantras are meaningless to be groundless.

Similarly, sentences addressing inanimate objects serve to praise the associated act. "Oṣadhe trāyasvainam" belongs to the yajamāna's shaving-ritual: addressing the darbha grass, "protect the yajamāna," the point is — if the grass itself protects the yajamāna seated for shaving, how much more should the one performing the shaving protect him. Likewise "śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ" ("listen, O stones"), recited before the dawn hymns (prātar-anuvāka): if even inanimate stones listen to these hymns, how much more attentively should the assembled learned Brahmins listen — this is the intended point.

This resolves the objection raised in "Artha-vipratiṣedhāt" — the alleged contradictions in "Aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam" (Aditi is both heaven and atmosphere) and "eka eva rudraḥ... sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrāḥ" (Rudra is one alone... yet thousands of Rudras exist).

"Guṇāvadhi-vipratiṣedhāt syāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.50)

यथा त्वमेव सिता त्वमेव मातेत्यत्र गौणप्रयोगादविरोधस्तद्वत् । एवमेकरुद्रदेवत्ये कर्मण्येको रुद्रः शतरुद्रदेवत्ये शतं रुद्रा इत्यविरोधः । यदुक्तं स्वाध्या...

यथा त्वम् एव सिता त्वम् एव मातेत्य् अत्र गौण-प्रयोगाद् अविरोधस् तद्वत् । एवम् एक-रुद्र-देवत्ये कर्मण्य् एको रुद्रः शत-रुद्र-देवत्ये शतं रुद्रा इत्य् अविरोधः । यद् उक्तं स्वाध्या... yathā tvam eva sitā tvam eva mātety atra gauṇa-prayogād avirodhas tadvat | evam eka-rudra-devatye karmaṇy eko rudraḥ śata-rudra-devatye śataṃ rudrā ity avirodhaḥ | yad uktaṃ svādhyā...

"Just as in 'you alone are my father, you alone are my mother,' the metaphorical usage removes any contradiction, so too here: in a rite dedicated to a single Rudra-deity, there is one Rudra; in a rite dedicated to a hundred Rudra-deities, there are a hundred Rudras — no contradiction. As for what was earlier said regarding svādhyāya..."

That is: just as calling someone "both father and mother" carries an evident metaphorical sense without contradiction, the "one Rudra"/"thousand Rudras" statements simply describe different ritual contexts invoking different numbers of Rudra-deities — no genuine inconsistency remains.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...this sowing the plant itself is protected, much more will the sower be" is the meaning of the one text. "If the very stones listen to the morning lesson, much more will learned brahmanas" is the meaning of the other.

As to the contradiction supposed to be involved in saying that Aditi is both Dyaus and Antariksha, his answer to that is in the next sutra.

Admit the metaphorical meaning, and there will be no contradiction.

It is just as in the sentence, You are my father and my mother, where the metaphorical meaning is apparent, and there is no contradiction. In the same way, too, in...

original p. 403

युमधीयानो माणवकः पूर्णिकायाः अवघातं न प्रकाशयितुमिच्छतीति तत्प्रोत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

(Regarding the earlier objection that a student engaged in rote study has no wish to convey meaning connected to Purnika's grain-pounding, a further answer follows.)

Sutra's meaning: since the metaphorical meaning indicated in the mantra is accepted, no room for genuine contradiction remains. In ordinary speech, "you alone are father, you alone are mother, you alone are everything" is a common expression — just as we don't take this literally, "aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam" doesn't literally mean Aditi is heaven and is the atmosphere; a secondary meaning must be grasped. Likewise, a rite addressed to a single Rudra invokes one Rudra-deity; one addressed to a hundred Rudras invokes a hundred — no contradiction arises.

Turning to resolve the Purnika/rote-recitation objection (from "svādhyāyavad-vacanāt"): the objector had argued that a mantra recited during rote study (illustrated by the woman "Purnika" pounding grain nearby) bears no genuine connection between mantra and act. The next sutra answers this.

"Vidyā-vacanam-asaṃyogāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.51)

वेदविद्याग्रहणकालेऽर्थस्य यदवचनं तदयज्ञसंयोगादुपपद्यते । न हि पूर्णिकाया अवघातको यज्ञसंयुक्तः । नापि माणवको यज्ञमनुतिष्ठति । अतो यज्ञानुष्ठारान्न तत्रार्थविवक्षा । यदुक्तं अम्यक्सा त इन्द्र । सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतूत्यादावर्थस्य ज्ञातुमशक्यत्वादनवबोध इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

वेद-विद्या-ग्रहण-कालेऽर्थस्य यद् अवचनं तद् अयज्ञ-संयोगाद् उपपद्यते । न हि पूर्णिकाया अवघातको यज्ञ-संयुक्तः । नापि माणवको यज्ञम् अनुतिष्ठति । अतो यज्ञानुष्ठारान् न तत्रार्थ-विवक्षा । ... veda-vidyā-grahaṇa-kāle'rthasya yad avacanaṃ tad ayajña-saṃyogād upapadyate | na hi pūrṇikāyā avaghātako yajña-saṃyuktaḥ | nāpi māṇavako yajñam anutiṣṭhati | ato yajñānuṣṭhārān na tatrārtha-vivakṣā | ...

"That meaning goes unconveyed during Vedic study is explained by the absence of any connection to an actual yajna. Purnika's pounding is not connected to a yajna, nor is the student performing one — hence, absent yajna-performance, there is no intention to convey meaning in that context. As for the claim that meaning cannot be determined in texts like 'amyaksā ta indra' or 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū,' an answer to that follows next."

That is: the student's silence on meaning during rote study isn't evidence mantras lack meaning generally — it simply reflects that neither Purnika's work nor the student's recitation is actually part of a yajna. Where no yajna is being performed, there's no occasion to intend conveying meaning at all — this doesn't undermine the mantra's meaning when genuinely used in ritual context.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...a sacrifice connected with one Rudra, there is one Rudra: in a sacrifice connected with a hundred Rudras, there are a hundred Rudras, and this without any contradiction in terms.

As to the remark that the boy engaged in study has no wish to throw light on what Purnika is doing his answer to that is in the next sutra.

The non-communication of knowledge here is due to the fact that there is no connection with the sacrifice.

If, at the time of studying the Veda, the meaning is not expressed, that is quite right. Because at such a time there is no connection with the sacrifice. The action of Purnika is not connected with the sacrifice. And the boy is not performing the sacrifice, Neither Purnika nor the boy are here assisting the sacrifice, and therefore it is that there is no desire on the boy's part to convey the meaning of what he is reciting.

As to the argument that there is no meaning in such a text as, for example, "amyak sa ta indra," or "srinyeva jarbhari turpharitu," because the meaning cannot be made out, his answer to that is in the next sutra.

original p. 404

Sutra's meaning: during rote practice/study, since the mantra bears no connection to any yajna-related ritual act, no meaning is conveyed. The objection holds that meaning-grasping fails to occur during Vedic study — but when mantras are genuinely applied in yajnas, real efforts at conveying and understanding meaning take place; during mere memorization, no such occasion arises. In the pestle-mantra case, since Purnika's husking isn't part of a yajna, no rule ties the mantra's recitation to the pounding — and the student's own recitation likewise isn't yajna-related. Where no yajna-connection exists, the absence of meaning-knowledge is simply not a flaw at all.

Resolving the "unintelligible mantras" objection ("avijñeyo'tha," objection 5):

"Śataḥ parama-vijñānam" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.52)

विद्यमान एवार्थः प्रमादालस्यादिभिर्विज्ञायते । तेषां निगम-निरुक्त-व्याकरणवशेन धातुतोऽर्थः परिकल्प्यते । तद्यथा । जर्भरी तुर्फरीति इत्येषां मन्त्राणां जर्भर्यादीन्यश्विनो रूपाणि । तेषु हि द्वित्वं लक्ष्यते । अश्विनं चेदं सूक्तम् आ अश्विनौ हंसारावित्यर्थः । सृ इति भर्तारावित्यर्थः । स्फर्फरीतं हंसारावित्यर्थः (Nirukta 2.13[?]) । इति । एवमन्यत्रापीत्यावश्यकम् । यदुक्तं प्रमाणान्तरसंयोगात्स्याच्च न स्यादिति तत्प्रोत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥

विद्यमान एवार्थः प्रमादालस्यादिभिर् विज्ञायते । तेषां निगम-निरुक्त-व्याकरण-वशेन धातुतोऽर्थः परिकल्प्यते । तद् यथा । जर्भरी तुर्फरीति इत्य् एषां मन्त्राणां जर्भर्यादीन्य् अश्विनो रूपाणि । तेषु हि द्वित्वं लक्ष्यते । अश्विनं चेदं सूक्तम्... vidyamāna evārthaḥ pramādālasyādibhir vijñāyate | teṣāṃ nigama-nirukta-vyākaraṇa-vaśena dhātuto'rthaḥ parikalpyate | tad yathā | jarbharī turpharīti ity eṣāṃ mantrāṇāṃ jarbharyādīny aśvino rūpāṇi | teṣu hi dvitvaṃ lakṣyate | aśvinaṃ cedaṃ sūktam...

"The meaning does exist, but goes unknown due to carelessness, laziness, or similar causes. In such cases, meaning must be constructed from the word's own verbal root, with the help of Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana. For example: in the mantra containing 'jarbharī turpharītu,' words like 'jarbhari' are forms referring to the Ashvins — their dual number is discernible, and this sukta is itself an Ashvin-hymn."

That is: the meaning is genuinely present in such mantras, but goes unnoticed through carelessness or inattention — not because it's inherently absent. Careful etymological analysis via Nirukta and grammar, cross-checked against parallel passages, reveals that even the famously obscure "jarbhari turpharitu" refers to the twin Ashvin deities, confirmed by the dual grammatical forms and the hymn's overall Ashvin-context.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The meaning is there, but it is not known.

The meaning is there, but from error, laziness or the like, it is not known. In the case of such texts a meaning must be conjectured from the root of the unknown word, with the help of parallel passages, the Nirukta and grammar. Take an example. Jarbhari, turpharitu and other words of the same kind in this hymn must be names of the Asvins. For we see that they are duals. And the hymn is an Asvin hymn, as is clear from the words...

original p. 405

One can indeed determine the meaning of such texts. For difficult words like these, gathering other Vedic passages using similar constructions, with Nirukta and grammar's help, one determines the underlying verbal root and infers meaning accordingly. Working through the cited example: "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" are clearly dual-number words, occurring in verse 6 of Rigveda Mandala 10, Sukta 106 — a sukta dedicated to the Ashvins, confirmed by that same sukta's own line "aśvinoḥ kāmam aprāḥ" ("you fulfilled the Ashvins' desire"). Therefore "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" refer to the Ashvin deities. The Nirukta itself, holding this same view, glosses "jarbharī" as "those who nourish/give shelter" and "turpharītū" as "those who destroy [obstacles]." The same method of inference applies to "amyak sā ta" and similar texts.

The ninth and final objection-sutra: "Anitya-saṃyogān mantrānarthakyaṃ." The Veda mentions non-eternal things — Pramaganda, Babara, Prātaḥsavana, and similar proper names of persons who lived and then perished. Either the claim that the Veda is beginningless (anādi) is false, the objector argues, or the Vedas have no meaning at all — mere recitation must be their sole purpose.

"Uktvā anitya-saṃyogaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.53)

प्रथमपादान्तिमाधिकरणे सोऽयमनित्यसंयोगदोष...

(Jaimini refers back to his own earlier treatment: this same objection regarding connection with non-eternal things was already raised and resolved in the final adhikarana of the Mimamsa-sutra's first pada — the answer given there applies equally here.)

"asvinoh kamam apra" occurring in it. Reasoning in this way the author of the Nirukta gives his explanation of these words. "Jarbhari," he says, is the same as bhartarau and "turpharitu" the same as hantarau. And the same method of inference must be applied to the text "amyak sa ta" and the like.

As for the argument that the Veda cannot be without beginning; because in it there is mention of non-eternal things such as, for example, king Pramaganda, his answer to that in the next sutra.

I have already dealt with the supposed connection with non-eternal things.

In the last adhikarana of the first pada of the Mimansa Sutra this objection, founded on the connection with non-eternal things, has been set out and disposed of, as...

उक्त्वा परिष्कृतः । तथा हि । तत्र पूर्वपक्षे वेदानां पौरुषेयत्वं वक्तुं काठकं कालापकमित्यादिपुरुषसंबन्धाभिधानं हेतूक्त्वा नित्यदर्शनाच्च (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.29) इति हेत्वन्तरं सूत्रितम् । कस्यायमर्थः । बबरः प्रावाहणिः अकामयत (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.1.3[?]) इत्यादि अनित्यानां बबरादीनामर्थानां दर्शनात्क पूर्वमसत्त्वाच्चौरुषेयो वेद इति तत्रोत्तरं सूत्रितम् । परं तु श्रुतिसामान्यात् (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.30) इति तस्यायमर्थः । यत्तु परं काठकादिसाम्यानं तत्त्ववचननिमित्तं । यत्तु परं बबराख्यनिमित्त दर्शनं तच्चापि सामान्यमात्रम् ।

(Jaimini's own summary, referring back to his earlier first-pada discussion: the objection there cited the human-derived names "Kathaka," "Kalapaka" (schools named after their teachers) and the appearance of transient proper names like "Babara" as evidence the Veda was composed by humans; the resolution held that such school-names simply reflect which sages transmitted a given recension, not authorship of the Veda's content itself, and that the "Babara" reference is a case of similar-sounding words rather than a genuinely non-eternal element within the Veda's own composition.)

Sutra's meaning: the matter of non-eternal things occurring in the Veda has already been addressed. In the closing portion of the first pada of Jaimini's sutras, while establishing the Veda's non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva), this same flaw regarding non-eternal things was resolved — Sayanacharya now summarizes that earlier resolution here, beginning with "tathā hi" ("that is").

The objection there held that the Vedas, like Kalidasa's own works, were composed by human authors — supported by two points: first, the connection to named persons via titles like "Kathaka," "Kalapaka," and similar Vedic school-names...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

follows. There, while engaged in putting forward the view to be controverted, Jaimini has adduced the occurrence of such titles as Kathaka and Kalapaka, as indicating the human origin of the Vedas. In the sutra "And because non-eternal things are mentioned" he adduces a second reason. The meaning is this. In the text "babarah pravahanir akamayata" mention is made of non-eternal things, such as Babara, a proper name, and the like. The Veda cannot have existed before these non-eternal things, and is therefore of human origin. The answer to this is in the sutra "Your second argument is based on a similarity of sounds only." The meaning of this is as follows. We have seen that the occurrence of such titles as Kathaka is due to the fact that sages like Katha taught the various versions of the Veda. Your second argument, drawn from the occurrence in the Veda of non-eternal things like...

original p. 407

...and the sutra "anitya-darśanāc ca" ("because non-eternal things are seen") further supports the Veda's supposed human origin — citing the mantra "babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata" and similar texts containing apparently non-eternal names, arguing these mantras couldn't predate the persons they name.

परं तु श्रुतिसामान्यमात्रम् ।

परं तु श्रुति-सामान्य-मात्रम् । paraṃ tu śruti-sāmānya-mātram |

"But this rests merely on a similarity of sounds."

This is Jaimini's answer: such words resemble ordinary words only in sound and letter-sequence, not in meaning. The siddhanta holds: "Kathaka," "Kalapaka," and similar terms denote different Vedic branches/schools; "Babara" and similar words merely resemble ordinary proper names in their letter-sequence — there was no actual person named "Babara." Rather, "babara" is the very sound wind makes while blowing — so "babaraḥ" here means "the wind that makes that sound," and "prāvāhaṇīḥ" means "one whose nature is to blow swiftly/forcefully." The same reasoning applies to words like "Pramaganda."

In this way, no flaw whatsoever remains regarding mantra-meaning — mantras genuinely exist to convey meaning, and each mantra should be applied precisely where its stated meaning holds genuine use.

A further doubt arises: the siddhanta-sutras have logically established that mantras reveal meaning and possess directly observable purpose — but one might object that no actual scriptural (śruti) statement supports this conclusion. Jaimini anticipates this and answers next.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Babara, really rests on a similarity of sounds only. There is no reference in the passage in question to a man called Babara. Babara is an onomatopoeic word. That being so, by the person who makes the sound ba-ba-ra is meant the god Vayu or the wind. The other word here, "pravahani," is also a name of Vayu so styled because he "pre-eminently travels" (prakarshena vahanasilah). Similar reasonings must be applied to other passages which appear to present a reference to non-eternal things.

We have thus got rid of each and every objection. At the sacrifice the texts are meant to be significant, and they are recited that they may convey their meaning,

But, it may be said, this thesis of yours, that the use of the recited texts at the sacrifice is a non-spiritual one, their purport being merely to convey their meaning, can be put by you only on probable grounds. You cannot produce a proof confirming this view from Scripture. He anticipates and answers this doubt in the next sutra.

original p. 408

"Liṅgo'padeśas tad-arthavat" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.58)

आग्नेय्याग्निध्रमुपतिष्ठेति श्रूयते । तस्यायमर्थः । अग्निदेवता यस्या ऋचः सेयमाग्नेयी । तयाग्निध्रस्थानमुपतिष्ठेति । अत्र ह्युपस्थानमुपदिशद्ब्राह्मणमग्ने नय (RV 1.14.1[?]) इत्येवंरूपोपस्थाने मन्त्रप्रतीकं पठित्वा नोपस्थितिं किं तु आग्नेयीत्याख्येनोपदिशति ।

आग्नेय्य् आग्निध्रम् उपतिष्ठेति श्रूयते । तस्यायम् अर्थः । अग्नि-देवता यस्या ऋचः सेयम् आग्नेयी । तयाग्निध्र-स्थानम् उपतिष्ठेति । अत्र ह्य् उपस्थानम् उपदिशद् ब्राह्मणम् अग्ने नय इत्य् एवं-रूपोपस्थाने मन्त्र-प्रतीकं पठित्वा नोपस्थितिं किं तु आग्नेयीत्य् आख्येनोपदिशति । āgneyy āgnidhram upatiṣṭheti śrūyate | tasyāyam arthaḥ | agni-devatā yasyā ṛcaḥ seyam āgneyī | tayāgnidhra-sthānam upatiṣṭheti | atra hy upasthānam upadiśad brāhmaṇam agne naya ity evaṃ-rūpopasthāne mantra-pratīkaṃ paṭhitvā nopasthitiṃ kiṃ tu āgneyīty ākhyenopadiśati |

"It is heard: 'one should approach the Agnidh's platform with an Āgneyī [verse].' Its meaning: that Rik whose deity is Agni is called 'Āgneyī' — one should approach the Agnidh's platform with such a verse. Here, the Brahmana, in prescribing this approach, does not simply cite the opening words of the actual verse ('agne naya...') — instead, it prescribes it using the descriptive term 'Āgneyī.'"

Sutra's meaning: ritual terms are used precisely to indicate meaning. "Āgneyyāgnidhram upatiṣṭheta" is a Brahmana statement indicating the mantra to recite while approaching the Agnidh's platform with one's wife for worship. "Āgneyyā" means "by the mantra whose presiding deity is Agni" — referring to the mantra beginning "agne naya." Rather than naming that mantra directly, the Brahmana uses the grammatically-derived (taddhita) term "āgneyī" ("Agni-related [verse]") — itself proof that the mantra is understood to carry genuine meaning, since only a meaning-bearing verse could be classified by its subject-deity this way. Since mantras thus demonstrably convey meaning, they must be recited at their proper application. Further proofs follow.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The references to mantras by a general description show that the meaning of the texts is taken into account.

There is the brahmana text "agney yagnidhram upatishtheta." The meaning of that is as follows. A verse which has Agni for its deity is styled an Agneyi verse. With such a verse approach the agnidhrasthana. Now here the brahmana, in enjoining the approach referred to, does not take the first two or three words of a verse and say "Approach with the verse, Agne naya &c." No. It uses Agneyi as a descriptive title of such verses. Since wherever Agni is chiefly made mention of in a verse, Agni is the deity of that verse. That being so the taddhita derivative Agneyi is a grammatically correct descriptive title of such verses. Therefore this injunction indicates that the mantra here is recognized as having a...

"Ūhaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.59)

प्रकृतानाम्नातस्य मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ समन्वेतार्थत्वाय तदुचितसदान्तरस्य प्रक्षेपेण पाठ ऊहः । शब्द्यथा । अन्वेनं माता मन्यतामनु पितानु भ्रातेति प्राकृते पशुविषये मन्त्रपाठः (Maitrayani Samhita 4.1.3.4[?]) । तस्य च मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ पशुद्वये सत्यन्वेना माता मन्यताम् इत्युक्त्ये कर्तव्ये इहैकस्मिन्त्रे व्याख्यारूपं ब्राह्मणमेवमाम्नायते । न माता वर्धते न पितेति ।

प्रकृतानाम् नातस्य मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ समन्वेतार्थत्वाय तद्-उचित-पदान्तरस्य प्रक्षेपेण पाठ ऊहः । शब्द्यथा । अन्वेनं माता मन्यताम् अनु पितानु भ्रातेति प्राकृते पशु-विषये मन्त्र-पाठः । तस्य च मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ पशु-द्वये सत्य् अन्वेना माता मन्यताम् इत्य् उक्त्ये कर्तव्ये इहैकस्मिन्त्त्रे व्याख्या-रूपं ब्राह्मणम् एवम् आम्नायते । न माता वर्धते न पितेति । prakṛtānām nātasya mantrasya vikṛtau samanvetārthatvāya tad-ucita-padāntarasya prakṣepeṇa pāṭha ūhaḥ | śabdyathā | anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrāteti prākṛte paśu-viṣaye mantra-pāṭhaḥ | tasya ca mantrasya vikṛtau paśu-dvaye saty anvenā mātā manyatām ity uktye kartavye ihaikasminttre vyākhyā-rūpaṃ brāhmaṇam evam āmnāyate | na mātā vardhate na piteti |

"Ūha (adaptation) means reciting a mantra, originally composed for one context, with an appropriately modified word substituted, so that it retains a fitting meaning when applied in a related but altered context. For example: 'anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrātā' ('may its mother, father, and brother approve of it') is the mantra-text prescribed for a single sacrificial animal. In the modified case of two animals, one might expect the dual form 'anvenā mātā manyatām' — yet the Brahmana's own explanatory gloss on this states: 'the mother is not increased, nor the father' [i.e., these terms remain singular regardless]."

Sutra's meaning: constructing suitable adapted words to fit a given context, when needed, is itself a proof that mantras carry meaning. The original mantra must sometimes be recited with slight modification across different contexts — changing certain words, or substituting others in their place — this practice is called ūha (adaptation), found here and there in ritual application. Consider the mantra recited while leading the sacrificial animal to the offering-place: "anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrātā" (may its mother, father, and brother approve of it)...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...meaning. And since the mantras have a meaning, it is clear that the object of the recitation of the mantras at the sacrifice is to convey that meaning.

In the next sutra Jaimini furnishes a second indication from Scripture of the doctrine that the mantras at the sacrifice are used with a view to their meaning.

Uha.

By uha is meant an alteration wrought upon a text to enable it to convey a modified but kindred meaning. For example. "Anvenam ('this') mata manyatam anu pitanu bhrata"

original p. 410

...its mother, father, and brother — may all these approve of this animal's sacrifice — this mantra is used as-is with a single animal. With two animals, it's modified to "अन्येनौ माता..." (anyenau mātā...); with many animals, to "अन्येनान् माता..." (anyenān mātā...) That is: the singular word becomes dual ("एनौ" enau, these two) or plural ("एनान्" enān, these), according to the animal-count. A Brahmana statement confirms this required adaptation, stating simply:

न माता वर्धते न पिता । na mātā vardhate na pitā | "The mother is not increased, nor the father."

Here, "vṛddhi" (increase) could mean either of two things: age-related growth (childhood through youth to old age), or grammatical number-change (the singular "mātā"/"pitā" becoming dual "mātarau"/"pitarau" or plural "mātaraḥ"/"pitaraḥ"). Age-related growth obviously cannot be denied — it's plainly observable. So the Brahmana's real point must be grammatical: the words "mātṛ" and "pitṛ" specifically should NOT change in number. Since this restriction applies only to those two words, it follows that the remaining word "enam" must instead take the appropriate dual or plural form depending on context. If mantras carried no meaning at all, why would this kind of careful word-adaptation even be necessary? This confirms that mantras do indeed convey genuine meaning.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...is the original form of a mantra referring to the sacrifice of an animal. When there are two animals to be sacrificed the form of this mantra is altered, and they say, "enau ('these two') mata manyatam." When there are more than two there is a different uha and they say "enan ('these') mata manyatam."

Of this mantra there is an interpretative brahmana, "Na mata vardhate na pita," "The mother does not increase, nor the father." Here the thought must arise, is the increase, which is in this brahmana forbidden, increase of the body, or is it increase of the word? By increase of the word of course is meant the change of the singular "matri" to the dual "matarau," or to the plural "matarah." Now it is not possible to prohibit increase of the body. For we see it increase before our eyes, according to the change from child to girl, from girl to woman. We are left with the increase of the word. And the special prohibition against any increase of the words matri and pitri in this text is intended to indicate that the other word enam is to be increased, according to the sense, to enau or enan. But if the meaning of the mantra is not intended to be conveyed by its recitation, then where is the necessity of introducing the dual when two beasts are to be sacrificed, or the plural when more than two beasts are to be sacrificed?

In the same matter he brings forward still another indication from scripture in the next sutra.

"Vidhi-śabdāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.60)

मन्त्रव्याख्यानरूपो ब्राह्मणिकः शब्दो विधिशब्द इत्युच्यते । स चैवमाम्नायते । शतं हिमाः शतं वर्षाणि जीव्यासमेत्येवैतदाह (Shatapatha Brahmana 2.3.4.10) इति । तत्र शतं हिमा इत्येतद्व्याख्येयमन्त्रस्य प्रतीकम् । अवशिष्टं तु तस्य तात्पर्यव्याख्यानम् । मन्त्रस्याविवक्षितार्थत्वे तु किं नाम तात्पर्यं मन्त्रे व्याख्यायेत । तस्माद्विवक्षितार्था मन्त्राः प्रयोगकाले स्वार्थप्रकाशनायैवोच्चार्यन्त इत्याह ॥

मन्त्र-व्याख्यान-रूपो ब्राह्मणिकः शब्दो विधि-शब्द इत्य् उच्यते । स चैवम् आम्नायते । शतं हिमाः शतं वर्षाणि जीव्यासम् इत्य् एवैतद् आह इति । तत्र शतं हिमा इत्य् एतद् व्याख्येय-मन्त्रस्य प्रतीकम् । अवशिष्टं तु तस्य तात्पर्य-व्याख्यानम् । मन्त्रस्याविवक्षितार्थत्वे तु किं नाम तात्पर्यं मन्त्रे व्याख्यायेत । तस्माद् विवक्षितार्था मन्त्राः प्रयोग-काले स्वार्थ-प्रकाशनायैवोच्चार्यन्त इत्य् आह ॥ mantra-vyākhyāna-rūpo brāhmaṇikaḥ śabdo vidhi-śabda ity ucyate | sa caivam āmnāyate | śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam ity evaitad āha iti | tatra śataṃ himā ity etad vyākhyeya-mantrasya pratīkam | avaśiṣṭaṃ tu tasya tātparya-vyākhyānam | mantrasyāvivakṣitārthatve tu kiṃ nāma tātparyaṃ mantre vyākhyāyeta | tasmād vivakṣitārthā mantrāḥ prayoga-kāle svārtha-prakāśanāyaivoccāryanta ity āha ||

"A Brahmana statement that takes the form of explaining a mantra is called a 'vidhi-śabda.' One such is recorded: 'śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam' ('may I live a hundred winters, a hundred years') — this is what is meant. Here, 'śataṃ himāḥ' is the pratīka (opening phrase) of the mantra being explained; the rest explains its purport. If the mantra carried no intended meaning at all, what purport could possibly be explained? This shows that mantras, carrying real intended meaning, are recited at their application specifically to reveal that meaning."

Sutra's meaning: vidhi-śabda words embedded in Brahmanas likewise support that mantras carry meaning. Brahmanas contain many mantra-explanatory statements (the earliest form of Vedic commentary) — such statements are called vidhi-śabda. In "śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam ity evaitad āha" (Shatapatha Brahmana 2.3.4.10), "śataṃ himāḥ" is the mantra-portion, and the rest explains its purport — that it means "may we live a hundred years." Had mantras no meaning, there would be no need to explain their purport at all. This too proves mantras carry genuine meaning.

(A closing summary verse from the Jaimini-nyaya-mala tradition, recapping that mantras like "uru prathasva" are shown to serve a directly observable purpose in ritual application, illuminated further by Brahmana explanation, rather than an exclusively unseen one — precise phrase-level construction is difficult to render with full confidence at this resolution, though the overall recapitulation is consistent with the preceding argument.)

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Because of vidhisabdas.

A clause in a brahmana explanatory of a mantra is called a vidhisabda. For example, take the brahmana "satam himah satam varshani jivyasmetyevaitad aha." Here the words "satam himah" are the pratika, or title consisting of the first two words of the mantra which is to be explained. The rest of the brahmana is the explanation of the mantra. But if the mantra is not intended to convey a meaning, why should the purport of a mantra be explained at all?

Chapter 9. Examination of the Authority of the Brahmana-Portion (the Vidhi/Injunctive Mantras)

Original title: "Brāhmaṇātmaka-mantrabhāgada prāmāṇyavicāravimarśeyu — vidhivākyapramāṇa samarthaneyu" Printed pages 412–419 of the source.

original p. 412

Here, the objector's (pūrvapakṣa) view is presented as a question, and the siddhanta as its answer.

Question: Do mantras like "uru prathasva" yield only an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit, or do they clarify actual ritual procedures — such as spreading the puroḍāśa — in the yajnas where they occur?

The objector's prima facie answer: since Brahmana statements already explain the acts to be performed in yajnas, mantras must be said to yield only unseen merit (puṇya).

Siddhanta: mantras do not yield merit alone as their fruit — the meanings they express are clearly useful for performing yajna-related acts. A directly observable (dṛṣṭa) fruit is always the superior explanation; mantras therefore do convey meaning, contrary to the claim that mere recitation is their only purpose.

A new question opens: granting the mantra-portion's authority, does the Brahmana-portion itself carry the same authority?

नन्वस्तु मन्त्रभागस्य प्रामाण्यम् । ब्राह्मणभागस्य तु न तदस्त्येक्ष्यते । तथा हि । द्विविधं ब्राह्मणम् । विधिरर्थवादश्चेति । तथा चासद्बन्धः । कर्मचोदना ब्राह्मणानि ब्राह्मणशेषोऽर्थवादः (Jaimini... 2.1.33[?]) इति । विधिरपि द्विविधः । अप्रवृत्तप्रवर्तनमज्ञातज्ञापनं चेति । यथा पुरोडाशं निर्वपन्ति दीक्षणीयायाम् (Shatapatha Brahmana 1.1[?]) इत्याद्या कर्मकाण्डगतविधयोऽप्रवृत्तिप्रवर्तकाः । आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् (Shatapatha Aranyaka 1.4.1[?]) इत्याद्यो ब्रह्मकाण्डगता अज्ञातज्ञापकाः । तत्र कर्मकाण्डगतानां जर्तिलैर्यवानाग्नौ जुहुयाद् वीरुधः कल्पयाग्ना वा (तैत्तिरीय संहिता 3.1.3.1[?]) इत्यादिविधीनां नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । प्रवृत्त्युद्यप्रवृत्युद्रव्यविधानेन सम्यगनुभवसाधनत्वाभावात् । अयोग्यत्वं च वाक्यशेषे समाम्नातम् । अनाहुतिर्वै जर्तिलाश्च गवीधु...

(Establishing that Brahmana passages fall into two categories — vidhi (injunction) and arthavāda (explanatory eulogy) — and that vidhi itself divides further into "initiating an unperformed act" and "revealing something unknown." (A dense sequence of specific Brahmana/Samhita citations working through cases where a stated ritual injunction is subsequently qualified or restricted by a related passage elsewhere — e.g., wild sesame and wild wheat being excluded as valid oblation-materials, and a dispute over whether the morning fire-offering must occur before or after sunrise. This passage argues that such internal qualifications show certain isolated Brahmana injunctions to be less than fully authoritative on their own. Let us accept the Samhita (mantra) portion as authoritative, as already established. But applying that same status to the Brahmana portion is not straightforward. Brahmanas fall into two kinds — vidhi (injunction) and arthavāda (explanatory statement). Apastamba's sutra defines them: "karma-codanā brāhmaṇāni" — statements that impel ritual acts are Brahmanas (vidhis); the remainder is arthavāda. Vidhi itself divides further into two kinds: those that initiate a not-otherwise-performed act, and those that reveal a previously unknown matter. Karma-kanda statements like "āgnāvaiṣṇavam..." and similar...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...It has been held that since the brahmanas also declare these rites, the mantras are recited for some virtue that lies in their recitation only: not so; their declaratory power is an immediate, temporal advantage, and that comes before a secondary spiritual advantage."

But, it will be said we admit the authority of the mantra portion of the Veda. The brahmana portion, however, cannot rightly be said to be authoritative, for the following reasons. The brahmana portion is of two kinds, called respectively vidhi and arthavada. So, for example, Apastamba says, "Some brahmanas relate to works, that is, are vidhis, precepts: and all the remaining brahmanas are of the nature of arthavada." Vidhis, too, are of two kinds, according as they enjoin the performance of something that has not been performed, or make known something that is not known. Such vidhis as, for example,

original p. 414

...belong to the first category. This statement's meaning: before beginning a yajna, the yajamana must undergo initiation (dīkṣā), called "dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi."

सोमयागे प्रवृत्तस्य यजमानस्य संस्कारो दीक्षणम् । तस्मै च संस्कारस्य हेतुः कर्मविशेषो दीक्षणीयाच्च्यवाच्यः ॥ (Sampranabhashya 6, Brahmana 1.1.1)

सोमयागे प्रवृत्तस्य यजमानस्य संस्कारो दीक्षणम् । तस्मै च संस्कारस्य हेतुः कर्म-विशेषो दीक्षणीयाच् च्यवाच्यः ॥ somayāge pravṛttasya yajamānasya saṃskāro dīkṣaṇam | tasmai ca saṃskārasya hetuḥ karma-viśeṣo dīkṣaṇīyāc cyavācyaḥ ||

"For the yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga, initiation (dīkṣaṇa) is the necessary consecration; the specific ritual act causing that consecration is termed 'dīkṣaṇīyā.'"

The yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga must undergo certain consecrations, including bodily purification — this purifying rite is called "dīkṣaṇīyā(-iṣṭi)," described in the Taittiriya Samhita's sixth kanda, first chapter, first anuvaka. In this iṣṭi, a puroḍāśa cake is offered to Agni and Vishnu together ("āgnāvaiṣṇava"). Since no one would undertake such an act without being told to, this statement counts as apravṛtta-pravartaka vidhi (initiating what wouldn't otherwise occur).

The second category of vidhi reveals previously unknown matters. "Ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" ("in the beginning, this was the Self alone") and similar statements on the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman belong to the brahma-kāṇḍa — the Aranyakas and Upanishads. Since such truths cannot otherwise be known, this category is called ajñāta-jñāpaka vidhi (revealing the unknown). Vidhi thus divides into these two kinds.

But within the karma-kāṇḍa, statements like "jartilayavāgvā..." (concerning forest-grown sesame and wheat as valid oblation materials) lack genuine authority — since the same scriptural tradition elsewhere states that forest-grown sesame and wheat are not suitable oblation materials. A statement permitting the use of unsuitable substances cannot itself be considered authoritative.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"agnavaishnavam purodasam nirvapanti dikshaniyayam," which fall under the karma section of the Veda, enjoin the performance of something that has not been performed. While such vidhis as, for example, "atma va idam eka evagra asit," which fall under the brahma section of the Veda, reveal something which was not previously known. Now of these two kinds there can, in the first place, be no authoritativeness about such vidhis, belonging to the karma section of the Veda, as, for example, "jartilayavagva va juhuyad gavidhukayavagva va" For these vidhis enjoin the use of substances which are not suitable for use, and they cannot therefore be said to be instruments of right knowledge. That the substances in question are not suitable for use is revealed in the rest of the sentence, "anahutir vai jartilas cha gavidhukas cha." For there the employment in the sacrifice of wheat and oil grown in the forest is...

original p. 415

Similarly, in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, and other Brahmanas, many matters are prohibited using phrases like "this should not be regarded" or "this should not be done that way." Consider two examples: the Aitareya Brahmana repeatedly condemns performing homa before sunrise as useless:

"tasmād udite hotavyam" — "therefore, homa should be performed only after sunrise" — stated again and again.

The Taittiriya Brahmana states similarly through "yad anudite... juhoti" and related passages — if homa is performed before sunrise, the offering goes entirely to Agni rather than reaching Surya; therefore the morning-homa (prātar-homa) must occur only after sunrise. Yet the same tradition also criticizes performing it after sunrise:

यदुदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रयुतायै शून्यायावसथायागच्छेत् । आद्यैव स्यात् । (Taittiriya Brahmana 2.1.2.1)

यद् उदिते सूर्ये प्रातर् जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रदुतायै शून्यायावसथायागच्छेत् । आद्यैव स्यात् । yad udite sūrye prātar juhuyāt | yathātithaye pradutāyai śūnyāyāvasathāyāgacchet | ādyaiva syāt |

"If one performs the morning homa after the sun has already risen — it is like a guest arriving at an empty house after the food meant for him has already been sent away; it would have been better offered promptly."

Thus, contradictory statements exist on this exact same point.

The Taittiriya Brahmana offers a mythological account explaining this: long ago, Prajapati (Brahma), preparing to offer havis to Agni, was approached by Surya, who insisted the offering be made to him instead. Agni and Surya then debated and reached an agreement: daytime homa belongs to Surya, nighttime homa belongs to Agni — a reasonable arrangement, since Surya's influence predominates by day and Agni's by night. Therefore, homa performed before sunrise (still counted as "night") belongs to Agni, while homa from sunrise to sunset belongs to Surya. Daytime homa thus belongs to Surya, nighttime homa to Agni.

A homa performed contrary to this arrangement, the argument holds, fails to reach its intended deity and becomes useless. Similarly, the Atiratra yajna's rule requiring the Shodashi-stotra and Shastra is directly contradicted by another passage prohibiting their use in that same rite. And while the Jyotishtoma yajna is said to secure heaven (with similar specific fruits attributed to other yajnas), none of these outcomes can be verified through direct experience — unlike "eating brings satisfaction," which is confirmed by observation. Since karma-kāṇḍa vidhi statements' promised fruits cannot be similarly verified, the objection concludes they carry no authority whatsoever.

Before proceeding, a clear understanding of yajnas' actual structure is needed — their main ritual components, subdivisions of injunction, method of performance, and technical vocabulary — to properly follow the Mimamsa-sutras' argument. We therefore briefly explain the classification of yajnas here.

Yajnas are of two kinds: सोमयज्ञ (Soma-yajña) and हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña) — Soma-juice as the offering-substance defines the former; ordinary havis (oblation material) the latter. Soma-yagas divide into three kinds:

एकाह (Ekāha) — completed within a single day. अहीन (Ahīna) — completed within two to twelve days. सत्र (Sattra) — continuing beyond twelve days.

Among Ekāhas, the most important is the ज्योतिष्टोम (Jyotiṣṭoma), itself of seven kinds (the "seven संस्था saṃsthā"):

  1. अग्निष्टोम (Agniṣṭoma) 2. अत्यग्निष्टोम (Atyagniṣṭoma) 3. उक्थ्य (Ukthya) 4. षोडशी (Ṣoḍaśī) 5. वाजपेय (Vājapeya) 6. अतिरात्र (Atirātra) 7. आप्तोर्याम (Āptoryāma)

Of these, Agnishtoma is the primary form, the remaining six being its variants — hence Agnishtoma is called the "prakṛti" (base form) and the other six the "vikṛti" (modified forms). In the Agnishtoma, the designated Stotras (hymns, or Sama-chants/mantras) are sung, and after each Stotra-recitation, the accompanying priests — Maitravaruna, Brahmanacchamsi, Achchavaka, and others...

original p. 418

Whether to include or omit a given Shastra remains disputed — the Sankhyayana-shrauta, Ashvalayana-shrauta, and Kaushitaki-brahmana all include the Shodashi, while the Aitareya Brahmana omits it entirely. In this yajna (Atiratra), the previous samstha's Stotra-Shastras are chanted through the night, with a Sandhi-stotra recited at sunrise — the continuous nighttime performance likely explaining the name "Atiratra" ("beyond/through the night"). Different Brahmanas count the resulting total Stotra-Shastras differently (some reaching 20, others differing by omitting the Shodashi) — genuine internal variation even within a single yajna's own description. Agnishtoma, Vajapeya, and Aptoryama see comparatively less common use.

A further, genuinely significant contradiction arises among the "revealing-the-unknown" (ajñāta-jñāpaka) vidhis of the brahma-kāṇḍa:

अज्ञातज्ञापकेषु ब्रह्मविधिष्ठ्वपि परस्परविरोधान्नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् (Aitareya Aranyaka 2.4.1[?]) इत्यैतरेयेण आमनन्ति । असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् (Taittiriya Aranyaka 7.2[?]) इति तैत्तिरीयकाः । सोऽयं विरोधः । तस्माद्येव विधिभागः सर्वोऽप्यप्रमाणमिति प्राप्ते ब्रूमः ॥

अज्ञात-ज्ञापकेषु ब्रह्म-विधिष्व् अपि परस्पर-विरोधान् नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । आत्मा वा इदम् एक एवाग्र आसीत् इत्य् ऐतरेयेण आम्नन्ति । असद् वा इदम् अग्र आसीत् इति तैत्तिरीयकाः । सोऽयं विरोधः । तस्माद् एव विधि-भागः सर्वोऽप्य् अप्रमाणम् इति प्राप्ते ब्रूमः ॥ ajñāta-jñāpakeṣu brahma-vidhiṣv api paraspara-virodhān nāsti prāmāṇyam | ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt ity aitareyeṇa āmnanti | asad vā idam agra āsīt iti taittirīyakāḥ | so'yaṃ virodhaḥ | tasmād eva vidhi-bhāgaḥ sarvo'py apramāṇam iti prāpte brūmaḥ ||

"Even among the brahma-kāṇḍa's 'revealing the unknown' vidhis, no authority exists, due to mutual contradiction. The Aitareyins state: 'ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was the Self alone). The Taittiriyas state: 'asad vā idam agra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was non-being alone). This is a direct contradiction. Given this, the entire vidhi-portion is claimed to be without authority — to which we now respond—"

Just as karma-kāṇḍa contains contradictions, the brahma-kāṇḍa does too — hence its statements are likewise claimed as unauthoritative. The Aitareya Aranyaka (Aitareya Upanishad 1.1) states that at the world's beginning, the Self (ātman) alone existed; the Taittiriya Aranyaka states instead that at the beginning, only "asat" (non-being/void) existed — a direct contradiction between these two Upanishadic statements.

Given that the entire vidhi-portion — both karma-kāṇḍa and brahma-kāṇḍa — stands accused of lacking authority, a resolution now follows, establishing the vidhi-portion's genuine authority.

The Aitareyins have a text, "atma va idam eka evagra asit." The Taittiriyas have one, "asad va idam agra asit." The two are contradictory.

Chapter 10. Examination of the Authority of the Arthavāda Portion

फलसिद्ध्यर्थमपूर्वं निर्णीतम् (Purva Mimamsa 2.1.3) इति पूर्वमीमांसायां प्रथमाध्यायस्य चतुर्थपादे कारणत्वेन चाकाशादिषु यथा व्यवदिष्टोक्तेः (Vedanta Sutra 1.4.14) इत्येष्टसूत्रे जगत्कारणे परमात्मनि श्रुतेर्विप्रतिपत्तिर्निराकृता । द्वितीयस्याध्यायस्य प्रथमपादारम्भाधिकरणे कैत्स्न्यपदेशान्नेति चेन्न धर्मान्तरेण वाक्यशेषात् (Vedanta Sutra 2.1.24[?]) इति सूत्रे तैत्तिरीयवाक्यगतस्यासच्छब्दस्य न शून्यपरत्वं किंत्वव्याकृत-स्थावस्थेति निर्णीतम् । तथा जैमिनिस्तोऽभिनवसूत्रे विधिश्च वाक्यं धर्मे प्रमाणमिति प्रतिज्ञायोक्ष्टिकसूत्रे तत्प्रामाण्यं समर्थयामास (Purva Mimamsa 1.1.5[?]) व्यासोऽपि शास्त्रयोनित्वसूत्रे (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.3) वेदान् शास्त्रस्य प्रामाण्यं प्रतिज्ञाय, तत्तु समन्वयात् (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.4) इत्यादिसूत्रैः समर्थयामास । तस्मादमीमांसकस्य कव पूर्वोक्तस्कान्यो दुष्परिहारः । अको विधिभागस्य प्रामाण्यं सुस्थितम् ॥

(A capstone argument citing the Vedanta-sutra and Purva-Mimamsa-sutra by name: showing that the apparent contradiction over the world's cause is resolved because "asat" (non-being) in the Taittiriya passage doesn't mean literal nothingness but rather the unmanifest/undifferentiated state — consistent with the Self being the world's true cause; and that both Jaimini and Vyasa establish the Veda's authority through their respective sutra-systems. The overall conclusion: the entire vidhi-portion's authority stands firmly established.)

Sutta's argument now resolves the objection fully: the statements "jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt gavīdhukayavāgvā vā" and "anāhutir vai jartilāś ca gavīdhukāś ca" (cited as contradictory) genuinely do lack authority — but without any actual flaw, since these vidhi-statements were never meant to be followed in the first place. The truly prescribed oblation-substance — goat's milk — appears shortly after, in "ajakṣīreṇa juhoti." Goat's milk is the excellent oblation-substance; jartila and gavidhuka were mentioned first, and then declared unsuitable, precisely to praise goat's milk by contrast — that is, jartila and similar substances...

...praise of kine and of horses were to say in a figure that there were no beasts beside them, and so deny the name of beast to goats and the like.

If you say here that in accordance with this reasoning vidhis such as that about forest grain, though rejected in the passage before us, must be authoritative in some other Sakha, just as goats and the like are beasts, though in that way of speaking they are declared not to be beasts, we will accept that. But they will be authoritative only to a follower of that Sakha. The case is on all fours with eating the food of a stranger which, forbidden in one stage of life, is lawful in another. Reasoning in this way we can resolve all contradictions between precepts or vidhis and prohibitions by referring them to differences in the man.

original p. 421

The vidhi-statements should be understood as arthavāda. Many such statements exist. The Taittiriya Brahmana states:

अपशवो वा अन्ये गोऽश्वेभ्यः । apaśavo vā anye go'śvebhyaḥ | "Apart from cows and horses, there are no [true] beasts."

This doesn't literally deny goats' status as animals — its real point is that cows and horses are superior in this context. There's a maxim:

न हि निन्दा निन्द्यं निन्दितुं प्रवर्तते, अपि तु विधेयं स्तोतुम् । na hi nindā nindyaṃ ninditum pravartate, api tu vidheyaṃ stotum | "Censure is not truly meant to condemn what's censured, but rather to praise what's prescribed."

Statements of censure aim to elevate what's prescribed, not genuinely denigrate what's censured. The same logic applies to jartila: its real point is praising goat's milk as the superior oblation-substance. If goats count as valid "beasts" in some other Vedic school, jartila might likewise be a valid oblation-substance there too — but this would apply only to followers of that particular school.

A household-duty example illustrates this same principle:

परस्साकरुणिः स्यात् । paras-sākaruṇiḥ syāt | (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.112)

— prohibits eating others' food for a householder;

भिक्षार्थी ग्राममाश्रयेत् । bhikṣārthī grāmam āśrayet |

— requires a sannyasi to beg for alms in the village (food from others being his only means);

ब्रह्मचारी स्थितो नैकमन्नमद्यादनापदि । brahmacārī sthito naikam annam adyād anāpadi |

— requires a Brahmachari student to eat from many households rather than just one, except in genuine hardship. What's prohibited in one life-stage (āśrama) is thus prescribed in another.

Following this same reasoning, mutually contradictory injunctions and prohibitions should be applied according to the specific person following them. Even mantras show this pattern across different schools (śākhā) — a rule stated in one context becomes prohibited in another. The Taittiriya Samhita contains the mantra:

न आयवस्थोपायवस्था देवो वः । nāyavastho-pāyavasthā devo vaḥ |

The same mantra appears in the Vajasaneyi Samhita too — but there, only "न आयवस्था देवो वः" (nāyavasthā devo vaḥ) appears, omitting "upāyavasthā" entirely. The Vajasaneyi Samhita's own Brahmana...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Just as, differences in the mantras being resolved by the division into Sakhas, the Taittiriyas have the text "vayavasthopayavastha;" the Vajasneyins altogether ignore, in the same text, the part "upayavastha;" on the other hand, in the Satapathabrahmana this part is recited, but only to be rejected. In the same way the Taittiriyas, in their "suktavaka" mantra, quote the reading of another Sakha, and reject it in favour of the reading of their own. The passage in which the reading of their another Sakha is rejected is "yad bruyat supavasana cha svadhyavasana cheti pramayuko yajamana syat." And the passage in which the other reading is enjoined is "supacharana cha svadhicharana chetyeva bruyat." A contradiction like this can only be resolved by a difference in the sacrificers. And the same rule must be applied to conflicting vidhis.

original p. 422

...the Shatapatha Brahmana debates the "nāyavastho-pāyavastha" reading and then rejects it, teaching instead the alternative: "sūpacaraṇā ca svadhicaraṇā cety eva brūyāt." Whichever reading is stated belongs to followers of that specific school (śākhā) — another school prescribes a different reading. In all such cases, the correct reading is determined by who recites or performs it. The same principle applies to vidhi-statements generally: whether a statement functions as injunction or prohibition must be judged relative to the specific person performing the act.

Turning to resolve the Ātman/Asat contradiction: "ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" means the Self alone existed before creation; "asad vā idam agra āsīt" means only the unmanifest form called "asat" existed — these two Shruti statements appear directly contradictory. The answer is given in the Brahma-sutra, first adhyaya, fourth pada, fourteenth sutra:

"कारणत्वेन चाकाशादिषु यथा व्यपदिष्टोक्तेः" "kāraṇatvena cākāśādiṣu yathā vyapadiṣṭokteḥ" (Vedanta Sutra 1.4.14)

(As with the sky and other elements, designated according to their causal role — the "asat" reference likewise describes Brahman's own unmanifest, pre-creative state as cause, not literal non-existence.)

Badarayana, and Jaimini following him, hold that all the Upanishads together establish one and the same underlying doctrine: that Brahman alone is eternal — a conclusion drawn from the Upanishads as a whole...

Take them in their order. In the Purva Mimansa, the tenth adhyaya, the eighth pada it is shown that the taking of the shodasi is optional. In the first pada of the second adhyaya the doctrine of fresh spiritual merit is established with the express view of proving the reality of rewards in a future world.
