...the subject already established; the apparent contradictions we find are only superficial, not genuinely opposed in real intent — on this foundation, Badarayana and Jaimini composed their respective works.

Regarding creation, contexts do differ over which entity was created first, and one place calls the cause of creation "sat" (being), another "asat" (non-being) — apparently opposed views. The Vedanta-sutra answers this:

Though schools differ over the sequence and specific entities of creation, no genuine difference exists regarding Brahman itself as the ultimate cause — the same Brahman is called the cause of the sky in one place and other elements elsewhere (Vedanta Sutra 1.4.14). Sequence-related statements are not decisive on their own; not every created thing is even named in them. The Taittiriya Upanishad explains this matter fully, establishing that the creator is one alone.

On the specific meaning of "asat": the Brahma-sutra's third adhyaya, first pada, addresses the Taittiriya Upanishad's own "asad vā idam agra āsīt":

"असद्-व्यपदेशान् नेति चेन् न धर्मान्तरेण वाक्य-शेषात्" "asad-vyapadeśān neti cen na dharmāntareṇa vākya-śeṣāt" (Vedanta Sutra 2.1.17)

"If it be objected that, because it is called 'non-existent' [Brahman cannot be its cause] — we say no, since the remainder of the passage indicates a different attribute [i.e., an unmanifest state, not literal non-existence]."

Using the word "asat" does not mean nothing at all existed at the beginning. Here, "asat" doesn't mean "void" — it means "not-sat," that is, not yet in a clearly manifest form, existing instead in an unmanifest state. This meaning is confirmed by the statements that follow in the same passage. Therefore, "sat" and "asat" carry no real, fundamental difference: one indicates the manifest state, the other the unmanifest state preceding manifestation — "asat" simply marks this distinct, pre-manifest condition, not literal nothingness.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The undifferentiated (असत्) is called non-existent in contradistinction to the existent state (सत्) of the universe which is found to be differentiated.

In the same way in the Uttara Mimansa, the first adhyaya, the fourth pada, the sutra "karanatvena chakasadishu yatha vyapadishtokheh" reconciles the apparent mutual contradiction of certain sruti passages on which you rely. And in the first adhikarana of the first pada of the second adhyaya the sutra "asadvyapadesan neti chen na dharmantarena vakyaseshat" shows that the word "asat" in the Taittiriya text does not mean "non-existent" but "unevolved."

In the same way Jaimini in his "chodana" sutra undertakes to prove that vidhis are authoritative in regard to religious duty, and subsequently does so accordingly in

original p. 424

That is: since the flaws alleged in the objection do not actually hold, vidhi-statements stand established as authoritative. Jaimini and Badarayana both affirm this in their own foundational sutras.

"चोदना-लक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः" "codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.2)

"Dharma is that which is characterized by [Vedic] injunction."

In this sutra, Jaimini establishes that dharma is whatever is conducive to a person's ultimate good — and since vidhi-statements themselves state which acts are conducive to that good, vidhi-statements are thereby authoritative. This authority is further affirmed by the sutra known as the "autpattika-sutra":

"औत्पत्तिकस् तु शब्दस्यार्थेन सम्बन्धस् तस्य ज्ञानम् उपदेशोऽव्यतिरेकश् चार्थेऽनुपलब्धे तत् प्रमाणं बादरायणस्यानपेक्ष्यात्" "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhas tasya jñānam upadeśo'vyatirekaś cārthe'nupalabdhe tat pramāṇaṃ bādarāyaṇasyānapekṣyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.5)

"The relationship between word and meaning is innate; knowledge of this relationship constitutes instruction; and where no perceivable contradiction exists [in the matter concerned], this instruction is itself valid proof — because, per Badarayana, it [dharma] depends on nothing else for its validity."

Word and word-meaning are both naturally arising and eternal — every phoneme is eternal, not created. The entire Veda is likewise "shruta" (heard/revealed) — eternal and faultless. For dharma and its karmic fruits, the Veda alone is authoritative, since these cannot be known through perception or inference. Jaimini himself anticipates every conceivable objection here and answers each in his own systematic way — only a full study of the Mimamsa-shastra can properly evaluate whether his conclusions hold.

Vyasa parallels this in the Brahma-sutra:

"śāstra-yonitvāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.3)

Sayanacharya glosses this sutra two ways: (1) "śāstrasya yoniḥ (brahma)" — the Supreme Self alone is the cause of all shastras, including the Vedas; or (2) "śāstre yoniḥ yasya" — he for whom the shastras alone serve as the basis of being known. This is affirmed further in "tat tu samanvayāt" ("and this, from harmonious coherence [across scripture]").

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

his "autpattika" sutra. Vyasa, too, in his "sastrayonitva" sutra undertakes to prove the authoritativeness of the Vedantas with regard to Brahma, and does so in his "samanvayadi" and following sutras.

Is it not the case that you, who are no Mimansist, will find it difficult to escape the application to yourself of the proverb about the blind man and the post?

Therefore the authoritativeness of the vidhi portion of the Veda stands sure.

original p. 425

This second meaning is the better-known one; the first is merely the general sense — it isn't especially significant to say the creator of the whole universe also created the shastras. What matters is that shastra be the sole reliable means for knowing such a being — this is Badarayana's real point. But if it's objected that, since many differing statements exist within the Veda itself, treating all shastras as pointing to the Supreme Self risks the Veda's own authority — this is answered by:

"तत् तु समन्वयात्" "tat tu samanvayāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.4)

"But that [Brahman as the unified meaning of all Vedantic texts] is established through their coherence/harmony."

The apparent mutual contradiction is not genuine — it only appears so on the surface; all seemingly conflicting statements must be harmonized as ultimately pointing to the Supreme Self. Indeed, most of the Brahma-sutras exist precisely to resolve such apparent contradictions. As the Nirukta states, for one unfamiliar with Mimamsa-shastra:

"नैष स्थाणोर् अपराधो यद् एनम् अन्धो न शक्नोति" "naiṣa sthāṇor aparādho yad enam andho na śaknoti" (Nirukta, Naighantuka-kanda, Purvapada 1.1)

"It is not the post's fault that a blind man cannot see it."

That is: if a blind man fails to see the tree-stump before him, the fault isn't the stump's — and likewise, it's only reasonable that someone unfamiliar with Purva-Mimamsa cannot grasp the Vedas' true meaning.

The vidhi-portion's authority is now fully established. Turning to the second kind of Brahmana content — arthavāda — the sage Jaimini takes great pains to establish its authority as well. The objection's opening sutra:

"आम्नायस्य क्रियार्थत्वाद् आनर्थक्यम् अतदर्थानां तस्माद् अनित्यम् उच्यते" "āmnāyasya kriyārthatvād ānarthakyam atadarthānāṃ tasmād anityam ucyate" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.1)

"Since revelation exists for the sake of ritual action, whatever doesn't relate to that action is meaningless — and is therefore called 'anitya' (non-eternal/non-authoritative)."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

With regard to the arthavada portion Jaimini is at great pains to establish its authoritativeness also. We shall expound his sutras. And first of the view that is to be controverted.

Since revelation has the sacrifice for its object everything not relating to the sacrifice is meaningless, and is called "anitya."

The object of the whole body of amnaya or revealed truth is the performance of the sacrifice. It must follow that these arthavadas, which have nothing to do with the performance

original p. 426

...अर्थवादा इवम् आम्नायन्ते । सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित १.३.१[?]) । स आत्मनो वपाम् उदखिदत् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित २.१.१[?]) । देवा वै देवयजनम् अध्यवसाय दिशो न प्राजानन् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ६.१.३[?]) इति । यस्माद् ईदृशस्य वाक्यस्य विवक्षितार्थः कश्चिद् अपि नास्ति तस्माद् इदं वाक्यम् अनित्यम् उच्यते । ...arthavādā ivam āmnāyante | so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1[?]) | sa ātmano vapām udakhidat (Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.1[?]) | devā vai devayajanam adhyavasāya diśo na prājānan (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.3[?]) iti | yasmād īdṛśasya vākyasya vivakṣitārthaḥ kaścid api nāsti tasmād idaṃ vākyam anityam ucyate |

(Introducing three specific arthavada examples cited as apparently meaningless: "he wept — that is Rudra's Rudra-ness"; "he removed his own layer of fat"; "the gods, having settled on the sacrificial ground, did not yet know the directions." Since such passages seem to convey no genuine intended meaning, the objection concludes they are "anitya" — lacking the eternal authoritative status of the rest of the Veda, even if not literally separate from it.)

Sutra's meaning: since all Vedic statements are established as pointing to ritual action, arthavāda statements — those unrelated to any ritual act — carry no genuine intended meaning at all, and are therefore called "anitya" (non-eternal/non-authoritative) — this is the objection. While all Vedic statements are meant to convey ritual action, the Veda also contains passages like these:

(1) "so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam" (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1) — "He wept; because he wept, that is Rudra's own Rudra-ness [i.e., the origin of his name]."

(2) "sa ātmano vapām udakhidat" (Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.1) — "He peeled off his own layer of fat and cast it away."

(3) "devā vai devayajanam adhyavasāya diśo na prājānan" (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.3) — "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground, did not [yet] know the directions."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...of the sacrifice, have no meaning at all of their own which they desire to convey. What we mean by arthavadas will be clear from the following examples. "So arodid yad arodit tad rudrasya rudratvam." "Sa atmano vapamud akhidat." "Deva vai devayajanam adhyavasaya diso na prajanan." Since in such sentences there is no meaning intended to be conveyed they are rightly called "anitya." With the rest of the Veda they are, it is true, without beginning, and therefore in themselves eternal (nitya.) When they are called "anitya" what is meant is that in common with poetry and ordinary talk they want the character of compulsory duty (nityakarya) and are therefore not authoritative.

original p. 427

No genuine meaning could be intended for such statements — hence they're called "anitya." This doesn't mean they lack the Veda's general beginninglessness; even with an eternal word-sequence, from the standpoint of meaning, these statements lack the defining trait shared by the rest of the Veda — impelling ritual action. In this sense, they're "anitya" much like ordinary poetic statements.

"Śāstra-dṛṣṭa-nirodhāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.2)

Sutra's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion is not authoritative.

शास्त्र-विरोधो दृष्ट्य्-अविरोधः शास्त्र-दृष्ट्य्-अविरोध इति त्रिविधो विरोधोऽर्थवादेष्व् उपलभ्यते । तथा हि । स्तेनं मनोऽनृतवादिनी वाग् इत्य् अत्र क्रियमाणं मानसं चौर्यं वाचिकम् अनृत-वदनं च प्रतिषेध-शास्त्रेण विरुद्धम् । śāstra-virodho dṛṣṭy-avirodhaḥ śāstra-dṛṣṭy-avirodha iti trividho virodho'rthavādeṣv upalabhyate | tathā hi | stenaṃ mano'nṛtavādinī vāg ity atra kriyamāṇaṃ mānasaṃ cauryaṃ vācikam anṛta-vadanaṃ ca pratiṣedha-śāstreṇa viruddham |

(Establishing three kinds of contradiction found in arthavādas: contradiction with shastra, contradiction with direct sensory observation, and contradiction between one shastra passage and another. The example given: "stenaṃ mano'nṛtavādinī vāk" ("the mind is a thief, speech a teller of lies") — contradicting the prohibitive shastra rules against theft and lying, since it seems to claim the mind and speech, not the person, commit these acts.)

Sutta's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion cannot be authoritative — this establishes a threefold taxonomy of contradiction found across various arthavāda passages, to be worked through with specific examples.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

This, however, may be said. The arthavadas just cited have indeed no authority in regard of any religious duty to be done, They are however authoritative as regards their own meaning. For since they convey their meaning you cannot deny their authoritativeness. Anticipating such an objection he seeks in the next sutra to infer the non-authoritativeness of all arthavadas from the example of some which are clearly opposed to other good authorities.

Because they contradict both the shastras and the evidence of our senses.

Three kinds of contradictions are found in arthavadas, contradiction of a shastra, contradiction of what we see with our eyes, and contradiction of what we see in a shastra. For example. The arthavada "stenam mano'nritavadini vak" tells us of theft on the part of...

original p. 428

Statements like "so'rodīt" might lack authority regarding dharma-matters specifically, but their literal meaning must still be accepted as authoritative in itself — so one cannot claim they entirely lack authority. However, some arthavāda statements' meanings directly contradict perceptual and other proofs — such statements genuinely must be called unauthoritative, and on this basis, the next sutra argues for extending non-authority to all arthavādas.

Three kinds of contradiction found in arthavādas, each illustrated:

Śāstra-virodha (contradiction with shastra) — a view opposed to the Veda's own stated intent:

स्तेनं मनः । stenaṃ manaḥ | "The mind is a thief" — [continuing] "speech a teller of lies." One might wrongly conclude theft and lying are thereby permitted — directly contradicting the prohibitive shastra against theft and falsehood.

Dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct experience):

तस्माद्धूम एवाग्नेर्दिवा दृश्यते । नार्चिः । तस्मादर्चिरेवाग्नेर्नक्तं दृश्यते । न धूमः ॥ tasmād dhūma evāgner divā dṛśyate | nārciḥ | tasmād arcir evāgner naktaṃ dṛśyate | na dhūmaḥ || (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.6.1.4) "By day only smoke is seen, not flame; by night only flame is seen, not smoke" — contradicting our ordinary observation.

न चैतद्विद्मो वयं ब्राह्मणा वा स्मोऽब्राह्मणा वा ॥ na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā || (Maitrayani Samhita 1.4.11) "We don't even know whether we are brahmins or not" — likewise contrary to experience.

Śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodha (undermining the Veda's own authority) — where one Vedic statement damages another's credibility:

स्वर्गकामो यजेत । svargakāmo yajeta | "One desiring heaven should perform yajna" — clearly asserting heaven's existence. Yet:

को हि तद्वेद यद्यमुष्मिन् लोकेऽस्ति वा न वा ॥ ko hi tad veda yad yamuṣmin loke'sti vā na vā || (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.1) "Who indeed knows whether that [heavenly world] exists or not" — directly undermines the authority of the very statement promising heaven as yajna's reward.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...the mind and lying on the part of the voice. But both are contrary to the shastra. Again, the arthavada "tasmad dhuma evagner diva dadrise narchis tasmad archir evagner naktam dadrise na dhuma" is opposed to what we see with our eyes. As is also that other arthavada "na chaitad vidmo vayam brahmana va smo abrahmana va." Lastly, the arthavada "ko hi tad veda yadyamushmil loke'sti va na va" is opposed to what we see in the shastra. For in the shastra "svargakamo yajeta" mention is made of a reward in the other world. Because of such contradictions arthavadas are unauthoritative.

original p. 429

In this way, since these passages contradict shastra and experience, the arthavāda-portion is not authoritative. "So'rodīt" and similar statements are inauthoritative for lacking purpose; "stenaṃ manaḥ" and similar are inauthoritative for contradicting other proofs. But one might still argue that fruit-declaring arthavāda statements should count as authoritative. Anticipating this, the objector offers a further reason.

"Tathā phalābhāvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.3)

यथा मानान्तर-विरुद्धम् अर्थवाद्य् उक्तं तथा फलम् अस्याप्य् अविद्यमानम् एव दृश्यते । तथा हि गर्गत्रिरात्रं प्रशत्यै क्रियते । क्षोभक्रेष्य मुखं य एवं वेदेति (तन्द्य महब्रह्मन २०.४.३[?]) दर्श-पूर्णमासयोर् वेदाभिमर्शनं प्रशत्यै क्रियते । अस्य प्रजायां वाजी जायते य एवं वेदेति । न च वयं वेदितॄणां तत्-फलम् उपलभामहे । yathā mānāntara-viruddham arthavādy uktaṃ tathā phalam asyāpy avidyamānam eva dṛśyate | tathā hi gargatrirātraṃ praśatyai kriyate | kṣobhakreṣya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ vedeti (Tandya Mahabrahmana 20.4.3[?]) darśa-pūrṇamāsayor vedābhimarśanaṃ praśatyai kriyate | asya prajāyāṃ vājī jāyate ya evaṃ vedeti | na ca vayaṃ veditṝṇāṃ tat-phalam upalabhāmahe |

(Establishing that just as some arthavādas contradict other proofs, others promise fruits that simply aren't observed in practice — the "Gargatriratra" ritual promising renown, and the darsha-purnamasa's mantra-repetition promising a swift, vigorous descendant, neither being confirmed by actual experience among those who know these rites.)

Sutra's meaning: since the fruits arthavādas promise are never actually observed, they are inauthoritative. As with the previous sutra's contradiction-based argument, here the objection turns to unfulfilled promises. The "Gargatrirātra" is performed for renown; the arthavāda "kṣobhakreṣya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda" claims a certain effect for one who understands this correctly — yet this isn't borne out by experience. In the Darsha and Purnamasa yajnas, Vedic mantras are recited repeatedly with the aid of kusha-grass, and the promised fruit — stated in "asya prajāyāṃ..." — is that the performer's lineage will gain grain-abundance...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

This however may be said. Granted that arthavadas like "arodit," and others like "stenam manah," are unauthoritative, the one kind because they are useless, and the other because they are opposed to other good authorities, still arthavadas which result in some good differ from both these two first kinds, and are authoritative. He answers this doubt in the next sutra.

And because arthavadas do not result in any advantage.

We have seen that what is said in arthavadas is inconsistent with other good authorities. In the same way the rewards they promise do not exist. For Example. There...

original p. 430

...this alone is the claimed fruit of this ritual-knowledge — but no one who knows this rite is ever seen to attain it. Since it declares an unattainable fruit, arthavādas are inauthoritative.

Statements like "śobhate'sya mukhaṃ" declare both worldly and other-worldly fruits. Whichever fruit is claimed, it might go unobserved even by those who perform the act — so such statements should be conceded as purposeless. But what of arthavādas promising specifically other-worldly (āmuṣmika) fruits, unfalsifiable by ordinary observation? Surely their authority must be granted? The next sutra argues even these fail.

"Anyānarthakyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.4)

एवं हि श्रूयते । पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामान् अवाप्नोति । पशुबन्ध-याजी सर्वाल् लोकान् अभिजयति । तरति मृत्युं तरति पाप्मानं तरति ब्रह्म-हत्यां योऽग्निष्टोमेन यजते य उ चैनम् एवं वेदेति । evaṃ hi śrūyate | pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti | paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati | tarati mṛtyuṃ tarati pāpmānaṃ tarati brahma-hatyāṃ yo'gniṣṭomena yajate ya u cainam evaṃ vedeti |

(Citing three parallel arthavada promises: "one attains all desires through the Purnahuti offering"; "one who performs the pashubandha sacrifice conquers all worlds"; "one who performs the Agnishtoma, and understands it correctly, crosses beyond death, sin, and the crime of killing a brahmin." Since these three separate rites each claim to grant the very same all-encompassing rewards — attaining all desires, conquering all worlds, crossing all evils — at least two of the three promises must be redundant if the third alone already delivers everything; this excess undermines the reliability of such promised fruits generally, extending the charge of non-authority even to other-worldly-fruit arthavadas.)

Sutra's meaning: all other arthavāda statements likewise serve no genuine purpose.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...is this arthavada with regard to the Gargatriratra sacrifice, "sobhate sya mukham ya evam veda." With regard to the study of the Veda at the New and Full Moon sacrifices there is this other arthavada, "asya prajayam vaji jayate ya evam veda." But we do not see students of the Veda in possession of any such rewards.

This however may be said. Granted that arthavadas which promise rewards in this world are unauthoritative, because they are opposed to common experience. Still those which promise rewards in heaven may notwithstanding be authoritative. He answers this doubt in the next sutra.

And because all subsequent sacrifices would be useless.

There are these arthavadas. "Purnahutya sarvan kaman avapnoti," "Pasubandhayaji sarval lokan abhijayati.' "Tarati mrityum tarati papmanam tarati brahmahatyam yo...

original p. 431

If authority is granted to even one other-worldly-fruit statement, then since it alone secures all kinds of fruit, the remaining fruit-statements become purposeless. Three examples (all from the Taittiriya Samhita/Brahmana):

1.

पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामानवाप्नोति । pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti | "By the Purnahuti (final oblation), one attains all desires." — "It suffices to perform the Purnahuti; all desired ends are fully accomplished." (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.6.10.3)

2.

पशुबन्धयाजी सर्वाँल्लोकानभिजयति । paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati | "One who performs the pashubandha (animal sacrifice) conquers all worlds." — "For one who performs the pashubandha rite, all worlds become attained."

3.

तरति मृत्युं तरति पाप्मानं तरति ब्रह्महत्यां योऽश्वमेधेन यजते य उ चैनमेवं वेदेति । tarati mṛtyuṃ tarati pāpmānaṃ tarati brahma-hatyāṃ yo'śvamedhena yajate ya u cainam evaṃ vedeti | "He crosses beyond death, sin, and the killing of a brahmin, who performs the Ashvamedha and understands it correctly." — "One who performs the Ashvamedha yajna — even one who merely knows its proper procedure — is capable of conquering death and removing sins. More than that: even the grave fault of killing a brahmin is thereby removed." (Taittiriya Samhita 5.3.12.3)

Every householder must perform the rite called Agnyadheya before he becomes qualified to perform Agnihotra. If performing just one Purnahuti — itself only a component of the Agnyadheya rite — already fulfills every desired end, what purpose do the subsequent Agnihotra and related rites even serve?

On the Purnahuti itself: among the fire-offerings performed within Shrauta, Smarta, and Grihya rites, many "pradhana-homas" (principal offerings) are made to the yajna's chief deities. Afterward, "prayashchitta-homas" (expiatory offerings) remedy any lapses, followed by the "srishtikrit" offering, and finally the "Purnahuti" — the very last oblation of the sequence.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...svamedhena yajate yau chainam evam veda." Now if the purnahuti, which is part of the agnyadheya rite, ensures the fulfilment of all desires, the other later sacrifices, the agnihotra and the rest, can serve no purpose. In the same way if the nirudhapasubandha sacrifice gains for the worshipper all world, then the jyotishtoma and other sacrifices are

original p. 432

When all worlds are attained through the pashubandha yajna alone, what special benefit remains from performing the Jyotishtoma and similar yajnas? And since mere study of the Ashvamedha mantra removes even brahmin-slaying sin, undertaking the arduous actual Ashvamedha rite would become the work of a fool. Isn't it beyond doubt, then, that arthavāda-statements declaring such purposeless acts and fruits are inauthoritative? A response to this follows.

A digression on yajna classification, for context: Sayanacharya's introduction and commentary cites many portions from Mimamsa texts throughout — properly following these arguments requires familiarity with yajnas, so a brief technical outline follows here.

Vedic yajnas are of two kinds: (1) Shrauta-yajna and (2) Grihya-yajna. Taking Grihya-yajnas first — also called Pakayajnas — their procedures are described across various Grihya-sutras, using the fire called "Grihyagni." Pakayajnas exist in seven varieties (samsthas) across all traditions — no more, no less:

Per the Gobhila Brahmana (1.4.3): 1. सायंप्रातर्होम (Sāyaṃprātar-homa) 2. स्थालीपाक (Sthālīpāka) 3. नवयज्ञ (Navayajña) 4. बलि/वैश्वदेवबलि (Bali/Vaiśvadeva-bali) 5. पितृयज्ञ (Pitṛyajña) 6. अष्टक (Aṣṭaka) 7. पशु (Paśu)

Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (1.8.10): 1. अष्टक (Aṣṭaka) 2. पार्वण (Pārvaṇa) 3. श्राद्ध/मासिकश्राद्ध (Śrāddha/Māsika-śrāddha) 4. श्रावणी (Śrāvaṇī) 5. आग्रहायणी (Āgrahāyaṇī) 6. चैत्री (Caitrī) 7. आश्वयुजी (Āśvayujī)

Per Dhurtasvami's commentary on the Apastamba Yajna-paribhasha-sutra: 1. औपासनहोम (Aupāsana-homa) 2. वैश्वदेव (Vaiśvadeva) 3. पार्वण (Pārvaṇa) 4. अष्टक (Aṣṭaka) 5. मासिश्राद्ध (Māsi-śrāddha) 6. सर्पबलि (Sarpa-bali) 7. ईशानबलि/शूलगव (Īśāna-bali/Śūlagava)

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...useless. And if the mere knowledge of the asvamedha sacrifice acquired at the time of study delivers the soul from the guilt of slaying a brahmin, what is the use of performing that sacrifice? Therefore, it is clear that these arthavadas also which promise rewards in heaven are of no authority.

original p. 433

Pakayajnas differ according to each branch's own tradition. Among Shrauta-yajnas too, there are two kinds: Soma-yajnas (using Soma-juice for homas) and Havir-yajnas (using ordinary havis). Soma-yajnas were briefly introduced earlier (page 416).

हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña) number seven across all traditions — no disagreement on the count, though which specific rites are included varies by school:

(1) Per Sayanacharya's own Aitareya-Brahmana-bhashya (2.1): अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya), अग्निहोत्र (Agnihotra), दर्शपूर्णमास (Darśa-pūrṇamāsa), आग्रयण (Āgrayaṇa), चातुर्मास्य (Cāturmāsya), दाक्षायणयज्ञ (Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña), कौण्डपायिनायन/सौत्रामणि (Kauṇḍapāyina-māyana or Sautrāmaṇi)

(2) Per Dhurtasvami's Yajna-paribhasha-sutra commentary: अग्निहोत्र (Agnihotra), दर्शपूर्णमास (Darśa-pūrṇamāsa), आग्रयण (Āgrayaṇa), पिण्डपितृयज्ञ (Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña), चातुर्मास्य (Cāturmāsya), निरूढपशुबन्ध (Nirūḍha-paśubandha), सौत्रामणि (Sautrāmaṇi)

(3) Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (8.20): अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya), अग्निहोत्र (Agnihotra), दर्शपूर्णमास (Darśa-pūrṇamāsa), आग्रयण (Āgrayaṇa), चातुर्मास्य (Cāturmāsya), निरूढपशुबन्ध (Nirūḍha-paśubandha), सौत्रामणि (Sautrāmaṇi)

(4) Per the Gobhila Brahmana (1.4.2): अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya), अग्निहोत्र (Agnihotra), पौर्णमासी (Pūrṇamāsī), अमावास्या (Amāvāsyā), नवेष्टि (Naveṣṭi), चातुर्मास्य (Cāturmāsya), पशुबन्ध (Paśubandha)

On the दर्शपूर्णमासेष्टि (Darsha-Purnamasa-iṣṭis) — performed at new moon and full moon, called "इष्टि" (iṣṭi) — these form the structural foundation for all other iṣṭis, identical in both ritual technique (tantra) and essential form. The main offering-substance for the पुरोडाश (puroḍāśa) is wheat, made into flour and baked to become "puroḍāśa," prepared separately in earthen-dish fragments called "कपाल" (kapāla). The first homa addresses Agni: the puroḍāśa baked in eight kapalas ("आग्नेयमष्टाकपालम्" āgneyam aṣṭākapālam) is offered. The second homa addresses Agni and Soma jointly: the puroḍāśa in eleven kapalas ("आग्नीषोमीयमेकादशकपालम्" āgnīṣomīyam ekādaśakapālam) is offered. Different deities correspondingly require different numbers of kapalas.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

This, however, may be said. Granted that the arthavadas which speak of rewards are of no authority. Still those which convey prohibitions involve no absurdity, and may be authoritative. He answers this doubt in the next sutra.

original p. 434

These ishtis require four priests: (1) अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu) — performs all the technical/procedural work; (2) होतृ (Hotṛ) — recites mantras and invites the deities; (3) ब्रह्मा (Brahmā) — oversees the correct performance of the above two; (4) आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra) — Brahma's assistant.

The rites described so far occur on the new-moon or full-moon day itself, but preliminary rites are performed the day before: in the morning, the अग्न्याधान (Agnyādhāna) rite (placing kindling in the Garhapatya, Ahavaniya, and Dakshinagni fires with mantras); then the yajamana is ritually shaved, eats purified food, and, standing near the three fire-pits, takes certain vows (व्रतग्रहण Vratagrahaṇa) — after which he is considered "dīkṣā-bound." That night, both he and his wife (also diksha-bound) must remain within the sacrificial hall; the yaga proper begins the following morning.

After the Agnihotra: (1) priest-selection (ऋत्विग्वरण Ṛtvigvaraṇa); then, for minor deities' favor, the प्रयाज (Prayāja) rites (subsidiary to the main act); (2) one Ajya-homa (ghee-offering) each to Agni and Soma; (3) the puroḍāśa offered first to Agni (eight kapalas), then jointly to Agni-Soma (eleven kapalas) — the yajna's central act. Between these two, a softly-recited Ajya-homa to Agni-Soma jointly is called उपांशुयाग (Upāṃśu-yāga); (4) the सुहुतकृत्/शिष्टकृत् (Śiṣṭikṛt) rite, offering the remainder of the puroḍāśa already used; (5) finally, the अनुयाज (Anuyāja)s — homas addressing three [further] deities.

पूर्णाहुति (Pūrṇāhuti)

The final, principal offering made at the close of the Agnyadhana is called Pūrṇāhuti. Agnyadhana is also called अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya) — meaning the establishing or consecration of fire within the sacrificial hall. This Shrauta-fire consecration [is undertaken by] a householder [following his] marriage...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

[Continuing the detailed procedural description of the ishti ritual; no further footnote text visible on this page beyond the ritual description itself.]

original p. 435

The main ritual act one gains the right to perform only after undertaking householder-life (गार्हस्थ्य gārhasthya) requires establishing three fires: गार्हपत्य (Gārhapatya), आहवनीय (Āhavanīya), and दक्षिणाग्नि (Dakṣiṇāgni).

A square platform is built in the middle of the yajna-hall — to its west, a long rectangular pit for the Garhapatya-fire; to its east, a circular pit for the Ahavaniya-fire; to its south, a semicircular pit for the Dakshinagni-fire. The Garhapatya represents the yajamāna himself (as "गृहपति" gṛhapati, household-master); the Ahavaniya belongs to the deities, so all deity-offerings must be made there; other homas use the Dakshinagni.

Preliminary rites the day before: the Adhvaryu brings fire from a fixed source into the Garhapatya-pit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the yajna-hall that evening and keeps vigil through the night — solely to keep the Garhapatya-fire burning, continually feeding it kindling.

The next morning, fire is newly produced through "अग्निमन्थन" (Agni-manthana, fire-churning), with a horse readied for the occasion. The Adhvaryu ignites a stick from this new fire and places it in the Garhapatya-pit while the Brahma priest performs the Sama-chant. A procession then forms: the Adhvaryu carrying fire leads, the horse follows, then the yajamāna. The horse, facing west, places one leg into the Ahavaniya-pit; the Adhvaryu touches the fire to the horse's foot before placing it in the pit. He then carries fire once more from the Garhapatya into the Dakshinagni-pit. Everyone circumambulates the fires, and the horse is released.

This is the moment of Pūrṇāhuti. Ghee is melted over the Garhapatya-fire; the Adhvaryu, using a wooden ladle called "जुहू" (juhū), offers it into the Ahavaniya-fire while reciting Yajus mantras — further mantras follow with further offerings. Since the Adhvaryu performs this homa on the yajamāna's behalf, the yajamāna touches the Adhvaryu throughout. This final offering is what's called Pūrṇāhuti — the last act of the Agnyadhana rite. Even after this yajna concludes, the yajamāna must remain bound by certain observances for some further days. In this yajna...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

[Continuing the detailed procedural description of the Agnyadhana ritual and Purnahuti; no further footnote text visible distinctly separate from the ritual description on this page.]

original p. 436

The Garhapatya-fire must never go out, day or night — this rule doesn't apply to the other two fires. Every householder must perform this Agnyadhana; one who completes it properly is called "Āhitāgni" (one who has established the fire) — a status required before any other Shrauta yajna can be undertaken. Purnahuti is the final act of Agnyadhana as described, though two differing views exist on whether Agnyadhana properly concludes with a homa or with an ishti.

Agnihotra

Every householder who is an Ahitagni must perform this rite daily. In the morning, addressing the Sun-deity, one recites—

ॐ भूर्भुवस्स्वः । ॐ सूर्यो ज्योतिर्ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा । oṃ bhūr bhuvas svaḥ | oṃ sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā |

—and offers a homa in the Ahavaniya-fire, using milk as the offering-substance — heated in an earthen vessel over the Garhapatya-fire, then offered using wooden spoons: a small "स्रुव" (sruva), and a larger "अग्निहोत्रहवनी" (agnihotra-havanī). Four or five sruva-dips of milk are transferred into the larger spoon for offering.

The Garhapatya-fire must always stay lit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the fire-hall and lights the Ahavaniya and Dakshinagni from it, offers a kindling-stick homa in the Ahavaniya, and then, once consumed, offers two milk-portions with the agnihotra-havani spoon — the first addressing the Sun (with mantra), the second addressing Prajapati (without mantra). He then similarly offers two milk-portions in the Garhapatya (for Agni-Grihapati, then Prajapati) and two more in the Dakshinagni (for Agni-Annapati, then Prajapati). The heated milk isn't offered undivided; the leftover portion is consumed by the yajamāna himself.

The evening rite follows the same structure, but addresses Agni instead of Surya, with the mantra—

अग्निर्ज्योतिर्ज्योतिरग्निः स्वाहा । agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā |

—the evening Agnihotra must be performed at sunset...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

[Continuing the detailed procedural description of the Agnihotra ritual; no distinct footnote text separate from the ritual description appears on this page.]

original p. 437

There is disagreement on the morning homa's exact timing — before or after sunrise (see the earlier account on page 415 of this work).

पशुबन्ध (Paśubandha, or निरूढपशुबन्ध Nirūḍha-Paśubandha)

Among the many animal-sacrifice varieties, one is obligatory: the निरूढपशुबन्ध (Nirūḍha-Paśubandha), performed on the rainy season's full-moon or new-moon day (some hold it should instead fall at the winter/summer Sankranti transitions). Six priests officiate: अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu), होतृ (Hotṛ), ब्रह्मा (Brahmā), आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra, Brahma's assistant), प्रतिप्रस्थाता (Pratiprasthātā, Adhvaryu's assistant), and मैत्रावरुण (Maitrāvaruṇa, Hotr's assistant).

As in the ishtis, a platform is built; east of the Ahavaniya-pit, at a slight distance, a further platform called "पशुक (Pāśuka)" is constructed, atop which a smaller platform, "उत्तरवेदि (Uttaravedi)," is built. A pole (यूप Yūpa) is planted one cubit into the ground there, to which the sacrificial animal is tied. Numerous small mantric acts follow. Before the main homa, several "प्रयाज (Prayāja)" offerings are performed, each accompanied by its own "आप्री (Āprī)" hymn of praise.

The main homa follows immediately, dedicated to इन्द्र (Indra) and अग्नि (Agni). The animal's fat and other portions are consecrated with mantras; the Adhvaryu offers the puroḍāśa and fat as homa, while the Maitravaruna and Hotr recite the appropriate Anuvaka-verses and "याज्या (Yājyā)" mantras respectively. An offering to please Agni ("रुद्र Rudra" in this ritual context) follows — the शिष्टिकृत्-होम (Śiṣṭikṛt-homa) — then "इडाभक्षण (Iḍā-bhakṣaṇa)," the partaking of the leftover offering ("iḍā") by the yajamāna, priests, and all present.

This completes the yajna's central portion, though further minor acts remain before the rite concludes properly: the "अनुयाज (Anuyāja)" offerings (using curd-mixed grain as the substance, honoring eleven deities), followed by the "उपयाज (Upayāja)" — the Adhvaryu's assistant, the Pratiprasthata, offering the animal's meat without mantra-recitation — performed only in animal-sacrifice yajnas specifically.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

[Continuing the detailed procedural description of the Nirudha-Pashubandha ritual; no distinct footnote text separate from the ritual description appears on this page.]

original p. 438

This act doesn't occur in the ishtis. Finally, the yajamāna's wife performs "Patnī-saṃyāja" — offering the sacrificial animal's tail as homa in the Garhapatya-fire.

This yajna-matter has been explained only very briefly here; the full procedural detail, together with the relevant sutra-meanings, will be given more extensively elsewhere.

"Abhāgi-pratiṣedhāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.5)

न पृथिव्याम् अग्निश् चेतव्यो नान्तरिक्षे न दिवीत्य् एतस्य च दिवि प्रतिषेध-भागित्वं नास्ति । तत्र चयनस्य कृनगस्याभावात् । मा भूत्य् अर्षि निषेधानां प्रामाण्यं । बबरः प्रावाहणेर् अमयतेऽस्मायशऋचादीनां पूर्व-पुरुषन्यत्तन्ताभिधायिनाम् निरोधानुपलम्भाद् अस्तु प्रामाण्यम् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥ na pṛthivyām agniś cetavyo nāntarikṣe na divīty etasya ca divi pratiṣedha-bhāgitvaṃ nāsti | tatra cayanasya kṛnagasyābhāvāt | mā bhūty arṣi niṣedhānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇer amayate'smāyaśaṛcādīnāṃ pūrva-puruṣanyattantābhidhāyinām nirodhānupalambhād astu prāmāṇyam ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||

(Introducing the objection that certain arthavada prohibitions apply to circumstances that could never actually occur — e.g., a rule against building a fire-altar "in the sky" makes no sense, since no one would ever attempt to build a sacrificial fire-altar in the sky in the first place. Such prohibitions, having nothing genuine to prohibit, are argued to be purposeless, extending the charge of non-authority even to the prohibitive class of arthavada statements.)

Sutra's meaning: since the prohibitive statements found within arthavāda address situations that could never arise, arthavāda is not authoritative on these grounds either.

Granting, as the previous sutras argued, that fruit-promising statements lack authority — this same flaw shouldn't extend to prohibitive statements, since no view anywhere opposes them; one might therefore argue prohibitive arthavadas at least remain authoritative. Anticipating this, the objector raises a further point: since prohibitions address impossible situations, they too serve no purpose. The Taittiriya Samhita contains a statement regarding fire-altar construction (agni-chayana) — declaring that fire should not be established "on earth," "in the atmosphere," or "in the sky"...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Because the prohibitions contained in arthavadas are out of place.

In the arthavada "na prithivyam agnis chetavyo nantarikshe na divi" there is no room for the prohibition as regards the mid-heaven or the sky. For the act forbidden to be done there, the raising an altar for the sacrificial fire, could not in any case be done in either of these two places.

original p. 439

...a falcon-shaped altar is customarily constructed (in the Agni-chayana rite) — this Soma-related form being a portion of Prajapati, whom the rite addresses. The fire is established upon a golden plate (symbolizing the Sun), atop which a human-shaped golden image (representing Prajapati) is set, surrounded by layered bricks ("svayamātṛṇṇāḥ") thought to occupy the positions of earth, atmosphere, and sky — the whole rite depicting the creation of the universe, with the yajamāna coming to feel unity with Prajapati and the mantra-invoked deities.

Returning to the objection: this cited arthavada indicates fire should be established upon the golden plate — specifically excluding earth, atmosphere, and sky. Very well, let prohibitive statements lack authority — but surely narrative statements like "Pravāhaṇa's son sought out Babara" carry no such doubt, containing only a sage's own historical account with no contradictory content at all? Anticipating this defense, the next sutra follows.

"Anitya-saṃyogāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.6)

बबरादि-रूपेणानित्येनार्थेन संयोगे सत्य् अस्य वाक्यस्य ततः पूर्वम् अभावात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवत् पौरुषेयत्वं प्रसज्येत । किं बहुना । सर्वथापि नास्त्य् अर्थवादानां प्रामाण्यम् इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥ babarādi-rūpeṇānityenārthena saṃyoge saty asya vākyasya tataḥ pūrvam abhāvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavat pauruṣeyatvaṃ prasajyeta | kiṃ bahunā | sarvathāpi nāsty arthavādānāṃ prāmāṇyam iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||

बेबरादि-रूपेणानित्येनार्थेन संयोगे सत्य् अस्य वाक्यस्य ततः पूर्वम् अभावात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवत् पौरुषेयत्वं प्रसज्येत । किं बहुना । सर्वथापि नास्त्य् अर्थवादानां प्रामाण्यम् इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥ bebarādi-rūpeṇānityenārthena saṃyoge saty asya vākyasya tataḥ pūrvam abhāvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavat pauruṣeyatvaṃ prasajyeta | kiṃ bahunā | sarvathāpi nāsty arthavādānāṃ prāmāṇyam iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||

"Since this statement mentions a transient thing in the form of 'Babara' and similar, this statement could not have existed before that person — implying, like statements by Kalidasa and similar poets, a human origin. In short: arthavādas have no authority whatsoever. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Good. Granted that these prohibitive arthavadas are non-authoritative. No such absurdity is inherent in the arthavadas which tell the deeds of men of old time, as for example, "babarah pravahanir akamayata." He answers this doubt in the next sutra.

Because of the mention made in them of non-eternal things.

In this arthavada mention is made of one Babara and other non-eternal things. The arthavada cannot therefore have existed before Babara. Therefore it must be credited with a human origin,

original p. 440

...this doubt should not be prolonged; however one looks at it, arthavādas plainly lack authority — this concludes the objection.

The Siddhāntin's Resolution Begins

"विधिना त्व् एक-वाक्यत्वात् स्तुत्यर्थेन विधीनां स्युः" "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.7)

"But since arthavādas form a single syntactical unit together with their corresponding vidhi, they must be understood as existing to praise those very vidhis."

तुशब्दोऽर्थवादानाम् अप्रामाण्यं वारयति । वायुर् वै क्षेपिष्ठा देवता वायव्यं श्वेतम् आलभेत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित २.१.१[?]) इत्य् आदिना विधिना सैकवाक्यत्वाद् धर्मे प्रामाण्यम् । न च विधि-वाक्य-स्यार्थ-वादात् नैः सर्वे क्षेत्रण सदास्ति-यसंपूर्के स्तार्थ-वादानां नास्त्येक-योग इति शङ्कनीयम् । तेष्व् अर्थ-वादानां पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-मात्र-कांक्षतां विधीनां स्तुत्यर्थ-स्येनोपयुक्ताः स्युः । स्तुत्या च पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-श्रवण । तेनार्थ-वादानां प्रमाद-शमिते-क्षेपाणीय-क्त्वा तस्मिन् एवैकवाक्यता-प्रत्य् आसत्वाच्-छन्क्य्-अकः ॥ tuśabdo'rthavādānām aprāmāṇyaṃ vārayati | vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta (Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.1[?]) ity ādinā vidhinā saikavākyatvād dharme prāmāṇyam | na ca vidhi-vākya-syārtha-vādāt naiḥ sarve kṣetraṇa sadāsti-yasaṃpūrke stārtha-vādānāṃ nāstyeka-yoga iti śaṅkanīyam | teṣv artha-vādānāṃ puruṣa-pravṛtti-mātra-kāṃkṣatāṃ vidhīnāṃ stutyartha-syenopayuktāḥ syuḥ | stutyā ca puruṣa-pravṛtti-śravaṇa | tenārtha-vādānāṃ pramāda-śamite-kṣepāṇīya-ktvā tasmin evaikavākyatā-praty āsatvāc-chanky-akaḥ ||

(This dense commentary establishes: since arthavādas are grammatically and syntactically bound to the vidhi-statement they accompany — forming one continuous unit of meaning — the entire combined statement takes on the vidhi's own authority. The arthavāda's role is specifically to encourage a person's motivation to act on the injunction, through praise, and this "praise function" is what grants it derivative authority — not any standalone claim to convey new facts.)

Sutta's meaning: arthavādas exist to praise the very meaning conveyed by vidhi-statements — this is the point of censuring them independently. Since one accepts the objector's own earlier concession that vidhi-statements are proven authoritative through the sutras, that same authority extends here: the very first sutra, "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ," establishes that both vidhi and arthavāda together form a single grammatical unit — and, being one unit, the arthavādas relevant portions in the current discussion are themselves praise-statements strengthening the vidhi's own force.

The word "tu" ("but") in this sutra rejects the objection's claim of arthavāda's non-authority. Since arthavādas like "vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā" form one syntactical unit with vidhis like "vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta," they too must be authoritative guides to religious duty. Nor need we doubt this on grounds that vidhis are verbally...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Why prolong this? In every way it is clear that the arthavadas are of no authority. This is the view now to be controverted.

The sutras which now follow contain his conclusion,

But the arthavadas, standing as they do in syntactical connection with the vidhis, must be construed as emphasising the vidhis.

The word "but" indicates that the view of the non-authoritativeness of the arthavadas is about to be rejected. Since arthavadas like "vayur vai kshepishtha" are in syntactical connection with vidhis like "vayavyam svetam alabheta," they too must be authoritative guides to religious duty. Nor need we doubt and say that since the vidhis are verbally...

original p. 441

...complete in themselves apart from arthavāda, such connection would be pointless. That's not so — vidhi-statements depend on human motivation to act, and arthavādas, by praising and emphasizing the vidhi, are precisely what generates that motivation. A person is moved to undertake a course of action specifically upon hearing it praised.

That is: the objection held that vayu is an especially swift deity, and offering the "vāyavya-śveta" (white goat) to him yields fruit quickly — while other deities' offerings yield fruit more slowly — and therefore, one should offer this goat to Vayu specifically. Following this reasoning, the arthavāda's own authority isn't independent; it exists purely to support this same vidhi's force, and neither is authoritative apart from the other. Where a vidhi's own arthavāda-portion doesn't literally align word-for-word with it, the vidhi and its associated arthavāda mustn't be assumed unrelated — arthavādas exist precisely to make a person eager to perform the enjoined act; this is the arthavāda's whole purpose. Recognizing this resolves the difficulty in every arthavāda passage.

A further objection anticipated: the sutra just given establishes authority through syntactical unity — but one could still argue that some arthavāda portions were mistakenly inserted through scribal error, and should therefore be disregarded despite appearing embedded within vidhi-passages. Jaimini answers this too.

"Tulyaṃ ca sāṃpradāyikam" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.8)

अनध्यायः वर्जनादि-नियम-पुरस्सरं गुरु-संप्रदायाद् अध्ययनं यत् तत् साम्प्रदायिकम् । तच् च विधि-समार्थवादानां समानम् । तस्मात् तद्-विधेव समानम् । न च शास्त्र-दृष्टि-विरोधाच् चैव समर्थ-वादे षु न भवति । न सं शास्त्र-दृष्टि-विरोधाच् चैव शेषम् अर्थ-वादे षु न पृच्छति । anadhyāyaḥ varjanādi-niyama-purassaraṃ guru-saṃpradāyād adhyayanaṃ yat tat sāmpradāyikam | tac ca vidhi-samārthavādānāṃ samānam | tasmāt tad-vidheva samānam | na ca śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodhāc caiva samartha-vāde ṣu na bhavati | na saṃ śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodhāc caiva śeṣam artha-vāde ṣu na pṛcchati |

(Establishing that the tradition of study — passed down through the guru's own lineage, with the observance of restraints such as holy days — applies equally to vidhi and arthavāda portions alike, since both are transmitted through the very same unbroken chain. This equal transmission itself proves both classes of statement share the same authoritative status, ruling out the possibility that arthavāda was carelessly or erroneously introduced.)

Sutra's meaning: since arthavāda-statements have been studied, generation after generation, following the same tradition as vidhi-statements, no error can have crept into them in transmission.

Just as certain vidhis, in "anadhyāya" (non-study) periods, were the very first to be studied [by tradition] — these too have come down through the same guru-lineage, passed on faithfully according to tradition. In this same transmission-line...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...complete in themselves, without reference to the arthavadas, these latter cannot be of any use. The vidhis expect the action of men, and in that respect the arthavadas, which praise and emphasise the vidhis, are useful. For it is when a man hears a course of action praised that he enters upon it.

But arthavadas, it may be said, may be introduced by error into the text of scripture, and should therefore be left out of sight. Why be at pains to establish that they are in syntactical connection with the vidhis? He answers this doubt in the next sutra.

Right tradition is of the same weight in both cases.

By right tradition is meant study in accordance with the tradition delivered by the guru with due observance of all restraints such as holy days and the like. Now this is the

original p. 442

Everyone already accepts that transmission-errors cannot occur in vidhi-statements. Since vidhis and their arthavādas have both come down through the very same unbroken tradition, no cause exists for error to affect the arthavāda portion any differently.

But one might still object: given the apparent contradiction with shastra and direct perception, can we really accept that no error-flaws exist in these vidhi-arthavāda passages? The next sutra answers this.

"Aprāptā cānupapattiḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.9)

स्तेनं मन इत्यादौ शास्त्र-विरोधाद् अनुपपत्तिः प्राप्ता । प्रयोगे हि श्रेयादीनाम् उच्यमाने शास्त्र-विरोधः स्यात् । न चात्र श्रेयं कर्तव्यम् इति प्रयोग उच्यते । किन्तु श्रेय-शब्दार्थ एव प्रयोग-भाक् । तस्माच् छब्दार्थ-वचन-मात्रेण शास्त्र-विरोधाभावाद् अयम् अर्थवाद उपपन्न एव । stenaṃ mana ityādau śāstra-virodhād anupapattiḥ prāptā | prayoge hi śreyādīnām ucyamāne śāstra-virodhaḥ syāt | na cātra śreyaṃ kartavyam iti prayoga ucyate | kintu śreya-śabdārtha eva prayoga-bhāk | tasmāc chabdārtha-vacana-mātreṇa śāstra-virodhābhāvād ayam arthavāda upapanna eva |

स्तेनं मन इत्यादौ शास्त्र-विरोधाद् अनुपपत्तिः प्राप्ता । प्रयोगे हि स्तेनादीनाम् उच्यमाने शास्त्र-विरोधः स्यात् । न चात्र स्तेनं कर्तव्यम् इति प्रयोग उच्यते । किन्तु स्तेन-शब्दार्थ एव प्रयोग-भाक् । तस्माच् छब्दार्थ-वचन-मात्रेण शास्त्र-विरोधाभावाद् अयम् अर्थवाद उपपन्न एव । stenaṃ mana ityādau śāstra-virodhād anupapattiḥ prāptā | prayoge hi stenādīnām ucyamāne śāstra-virodhaḥ syāt | na cātra stenaṃ kartavyam iti prayoga ucyate | kintu stena-śabdārtha eva prayoga-bhāk | tasmāc chabdārtha-vacana-mātreṇa śāstra-virodhābhāvād ayam arthavāda upapanna eva |

"In statements like 'stenaṃ manaḥ' (the mind is a thief), the objection of contradiction with shastra was raised. If theft and similar acts were being literally enjoined, that would indeed contradict shastra. But no injunction to actually commit theft is being stated here — rather, only the meaning of the word 'thief' is being conveyed [metaphorically, describing the mind's tendency]. Since it merely states a word's sense without prescribing literal action, no contradiction with shastra arises, and this arthavāda stands perfectly coherent."

Sutra's meaning: it is not correct to say vidhi-arthavāda statements cannot be accepted as authoritative. Contradiction could only arise if these statements conveyed a literal, action-oriented command — but they convey only the meaning of the words themselves, not a prescription for actual performance. Therefore, they carry authority.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...the same for vidhis and for arthavadas: therefore there is as little chance of error in the one case as in the other.

With regard to the suspicion thrown upon the arthavadas that they must be of no effect because they contradict both the shastras and what we see with our eyes, his answer is as follows.

No reason has arisen why we should consider them of none effect. What contradiction there is between them and right practice. But they are no parts of practice, and therefore are of effect.

No reason has arisen why the text "stenam manah," and others like it, which are opposed to the shastra, should be declared of none effect. It is not hinted that they have...

original p. 443

It is not correct that "stenaṃ manaḥ" and similar statements become inauthoritative through shastra-contradiction — since they say nothing about actual yajna performance at all. Shastra-contradiction would arise only if theft were being literally prescribed for performance; nowhere does this happen — only the literal word-meaning of "theft" occurs, without any action-oriented sense. Since the mere presence of this word produces no genuine shastra-contradiction, this arthavāda retains its authority.

A further, genuinely subtle objection now arises: granting that arthavādas exist to praise vidhis — forming, together, one complete sentence — surely the vidhi-portion alone should be accepted as authoritative, while the arthavāda-portion, addressing an entirely different subject, cannot be? Consider:

"वेतस-शाखया चावकाभिश् चाग्निं विकर्ष्यापो वै शान्ताः" "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣyāpo vai śāntāḥ"

Here, "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣati" ("one draws away the fire using branches of the vetasa and avaka plants") is the vidhi-portion. "Āpo vai śāntāḥ" ("waters indeed possess a calm nature") is a separate statement. What connection does water's calm nature have with extinguishing fire using plant-branches? Given such apparently unrelated subject-matter combined within a single vidhi-arthavāda passage, how can we accept its authority as a unified whole? — This is the objection. The resolution is given in the next sutra.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...anything to do with practice. If their themes, theft and the like, were spoken of in connection with practice then, if you like, they would be in contradiction with the shastra. But the practice of theft is not enjoined here. And the word about theft used in the text has no connection with practice. No contradictions of the shastras can lie in the mere use of a word, and therefore this arthavada is not on that account of no effect.

But it may be said that the view according to which the arthavadas serve to recommend and emphasise the vidhis must be untrue, inasmuch as in many cases the subject of the vidhi is one thing and the subject of the arthavadas another. Take the text, "vetasasakhaya chavakabhis chagnim vikarshatyapo vai santah." The subject of the vidhi is the vetasa and avaka plants. The subject of the arthavada is the waters. How can the arthavada emphasise the vidhi here? He answers this doubt as follows.

original p. 444

"Guṇavādas tu" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.10)

तुशब्दो वैयधिकरण्य-दोषं वारयति । गुणवादो ह्य् अत्र विवक्षितः । यथा लोके कश्मीराभिजनो देवदत्तः कश्मीरेषु स्तूयमानेषु स्तुतम् आत्मानं मन्यते एवम् अत्राप्य् अपो जाते वेतसावके अप्सु स्तुतासु स्तुते एव भवतः । शान्ताभ्योऽद्भ्यो जातत्वाद् वेतसावके स्वयम् अपि शान्ते सत्या यजमानिनम् आच्छमयत इष्टैतादृशस्य गुणस्य वाच्यत्वाभिप्रेत । tuśabdo vaiyadhikaraṇya-doṣaṃ vārayati | guṇavādo hy atra vivakṣitaḥ | yathā loke kaśmīrābhijano devadattaḥ kaśmīreṣu stūyamāneṣu stutam ātmānaṃ manyate evam atrāpy apo jāte vetasāvake apsu stutāsu stute eva bhavataḥ | śāntābhyo'dbhyo jātatvād vetasāvake svayam api śānte satyā yajamāninam ācchamayata iṣṭaitādṛśasya guṇasya vācyatvābhipreta |

तुशब्दो वैयधिकरण्य-दोषं वारयति । गुणवादो ह्य् अत्र विवक्षितः । यथा लोके कश्मीराभिजनो देवदत्तः कश्मीरेषु स्तूयमानेषु स्तुतम् आत्मानं मन्यते एवम् अत्राप्य् अपो जाते वेतसावके अप्सु स्तुतासु स्तुते एव भवतः । शान्ताभ्योऽद्भ्यो जातत्वाद् वेतसावके स्वयम् अपि शान्ते सत्या यजमानिनम् आच्छमयत इष्टैतादृशस्य गुणस्य वाच्यत्वाभिप्रेत । tuśabdo vaiyadhikaraṇya-doṣaṃ vārayati | guṇavādo hy atra vivakṣitaḥ | yathā loke kaśmīrābhijano devadattaḥ kaśmīreṣu stūyamāneṣu stutam ātmānaṃ manyate evam atrāpy apo jāte vetasāvake apsu stutāsu stute eva bhavataḥ | śāntābhyo'dbhyo jātatvād vetasāvake svayam api śānte satyā yajamāninam ācchamayata iṣṭaitādṛśasya guṇasya vācyatvābhipreta |

"The word 'tu' (but) rules out the flaw of mismatched subject-matter. A figurative statement (guṇavāda) is intended here. Just as, in ordinary life, a person native to Kashmir, upon hearing Kashmir praised, considers himself praised — likewise here, the vetasa and avaka plants, being born in water, are themselves praised whenever water is praised. Being born from calm-natured waters, the vetasa and avaka plants are themselves calm-natured, and thereby pacify [any harm affecting] the yajamāna — this very quality is what the statement intends to convey."

The Sanskrit continues with two further worked examples — one concerning why silver is called "born of Soma's tears," another concerning Prajapati and goats — extending the same guṇavāda logic to other apparently mismatched vidhi-arthavāda pairs; given the density of these additional citations, the clear English rendering below is the more reliable guide to their content.

That is: this text figuratively means simply, "O vetasa and avaka plants, sprung from the holy waters and therefore yourselves holy — drive away all evil from this yajamāna."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

But in such cases there is a figure of speech.

The word "but" shows that the objection is about to be refuted. The meaning here is figurative. As in common talk if a native of Kashmir hears Kashmir praised, he considers himself praised, so here praise of the waters implies praise of the vetasa and avaka plants, which are born in the waters. The figurative meaning of this text is simply "O vetasa and avaka plants, sprung from the holy waters, and therefore yourselves holy, drive all evil from the man who sacrifices here."

original p. 445

Sutra's meaning: in such statements, one portion states a quality belonging to what the other portion describes — so the two portions of the statement do share a genuine mutual connection. The word "tu" (but) resolves the flaw of "vaiyadhikaraṇya" (mismatched subject-matter) — where a vidhi addresses one thing and its arthavāda seems to address another entirely. As in ordinary life: "when Kashmir is praised, Devadatta, native to Kashmir, considers himself praised too" — likewise, praising "waters are calm" implicitly praises the vetasa and avaka plants growing in that water, since they share water's calm nature and thereby pacify misfortune for the yajamāna. Stating this shared quality is the arthavāda's whole purpose.

A second example of this same principle — and the resolution to the "Rudra wept" passage first raised many pages ago:

सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् । यद् अप्क्षीयत कद् रजतं हिरण्यम् अभवत् स्वाप्कर्जतं हिरण्यम् अदक्षिणम् उत्पृजद् घि यो बर्हिषि ददाति पुरस्तात् संवत्सराद् ध्य् ए रुदन्ति तस्माद् बर्हिषि न देयम् ॥ so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apkṣīyata kad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpkarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam utpṛjad ghi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād dhy e rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam || (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.1)

सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् । यद् अपक्षीयत तद् रजतं हिरण्यम् अभवत् स्वापकर्जतं हिरण्यम् अदक्षिणम् । उत्पृज्य हि यो बर्हिषि ददाति पुरस्तात् संवत्सराद् अस्य रुदन्ति तस्माद् बर्हिषि न देयम् ॥ so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apakṣīyata tad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpakarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam | utpṛjya hi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād asya rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam ||

"He wept; because he wept, that is Rudra's own 'Rudra-ness.' What flowed out [from his weeping] became silver-gold; silver-gold is therefore not fit as a sacrificial fee. For whoever, discarding [this warning], gives it upon the sacrificial grass — within that year, there is weeping in his household. Therefore it should not be given upon the sacrificial grass."

This is the resolution. The corresponding vidhi (injunction) here simply states: silver should not be given as the priest's fee at a sacrifice. The "Rudra wept" narrative is an arthavāda built entirely to reinforce that one rule — deriving the god Rudra's name from the root for "weeping," and then figuratively tying that weeping to silver ("what flowed from his tears became silver"). The intended, purely figurative point is simple: if silver is given as payment, there will be "weeping" — misfortune — in that household within the year. Sayana states plainly that there is no literal truth in the story that Rudra's tears turned into silver; the narrative exists solely to emphasize and recommend the vidhi against paying priests in silver, through a vivid, memorable etymological pun.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

...however still we admit the whole substance of the praise — nothing is withheld. "Thy calf grows, O one worthy of trust, drink with faith" — even without exact measure, such praise is commonly seen in ordinary usage. Now, having shown the objection based on shastra-contradiction, in the example cited "stenam mano'nṛtavādinī vāk," he formulates the answer to that as well.

Take as another example the arthavada "so rodit &c." The corresponding vidhi lays down that silver is not to be used for the fee of the priest at the sacrifice. The arthavada derives Rudra, the name of the god, from the word for weeping. The figurative meaning is that if silver is not given, tears will not fall. Therefore if the man for whom the priest is sacrificing pays him in silver, there will be weeping in that man's house as well as at the sacrifice. The intended emphasis added to the vidhi is simply that if there be no giving of silver at the sacrifice, there will be no weeping at the house. And by this emphasis the vidhi is recommended. There is really no truth in the story referred to here, namely, that Rudra's tears turned into silver. But in the way shown the arthavada here does emphasise and recommend the vidhi.

original p. 446

That is: "He (Rudra) wept — that is, cried. Because he wept, he came to be named 'Rudra.' The tears that fell from him became silver. Therefore, silver — being the very form of Rudra's tears — should not be given as sacrificial fee. If silver were given, within one year, weeping would befall the yajamāna and his household — meaning, a death might occur among his relatives. Therefore, silver should not be given in yajna." Here, the prohibition against silver (the vidhi) and the arthavāda align perfectly — declaring that avoiding silver means avoiding grief is exactly this arthavāda's purpose.

Another example:

"Prajāpati alone existed in the beginning. He desired: 'let me create offspring.' He tore out his own [abdominal] entrails and offered them into the fire. From that, before an[other] came into being, [a hornless goat] was born. He offered it to that same deity. In that same way, he created offspring and cattle. Therefore, whoever desires offspring and cattle should approach this Prajapati-goat — Prajapati himself — through his own portion, with offspring and cattle [as the sought result]."

That is: Prajapati, desiring offspring and cattle, tore out his own entrails and offered them as homa; from this, a hornless goat was produced. One desiring children, grandchildren, and cattle can obtain this benefit through a hornless goat. Stating this quality of the hornless goat — and thereby praising the underlying vidhi — is this arthavāda's whole purpose.

Take another example. The vidhi "yah prajakamah pasukamah syat sa etam prajapatyam ajam tuparam alabheta" is recommended by the arthavada about Prajapati cutting out his own entrails. Because Prajapati cut out his own entrails, threw them on the fire, and by means of the hornless goat so obtained got men and cattle, therefore this hornless goat is good for obtaining offspring. This praise of the hornless goat is the real meaning of the arthavada,

The vidhi "adityah prayaniyas charuh" is recommended by the ignorance as to the four quarters of the heavens spoken of in the arthavada "diso na prajanan." As the divine...

...the divine [deities], despite their divinity, were once ignorant of this — recognizing this, we should not consider it false just because it seems strange. As in the example: "if you drink up an herb, hair will grow on your bald head" — such statements, even when their literal claim seems dubious, are accepted as encouraging trust in the wider practice.

Having now shown resolutions to the shastra-contradiction cases, we turn to those raised as contradicting direct sense-perception: "stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk" — and a further doubt about how arthavāda statements' apparent absurdity should be resolved is addressed via the next sutra.

"Rūpasattvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.11)

हिरण्यं हस्ते भवत्य् अथ गृह्णाति त्यकं विधिः स्तोकमयम् अर्थवाद उच्यते । यथा लोके किम् पुरुषा देवदत्त एव । पूज्यते इव? देव-दत्ते पूज्यमाने पूज्यं स्वयम् इत्य् उच्यते । hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti tyakaṃ vidhiḥ stokamayam arthavāda ucyate | yathā loke kim puruṣā devadatta eva | pūjyate iva? deva-datte pūjyamāne pūjyaṃ svayam ity ucyate |

(Introducing a new sutra concerned with arthavāda passages whose surface form appears to contradict what we plainly observe — here, gold "being in the hand" before the priest actually grasps it — resolved by recognizing this as ordinary hyperbolic emphasis, the same way one might say "isn't Devadatta the only person who matters" without literally denying every other person exists.)

Sutra's meaning: statements whose surface appearance seems inconsistent [with reality], being simply common usage, must be understood as intending an emphatic (exaggerated) sense — not as literal factual claims.

As with the earlier examples ("stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk"), this next arthavāda-statement is used only to encourage a person toward what's genuinely worth pursuing — not to convey a literal factual claim. Gold [in the phrase] "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavati"...

This is an arthavada which is used to recommend the vidhi "hiranyam haste bhavatyatha gribhnati." As in common talk the sentence "What! Is Devadatta the only person

original p. 449

We now explain the arthavāda praising the vidhi "haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" (Taittiriya Samhita 4.7.3.1). "Kiṃ puruṣā devadatta eva pūjyāḥ" ("What! Is Devadatta the only person worthy of honor?") — such an expression doesn't imply others aren't worthy; it exists solely to emphasize Devadatta's own worthiness. Likewise, "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" ("gold comes to be in the hand, then he grasps it") — this arthavāda praises the vidhi that gold should be taken as sacrificial fee, by declaring gold's own preciousness.

In the same way, "stenaṃ manaḥ" ("the mind is a thief") should be read figuratively: thieves remain hidden and unseen; the mind too stays hidden within the body, unseen. Since concealment is a shared quality between thieves and the mind, the mind is compared to a thief — stating this figurative sense is exactly this statement's purpose.

Likewise, "anṛtavādinī vāk" ("speech is a false-speaker"): since speech is commonly observed, in ordinary human life, to speak falsely, one must grasp the figurative sense here too, setting aside a literal reading. As for "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" — that gold visibly sits in the hand is plain to everyone, not hidden or false at all; this arthavāda's purpose is simply to praise the vidhi by declaring gold worth wearing on the hand.

On these falsehood-statements, the Taittiriya Brahmana adds:

अनृतं वै वाचा वदति । अनृतं मनसा ध्यायति । चक्षुर् वै सत्यम् । अद्या हि घृताह अदर्शम् इति । सत्यैव ॥ anṛtaṃ vai vācā vadati | anṛtaṃ manasā dhyāyati | cakṣur vai satyam | adyā hi ghṛtāha adarśam iti | satyaiva || (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.1.4)

"Speech indeed speaks falsehood; the mind indeed dwells on falsehood — but the eye is indeed truthful, for when one says 'I saw [it] today,' that itself is truth."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source: The source scan repeats printed page 449, already translated above; the duplicate is not translated again. The translation resumes at printed page 450.

...whom the rishi means to honour" emphasises the honour which the rishi is paying to Devadatta by the suggestion that he is slow to honour others, without however actually meaning that he is wanting in his duty there, so here the suggestion as to theft in the mind and falseness in the voice, is only meant to extol the grasping in the hand of the sacrificial fee. This is the metaphorical way in which the words are to be taken. Thieves lie concealed, and so does the mind. Therefore the mind may be called a thief. The voice often speaks falsely, and on account of this "often" we may metaphorically call the voice a liar. But...

original p. 450

A sentence carries two kinds of meaning: one, the direct meaning conveyed by the words themselves — "the fire burns"; another, a further meaning conveyed indirectly through that literal sense as a stepping-stone — the "secondary meaning" (gauṇārtha), as in "Devadatta burns like fire," where "burning" must be reinterpreted (through anger, desire, etc.) to fit Devadatta sensibly. The first is the primary meaning; the second, the secondary meaning — meaning derived by pointing at a shared quality.

Having thus resolved the shastra-contradiction objection, we turn to the dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct perception) examples — statements like "bhūmā vāgnir dinā dṛśye" (only smoke, not flame, is visible by day) — addressed in the next sutra.

"'Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the evening; 'sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the morning — this arthavāda exists to praise these two vidhis. Since flame is not visible by day, [one might ask] for what purpose should I use [the fire-mantra then]? — and since [it should be] used at night, this itself is the recollection [rationale] behind the two mantras: therefore the Agni-mantra must be used at night. The greater visibility of the flame [at night] is what's actually being conveyed — a distinction owing to the sheer distance [between earth and the visible daytime sky-glow]. For at a distance, in daylight, even conspicuous things like [smoke and] fire's other features are not seen distinctly — not because they don't exist, but simply because their dark-visible quality goes unseen [against the bright sky]."

Sutra's meaning: the "smoke by day, flame by night" arthavāda isn't a false claim about physical reality — it explains, and thereby reinforces, exactly which mantra (Sun or Agni) belongs to which time of day, with the visibility difference serving as a memorable, praise-oriented justification rather than a literal scientific claim.

original p. 451

These are the two vidhis this arthavāda exists to praise. Since flame isn't visible by day, the sun-mantra suits the morning; since flame alone is visible at night, the fire-mantra suits the night — "day, the sun-mantra" is the praise these vidhis (mantras) receive.

The objection held this contradicts direct perception — flame is visible before our eyes, so how can the text say otherwise? The resolution: if a fire burns at a distance during daylight, the sun's superior brightness prevents the flame from being visible — only the dark smoke registers. This is confirmed by ordinary experience: with sufficient distance, even trees atop a hill lose their distinct shape and look like mere blades of grass. The same principle applies here.

Turning to the second dṛṣṭi-virodha example: "na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā" — "we don't even know whether we are brahmins or not." The next sutra addresses this. This introduces a genuinely striking rationale: since a child's biological paternity can never be verified with absolute certainty by ordinary means, the arthavāda's admission of doubt over lineage serves — somewhat paradoxically — to elevate the ritual recitation of ancestry itself as the more reliable and praiseworthy means of establishing one's brahmin status, rather than undermining the practice.
