"Next, Grammar should be studied for conciseness' sake. Brihaspati taught Indra the science of words for a thousand years of the gods, giving him one word after another. He never got to the end. Yet Brihaspati was the teacher, and Indra was the scholar, and the lesson lasted for a thousand years of the gods. And still he did not get to the end. Nowadays if a man is long-lived, he may reach a hundred years. How can he apprehend, much less learn to use rightly, all words if taught them word by word?

"Lastly, Grammar should be studied for the removal of doubts. The priests recite the text 'sthulaprishatim agnivarunam anadvahim alabheta.' Here no one but a grammarian can say how the compound 'sthulaprishati' is to be taken. He decides by the accent. If the acute accent were on the last syllable of the compound, the word would be a karmadharaya. As it is, the compound has the accent of its first member, and it is therefore a bahuvrihi.

original p. 562

"Moreover, there are these further uses of Grammar":

तेऽसुरः दुष्टः शब्दः यदधीतम् यस्तु प्रयुङ्क्ते अविद्वान्सह विभक्तिं कुर्वन्ति यो वा इमं चत्वारि उतत्वः सक्तुमिव सरस्वतीं दसम्यं पुत्रस्य सुदेवोऽसि वरुणः । te'suraḥ duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ yad adhītam yas tu prayuṅkte avidvān saha vibhaktiṃ kurvanti yo vā imaṃ catvāri uta tvaḥ saktum iva sarasvatīṃ dasamyaṃ putrasya sudevo'si varuṇaḥ | (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)

"'Te'suraḥ, duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ, yad adhītam, yas tu prayuṅkte, avidvān saha, vibhaktiṃ kurvanti, yo vā imaṃ, catvāri, uta tvaḥ, saktum iva, sarasvatīm, dasamyaṃ putrasya, sudevo'si varuṇaḥ.'"

"Te'suraḥ" (The Asuras)

हेळयो हेळयः इत्यसुरा उच्चरन्तः पराजिता । तस्माद्ब्राह्मणेन म्लेच्छितवै नापभाषितवै मलेच्छो ह वा एष यदपशब्दः ॥ heḷayo heḷayaḥ ity asurā uccarantaḥ parājitāḥ | tasmād brāhmaṇena mlecchitavai nāpabhāṣitavai | mlecchо ha vā eṣa yad apaśabdaḥ || (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)

"The Asuras shouted 'heḷayo heḷayaḥ' (he 'rayo he 'rayaḥ) and were defeated. Therefore a brahmin should not speak the language of the barbarian, should not use bad forms. The word 'mleccha' here is equivalent to 'apaśabda' [incorrect speech]. Let us study Grammar that we may not be Mlecchas."

"Duṣṭaḥ Śabdaḥ" (The Corrupted Word)

दुष्टः शब्दः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह । स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥ duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāg-vajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt || (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)

"A word with a wrong accent or a wrong letter is used in vain since it does not convey the same meaning: it is a spoken thunderbolt that will destroy the sacrificer, as, for example, the word 'indraśatru' with the accent misplaced."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Moreover there are these further uses of grammar. 'Te'surah, dushtah sabdah, yad adhitam, yas tu prayunkte, avidvansaha, vibhaktim kurvanti, yo va imam, chatvari, uta tvah, saktum iva, sarasvatim, dasamyam putrasya, sudevo 'si varuna.'"

'Te'surah.

"The Asuras shouted 'helayo helayah' (he 'rayo he 'rayah) and were defeated. Therefore a brahmin should not speak the language of the barbarian, should not use bad forms. The word 'mlechchha' here is equivalent to 'apasabda.' Let us study grammar that we may not be Mlechchhas.

"Dushtah sabdha.

'A word with a wrong accent or a wrong letter is used in vain since it does not convey the same meaning: it is a spoken thuuderbolt that will destroy the sacrificer, as, for example, the word indrasatru with the accent misplaced.'

original p. 563

Now let us critically examine the grammatical discussion that stands as the principal matter among the Veda's Angas. Grammar accepts and orders the roots (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), word-forms, and their meaning-determinations in the appropriate contexts where they apply. As it was said before, this too has its basis in the Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa—

वाग्वै पराच्यव्याकृतावदत् एते देवा इन्द्रमब्रुवन् इमां नो वाचं व्याकुर्विति सोऽब्रवीद्वैषा मह्यं चैव वायवे च सह गृह्णाथा इति तस्मादिन्द्रवायू सहैव गृह्णाति तामिन्द्रो मध्यतोऽवक्रम्य व्याकरोत् तस्मादियं व्याकृता वागुद्यते ॥ vāg vai parācy avyākṛtāvadat | ete devā indram abruvan imāṃ no vācaṃ vyākuruv iti | so'bravīd vaiṣā mahyaṃ caiva vāyave ca saha gṛhṇāthā iti | tasmād indra-vāyū sahaiva gṛhṇāti | tām indro madhyato'vakramya vyākarot | tasmād iyaṃ vyākṛtā vāg udyate || (Taittiriya Samhita 6.4.7.3; see page 558 above)

Meaning: in the beginning, Speech spoke unclearly (avyākṛta — undivided), rendering it useless [for correctly conveying meaning]. Then the gods approached Indra, asking, "Divide this Speech of ours [into parts] for us." He agreed, saying, "Give this offering jointly to me and to Vayu." Because of this, [the offering] is given jointly to Indra and Vayu even now (this is called "Aindravāyava" — a specific offering-related Dharma tradition). Both deities accepted the offering. Then Indra took hold of Speech at her very middle and divided her methodically. That is why what we now recite is "vyākṛta vāk" — Speech that has been analyzed and divided into her proper constituent parts.

Grammar itself was, in ancient times, composed in the earliest period — vast in extent, like the ocean itself. The roots, suffixes, words, and sentences were originally undivided (agrantha, unarranged into a systematic textual form). Then, out of desire for the fulfillment [of ritual duties], the gods approached Indra alone specifically, and by combining the powers of Vayu and Soma-Rasa-graha with him, established a fixed order — and thus, from that point on, this speech came to be arranged in a systematic, divided fashion, namely: words, roots, and suffixes, distinguished from one another. Because of this, the wisest sages, from Pāṇini onward, arranged this speech (that is, established a grammatical treatise) in a fixed, methodical form — this is the understood significance here.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Let us study Grammar that we may not be guilty of using wrong forms.

"Yad adhitam.

'A text learned but not understood and so recited is like dry fuel thrown where no fire is: it will never blaze up.'

"Let us study Grammar that we may not learn the Veda without understanding its meaning.

original p. 564

Regarding what specific purpose this Grammar serves, later scholars, in their own tradition, have stated—

रक्षोहागमलाघवसंदेहाः प्रयोजनमिति । rakṣohāgamalāghavasandehāḥ prayojanam iti | (Katyayana's Vartika; see page 559 above)

"Rakṣā (protection), ūha (adaptation), āgama (scriptural priority), lāghava (brevity), and sandeha-removal — these are the purposes [of Grammar]." Vararuchi has clearly set out these five purposes in his own vārtika-treatise.

Rakṣā (Protection): since Vedic mantras have come down through the ages, doubts arise concerning whether their forms have been corrupted, whether some deviation has crept into the words as transmitted. Precisely to remove such doubts and to protect the Veda's genuine form from corruption, Grammar is necessary. Without knowing Grammar, one cannot distinguish which letters, among those forming a word, are genuinely correct and which have been altered — nor determine, through Grammar's principles, the correct application of the mantras. Hence, without knowledge of Grammar, one cannot properly identify errors of accent, wrong letters, and similar deviations.

Ūha (Adaptation): the words found in the Vedic mantras — nouns, verbs, and similar forms — are not always used explicitly in their fully expanded application; often, the application must be inferred and understood [i.e., adapted to the specific ritual context]. This too requires proficiency in Grammar. Where the mantras must be modified [in case, number, gender] for ritual employment — this adaptation likewise cannot be accomplished without knowledge of Grammar.

Āgama (Scriptural Priority): the Brahmin who desires knowledge must study and understand not only the Veda itself, but also the dharma expressed through its established, systematic form — this too the shastras declare. Among the six Angas of the Veda, Grammar holds the foremost place. Effort spent studying this principal Anga will prove fruitful. Therefore, Grammar should be studied.

Lāghava (Brevity): to know the Veda with genuine ease, one must study Grammar. Once, when the sage Brihaspati desired to teach the science of words to Indra, he explained it word by word — an approach that even after a thousand celestial years, remained incomplete. Grammar's own systematic method (through its structured rules on roots, suffixes, and the like) accomplishes in a single stroke what such an exhaustive word-by-word approach never could.

Sandeha (Removal of Doubt): even one who knows how to distinguish between correct and incorrect forms may occasionally have doubts about a particular word's status. If, at such a time, one lacks the ability to apply Grammar's rules, one cannot resolve the doubt.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Yas tu prayunkte.

'He who knows how to put words together, and skilful in discriminating between them, uses them rightly on occasion, obtains endless victory in heaven: but he is injured by bad forms.'

"Who is injured? The same man, he who knows how to put words together. For he who knows what the right forms are must also know what the wrong forms are. And if

original p. 565

...religious merit accrues to him from his knowledge of the right form, religious demerit must accrue to him from his knowledge of the wrong form. In fact, more demerit than merit. For wrong forms are many, right are few. Every word has many corruptions. Take the word

गौः । gauḥ |

Corrupt forms of it are

गवी, गोणी, गोपोतलिका । gavī, goṇī, gopotalikā |

and the like. As for the man who does not know how to put words together, his ignorance is his safety."

Asaṃdeha (Freedom from Doubt): knowing the meanings of words correctly is called freedom from doubt (asaṃdeha). This is a fundamental requirement for grammatical study. Understand it this way—

स्थूलपृषती मासि आलभेत । sthūlapṛṣatī māsi ālabheta |

— this sentence involves ambiguity: how should the compound "sthūlapṛṣatī" be understood? Or should one understand it as—

स्थूलः पृषती । sthūlaḥ pṛṣatī |

—(great and spotted — meaning a bull that is both great and spotted)? Or as a karmadhāraya compound meaning "the great-spotted-one"? Without knowledge of Grammar, this cannot be resolved. Only a grammarian, on the basis of the accent, can determine whether this is a bahuvrīhi or a karmadhāraya compound, and thereby settle the meaning correctly. Here, in this sentence, the accent falls on the compound's first member — establishing it definitively as a bahuvrīhi, meaning "one who possesses great spots," rather than "great and spotted" as a mere descriptive pairing. This kind of doubt-resolution is Grammar's chief use. Therefore, Grammar should be studied to remove such doubts.

The sutras of these [purposes] are as follows: rakṣā, śabdaḥ, uditvaṃ, iyaśca, prayukte, avidvāṃsa, vibhaktiṃ kurvanti, yo vā imāṃ, catvāri, uta tvaḥ, saktum iva, sāraśvatīṃ, dasamyaṃ putrasya, sudevoṣi varuṇeti ||

Devāsurāḥ (Gods and Asuras): it is said that in ancient times, gods and demons — belonging to the same lineage — became rivals for supremacy over the three worlds. Then, both sides ("devāḥ" and "asuraḥ")...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

religious merit accrues to him from his knowledge of the right form, religious demerit must accrue to him from his knowledge of the wrong form. In fact, more demerit than merit. For wrong forms are many, right are few. Every word has many corruptions. Take the word gauh. Corrupt forms of it are gavi, goni, gopotalika, and the like. As for the man who does not know how to put words together, his ignorance is his safety.

original p. 566

(In place of the letter "l" [in certain dialectal pronunciations, sounds shift]) — using "r" in place of "l" pronounces "layaḥ" as "rayaḥ" ("layaḥ" = destruction; "rayaḥ" = wealth) — and speaking this way, if "layaḥ" (destruction) is [mistakenly] spoken as "layaḥ" (with a corrupted, garbled sound), it becomes offensive to a brahmin's ears. That is why one should avoid speaking corrupted speech (mleccha-speech). And that "corrupted speech" (apaśabda) itself is precisely what must not be uttered — a corrupted word must be studiously avoided; Grammar should therefore be studied specifically to avoid such corrupted speech.

"Duṣṭaḥ Śabdaḥ" (The Corrupted Word) — this term has already been discussed above (see page 552 [the indraśatru account]). It occurs in the Nirukta's own Shikshadhyaya as follows:

दुष्टः शब्दः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह । स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥ duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāg-vajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt || (Nirukta 1.9)

Whether wrong in accent or wrong in letter — a word used incorrectly does not convey its intended meaning at all. Whether the fault lies in accent or arises through incorrect meaning, this indicates a corrupted word. This shows the meaning being conveyed as fault-bearing. Because of this defective usage, [the mantra] harms the sacrificer, just as we've seen, in a similar manner, with the "indraśatru" example — [it] causes the yajamāna to be struck down. From this discussion, we've seen the various flaws that can arise. Therefore, to avoid producing a corrupted word, one must study Grammar.

"Yad Adhītam" (What Has Been Studied) — from the Nirukta (1.18), stated thus—

यदधीतमविज्ञातं निगदेनैव शब्द्यते । अनग्नाविव शुष्कैधो न तज्ज्वलति कर्हिचित् ॥ yad adhītam avijñātaṃ nigadenaiva śabdyate | anagnāv iva śuṣkaidho na taj jvalati karhicit || (Nirukta 1.18)

Meaning: whatever is studied by rote alone, without understanding, and merely recited mechanically, without genuine comprehension of the Veda's meaning — it will never blaze up, like dry fuel thrown where there is no fire, never bursting into flame. Therefore, one should study Grammar specifically in order to understand the Veda's meaning correctly.

"Yas tu Prayuṅkte" (He Who Rightly Applies It) — [regarding] the use of words, and the skill applied in a given context; how one should properly apply each — this is what one must know. On this matter, the authors of the Kaśikā and similar grammatical treatises say—

यस्तु प्रयुङ्क्ते कुशलो विशेषे शब्दान्यथावद्व्यवहारकाले । yas tu prayuṅkte kuśalo viśeṣe śabdān yathāvad vyavahāra-kāle | (see page 564 above)

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"This is a hard saying. Ignorance ought not to be safety. The man who slays a brahmin or who drinks wine in ignorance would, I presume, fall from caste despite his ignorance. Who then is it that is injured? The man who does not know how to put words together. As for the man who knows his knowledge is his safety.

original p. 567

सोऽकनन्तेमाप्रोत्येति जयं परत्रे वाग्योगविद्दुष्यति चापशब्दैः ॥ so'kanantemāprotyeti jayaṃ paratre vāg-yoga-vid duṣyati cāpaśabdaiḥ || (Kashika/grammatical tradition, on the value of correct usage)

Meaning: one who has skillfully mastered the proper use of speech, applying it correctly according to worldly needs, attains victory in the beyond as well. But one who is ignorant of the proper joining and application of speech is contaminated by corrupted forms (apaśabda).

Here it must be understood what constitutes the "fault" of a corrupted word's use. Concerning this: is the use of a corrupted word — that is, an improper word — itself a fault? Or does merely knowing that a word is corrupted, without actually using it, also become fault? Precisely because of this discussion, using a corrupted word is a true dharma-violation. In that sense, whether from mere knowledge of a corrupted word or from actually using it, an adharma (or, indeed, a sin) results. Ordinarily, corrupted forms are far more numerous than correct forms. Corrupted forms exist in great abundance. For example — "gauḥ" (cow) — and its many corrupt variations, such as "gāvī," "goṇī," "gopotalikā," and similar, are widely known.

Once, a certain man, from lack of grammatical knowledge, is said to have used a corrupted form without even knowing it was corrupted. If asked, can he escape blame simply because he acted out of ignorance rather than deliberate intent? — even so, ignorance is customarily excused as a defense. Whether or not a brahmin knew, if he committed some transgression, or created some fault through incorrect performance, does he not still bear consequences for it? Similarly, even one who commits a mistaken utterance without knowing it — precisely because he lacks the knowledge to know that his usage is corrupt — such a person does not incur the fault of adharma. This shows why "avidvāṃsaha" (ignorance) is discussed — merely knowing many words and their applications, without also knowing dharma, still leaves one properly usable in speech.

Jaimini and other Mīmāṃsakas insist one must know what constitutes dharma, and equally know what constitutes adharma — precisely for this purpose. Both must be known: to perform dharma, and to avoid adharma. Even here [in the Śikṣā's own account], "śabda" (correct word) and "aśabda" (incorrect word)...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Avidvansah.

'But the unlearned, who do not know that, in responding to a salutation they should protract the vowel—in approaching them he should simply say, as he would to a woman, Here am I.'

original p. 568

...one must know both. Knowing the correct word, and knowing how it should be applied; knowing the incorrect word, and knowing how it should be avoided in application — for this very reason, Grammar should be studied.

"Avidvāṃsaha" (The Ignorant) — regarding this term, since it discusses those who are ignorant of Grammar, it has been treated already in similar contexts. Since it discusses persons devoid of grammatical knowledge, it treats the fault of using improper forms — this is given here as an example—

अविद्वांसः प्रत्यभिवादे नानोऽयं ये न पुंसि विदुः । कामं तेषु तु विप्रेष्यं स्त्रीष्विवानायं वदेदिति ॥ avidvāṃsaḥ pratyabhivāde nāno'yaṃ ye na puṃsi viduḥ | kāmaṃ teṣu tu vipreṣyaṃ strīṣv ivānāyaṃ vaded iti || (Nirukta 1.19)

"But the unlearned, who do not know that, in responding to a salutation, they should protract the vowel — in approaching them, he should simply say, as he would to a woman, 'Here am I.'"

Meaning: in this verse (which appears in the first chapter, describing the ordinary applications typically found), it is said that when responding to a salutation, one's own [family or personal] name should be pronounced with a lengthened vowel [as a mark of grammatical propriety]. Those unlearned people who do not know this rule instead pronounce it in an ordinary manner, as one would when addressing a woman [informally]. This is spoken of here as an example of erroneous practice. In this way, in a person's daily life as well, such improper practices are known to occur. This shows that even after studying and gaining scholarly proficiency, without also thoroughly mastering Grammar, one cannot avoid this kind of fault in ordinary word-usage. Since even scholars versed in the shastras are exposed to this risk, Grammar's importance is beyond dispute; without knowledge of Grammar, no genuine honour attaches [to one's learning]. Therefore, Grammar should be studied.

"Vibhaktiṃ Kurvanti" (They Perform the Division) — the priests who properly know the words to be recited (that is, the principal words belonging to the yajna, and the words belonging to that portion) must be studied for their correct application. Without knowledge of Grammar, this precept cannot be properly complied with. For this reason too, Grammar should be studied.

प्रयाजाः सविभक्तिकाः कार्त्स्न्या इति — prayājāḥ savibhaktikāḥ kārtsnyā iti — "The priests recite the text 'prayajah savibhaktikah karyah.' But without Grammar this precept cannot be complied with. Let us study Grammar then for this reason."

"Yo Vā Imām" (He Who [Analyses] This [Speech]) — this well-known text of the Rig Veda declares that whoever fully knows word, accent, and letter — one must know these matters, distinguishing each accent, each letter, in due order—

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Let us study Grammar that we may not be treated like women.

"Vibhaktim kurvanti.

"The priests recite the text 'prayajah savibhaktikah karyah.' But without Grammar this precept cannot be complied with. Let us study Grammar then for this reason.

"Yo va imam.

"He who can analyse speech, word by word, accent by accent, letter by letter, he and he only is fit to be a priest."

original p. 569

...according to the rules — only such a person is fit to be a priest. One who cannot properly divide sentences, syllables, or word-portions; who cannot distinguish accent-differences, letter-differences, or the boundaries within a compound; who cannot properly identify [ritually] related words — such a person is unfit to serve as priest in yajna and similar rites. Therefore, only one who is thoroughly versed in Grammar is fit for priesthood.

Here, to illustrate the analysis of words and accented letters, the Nirukta gives the following example—

वायुर्वा यज्ञो दर्शतेव सोमा अरंकृताः । तेषां साकं श्रुधीहवम् ॥ vāyur vā yajño darśateva somā araṃkṛtāḥ | teṣāṃ sākaṃ śrudhī havam || (Vajasaneyi Samhita 1.2.1)

This mantra occurs in the Gayatri-chandas [meter]. Its word-division is: "vāyur vā yajño darśate | ime somā araṃkṛtāḥ ||" — meaning [that is how it should be understood].

Here, "darśakeṣu" [visible things] — should it be understood as "darśaka" [one who sees] or "ime" [these]? The letter division is: t + ime, two separate letters combining. Where sandhi occurs, adjacent letters join together. This slight variation causes doubt within the interpretation. "Te" indicates a word, and following "anudātta," its accent varies. This word, distinct from the letter "i," is a separate letter carrying its own accent, differing from "te."

This way, in this manner, there are many divisions to be made — for example, "dīrgha" [long syllable] versus "avagraha" [separated word], and "vāṃ" versus "ahaṃ" [I], and "khu" (namely "sāṃ ne sūnu" — see page 549 above) — "dīrghākṣare pṛṣṭhaṃ vā abhavat, sphā ne sūnu = saḥ | khu | naḥ | sūnuḥ" — the accent differs by syllable-length in each case. All these matters require careful precision; anyone wishing to fully master this discipline must study Grammar with genuine effort. This too is a reason why one must study Grammar.

"Catvāri" (Four)

This particular topic is important — regarding it, our own tradition cites this verse (found on folio 40)—

चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य । त्रिधा बद्धो वृषभो रोरवीति महो देवो मर्त्यां आ विवेश ॥ catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa || (Rigveda Samhita 4.58.3)

"With four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands in Bull, penned up in three places roars mightily; a great god has entered mortals."

Since this mantra's meaning cannot easily be determined through common understanding, it remains obscure to most, given its many possible interpretations. This mantra is described as one belonging to a rishi named "Vena" (yathāsvaru; see Nirukta 5.2[?]). It is a "sāmayanā" [collective] mantra — its sense taken together, and its application through Agni, Surya, and Apa (waters), and through the Gopura (metaphorical bull) with its four "kṣapa" (horns), the wise say. Some also expound it grammatically according to the analysis of the "rukchandas" [Vedic prosody] tradition.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"Let us study Grammar that we may be fit to be priests.

"Chatvari.

'With four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands in Bull, penned up in three places roars mightily; a great god has entered mortals.'

original p. 570

Ancient scholars have explained this mantra's meaning in various ways, according to whichever deity is taken as primary in the intended sense; even in our own tradition, this mantra has been interpreted in several distinct ways. Grammatically, they explain the meaning as follows —

चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य । त्रिधा बद्धो वृषभो रोरवीति महो देवो मर्त्यां आ विवेश ॥ catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa || (Rigveda Samhita 4.58.3; see page 569 above)

From this, the following meanings can be explained:

Catvāri Śṛṅgā (Four Horns) — from the standpoint of Grammar: noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga), and particle (nipāta) — these are the four kinds of word-categories.

Trayo Asya Pādāḥ (Its Three Feet) — past (bhūta), present (bhavat), and future (vartamāna) — these are the three time-divisions.

Dve Śīrṣe (Two Heads) — nominal endings (subanta-padas) and verbal endings (tiṅanta-padas) — these two types of word-terminations.

Sapta Hastāso Asya (Its Seven Hands) — the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh cases (vibhakti) — these seven case-endings.

Tridhā Baddhaḥ (Bound in Three Places) — held fast by the three articulatory places: throat, chest, and head — these three points [of pronunciation].

Vṛṣabhaḥ (The Bull) — since it showers down (varṣaṇa) blessings upon what is desired, it is called Vṛṣabha (the Bull, "the shower-er").

Roravīti (It Roars Mightily) — from the root "ru," meaning to make a sound (śabda-karma) — hence its use here.

Mahoo Devaḥ (The Great God) — the great deity, referring to the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa) itself.

Martyān (Into Mortals).

Ā Viveśa (Has Entered) — meaning: has entered into, taken possession of. That great deity — namely Grammar itself — has entered into mortal beings [i.e., speakers] and dwells within them.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"The four horns are the four kinds of words,—the noun, the verb, the preposition, and the particle;—the three hands are the three times; the two heads are the nominal and verbal terminations: the seven hands are the seven cases; the three times in which the Bull is penned are the breast, the throat and the head. He is called here a Bull (vrishabha), because he rains down (varshana) blessings. 'Roravīti,' from the root 'ru' to make a noise. A great god has entered mortals. Let us study grammar that we may attain to union with this great god.

original p. 571

Or this verse may be quoted under the heading "Catvāri" — since it belongs to the sutra as an illustrative example, we may cite here another well-known verse—

चत्वारि वाक्परिमिता पदानि तानि विदुर्ब्राह्मणा ये मनीषिणः । गुहा त्रीणि निहिता नेंगयन्ति तुरीयं वाचो मनुष्या वदन्ति ॥ catvāri vāk parimitā padāni tāni vidur brāhmaṇā ye manīṣiṇaḥ | guhā trīṇi nihitā neṃgayanti turīyaṃ vāco manuṣyā vadanti || (Rigveda Samhita 1.164.45)

"There be four divisions of speech: brahmins who are wise know all four; but three lie hid in their secret place and do not move; the fourth part of speech men speak."

"Manīṣiṇaḥ" means "manasā īśinaḥ" (those who are masters through the mind). "Guhā" is a Vedic form for "guhāyam" (in the secret place), as is also "nihitā" for "nihitāni" (placed/deposited). "Turīyaṃ vāco manuṣya vadanti" — that is, it is the fourth part of speech only that is current among men.

This particular verse too has been explained in various ways by many scholars — differing interpretations arise from the differing systems each scholar follows. In deciding its precise meaning, various learned authorities have explained the matter in different ways—

Om-kāra (the syllable Om, the "praṇava") is the great, non-decaying, imperishable [primal sound]. Nāma (name) is called "bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ" — the vyāhṛti-forms, said to number four. Nāma (noun), ākhyāta (verb), upasarga (preposition), nipāta (particle) — these are the four kinds of speech, according to Vyākaraṇa's own account.

Mantra, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, lokakṣaṇa-vyāhāra — the [four-part] division as understood by ordinary human beings is one view. Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Vyāvahārika-bhāṣā (practical/ordinary speech) — this is another classification. Sparśa, sparśī, kramīkṛta and the "vyāvahārikī" (practical) speech — such is another accepted account.

Paśyantī, madhyamā, and vaikharī — [along with a fourth] — these terms are used by some scholars to explain the fourfold division.

In this way, the ancients have set forth many kinds of interpretation — brahmins, wise in mind, know all these fourfold divisions. Of these four, three remain hidden and unmoving in their secret place; it is only the fourth portion of speech that ordinary humans commonly utter — this much is the accepted meaning, held by many across different systems.

The meaning of the word "muktārtha" [liberated/complete sense] is that speech has four distinct kinds. Grasping this well, brahmins who genuinely know [this doctrine] understand: among these four kinds of speech-categories, in three of them exist countless forms — but in only one does the ordinary usage practiced by human beings actually occur. That which remains, unspoken and unmoving in most cases, is what most people are unaware even exists. Here, the terms "manīṣiṇaḥ" and "brāhmaṇāḥ" are used interchangeably, discussed together, and their meaning...

यत्रा सखायः सख्यानि जानते सक्तुमिव तितउना पुनन्ति । अत्रा धीरा धिय एनाभिरेकं गूहन्ति गुह्यमविशेषु शीकैः ॥ yatrā sakhāyaḥ sakhyāni jānate saktum iva titaunā punanti | atrā dhīrā dhiya enābhir ekaṃ gūhanti guhyam aviśeṣu śīkaiḥ || (Rigveda Samhita 10.71.2)

Meaning: the word "saktu" (ground grain/meal) here — its derivation according to Grammar can be traced through the verbal root "√sac" (to associate/adhere), yielding the sense of "that which is difficult to purify [thoroughly]." Alternatively, deriving it through metathesis (letter-transposition) from the root "√kas" (to move/shine), it may instead convey the sense of "capability" (śakti). This shows how the very meaning of a single word — its etymological source, and hence its true sense — depends entirely on grammatical analysis.

This mantra, whether taken as expressing the science of speech (vāk-śāstra), or as describing the structure of grammar (vāk-svarūpa) itself, is a difficult one, requiring the discipline called "grammar" (śabda-śāstra) to properly navigate its path. Who, then, is capable of understanding it? Only the authorities on Grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) themselves.

Therefore, to avoid having to perform such expiatory rites, one should study Grammar.

"'Let him name the boy on the tenth day after his birth. He must make the name of the sonants, with y, r, l or v in the beginning or middle, and the visarga at the end, of two syllables or four, a kṛt-formation, and not ending in a taddhita.' But without a knowledge of..."

Meaning: the person's name should either begin with, or have in its middle, a semivowel (y, r, l, or v) [i.e., an "antasthā" consonant], and should end with the visarga. It should be two syllables in length, or four; it should be formed as a "kṛt"-derivative (from a verbal root, via primary suffixes), and must never be a "taddhita"-derivative (a secondary derivative formed from another noun). Whoever wishes to properly assign a name according to these precise grammatical rules must, without exception, possess knowledge of Grammar; without it, this precept cannot be properly carried out.

वायोर्भगान्तमन्तरिक्षदेवतानां सूर्यादि देवपत्न्यन्तं दिवि देवतानाम् ॥ vāyor bhagāntam antarikṣa-devatānāṃ sūryādi devapatny-antaṃ divi devatānām ||

"Let the section from Vayu to Bhaga be for the gods in mid-air; and that from Surya to Devapatnyah for the gods in heaven."

"So the whole Samāmnāya from 'Gauḥ' to 'Devapatnyaḥ' is studied."

Nighaṇṭu is a well-established name for a book which contains chiefly lists of synonyms. As for example, such books as Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha, and others are spoken of as the "ten Nighaṇṭus." In the same way, the first chapter of our book, which gives a list of synonyms, is called a Nighaṇṭu. There are three adhyāyas in this chapter. In the first, we have names of things, such as the earth and the other worlds, and space and time; in the second, we have the names of things such as men and the limbs of men; in the third, we have qualities, such as multitude or shortness, belonging to both classes of things.

This is what the following verse conveys:

प्रथमाध्याये भूम्यादि-लोकानाम् आकाश-कालयोश्च नामानि । द्वितीये पुरुषादीनां तदङ्गानां च संज्ञाः स्युः । तृतीये तूभयोरपि साधारणा बहुत्वाल्पत्वादि-गुणवाचकाः शब्दāḥ || prathamādhyāye bhūmyādi-lokānām ākāśa-kālayoś ca nāmāni | dvitīye puruṣādīnāṃ tad-aṅgānāṃ ca saṃjñāḥ syuḥ | tṛtīye tūbhayor api sādhāraṇā bahutvālpatvādi-guṇa-vācakāḥ śabdāḥ ||

Even the very authorship of this book (Nighaṇṭu) is not settled with certainty among scholars. Regarding its origin, some hold varying views — but its own arrangement, its chapter-and-verse organization, and its authoritative status regarding synonym-lists are firmly established, notwithstanding disagreements about its precise authorship. There is no dispute regarding all this. Its content bears directly on the science of etymology (Nirukta) and its practical application, being useful for that purpose (page 576 discussion, above).

Therefore, this concludes the summary of the Devata-Anga's Nirukta discussion.

Continuing the extensive discussion on the science of etymology (Nirukta) and its practical application, the current explanation now also touches on grammar's own connection to it. There is no separate helpful resource for this beyond the treatise itself, so the author gives the relevant details directly. Since establishing this particular subject matter requires knowledge that only Grammar can supply, its inclusion here is entirely appropriate.

On this point, the verses at the start of the Nirukta's own commentary state—

आद्यं नैघण्टुकं काण्डं द्वितीयं नैगमं तथा । तृतीयं दैवतं चेति समाम्नायस्त्रिधा स्थितः ॥ गौरादि पापूरणपर्यन्तमाद्यं नैघण्टुकं मतम् । जहादि व्यवसानान्तं नैगमं संप्रचक्षते ॥ अग्न्यादिदेवपत्न्यन्तं देवताकाण्डमुच्यते । अग्न्यादिदेवी ऊर्जाहुत्यन्तक क्षितिगतो गणः ॥ वाय्वादिदेवो भगान्ताः स्वन्तरिक्षस्थ देवताः । सूर्यादिदेवपत्न्यन्ता द्युस्था देवता इति ॥ गणादिदेवपत्न्यन्तं समाम्नायमधीयत इति ॥

ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ kāṇḍaṃ dvitīyaṃ naigamaṃ tathā | tṛtīyaṃ daivataṃ ceti samāmnāyas tridhā sthitaḥ || gaurādi pāpūraṇa-paryantam ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ mataṃ | jahādi vyavasānāntaṃ naigamaṃ saṃpracakṣate || agnyādi-devapatny-antaṃ devatā-kāṇḍam ucyate | agnyādi devī ūrjāhutyantaka kṣiti-gato gaṇaḥ || vāyv-ādi-devo bhagāntāḥ svāntarikṣa-stha devatāḥ | sūryādi-deva-patyantā dyu-sthā devatā iti || gaṇādi-deva-patny-antaṃ samāmnāyam adhīyata iti ||

"The first section (kāṇḍa) is Naighaṇṭuka, the second is likewise Naigama, and the third Daivata — thus the Samāmnāya stands in three parts. From 'gauḥ' up to 'pāpūraṇa' is held to be the first, Naighaṇṭuka; from 'jahā' to 'vyavasāna' is proclaimed as Naigama. From 'agni' up to 'devapatnī' is called the Devatā-kāṇḍa; from Agni's own [group] up to Ūrjāhuti is the host of deities dwelling on Earth. From Vāyu onward, ending with Bhaga, are the deities dwelling in the mid-region (antarikṣa); from Sūrya onward, ending with the Devapatnīs, are the deities dwelling in heaven (dyuloka). Thus, from 'gaṇa' onward, ending with 'devapatnī,' the Samāmnāya is studied."

Meaning: in this way, this Nirukta-treatise has five sections — that is, three kāṇḍas (Naighaṇṭuka, Naigama, Daivata), further subdivided into the earth-region, the mid-region, and the heaven-region within the Daivata portion itself. The word "nigama" means Veda. For Yaska, when citing a Vedic text, constantly uses the formula, "And there is a nigama with regard to this." Because the second chapter, which is the fourth adhyāya, deals with words that, for the most part, occur in the Veda, it is therefore called Nigama.

The reason why the third chapter, which is the fifth adhyāya, is called Daivata is plain.

The whole book, consisting of five adhyāyas or three chapters, is thus called Nirukta, because it teaches the meanings of words that stand in the lists perfectly independent of each...

other. Yaska composed the commentary on it in twelve adhyāyas, beginning

समाम्नायः समाम्नातः । samāmnāyaḥ samāmnātaḥ |

and ending

तस्यास्तस्यास्तद्भाव्यमनुभवत्यनुभवति । tasyas tasyas tad-bhāvyam anubhavaty anubhavati |

This commentary also is called Nirukta. Because the supposed elements of each word are here fully (nir) set out (ukta). For in his book, after having declared the fourfold division of words into nouns, verbs, prepositions, and particles, Yaska declares that particles fall into (nipatanti) various meanings. Having thus analysed the term "nipāta," he gives an example. "Na" means only prohibition in common talk: in the Veda it means both (prohibition and comparison). In the text

नेन्द्रं देवममंसत । nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |

it means prohibition. In the text

दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् । durmadāso na surāyāṃ |

Meaning: the etymological ("Vaikārthavāchi") sense, wherever a single word denotes a whole class of meaning through one root's own natural sense, is regarded as one such usage encoded in this treatise — this is what "nipāta" (particle) refers to. Among particles, there is also a subdivision into those used in the sense of comparison and those used otherwise. This treatise, in its own opening chapters, discusses different applications of the word "artha" and their fourfold classification, and also treats "aupacārikatva" (figurative usage) or "nipāta" (untranslatable particles).

In the beginning chapters, various types are discussed: root-analysis, letter-derivation, day, night, and time-related words, along with words carrying meanings of substance. In the middle chapters, useful discussions of household-related words, actions, and their derivation appear. In the final chapters, virtues and defects belonging to the qualities discussed in earlier chapters are treated more fully.

The Nigama section of the Veda deals with well-known, non-obscure sentences drawn from various parts of the Veda, and clarifies their exact meaning; scholars refer to this specifically as forming the "Nigama-kāṇḍa." In this section, ordinary Vedic sentences are cited and their meanings clearly resolved, distinguishing this section as belonging to the "Nigama" division.

In the third section — the fifth adhyāya — the deities discussed are called "Devatā." This is why it is termed the "Devatā-kāṇḍa."

These three sections make up the full text. Since this treatise gives the derivations of unusual (obscure) words found scattered throughout the Veda, the text is called "Nirukta." Yaska defines these obscure words as belonging to the categories: noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga), and particle (nipāta); and states that particles convey various meanings depending on context. Having analyzed the term "nipāta" this way, he gives an example. "Na" ordinarily means only prohibition in common speech; but in the Veda, it carries both senses — prohibition and comparison. In the text—

नेन्द्रं देवममंसत । nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |

—it means prohibition. In the text—

दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् । durmadāso na surāyāṃ |

—...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

other. Yaska composed the commentary on it in twelve adhyayas, beginning 'samamnayah samamnatah' and ending 'tasyas tasyas tadbhavyam anubhavatyanubhavati.' This commentary also is called Nirukta. Because the supposed elements of each word are here fully (nir) set out (ukta). For in his book, after having declared the fourfold division of words into nouns, verbs, prepositions and particles, Yaska declares that particles fall into (nipatanti) various meanings. Having thus analysed the term 'nipata,' he gives an example. 'Na' means only prohibition in common talk: in the Veda it means both (prohibition and comparison). In the text 'nendram devam amansata,' it means prohibition. In the text 'durmadaso na 'surayam,'

original p. 580

it means comparison. This is the example given in the Nirukta for the double use of the particle 'na,' as meaning both 'no' and 'if' in the Veda, whereas in common talk it means 'no' only. We shall have frequent occasion in the course of our commentary to cite similar etymologies given by this author.

Nor need it be feared that these etymologies have no foundation in fact. For some of them are given in the brahmanas.

इन्द्रं वा एष अहुतीः इति तस्मादिन्द्रो नाम । अप्रथयदिति तस्मात्पृथिवी नाम ॥ indraṃ vā eṣa āhutīr iti tasmād indro nāma | aprathayad iti tasmāt pṛthivī nāma ||

"This is that in virtue of which the āhutis are so called." Therefore they call him "Indra." "Because he stretched it out (aprathayat)," that is why the earth (pṛthivī) is so called.

The author himself will also be found citing brahmanas in proof of the etymologies he gives.

It is true that the etymology of some words can be learned from Grammar. But not all. Wherefore the author says—

तदिदं विद्यास्थानं व्याकरणस्य केवलं शब्दलक्षणे न सर्वेषां पदानां निर्वचनं सिद्ध्येत् । tad idaṃ vidyā-sthānaṃ vyākaraṇasya kevalaṃ śabda-lakṣaṇe na sarveṣāṃ padānāṃ nirvacanaṃ siddhyet |

"Therefore this science is the essence of Grammar and establishes the proper sense of the words. Therefore the Nirukta is useful towards the understanding of the Veda."

Meaning: it means comparison as well, not merely prohibition. This is precisely the illustration the Nirukta itself gives — how the particle "na" carries a double sense within the Veda, though in ordinary conversational usage it means only "no." Throughout our own commentary, we shall have frequent occasion to cite similar etymological derivations given by this author (Yaska), and there is no need to fear that such derivations have no factual grounding — many of them are directly supported by statements found in the Brahmana portions themselves.

For example: "This offering (āhuti) belongs to him — therefore he is named Indra." "He stretched out (aprathayat) [the earth] — therefore the earth is called Pṛthivī." Such etymological explanations, based on scriptural authority, are found scattered throughout many places, and our author (the composer of the Nirukta) himself cites such Brahmana-passages in support of the etymologies he offers.

It is true that some words' etymologies can indeed be derived through Grammar alone. But this doesn't hold for all words — Grammar's own rules cannot, by themselves, fully derive the meanings of every single word. Therefore, the author of this treatise states:

"Therefore, this branch of learning (Nirukta) exists as a specialized supplement to Grammar."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

it means comparison. This is the example given in the Nirukta for the double use of the particle 'na,' as meaning both 'no' and 'if' in the Veda, whereas in common talk it means 'no' only. We shall have frequent occasion in the course of our commentary to cite similar etymologies given by this author.

Nor need it be feared that these etymologies have no foundation in fact. For some of them are given in the brahmanas. 'This is that in virtue of which the ahutis are so called.' Therefore they call him 'Indra.' 'Because he stretched it out (aprathayat), that is why the earth (prithivi) is so called.' The author himself will also be found citing brahmanas in proof of the etymologies he gives.

It is true that the etymology of some words can be learned from Grammar. But not all. Wherefore the author says 'Therefore this science is the essence of Grammar and establishes the proper sense of the words.' Therefore the Nirukta is useful towards the understanding of the Veda.

"Kāryeṣu sādarasādhakaṃ ca" (see page 579 above) — for this reason, this shastra (Nirukta) properly determines the meanings of words that are not otherwise settled by any means. Therefore, Nirukta must be studied specifically for the sake of the Veda's meaning.

The Fifth Anga: Chandas (Metrics)

Just as, in the sacrificial rites, various matters are described as ritually obligatory in certain cases—

गायत्र्युष्णिगनुष्टुब्बृहती पङ्क्तिस्त्रिष्टुब्जगत्यौ छन्दांसि सप्त । gāyatry-uṣṇig-anuṣṭub-bṛhatī-paṅktis-triṣṭub-jagatyau chandāṃsi sapta |

"As, for example, in the text, 'Therefore seven plus four metres are recited in the prataranuvakya.' Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, are the seven metres. The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables. The Uṣṇik has four more, and thus consists of twenty-eight syllables. So the others may be worked out, as the Anuṣṭubh for example, each containing a greater number of syllables than the one before."

Let me give another text:

ब्राह्मणं गायत्र्या यजेत् क्षत्रियं त्रिष्टुभा । brāhmaṇaṃ gāyatryā yajet kṣatriyaṃ triṣṭubhā |

"He should say the fire for a Brahmin with Gāyatrī verses, for a Kshattriya with Triṣṭubh verses, and"...

Meaning: because in ritual matters, certain specific meters are prescribed as obligatory to use in various contexts, one must study the science of metrics (Chandas-shastra) in order to properly know these meters, distinguish them correctly, and apply the right meter in the right context. This is precisely why the fifth Anga — Chandas — exists and must be studied.

On this point, our own tradition gives the following explanation. The seven principal meters are: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables; Uṣṇik has four syllables more, thus consisting of twenty-eight; and continuing in this manner, each subsequent meter contains four syllables more than the one preceding it — thus Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and finally Jagatī, each increasing progressively.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

So, too, is Chhandas or the book on metres. Because throughout the ritual certain metres are declared to be obligatory in certain cases. As, for example, in the text, "Therefore seven plus four metres are recited in the prataranuvakya." Gayatri, Ushnik, Anushtubh, Brihati, Pankti, Trishtubh are the seven metres. The Gayatri consists of twenty-four syllables. The Ushnik has four more, and thus consists of twenty-eight syllables. So the others may be worked out, as the Anushtubh for example, each containing a greater number of syllables than the one before. Let me give another text. "He should say the fire for a Brahmin with Gayatri verses, for a Kshattriya with Trishtubh verses, and

original p. 582

for a Vaishya with Jagatī verses." Now in a matter of this kind, it is not easy without the Chhandas book to apprehend the distinction between the different metres, as that is laid down in the technical rules given there. I can quote a third text—

गायत्रीभिर्ब्राह्मणस्याग्निं यजेत् त्रिष्टुभा राजन्यस्य त्रिष्टुभा वैश्यस्य जगत्या । ओतत्तत्त्वं यजेत् ॥ gāyatrībhir brāhmaṇasyāgniṃ yajet triṣṭubhā rājanyasya triṣṭubhā vaiśyasya jagatyā | otat tattvaṃ yajet || (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.8[?])

"With Gāyatrī verses one should sacrifice the fire for a Brahmin, with Triṣṭubh verses for a Kshatriya, with Triṣṭubh verses for a Rajanya, with Jagatī verses for a Vaishya."

Meaning: the proper procedure for the fire-establishment rite (Agnyādhāna) for a Brahmin is to use Gāyatrī-metered mantras; for a Kshatriya, it must be done with Triṣṭubh-metered mantras; for a Vaishya, one must use Jagatī-metered mantras. In this way, this treatise establishes precisely which meters apply to which specific rites for each of the three classes.

Regarding some mantras where the meter itself is not directly specified, there are procedures that use a "mixed" (miśra) arrangement — for example, using Sāmi-baddha (partially combined) verses, or various such technical combinations, discussed within the treatise's own rules.

Fourth, one should know the "ānṛtya" [truth/falseness-related] and other specific chandas-related terms discussed here for practical use in various rites.

I can also cite another text:

यो ह वा अविदितार्ष-च्छन्दो-दैवतेन मन्त्रेण योजयति स्खलितं गच्छति कूपे वा पतति भूयश्च तस्मादृचā yajño'vidvāṃsam eva śāsti prakāśyate iti ॥ yo ha vā avidita-arṣa-chando-daivatena mantreṇa yojayati skhalitaṃ gacchati kūpe vā patati bhūyaś ca tasmād ṛcā yajño'vidvāṃsam eva śāsti prakāśyate iti ||

"The man who sacrifices or teaches by means of a mantra whose rishi, metre, and devatā he does not know, runs up against a post, or falls into a well, or perishes utterly: his guilt is increased. Therefore for every mantra he must know all these."

Meaning: whoever performs a yajna or teaches a mantra without knowing the rishi (its seer), chandas (its metre), or devatā (its deity), stumbles as he goes, or falls into a well; his fault becomes even greater than before. Therefore, one must know the rishi, meter, and deity of every mantra one recites.

Therefore, the Chhandas book on metres is useful for this knowledge.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

for a Vaisya with Jagati verses. Now in a matter of this kind, it is not easy without the Chhandas book to apprehend the distinction between the different metres as that is laid down in the technical rules given there. I can quote a third text. "The man who sacrifices or teaches by means of a mantra whose rishi, metre and devata he does not know, runs up against a post, or falls into a well, or perishes utterly: his guilt is increased. Therefore for every mantra he must know all these."

Therefore the Chhandas book on metres is useful for this knowledge.

The Sixth Anga: Jyotiṣa (Astronomy) — Its Purpose and Significance Determined

original p. 583

The use of the Jyotiṣa is thus given in that book itself: "To establish the times and reasons for sacrifices." There are texts prescribing all manner of times. The text "saṃvatsaraṃ" and similar refers to periods of years. The text "vasante" and similar refers to months. The text "māsi māsi" and similar refers to months. The text "yaṃ kāmayeta" refers to half-months. The text "ekāṣṭakāyāṃ" and similar refers to days. The text "kṛttikāsu" and similar refers to the nakṣatras (lunar mansions).

संवत्सरं वा ऋतवो मासाश्च ॐ ब्राह्मणेनाग्निर्माधीयीत । गृह्णे राजन्य आधीयेत । शरदि वैश्य आधीयेत ॥ saṃvatsaraṃ vā ṛtavo māsāś ca oṃ brāhmaṇenāgnir ādhīyeta | gṛhṇe rājanya ādhīyeta | śaradi vaiśya ādhīyeta || (Taittiriya Samhita 5.2.7[?])

"A Brahmin should establish the fire in spring; a Kshatriya should establish it in summer; a Vaishya should establish it in autumn."

मासि मासि पुष्ट्यार्थं गृह्णे च गृह्ण्य आधीयते इति मासविधयः । यं कामयेत वशीयासमिति पक्षविधिः । māsi māsi puṣṭy-arthaṃ gṛhṇe ca gṛhya ādhīyate iti māsa-vidhayaḥ | yaṃ kāmayeta vaśīyāsam iti pakṣa-vidhiḥ |

"Month by month" and similar [texts refer to] monthly regulations for the sake of prosperity. "Yaṃ kāmayeta" [expressing whatever a person] desires — this is the fortnight-regulation. "Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ" is the day-regulation. "Kṛttikāsu" is the nakṣatra-regulation.

This is the meaning: the Jyotiṣa serves the purpose belonging to yajnas and similar rites specifically because the treatise itself declares this. Since all yajnas and similar acts must be performed at their properly appointed times, determining that time correctly is the primary purpose which the science of Jyotiṣa serves. The mantras used in performing yajnas must be known together with their proper timings, and these are specified in various places throughout the Veda—

"To establish the reasons and times for sacrifices" — one should establish this by knowing the proper measure of the year's timing [and so on].

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The use of the Jyotisha is thus given in that book itself. "To establish the times and reasons for sacrifices." There are texts prescribing all manner of times. The text 'samvatsaram &c.' refers to periods of years. The text 'vasante &c.' refers to months. The text 'masi mase, &c.' refers to months. The text 'yam kamayeta' refers to half months. The text 'ekashtakayam, &c.' refers to days. The text 'krittikasu, &c.' refers to the nakshatras.

Therefore the Jyotisha is useful for determining the times and seasons proper for sacrifices.

original p. 584

"Saṃvatsaram-mukhyaṃ bṛhatyā" (see page 583 above) — this too establishes the correct measure of the year's timing.

वसन्ता ब्राह्मणस्याग्निमाधीयेत । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्य भवति । मुखं वा एतद्संवत्सरस्य यद्वसन्तः । यो वसन्ते ब्राह्मणमाधत्ते मुखत एव भवति । अथो योऽभिजितं वसन्तमेव प्रजापतिमाधत्ते । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्यादधीत ग्रीष्मो वै राजन्यस्य ऋतुः । शरदि वैश्यस्यादधीत शरत् वै वैश्यस्य ऋतुः ॥ vasantā brāhmaṇasyāgnim ādhīyeta | grīṣme rājanyasya bhavati | mukhaṃ vā etad-saṃvatsarasya yad vasantaḥ | yo vasante brāhmaṇam ādhatte mukhata eva bhavati | atho yo'bhijitaṃ vasantam eva prajāpatim ādhatte | grīṣme rājanyasyādadhīta grīṣmo vai rājanyasya ṛtuḥ | śaradi vaiśyasyādadhīta śarad vai vaiśyasya ṛtuḥ || (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.2)

Meaning: in spring, one should establish the fire for a Brahmin; in summer, for a Kshatriya. Spring is indeed the face (mukha) of the year. Whoever establishes the fire for a Brahmin in spring establishes it, as it were, "by the face" [the beginning/head of the year]. Moreover, whoever establishes the fire in spring establishes it under Prajapati himself as the presiding deity of that season. One should establish the fire for a Kshatriya in summer, for summer is indeed the Kshatriya's own proper season. One should establish the fire for a Vaishya in autumn, for autumn is indeed the Vaishya's own proper season.

In this way, the science of Jyotiṣa determines the appropriate season for the Agnyadhana rite. Similarly, for the shraddha (memorial) rites, the specific month must be known; the science of Jyotiṣa serves this purpose too—

"Māsi māsi puṣṭyārthaṃ śrāddhaṃ gṛhya" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the monthly regulations for shraddha-performance.

"Yaṃ kāmayeta vaśīyāsam iti kaṃ pūrva-pakṣe yojanīyaṃ" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the fortnight-measure regulations.

"Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ dīkṣerann......phalāgnīṃ pūrṇamāsi dīkṣerann" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the day-timing regulations.

"Prātar-ūrjo hoti, sāyaṃ jñu hoti" (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.7.11.1[?]) and similar [texts] give the daily timing regulations.

"Kṛttikāsu agnim ādadhīta" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.2) and similar [texts] give the nakṣatra-timing regulations.

Since it is by knowing the times determined through this science that all the required texts and other treatises are correctly employed, the Jyotiṣa and its own useful application should be understood here.

That these six books, which we have shown to be helps to the understanding of the Veda, are 'Angas' or limbs of the Veda, is declared in the Śikṣā itself:

छन्दः पादौ तु वेदस्य हस्तौ कल्पोऽथ उच्यते । ज्योतिषामयनं चक्षुर्निरुक्तं श्रोत्रमुच्यते ॥ शिक्षा घ्राणं तु वेदस्य मुखं व्याकरणं स्मृतम् । तस्मात्साङ्गमधीत्यैव ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥ chandaḥ pādau tu vedasya hastau kalpo'tha ucyate | jyotiṣām ayanaṃ cakṣur niruktaṃ śrotram ucyate || śikṣā ghrāṇaṃ tu vedasya mukhaṃ vyākaraṇaṃ smṛtam | tasmāt sāṅgam adhītyaiva brahmaloke mahīyate || (Panini Shiksha, verses 41-42)

"'Chhandas is the feet of the Veda, and Kalpa is declared to be its hands: Jyotisha is called its eye, and the Nirukta its ear. Śikṣā is the Veda's nose, Grammar they call its face: therefore he who studies the Veda along with these its limbs will be great in heaven.'"

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

That these six books which we have shown to be helps to the understanding of the Veda are 'Angas' or limbs of the Veda is declared in the Siksha itself:

"Chhandas is the feet of the Vada, and Kalpa is declared to be its hands: Jyotisha is called its eye, and the Nirukta its ear.

"Siksha is the Veda's nose Grammar they call its face: therefore he who studies the Veda along with these its limbs will be great in heaven."

Chapter 18. Why Knowledge of the Puranas, Nyaya, and Other Disciplines Is Necessary for Understanding the Veda's Meaning; and the Marks of One Unqualified to Receive That Knowledge

Original title: "Vēdārthajñānakke Purāṇa-Nyāyādi itara vidyegaḷa jñānavu avaśyakavu — vēdārthajñānakke adhikāriyilladavana lakṣaṇagaḷu" Printed pages 585–593 of the source.

original p. 585

Meaning: for the Veda, Chandas is likened to its feet, Kalpa to its hands, Jyotiṣa to its eyes, Nirukta to its ears, Śikṣā to its nose, and Grammar is said to be its face. Therefore, one who studies the Veda together with these six limbs is greatly honoured in the world of Brahma.

That the Puranas and Similar Texts, Together with the Fourteen Sources of Knowledge, Also Serve to Determine the Veda's Meaning

That the Puranas, and similar texts, are, like the Angas, useful for a better understanding of the Veda, is recorded by Yajnavalkya:

पुराणन्यायमीमांसाधर्मशास्त्राङ्गमिश्रिताः । वेदाः स्थानानि विद्यानां धर्मस्य च चतुर्दश ॥ purāṇa-nyāya-mīmāṃsā-dharma-śāstrāṅga-miśritāḥ | vedāḥ sthānāni vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca caturdaśa || (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.3)

"The Puranas, the Nyaya, Mimansa, and Dharma-shastras, the Vedas with their Angas, these be the fourteen sources of the sciences and of dharma."

Elsewhere, too, it is thus recorded—

Ṣaḍaṅgaṃ vedam (the Veda together with its six Angas), purāṇa-nyāya-vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca sāṃgraha-yoga-jñāneṣu, together with these treatises, serves the purpose of properly understanding the Veda's meaning — this is what the passage establishes. Puranas and Itihasas [histories], the vidyā-sthānas (sources of learning) — the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other systems — number fourteen in total, said the ancients—

Given [some texts hold] eighteen Puranas [and further extensions], this ["ṛg-yajuḥ-sāmātharvāḥ..."] enumeration itself makes clear the fourteen [sources]. It includes the four Vedas together with their Angas: Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, Jyotiṣa — [six] — plus the Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya-vistara, Purāṇa, and Dharma-shastra — bringing the total count to fourteen sources.

Among these fourteen, Mīmāṃsā [and its allied disciplines] serve to determine the Veda's own meaning through examination of doubtful passages, resolving contradictions, and clarifying obscure statements — its work is indispensable. The Nyāya-shāstra establishes valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and logical reasoning necessary to settle disputed points that arise in interpreting scriptural statements.

The Purāṇas contain ancient histories illustrating dharma through concrete narrative — kings, sages, and their deeds — thereby making abstract Vedic injunctions vivid and comprehensible to ordinary understanding. The Dharma-shastras (Manu and similar authors) systematize the specific practical rules of conduct (varṇāśrama-dharma) that the Veda itself only briefly touches upon, elaborating them into a complete, coherent code applicable to daily life.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

That the Puranas, &c. are, like the Angas, useful for a better understanding of the Veda, is recorded by Yajnavalkya:

"The Puranas, the Nyaya, Mimansa and Dharma shastras, the Vedas with their Angas, these be the fourteen sources of the sciences and of dharma."

Elsewhere, too, it is thus recorded.

original p. 586

Now, in order to show that the Puranas and similar texts likewise serve to help determine the Veda's own meaning, Yajnavalkya himself states:

पुराणन्यायमीमांसाधर्मशास्त्राङ्गमिश्रिताः । वेदाः स्थानानि विद्यानां धर्मस्य च चतुर्दश ॥ purāṇa-nyāya-mīmāṃsā-dharma-śāstrāṅga-miśritāḥ | vedāḥ sthānāni vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca caturdaśa || (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.3; see page 585 above)

Meaning: Puranas, Nyaya-shastra, Mimamsa, Dharma-shastra, and the Vedas together with their six Angas — mixed together — comprise the fourteen sources (sthāna) of both learning (vidyā) and dharma. And likewise in the Mahabharata—

इतिहासपुराणाभ्यां वेदं समुपबृंहयेत् । बिभेत्यल्पश्रुताद्वेदो मामयं प्रहरिष्यति ॥ itihāsa-purāṇābhyāṃ vedaṃ samupabṛṃhayet | bibhety alpa-śrutād vedo mām ayaṃ prahariṣyati || (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1.267)

"A man should strengthen the Veda by means of the Itihasas and Puranas: the Veda is afraid of the man of little learning, lest he should hurt it."

Meaning: history and purāṇic narrative should be used together to broaden and reinforce Vedic understanding. The Veda [itself is described as] fearful of the man with little learning — apprehensive that such a person, through his limited understanding, might do it harm [misinterpret or misapply it].

The stories of Harishchandra, Nachiketa, and the like, told in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, Kathaka, and other Shakhas, which are useful for the better understanding both of dharma and of brahma, are explained in the Itihasa books. The statements found in the Upanishads concerning the creation, the preservation, and the absorption of the world are explained in the Brahma, Padma, Vaishnava, and other Puranas. Compare the well-known verse, "Sargaśca pratisargaśca."

Meaning: Itihasa and Purana strengthen and confirm the meaning found within the Veda. It should be understood that ancient and traditional matters — the Veda's own supporting narrative context — are made firm through these Itihasas and Puranas. Since the Veda is described as fearful of one whose learning is shallow, this indicates: if a person with little genuine understanding grasps only the surface meaning of the Veda (its own scriptural expression), he may inadvertently do it harm through misapplication — this is what is meant here.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

"A man should strengthen the Veda by means of the Itihasas and Puranas: the Veda is afraid of the man of little learning, lest he should hurt it."

The stories of Harischandra, Nachiketa and the like told in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, Kathaka and other Sakhas which are useful for the better understanding both of dharma and of brahma, are explained in the Itihasa books. The statements found in the Upanishads concerning the creation, the preservation, and the absorption of the world explained in the Brahma, Padma, Vaishnava and other Puranas. Compare the well-known verse, 'Sargascha pratisargascha.'

original p. 587

Other Puranas — Skanda, Vishnu, and others — are also useful for understanding dharma and brahma alike. The Puranas illustrate, through narrative, the meanings underlying various commands and prohibitions found scattered throughout the Veda. These matters are dealt with extensively and clearly within these treatises. Among the various treatises discussing origins (utpatti), the deeds of Muni-descended lineages, Manu's own lineage, and battles between gods and demons are given in detail; and dynastic genealogies, too, are described as belonging to the Vaṃśānucharita [dynastic-history] portion of the Puranas. Scholars declare that the characteristic features of the Puranas are these—

सर्गश्च प्रतिसर्गश्च वंशो मन्वन्तराणि च । वंशानुचरितं चेति पुराणं पञ्चलक्षणम् ॥ sargaś ca pratisargaś ca vaṃśo manvantarāṇi ca | vaṃśānucaritaṃ ceti purāṇaṃ pañca-lakṣaṇam || (Vishnu Purana 3.6.24; Amarakosha 1.6.5)

Meaning: creation (sarga), re-creation [after periodic dissolution] (pratisarga), dynastic genealogy (vaṃśa), the ages of the Manus (manvantara), and dynastic history (vaṃśānucharita) — these are the five defining characteristics of a Purana.

Ordinary subjects treated in the Puranas include: descriptions of well-known holy places, the qualities of various persons, causes underlying particular matters, and similar topics — each Purana, according to its own scope, covers such subjects in detail. It's understood that these matters, scattered across many Puranas, are difficult for ordinary people to piece together on their own.

In Nyaya-shastra, discussions of pramāṇa (valid means of knowledge), prameya (objects of knowledge), saṃśaya (doubt), prayojana (purpose), and dṛṣṭānta (example) are among the topics treated. Determining the specific meaning of a given text requires knowing these categories precisely; establishing which meaning is correctly authoritative for a given passage becomes possible only through such careful analysis.

How the Purva and Uttara Mimamsas help to a better understanding of the Vedas is clear enough.

In the Smritis of Manu, Atri, Vishnu, Harita, and other writers, injunctions found in the Vedas, such for example as that concerning the evening prayer, are extended and developed. The text "tad u ha va ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāḥ sandhyābhivādaya gāyatrī-bhimantritā apa ūrdhvaṃ vikṣipanti," and similar, is a command to say the evening prayer. That other, "pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pravartante," is a command to perform the so-called great sacrifices. Other instances of commands given in the Veda and developed in the Smritis can be found.

Since in this way the Puranas are a help to a better understanding of the Veda, the name "vidyāsthāna" (strongholds of wisdom) is rightly, in Yajnavalkya's verse above, applied to them.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

Nyaya investigates the sixteen categories, and only by its help can we decide that such and such a text rather than some other is the authority for a particular meaning.

How the Purva and Uttara Mimansas help to a better understanding of the Vedas is clear enough.

In the Smritis of Manu, Atri, Vishnu, Harita and other writers, injunctions found in the Vedas, such for example, as that concerning the evening prayer, are extended and developed. The text 'tad u ha va ete brahmavadinah puryabhimukhah samdhyavayam gayatrabhimantrita apa urdhvam vikshipanti, &c. is a command to say the evening prayer. That other 'pancha va ete mahayajnah satatam pratryanta, &c.,' is a command to perform the so-called great sacrifices. Other instances of commands given in the Veda and developed in the Smritis can be found.

Since in this way the Puranas are a help to a better understanding of the Veda the name vidyasthana (strongholds of wisdom) is rightly in Yajnavalkva's verse above applied to them.

original p. 588

तदु ह वा एते ब्रह्मवादिनः पूर्वाभिमुखाः संध्यायां गायत्रीयाभिमन्त्रिता अप ऊर्ध्वं विक्षिपन्ति ॥ tad u ha vā ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāḥ saṃdhyāyāṃ gāyatrīyābhimantritā apa ūrdhvaṃ vikṣipanti || (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.11.1)

Meaning: this is what is stated — those who know brahma, facing east, at twilight-time, consecrate the [sacred water] with the Gayatri mantra and then cast it upward, toward the sun as it rises before them (that is, [perform] the "arghya"-offering) — this is the specific procedure enjoined for the twilight-prayer.

And also: "Pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pravartante" (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.10) — this and similar [texts], declared as commands, establish the requirement to continually perform the [five] great sacrifices. In this way, the same procedures found here and there [in various Vedic texts] are elaborated more fully in various Smritis; a careful study of both together allows one to properly grasp these matters.

The topics briefly touched upon in the Puranas and similar texts must also be properly correlated with the Veda's own meaning; those able to do so provide genuine help — this is why they are called "vidyā" (branches of learning).

These Puranas and similar texts are said to number fourteen because they comprise: the four Vedas, the six Angas, the Puranas, Nyaya-shastra, Mimamsa, and Dharma-shastra — treating these each as one unit, that makes fourteen sources of learning altogether. But if one asks whether other branches of learning exist beyond these, [the answer is] many more indeed exist. Regarding the Veda's own meaning specifically, these fourteen branches of learning are understood to be the qualified authorities for that purpose — [other branches, being useful] for different purposes (such as medicine, for instance), are each authoritative in their own separate fields. Yaska cites four verses from another Shakha declaring who alone is worthy [to receive this wisdom]—

The first is this:

विद्या ह वै ब्राह्मणमाजगाम गोपाय मा शेवधिष्टेऽहमस्मि । असूयकायानृजवेऽनृतायाशीलाय मा ब्रूया वीर्यवती तथा स्याम् ॥ vidyā ha vai brāhmaṇam ājagāma gopāya mā śevadhis te'ham asmi | asūyakāyānṛjave'nṛtāyāśīlāya mā brūyā vīryavatī tathā syām || (Nirukta 2.4)

"Wisdom came to the brahmin and said, 'Protect me for I am your treasure: do not teach me to the scornful or the knavish or the sensual man; so shall I be strong.'"

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The four Vedas, with the six Angas, the Puranas, the Nyaya, Mimansa and Dharma shastras, are the fourteen strongholds of Wisdom. Who is able to lay hold upon her? There are four verses from another Sakha which declare who alone are worthy. Yaska quotes them.

The first is this.

"Wisdom came to the brahmin and said, Protect me for I am your treasure: do not teach me to the scornful or the knavish or the sensual man; so shall I be strong."

विद्याभिमानिनी देवता ब्राह्मणमुपदेष्टारमाचार्यमाजगाम । आगत्य चैवं प्रार्थयामास हे ब्राह्मण मामवनद्धिकारिणेच्छन्दुरुषार्थेच्छुरस्मि । तादृश्यं तुभ्यं तदुपदेष्टरि त्वयि च योग्यमूनं करोमि । यत्खार्जनेन विद्यां नाभ्यर्जते विद्यां नाभ्यर्जते यश्च मनोदन्धाचारनियतो न भवति । तादृशे भव्यक्ष्यशिक्षाभावेभ्यो मां न ब्रूयात् । तथा सति तव हृदये स्थित्वा फलप्रदा भवेयम् ॥ vidyābhimāninī devatā brāhmaṇam upadeṣṭāram ācāryam ājagāma | āgatya caivaṃ prārthayāmāsa he brāhmaṇa mām avanaddhikāriṇecchan durūṣārthecchur asmi | tādṛśyaṃ tubhyaṃ tad-upadeṣṭari tvayi ca yogyam ūnaṃ karomi | yat khārjanena vidyāṃ nābhyarjate vidyāṃ nābhyarjate yaś ca mano-dhandhācāra-niyato na bhavati | tādṛśe bhavyakṣyaśikṣā-bhāvebhyo māṃ na brūyāt | tathā sati tava hṛdaye sthitvā phala-pradā bhaveyam ||

Meaning: the goddess who is immanent in all learning came to the brahmin teacher, that is, to the Acharya, and thus besought him: "O brahmin! protect me, do not teach me to him that is unworthy. I am for a treasure to you, giving you all that a man can desire. He that does despite to me, or to you who teach me — he that does not follow learning uprightly, he that does not keep his body under by due observance of the rules about bathing, rinsing the mouth, and the like before lessons — to all such pupils, who are pupils in appearance only, do not teach me. So shall I abide in your heart and bear fruit."

Next the second verse.

यमात्मने कुर्वते नित्यं संप्रयच्छन्नमृतं वदति । तं मन्येते पितरं मातरं च तस्मै न द्रुह्येत्कतमच्चनाहः ॥ yam ātmane kurvate nityaṃ samprayacchann amṛtaṃ vadati | taṃ manyete pitaraṃ mātaraṃ ca tasmai na druhyet katamac canāhaḥ || (Nirukta 2.4)

"He who fills the ears with truth, but not so as to hurt, and who adds thereto nectar, he is the pupil's father and mother, and should in no wise be injured by him."

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The goddess who is immanent in all learning came to the brahmin teacher, that is, to the Acharya, and thus besought him Oh brahmin! protect me, do not teach me to him that is unworthy. I am for a treasure to you, giving you all that a man can desire. He that does despite to me, or to you who teach me—he that does not follow learning uprightly, he that does not keep his body under by due observance of the rules about bathing, rinsing the mouth, and the like before lessons—to all such pupils, who are pupils in appearance only, do not teach me. So shall I abide in your heart and bear fruit.

Next the second verse.

"He who fills the ears with truth, but not so as to hurt, and who adds thereto nectar, he is the pupil's father and mother, and should in no wise be injured by him."

original p. 590

Meaning: the first verse contained a prohibitory rule for the teacher: this has one for the pupil. By "सत्य" (satya, "truth") is meant the Veda, called so as being the opposite of worldly talk, which is untrue, and not conducive to man's chief end. "यमात्मने कुर्वते नित्यम्" (yam ātmane kurvate nityaṃ) — the teacher who completely fills his pupil's ears with the words of the Veda. The root "तृणत्ति" (tṛṇatti, to fill/pierce), by the force of its prefix "सम्" (sam), and from the context, takes a meaning different from the usual one. The meaning is "whoever recites the Veda to him." How? "अमृतं वदति" (amṛtaṃ vadati) — so as not to give him pain. If the boy be dull and unable to learn a verse or a half verse at a time, the teacher, in order to avoid giving him...

In this way, the pupil's own defining qualities — appropriate to receiving proper instruction from a qualified Acharya (teacher) — are established for the pupil's benefit as well. This too is a distinct benefit — namely, the teaching of the Veda's own meaning becomes possible. Regarding this matter, the Veda-mantra taken up here for illustration [is the one whose meaning we've been examining]: whatever action the Acharya takes with his student — whether accepting him for instruction, guiding his conduct, or teaching him respectfully — through all such acts, he cultivates the qualities properly belonging to a genuine teacher. The verse states: whether it be a whole [verse] or half, if the student cannot grasp it properly, or if he errs in reciting the mantra, [the teacher should not cause him pain by harsh correction] — thus it is said. Because [causing pain to a student] is not consistent with proper conduct, one should not [act this way]. Furthermore: the deity presiding over knowledge (Sarasvati/Vagdevata) is spoken of as the fitting recipient of the offering here — and it is entirely proper that the student's own conduct be modeled after this virtue.

This entire matter [these four verses cited by Yaska], being the Acharya's own combined [pedagogical wisdom], should be understood as primarily concerned with the pupil. Previously established as such, this concerns [proper conduct in] the teacher-student relationship, and the human aim it serves. The main purpose behind [reciting] these body-related verses is this: [that the transmission of knowledge itself should never become a source of harm].

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

The first verse contained a prohibitory rule for the teacher: this has one for the pupil. By 'the truth' is meant the Veda, called so as being the opposite of worldly talk, which is untrue, and not conducive to man's chief end. The teacher who completely fills his pupil's ears with the words of the Veda. The root 'trinatti' by the force of its prefix a, and from the context, takes a meaning different from the usual one. The meaning is 'who ever recites the Veda to him.' How? So as not to give him pain. If the boy be dull and unable to learn a verse or a half verse at a time, the teacher, in order to avoid giving him

original p. 591

pain, makes him learn the fourth part of a verse, or even the eighth part. What more? "Adding thereto nectar." By "nectar" is meant the sense of the Veda, as distinguished from the new words. Because it makes a man a god, or procures for him final release. "Adding thereto nectar" means giving him that. Such a teacher, the pupil, who is a pupil indeed, must regard as his chief father and mother. Why are his father and mother according to the flesh not chief? Because they gave him at his first birth his worthless fleshly body only. The pupil must not injure in any way whatever his teacher, who is thus in the highest sense his father and his mother.

Manu himself, in his own Smriti, establishes this meaning in the following verse—

उत्पादकब्रह्मदातोर्गरीयान् ब्रह्मदः पिता । ब्रह्मजन्म हि विप्रस्य प्रेत्य चेह च शाश्वतम् ॥ utpādaka-brahmadātor garīyān brahmadaḥ pitā | brahma-janma hi viprasya pretya ceha ca śāśvatam || (Manu Smriti 2.146)

"Between the natural father and the giver of sacred learning, the giver of sacred learning is the more venerable father; for the birth through the Veda is eternal, both here and hereafter, for the brahmin."

Next the third verse.

अध्यापिता ये गुरुं नाद्रियन्ते विप्रा वाचा मनसा कर्मणा वा । युष्मैव ते न गुरोर्भोज्यनीया स्तस्यैव ताज्ज्ञप्ति शृतं तदिति ॥ adhyāpitā ye guruṃ nādriyante viprā vācā manasā karmaṇā vā | yuṣmaiva te na guror bhojanīyā stasyaiva tāj jñaptiḥ śrutaṃ tad iti || (Nirukta 2.4)

"But those brahmins who have received instruction, yet do not honour their teacher in thought, word, and deed, as they ought — not to be protected by their teacher, so neither will the holy revelation which they have learned protect them."

Meaning: those brahmin students who, having received instruction from their teacher regarding the Veda's meaning, do not thereafter honour him through mind, speech, and bodily action — such students should not be [further] taught or supported by their teacher. And since these students fail to properly honour their teacher, the Veda's own knowledge that they have thus far received will not, in the end, genuinely protect them or bear fruit for them.

Meaning [continuing the third verse's explanation]: among those who have engaged in the study of the Veda's meaning and made effort to understand it thoroughly, some, out of disrespect toward their teacher, disregard his instruction, do not honour his wishes, and behave with contempt toward him. Such disciples, though outwardly appearing to be genuine students of their teacher, are not so in the eyes of wise men. Since these students fail in their proper duty toward the teacher, the Vedic knowledge they've received will not ultimately protect or benefit them.

"Those wicked brahmins, who after having been taught do not honour their teacher by respectful language, thought for his interests and obedience to his commands, are his pupils in appearance only, and ought not to be protected by him. They are unworthy of his favour: he will not have compassion on them. And as he will not protect them, so neither will the Veda, which he has taught them, protect these wicked pupils. It will not bear them fruit."

यमेव विद्याः शुचिमप्रमत्तं मेधाविनं ब्रह्मचर्योपपन्नम् । यस्मै न द्रुह्येत्तस्मैचनाह तस्मै मा ब्रूया निधिपाय ब्रह्म ॥ yam eva vidyāḥ śucim apramattaṃ medhāvinaṃ brahmacaryopapannam | yasmai na druhyet tasmai canāha tasmai mā brūyā nidhipāya brahma || (Nirukta 2.4)

"But if there be one whom you know to be pure, eager to hear, intelligent, and chaste, who will never do you harm, teach me to him, Oh brahmin! he will protect me, your treasure."

Meaning [Sayana's summary]: to the Acharya who is himself the leading teacher, thoroughly versed and pure in conduct — to such a well-disciplined, discerning pupil, one who is chaste and disciplined, and who will never bring harm — to him alone should knowledge be taught. Such a student will indeed protect me, [Vidya herself says,] your treasure, and preserve the Veda's own meaning faithfully.

॥ Iti Sāyaṇācārya-kṛtā Ṛgveda-Bhāṣya-Bhūmikā Samāptā ॥

॥ इति सायणाचार्यकृता ऋग्वेदभाष्यभूमिका समाप्ता ॥

"Thus ends the Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika, composed by Sayanacharya."

This marks the formal close of Sayana's introductory preface (Bhumika) to his Rigveda commentary. What follows next, according to the chapter opening below, is the beginning of the discussion proper on the mantra's own defining characteristics — turning at last from the preface's extensive philosophical program (spanning the Veda's nature, the mantra/brahmana distinction, the authority debates, the Angas, and the qualifications of student and teacher) to the commentary's actual verse-by-verse work.
