It will not bear them fruit.

Next the fourth verse.

"But if there be one whom you know to be pure, eager to hear, intelligent, and chaste, who will never do you harm, teach me to him, Oh brahmin! he will protect me, your treasure."

Final Page of the Bhūmikā

Meaning: to such a pupil — one who is not unruly, who is intelligent, who refrains from laziness, and who diligently observes the rules of brahmacharya (celibate discipleship) — the leading student among all, in whom trust may rightly be placed, should the [Veda-personified deity, i.e., the Vidyā] be taught. This alone is worthy of honour. In this way, having made her request that the teacher, upon finding a worthy and virtuous student who faithfully observes the discipline, should teach him the knowledge of the Veda, Manu Smriti gives this very verse—

यमेव तु शुचिं विद्यान्नियतं ब्रह्मचारिणम् । तस्मै वां ब्रूहि विप्राय निधिं कामप्रवादिने ॥ yam eva tu śuciṃ vidyān niyataṃ brahmacāriṇam | tasmai vāṃ brūhi viprāya nidhiṃ kāma-pravādine || (Manu Smriti 2.114; Nirukta 2.4)

"O Teacher, teach me wisdom in the form of the Veda. To him whom you know to be a pupil indeed, pure, eager to hear, intelligent, and chaste, and who will never do you harm: he will protect your treasure. At such a request made to him by the Goddess of learning, the teacher will teach him, who is a pupil indeed, the knowledge of the Veda."

Therefore we will now explain the Rig-Veda in accordance with its six Angas.

इल्लिगे सायणाचार्यरिंद रचितवाद ऋग्वेदभाष्यभूमिकेयु समाप्तवादुदु.

ಇಲ್ಲಿಗೆ ಸಾಯಣಾಚಾರ್ಯರಿಂದ ರಚಿತವಾದ ಋಗ್ವೇದಭಾಷ್ಯಭೂಮಿಕೆಯು ಸಮಾಪ್ತವಾದುದು.

"Here ends the Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika, composed by Sayanacharya."

At such a request made to him by the Goddess of learning, the teacher will teach him, who is a pupil indeed, the knowledge of the Veda.

Therefore we will now explain the Rig-Veda in accordance with its six Angas.

PART III: The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā with Sāyaṇa's Commentary (Mādhavīya Vedārtha-Prakāśa)

Title Page

॥ श्री गणाधिपतये नमः ॥ Śrī Gaṇādhipataye Namaḥ "Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas [Ganesha]."

अथ श्रीसायणाचार्यविरचिता माधवीय वेदार्थप्रकाश संहिता। Atha Śrī-Sāyaṇācārya-viracitā Mādhavīya Vedārtha-prakāśa Saṃhitā | "Now [begins] the Mādhavīya Vedārtha-prakāśa Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Sāyaṇācārya."

अस्माभिः विद्वन्निरचितकर्णाटकभाषानुवादयुता asmābhiḥ vidvan-nirachita-karṇāṭaka-bhāṣānuvāda-yutā "— accompanied by a Kannada-language translation composed by this humble scholar —"

ऋग्वेदसंहिता Ṛgveda Saṃhitā "The Rigveda Samhita"

॥ प्रथमं मण्डलम् ॥ Prathamaṃ Maṇḍalam "Book One (Maṇḍala I)"

Invocation

ॐ वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युः स्मृत्वा वन्दे तमादिगणम् ॥ oṃ vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānām upakrame | yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syuḥ smṛtvā vande tam ādigaṇam ||

"At the outset of every undertaking, the wise — Bṛhaspati (Lord of Speech) and others — having bowed to whom become accomplished in their aims: remembering him, I too salute that same foremost of the Gaṇas [Ganesha]."

Śrī Sāyaṇācārya, in his Rigveda-Bhāṣya-Bhūmikā, having extensively examined — with the help of works such as Mīmāṃsā, Vyākaraṇa, and Dharma-shāstra — many profound topics (the Veda's defining characteristics, the Veda's authority, the Veda's non-human origin, the matter of Vedic study, the subject-matter the Veda expounds, a close exposition of the Vedāṅgas, who is qualified to receive Vedic knowledge, and so on), now, before beginning this Vedic commentary proper, briefly states — as an introductory matter — both the division-scheme of the Aṣṭaka-adhyāyas found in the Rigveda, and the matter of the mantras' ritual application (viniyoga), and thus opens the treatise itself.

तदर्थमृग्वेदोक्तार्थः षडङ्गानुसारेण व्याख्यायते । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मके वेदे ब्राह्मणस्य मन्त्रव्याख्यानोपयोगित्वादादौ ब्राह्मणमारभ्य काण्डशः व्याख्यातम् । अथ तत्र तत्र ब्राह्मणोदाहरणेन मन्त्राख्यः संहिताग्रन्थो व्याख्यातव्यः ॥ tad-artham ṛgvedokta-arthaḥ ṣaḍ-aṅgānusāreṇa vyākhyāyate | mantra-brāhmaṇātmake vede brāhmaṇasya mantra-vyākhyānopayogitvād ādau brāhmaṇam ārabhya kāṇḍaśaḥ vyākhyātam | atha tatra tatra brāhmaṇodāharaṇena mantrākhyaḥ saṃhitā-granthaḥ vyākhyātavyaḥ ||

"For this purpose, the sense stated in the Rigveda is expounded following the six Aṅgas. Since, in the Veda — which consists of mantra and brāhmaṇa together — the Brāhmaṇa is useful for explaining the mantra, [the commentary] has been expounded section by section (kāṇḍaśaḥ), beginning first with the Brāhmaṇa. Now, citing the Brāhmaṇa at each relevant point, the Saṃhitā-text — that is, the mantras — is to be expounded."

Up to this point, in the Bhāṣya-Bhūmikā, we have broached many topics; at its close we discussed who is qualified for the Veda — that is, who should undertake to know the Veda and its meaning? What qualities should such a person possess? In what manner should study be undertaken? [How should its] meaning...

original p. 596

...tell whom to trust? What matters should be broached? What is the meaning to be conveyed? — all these matters we have already explained. Now we shall begin expounding the topics belonging to the Bhashya-Bhumika of the Rigveda proper.

That the Veda should be studied together with its meaning has already been stated. In explaining the mantra-portion, however, familiarity with the Brahmana-portion is essential, since [the commentary] first began with the Brahmana and proceeded section by section (kāṇḍaśaḥ). Now, the commentary on the Rigveda's Samhita-portion — that is, its mantras — is to be undertaken, citing the corresponding Brahmana-passages as relevant at each point.

स चाग्निमीळ इत्यारभ्य यथा वः सुसातेत्यन्तोऽष्टकाण्ड्ये दशमण्डलेऽष्टाध्यायैः पञ्चाशीत्यनुवाकैः सहस्राधिकसूक्त्या द्विसहस्राधिकवर्गया दशसहस्राधिकर्क्संख्यया ऋग्भ्योऽपेतः । तस्य च ग्रन्थस्य कृत्स्नस्यास्यामाम्नातक्रमेणैव सामान्यविनियोगो ब्रह्मयज्ञपाठपूर्वमेवाभिहितः । विशेषविनियोगस्तु कतौ सूत्रकारेण प्रदर्शितः । स च त्रिविधः । सूक्तविनियोगस्त्वचादिषड्विनियोग एकैकस्या ऋचो विनियोगश्चेति ॥ sa cāgnimīḷa ity ārabhya yathā vaḥ susāteti-anto'ṣṭakāṇḍye daśa-maṇḍale'ṣṭādhyāyaiḥ pañcāśīty-anuvākaiḥ sahasrādhika-sūktyā dvisahasrādhika-vargayā daśasahasrādhika-ṛk-saṃkhyayā ṛgbhyo'petaḥ | tasya ca granthasya kṛtsnasyāsyām āmnāta-krameṇaiva sāmānya-viniyogo brahma-yajña-pāṭha-pūrvam evābhihitaḥ | viśeṣa-viniyogas tu katau sūtra-kāreṇa pradarśitaḥ | sa ca trividhaḥ | sūkta-viniyogas tv acādi-ṣaḍ-viniyoga ekaikasyā ṛco viniyogaś ceti || (the precise digits in this dense enumeration were read with care but the scan resolution leaves a couple of them, noted below, less than fully certain)

"That [Samhita], beginning with 'agnimīḷe' and ending with 'yathā vaḥ susāte,' is furnished, in the eight-Ashtaka division, with ten Maṇḍalas, sixty-four (eight-times-eight) Adhyāyas, eighty-five Anuvākas, a little over one thousand Sūktas, a little over two thousand Vargas, and a little over ten thousand Ṛks. The general application (sāmānya-viniyoga) of this entire text, in its own recited sequence, has already been stated in connection with the Brahma-yajña recitation. The specific application (viśeṣa-viniyoga), however, has been shown by the Sūtra-authors in the ritual texts themselves. This specific application is of three kinds: application of a whole Sūkta, application of a group of six verses beginning with a given one (ācādi-ṣaḍ), and application of a single Ṛk individually."

Meaning: the Rigveda Samhita we are about to expound begins with "agnimīḷe" and ends with "yathā vaḥ susāte." We have already described this division-scheme of the Rigveda earlier (see our discussion above). In total, the Rigveda Samhita is divided into eight Ashtakas, and each Ashtaka is further divided into eight Adhyayas. The number of Vargas within each Adhyaya, however, is not uniform — where shorter-syllabled meters such as Gayatri predominate, that Adhyaya contains more Vargas; where longer-syllabled meters such as Jagati predominate, that Adhyaya contains fewer Vargas. The overall length of each Adhyaya thus remains roughly, though not perfectly, equal. Following this scheme, the Rigveda has sixty-four Adhyayas in total (eight Ashtakas × eight Adhyayas each). This arrangement was established for ease of study and has been followed since ancient times.

The Mandala-division-scheme is a different system — older than the Ashtaka-scheme. Following the lineages of the mantra-seeing rishis, each Mandala generally contains mantras "seen" (dṛṣṭa) by one principal rishi together with his descendants or disciples. The Rigveda contains ten such Mandalas. A small number of Mandalas — the text names them, though the exact digits are not fully certain at this scan resolution — do not strictly follow this single-rishi-family pattern, instead containing mantras seen by many different rishis; this matter has already been discussed earlier.

Therefore, it is said that the Rigveda contains: eight Ashtakas, ten Mandalas, sixty-four Adhyayas, eighty-five Anuvakas, a little more than one thousand Suktas, a little more than two thousand Vargas, and more than ten thousand Riks (verses).

Embedded English translation, as given in the source: This page's footnote continues technical points on the threefold viniyoga scheme discussed above; the Kannada explanatory prose has been translated in full in the main text above.

original p. 597

Since we have already discussed the Veda's own division-scheme earlier, at some length, in the relevant context, it is not necessary to repeat those matters point by point here.

प्रत्यक्षेणानुमित्या वा यस्तूपायो न बुध्यते । एतं विन्दन्ति वेदेन तस्माद्वेदस्य वेदता ॥ pratyakṣeṇānumityā vā yas tūpāyo na budhyate | etaṃ vindanti vedena tasmād vedasya vedatā || (see earlier discussion in the Bhūmikā, under the Nirukta Aṅga)

"That means [of knowledge] which cannot be grasped either through direct perception or through inference — this alone is made known through the Veda; therefore the Veda derives its very name 'Veda' [from the root vid, 'to know']."

Meaning: whatever cannot be established through the ordinary means of knowledge — direct perception or inference — is made knowable solely through the Veda; it is for this reason that "the Veda" bears the very name "Veda," from the root "vid" (to know), signifying that which makes known what is otherwise unknowable.

As stated in the Puranas and similar texts: the Rigveda has twenty-one (21) shakha-divisions; the Yajurveda has one hundred (100) shakha-divisions (of these, Shukla-Yajurveda has fifteen shakhas, and Krishna-Yajurveda has eighty-six shakhas, together making one hundred); the Samaveda has a thousand shakhas; and the Atharvaveda has nine shakhas. Of these many shakhas, a great number have been lost over the course of time and are no longer in use today — only a few are still available.

Every Veda comprises two kinds of portions: the mantra-portion (Samhita) and the Brahmana-portion.

मन्त्रे ब्राह्मणयोर्वेदनामधेयम् । mantre brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam | "'Veda' is the name applied to mantra and Brahmana together."

The shakhas belonging to each Veda are as follows: for the Rigveda — the Shakala-shakha and, among the ancient shakhas, the Bashkala-shakha and similar; for the Yajurveda — the Kanva and Madhyandina shakhas of the Shukla branch, and the Taittiriya shakha among others of the Krishna branch; for the Samaveda — the Kauthuma, Ranayaniya, and Jaiminiya shakhas among others; for the Atharvaveda — the Shaunaka and Paippalada shakhas among others. Among these, the shakhas still available in full, or largely intact, are relatively few.

This shakha — the one we are here expounding — follows Ashvalayana's own sutra-tradition. According to Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra, the Rigveda Samhita's division into Mandalas is followed, alongside the Ashtaka-division discussed earlier. The Samhita's own arrangement into these divisions has already been described.

Vedic meters (chandas): there are seven principal meters — Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī — the...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 598

These are the principal meters. Each meter has many sub-varieties, which we have already explained at length with examples earlier (see our discussion above). The seven meters mentioned above, beginning with Gayatri, have respectively 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48 syllables.

In the second group — अतिजगती, शक्करी, अतिशक्करी, अष्टिः, अत्यष्टिः, धृतिः, अतिधृतिः (Atijagatī, Śakvarī, Atiśakvarī, Aṣṭiḥ, Atyaṣṭiḥ, Dhṛtiḥ, Atidhṛtiḥ) — these seven meters have respectively 52, 56, 60, 64, 68, 72, 76 syllables.

In the third group — कृतिः, प्रकृतिः, आकृतिः, विकृतिः, संकृतिः, अभिकृतिः, उत्कृतिः (Kṛtiḥ, Prakṛtiḥ, Ākṛtiḥ, Vikṛtiḥ, Saṃkṛtiḥ, Abhikṛtiḥ, Utkṛtiḥ) — these seven meters have respectively 80, 84, 88, 92, 96, 100, 104 syllables.

When stating the totals for Ashtakas, Adhyayas, Vargas, and the rest, the Bhashyakara [Sayana] does not give an exact figure, but instead uses the general expression "ईषदधिक" (īṣad-adhika, "a little more than"). This is because — although the counts of Mandala, Anuvaka, Ashtaka, and Adhyaya are not disputed — genuine differences of opinion exist regarding the counts of Suktas, Vargas, and mantras (Riks). For example: in the ninth Mandala, [certain] single-rik hymns are called by [special] names. Ten such Vālakhilya-sūktas are absent from some shakhas' texts. Some include these khila-sūktas (supplementary hymns) within the Samhita; others do not. This is why differences arise in the count of Suktas.

Regarding the count of Vargas: generally, a group of roughly five Riks is treated as one Varga. If a Sukta contains 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 2 Riks, that entire Sukta itself is counted as a single Varga. A Sukta containing 8 Riks is treated by some as a single Varga, and by others as two Vargas. This too causes differences in the Varga-count.

Regarding the count of Riks: in many places there occur Riks in the "dvipadā virāṭ" meter. Some scholars count these as Riks having three padas (that is, half of a full Rik's normal extent), while others hold that "dvipadā" is merely the meter's own name, and that — like every other meter — it too actually comprises four padas in full. According to the first view, three padas (half a Rik) count as one whole Rik; according to the second view, four padas (a complete first-half plus second-half) count as one Rik. This too is a source of variation in the total Rik-count. Taking all of this into account, the Bhashyakara generally states the Varga and related counts using the qualifier "īṣad-adhika" (a little more than), rather than an exact figure.

Now let us examine the matter of the mantras' application (viniyoga). Viniyoga means: the rule that a given mantra should be employed in a given ritual context. Since mantras are used according to the specific rite being performed, viniyoga is thus tied to that rite (karma). This scheme of application is of two kinds: general (sāmānya) and specific (viśeṣa). Reciting all the mantras of this Rigveda Samhita in their entirety — as in the Brahma-yajna, japa, complete recitation (pārāyaṇa), and similar practices — is called the mantras' "general application." In yajnas and other rites, and likewise in other ritual observances — that is, in the japa and similar practices undertaken to realize one's chosen deity — the [specific] application...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 599

...belonging to each individual mantra is determined. This specific application is itself of three kinds: application of a whole Sukta, application of a group of Suktas, and application of a single mantra.

तत्राग्निमीळ इति सूक्तमस्य प्रातरनुवाके आग्नेये कृतौ विनियुक्तम् । स विनियोग आश्वलायनेन चतुर्थाध्यायस्य त्रयोदशे खण्डे सूत्रितः ॥ tatrāgnimīḷa iti sūktam asya prātar-anuvāke āgneye kratau viniyuktam | sa viniyoga āśvalāyanena caturthādhyāyasya trayodaśe khaṇḍe sūtritaḥ || (this passage and the several dense technical sentences following it, concerning further sub-rules from Ashvalayana's own sutras on the exact application of individual verses within this sukta, were read with care but the source's compressed technical Mimamsa terminology could not be transcribed with full syllable-level confidence at this resolution)

"There, the sukta 'agnimīḷe' is applied by him [Ashvalayana] to the Āgneya rite within the Prātar-anuvāka. This application is laid down by Āśvalāyana in the thirteenth section of the fourth Adhyāya [of his Shrauta-sutra]."

In the relevant context, since the "agnim īḷe" sukta is recited within the ritual (kratu) belonging to the Prātar-anuvāka (morning-recitation) portion, this constitutes the prescribed application (viniyoga) for this sukta.

In the Soma-yaga, on the night preceding the pressing-day (sutyā-dina), from midnight until dawn, three deities — Agni, Uṣas, and the Aśvin-deities — are praised using the seven meters beginning with Gāyatrī. The act of praising a particular deity in this way is called the "kratu" connected with that deity: praising Agni is the Āgneya-kratu; praising Uṣas is the Auṣasya-kratu; praising the Aśvins is the Āśvina-kratu — these are the three kratus [of this section]. Since these are recited a little before dawn, this rite as a whole is called the Prātar-anuvāka (the morning recitation). Within this Prātar-anuvāka, when performing the Āgneya-kratu — that is, when reciting the Agni-related sukta — this very sukta, "agnim īḷe," is recited. This is precisely the application (viniyoga) of this sukta.

Ashvalayana states, at the close of the fourth Adhyaya of his own Shrauta-sutra, in a passage belonging to the Nirvapa section: "āvā no agna iti ṣaḍagnimāḷāgnis dhūta-sam iti" — [our reading of this particular closing citation likewise remains a hedged, best-effort transcription]. When discussing the application of the mantras within his sutra, Ashvalayana refers to one specific instance...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 600

When a sutra states a citation in full, one should understand that only that particular Rik's application is being given. When a sutra states merely the opening of a sukta, in less than a single full pada, one should understand that the application is being given to the entire sukta. As stated in the definitional sutra (paribhāṣā-sūtra):

सूक्तं सूक्तादावृचि एकस्मिन् पादे । sūktaṃ sūktādāv ṛci ekasmin pāde | (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra, Paribhasha 1.1)

— meaning: if the sukta's opening portion is stated using less than one full pada, the application should be understood to cover the whole sukta.

In the sutra quoted above — "āvā no agna iti ṣaḍ agnimāḷer agniṃ dhūtakam" — "āvā no agna iti ṣaṭ" indicates that the mantra beginning "āvā no agne" is the sixth Rik in its sukta. Since it is cited only up to that extent, this sutra's meaning is that the application given here covers only that sixth Rik specifically — not the whole sukta.

Having thus stated the application of a complete sukta, the application of a single Rik — "agnimīḷe" — is now stated. This sukta's very first mantra, "agnimīḷe," is used as the Yājyā-mantra when performing the Pavamāna [rite]. In the first section of the second Adhyaya of the Shrauta-sutra, this Rik's application is stated through the sutra:

साध्यान्निश्चा अभियुजोऽग्निमाळे पुरोहितमिति संयाज्ये । sādhyānniścā abhiyujo'gnimāḷe purohitam iti saṃyājye |

Here, since the first padas of the Riks "sādhyānniścā abhiyujaḥ" and "agnimīḷe purohitam" are each cited in full, one should understand that the application is given only to those two specific Riks. There is a governing sutra: "ṛtaṃ pāda-grahaṇe" (Adhyaya 1.1) [a single-pada citation refers only to that pada]. Since the sutra uses the word "saṃyājye," this indicates the application is specifically within the homa belonging to the Svishtakrit category.

In Shrauta-related rites, the ritual act of properly producing fire through churning (manthana) and similar prescribed methods is called "Ādhāna." This Ādhāna is of three kinds: ending in Pūrṇāhuti, ending in Homa, and ending in Ishti. Among these, in the third — the Ishti-ending procedure — three homas are performed. For the first (Pavamāneṣṭi) homa, the deities are Agni and Agniṣavamāna; for the second homa, the deities are Agniḥ Savakaḥ and Agniḥ Śuciḥ; for the third homa, the principal deities are Agniṣomau, Indrāgnī, Viṣṇu, and Aditi. Among these three, in the second — when performing the Svishtakrid-homa — the mantra "sādhyānniścā abhiyujaḥ" is used as the Puronuvākyā-mantra, and the Rik "agnimīḷe purohitam" is used as the Yājyā-mantra.

When performing homa addressed to specific deities, one first calls the deities to mind and invokes them by reciting a Rik. This [invoking] Rik is called the "Puronuvākyā"...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 601

...and is so called. Thereafter, having called the deity to mind and invited it, one performs homa reciting another Rik. This Rik is called the "Yajya." Both are together termed the Puronuvakya-Yajya pair. Application-statements always begin by stating the Puronuvakya first and the "anantara" (subsequent) mantra afterward — this is the settled order.

Regarding the Paribhasha-sutra — "sāmānyāt siṣṭāḥ" and similar — since it begins by naming the Puronuvakya first, one should understand this to be the fixed sequence for citing the two mantras. On this point, there is a well-known verse in the fourth adhyaya of the Purushartha-nushasana's own Nyaya-mala-vistara commentary:

पुरोनुवाक्या या याज्या विकल्प्या वा समुच्चिता । विकल्प्यास्यैषैव देवतायाः प्रकाशनात् ॥ puronuvākyā yā yājyā vikalpyā vā samuccitā | vikalpyāsyaiṣaiva devatāyāḥ prakāśanāt ||

पुरोनुवाक्या समाख्यानाध्यैवास्य समुच्चितः । देवताप्रकाशनकार्यास्यं कश्चात् युग्मैरोर्यार्था विकल्पस्यै युग्मगतयोरिति चेत् नैवम् । पुरोनुवाक्येति समाख्या उत्तरकालीनयाज्यामन्त्रेणानुपसृप्तेः । किं च— puronuvākyā samākhyānādhyaivāsya samuccitaḥ | devatā-prakāśana-kāryāsyaṃ kaścāt yugmair oryārthā vikalpasyai yugmagatayor iti cet naivam | puronuvākyeti samākhyā uttarakālīna-yājyā-mantreṇānupasṛpteḥ | kiṃ ca— (this technical Mimamsa-verse passage remains genuinely dense at this resolution and is presented as a best-effort reading)

"puronuvākyāmanūṣye yājyayā juhoti" — "puronuvākyām anūṣya yājyayā juhoti | this text of Scripture ["having recited the Puronuvakya, one performs the homa by means of the Yajya"] plainly requires an explicit ordering — the Puronuvakya's citation precedes the Yajya's own act of oblation."

The Puronuvakya and Yajya mantras both refer to the same deity. Therefore, during the yajna's performance, one might ask: should only the Puronuvakya be recited, or only the Yajya, or both? Since the sutra states "samucchitayaḥ" (combined/joined together), it means both mantras must be recited. But here a doubt arises: in a single yajna — indeed, within a single rite — directed toward one specific deity, why should two mantras of identical purport be required? If one might suppose that a single mantra alone cannot accomplish the task — that is not correct. Rather: first, one must call the deity to mind and invite it; for this, the mantra called Puronuvākyā is recited ("puronuvākyā" meaning "that which is recited first, or at the outset"). Thereafter, considering that the deity has accepted the invitation and arrived at the sacrificial altar, one performs the homa — the offering of the oblation — through the Yājyā-mantra. Therefore, these two mantras — first the Puronuvakya, then the Yajya — must indeed be recited in that order; this is the settled doctrine (siddhānta) established by both the Mīmāṃsakas and the Sūtra-authors, and both mantras must be recited without exception. On this very point—

पुरोनुवाक्यामनूष्य याज्यया जुहोति । puronuvākyām anūṣya yājyayā juhoti | "Having recited the Puronuvakya, one performs the homa with the Yajya"

— confirms that the Puronuvakya must first be recited, and only thereafter should the homa be performed using the Yajya-mantra...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 602

...(in the Kratu), one should reflect accordingly. Moreover, since the Puronuvakya's application is understood to precede the deities' own act of being called to mind, and since the Yajya's application is not stated as belonging to any other set of homa-related rules, both these mantras should be understood accordingly. This is why the word "samuccitayaḥ" is employed [in the sutra].

एकर्चाग्निमित्यादिसूक्तं नवर्चम् । "अग्निं नव मधुच्छन्दा वैश्वामित्रिः" इत्यनुक्रमणिकायामुक्तत्वात् (अनु. १-४) । विश्वामित्रपुत्रो मधुच्छन्दोनामकस्य सूक्तस्य द्रष्टृत्वाद्ऋषिः । ekarcāgnim ity-ādi sūktaṃ navarcam | "agniṃ nava madhucchandā vaiśvāmitriḥ" ity anukramaṇikāyām uktatvāt (anu. 1-4) | viśvāmitra-putro madhucchando-nāmakasya sūktasya draṣṭṛtvād ṛṣiḥ |

"This sukta, beginning with the single verse 'agnim...,' consists of nine Riks — as stated in the Anukramanika (index): 'Agni [is praised in] nine [verses] by Madhuchandas Vaishvamitra' (Anukramanika 1.4). Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra, is the 'rishi' [seer] of this sukta, being the one who directly perceived (draṣṭṛ) it."

On the etymology of "rishi": from the root "ṛṣ" (to go/move) — per the Unadi-sutra rule "sarva-dhātubhya inn" (Unadi 4.119) and "igupadāt kit" (Unadi 4.104) — [one who, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, directly] perceives, without dependence on ordinary sense-organs, the Veda [as it truly is]. This much is stated. As it is said:

अजान् ह वै पूर्वं तपस्यमानास्तप्त्वा स्वयंभुव आभिणर्त्यृषयोऽभवन् । ajān ha vai pūrvaṃ tapasyamānās taptvā svayambhuva ābhiṇarty ṛṣayo'bhavan | (Kaushitaki Aranyaka 2.9) (this specific citation remains a best-effort reading at this resolution)

"In the beginning, those who performed austerity (tapas), having practiced it, became 'rishis' through the direct favour of the Self-existent [Svayambhu]."

In this same way, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the direct perception of the supra-sensory Veda [by the earliest seers] establishes their status as "rishi" — this much is affirmed.

युगान्ते चास्य निःश्वासादेतद्व्येतीहासात्तदृषयः । लेभिरे तपसा पूर्वमनुज्ञाताः स्वयंभुवेति ॥ yugānte cāsya niḥśvāsād etad vyetīhāsāt tad ṛṣayaḥ | lebhire tapasā pūrvam anujñātāḥ svayambhuv eti || (this closing verse likewise remains a best-effort reading)

Now let us examine the discussion begun in the "agnimīḷe" sukta. As stated in the Anukramanika: "agniṃ nava madhucchandā vaiśvāmitriḥ" — "agnimīḷe" is the first mantra in this sukta belonging to Vishvamitra's son [Madhuchandas]. Since this sukta's Rishi is the son of Vishvamitra, one should understand that a comparable status applies wherever this Rishi is cited.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 603

"Rishi" derives grammatically from the root "ṛṣ" (to go/move). Before the root "ṛṣ," the affix "in" is added, per the Unadi rule; the resulting form, with "ṛ" changed to guṇa, becomes "arṣi," and further, since a "vidhi" (rule) states this specific combination applies, it becomes "ṛṣi." Since the term denotes one who is qualified by this rule, "ṛṣ" + "in" together yield "ṛṣi."

Why should we take the trouble to know a mantra's rishi? The reason is stated as follows: those who compose or discover [a mantra] at the very beginning — that is, at the start of creation (or, according to some, at the start of the cosmic cycle) — are called the rishis for that mantra. It is they who hold the credit for it. Later, brahmins who wish to make use of that mantra, out of respect and gratitude toward that rishi, must know and recite his name whenever they recite the mantra, so that the rishi remains pleased. Elsewhere, it is likewise stated that the rishi is himself worthy of honour precisely because of this connection to the mantra.

Where knowledge of the rishi and the rest is absent, the resulting fault (pratyavāya) is established [by scripture]:

अविदित्वा ऋषिं छन्दो दैवतं योगमेव च । योऽध्यापयेज्जपेच्चैवापि पापीयान् जायते तु सः ॥ avidītvā ṛṣiṃ chando daivataṃ yogam eva ca | yo'dhyāpayej japec caivāpi pāpīyān jāyate tu saḥ ||

"Whoever, without knowing the rishi, the meter, the deity, and the [proper ritual] application, either teaches a mantra or recites it in japa — he becomes exceedingly sinful."

ऋषिच्छन्दोदैवतानि ब्राह्मणार्थं स्थिराध्यषि । अविदित्वा प्रयुञ्जानो मन्त्रकण्टक उच्यते इति ॥ ṛṣi-chando-daivatāni brāhmaṇārthaṃ sthirādhyaṣi | avidītvā prayuñjāno mantra-kaṇṭaka ucyate iti ||

"One who employs a mantra without knowing its rishi, meter, and deity — essential for the Brahmana's own purpose — is called a 'thorn in the mantra' [a source of blemish and danger to it]."

That knowledge of the vidhi (application) is likewise required is established:

स्वरो वर्णोऽक्षरं मात्रा विनियोगोऽर्थ इव च । मन्त्रं जिज्ञासमानेन वेदितव्यं पदे पदे इति ॥ svaro varṇo'kṣaraṃ mātrā viniyogo'rtha iva ca | mantraṃ jijñāsamānena veditavyaṃ pade pade iti ||

"One who genuinely desires to understand a mantra must know, at every single word: its accent (svara), its letters (varṇa), its syllable-count (akṣara), its quantity (mātrā), its ritual application (viniyoga), and equally its meaning (artha)."

One must know the mantra's own deities, along with their names, to properly recite the Vedic mantras and understand their meaning. Likewise, one must know the deity-related names...

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 604

...and the deity-related names one should know in order to properly understand a mantra's precise sense — this we shall explain: whether the person addressed is Agni, or another deity, or some inanimate object or human being being invoked, we shall clarify. Moreover, one must know the meter (chandas) governing the mantras of each rishi — understanding this correctly settles the mind. When reciting the Veda, knowing the mantra's own accent-application (svara-viniyoga) is likewise required for correct performance. Having studied [these matters], we should now clarify their meaning as understood by scholars — for those undertaking systematic study, one should know: the accent (svara), the letters (varṇa), the syllable-count (akṣara), and other such particulars belonging to the mantra, applying at each step, as befits the Mimamsa-shastra's own established method (which, in due course, we shall likewise examine).

अग्निमित्यादिसूक्तस्य छन्दोऽनुक्रमणिकायां युधीष्टं नोक्तं तथापि परिभाषायामेवमुक्तम् । "अदौ गायत्रं प्राग्घिरण्यस्तूपाच्छ्रात्" (अनु. १-३-७४) इति । हिरण्यस्तूप-ऋषिकं वज्रकेतो मन्त्रेषु प्रकृतेषु शतकेषु पाशीनेषु मन्त्रेषु सामान्येन गायत्रं भवद इत्यर्थः । पुरुषस्य पापसंबन्धं वारयितुमाश्चादिकत्वाच्छ्रुण्डे इत्यच्छ्रुण्डे भावदयोकते । भावदयन्ति हश वा दिनं भवदाणसि शासा- कर्मण इति । agnim ity-ādi sūktasya chando'nukramaṇikāyāṃ yudhīṣṭaṃ noktaṃ tathāpi paribhāṣāyām evam uktam | "ādau gāyatraṃ prāg-hiraṇyastūpāc chrāt" (anu. 1.3.74) iti | hiraṇyastūpa-ṛṣikaṃ vajraketo mantreṣu prakṛteṣu śatakeṣu pāśīneṣu mantreṣu sāmānyena gāyatraṃ bhavaty arthaḥ | (this technical passage on meter-default rules and the following material remain a best-effort reading at this resolution, given the source's density here)

Meaning: although the meter for suktas beginning with "agnim..." is not explicitly stated in the Anukramanika [in every instance], the Paribhasha (general rule) states: from the very beginning up through the Hiranyastupa-rishi's own hymns, Gayatri is to be understood as the default meter, unless otherwise specified — this is the sense.

One should know the mantras' own deity-related names before reciting them, along with correctly understanding their meaning. Now we shall discuss the Sukta's own deities: the sukta's rishi and meter having already been stated (Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra; Gayatri meter), its deity too is likewise to be understood.

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 605

...is connected to the [ritual] purpose. Or, in the various rites performed [in yajnas] with fire, the danger arising from an unintentional offense is warded off; this is called "bhadra" (auspicious/protective). On this very subject, one sutra states—

प्रजापतिर्हि सुतनुः स क्षुरपविर्भूत्वा शिष्टक्ये देवा बिभ्यकौ नोऽसानौनं श्रीयॆभिरधाभैद्युत्क्रोशायौन दशाम् भगदस्त्यम् । (this citation remains a genuinely uncertain, best-effort reading at this resolution)

— indicating that a person who fears such harm should recite this consecrated mantra to protect his own life (dhāraṇā-vidhi), invoking the deities as appropriate. It is for this reason that these are called "bhandas" (protective verses); the elders have accordingly held that "bhandas" and "bhadra" carry the same underlying sense.

Having explained the rishi and meter, we now explain the meaning of the term "deva" (deity):

दिवा वै नो भूदिति तद्देवानां देवत्वम् । divā vai no bhūd iti tad devānāṃ devatvam | (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.3.8.8[?]) "'We shine by our own light' — thus [say] the deities. That itself is the 'devatva' [deity-nature] of the deities."

The root "dīvyati" means "to shine, to illuminate." Scripture states that the very word "deva" arises from this root. "Being illuminated through the mantra" means: since a being is praised (and thereby made resplendent) through a mantra, it is accordingly called a "deva." In this "agnimīḷe" sukta, since Agni is the one being praised, Agni alone is the deity of this sukta.

As the Anukramanika also states:

मण्डलादिष्टाग्नेयमृग्दात् । maṇḍalādiṣṭāgneyam ṛg-dāt | "The opening Rik at the head of each Mandala pertains to Agni [or, in certain Mandalas, to Indra]."

— that is, for the suktas standing at the very beginning of each Mandala, the presiding deity is either Agni or Indra. Since this sukta is the very first sukta of the very first Mandala, Agni alone is its deity.

The Blessed Veda-Puruṣa himself now speaks this sukta's first Rik, as follows—

Embedded English translation, as given in the source:

original p. 606

The First Sūkta (Ṛgveda 1.1) — agnim īḷe purohitam

The First Mantra of the Rigveda

॥ ॐ ॥

॥ Maṇḍala — 1 ॥ Anuvāka — 1 ॥ Sūkta — 1 ॥ ॥ Aṣṭaka — 1 ॥ Adhyāya — 1 ॥ Varga — 1–2 ॥ ॥ Rik-numbers contained in this sukta: 1–9 ॥

Ṛṣi — Madhucchandā Vaiśvāmitraḥ (Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra) Devatā — Agniḥ (Agni) Chandaḥ — Gāyatrī (the Gayatri meter)

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ (the accented continuous-recitation text) ॥

अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं य॒ज्ञस्य॑ दे॒वमृ॑त्विज॑म् । होता॑रं रत्न॒धात॑मम् ॥१॥

agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhā́tamam ||1||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ (the word-separated text) ॥

अग्निम् । ईळे । पुरः-हितम् । यज्ञस्य । देवम् । ऋत्विजम् ॥ होतारम् । रत्न-धातमम् ॥१॥

agnim | īḷe | puraḥ-hitam | yajñasya | devam | ṛtvijam || hotāram | ratna-dhātamam ||1||

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam (Sāyaṇa's Sanskrit commentary) ॥

अग्निनामके देवम् ईळे । स्तौमि । ईड स्तुतौ । धा. २४-४ । इति धातुः, डकारस्य ळकारो बह्वचि आर्धधातुके सम्प्रदायप्राप्तेः । तथा च प्रकृतौ अज्झ्यधस्थडकारस्य ळकारं बह्वचा जगुः । अज्झ्यधस्थभकारस्य ळकारं वा यथाक्रमम् इति । निरुक्ते हॊता प्रियोज्यात् पदं होता स्वा इति लभ्यते । ईड्यम् अग्निम् । यज्ञस्य पुरोहितम् । यथा राज्ञः पुरोहितस्तद्भृत्यं संपादयति तथाग्निरपि यज्ञस्वाभीष्टिकं होमं संपादयति । यद्वा । यज्ञस्य संबन्धिनि पूर्वभागे आहवनीयरूपेणास्थितम् । पुनः ईदृशम् । देवं दानादिगुणयुक्तम् । पुनः ईदृशम् । होतारम् ऋत्विजम् । देवानां यज्ञेषु होतृनामक ऋत्विगेव । तथा च श्रूयते । अग्निर्वै...

agni-nāmake devam īḷe | staumi | īḍa stutau | dhā. 24-4 | iti dhātuḥ, ḍakārasya ḷakāro bahvaci ārdhadhātuke sampradāya-prāpteḥ | tathā ca prakṛtau ajjhyadhastha-ḍakārasya ḷakāraṃ bahvacā jaguḥ | ajjhyadhastha-bhakārasya ḷakāraṃ vā yathākramam iti | (nirukte) hotā priyojyāt padaṃ hotā svā iti labhyate | īḍyam agnim | yajñasya purohitam | yathā rājñaḥ purohitas tad-bhṛtyaṃ sampādayati tathāgnir api yajña-svābhīṣṭikaṃ homaṃ sampādayati | yadvā | yajñasya sambandhini pūrva-bhāge āhavanīya-rūpeṇāsthitam | punaḥ īdṛśam | devaṃ dānādi-guṇa-yuktam | punaḥ īdṛśam | hotāram ṛtvijam | devānāṃ yajñeṣu hotṛ-nāmaka ṛtvig eva | tathā ca śrūyate | agnir vai... (the two brief grammatical citations on the ḍa-to-ḷa shift are best-effort readings given their compressed technical form)

Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary: "I praise (īḷe) the deity named Agni. [The verb] 'īḷe' derives from the root 'īḍ,' meaning 'to praise' (Dhatupatha 24.4); by grammatical convention, the root's 'ḍ' becomes 'ḷ' before a vowel-beginning ārdhadhātuka affix. Correspondingly [certain sutras confirm this]: '...the letter ḍ standing between vowels becomes ḷ before a vowel-initial [affix]... the letter bh standing between vowels similarly becomes ḷ in due sequence.' In the Nirukta, the word 'hotā' [priest/invoker] is derived from a root meaning 'to call' — 'hotā' is thus obtained as meaning 'one who calls' [i.e., invokes the gods].

'Īḍyam agnim' — the praiseworthy Agni. 'Yajñasya purohitam' — just as a king's Purohita (chief priest/minister) accomplishes tasks on the king's behalf, so too Agni accomplishes the yajna's own desired oblation. Alternatively: [Agni] stands established in the front portion connected with the yajna, in the form of the Āhavanīya fire. Again, of this same [Agni]: 'devam' — endowed with qualities such as generosity and the like. Again, of this same [Agni]: 'hotāram ṛtvijam' — among the gods' own priests at sacrifices, [Agni] is indeed the one bearing the name 'Hotṛ,' [acting as] their ritual-priest. And thus it is heard in scripture: 'Agnir vai...'"

original p. 607

Sāyaṇa's Commentary on Verse 1, continued

देवानां होता । ऐ. ब्रा. ३-७ । इति । devānāṃ hotā | ai. brā. 3-7 | iti | "'[Agni is] the Hotr of the gods' (Aitareya Brahmana 3.7)."

"Ratna-dhātamam" — the one who, most abundantly (atiśayena), bestows or holds (dhārayitāram) the treasures (ratnāni) that take the form of a yajna's own fruits — that is, "the bestower of treasures most abundant."

Here, the word "Agni" is shown to admit of many derivations, following Yāska's own established method in the Nirukta. The extended etymological passage that follows here — deriving "Agni" variously from roots meaning "to lead," "to shine," "foremost," and similar, in the classical Nirukta multi-derivation style, along with several further Vedic citations supporting each derivation — is presented in the source in a very tightly compressed technical register. Given the genuine risk of mis-transcribing such dense etymological Sanskrit with false confidence, this passage is flagged here for careful, unhurried re-reading in a future pass, rather than rendered now from an uncertain reading.

The overall sense of this first Rik, as conveyed by the mantra itself, is this: "I praise Agni — the household-priest (purohita) of the sacrifice, its divine ritual-priest (ṛtvij), its invoking-priest (hotṛ), the one who most abundantly bestows treasures."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (word-by-word meaning) ॥

अग्निम् (agnim) — Agni ईळे (īḷe) — I praise पुरोहितम् (purohitam) — the household-priest [of the sacrifice] यज्ञस्य (yajñasya) — of the yajna देवम् (devam) — the divine one ऋत्विजम् (ṛtvijam) — the ritual-priest होतारम् (hotāram) — the invoking-priest रत्नधातमम् (ratna-dhātamam) — the one who most abundantly bestows treasures.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ (overall sense) ॥

I praise Agni, who serves as the household-priest of the sacrifice, its own divine ritual-priest, its invoking-priest, and who most abundantly bestows treasures [upon the sacrificer]. This page continues Sāyaṇa's etymological support for "ratna-dhātamam" and then opens the formal grammatical derivation (prakriyā) of the verse's individual words. Working through it carefully below: recognizable roots, well-known citations, and the overall logical structure of the argument are given with confidence; specific numeric sūtra-citations that could not be independently confirmed against the standard Aṣṭādhyāyī are marked with "[sūtra-ref uncertain]" rather than presented as verified — this is a deliberately more cautious register than the rest of this translation, given how easily a single misread digit here becomes a fabricated citation.

original p. 608

Grammatical Analysis (Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā) of Verse 1

धनानां दातृतमम् । नि. २-१५ । इति । dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam | ni. 2.15 | iti | "'The greatest giver of wealth' (Nirukta 2.15)."

This further supports "ratna-dhātamam" through an independent Nirukta citation — Yaska himself glosses a closely related term as "dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam" ("the greatest bestower of riches"), lending etymological support to Sayana's own gloss of "ratna-dhātamam" above.

Turning now to the grammatical derivation itself: the root "īḍ" (from which "īḷe" derives) belongs to a verb-class where its meaning is "praise" (stuti) — this sense is well-established (prasiddha). Although the root admits multiple senses even where well-known, by the governing convention (nyāya), the specific senses of "asking/requesting" (yācanā) and "invoking with reverence" (adhyeṣaṇā, closely tied to pūjā, worship) are the ones appropriate here, and the word is explained accordingly.

On "purohitam": the word is analyzed as a compound — "puraḥ" (in front) + "hitam" (placed) — meaning "one placed in front" [i.e., stationed before the sacrificer as his priest/protector], following the standard krit-formation for such compounds. [The specific sutra-citations governing this compound's exact formation, visible in the source at this point, could not be confirmed with full confidence and are not reproduced as numbered citations here.]

On "devam": derived from the root "div" (to shine/sport/play), with the appropriate primary affix, yielding "deva" in the sense of "the shining/resplendent one."

On "hotāram": derived from the root "hu" (to call/invoke, or, in ritual context, to offer oblation), with the agentive affix "tṛc" (or an equivalent krit-affix), yielding "hotṛ" — "one who invokes/offers" — here declined in the accusative "hotāram."

On "ṛtvijam": analyzed as a compound of "ṛtu" (season/proper time) and a form of the root "yaj" (to sacrifice) — "one who sacrifices at the proper/appointed time" — the standing grammatical explanation for this well-established ritual term.

On "ratna-dhātamam": "ratna" (treasure) + "dhā" (to hold/bestow, the same root seen in "dhātṛ") + the superlative affix "tamap," yielding "dhātamam" — "most abundantly bestowing" — hence "the one who most abundantly bestows treasures," as already given in the Pratipadartha above. A number of further short technical notes on accent-placement (svara) for each derived form appear interspersed in the source at this point; these follow standard rules for the placement of udātta accent on krit and taddhita formations, but the specific accent-mark-by-syllable detail is not reproduced here with full confidence, consistent with the same caution noted for the Shiksha Anga's accent-classification passages earlier in this project.

On a genuinely careful second pass, I can confirm the general subject matter with confidence but not the specific sutra-numbers themselves at this scan resolution — presenting invented digits here would recreate exactly the failure this cautious approach exists to avoid, so they are not reproduced.

What this page is doing, with confidence: it continues determining the correct accentuation (udātta/anudātta placement) for the compound words already derived on the previous page — particularly "puro-hitam" (a compound whose accent depends on which member is treated as dominant) and "ratna-dhātamam" (where the superlative affix "tamap" has its own accent-governing rules). The discussion applies the standard grammatical principle that a compound's accent is determined by rules specific to its formation-type (here, apparently treated as governed by the rules for upapada or samāsānta compounds), rather than by the default accent of either member alone.
