॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (word-by-word meaning, given here in fuller form) ॥

यज्ञस्य (yajñasya) — for the yajna (of the yajna) | पुरोहितम् (purohitam) — who acts as the ācārya who conducts the yajna, or as its purohita | देवम् (devam) — the resplendent one, or the one generous in giving | होतारम् ऋत्विजम् (hotāram ṛtvijam) — who is the principal ritvij called "Hotṛ" among those performing the yajna for the gods | रत्नधातमम् (ratna-dhātamam) — who bestows upon the sacrificer, as the yajna's fruit, jewels and other excellent things | अग्निम् (agnim) — the deity named Agni | ईळे (īḷe) — I praise.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ (overall sense) ॥

I praise the deity named Agni — who stands in the foremost place within the yajna as its Purohita; who is present in the yajna as its own directly-embodied deity; who, among the four principal ritvijs — Brahmā, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ — serves specifically as the Hotṛ-priest; and who graciously bestows upon the performing yajamāna wealth in the form of jewels and similar treasures.

॥ English Translation ॥

I praise (with hymns) Agni, the chief priest of the sacrifice, the bright one, the invoking priest, the greatest giver of reward.

॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ (special topics) ॥

In this Rik, the one who says "I shall praise" is the priest called the Hotṛ. In praising Agni here, only matters connected with the yajna are described — the qualities properly belonging to those who bear the principal roles within a yajna are here attributed to Agni himself. The word "purohitam" signifies either the chief ācārya who officiates the yajna, or, [more generally,] a brāhmaṇa [in that role]...

original p. 611

...or, alternatively, it refers to the Adhvaryu — the priest who accomplishes the majority of the practical tasks within the yajna — because "purohitam" (puraḥ + hitam) means: one who, during the yajna's performance, sits foremost, ahead of everyone else, and carries out the yajna's own tasks. "Yajñasya devam" means: Agni alone is the directly-visible deity within the yajna. The other deities are not visible to us. Moreover, since the oblations meant for other deities are all offered through Agni himself as the medium, there is no greater giver within the yajna than Agni. "Ṛtvijam" may refer to any one of the four principal ritvijs, beginning with Brahmā. "Hotāram" means the ritvij associated with the invoking/Homa-offering — but since it is well established that Agni himself brings the other deities to the sacrificial altar (sa devān eha vakṣati, "he shall bring the gods here," as stated explicitly in the very next Rik), he is accordingly called "hotāram." "Ratna-dhātamam" means: one who bestows, as the fruit of the yajna, jewels and similar things upon the yajamāna. There is an established usage whereby "ratna" refers not only to gems such as diamonds, but to any excellent or superior object generally. Hence the meaning: one who gives the yajamāna wealth, grain, cattle, jewels, and other such excellent things, as needed.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

For this first sukta of the first Mandala, it is stated that the rishi is Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra. From this sukta through the tenth sukta — that is, across a total of ten suktas — this same Madhuchandas remains the rishi. This rishi Madhuchandas is one of the sons of the rishi Vishvamitra. That Vishvamitra was himself the son of Gadhi is stated both in the Aitareya Brahmana (2.12) and the Jaiminiya Brahmana (1.317[?]). In the Rigveda's own comprehensive index (Sarvanukramanika), he is said to be the son of Kushika's son Gadhi. Only in the Panchavimsha Brahmana (21.12.2[?]) is Vishvamitra instead described as a king born in the lineage of a king named Jahnu.

For the Rigveda's third Mandala, this same Vishvamitra, son of Gadhi, is the rishi — that Mandala contains 71 suktas. Logically, these ten suktas belonging to Vishvamitra's son Madhuchandas ought to have been included within the third Mandala. Why they were not so included, and instead came to stand at the head of the first Mandala, remains unknown.

This sukta contains a total of nine Riks, all having Agni as their deity. Ordinarily, a single sukta has only one rishi; yet it is occasionally found that a single sukta has several. The same holds for deities — a sukta may have one deity, or many. Likewise, a sukta's verses may all share one meter, or differ. For the present sukta we are expounding — "agnimīḷe" — across all nine of its Riks, there is a single rishi (Madhuchandas), a single deity (Agni), and a single meter (Gayatri).

original p. 612

Should it not be "agnimāḍe" rather than "agnimīḷe"? [This is explained:] per the sutra "īḍa stutau" (Dhatupatha 24.4), the form "īḷe" arises from the root "īḍ." In place of the letter "ḍa," the major grammarians employ the letter "ḷa" in certain contexts. This is a long-established, traditional convention—

अज्झ्यधस्थडकारस्य ळकारं बह्वचा जगुः । अज्झ्यधस्थढकारस्य ळ्हकारं वै यथाक्रमम् ॥ इति ॥ ajjhyadhastha-ḍakārasya ḷakāraṃ bahvacā jaguḥ | ajjhyadhastha-ḍhakārasya ḷhakāraṃ vai yathākramam || iti ||

"The letter 'ḍa,' standing between vowels, is pronounced as 'ḷa' before a vowel-beginning [affix]; the letter 'ḍha,' standing between vowels, likewise becomes 'ḷha,' in the same manner."

That is: when "ḍa" occurs between two vowels ("aj" here meaning the class of vowel-sounds), it is pronounced as "ḷa." Here, when "īḍe" is to be spoken: ī + ḍa + e = "īḷe" results. Since the "ḍa" falls between the two vowels "ī" and "e," it becomes "ḷa," and the whole word becomes "īḷe." Correspondingly, wherever "ḍha" occurs in the same position, it becomes "ḷha." For example:

आषाळ्हं यां प्रतनासु पश्वम् । āṣāḷhaṃ yāṃ pratanāsu paśvam | (Rigveda Samhita 1.100.3[?])

Many commentators construct many different derivational analyses for the word "Agni." Generally, following grammatical sutras, they devise various component-meanings that happen to fit with Agni's own well-known qualities. But it cannot be said with certainty that these are the word's actually intended meaning, or the original poet's own sense. In Sanskrit, with the aid of grammar and verbal roots, it is far from impossible to construct some meaning in almost any direction one wishes. Yet it is difficult to simply accept that the many words used throughout the Veda — deity-names especially — actually contain such elaborate component-meanings, achievable only through such intricate grammatical machinery. The Veda's own language tends toward simplicity, stating its intended sense directly; a compound of more than two elements is itself a rarity there. Given this, some scholars decline to set aside a word's natural sense in favor of derivations achievable only through comparatively late-arising grammatical apparatus.

However, it is no fault of the Bhashyakara [Sayana] that "Agni" has been explained in so many ways — for, following precisely what is already stated regarding this word in the Brahmanas and in the Nirukta, the meaning has been worked out with grammar's assistance. We shall now explain some of the principal derivations among these.

अथातोऽनुक्रमिष्यामोऽग्निः प्रथमस्थं प्रथमं व्याख्यास्यामोऽग्निः कस्मादग्रणीर्भवत्यग्रं यज्ञेषु प्रणीयतेऽग्रं यज्ञं नयति सन्नमानो वा क्रोशनो भवतीति स्थौलाष्ठीविः । क्रोशनयति न स्नेयति तृप्तेराख्यातेभ्यो जायत इति शाकपूणिः । athāto'nukramiṣyāmo'gniḥ prathama-sthaṃ prathamaṃ vyākhyāsyāmo'gniḥ kasmād agraṇīr bhavaty agraṃ yajñeṣu praṇīyate'graṃ yajñaṃ nayati sannamāno vā krośano bhavatīti sthaulāṣṭhīviḥ | krośanayati na sneyati tṛpter ākhyātebhyo jāyata iti śākapūṇiḥ | (Nirukta 7.14) (the remainder of this Nirukta passage on this page continues with further, highly compressed etymological reasoning — deriving pieces of "Agni" variously from roots connected with "aṅga," "nī," and "dah" — which is not reproduced further here with full confidence, consistent with the cautious approach adopted for this register of text)

"Now, hereafter, we shall proceed [to explain the deity-names in order]. Since Agni stands first [in the list], we explain him first. Why is Agni called 'agraṇī' (foremost-leader)? Because he is led at the forefront in sacrifices, or because he leads the sacrifice forward. Or — he becomes so through bending low, or through crying out — thus says Sthaulāṣṭhīvi. [Regarding the sense 'krośana,' crying out, as against 'na sneyati,' not becoming smooth:] it is born from verbal roots (ākhyāta) — thus says Śākapūṇi."

Meaning: Yaska, in his Nirukta, having decided to explain the deity-names in the order they occur, takes up Agni first, since Agni stands first among them. Two ancient authorities are cited for the etymology of "agraṇī" (one who leads at the forefront) — Sthaulashthivi holding one view, Shakapuni offering a related but distinct grammatical explanation...

original p. 613

The meaning of this is: it is generally customary to state defining marks for all deities alike; accordingly, we shall now provide a special explanation of "Agni" from the standpoint of its component-meaning. Since Agni the deity is said to exist both on earth and in heaven, we first explain his form as present on earth. In explaining how the word "Agni" came to bear this name, the answer "agraṇe" may be given. "Agraṇe" means: one who himself leads the divine army, or who serves as its foremost leader (nāyaka). This is one reason for the name.

Moreover, a Brahmana passage states:

अग्निर्देवानां सेनानीः । agnir devānāṃ senānīḥ | "Agni is the general (senānī) of the gods' army."

Following this, the Aitareya scholars state in their own Mantra-Brahmana:

अग्निर्मुखं प्रथमो देवतानाम् । agnir mukhaṃ prathamo devatānām | (Aitareya Brahmana 1.4) "Agni is the face — the foremost among the deities."

Elsewhere in the same Brahmana:

अग्निर्वै देवानामवमः । agnir vai devānām avamaḥ | (Aitareya Brahmana 1.1) "Agni is indeed the nearest of the deities [to men]."

And in the Taittiriya Brahmana:

अग्निरग्रे प्रथमो देवतानाम् । agnir agre prathamo devatānām | (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.4.2.1[?]) "Agni, at the forefront, is the first among the deities" — and also "agnir avamo devatānām" ["Agni is the nearest of the deities"].

From these examples, Agni is established as first among the deities, standing at the forefront, serving as their leader.

Because of this, in the sacrificial rites generally, fire is first carried from the Gārhapatya fire-pit onward to the Āhavanīya fire-pit standing in the eastern direction — and it is from this "carrying forward" (agra-nayana) that Agni comes to bear his name; this is the second reason.

Furthermore, since Agni, offering up his very own body, burns kindling and similar fuel, and likewise cooks the oblation in homas and similar rites — through this self-consuming, self-propelling action — Agni comes to bear his name; this is counted among the third such reasons.

The Nirukta-scholar Sthaulāṣṭhīvin, son of the great sage Sthaulāṣṭhīva, holds that Agni's very nature — burning continuously, without pause or restraint — accounts for the name: from a root meaning "to behave harshly" (krośa) comes "krośayati"; "na krośayati" gives "akroṣaṇaḥ" — that is, [Agni] burns wood and similar material mercilessly, without the gentleness [that quality's absence implies].

Another Nirukta-scholar, Śākapūṇi (son of Śakapūṇi, also known by the name Rathītara), holds that the word "Agni" arises from three separate roots: the precise Dhatupatha reference-numbers for the second and third roots, and a fourth root the passage appears to introduce at the very bottom of this page, remain uncertain at this resolution and are not asserted as verified citations

इण् गतौ इति धातुः (धा. २४-२५) । iṇ gatau iti dhātuḥ (dhā. 24.25) | — "'iṇ,' in the sense of 'going'" —

अक्ष्णोतेर्वा तृप्रक्षणकाङ्क्षिषु इति धातुः । akṣṇoter vā tṛpra-kṣaṇa-kāṅkṣiṣu iti dhātuḥ | — [a root connected with desiring/aspiring] —

दघ्नोतेर्वा दह भस्मीकरणे इति धातुः । daghnoter vā daha bhasmīkaraṇe iti dhātuḥ | — "'dah,' in the sense of 'reducing to ash [by burning]'" —

original p. 614

The word "Agni" is thus formed from the sounds "a," "g," and "ni": the "a" comes from "ayana" (a form derived from the root "iṇ," "to go," via "eti"); the "g" comes either from the root "ac" (whose "k" becomes "g" by substitution) or from "dagdha" (a form of "dah," "to burn, reduce to ash"); and the long "nī" — from "nayati," a form of the root "nī" ("to lead/obtain") — is shortened to "ni." These three — ā + g + ni = Agni — combine, formed from the three roots discussed above. Since Agni comes to the sacrificial ground and, by offering up his own body, burns the kindling and similarly causes the oblation to be cooked, this deity accordingly bears the name "Agni" — this is the overall sense.

Since the praise of this deity Agni — bearing this full range of meaning — is the principal subject of this Rik, this mantra is well known by the name "agnimīḷe." The sage Yāska himself explains this very Rik in his Nirukta, as follows:

अग्निमीळेऽग्निं याचामीळिध्येषणकर्मा पूजाकर्मा वा पुरोहितो व्याख्यातो यज्ञस्य देवो दानाद्वा दीपनाद्वा द्योतनाद्वा द्युस्थानो भवतीति वा यो देवः सा देवता होतारं ह्वातारं जुहोतेर्होतेर्वाभोरत्नधातमं रमणीयानां धनानां दातृतमम् ॥ इति (नि. ७-१५) agnim īḷe'gniṃ yācāmi īḍi-adhyeṣaṇa-karmā pūjā-karmā vā purohito vyākhyāto yajñasya devo dānād vā dīpanād vā dyotanād vā dyu-sthāno bhavatīti vā yo devaḥ sā devatā hotāraṃ hvātāraṃ juhoter hoter vā abhoḥ ratna-dhātamaṃ ramaṇīyānāṃ dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam || iti (Nirukta 7.15)

"'Agnim īḷe' — 'I entreat Agni'; [the root 'īḍ'] carries the sense of asking (adhyeṣaṇa) or of worship (pūjā). 'Purohita' has already been explained. 'Devaḥ' [of the yajna] — [Agni is called 'deva'] either from 'dāna' (giving), 'dīpana' (illuminating), or 'dyotana' (shining) — or because he abides in the region of the sky (dyu-sthāna); whoever is thus 'deva' constitutes 'devatā.' 'Hotāram' — the one who calls (hvātāram), from the root 'hu' (to invoke or to offer). 'Ratna-dhātamam' — the greatest giver (dātṛtamam) of desirable riches (ramaṇīyānāṃ dhanānām)."

Meaning: the root "īḍ" is well known to carry a sense connected with praise. Following the accepted principle that roots may carry multiple senses, the meanings "entreaty" (yācñā), "asking/invocation" (adhyeṣaṇā), and "worship" (pūjā) have all been assigned to the root "īḍ," and the verse is explained accordingly here.

The word "purohita" was already explained in the Nirukta's second chapter (2.13), in the course of commenting on the Rik "yeṣṭe vāpiḥ śaṃ kenāve purohitaḥ" (Rigveda Samhita 10.14.2[?]) — that is, "puraḥ hitaṃ dadhāti purohitaḥ": one who stands in front, [specifically] in front of the sacrificer [facing him] during the yajna. The Yajurvedins too gloss it as "puro hitaṃ dadhate" — one standing in front, that is, in the foremost position. The word "purohita" carries the established sense of the principal ācārya who properly conducts yajnas and similar rites according to shastric injunction. In this Rik, since the qualities of the Hotr and other ritvijs are attributed to Agni in this praise, "purohita" may equally be understood here as "chief ācārya." This word "purohita" occurs only in a few places within the Rigveda itself. Though the Bhashyakara [Sayana] clearly explains this word's sense as "chief ācārya" there, in the Krishna-Yajur[veda]...

original p. 615

In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda:

विश्वरूपो नै त्वाष्ट्रः पुरोहितो देवानाम् । viśvarūpo nai tvāṣṭraḥ purohito devānām | (Taittiriya Samhita 2.5.1[?]) "Vishvarupa, son of Tvashtri, was the purohita of the gods."

And:

बृहस्पतिर्देवानां पुरोहित आसीच्छन्दःसाराणां कार्षणसुराणाम् । bṛhaspatir devānāṃ purohita āsīc chandaḥsārāṇāṃ kārṣaṇa-surāṇām | (Taittiriya Samhita 3.4.10[?]) "Brihaspati was the purohita of the gods; Shanda and Marka were the purohitas of the demons (daityas)."

In these instances, "purohita" is used in the sense of the chief ācārya who conducts ritual performances (High Priest).

On "devam": the word "deva" expresses senses connected with giving (dāna), illuminating (dīpana), and shining (dyotana). It derives from the root "div," "to shine." "Devam" thus means "one who shines, one who illuminates" — that is, "a deity." Alternatively, taken as "giver [of vigor] to the yajna," it means one who plays the principal role within it — since the yajna cannot be accomplished without Agni at all, this is the sense. Since "deva" and "devatā" are synonymous terms bearing identical meaning ("deva" masculine, "devatā" feminine), the deity meant in this mantra need not be thought to be anyone other than Agni himself.

On "ṛtvijam":

ऋतौ युज्यते इति ऋत्विक् । ṛtau yujyate iti ṛtvik | (cf. Panini Ashtadhyayi 3.2.59) "One who is engaged/employed at the proper season [or appointed time] is called 'ṛtvik.'"

Though "ṛtvij" is used generally for anyone engaged in reciting mantras and similar duties during a ritual, it more specifically denotes one of the four who bear the principal roles in a yajna: Brahmā, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ. Since the word "hotāram" immediately follows "ṛtvijam" in this Rik, the Bhashyakara and many other commentators hold that the specific reference here is to the ritvij called Hotṛ.

On "hotāram": the word "hotṛ" derives from the root "hve" (to invoke, to call) — hence "one who invokes the deities." This sense is reinforced by the very next Rik, which states "sa devān eha vakṣati" ("he shall bring the gods here"). The sage Baurṇavābha holds the alternative view that "hotṛ" instead derives from "juhoti" (to perform homa). For the word "hotṛ," this [alternate derivation]...

original p. 616

Both meanings apply. In connection with Agni, the word "hotāram" has frequently been used alongside "ṛtvijam" in many places across the Rigveda:

नि त्वा यज्ञस्य साधनमग्ने होतारमृत्विजम् । नि त्वा होतारमृत्विजम् । त्वां यज्ञेष्वृत्विजमग्ने होतारमीळते । मन्द्रं होतारमृत्विजं चिकित्वांसं विभावसुम् । ni tvā yajñasya sādhanam agne hotāram ṛtvijam | ni tvā hotāram ṛtvijam | tvāṃ yajñeṣv ṛtvijam agne hotāram īḷate | mandraṃ hotāram ṛtvijaṃ cikitvāṃsaṃ vibhāvasum | (this cluster of formulaic parallel citations, and their specific chapter-verse locators, remain a best-effort reading at this resolution)

— and so on. As shown above, many rishis, in praising Agni, use the two words "hotāram" and "ṛtvijam" together. Since the Hotṛ's role in a yajna is especially prominent, the custom of calling Agni himself "Hotṛ" may well have arisen from this frequent pairing.

On "ratna-dhātamam": Yaska, in the Nirukta's second chapter, explains "ratna" alongside other words denoting wealth. Anything pleasing or delightful is called "ratna"; it may also mean simply "an excellent object." Here, primarily, "ratna" carries the sense of wealth (aiśvarya). "Dhātamaḥ" is used in the sense of "giving." In the Rigveda, it is generally found that where the sense "to give" (dadāti) is intended, the root "dadhāti" is used instead. For example:

प्रातर्रत्नं प्रातरित्वा दधाति । prātar ratnaṃ prātaritvā dadhāti | (Rigveda Samhita 1.125.1[?])

In this verse, the rishi Kakṣīvān describes a donation made by a king named Svanaya. Here "ratna" clearly means gold and similar wealth, or cattle and other excellent possessions, as becomes evident from the words used in the following verses. "Dadhāti" here means simply "giving" (dadāti). Similarly, in passages such as:

रायस्पोषं यजमानेषु धत्ते । प्रजां पुष्टिं भूतिमस्मासु धत्ते । rāyas poṣaṃ yajamāneṣu dhatte | prajāṃ puṣṭiṃ bhūtim asmāsu dhatte | (Rigveda Samhita 7.48.2[?])

— "dhatte" is likewise used in place of "dadāti." All of this draws upon Yaska's own explanation, as the Nirukta's author, of this mantra.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (Grammatical Process) ॥

हयास्तूपरङ्गेन्द्रा नत्वा तत्वार्थदौ ब्रुवे । ऋतिं देष्या पाणिनीयमाक्ष्णोशो मार्गपोक्तः ॥ (this brief opening verse to the grammar section remains a best-effort reading, its precise sense unclear even after careful re-examination)

The word "Agni" arises from the root "ag," meaning "to go" — per the Unadi rule "aṅger ṇa-lopaś ca" (Unadi Sutra, precise number uncertain): before the root "ag," the affix "ni" is added; moreover, [a rule governs] the loss of the nasal "n" [in the root]...

original p. 617

...the elision also occurs; by this rule, the affix "ni" comes after the root "ag." Since the "i" in the root "ag" bears the designation "it" (a marker later dropped), by the rule "idito nuṃ dhātoḥ" (Panini 7.1.58) — a nasal "n" is added after the final vowel of a root so marked — the resulting nasal then undergoes its own elision by a further rule. "Aṅgati iti agniḥ" — "he who moves/goes forth" is "Agni" — that is, because he carries the oblation up to the deities in heaven, he bears this name. Several further accent-rule citations follow, working out that the resulting word "Agni" has its "a" as anudātta and its "i" as udātta — this is confirmed by the accent marks already seen on "agním" in the Saṃhitā-pāṭha itself. The specific chain of Ashtadhyayi sutra-numbers cited here — governing root-accent, affix-accent, and the eventual "ekādeśa" [single-substitute] accent rule for the accusative "agnim" — is presented with the same caution as elsewhere in this section, though the overall grammatical logic and its conclusion are clear and consistent with the verse's own printed accentuation.

Here the discussion turns to a foundational methodological question in Sanskrit grammar itself:

नामान्याख्यातजानीति शाकटायनस्य नैरुक्ते समये । न सर्वाणीति गार्ग्ये वैयाकरणानां चैके । nāmāny ākhyāta-jāneti śākaṭāyanasya nairukte samaye | na sarvāṇīti gārgye vaiyākaraṇānāṃ caike | (Nirukta 1.13)

"'All nouns are born from verbs' — this is Śākaṭāyana's own view, within the Nirukta's own convention. 'Not all [nouns are so derived]' — this is Gārgya's view, and that of some grammarians as well."

Śākaṭāyana, himself a Nirukta-author, holds that every nominal stem (prātipadika) derives from a verbal root (dhātu). In Gārgya's own view, however, the word "Agni" is "akhaṇḍa" — that is, an underived, indivisible nominal stem, admitting no division into root and affix. In this [Gargya's] view...

original p. 618

उदात्तं (फिट् सू. १) । udāttaṃ (phiṭ sū. 1) | "'Phiṭ' [denotes] a nominal stem (prātipadika); its final [syllable] takes the udātta accent."

By this rule, "agni" as a prātipadika likewise has udātta accent on its final syllable. When the accusative ending "am" is applied, the same grammatical process as before should be understood to apply.

Yaska himself favors three derivations of the word "Agni":

अग्रं नयतीत्यग्रणिः, अग्रं प्रति प्रीयत इत्यग्निः, अङ्गं नयतीत्यग्निः । agraṃ nayatīty agraṇiḥ, agraṃ prati prīyata ity agniḥ, aṅgaṃ nayatīty agniḥ |

"'He who leads forward' is Agraṇi; 'he who inclines with delight toward the forefront' is Agni; 'he who leads the body/limb onward' is Agni."

The great sage Sthaulāṣṭhīvi instead offers: "akṣṇo'payatīty agniḥ" — "he who removes affliction from the eye is Agni." In these derivations, the division into root and affix must be constructed as appropriate in each case.

On this very point, Yaska states one of the Nirukta's own foundational methodological statements:

अथ निर्वचने तेष्वेषु पदेषु स्वरसंस्कारौ समर्थः प्रादेशिकेन गुणेनान्वितौ स्यातां तथा तानि निब्रूयात्, अप्रादेशिके विकारीर्थनि परीक्षिते केनचिद् दृष्टिसामान्येन, असिध्यमाने सामान्ये स्वक्षरवर्णसामान्यान् निब्रूयाच्चैव न निब्रूयात् ॥ atha nirvacane teṣv eṣu padeṣu svara-saṃskārau samarthaḥ prādeśikena guṇenānvitau syātāṃ tathā tāni nibrūyāt, aprādeśike vikārīrthani parīkṣite kenacid dṛṣṭi-sāmānyena, asidhyamāne sāmānye svākṣara-varṇa-sāmānyān nibrūyāc caiva na nibrūyāt || (Nirukta 2.1)

"Now, in etymological explanation: in whichever words the accent and grammatical processing prove capable [of derivation] and are found connected with a rootward (prādeśika) sense-quality, one should explain them accordingly. Where such a root-connection is absent, but some general resemblance can still be discerned through a certain manner of observation, [one may explain by that resemblance]. Where even that general resemblance cannot be established, one may resort to mere resemblance of individual letters and sounds — or else one need not attempt an explanation at all."

Meaning: where a word's accent and grammatical derivation (via root and affix) can be properly connected to its intended sense through standard grammatical procedure, one should explain it that way — this is the strongest kind of explanation. Where this isn't available, a general resemblance of sense, discernible by some means, may serve instead. Where not even that can be shown, mere resemblance of individual sounds may be invoked as a last resort. Taking "Agni" as the example: the derivation "aṅgati ity agniḥ" — where root, affix, and accent-pattern are all fully established through grammar — satisfies this strongest, first kind of explanation.

Where the root's own sense does not directly apply to the intended meaning, one may instead follow a Brahmana-passage's own usage, or an intended qualifying sense applied to a deity, adapting the general action-sense (kriyā-sāmānya) of the root so that the intended meaning still emerges from the word. In "agraṃ nayati ity agni" [as above], the general notion of "leading" is what grounds the word "Agni" here. Where even this general action-sense proves unavailable, one should form the etymology on the basis of mere resemblance of syllables or letters (akṣara-sāmānya / varṇa-sāmānya). When "akṣṇo'payatīty agniḥ" is analyzed this way, "akṣṇaḥ" — per the lexicon's sense "akṣo nānā-pratiṣedhe" — carries a negating sense with an initial "a"-sound; since the word "Agni" likewise begins with the sound "a," this derivation rests on mere sound-resemblance (akṣara-sāmya). "Akṣara" here means a meaning-bearing sound. Śākapūṇi's own derivation proceeds by mere letter-resemblance (varṇa-sāmya) — noting only that both words happen to share the sound "g." Thus, an etymological explanation should never be abandoned outright, by whichever of these means it can be achieved — this is the sense of Nirukta 2.1.

original p. 619

This confirms that the word "īḷe" is properly svara-accented as derived above. Continuing with "timbū" and similar forms [a brief transitional note], the same accent process applies.

On "purohitam" — its grammatical derivation:

आयं पुरो भुवः । āyaṃ puro bhuvaḥ | (Taittiriya Samhita 4.3.2.1[?])

— here "puraḥ" is accented on its final syllable (antodātta). The word "puraḥ" itself derives from "pūrva," per the rule:

पूर्वाधरावरादिभ्यो दिक्देशकालेष्वस् । pūrvādhara-avarādibhyo dik-deśa-kāleṣv asa (cf. Panini Ashtadhyayi 5.3.39)

— the taddhita affix "as," expressing direction, place, or time, is added after words such as "pūrva," "adhara," and "avara." When this affix is applied, "pūrva" takes the substitute "pur," yielding "pūrva + as = puras" — and with visarga, "puraḥ." Since the vowel here belongs to the affix "as," by the rule "ādyudāttaś ca" (Panini 3.1.3) — the affix's own initial letter takes udātta — "puraḥ" becomes antodātta [accented on its final syllable].

On "hitam": from the root "dhā" (ḍudhāñ, "to hold, to nourish") — before the affix "kta," per the rule "dadhāter kit" (Panini 7.4.42), the substitute "hi" replaces "dhā." The resulting "hita" thus takes udātta accent on its final syllable.

When "puraḥ" and "hitam" combine as a compound — per the general rule that a compound's final member ordinarily governs accent, with the specific exception applying here for this type of tatpurusha formation — the compound "purohitam" results, accented accordingly on the vowel following the combination. Several further specific citation-chains on this page — governing sandhi between the visarga of "puraḥ" and the initial "h" of "hitam," and the precise accent-retention rule for this particular tatpurusha type — involve highly compressed technical shorthand that could not be independently confirmed at full confidence and are not reproduced as specific numbered sutras here. This page continues the grammatical derivation in the same dense register — working through "yajñasya" from the root "yaj" [devapūjāyām, "in the sense of worshipping the gods"], and beginning the derivation of "devam." Given the density of specific sutra-citations here, the following summarizes the confirmed content rather than reproducing every numbered reference.

original p. 620

On "yajñasya": derived from the root "yaj," meaning "devapūjā" (worship of the deities) — through the standard krit-affix process yielding the noun "yajña" ("sacrifice, act of worship"), here declined in the genitive "yajñasya" ("of the sacrifice").

The passage also revisits "hotāram" and "ratna-dhātamam" from a grammatical standpoint, confirming: "hotāram" as derived from the root "hu" (to invoke/offer) with the agentive "tṛc" affix, appropriately accented; and "ratna-dhātamam" as "ratna" (from a root connected with "delighting") compounded with "dhātamam," itself "dhā" (to bestow) plus the superlative affix "tamap" — consistent with the meaning already established in the Pratipadartha above.

On "devam": the derivation opens from the root "div," "to shine/sport," with the appropriate primary (kṛt) affix yielding "deva" — "the shining one" — the grammatical derivation matching the sense already given in Sayana's own bhashya-prose earlier. As with the preceding grammar-heavy pages, the specific chain of Ashtadhyayi sutra-numbers governing each accent-shift and affix-substitution in this derivation sequence is not reproduced verbatim here, consistent with the cautious approach adopted for this register of text throughout this project. This page continues and concludes the grammatical derivation of "hotāram" and "ratna" — confirming the accent patterns already established in the Pratipadartha, via the same dense sutra-citation register as the preceding pages, summarized here rather than reproduced verbatim.

original p. 621

On "ratna": the word is analyzed as neuter, derived through a krit-affix from a root connected with "delighting" or "taking pleasure in" — confirming the sense already given above ("a delightful/excellent thing," hence "treasure"). The compound "ratna-dhātamam" follows standard tatpurusha-compound accentuation rules, with the superlative "tamap" affix retaining its own accent per the general principle governing such formations.

Having thus explained, at length, both the meaning and the grammatical derivation of the first Rik, [the commentary] now proceeds to state the meaning of the second Rik.

original p. 622

The Second Mantra of the Rigveda

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अ॒ग्निः पूर्वे॑भि॒रृषि॑भि॒रीड्यो॒ नूत॑नैरु॒त । स दे॒वाँ एह व॑क्षति ॥२॥

agníḥ pū́rvebhir ṛ́ṣibhir īḍyó nū́tanair utá | sá devā́m̐ éha vakṣati ||2||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अग्निः । पूर्वेभिः । ऋषिभिः । ईड्यः । नूतनैः । उत । सः । देवान् । आ । इह । वक्षति ॥२॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अयमग्निः पूर्वेभिः पुराकैर् अङ्गिरःप्रभृतिभिर् ऋषिभिर् ईड्यः स्तुत्यः, नूतनैर् उत इदानींतनैर् अप्यृषिभिः स्तुत्यः । सोऽग्निः स्तुतः सन्न् इह यज्ञे देवान् विभूर्जान् आ वक्षति । वह प्रापणे इति धातुः । ayam agniḥ pūrvebhiḥ purākair aṅgiraḥ-prabhṛtibhir ṛṣibhir īḍyaḥ stutyaḥ, nūtanair uta idānīṃtanair apy ṛṣibhir stutyaḥ | so'gniḥ stutaḥ sann iha yajñe devān vibhūrjān ā vakṣati | vaha prāpaṇe iti dhātuḥ |

Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary: "This Agni is worthy to be praised (īḍya, stutya) by the ancient rishis of former times — Aṅgiras and others; and equally worthy to be praised by present-day rishis as well. That Agni, thus praised, brings the gods, [laden] with their [ritual] portions, here to this yajna. The root 'vah' [here as 'vakṣati'] carries the sense of 'conveying, bringing.'" The remainder of this page continues into the same dense grammatical-derivation register seen throughout the preceding pages — working through the accent and formation of "pūrvebhiḥ," "ṛṣibhiḥ," "īḍyaḥ," "nūtanaiḥ," "uta," and the sandhi/accent treatment of "devān" before "eha" — citing a long chain of specific Ashtadhyayi sutras. Consistent with the cautious approach adopted for this register throughout this project, these specific numbered citations are not reproduced verbatim here; a dedicated pass with a standard Ashtadhyayi reference would be needed to transcribe them reliably. The grammatical-derivation section concludes at the top of this page, working through "vakṣati" and confirming the accent-pattern of the whole verse, in the same dense register as before.

original p. 623

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

अग्निः (agniḥ) — the deity Agni | पूर्वेभिः ऋषिभिः (pūrvebhiḥ ṛṣibhiḥ) — by many ancient rishis, such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and others | ईड्यः (īḍyaḥ) — is praised | उत (uta) — and | नूतनैः (nūtanaiḥ) — by present-day [rishis] such as us, and by other rishis who are our contemporaries | ईड्यः (īḍyaḥ) — is worthy of being praised, that is, is [likewise] praised | सः (saḥ) — that Agni | देवान् (devān) — the deities invoked in the yajna | इह (iha) — here, that is, to the yajna-ground | आ वक्षति (ā vakṣati) — brings, [may he] bring.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

This Agni, whom I now praise, has been praised by many great sages in ancient times. In the present age too, I myself, along with other rishis who are my contemporaries, praise Agni. May this Agni — thus worthy of praise by rishis of both past and present ages — bring here the deities whom we invoke, so that they may accept their portion of the oblation in the yajna we now perform.

॥ English Translation ॥

Agni is a god to be praised by sages ancient and by sages modern. May he bring the gods hither.

॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ ॥

This Rik's meaning is straightforward — it contains nothing difficult or ambiguous. Since it is said that Agni exists both on earth and in heaven, the principal rishi here prays that Agni bring the deities dwelling in heaven down to the sacrificial altar.

original p. 624

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

Since this Rik states "pūrvebhiḥ ṛṣibhiḥ" (by ancient rishis), it becomes clear that suktas even more ancient than this one existed, composed by rishis even more ancient than the present one. This "agnimīḷe" sukta, though standing at the very head of the Rigveda, is by no means itself the most ancient composition. Suktas evidently far older than this one were already current in this rishi's own time, and appear — from the way they were handed down — to have been taught traditionally from a considerably earlier period still. Even examined purely from the standpoint of linguistic style, a good many suktas can be found that are more archaic, more ambiguous in sense, and built from more obscure word-combinations than this one.

Some rishi-names earlier than the present one may be given as follows:

In the lineage of the rishi Bhṛgu — Bṛhaspati, Ayāsya, Ajarvan(?), Dadhyañc, Vyaśva(?), Saṃvarta, Ucithya(?), Ucathya, Bharadvāja, Dīrghatamas, Sudhanvan, Ṛbhu, Vibhvan(?), Vāja, Kavandhya(?), Vicāra, and others.

In the lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras — Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others, as well as those of the present rishi's own family: Kuśika, Gādhin, Viśvāmitra, and others.

Since the names of these rishis appear within the Veda itself, all of them are established as having directly perceived (draṣṭṛ) their respective mantras in praising Agni. Among such rishis, there may well have been many others whose very names are unknown even to me [the commentator, Venkatarao himself is speaking here]; the suktas they composed are no longer available to us today. They may have composed many suktas not now found within the Rigveda at all — but since these fell out of use, they remain inaccessible to us. Since only the suktas actually preserved within the Rigveda have come down to us, it is only the matters contained in these that we are able to examine.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (Grammatical Process) ॥ This section opens the grammatical derivation of "pūrvebhiḥ" and the remaining words of Rik 2, in the same dense sutra-citation register as before. This page continues the grammatical derivation of "pūrvebhiḥ," "ṛṣibhiḥ," and "nūtanaiḥ" in the same dense register as before — working through affix-application, accent-rules, and the specific declined forms, with the derivation of "ṛṣi" itself touched on again in connection with the rishi-etymology discussed earlier in this project (see printed page 602 above, the "ṛṣ" root discussion). The page also appears to discuss variant grammatical schools' differing accounts of how "pūrvebhiḥ" receives its instrumental-plural accent. Consistent with the cautious approach maintained throughout this technical register, the specific chain of numbered sutra-citations here is not reproduced verbatim. This page continues the dense grammatical derivation of "nūtanaiḥ" and "uta," working through affix-formation and accent rules via the standard sutra-citation register. It touches briefly on the classification of "ṛṣi" as belonging to a specific noun-group (gaṇa) for declension purposes, and discusses accent-retention rules for compounds ending in these forms. Consistent with the established approach for this register, the specific numbered citations are not reproduced verbatim here. This page continues the dense grammatical derivation, now working through "saḥ," "devān," and the verb "vakṣati" — covering pronoun-declension rules, the "ṛ→ar" substitution for roots of this class, and accent-retention through the Ashtadhyayi's internal "asiddha" (treated-as-not-yet-applied) rule for certain sandhi operations. As with the preceding grammar-heavy pages, the specific numbered sutra-chain is not reproduced verbatim here, consistent with the cautious approach maintained for this register throughout this project.
