The grammatical derivation of Rik 2 concludes at the top of this page, closing with a brief note that the accent-marks visible in the printed Saṃhitā text follow directly from the derivation just completed.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अ॒ग्निना॑ र॒यिम॑श्नव॒त् पोष॑मे॒व दि॒वेदि॑वे । य॒शसं॑ वी॒रव॑त्तमम् ॥३॥

agnínā rayím aśnavat póṣam evá divé-dive | yaśásaṃ vīrávattamam ||3||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अग्निना । रयिम् । अश्नवत् । पोषम् । एव । दिवेऽदिवे । यशसम् । वीरवत्तमम् ॥३॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

यो'यं होत्रा स्तुत्योऽस्य नाग्ना निमित्तभूतेन यजमानो रयिं धनम् अश्नवत् प्राप्नोति । पोष्यं रयिम् । दिवे दिवे पोषणेव प्रतिदिनं पुष्यमानतया वर्धमानम् एव, न तु कदाचिद् अपि क्षीयमानम् । यशसं दानादिना यशोयुक्तम् । वीरवत् अतिशयेन पुत्रपौत्रादि-वीरपुरुषोपेतम् । अति हि धने पुरुषाः संपद्यन्ते । रयिशब्दो माघमित्यादिधननामसु पठितः । तत्र फिट् स्वरः । अश्नवत् अशेर्मा-... yo'yaṃ hotrā stutyo'sya nāgnā nimitta-bhūtena yajamāno rayiṃ dhanam aśnavat prāpnoti | poṣyaṃ rayim | dive dive poṣaṇeva pratidinaṃ puṣyamānatayā vardhamānam eva, na tu kadācid api kṣīyamānam | yaśasaṃ dānādinā yaśo-yuktam | vīravat atiśayena putra-pautrādi-vīra-puruṣopetam | ati hi dhane puruṣāḥ sampadyante | rayi-śabdo māgham ity-ādi-dhana-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ | tatra phiṭ svaraḥ | aśnavat aśer mā-...

Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary: "Through this Agni, who is worthy of praise by the Hotṛ, and who serves as the [instrumental] cause — may the sacrificer obtain wealth (rayi); 'aśnavat' means 'may he obtain.' 'Poṣyam rayim' — wealth that is [continually] nourished. 'Dive dive' — day by day, ever growing through such continual nourishment, never at any time diminishing. 'Yaśasam' — endowed with fame, through generosity and similar virtues. 'Vīravat[-tamam]' — endowed, in the highest degree, with heroic men such as sons and grandsons; for indeed, men [descendants] are what truly complete [and enrich] wealth. The word 'rayi' is listed among the terms for wealth, such as 'māgham' and similar; for it, the Phit-sutra's own accent rule applies. 'Aśnavat' derives from the root 'aś'..." The remainder of this page continues into the grammatical derivation, in the same dense register as before. The grammatical-derivation section concludes at the top of this page.

original p. 629

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(यजमानः) — (the sacrificer) | अग्निना (agninā) — by Agni, who has been praised by the Hotṛ | दिवेदिवे (dive-dive) — day by day | पोषमेव (poṣam eva) — that which is continually nourished/increasing | रयिम् (rayim) — wealth, or prosperity | यशसम् (yaśasam) — the renown that comes through generosity and similar virtues | वीरवत्तमम् (vīravattamam) — brave sons, servants, and similar men, in the highest measure | अश्नवत् (aśnavat) — may [he] obtain.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

When the Hotṛ praises Agni, may Agni, pleased by this praise, bestow upon the sacrificer who performs the yajna: wealth and prosperity, renown, and valorous sons together with servants and other members of his household. The wealth Agni bestows should not merely last for some time and then dwindle away — rather, it should keep increasing day by day, bringing the sacrificer continual joy. This is the intended sense.

॥ English Translation ॥

Through Agni, may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity which increases day by day accompanied by renown and a host of brave followers.

॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ ॥

The Hotṛ, having praised Agni, prays that Agni may graciously grant the sacrificer wealth and prosperity, fame, and brave sons, servants, and the like. The sense is that whatever wealth Agni gives should increase day by day, and never diminish. Alternatively, through the specific phrase "dive-dive" (on every single day), the further sense emerges: may Agni continue giving such wealth on each and every day, without interruption.

original p. 630

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Rayim" means wealth, as the Nirukta itself states. The word "rāyaḥ" expresses this same sense. "Rāyaḥ" is commonly paired with the word "poṣa" throughout the Vedas. For example:

रायस्पोषं यजमानेषु धत्तम् । रायस्पोषेण सचीय सुवीरः । rāyas poṣaṃ yajamāneṣu dhattam | rāyas poṣeṇa sacīya suvīraḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 7.43.3[?]; 1.151.1[?])

— and so on. Here, the Bhashyakara explains "poṣa" as "abhivṛddhi" (increase). This meaning fits well here, though "poṣa" often carries a somewhat distinct sense elsewhere in the Rigveda:

भूरि पोषं स धत्ते वीरवद्गृहः । दधद् रयिं मयि पोषम् । पोषं रयीणामरिष्टिं तनूनाम् । bhūri poṣaṃ sa dhatte vīravad gṛhaḥ | dadhad rayiṃ mayi poṣam | poṣaṃ rayīṇām ariṣṭiṃ tanūnām | (Rigveda Samhita 8.23.21[?]; 7.66.11[?]; 3.51.8[?])

In these verses, "poṣa" primarily means "nourishment, plumpness," though the sense of "increase" is also implied.

"Aśnavat" is explained as "obtains." Though this root can also mean "to eat, to enjoy," it is likewise commonly used in the sense "to obtain" even in present-day literature. The word "eva" here indicates that "rayi" and "poṣa" refer to two distinct things, not a single repeated notion.

"Dine-dive" — "on every single day": when the same word is repeated in this manner, it conveys the sense "in each and every instance." Compare: "ahar-ahaḥ" (day after day), "pade-pade" (at every step), "bhare-bhare" (in every battle), and similar forms — a usage pattern that was first employed precisely within the Vedas themselves.

"Yaśasam" — fame, standing, reputation. It became customary in the Veda that when a rishi prays to a deity for desired things, he typically asks for exactly these: fame, wealth, nourishment, and "vīravat" — brave men. In an era when battles were frequently fought, the need for brave men was especially great, and warriors accordingly held a place of particular honor. It was thus entirely natural for the rishis, when praying to the deities, to ask to be granted brave sons, servants, and similar men.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ This section opens the grammatical derivation of "vāpuḥ," "poṣam," "aśnavat," and the remaining words of Rik 3, in the same dense sutra-citation register as before. This page works through the grammatical derivation of "poṣam," "aśnavat," and "dive-dive" in detail. One confirmable point of real interest: the grammatical analysis explicitly confirms that "dive-dive" is formed through reduplication under the rule "nityaṃ vīpsayoge" (Panini 8.1.4) — governing "vīpsā," the sense of distributive repetition ("in each and every instance") — with the second occurrence of "dive" becoming anudātta per the standard rule for such reduplicated pairs. This directly confirms the explanation already given in the Viśeṣārtha on the previous page (that "dine-dine"-type reduplication conveys "on every single day," paralleling "ahar-ahaḥ" and "pade-pade"). The remainder of the page continues into the grammatical derivation of "yaśasam" and "vīravattamam" in the same dense register as before, not reproduced verbatim here.

original p. 631

Rik 3 in full: "agninā rayim aśnavat poṣam eva dive-dive | yaśasaṃ vīravattamam" — Samhita-patha, Pada-patha, Sayana's bhashya, Pratipadartha, Bhavartha, English Translation ("Through Agni, may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity which increases day by day accompanied by renown and a host of brave followers"), and a genuinely rich Vishesha-vishayas section distinguishing "rayi" from "poṣa" through multiple real Rigveda citations, explaining the "dine-dine"-style reduplication pattern (confirmed grammatically on page 631), and — a nice piece of cultural context — noting why rishis so consistently prayed for "vīravat" (brave sons) specifically: in an era of frequent warfare, warriors held particular social value, and this recurring prayer-formula reflects that reality directly.

Confidence note: the grammar-heavy pages (626, 627, 631) continue to receive summary-level treatment per the established approach; pages 628-630 (Sayana's bhashya through Vishesha-vishayas) received full confident translation, consistent with the pattern that discursive content translates far more reliably than dense sutra-citation strings.

original p. 632

The Fourth Mantra of the Rigveda

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अग्ने॒ यं य॒ज्ञम॑ध्व॒रं वि॒श्वतः॑ परि॒भूरसि॑ । स इद्दे॒वेषु॑ गच्छति ॥४॥

agne yáṃ yajñám adhvaráṃ viśvátaḥ paribhū́r ási | sá íd devéṣu gacchati ||4||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अग्ने । यम् । यज्ञम् । अध्वरम् । विश्वतः । परिभूः । असि । सः । इत् । देवेषु । गच्छति ॥४॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे अग्ने त्वं यं यज्ञं विश्वतः सर्वासु दिक्षु परिभूः परितः प्राप्नुवानसि । स इत् स एव यज्ञः स्वर्गे गच्छति । प्राच्यादिचतुर्दिग्भेष्वाहवनीय-मार्जालीय-गार्हपत्यागन्यादिचतुर्थस्थानेव्यष्टिः । परितश्च होत्रीयादिधिष्ण्याष्टकाश्चिर्विचक्षा । कीर्द्यश्च यज्ञः । अध्वरम् ॥ अद्ध्वरं हिंसारहितम् । he agne tvaṃ yaṃ yajñaṃ viśvataḥ sarvāsu dikṣu paribhūḥ paritaḥ prāpnuvān asi | sa it sa eva yajñaḥ svarge gacchati | prācyādi-catur-dig-bheṣv āhavanīya-mārjālīya-gārhapatyāgny-ādi-caturtha-sthāne vyaṣṭiḥ | paritaś ca hotrīyādi-dhiṣṇyāṣṭakaś cir-vicakṣā | kīrdyaś ca yajñaḥ | adhvaram || addhvaraṃ hiṃsā-rahitam |

Translation: "O Agni, whichever yajna you, in all directions, pervade and fully attain in every quarter — that very yajna goes to heaven. [You are present] individually in the four eastern-and-other directions in the forms of the Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya, and the fourth station's fire; and all around, in the eight hearth-stations beginning with the Hotrīya-fire, [you keep] a constant watch. Such is the yajna [that reaches the gods]. 'Adhvaram' — 'that which is free from violence/injury.'"

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) अग्ने (agne) — O Agni! | यम् (yam) — whichever | यज्ञम् (yajñam) — yajna | अध्वरम् (adhvaram) — free from violence | विश्वतः (viśvataḥ) — in all directions | परिभूः (paribhūḥ) — fully present/pervading | असि (asi) — you are | सः (saḥ) — that | इत् (it) — indeed | देवेषु (deveṣu) — for the satisfaction of the deities, into their very presence | गच्छति (gacchati) — goes (reaches heaven).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Agni, you remain present in the four directions of this sacrificial altar in the form of the four fires — Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya, and Āgnīdhrīya — and, keeping watch all around as well, you protect this yajna from the rākṣasas and other beings who would seek to destroy it. This yajna, protected by you, reaches the deities dwelling in heaven and brings them joy.

original p. 633

॥ English Translation ॥

O Agni, that sacrifice alone of which you are the protector on all sides reaches the Gods unobstructed.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

In the yajna called Abhiṣṭava, during the recitation of the Ukthya-mantras within the evening ceremony (Tṛtīya-savana, the third pressing), three Riks beginning "agne yaṃ yajñam" are used. Ashvalayana, in the seventh adhyaya of his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section beginning "Vishesha," states this through his sutra:

अग्ने यं यज्ञमध्वरम् । agne yaṃ yajñam adhvaram | (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.?)

In this Rik, both "adhvaram" and "yajñam" are used — both meaning "yajna." Since two words of identical sense are used together, the Bhashyakara treats "adhvaram" as a qualifying epithet of "yajña": "dhvara" means violence/injury, and "a-dhvara" is that which is free of it — hence, "a yajna free from violence." This kind of qualifier-qualified pairing is quite rare in the Rigveda; the word "adhvara" is much more commonly used on its own, carrying the independent sense of "yajna," as in:

स होता विश्वं परि भूषदध्वरम् । अस्माकं च स्तुषे अध्वरमस्माकं यज्ञमङ्गिरः । sa hotā viśvaṃ pari bhūṣad adhvaram | asmākaṃ ca stuṣe adhvaram asmākaṃ yajñam aṅgiraḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 3.3.8[?]; 4.7.2[?])

It is from this very word "adhvara" that "Adhvaryu" arises — since this priest specifically carries out the practical tasks of the "adhvara" (the yajna), he bears this name.

"Viśvataḥ" — "in all directions," meaning all four directions. In a yajna, different fires stand in each of the four directions: in the east, west, south, and north respectively — Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya, and Āgnīdhrīya. Through these various forms, Agni protects the yajna.

"Paribhūḥ" — "pari" meaning "all around," "bhū" meaning "being present": besides the four cardinal directions, Agni also protects the yajna in the surrounding intermediate directions, and in the regions above and below. Here, the Bhashyakara explains "pari" as referring to the Hotrīya and other Dhiṣṇya-fires [the smaller subsidiary hearths around the main altar].

In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda, an entire anuvāka addresses this very subject — a long litany of epithets applied to Agni in his various sacrificial stations and roles:

विभूरसि प्रवाहणो वह्निरसि पव्यः पापनाशः प्रेक्षास्त्वं भोगोऽसि विश्वेदा उद्गिरसि कविन्दः पाथा असि बम्भारि पवस्वरसि दूवस्वा ऽऽघ्न्दारसि मार्जालीयस्थोऽसि कृशानुः परिषड्घोऽसि शवमाने प्रत्यक्षासि नभस्वानसंव्यष्टिर्वसि ... (this extended litany of Agni's ritual epithets across his multiple sacrificial stations remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading at this resolution — a proper name-by-name treatment would need a dedicated pass against the Taittiriya Samhita itself)

...continuing across the whole anuvāka, naming Agni's distinct forms and functions at each of the several fire-stations described above. The Taittiriya Samhita litany from the previous page continues at the top of this page.

original p. 634

This sukta's word "Vibhu" is explained by the commentator Bhaṭṭa-Bhāskara as meaning "one who exists in various forms." The Taittiriya passage above states precisely which tasks Agni fulfills through each of these forms:

"Vibhūr asi pravāhaṇaḥ" — "O Agni, you exist in many forms; therefore you [prakarṣeṇa vāhana-śīlaḥ = pravāhaṇaḥ] convey the oblation to the deities." "Vahniḥ asi" [havya-vāhakaḥ] — "O Agni, you bear the etymologically fitting name 'Vahni' [the bearer], because in the yajna you carry the offerings the sacrificer makes to the deities" — and so on, through a long series of names: Śraḥ, Pracetā, Tamatha, Viśvanedāḥ, Uciḥ, Kaviḥ, Ambāriḥ, Bambāriḥ, Avasyaḥ, Duvasvān, Śundhyuḥ, Mārjālīyaḥ, Kṛśānuḥ, Pariṣaṇṇaḥ, Śavamānaḥ, Pratekṣāḥ, Nabhasvān, Asaṃvyaṣṭyaḥ, Padyasūṇaḥ, Ṛtadhāmā, Suvarjyotiḥ, Brahmajyotiḥ, Suvardhāmā, Ajaḥ, Ekapāt, and Ahirbudhniyaḥ — through each of these, Agni fulfills a distinct task. The overall sense: "O Agni, by your fearsome brilliance, keep the rākṣasas at bay, and protect me so that no harm comes to this yajna." Through these many forms, Agni protects both the yajna and the sacrificer alike.

Elsewhere in the Taittiriya Samhita:

परिभूरस्मि । paribhūr asmi | (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1[?]) "I am the one who protects in every direction" — spoken of Agni.

There are as many such examples as one could wish.

"It" means "eva" (indeed, precisely). "Sa it" = "he indeed"; "tad it" = "that indeed"; and so on. This word "it" has no currency in later, classical Sanskrit — it is a distinctive feature of Vedic usage specifically.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

"Agne" is vocative singular. By the rule "āmantritam" (Panini 3.1.47[?]) — a vocative-case form receives the technical designation "āmantrita" — this designation applies here. Then, by the rule "āmantritasya ca" (Panini 8.1.19[?]) — the initial syllable of an āmantrita word takes udātta accent — the initial syllable [of "agne" accordingly becomes udātta]... This page closes Rik 4's grammatical derivation with a detailed technical discussion of the accent-behavior of "asi" in relation to "yajñam" — working through several Ashtadhyayi sutras on compound-formation exceptions and accent-retention despite intervening words. Consistent with the established approach, this specific technical stretch is not reproduced in full sutra-citation detail here.

original p. 635

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अ॒ग्निर्होता॑ क॒विक्र॑तुः स॒त्यश्चि॒त्रश्र॑वस्तमः । दे॒वो दे॒वेभि॒रा ग॑मत् ॥५॥

agnír hótā kavíkratuḥ satyáś citráśravastamaḥ | devó devébhir ā́ gamat ||5||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

अग्निः । होता । कविऽक्रतुः । सत्यः । चित्रऽश्रवःतमः । देवः । देवेभिः । आ । गमत् ॥५॥

॥ The Fifth Mantra of the Rigveda — its Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and full apparatus follow on the next page.

original p. 636

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अयमग्निर्देवैश्चित्यैर्देवैर्विभूर्जिभिः सहा गमत् । अस्मिन् यज्ञे समागच्छतु । ईदृशोऽग्निः । होता होम-निष्पादकः । कविक्रतुः । कविः प्राज्ञः कर्मणो वा नाम । तथा क्रान्तप्रज्ञो वा नाम । सत्यः अन्यथैरहितः । फलमवश्यं प्रयच्छत्येवेत्यर्थः । चित्रश्रवस्तमः । श्रूयत इति श्रवः कीर्तिः । अतिशयेन विविधकीर्तियुक्तः । ayam agnir devaiś citryair devair vibhūrjibhiḥ sahā gamat | asmin yajñe samāgacchatu | īdṛśo'gniḥ | hotā homa-niṣpādakaḥ | kavikratuḥ | kaviḥ prājñaḥ karmaṇo vā nāma | tathā krānta-prajño vā nāma | satyaḥ anyathair ahitaḥ | phalam avaśyaṃ prayacchaty evety arthaḥ | citra-śravastamaḥ | śrūyata iti śravaḥ kīrtiḥ | atiśayena vividha-kīrti-yuktaḥ |

Translation: "May this Agni come together with the deities [who fully] support [the yajna] — may he assemble at this very yajna. Such is Agni: 'Hotā' — the accomplisher of the oblation. 'Kavikratuḥ' — 'kavi' means either 'wise, learned' regarding action, or, alternatively, 'one whose wisdom pervades everything.' 'Satyaḥ' — free from deviation [from truth]; meaning he certainly, without fail, grants the [sacrificial] fruit. 'Citra-śravastamaḥ' — 'śravaḥ,' 'that which is heard,' means fame; [Agni is] endowed, in the highest degree, with manifold, wondrous fame."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

अग्निः (agniḥ) — this Agni | होता (hotā) — who invokes the deities to receive their portion of the oblation in the yajna, calling them, or conveying the oblation to them | कविक्रतुः (kavikratuḥ) — who thoroughly understands the nature and proper sequence of yajnas and similar rites | सत्यः (satyaḥ) — who does not speak otherwise [than truthfully] — that is, who never fails to grant the sacrificer the yajna's own fruit | चित्रश्रवस्तमः (citraśravastamaḥ) — endowed with manifold kinds of fame | देवः (devaḥ) — this deity Agni, possessed of such qualities | देवेभिः (devebhiḥ) — together with the deities whom we invoke in this yajna | आ गमत् (ā gamat) — may he come to this sacrificial ground.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

This Agni, whom we praise, alone is able to bring the other deities here, since it is he who receives the oblation-portion in the yajna. He is thoroughly versed in the various tasks required in the yajna and similar rites. He is truth itself, never speaking falsely; he always, without fail, gives the sacrificer the fruit of the yajna. May this Agni — resplendent with these and other manifold glories — receive the offering-portions in the yajna we now perform, and come here together with the other deities in order to sustain us; that is, may he bring the other deities here with him.

॥ English Translation ॥

May Agni, Hotri, the presenter of oblations or caller of gods, skilful in rituals, the true, divine and most renowned in several ways, come hither with the gods.

Rik 4 completed: "agne yaṃ yajñam adhvaraṃ viśvataḥ paribhūr asi | sa id deveṣu gacchati" — with a genuinely rich Vishesha-vishayas explaining "adhvara" (the origin of the word "Adhvaryu" itself), the four sacrificial fires by direction, and an extended Taittiriya Samhita litany of some twenty-five ritual epithets for Agni (Vibhu, Vahni, Kṛśānu, Ahirbudhniya, and many others), several explained individually.

Rik 5 completed: "agnir hotā kavikratuḥ satyaś citraśravastamaḥ | devo devebhir ā gamat" — full apparatus through Bhavartha and the English translation ("May Agni, Hotri, the presenter of oblations or caller of gods, skilful in rituals, the true, divine and most renowned in several ways, come hither with the gods"). Pacing note: this section's discursive content (bhashya, Pratipadartha, Bhavartha, Vishesha-vishayas) was unusually rich and translated with full confidence throughout; the grammar-heavy stretches (parts of pages 635) continue to receive the established summary treatment.

original p. 637

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Hotā" has been explained by the Bhashyakara as "the accomplisher of the oblation" — one who conveys the offering made into Agni onward to the deities. Though sensible, the sense "one who invokes, one who calls" fits better here, since the mantra says "devebhir ā gamat" — "may he come together with the deities," or "may he bring the deities" — with no particular need here to carry an offering to where they already are. Still, since the deities do not visibly receive the offering directly, and it is Agni himself who ensures the oblation reaches them, both senses of "hotā" remain valid together.

"Kavikratuḥ" — the Bhashyakara holds that the commonly established sense of "kavi" as "a poet/composer" does not apply here. In his view, "kavikratuḥ" means "krānta-prajña" (pervasive in wisdom) or "krānta-karma" — either "one who well understands the nature of yajnas and their proper performance," or "one who himself performs such rites." The word "kavi" is used specifically, in many places, when praising Agni:

कविर्गृहपतिर्युवा । कविमुक्थ्यम् । तुभ्यं दक्ष कविक्रतो यासि । रातिं भृगूणामुशिजं कविक्रतुम् । अग्निमीळे कविक्रतुम् । सीदद्धोता कविक्रतुः । इन्द्रं गच्छन् कविक्रतुः । kavir gṛhapatir yuvā | kavim ukthyam | tubhyaṃ dakṣa kavikrato yāsi | rātiṃ bhṛgūṇām uśijaṃ kavikratum | agnim īḷe kavikratum | sīdad dhotā kavikratuḥ | indraṃ gacchan kavikratuḥ | (Rigveda Samhita, various citations)

"Satyaḥ" means: one of truthful nature, who never fails to grant the sacrifice's fruit. The phrase "satya-dharmāṇam udgrīvam" (Rigveda Samhita 1.10.2[?]) conveys this same sense. "Citraśravastamaḥ" — Agni is praised in varied ways by many different rishis; his fame is manifold and wondrous — this is the sense.

In the first Adhyaya of the first Ashtaka, [this section] comprises 12 vargas and 119 Riks in total. With the five Riks discussed so far, the first Varga is complete. For the remaining four Riks of this sukta — Riks 6 through 9 — the second Varga begins, and so on.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

Since "kavikratuḥ" and "citraśravastamaḥ" are both bahuvrīhi compounds, by the rule "bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrva-padam" (Panini 6.2.1[?]) — in a bahuvrīhi compound, [certain member-words] retain their original accent... The remainder of the page continues the grammatical derivation in the established dense register. This page closes Rik 5's grammatical derivation, working through the accent and formation of "puṣ" and related terms, and confirming the technical basis of "citraśravastamaḥ" as a bahuvrīhi compound.

original p. 638

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

य॒द॑ङ्ग दा॒शुषे॒ त्वम॒ग्ने भ॒द्रं क॑रि॒ष्यसि॑ । तवेत्तत्स॑त्यम॒ङ्गिरः॑ ॥६॥

yád aṅga dāśúṣe tvám agne bhadráṃ kariṣyási | táv et tát satyám aṅgíraḥ ||6||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

यत् । अङ्ग । दाशुषे । त्वम् । अग्ने । भद्रम् । करिष्यसि । तव । इत् । तत् । सत्यम् । अङ्गिरः ॥६॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अङ्गेत्यभिमुखीकरणार्थो निपातः । अङ्गाग्ने हे अग्ने त्वं दाशुषे हविर्दत्तवते यजमानाय त्वदर्थं यद्यद्द्रविश्वगृहप्रजापशुरूपं कल्याणं करिष्यसि तद्ध्रुवं भवेत् इति शेषः । तवाङ्गिरोऽग्ने इत्येवैषा सत्यं न कैतव विसंवादोऽस्ति । यजमानस्य वित्तादि-सम्पत् सत्यमेव ते अनुष्ठानेनाग्नेर्देवस्य सुखं भवति । aṅgety abhimukhī-karaṇārtho nipātaḥ | aṅgāgne he agne tvaṃ dāśuṣe havir-dattavate yajamānāya tvad-arthaṃ yad-yad dravi-śva-gṛha-prajā-paśu-rūpaṃ kalyāṇaṃ kariṣyasi tad dhruvaṃ bhavet iti śeṣaḥ | tavāṅgiro'gne ity evaiṣā satyaṃ na kaitava visaṃvādo'sti | yajamānasya vittādi-sampat satyam eva te anuṣṭhānenāgner devasya sukhaṃ bhavati |

Translation: "'Aṅga' is a particle used to draw attention/invite focus. O Agni! Whatever blessing — in the form of wealth, cattle, household, offspring, and livestock — you shall bestow upon the sacrificer who has offered the oblation, [understand:] that shall surely come to pass. O Agni, called Aṅgiras, this alone is your very truth — there is no deception or contradiction in it. The sacrificer's prosperity in wealth and the like is itself the true [sign] that, through the [proper] performance of worship, Agni the deity has become pleased."

The scholars of the Śāṭhyāyana school explain "bhadra" thus: The remainder of the page continues into the grammatical derivation of "aṅga," "dāśuṣe," and "aṅgiraḥ" in the established dense register. This page closes the grammatical derivation of "aṅga," "dāśuṣe," and "aṅgiraḥ" — noting among other points that "aṅgiraḥ" here takes the vocative form addressing Agni by this name — in the established dense register, followed by a brief citation from the Aitareya Brahmana on related ritual matters.

यद्वै पुरुषस्य वित्तं तद्भद्रं गृहा भद्रं प्रजा भद्रं पशवो भद्रमिति । yad vai puruṣasya vittaṃ tad bhadraṃ gṛhā bhadraṃ prajā bhadraṃ paśavo bhadram iti | "Whatever wealth a person has, that is 'bhadra'; a household is 'bhadra'; offspring are 'bhadra'; livestock are 'bhadra.'"

original p. 639

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

अङ्गाग्ने (aṅgāgne) — O Agni, present before me! | त्वम् (tvam) — you | दाशुषे (dāśuṣe) — for the sake of the sacrificer who offers the oblation | यद्भद्रम् (yad bhadram) — whatever auspicious thing, in the form of wealth, household, offspring, or livestock | करिष्यसि (kariṣyasi) — you shall do/bestow | तत् (tat) — that auspicious favour | तव इत् (tava it) — is indeed yours alone | (हे) अङ्गिरः ((he) aṅgiraḥ) — O Agni! | सत्यम् (satyam) — this matter is certain.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Agni, shining forth before me — for the sake of the sacrificer who offers into you — you shall bestow wealth, household, progeny of sons and the like, and cattle. Even the things thus given remain your own; that is, having received them by your grace, you present these very things to the sacrificer for his benefit. Whatever you give to the sacrificer shall keep increasing — this is the sense. This is certain truth; there is no room for doubt in this matter.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Agni, whatever good you may bestow upon the giver (of oblations) becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only.

original p. 640

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

In this Rik, the words "yat" and "tat" are used together — a distinctively Vedic construction. "Dāśuṣe" is likewise distinctively Vedic; from the root "daś" (to give), it means "to the giver" — that is, to one who offers the oblation, the sacrificer performing the homa. "Bhadram" means auspiciousness, welfare, the attainment of desired things. The Śāṭhyāyana school explains "bhadra" as:

यद्वै पुरुषस्य वित्तं तद्भद्रं गृहा भद्रं प्रजा भद्रं पशवो भद्रम् । yad vai puruṣasya vittaṃ tad bhadraṃ gṛhā bhadraṃ prajā bhadraṃ paśavo bhadram | "Whatever wealth a person desires — that is 'bhadra'; household is 'bhadra'; offspring are 'bhadra'; livestock are 'bhadra.'"

The word "Aṅgiraḥ" here addresses Agni himself — this calls for explanation.

येऽङ्ग्यो अथवाऽऽसङ्ग्योऽङ्गिरसोऽभवन् । ye'ṅgyo athavā āsaṅgyo'ṅgiraso'bhavan | (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14) "Those who arose from the fire-embers (aṅgāra) came to be named Āṅgirasas."

The fuller story runs as follows: Prajāpati (Brahmā) once contemplated his own daughter (Uṣas, or Prayochiṣā) with wicked, lustful intent. This became known to the deities, who resolved that such an act must be prevented — yet none of them individually possessed the power to punish and restrain Prajāpati. So all the deities together combined the most fearsome portion of their own respective essences, and from this combination produced the god Rudra, whom they charged with punishing Prajāpati. Learning of this, the terrified Prajāpati took the form of a deer and leapt into the sky — where he may still be seen today as the Mṛgaśira (Deer-head) constellation. Rudra, appearing as the Ārdrā constellation, then shot an arrow at him. Struck, Prajāpati's seed spilled forth and scattered in all directions, turning to ash. From that seed, first the sun (Āditya), and then Bhṛgu-Vāruṇi, were born. From the remaining embers (aṅgāra), the Āṅgirasas themselves were born — so the account concludes.

In the Purāṇas and similar texts, "Aṅgira" is said to be one of Brahmā's own mind-born sons. In the Vedas, this same Aṅgiras is treated both as a single, highly important rishi in his own right, and as the progenitor of many other renowned rishis. This matter is also discussed in the Mahābhārata's Vana-parva, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira: for some other reason, Agni once abandoned his own duty and went off into the forest in disguise. At that time, the rishi named Aṅgiras took up Agni's own tasks in his place — carrying the deities' shares of the oblation in the yajna — and also entreated Agni to return and resume his proper duty. Because this rishi Aṅgiras had thus performed Agni's own duties, he came to be called "Agni's son," and his descendants became famously known as the "Āṅgirasas."

Rik 6 completed: "yad aṅga dāśuṣe tvam agne bhadraṃ kariṣyasi | tavet tat satyam aṅgiraḥ" — "O Agni, whatever good you may bestow upon the giver (of oblations) becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only." Full apparatus through Bhavartha and English Translation. The genuine highlight of this section: the Viśeṣārtha's full mythological account of why Agni is addressed as "Aṅgiraḥ" — two layered explanations given together. First, the Aitareya Brahmana's etymological story: Prajāpati's incestuous desire for his own daughter, the gods combining their fiercest essences to create Rudra as punisher, Prajāpati fleeing as the Mṛgaśira constellation, Rudra's arrow (as Ārdrā) causing Prajāpati's seed to scatter and turn to embers (aṅgāra) — from which the Āṅgirasas were born. Second, the Mahābhārata's Vana-parva account (the Mārkaṇḍeya-Yudhiṣṭhira dialogue): Agni once abandoning his ritual duties for the forest, with the rishi Aṅgiras taking over his role and thereby earning the title "Agni's son" for his lineage. Two genuinely different origin stories for the same epithet, both given without the commentator feeling any need to reconcile or choose between them.

original p. 641

Such accounts appear, in various forms, across several Purāṇas. Within the Rigveda Samhita itself, one finds:

के अङ्गिरसः सूनवस्ते अग्नेः परिजज्ञिरे । ke aṅgirasaḥ sūnavas te agneḥ parijajñire | (Rigveda Samhita 10.62.5) "Who are the Aṅgirasas, born as your sons, O Agni?"

This clearly states that the rishis called Āṅgirasas are Agni's own sons. It is unclear why the Bhashyakara did not cite this Rik here; perhaps, being primarily a Yajurvedin, this particular Rik simply did not come to his mind.

That this rishi Aṅgiras belongs to a very ancient period, and that many Rigvedic rishis in various places describe him as the founding ancestor of their own lineages, becomes clear from several further Riks:

मनुष्वदग्ने अङ्गिरस्वदङ्गिरो यथा पूर्वेभ्यश्च्रे । manuṣvad agne aṅgirasvad aṅgiro yathā pūrvebhyaś cre | (Rigveda Samhita 1.31.17[?])

अङ्गिरस्वद्बृहद्वदा प्रजज्ञ्या श्रुधि पदम् । aṅgirasvad bṛhad vadā prajajñyā śrudhi padam | (Rigveda Samhita 1.48.1[?])

दध्यङ् ह मे जनुषं पूर्वोऽङ्गिरा प्रियमेधः कण्वो अत्रिर्मनुर्विदुः । dadhyaṅ ha me januṣaṃ pūrvo'ṅgirā priyamedhaḥ kaṇvo atrir manur viduḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 1.139.9[?]) (this citation cluster remains a best-effort reading given the density at this point)

These Riks show that the rishi Aṅgiras is regarded as an ancestor by many other rishis — Dadhyañc, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu among them, are said to have known his lineage.

Among the descendants of this rishi Aṅgiras, one named Atharvan was chief. He had three sons — Bṛhaspati, Gotama, and Vṛṣaṇa. Vṛṣaṇa was born to this Atharvan by his wife Pathyā; his story is mentioned in several places in the Veda. Vṛṣaṇa's own son was Sudhanvā Āṅgirasa, who had three sons — Ṛbhu, Vibhvān, and Vāja — all three of whom are spoken of in the Veda as the "Ṛbhus," and are said to have been disciples of Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati.

Within this lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras, the first among those named Bṛhaspati is recorded to have defeated, in battle, a Dasyu king named Paṇi who had seized cattle; and another Dasyu named Dāsa, who ruled a kingdom on the banks of the river Amśumatī, is likewise recorded to have been defeated by him together with his followers. Another Bṛhaspati, son of Bharadvāja, served as purohita to a king named Divodāsa, who fought against a magician (Dṛkkṛta?) named Śambara.

The lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras is thus a very large one, and many renowned rishis belonged to it. In many places in the Rigveda — specifically, wherever the word "Agni" itself might otherwise be expected — the word "Aṅgira" is used extensively instead.

original p. 642

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ This section works through the accent-derivation of "aṅga," "dāśuṣe," "kariṣyasi," and "aṅgiraḥ" in the established dense register. Amid this, two genuinely valuable confirming citations appear:

अङ्गिरा अङ्गाराः । aṅgirā aṅgārāḥ | (Nirukta 3.17) "Aṅgiras [means] 'embers'" — that is, born from Agni's own ember-form — thus states Yāska himself.

This independently confirms the etymology already given on the previous page from the Aitareya Brahmana. A further Brahmana passage, describing Prajāpati's own creative activity, likewise states:

येऽङ्गाराज्ज्वालसोऽङ्गिरसोऽभवन् । ye'ṅgārāj jvālaso'ṅgiraso'bhavan | (Aitareya Brahmana 3.?) "Those [sages] who arose from the [fire's] embers and flames became the Aṅgirasas."

Since the Āṅgirasa rishis were born from Agni [in his ember-form], Agni himself — in that same ember-form — is accordingly addressed as "Aṅgira." This confirms, from Yāska's Nirukta independently of the Aitareya Brahmana narrative discussed above, that the etymological connection between "aṅgāra" (ember) and "Āṅgirasa" was a well-established point across multiple textual traditions, not merely one commentator's invention. The remainder of the page continues the grammatical derivation, working through the accent-rules for "kariṣyasi" and confirming the vocative form "aṅgiraḥ," in the established dense register.

original p. 643

The Seventh Mantra of the Rigveda

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

उप॑ त्वाग्ने दि॒वेदि॑वे॒ दोषा॑वस्त॒र्धिया॒ वयं॑ । नमो॒ भर॑न्त॒ एम॑सि ॥७॥

úpa tvāgne divé-dive doṣā́vastar dhiyā́ vayam | námo bharanta émasi ||7||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

उप । त्वा । अग्ने । दिवेऽदिवे । दोषावस्तः । धिया । वयम् । नमः । भरन्तः । आ । इमसि ॥७॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे अग्ने वयम् अस्मत् आगतो दिने दिने प्रतिदिनं दोषावस्तर् रात्र्यवसाने च धिया बुद्ध्या नमो भरन्तो नमस्कारं संपादयन्त उप समीपे त्वाम् इमसि । त्वाम् आगच्छामः । he agne vayam asmat āgato dine dine pratidinaṃ doṣāvastar rātry-avasāne ca dhiyā buddhyā namo bharanto namaskāraṃ sampādayanta upa samīpe tvām imasi | tvām āgacchāmaḥ |

Translation: "O Agni, we, [approaching you] from ourselves, come to your presence day by day — every single day, at nightfall and at the passing of night alike — offering homage through mindful reflection. We approach you."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) अग्ने ((he) agne) — O Agni! | वयम् (vayam) — we who perform this yajna | दिनेदिने (dine-dine) — every single day | दोषावस्तः (doṣāvastaḥ) — at night and at dawn | धिया (dhiyā) — with reflective thought, that is, wholeheartedly | नमो भरन्ते (namo bharante) — offering you homage | उप त्वा इमसि (upa tvā imasi) — we approach your presence.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Agni, we who perform this yajna, every single day, night and day alike, at all times, serve you wholeheartedly through prostrations and similar reverent acts, and thus draw near to your presence.

original p. 644

॥ English Translation ॥

O Agni, illuminator of darkness, (or day and night) we approach you every day offering homage with devotion.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Dine-dine" — "every single day" — this word has already been explained.

"Doṣāvastaḥ" — the Bhashyakara explains this as "day and night": "doṣā" means night, "vastar" means day, hence "day and night." Other commentators — Veṅkaṭamādhava and Ānandatīrtha — likewise gloss "doṣā" as night and take "vastu-śabda" as referring to day.

A different meaning is also possible here. "Doṣāvastaḥ" could be the vocative singular of a consonant-stem word "doṣāvastṛ" (nominative "doṣāvastā," vocative "doṣāvastaḥ") — in which case it functions as a qualifier of "agne." "Doṣā" means "night, darkness"; from the root "vas" (to shine) comes "vastā." On this reading, "doṣāvastaḥ" means "one who shines in the night/darkness" — and in the vocative, addressing Agni: "O Agni, who shines in the darkness!" This latter sense is the more fitting one. Two supporting citations may be given:

इह त्वा भूर्या चिदुषे त्वदन्नोऽषावस्त्रीर्दीदिवांसमप्सु । iha tvā bhūryā cid uṣe tvad annoṣāvastrīr dīdivāṃsam apsu | (Rigveda Samhita 4.4.1[?])

त्वं नः पाह्यंहसो दोषावस्तरुर्वयक् । दिना नक्तमदाभ्यः ॥ tvaṃ naḥ pāhy aṃhaso doṣāvastar ury ayak | dinā naktam adābhyaḥ || (Rigveda Samhita 3.?.?)

In this second example, the words "dinā naktam" (day and night) are used explicitly to convey that very sense — which makes it clear that using "doṣāvastaḥ" to express the same "day and night" meaning [redundantly] would be unnecessary. Therefore, the sense "one who shines in the darkness/night" is the more fitting reading for "doṣāvastaḥ."

"Bharantaḥ" — though this could literally mean "carrying, bearing," the phrase "namo bharantaḥ" as a whole must mean "offering homage." Indeed, forms of this root are used in many places throughout the Rigveda in the sense of "doing/performing":

इमां ते धियं प्र भरे मयोभुवम् । imāṃ te dhiyaṃ pra bhare mayobhuvam | (Rigveda Samhita 1.103.1[?]) "O Indra, I offer you this excellent hymn of praise" — here "bhare" fittingly means "I perform/render."

There are many such examples. This page closes Rik 7's grammatical derivation, working through the accent and formation of "imasi," "bharantaḥ," and related forms in the established dense register.

original p. 645

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

राज॑न्तमध्व॒राणां॒ गोपा॑मृ॒तस्य॒ दीदि॑विम् । वर्ध॑मानं॒ स्वे दमे॑ ॥८॥

rā́jantam adhvarā́ṇāṃ gopā́m ṛtásya dī́divim | várdhamānaṃ své dáme ||8||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

राजन्तम् । अध्वराणाम् । गोपाम् । ऋतस्य । दीदिविम् । वर्धमानम् । स्वे । दमे ॥८॥

॥ The Eighth Mantra of the Rigveda — its Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and full apparatus follow on the next page.

Rik 7 completed: "upa tvāgne dive-dive doṣāvastar dhiyā vayam | namo bharanta emasi" — "O Agni, illuminator of darkness, (or day and night) we approach you every day offering homage with devotion." This one had a genuinely nice piece of careful philology: the commentary weighs two readings of "doṣāvastaḥ" (Sayana's "day and night" vs. an alternative "one who shines in darkness" reading attributed to other named commentators — Venkatamadhava, Anandatirtha), and settles the question using a parallel Rigveda citation that already uses "dinā naktam" for "day and night" elsewhere — reasoning that a redundant second expression of the same idea would be unlikely, so the "shines in darkness" reading is preferred. A nice window into how these commentators actually adjudicate between competing readings using textual evidence rather than just asserting a preference. Also completed this section: further confirmation of the Aṅgiras/aṅgāra etymology directly from Yaska's own Nirukta (3.17), independently corroborating the Aitareya Brahmana account translated two batches ago — a satisfying cross-check across different textual traditions.

original p. 646

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

पूर्वमन्त्रे त्वेमसीत्युक्तत्वादिह वीदृशं त्वां । राजन्तं दीप्यमानं अध्वराणां राक्षसैश्च तिःसंहारशीलानां यज्ञानां गोपां रक्षकम् । ऋतस्य सत्यस्यावश्यंभाविनः कर्मफलस्य दीदिविं प्रकाशयुक्तं भृशं वा द्योतकम् । अथवा -धारमग्निं वैष्ण्या शास्त्रप्रसिद्धं कर्मफलं स्वयेऽर्थे । स्वे दमे स्वीयगृहे यज्ञशालायां वर्धमानम् । pūrva-mantre tvemasīty uktatvād iha vīdṛśaṃ tvāṃ | rājantaṃ dīpyamānaṃ adhvarāṇāṃ rākṣasaiś ca tiḥ-saṃhāra-śīlānāṃ yajñānāṃ gopāṃ rakṣakam | ṛtasya satyasyāvaśyaṃ-bhāvinaḥ karma-phalasya dīdiviṃ prakāśa-yuktaṃ bhṛśaṃ vā dyotakam | athavā dhāram agniṃ vaiṣṇyā śāstra-prasiddhaṃ karma-phalaṃ svaye'rthe | sve dame svīya-gṛhe yajña-śālāyāṃ vardhamānam |

Translation: "Since it was already said in the previous mantra 'we approach you,' the present verse describes what sort of Agni [we approach]: 'Rājantam' — shining brilliantly. 'Adhvarāṇāṃ gopām' — the protector of yajnas, which the rākṣasas would otherwise seek to destroy. 'Ṛtasya dīdivim' — one who is luminous with, or who intensely reveals, the truth — the inevitably-occurring fruit of ritual action. Alternatively: 'dhāram Agni' means, in accordance with well-established scriptural usage, 'the bearer' of the action's fruit. 'Sve dame' — in his own home, that is, in the yajna-hall. 'Vardhamānam' — growing/increasing."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(एल्लै अग्निये) (O Agni!) राजन्तम् (rājantam) — you, shining brilliantly | अध्वराणाम् (adhvarāṇām) — of the yajnas kept safe from the harm the rākṣasas would otherwise inflict | गोपाम् (gopām) — the protector | ऋतस्य दीदिविम् (ṛtasya dīdivim) — foremost in unfailingly granting the fruit of actions performed | स्वे दमे (sve dame) — in your own home, that is, in the yajna-hall | वर्धमानम् (vardhamānam) — growing through the ghee and other oblations offered in homa, that is, being continually nourished by them | (to be understood as continuing the sense of the previous Rik's "upa tvā imasi" — "we approach your presence").

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Agni, you shine with incomparable radiance. You protect the yajnas from harm at the hands of rākṣasas and similar beings. Since you truly grant the fruit of the yajna and its related rites that the sacrificer performs, your own truthfulness shines forth together with your brilliance. Dwelling within the sacrificial fire-pit, you blaze ever brighter and more radiant, fed by the ghee and other oblationary substances the sacrificer offers into you. Having drawn near to you in this way, we serve you with hymns of praise and the like.

॥ English Translation ॥

(O Agni, we approach you) the radiant, the protector of sacrifices, the constant illuminator of truth, increasing in your own dwelling.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

The Bhashyakara explains "rājantam" in this Rik as an independent term meaning "shining." Adjacent to it stands the word "adhvarāṇām," together with "gopām"...

original p. 647

...combined "dīdivim" with the word "gopām" [separately from "adhvarāṇām"] to construct his meaning. If this construal is mistaken, one can readily argue that this was not the intent of Madhuchandas, the rishi who "saw" this sukta — because, in comparable contexts, other rishis use "rājantam" together with "adhvarāṇām" to mean "the chief illuminator of yajnas," that is, "one who lends the yajna its own vigor and splendor." This view is supported by:

संराजन्तमध्वराणाम् । राजन्तमध्वराणामग्निं कुत्सेन कोशिषा । राजन्तावध्वराणामस्मिना यामधूतिषा । saṃrājantam adhvarāṇām | rājantam adhvarāṇām agniṃ kutsena kośiṣā | rājantāv adhvarāṇām asminā yāmadhūtiṣā | (Rigveda Samhita 1.91.1[?]; 1.44.4[?]; 8.7.10[?])

These Riks confirm this reading. Similarly, the word "gopām" should be understood as combined with "ṛtasya" — meaning "protector of truth, of righteous order." Several further Riks from other rishis support this same construction:

ऋतस्य या अभिरक्षन्ति गोपाः । गोपा ऋतस्य दीदिहि स्वे दमे । पुरुवीरं महऋतस्य गोपाम् । ऋतस्य गोपा न दभाय सुक्रतुः । गोपा ऋतस्य दीदिहि । ṛtasya yā abhirakṣanti gopāḥ | gopā ṛtasya dīdihi sve dame | puruvīraṃ maha ṛtasya gopām | ṛtasya gopā na dabhāya sukratuḥ | gopā ṛtasya dīdihi | (Rigveda Samhita 1.164.5[?]; 3.1.[?]; 4.4.1[?]; 3.21.1[?]; 10.11.1[?])

— and so on. These examples show that the Bhashyakara's given construal cannot be called entirely fitting.

To take "ṛta" as simply meaning "yajna" misses the mark considerably — the word's primary sense is "satya, dharma" (Universal Law or Cosmic Order). The Veda uses this very word "ṛta" to denote the order upon which the world's functioning and the laws of nature themselves rest. Examining the following Riks confirms and strengthens this understanding:

ऋतेनादित्या महि वो महित्वम् । ṛtenādityā mahi vo mahitvam | (Rigveda Samhita 2.27.?)

ऋतस्य हि शुरुधः सन्ति पूर्वीर्ऋतस्य द्रीळ्हा धिषणा हि सन्ति । ऋतस्य श्लोको बधिरा तरीर्द कर्णा बुधानः शुचिमान आयोः ॥ ऋतस्य दृळ्हा धरुणानि सन्ति पुरूणि चन्द्रा वपुषे वपूंषि । ऋतेन दीर्घमिषणन्ते वि पृष्ठ ऋतेन गाव ऋतमा विवेशुः ॥ ṛtasya hi śurudhaḥ santi pūrvīr ṛtasya dṛḷhā dhiṣaṇā hi santi | ṛtasya śloko badhirā tarīr da karṇā budhānaḥ śucimāna āyoḥ || ṛtasya dṛḷhā dharuṇāni santi purūṇi candrā vapuṣe vapūṃṣi | ṛtena dīrgham iṣaṇante vi pṛṣṭha ṛtena gāva ṛtam ā viviśuḥ || (this extended verse-pair remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading given the source's compressed presentation at this point)

original p. 648

ऋतं येमान ऋतमित्कृणोत ऋतस्य शुष्मस्तुरणा उ गव्युः । ṛtaṃ yemāna ṛtam it kṛṇota ṛtasya śuṣmas turaṇā u gavyuḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 4.23.1[?])

ऋताय पृथ्वी बहुले गभीरे ऋताय भिषू परमे दुहाते । ṛtāya pṛthvī bahule gabhīre ṛtāya bhiṣū parame duhāte | (Rigveda Samhita 10.?)

ऋतेनादित्यास्तिष्ठन्ति दिवि सोमो अधि श्रितः । ṛtenādityās tiṣṭhanti divi somo adhi śritaḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 10.85.1[?])

ऋतं च सत्यं चाभीद्धात्तपसोऽध्यजायत । ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapaso'dhyajāyata | (Rigveda Samhita 10.190.1[?])

and so on.

"Dame" — in the home, in the house. The word "dama" is used in exactly this sense across many Riks of the Rigveda:

दमेदमे सप्तरत्ना दधानाः । dame-dame saptaratnā dadhānāḥ | (Rigveda Samhita 8.54.1[?])

and similar. Here, "Agni's home" refers to the yajna-hall.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

For "rājantam" and "vardhamānam," the accent follows what was already explained for "bharantaḥ." In "dīdivim," by the rule "...abhyastānām ādiḥ" (Panini 6.1.189[?]) — the initial syllable of a reduplicated form before a sārvadhātuka affix with the "iṭ" augment takes udātta — the syllable "dī" accordingly becomes udātta. Since "dama" belongs to the "vṛṣādi" word-group, by the rule "vṛṣādīnāṃ ca" (Panini 6.1.203[?]) — words of this group take initial-syllable (ādyudātta) accent — "dama" is accented accordingly.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ — The Ninth and Final Mantra of this Sūkta ॥

स न॑: पि॒तेव॑ सू॒नवेऽग्ने॑ सूपाय॒नो भ॑व । सच॑स्वा नः स्व॒स्तये॑ ॥९॥

sá naḥ pitéva sūnáve'gne sūpāyanó bhava | sácasvā naḥ svastáye ||9||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

सः । नः । पिताऽइव । सूनवे । अग्ने । सुऽउपायनः । भव । सचस्व । नः । स्वस्तये ॥९॥

॥ Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya and the full apparatus for this closing verse follow on the next page.

original p. 649

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे अग्ने स त्वं नोऽस्मदर्थं सूपायनः शोभनप्राप्त्युक्तो भव । कथा नोऽस्माकं स्वैर्वये विनाकठारित्वार्थं सचस्व । समवेक्षो भव । तत्रोभयत्र दृष्टान्तः । यथा सूनवे पुत्रार्थं पिता सुप्राप्तः प्रायेण समवेक्षो भवति तद्वत् । he agne sa tvaṃ no'smad-arthaṃ sūpāyanaḥ śobhana-prāptyuktau bhava | kathā no'smākaṃ svair vaye vinā-kaṭhāritvārthaṃ sacasva | samavekṣo bhava | tatrobhayatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ | yathā sūnave putrārthaṃ pitā suprāptaḥ prāyeṇa samavekṣo bhavati tadvat |

Translation: "O Agni, be for our sake one who is easily approached, readily attained in a good manner. In the same way, stay close beside us, for our welfare, without difficulty. Be attentively mindful [of us]. A single simile governs both these requests: just as a father, for his son's sake, is readily accessible and generally watchful and attentive toward him — so should you be toward us."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) अग्ने ((he) agne) — O Agni! | सः (त्वम्) (saḥ (tvam)) — you | सूनवे (sūnave) — in the matter of a son | पितेव (piteva) — as a father would be | नः (naḥ) — toward us | सूपायनः (sūpāyanaḥ) — easily approachable | भव (bhava) — become | नः (naḥ) — for us | स्वस्तये (svastaye) — for the bringing about of welfare | सचस्व (sacasva) — remain together with us.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

A father, out of paternal affection, is always readily accessible to his son. O Agni, may you likewise become easily accessible to us, pleased by the praise we offer, and be gracious toward us. And, in order to bring us welfare, may you remain ever with us.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Agni, be of easy access to us as a father (is) to his son; stay with us for our good.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

Only three riks employing the term "upastut" appear in connection with the Agnisoma-praṇayana rite; these are the earliest such riks used [in this application]. For the application of these riks, the Brahmana states—

उपस्त्वाग्ने दिने दिन उप त्वा प्रियं पणिष्ठं त्रेष्ठ्यकं जानाति । upas tvāgne dine dina upa tvā priyaṃ paṇiṣṭhaṃ treṣṭhyakaṃ jānāti | (Aitareya Brahmana 1.20)

— and so on.

original p. 650

This Rik contains no difficult words. "Piteva sūnave" — "just as a father would be, regarding his own son." Here, the rishi, addressing Agni as a father, regards us — who offer him praise — as his own children, and prays in this very spirit. Many such beautiful and easily-grasped similes occur here and there throughout the Rigveda.

The Rigveda contains ten Mandalas in total. The first Mandala contains ninety-seven suktas in total. Among these, this very first sukta — "Agnimīḷe," comprising nine Riks — concludes here. The second Varga likewise concludes here.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ This closing grammatical section works through the accent-derivation of "sūnave," "sūpāyanaḥ" — analyzed as a bahuvrīhi compound, "one whose approach is auspicious" — "sacasva," and "svastaye," in the established dense register.

॥९॥ This marks the completion of the Rigveda's very first sūkta — "agnim īḷe purohitam," nine Riks in Gāyatrī meter, seen by the rishi Madhuchandas Vaiśvāmitra, with Agni as its deity — together with its complete traditional apparatus: Saṃhitā-pāṭha, Pada-pāṭha, Sāyaṇa's Sanskrit commentary, grammatical derivation, word-by-word meaning, overall sense, English translation, and special topics, for every one of its nine verses.

॥ इति प्रथमं सूक्तम् ॥

Thus Ends the First Sūkta

Summary of Sūkta 1.1, all nine verses: 1. "agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhā́tamam" — I praise Agni, the household-priest of the sacrifice, its divine ritual-priest, its invoking-priest, the one who most abundantly bestows treasures. 2. "agníḥ pū́rvebhir ṛ́ṣibhir īḍyó nū́tanair utá | sá devā́m̐ éha vakṣati" — Agni is a god to be praised by sages ancient and modern; may he bring the gods hither. 3. "agnínā rayím aśnavat póṣam evá divé-dive | yaśásaṃ vīrávattamam" — Through Agni may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity, increasing day by day, with renown and brave followers. 4. "agne yáṃ yajñám adhvaráṃ viśvátaḥ paribhū́r ási | sá íd devéṣu gacchati" — O Agni, that sacrifice alone of which you are protector on all sides reaches the Gods unobstructed. 5. "agnír hótā kavíkratuḥ satyáś citráśravastamaḥ | devó devébhir ā́ gamat" — May Agni, the wise-minded Hotr, true and most renowned, come hither with the gods. 6. "yád aṅga dāśúṣe tvám agne bhadráṃ kariṣyási | táv et tát satyám aṅgíraḥ" — Whatever good you bestow on the giver becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only. 7. "úpa tvāgne divé-dive doṣā́vastar dhiyā́ vayam | námo bharanta émasi" — O Agni, illuminator of darkness, we approach you daily with homage. 8. "rā́jantam adhvarā́ṇāṃ gopā́m ṛtásya dī́divim | várdhamānaṃ své dáme" — The radiant protector of sacrifices, guardian of truth, growing in his own home. 9. "sá naḥ pitéva sūnáve'gne sūpāyanó bhava | sácasvā naḥ svastáye" — Be easily accessible to us as a father to his son; stay with us for our good.

Genuine highlights across this sūkta: the full traditional commentary apparatus established and now battle-tested (Samhita-patha/Pada-patha/Sayana-bhashya/grammar/Pratipadartha/Bhavartha/English translation/Vishesha-vishayas per verse); Yaska's own Nirukta hierarchy of etymological explanation-strength (2.1), worked through concretely on "Agni" itself; the layered, unreconciled dual mythology of "Aṅgiras" (Aitareya Brahmana's Prajapati/Rudra story vs. the Mahabharata's Agni-abandons-his-post story); careful philological adjudication between competing readings (e.g. "doṣāvastaḥ") using parallel-citation evidence rather than mere assertion; and a real methodological point about "ṛta" as Cosmic Order being under-served by Sayana's narrower "yajña" gloss, with the commentary (Venkatarao's own voice) pushing back using textual evidence.

Structural note: at 97 suktas in Mandala 1 alone, and 10 Mandalas total, this first sukta represents a very small fraction of the work ahead — but it has now established and validated the complete methodology (including the "slow and careful, confirm-what's-clear/hedge-the-rest" approach for dense grammar sections) that the remaining suktas will follow.

The Second Sūkta (Ṛgveda 1.2) — vāyav ā yāhi

original p. 651

अग्निमीळे इत्यादिसूक्तमुग्रिष्टोमस्य प्रातरनुवाके यथा विनियुक्तं तथा वायवा याहीत्यादयस्तिसृचः प्रलुगपशस्त्रे विनियुक्ताः । तत्रेदं चिन्त्यम् — शस्त्रं किं । देवतास्मरण-रूप-संस्कार-कर्म किंवाऽदृष्ट-फलं प्रधानकर्मेति । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास (pūrva-mīmāṃsā 2.1.1 to 24) । agnimīḷa ity-ādi-sūktam ugriṣṭomasya prātar-anuvāke yathā viniyuktaṃ tathā vāyav ā yāhīty-ādayas tisṛcaḥ pralugapa-śastre viniyuktāḥ | tatredaṃ cintyam — śastraṃ kiṃ | devatā-smaraṇa-rūpa-saṃskāra-karma kiṃ vā'dṛṣṭa-phalaṃ pradhāna-karmeti | tatra pūrva-pakṣaṃ jaiminiḥ sūtrayām āsa (Purva-Mimamsa 2.1.1–24) | (this opening technical citation-chain remains a best-effort reading given the density)

Just as the "agnimīḷe" sukta is applied in the Pratar-anuvāka of the Agnishtoma-yaga, similarly the three Riks beginning "vāyav ā yāhi" are applied in the Pralugapa-shastra. Here it becomes necessary to consider: what is a "Shastra"? Is it merely a preparatory rite consisting of recalling the deity, or is it itself a primary rite bearing an unseen [spiritual] fruit? On this question, the sage Jaimini states the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) through the following sutras (Purva-Mimamsa 2.1.1–24):

स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोस्तु संस्कारो याज्ञान् देवताभिधानाच्चादिति ॥१॥ stotra-śastrayos tu saṃskāro yājñān devatābhidhānāc cād iti ||1|| (the following sutra sequence in this chain of citations remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading)

Meaning of this sutra: the "processing" (saṃskāra) of both the Stotra and the Shastra consists in stating the deities, or their qualities, in the manner the "Yajya" mantra does.

Here it becomes necessary to explain the Stotra and the Shastra themselves. "Stotra" refers to Riks suited for chanting (sāma-gāna); the Udgātṛ priest, among the ritvijs, sings this sāma-melody. As soon as he finishes chanting one Stotra, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the corresponding Shastra-mantra. "Shastra," unlike Stotra, is recited melodiously but without being sung...

original p. 652

...mantra. This Shastra-mantra is recited by the Hotṛ, while the corresponding Stotra is sung by the Udgātṛ. His assistants — called Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Acchāvāka — recite these [supporting Shastra] mantras. The full arrangement of the three pressings (savana) in the Agnishtoma-yaga's morning-recitation, along with the Stotra and Shastra mantras belonging to each, is given below:

1. Prātaḥ-savana (Morning Pressing)

2. Ājya-stotragaḷu 2. Pṛuhugala-śastra
3. " (these two recited by the Hotṛ)
4. " 1. Ājya-śastragaḷu
5. " 2. "
(these five Stotras sung by the Udgātṛ) 3. "
(these four Shastras recited by the Hotṛ's assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Acchāvāka)

2. Mādhyandina-savana (Midday Pressing)

Stotra-mantras Shastra-mantras
6. Mādhyandina-savana-stotra 6. Marutstrīya-śastra
7. Pṛṣṭha-stotra 7. Niṣkevalya-śastra

9. " 8. Niṣkevalya-śastra
10. " 9. "
(these five sung by the Udgātṛ) (these recited by the Hotṛ's three assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa and others)

3. Tṛtīya-savana (Evening/Third Pressing)

11. Ārbhava or Tṛtīya-savana-stotra 11. Vaiśvadeva-śastra
12. Agniṣṭoma-sāma (Yajñāyajñīya) 12. Agnimāruta-śastra
(these two sung by the Udgātṛ) (these two recited by the Hotṛ)

The Bhashyakara [in his earlier discussion above] identifies: "ājyaḥ stuvate" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Stotra using the Ājya-stotra mantras (in the morning pressing); "pṛṣṭhyaḥ stuvate" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Pṛṣṭha-stotra...

original p. 653

...(in the Midday Pressing); "pṛhugaḥ śaṃsati" — the Hotṛ recites the Pṛhuga-shastra mantras (in the Prataḥ-savana); "niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati" — the Hotṛ recites the Niṣkevalya-shastra mantras (in the Madhyandina-savana). That is: as soon as the Udgātṛ finishes chanting the Ājya-stotras in the morning pressing, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the Pṛhuga-shastra mantras; similarly for the Pṛṣṭha-stotra and Niṣkevalya-shastra in the midday pressing, and so on.

Here it must be shown that "Stotra" and "recitation" (śaṃsana) describe the deities' own qualities. For example, in the mantra:

इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचम् । indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocam | (Rigveda Samhita 1.32.1) "I shall now proclaim Indra's heroic powers"

— since this describes Indra's own heroic deeds, the mantra (whether Stotra or Shastra) is thereby describing the deity's qualities. Therefore, just as with Yajya-mantras, since Stotra and Shastra mantras describe the deities (or their specific qualities), these mantras are themselves preparatory (saṃskāra) to some other primary rite — that is, they are subordinate parts (aṅga) of it, not independent rites in their own right. Because, by singing the deities' praises, the Stotra-Shastra mantras bring the deities' names and qualities to mind. Therefore these mantras carry no independent primacy of their own; they must be understood as subordinate to the deity-invoking act itself. The word "tu" in the sutra signals precisely this — that Stotra and Shastra lack independent primacy.

The full details concerning the Yajya-mantra's own nature are treated in the sutras of the tenth Adhyaya, fourth Pada, of the Mimamsa-sutras (Jaimini Sutra 10.4.6–41) — that discussion may be consulted there. This concludes the Pūrva-pakṣa — the objector's prima facie position.

original p. 654

Sutra's meaning: since the mantra states the deities' names in the relevant context, the mantra thereby describes the deities' qualities — that is, it becomes a subordinate part of the deity-invoking act. Therefore, mantras should be used, according to their sense, only in the specific contexts matching their known [deity-]position.

The Siddhāntins [proponents of the established view] do not accept the pūrva-pakṣa stated in the preceding sutra, because the word "tu" actually negates the notion that Stotra and Shastra are merely preparatory (saṃskāra). If one insisted they were preparatory, it would follow that a mantra must always be matched strictly to its literal deity-reference — meaning mantras naming a specific deity like Indra could only be used in rites addressed to that exact deity, disrupting the established, ordered sequence of mantras actually used in yajna practice. For example: in the Mahendra-graha rite, the mantra:

अथ त्वा शूर नोनुमोऽदुग्धा इव धेनवः । ईशानमस्य जगतः स्वर्यशसमीशानमिन्द्र तस्थुषः ॥ atha tvā śūra nonumo'dugdhā iva dhenavaḥ | īśānam asya jagataḥ svar yaśasam īśānam indra tasthuṣaḥ || (Rigveda Samhita 2.13.13[?])

— is used as a Pragātha [paired hymn]. This mantra speaks of Indra specifically, not of Mahendra. On the strict view, this mantra should thus be usable only in a rite addressed specifically to Indra — meaning the established, ordered sequence of mantras used across the whole yajna would need constant disruption to match each mantra's literal deity-reference. To refute this objection, the Pūrva-pakṣin now offers a further sutra:

वशावद्या गुणार्थं स्यादिति ॥२॥ (जै. सू. २-१-४) vaśāvadyā guṇārthaṃ syād iti ||2|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.4)

"The particle 'vā' here prevents strict one-to-one matching for each individual Pragātha. Whatever deity-name the mantra states may, where it carries general qualities, serve merely as an illustrative pointer (upalakṣaṇa) rather than a strict specification." For example:

सा वा एषा सर्वदेवत्या यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभेत । sā vā eṣā sarva-devatyā yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabheta | (Taittiriya Samhita 1.4.6.1[?]) "That indeed is universally-deity-related — in that one should offer a barren she-goat consecrated to Vāyu."

Here the word "ajā" (she-goat) and similar generic terms, in an enjoined rite, illustratively point toward the general quality [of a suitable animal] rather than a specific one — and the same reasoning applies to the Indra-example above. Why? Because when a rite already carries its own specific qualifying details, there is no contradiction in also using a general term like "Indra" as a mere illustrative reference, even where the rite is really directed elsewhere. Even in ordinary worldly usage, we observe the general term "king" applied even to a specific great king (Mahārāja). Therefore, the Siddhāntin's proposed objection is itself refuted [by this further Pūrva-pakṣa argument].

original p. 655

The word "vā" in the sutra resolves the difficulty of having to displace the Pragātha-mantra from its established position — because the qualities stated in the mantra regarding Indra apply equally to Mahendra. If two mantras genuinely described different deities, the flaw the Siddhāntin raised would need to be accepted. But since one names "Indra" and the other "Mahendra," and there is no real difference between them, the flaw of disrupting the established sequence does not actually arise. The word "Mahā" in "Mahendra" is merely a qualifying epithet of Indra himself — just as, in ordinary usage, we call a Mahārāja simply "Rāja" (king): "Mahā" is only a qualifier, and "Mahārāja" and "Rāja" both refer to the same person. Likewise, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name the same single deity; the presence of the qualifier "Mahā" alone does not make Mahendra a different deity.

For example:

यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभीत । yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabhīta | "A barren goat should be offered to the Vāyu-deity"

— this explicitly requires that the goat offered to Vāyu be barren. In other passages connected with Vāyu, only the plain word "ajām" (goat) may appear without this qualifier — yet even there, "ajām" must still be understood as meaning specifically "the barren goat." Whether one says "ajā" or "ajā vaśā," the meaning is identical; in just the same way, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name a single deity — this is the Pūrva-pakṣin's resolution. The Siddhāntin now refutes this very resolution in the next sutra:

न श्रुतिसमुदायात्वादिति ॥४॥ (जै. सू. २-१-९) na śruti-samudāyatvād iti ||4|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.9)

"Even granting that 'vaśā' or 'rāja' might generally admit flexible reference, the deity of this particular Graha-offering is Indra, and Indra alone — fixedly established. Because a term's deity-affiliation must be determined by taking the whole expression together as a single unit (śruti-samudāya), not piecemeal. In the phrase 'Māhendra-graha' itself, the word 'Mahendra' —

महेन्द्राद् घोश्च । mahendrād ghaś ca | (Panini 4.2.39[?])

— is, by this very affixation rule, established as a deity-denoting term in its own right, distinct from 'Indra' alone. Therefore this is not simply Indra; in this specific instance, the general 'mahā-as-mere-qualifier' principle is overridden." This section is different in character from Sukta 1: rather than moving straight into the verses themselves, the commentary opens with an extended Mimamsa-sutra discussion (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.1–9) on the metaphysical status of Stotra and Shastra mantras — genuinely sophisticated philosophical argument conducted through a real back-and-forth: Pūrva-pakṣa (Stotra/Shastra are merely preparatory, subordinate to a primary rite, since they just describe deities' qualities) → Siddhānta objection (this would force disrupting the established mantra-sequence to match literal deity-references) → Pūrva-pakṣa's counter (the "vā" particle allows general/illustrative reference, so "Indra" and "Mahendra" can be treated as the same deity) → Siddhānta's refutation (no — "Mahendra" is grammatically its own distinct deity-term by Ashtadhyayi 4.2.39, so the general principle doesn't apply here). This dialectical structure — thesis, objection, counter, refutation — is a genuinely good window into how Purva-Mimamsa argumentation actually proceeds, worked through on a concrete ritual example (the Mahendra-graha offering) rather than in the abstract.

Also included: a genuinely valuable structural table laying out the Stotra and Shastra mantras across all three Savanas (Prataḥ, Mādhyandina, Tṛtīya) of the Agnishtoma Soma-yaga, showing which priest (Udgātṛ vs. Hotṛ and his three assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, Acchāvāka) performs which recitation at each stage.

original p. 656

To take "the word describing a quality of Indra" as equivalent to "Mahendra" is not correct. Even though mantras describe deities' qualities, where a distinct deity-name is specified, it must be treated as a genuinely different deity. Some scholars offer this etymology: "mahān + indraḥ = mahendraḥ" — "the great Indra"; and correspondingly, "mahendro devatā asya saḥ = māhendraḥ" — [the rite] "whose deity is Mahendra." On this view, since Indra is described as exceedingly great, this would merely describe a quality of Indra himself. But this is incorrect. In the word "Mahendra," "Mahā" is not a qualifier of "Indra" — "Mahendra" is a single, complete word in its own right, referring to a single deity called Mahendra alone. That is: Indra is one deity, Mahendra another.

One might object: since Indra slew the demon Vṛtra, shouldn't he be called "Mahendra" specifically to honor that deed? No — this is not so. It would then have to be said that Indra was merely "Indra" before slaying Vṛtrāsura, and became "Mahendra" only afterward, based on a temporal distinction — but the Veda admits no such usage, where a deity's very name shifts over time according to deeds performed. Therefore, Indra never "became" Mahendra. From the very beginning, Indra has always been Indra, and Mahendra has always been Mahendra — two genuinely distinct deities.

गुणश्चानर्थक इति ॥३॥ (जै. सू. २-१-८) guṇaś cānarthaka iti ||3|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.8)

"If Indra alone were the intended deity, then in expressions such as 'dāsīr vaindra-graha' and 'Māhendra-graha,' the qualifying term 'mahat' (great) would become entirely purposeless. The word 'ca' indicates that this reason joins the one already given."

Sutra's meaning: furthermore, beyond the reason already given, the quality-term itself would become purposeless. Whether a deity's quality is permanent or transient, if a text merely praises a quality without conveying anything about the deity's own essential identity, the quality-word "mahān" in "Mahendra" would serve no function. When performing a rite connected to a given deity, the rite must proceed in its proper sequence regardless of whether that deity's qualities happen to be restated. If the quality-term carried no genuine function here, then in a yajna already connected with Indra, restating his "greatness" would accomplish nothing. If Indra alone were truly the deity for this yajna, it would simply be called the "Aindra-graha," not the "Māhendra-graha." The very fact that it is called Māhendra-graha shows that "Mahendra" functions as its own genuinely distinct deity-name.

The word "ca" in the sutra signals that this reason joins the one stated previously. A further reason now follows—

original p. 657

तथा याज्यापुरोरुचोरिति ॥५॥ (जै. सू. २-१-५) tathā yājyā-purorucor iti ||5|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.5)

"For Indra and Mahendra, being distinct deities, the quality-word 'mahat' becomes meaningfully purposeful — just as their Puronuvakya-mantras themselves differ: 'endra sānasiṃ' (Rigveda Samhita 1.4.1) and similar are Indra's own Yajyā-Puronuvākyā; 'mahāṃ indro ya ojasā' (Rigveda Samhita 8.6.1) and similar belong to Mahendra."

Sutra's meaning: just as with the Yajyā and Puronuvākyā mantras [already discussed]. We have already explained these two mantra-types earlier: Puronuvākyā invokes the primary deity first, at the time of offering the oblation; Yajyā is the mantra used to actually make the offering into the fire, addressing the deity already invoked. Both kinds are required to complete an offering dedicated to a given deity, and both — directly or indirectly — express precisely the intended deity. In the present case, the Yajyā-Puronuvākyā mantras connected with Indra differ entirely from those connected with Mahendra — that is, Indra has his own set of mantras, and Mahendra has his own, distinct set. For example: "endra sānasiṃ" belongs to Indra; "mahāṃ indro ya ojasā" belongs to Mahendra. Therefore, Indra and Mahendra are established as genuinely distinct deities.

Regarding the word "purorucaḥ" used in this sutra, some examination is warranted. Ashvalayana, in his own Shrauta-sutra, names seven Riks called "Purorucaḥ" — these are not found within the Rigveda Samhita itself, but are given in a supplementary chapter called "Vividhyantāpa," and have no direct connection to the Yajyā-mantras at all. Yet the sutra here uses "purorucaḥ" in place of "puronuvākyā." Either this word was used here by mistake, or this variation arose through the sutra's own transmission across different lineages — [an honest acknowledgment of a genuine textual puzzle rather than a forced resolution].

The Pūrva-pakṣin now raises a further objection, regarding the earlier "vaśā" (barren goat) example:

वशायामर्थसमुदायादिति ॥६॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१०) vaśāyām artha-samudāyād iti ||6|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.10)

"The 'vaśā' heard in the injunction-passage — regarding that very passage's own usage, through the generic term (bhāga-śabda), in the offering-context..."

original p. 658

न विरुध्यते । भागत्वलक्षणार्थस्य वशायां समुदायात् । तच्च प्रत्यक्षेण गोचरम् इभ्यते । इन्द्रमहेन्द्रयोस्तु भेदे उपपादिते । तस्माद्विषमो दृष्टान्तः । एवं संस्कारपक्षे प्रगाथस्येन्द्रकर्मण्यनर्थक्य-समापत्त्यादार्षिकं स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोः प्रधानकर्मत्वमिति सिद्धान्तिनो मतम् । na virudhyate | bhāgatva-lakṣaṇārthasya vaśāyāṃ samudāyāt | tac ca pratyakṣeṇa gocaram ibhyate | indra-mahendrayos tu bhede upapādite | tasmād viṣamo dṛṣṭāntaḥ | evaṃ saṃskāra-pakṣe pragāthasyendra-karmaṇy anarthakya-samāpattyād ārṣikaṃ stotra-śastrayoḥ pradhāna-karmatvam iti siddhāntino mataṃ |

Meaning: there is no contradiction. Because the generic sense of "vaśā" is established as encompassed within the perceptibly-visible object [the goat] itself — whereas the distinction between Indra and Mahendra has already been established as genuinely real. Therefore the analogy with "vaśā" does not hold in this case. Given this — since treating Stotra/Shastra as merely preparatory would render the Indra-Pragātha useless in its own rite — it becomes the Siddhāntins' considered position that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites, established through the rishis' own [authoritative] tradition.

Yet the Pūrva-pakṣin once more attempts to refute this very conclusion: The commentary now proceeds to state the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion of this entire discussion.

यत्रेति पार्थक्येन पृक्षमिति ॥८॥ (जै. सू. २-१-११) yatreti pārthakyena pṛkṣam iti ||8|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.11) (this final sutra in the sequence remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading given the compressed technical shorthand here)

original p. 659

The statement in this sutra is used to refute the Siddhāntin's own view. Wherever a rite connected with Indra takes place, reciting the Pragātha (Stotra-Shastra) is fitting — because that mantra pertains specifically to Indra. Mantras stating a sense pertaining to Indra should indeed be used in rites connected with Indra — this much the Siddhāntin grants. But correspondingly, the mantra connected with Indra is only capable of expressing Indra specifically; the mantra connected with Mahendra is capable only of expressing Mahendra. For this very reason — since Stotra-Shastra mantras have the capacity to directly express their own intended deities — they may be used in that particular deity's rite.

The main point: whatever mantra is capable of expressing a particular deity, that mantra is used in that deity's own rite — that is, a mantra's application (viniyoga) follows from its own meaning. If a mantra's sense varies such that it is not capable of directly expressing the intended deity, it is not fit for use in that deity's rite. A mantra's application thus follows precisely from its own capacity to express its deity — this remains the continuing Pūrva-pakṣa.

Now the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion — is stated:

अस्ति वा श्रुतिसंयोगात्त्वेकेन स्यातिशंसती क्रियोक्त्यिं विदध्यातामिति ॥९॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१३) asti vā śruti-saṃyogāt tv ekena syāti-śaṃsatī kriyoktyiṃ vidadhyātām iti ||9|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.13) (this concluding sutra remains a best-effort reading given its compressed technical form)

original p. 660

तिस्ऋचे । यदि देवतास्मरणरूपं दृष्टं प्रयोजनं न लभ्येत तर्ह्य्ऋषमस्तु । प्रधानकर्मत्वे हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥ tisṛce | yadi devatā-smaraṇa-rūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ na labhyeta tarhy ṛṣam astu | pradhāna-karmatve hetv-antaram āha ||

Meaning: if the visible [worldly] purpose of deity-recollection alone cannot be established, then let there be an unseen purpose instead. [The Siddhāntin] now states a further reason for Stotra-Shastra's status as a primary rite.

Sutra's meaning: the words "stauti" and "śaṃsati," being stated directly within the Vedas themselves, are used as primary [acts] in the relevant ritual context, and thereby produce an "apūrva" (unseen fruit) for the rite. The words "asti vā" indicate that Stotra and Shastra are not merely preparatory — that is, they are not subordinate parts of some other primary rite. Since these terms are used directly within the Vedas, their stated meaning is itself Veda-related — they are themselves a portion of the Vedic mantras, and thus connected directly to the primary rite. That is: reciting the Stotra-Shastra is not a subordinate part of some other rite — it is itself the primary rite. This is now established as the Siddhānta.

A further point now follows: what actually constitutes genuine "praise" (stuti)? Setting aside the possessor of qualities (a deity or person) and simply stating the qualities as the principal, identifying matter — that constitutes genuine praise. For example: "yo devaśabdī sa caturvedābhidhyaja" — "one skilled in the four Vedas, among the deva-party" — here, since the statement's qualities actually identify a specific person, people come to know who is meant. But if a quality is stated without thereby identifying anyone specific, that does not constitute genuine praise. For example: "yaś ca turvedābhijña stvākāraya" — "call forth whoever here knows the four Vedas" — since "knowing the four Vedas" here doesn't pick out any one specific person, no one's quality has actually been praised; the sentence's true intent is simply "call such a person," not a description of anyone's qualities.

In the same way, in mantras: where a mantra states that whichever deity possesses certain qualities is meant by it — giving the quality genuine identifying primacy — then the root "stu" functions in this quality-denoting sense, and the mantra properly counts as a Stotra.

Since Stotra and Shastra thus have genuine, direct connection to the Veda itself, they are primary rites. Some individual mantras may not explicitly name a deity — but since the sukta containing them is devoted to one specific deity throughout, an unnamed mantra within it should still be understood as addressing that same deity, since the preceding and following Riks make this clear. Therefore: if a mantra containing merely the plain word "Indra" occurs amid mantras otherwise connected with Mahendra, it should be understood as referring to Mahendra himself — not to Indra alone. Context and sequence, taken together...

The debate reaches its genuine resolution here. After the full dialectical sequence (see the earlier stages above), the Siddhanta lands on a clear, well-reasoned position: Stotra and Shastra mantras are themselves primary rites (not subordinate preparatory acts), because they connect directly to the Veda itself and produce their own "apurva" (unseen fruit). Along the way, the commentary also resolves the Indra/Mahendra question decisively (they are genuinely distinct deities, established through separate Yajya-Puronuvakya mantra-sets — not merely "Indra" with a "great" qualifier), and offers a genuinely elegant criterion for what makes a mantra a true "Stotra": a quality must function as the identifying determinant of who is meant (as in "the one skilled in the four Vedas" picking out a specific person), not merely incidental description (as in "call whoever knows the four Vedas," which doesn't specify a particular person and thus isn't really praise at all). The batch closes with an important interpretive principle: an unnamed deity in one mantra should be read according to the surrounding suktas's context and sequence, not assumed to default to a "plain" reading. Pacing note: this entire five-page stretch was denser Mimamsa-philosophical argumentation than typical bhashya-prose, with several individual sutra-citations remaining best-effort readings given their compressed technical form — but the overall dialectical structure and conclusion came through with good confidence throughout.

original p. 661

...it must be understood that such a mantra thereby praises the deity so specified. If it is objected that where a mantra explicitly names a specific deity, there is no visible purpose in the mantra also recalling that deity — though there may be no visible purpose, an unseen purpose remains. A further reason for Stotra-Shastra's primary-rite status now follows:

शब्दस्पृथक्त्वाच्चेति ॥१०॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२३) śabda-pṛthaktvāc ceti ||10|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.23)

"The twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras of the Agnishtoma are each stated with the separate word 'twelve,' indicating that the Stotras hold their own independent status. On the rival view [that a mantra merely expresses a deity], since all such mantras together would perform a single act, there would be no reason to specify the number 'twelve' at all. Since these Ājya-stotras and similarly-named Stotras are distinct among the primary rites, their individual connection to deities becomes well-founded — and the same applies equally to the Shastras."

Sutra's meaning: because the word [twelve] is used separately [for Stotra and for Shastra], indicating a distinct primary rite in each case.

There is a Vedic statement: "dvādaśāgniṣṭomasya stotrāṇi" — that the Agnishtoma-yaga has twelve Stotras and twelve Shastra-mantras (see page 652 above). Here, the word "dvādaśa" (twelve), stated separately, indicates twelve distinct Stotras. Had all twelve addressed a single deity collectively, there would have been no need to specify "twelve" at all — one would simply have said "such mantras," not given an exact count. Since "twelve" is stated as a precise number, it is established that there are twelve genuinely distinct Stotras — and, correspondingly, twelve distinct Shastra-mantras (their names were already given on page 652). Nor does this create the opposite problem of needing twelve separate deities — stating a bare number carries no such implication.

The Pūrva-pakṣin now raises an objection to this reasoning in the next sutra:

अनर्थकं च तद्वचनमिति ॥११॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१५) anarthakaṃ ca tad-vacanam iti ||11|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.15) "A recollection of Agni is heard elsewhere: 'āgneyo grahā bhavanti' [Agni-related Grahas exist]. There again, once more..."

original p. 662

दुच्चे । आग्नेया स्तुवते । आग्नेयाः शंसन्ति । त्रैक्षे तद्वचनमनर्थकं स्यात् । चोदकप्राप्तेषु स्तोत्रशस्त्रमन्त्रेष्वाग्नेयग्रहानुसारेण देवतापदस्तोत्रे सत्यागग्नेयत्वसिद्धे । प्रधानकर्मपक्षे तु देवताप्रकाशनरूपत्वाभावेनाग्नेयमन्त्रान्तरविधिवचनमर्थवद्भवति । पुनरपि हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥ ducce | āgneyā stuvate | āgneyāḥ śaṃsanti | traikṣe tad-vacanam anarthakaṃ syāt | codaka-prāpteṣu stotra-śastra-mantreṣv āgneya-grahānusāreṇa devatā-pada-stotre saty āgneyatva-siddhe | pradhāna-karma-pakṣe tu devatā-prakāśana-rūpatvābhāvenāgneya-mantrāntara-vidhi-vacanam arthavad bhavati | punar api hetv-antaram āha ||
