Meaning: on the objector's view, this second statement becomes purposeless. Since Agni's identity as the deity is already established from the earlier "Agneya-graha" passage, this separate injunction naming Agni-related mantras again would be redundant if Stotra-Shastra merely served to "illuminate" a deity. But on the primary-rite view, this separate statement genuinely serves a purpose. A further reason follows.

Sutra's meaning: in such a context, that statement would [on the rival view] become purposeless.

In the Veda: "āgneyā grahā bhavanti" — "Agni-related substances become the Grahas here" — meaning one should praise Agni. Elsewhere, addressing the same matter: "āgneyāḥ stuvate" and "āgneyāḥ śaṃsanti" — meaning one should perform Stotra using specifically Agni-related mantras or suktas. If the sole purpose were simply to establish that Agni should be praised, wouldn't the first statement alone have sufficed? What does the second add? On the Siddhānta's own reading, however, both statements serve genuine, distinct purposes: the first establishes that Agni is the deity here; the second establishes which specific mantras should be used to praise him. Both scriptural statements thus receive a coherent, non-redundant reading. A further reason follows:

अन्यश्चार्थः प्रतीयत इति ॥१२॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२१) anyaś cārthaḥ pratīyata iti ||12|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.21)

"It was earlier stated that Stotra and Shastra are mutually connected — and connection holds between two distinct things, not within a single thing alone. Therefore a genuine difference in meaning between Stotra and Shastra is thereby implied — a difference that cannot arise on the mere-preparatory view, since 'illuminating a deity' would be a single, identical function for both. On the primary-rite view, however, the distinction is naturally established: whatever is accomplished through a sung mantra is called Stotra; whatever is accomplished through an unsung, recited mantra is called Shastra."

Sutra's meaning: [the terms] convey genuinely distinct meanings from one another.

In the Veda: "sambaddhe vai stotra-śastre" — Stotra and Shastra mantras are mutually connected...

original p. 663

...it is said. "Connection" here means holding between two distinct things, not existing for one thing alone — and to speak of genuine connection, the two objects must be distinct while sharing some point of commonality. This shows that the words describing Stotra and Shastra as "preparatory" must carry genuinely different meanings for each — a single "preparatory" description could not otherwise sustain any real distinction. Because if both merely supported one single deity-illuminating rite, they would in effect be the same rite, with no mutual difference possible. But when Stotra and Shastra are understood as primary rites, their meanings genuinely diverge. Though the underlying roots share a common basic sense, "Stotra" refers specifically to a mantra capable of being sung/chanted, while "Shastra" refers to a mantra recited melodiously but without singing. This is itself stated directly in the Veda, requiring no further proof. A further reason follows:

अभिधानं च कर्मण इति ॥१३॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२६) abhidhānaṃ ca karmaṇa iti ||13|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.26)

"Just as the primary rite is expressed through the accusative case, as in 'agnihotraṃ juhoti' — similarly, 'pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati' likewise carries a distinct meaning through this same construction. Therefore, Stotra-Shastra must be understood as primary rites."

Sutra's meaning: since "Stotra" and "Shastra," combined with the accusative case, indicate an action, they must be understood as primary rites.

Earlier, when explaining the sutra "śaktyanuṣṭhirāiṣām" (see page 501), we established that when the accusative case names an action within a sentence, that action becomes the sentence's primary rite — just as "agnihotram" bears the accusative and is primary in "agnihotraṃ juhoti." Correspondingly, in "pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati," the word "pṛhugam" likewise indicates a primary rite. Therefore, Stotra and Shastra are primary rites. A further reason follows:

फलनिर्वर्तकत्वादिति ॥१४॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२४) phala-nirvartakatvād iti ||14|| (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.24)

स्तुतस्य स्तुतमसि । stutasya stutam asi | (Taittiriya Samhita 1.2.2.1)

"Here, only the fruit of the Stotra itself is directly stated, in the closing portion following the completion of the Stotra-mantra's recitation:"

इन्द्रियावन्तं वनामहे घृतेनाक्तिमजिमिषम् । indriyāvantaṃ vanāmahe ghṛtenāktim ajim iṣam | (Taittiriya Samhita 1.2.2.1)

"...not..."

original p. 664

देवताप्रयुक्तं फलमाम्नातं । अतो न देवतासंस्कारः किंतु प्रधानकर्मेति स्थितं । devatā-prayuktaṃ phalam āmnātaṃ | ato na devatā-saṃskāraḥ kiṃtu pradhāna-karmeti sthitaṃ |

Meaning: the fruit stated here is not one merely accruing via the deity — therefore Stotra-Shastra are not preparatory to deity-worship, but are established as primary rites in their own right.

The fuller sense: it is well known that certain mantras within suktas yield desired fruits through their recitation. For fruit to genuinely accrue, mantras must be independent and primary — this could not hold if they were merely preparatory, subordinate parts. In ordinary life, when pursuing an important task, we rely on the chief person capable of accomplishing it, not on his servants, who lack that capacity themselves. In the same way, since Stotra-Shastra mantras are primary within their own rite, they are capable of yielding both seen and unseen fruits. The Vedic statement "stutasya stutam asi" itself states the fruit obtained through Stotra; likewise "indriyāvanto vanāmahe ghṛtenāktim ajim iṣam" states Stotra's own fruit specifically — not a fruit given by the deity directly. Therefore Stotra and Shastra are not subordinate to deities — they are primary rites.

Given this, in variant/subordinate rite contexts, the fruit must be inferred accordingly. On the rival "preparatory" view, one would also have to infer, in such variant contexts, some other deity's name-term even where absent from the mantra — which is untenable. To avoid this, Stotra-Shastra's status as primary rites has been established. This same matter is confirmed in the tenth Adhyaya of Jaimini's own Sutras:

ग्रहाणां देवतास्तुत्ये स्तुतशस्त्रयोः कर्मत्वाद्विकारः स्यात् । grahāṇāṃ devatā-stutye stuta-śastrayoḥ karmatvād vikāraḥ syāt | (Purva-Mimamsa 10.4.46)

On this matter, summary verses from the Nyāya-mālā-Vistara commentary are cited:

प्रलुगं शंसतीत्यादौ गुणकोक्ता प्रधानता । दृष्ट्वा देवस्मृतिस्त्वेव गुणता स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोः ॥ स्तुत्येफलस्य स्युतिशस्त्रैर्द्वयोः श्रौतार्थबाधनं । तेनादृष्टमुपेत्यापि प्राधान्यं श्रुतये मतम् ॥ (जै. न्या. वि. २-१-५) pralugaṃ śaṃsatīty ādau guṇakoktā pradhānatā | dṛṣṭvā deva-smṛtis tv eva guṇatā stotra-śastrayoḥ || stutye-phalasya stuti-śastrair dvayoḥ śrautārtha-bādhanaṃ | tenādṛṣṭam upetyāpi prādhānyaṃ śrutaye mataṃ || (Jaimini Nyāyamālā-Vistara 2.1.5)

"In 'pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati' and similar expressions, what is stated through the qualifying accusative term is itself the primary matter; the visible recollection of the deity that results is merely a secondary quality of Stotra and Shastra. Since scripture's own sense would otherwise be contradicted regarding the fruit that accrues to both through recitation, it is understood that scripture intends primacy for them, granted even by way of an unseen fruit." This section completed the debate's remaining threads and closed it out properly: the "twelve Stotras/twelve Shastras" argument (a precise stated number proves twelve distinct rites, not one collective act); the resolution of an apparent redundancy between two scriptural statements about Agni (one establishes that Agni is the deity, the other establishes which specific mantras to use — genuinely different functions, not repetition); the demonstration that "Stotra" and "Shastra" carry genuinely distinct meanings (sung vs. recited-unsung), which only makes sense if both are primary rites rather than a single subordinate function; a grammatical proof via the accusative case construction (parallel to "agnihotraṃ juhoti"); and finally the decisive argument from fruit-bearing capacity — Stotra/Shastra mantras are shown, from direct Vedic statements, to yield their own fruit through recitation, which only a primary rite (not a subordinate part) could do. The whole argument is capped with summary verses from the Nyāyamālā-Vistara commentary, cleanly restating the final position.

This closes out what has been a genuinely substantial excursus into Purva-Mimamsa methodology — likely serving as the interpretive foundation the commentary will lean on whenever Stotra/Shastra application questions arise for the rest of the text. The actual verses of Sukta 2 ("vāyav ā yāhi") should now follow directly.

original p. 665

This is said. These two verses condense and summarize everything discussed so far. The statements "pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati, niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati, ājyaṃ stuvate, pṛṣṭhyaṃ stuvate" are simply instructions used within the Agnishtoma-yaga. "Pṛhuga" and "Nishkevalya" name Shastra-mantras; "Ajya" and "Prishtha" name Stotra-mantras. Riks used to praise deities without being sung are called "Shastra"; mantras suited to chanted praise are called "Stotra." These Stotra-Shastra mantras are themselves primary, each bearing its own distinct fruit.

If it were said instead that these mantras are merely preparatory, this would force the roots "stu" and "śaṃs" to be understood as describing only a deity's quality — with no primary sense of their own. But a sentence like "Devadattaḥ caturvedābhijñaḥ" (Devadatta, knower of the four Vedas) constitutes genuine praise precisely because it identifies a specific person; if no such connection existed, no genuine praise would be possible. Therefore, Vedic injunctive statements such as "ājyena devaṃ prakāśayet" (one should illuminate the deity through Ajya) would lose their primary sense entirely on the rival view. To avoid contradicting scripture, one must accept that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites — bearing, if not visible purpose, then certainly an unseen one (adṛṣṭa-phala).

In the Agnishtoma, the Hotṛ, commanded before sunrise, should recite the Prātar-anuvāka. This is stated in a single chapter of the Aitareya Brahmana:

देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यः प्रेषितोऽनुब्रूयाद्धृतीचारणायृगादि ब्राह्मणम् । devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ preṣito'nubrūyād dhṛtī-cāraṇāya ṛg-ādi brāhmaṇam | (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)

Within this Prātar-anuvāka, the "agnimīḷe" sukta forms a part — this has already been explained [in Sukta 1]. In the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-Grahana, the Hotṛ is to recite the Pralugat-Shastra — which consists of the sukta beginning "vāyunā yāhi" [Sukta 2 itself]. This is confirmed both in the relevant Brahmana section and in Ashvalayana's own Shrauta-sutra (5.10[?]).

The Anukramaṇikā [index] entry for this sukta reads:

वायो नायहि । इन्द्रवाय्वादित्यमैत्रावरुणाश्च त्रयो देवताः, पालुगत-देवता इति । vāyo nāyahi | indra-vāyu-āditya-maitrāvaruṇāś ca trayo devatāḥ, pālugata-devatā iti | "'Vāyav ā yāhi' — with Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, and Mitra-Varuṇa as its three deities — a Prāluga-deity sukta."

Its meaning: "vāyunā yāhi" and so on is a nine-versed sukta.

original p. 666

"Agniṃ nava" — the word "nine" continues from the preceding count. Of this sukta's [nine] Riks: the first has Vāyu as deity; the second, Indra-Vāyu; the third, Mitra-Varuṇa. [The commentary then notes the next sukta too, beginning "aśvinā," twelve Riks:] the first has the Ashvins; the second, Indra; the third, Vishvadeva; the fourth, Sarasvata. In its remaining Riks, Vāyu and similar deities, together with Sarasvatī, are the deities treated within the Pralugata-Shastra as a whole. Madhuchandas continues as the rishi [as in Sukta 1], and correspondingly the meter remains Gāyatrī.

The first Rik, addressed to Vāyu, serves as one Puronuvākyā belonging to the Indra-Vāyu-graha offering — this too is recorded in the Brahmana:

वायुना पूर्वा पुरोनुवाक्येन्द्रवायव्ऋग्भिरा । vāyunā pūrvā puronuvākyendravāyav ṛgbhirā | (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)

and confirmed in the Sutra thus:

वायुना याहि दर्शतेन्द्रवायू इमे सुता इत्यनुवाक्ये । vāyunā yāhi darśata indravāyū ime sutā ity anuvākye | (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10[?])

On the day of the Agnishtoma when the Soma juice is crushed and extracted — called "Sutya-dina" or "Stutya-dina" — on that morning, before sunrise (after the previous midnight has passed, but before dawn), the Adhvaryu speaks the directive (Praiṣa-mantra) to the Hotṛ: "devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ hotar anubrūhi," and the Hotṛ then immediately recites the Prātar-anuvāka mantras. This is stated in the Aitareya Brahmana itself:

देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यो होतरनुब्रूहीत्यध्वर्युः । devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyo hotar anubrūhīty adhvaryuḥ | (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)

These Prātar-anuvāka mantras include the "agnimīḷe" mantras and others [i.e., all of Sukta 1] — their application has already been explained.

We shall now describe, in careful detail, the sequence the Hotṛ follows when reciting the Prātar-anuvāka. In the yajna, the Adhvaryu — who directs the Hotṛ, the primary ritvij — must periodically instruct the other ritvijs to perform their respective tasks; such directive statements are called "Praiṣas." Here, the Adhvaryu addresses the Hotṛ: "O Hotṛ! Recite the Prātar-anuvāka mantras, addressing the deities." Upon this, the Hotṛ proceeds to the vicinity of the Āgnīdhra fire-pit and, for the sake of a mantra-linkage, offers one Ājya-oblation into the Āhavanīya fire and two into the Āgnīdhra fire, following the prescribed mantras. He then enters the Havirdhāna-hall (where the Soma-cart is kept) through its eastern doorway, sits near the yoke of the carts there, and recites this mantra first—

original p. 667

आप्रे रेवतीक प्रयज्ञा हि वसुक क्रतुं च भद्रं बिभृथामृतं च । रायश्च स्था स्वश्च शंख्रिके सरस्वती कद्वणके वयो धात् ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-११०-१) (this opening mnemonic verse remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading given its compressed form)

Following this, the Hotṛ addresses Agni, Uṣas, and the Aśvin-deities in turn, reciting the Prātar-anuvāka mantras — in three portions. Mantras addressing Agni belong to the "Āgneya-kratu"; those addressing Uṣas, to the "Auṣasya-kratu"; those addressing the Aśvins, to the "Āśvina-kratu." Within each of these kratus, there are seven distinct sections, each in a different meter — Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇik, Jagatī, and Paṅkti. These mantras — not fewer than a hundred in total — must be recited continuously from midnight until dawn. Depending on context, they are recited in one of seven accent-registers, including upāṃśu-svara and mantra-svara. Among these Prātar-anuvāka mantras, within the Āgneya-kratu's own portion, the "agnimīḷe" sukta is included — already expounded above.

Now, in the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-grahaṇa, the Hotṛ must recite the Shastra-mantra called the "Pralugat-shastra." This Shastra-mantra includes the mantras of this present, second sukta, beginning "vāyunā yāhi."

It is worth explaining here what "Prātaḥ-savana" (the morning pressing) actually means. In the Soma-yaga, the Soma creeper's juice is crushed out with stones, and, following prescribed mantra-procedures, homa and similar rites are performed with that juice for the deities' satisfaction — after which the sacrificer and his ritvijs drink the Soma juice. There are seven varieties of Soma-yaga, traditionally called by the seven "Soma" designations: Agnishtoma, Atyagnishtoma, Ukthya, Shodashi, Atiratra, Aptoryama, and Vajapeya. Among these, the Agnishtoma-yaga is the foundational form — that is, it serves as the base from which the remaining six Soma-yagas derive, through certain modifications.

We shall summarize the Agnishtoma-yaga's procedure here. Its full, prescribed treatment is given at length in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda, Kanda 6, Adhyayas 1–8. Since explaining this rite's own form requires clarifying many technical terms — and since doing so fully would make this work excessively long — only the Sanskrit verses summarizing the rite's structure are given here, together with a Kannada explanation of only those points genuinely useful for the present context:

A concise summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure: This section established: Sukta 2's full structure (nine Riks, rishi Madhuchandas continuing from Sukta 1, Gayatri meter, three deities across its three verses — Vayu, Indra-Vayu, Mitra-Varuna — plus its role as one Puronuvakya for the Indra-Vayu-graha offering); the detailed procedural sequence of the Agnishtoma's Pratar-anuvaka (the Adhvaryu's Praisha-command to the Hotr, the Ajya-oblations at the Agnidhra fire, entering the Havirdhana-hall); and a genuinely useful overview of the seven Soma-yaga types (Agnishtoma, Atyagnishtoma, Ukthya, Shodashi, Atiratra, Aptoryama, Vajapeya), with Agnishtoma identified as the foundational form from which the other six derive through modification. The commentary now opens a condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma's full ritual structure — explicitly flagged as abbreviated, since the full technical treatment lives in the Taittiriya Samhita's sixth Kanda (Adhyayas 1-8) and would otherwise make the commentary unwieldy.

अथाग्निष्टोमसंज्ञेन ज्योतिष्टोमेन याजयेत् । स पूर्वमृत्विजो वृत्वा देवभावमिनिश्चये ॥ athāgniṣṭoma-saṃjñena jyotiṣṭomena yājayet | sa pūrvam ṛtvijo vṛtvā deva-bhāvam iniścaye ||

We are now positioned right at the threshold of the actual Samhita-patha for Sukta 2's first verse ("vāyav ā yāhi"). This page continues the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure begun on the previous page — roughly fifteen further couplets in a dense, technical, versified register, evidently walking through the ritual's major stages in sequence: the Dīkṣaṇīya rite (consecration of the sacrificer), the purchase and consecration of the Soma creeper (soma-kraya), the Pravargya rite, the Upasad days, and the various preparatory homas leading up to the Sutyā (pressing) day itself. Recognizable technical terms include "dīkṣaṇīyam," "somam," "pravargya"-related forms, and "upasad" — but the verses compress a great deal of ritual-procedural detail into terse poetic Sanskrit, using specialized vocabulary not always glossed in the surrounding prose. Rather than risk a fabricated word-by-word rendering of this densely versified technical summary, this page is characterized here at the level of its subject matter; a fully confident line-by-line translation would need careful cross-referencing against the Taittiriya Samhita passages (6th Kanda) that the verses are themselves summarizing — precisely the source Sayana names on the previous page as containing the full prescribed detail. This page completes the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure, continuing through roughly fifteen further couplets in the same dense technical register — evidently covering the remaining ritual stages: the Soma-purchase sequence, further preparatory rites, the building of the sacrificial altar (vedi) and fire-pits, and the approach to the Sutyā day itself. As with the preceding two pages, this dense versified portion is characterized here at the subject-matter level rather than translated line-by-line, for the same reasons given above.

original p. 668
original p. 669

The clear prose that closes this summary is genuinely valuable and is translated in full:

इदम् अग्निष्टोमयागद संक्षेप विवरणे । अग्निष्टोमयागदल्लि हन्नेरड स्तोत्रगळा हन्नेरड शस्त्रगळा उपयोगिसल्पडुववु । इतर अत्यग्निष्टोमादि सोमयागगळल्लि ई स्तोत्र-शस्त्रगळ संख्येयु अधिकवागिरुवुदु । सोमयागदल्लि यज्ञमाडुव यजमाननु...

"This is the concise description of the Agnishtoma-yaga. In the Agnishtoma-yaga, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras are used. In the other Soma-yagas — Atyagnishtoma and similar — the number of these Stotras and Shastras is greater. In the Soma-yaga, the sacrificer (yajamāna) who performs the rite..." This confirms, directly from the source, the exact "twelve Stotras, twelve Shastras" structure already established through the ritual table on page 652 and the Mimamsa argument on page 661 — a satisfying cross-confirmation of the earlier discussion.

original p. 670

A Soma-yaga may have a single sacrificer, or as many as sixteen ritvijs. In some Soma-yagas, many sacrificers together, along with an even larger number of ritvijs, participate. Such a Soma-yaga, performed jointly by many people together, is called a "Sattra." This Sattra-yaga is of two kinds: one performed continuously over twelve days, and another performed over a full year. The year-long Sattras are themselves of many kinds — Ganamayana, Adityanamayana, Angirasamayana, and others — of which Ganamayana serves as the foundational form underlying all the rest.

"Abhiplava" is the name given to a Soma-yaga performed over six days. This too is of two kinds: Abhiplava and Prishthya. The great sage Ashvalayana describes the defining character of both: "ubhayato-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam" and "antarataś-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam." That is: in a six-day Soma-yaga where the first and last days are performed like the Agnishtoma-yaga, and the remaining four days like the Ukthya Soma-yaga, that special form is called "Abhiplava." "Prishthya" refers to the variant Soma-yaga where the first and fourth days are performed like Agnishtoma, and the remaining days like Ukthya.

In the Agnishtoma-yaga, the day when the Soma juice is pressed and extracted is called "Sutya-dina." Since Stotra and Shastra mantras are recited during the time of extracting the Soma juice, this day is also called "Stutya-dina." On this day, in the early morning — that is, after the previous night's midnight has passed, but before sunrise, from when the birds' calls first begin until the earliest light of dawn — the mantras called the Pratar-anuvaka must be recited to completion. This Pratar-anuvaka comprises three portions: the Agneya-kratu (Riks connected with Agni), the Auṣasya-kratu, and the Aśvina-kratu. Each portion must contain numerous mantras spanning the seven meters — Gayatri, Anushtubh, Trishtubh, Brihati, Ushnik, Jagati, and Pankti.

After reciting the Pratar-anuvaka, the rite called "Prataḥ-savana" takes place. "Savana" means: crushing the Soma creeper with stones and extracting its juice. This rite occurs at three separate times: extraction in the morning is called "Prataḥ-savana"; extraction at midday is called "Madhyandina-savana"; extraction in the evening is called "Tritiya-savana."

Across these three Savanas together, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras must be recited in total. We have already explained their sequence on page 652.

During the recitation of the Pratar-anuvaka mantras, the sukta "agnimīḷe" is recited — its application has already been explained. Now, the second sukta, "vāyunā yāhi"...

original p. 671

...the nine-versed sukta; and the third sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," comprising twelve Riks, are to be recited by the Hotṛ during the recitation of the mantras called the "Pralugat-shastra." The sequence of these Pralugat-shastra mantras runs as follows — mantras praising the seven deities: Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā, Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ, and Sarasvatī. Each deity is addressed by three Riks in turn. In this nine-versed sukta "vāyunā yāhi": the first three Riks address Vāyu; Riks four through six address Indra-Vāyu; Riks seven through nine address Mitrā-Varuṇā. In the following sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ": Riks one through three address the Aśvins; four through six, Indra; seven through nine, Viśve-devāḥ; and nine through twelve, Sarasvatī. Together, these two suktas thus contain the Shastra-mantras for all seven deities, in seven groups of three Riks each. The Hotṛ recites these — this second Pralugat-shastra — in the morning pressing, immediately after the Udgātṛ has sung the Ājya-stotra, following the earlier-recited [Sukta 1]. This is the application (viniyoga) of both this sukta and the following, third sukta.

This application is confirmed in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the section beginning "gṛhe'laṃ" (Aitareya Brahmana 3.1), and also by Ashvalayana himself in his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section beginning "stotram agre śakrāt" (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10). The Anukramaṇikā states this as follows:

वायो वायस्त्वं प्रे वायनस्त्वंत्रावरुणास्त्वाचि अग्निना द्वादशाश्च्वैन्द्रैश्वदेवसारस्वास्त्वैचास्त्वैचा प्रुलगदेवता । (this compressed Anukramaṇikā entry remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading; its overall sense, however, is confirmed by the clear surrounding prose)

That is: in the sukta "vāyav ā yāhi," each set of three Riks in turn is assigned one deity — Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā — and in the sukta "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," the following four deities — Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ, Sarasvatī — are similarly praised, three Riks each. All seven of these deities together bear the name "Pralugat-devatāḥ."

Regarding this sukta "vāyav ā yāhi" — as with the preceding "agnimīḷe" sukta, its meter throughout is Gāyatrī. The sukta's first three Riks are Vāyu-related. Among them, the first Rik serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Vāyu-deity, and the second Rik serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Indra-Vāyu [offering] — this application is stated directly.

Ashvalayana likewise states, in his own Shrauta-sutra:

वायुना याहि दर्शते न्द्रवायू इमे सुता इत्यनुवाक्ये । vāyunā yāhi darśate indravāyū ime sutā ity anuvākye | (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10[?])

— that is: "vāyunā yāhi darśata" serves as one Puronuvākyā, and "indravāyū ime sutā" as another — this states the application of these Riks.

original p. 672

Sūkta 2, The First Mantra

॥ Sūkta 2 ॥

॥ Maṇḍala — 1 ॥ Anuvāka — 1 ॥ Sūkta — 2 ॥ ॥ Aṣṭaka — 1 ॥ Adhyāya — 1 ॥ Varga — 3–4 ॥

॥ Rik-numbers contained in this sukta: 1–9 ॥

Ṛṣi — Madhucchandā Vaiśvāmitraḥ Devatā — Riks 1–3: Vāyu; Riks 4–6: Indra-Vāyu; Riks 7–9: Mitrā-Varuṇau Chandaḥ — Gāyatrī

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वा॒यवा या॑हि दर्श॒तेमे सोमा॒ अर॑ङ्कृताः । ते॒षां पा॑हि श्रु॒धी हव॑म् ॥१॥

vāyav ā́ yāhi darśatéme sómā araṅkṛtā́ḥ | teṣā́ṃ pāhi śrudhī́ hávam ||1||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो इति । आ । याहि । दर्शत । इमे । सोमाः । अरंकृताः ॥ तेषाम् । पाहि । श्रुधि । हवम् ॥१॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

दर्शत हे दर्शनीय वायो कर्मश्येतिस्किन्ना याहि । आगच्छ । त्वदर्थमिमे सोमा अरंकृताः । अभिषवादिसंस्कारोऽलंकारकः । तेषां तान् सोमान् । यद्वा । तेषामेक देवमित्याधारकः । पाहि । स्वीयं भागं पिबेत्यर्थः । तत्पानार्थं हवनस्त्वयमाह्वानं श‍ृणु । darśata he darśanīya vāyo karmaśyetiskinnā yāhi | āgaccha | tvadartham ime somā araṅkṛtāḥ | abhiṣavādi-saṃskāro'laṃkārakaḥ | teṣāṃ tān somān | yadvā | teṣām eka devam ity ādhārakaḥ | pāhi | svīyaṃ bhāgaṃ pibety arthaḥ | tat-pānārthaṃ havanas tvayam āhvānaṃ śṛṇu |

Translation: "'Darśata' — O beautiful, gracious Vāyu! Come! Come here! For your sake, these Soma-drops have been readied — that is, embellished through pressing and the other preparatory processes. 'Teṣām' — of those Somas [drink]; or alternatively, this may refer to the single, sustaining deity presiding over them. 'Pāhi' — drink, that is, partake of your own share. For that purpose, hear this our summoning call!"

This is confirmed by the Nirukta: The grammatical derivation of "darśata" then follows, in the established dense sutra-citation register. This section completed: the dense versified Sanskrit summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's full procedure (honestly characterized rather than force-translated, given its compressed technical register); a genuinely valuable confirmation that Agnishtoma uses exactly twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras (cross-confirming the earlier structural table and Mimamsa argument); clear explanations of Sattra-yagas, the Abhiplava/Prishthya distinction, and the three Savanas (Prataḥ, Madhyandina, Tritiya); the complete structural breakdown of the seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra spanning Suktas 2 and 3 (Vayu, Indra-Vayu, Mitra-Varuna in Sukta 2; Ashvins, Indra, Vishvedevah, Sarasvati in Sukta 3, three Riks each); and finally — Sukta 2's formal header (rishi Madhuchandas continuing, Gayatri meter, deities by Rik-range) and the complete Samhita-patha, Pada-patha, and Sayana-bhashya for its first verse: "vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṅkṛtāḥ | teṣāṃ pāhi śrudhī havam" — "O Vayu, come, thou beautiful one: these Soma-drops are made ready. Drink of them; hear our call" — with a genuine Nirukta citation (10.2) confirming the same reading.

वायुनायाहि दर्शनीयेमे सोमा अरंकृता अलंकृतास्तेषां पिब शृणु नो स्तवानम् । vāyunāyāhi darśanīyeme somā araṅkṛtā alaṅkṛtās teṣāṃ piba śṛṇu no stavānam | (Nirukta 10.2[?]) "O Vāyu, come, you who are beautiful to behold; these Soma-drops are prepared, adorned; drink of them, hear our praise-call."

This closes what has been a substantial introductory apparatus for Sukta 2 — considerably longer than Sukta 1's own opening, reflecting the genuine complexity of the Pralugat-Shastra's multi-sukta, multi-deity structure within the Agnishtoma's morning pressing. The grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 concludes at the top of this page, working through "darśata" (a formation from the root "dṛś" with the affix "ataC"), "araṅkṛtāḥ" (the compound "alam-kṛta," with the substitution of "r" for "l" as a Vedic feature), "pāhi," and "śrudhi" — including the point that the accent of "pāhi" is lost through the rule for verbs following a vocative, and that the long vowel in "śrudhī" arises in the Saṃhitā. As throughout, the chain of specific numbered sutras is not reproduced verbatim.

original p. 673

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

दर्शत (darśata) — one worthy of being looked upon, that is, one of beautiful form | (हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | आ याहि (ā yāhi) — come (to this yajna we are performing) | इमे सोमाः (ime somāḥ) — these Soma-juices (the pressed Soma-juice that has been prepared) | अरंकृताः (araṅkṛtāḥ) — made ready, that is, embellished, by the pressing and other preparatory rites (made fit for drinking) | तेषाम् (teṣām) — of those Soma-juices, or from among those Soma-juices, your share | पाहि (pāhi) — drink | हवम् (havam) — the invocation we make (for the sake of the Soma-drinking) — the calling | श्रुधि (śrudhi) — hear.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Vāyu, your form is exceedingly beautiful. We have here, in this yajna, pressed out the Soma juice in the prescribed manner, and — through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like — refined it and made it ready for drinking. Hear the invocation we make with these mantras, come here, and drink this Soma-juice.

॥ English Translation ॥

Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation.

original p. 674

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Somāḥ" — the Veda contains many mantras concerning Soma; the entire ninth Maṇḍala is devoted to praise of Soma. When many deities are being invoked, Soma is called to come to the yajna so that they may drink it. Many yajnas are connected with Soma, of which the Agniṣṭoma is chief. In this yajna, only a single animal (a goat) is offered to Agni. Through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like, the Soma is drawn out in the prescribed manner at all three pressings, consecrated, and drunk by the sacrificer and the ritvijs. In the other Soma-yajnas too, the same order is followed with certain variations.

What, then, is "Soma"? This needs some examination. Soma is a particular kind of creeper (a climbing plant). Its juice is extracted by placing it on a stone and crushing it with another stone. The lower stone is called "adri" (Rigveda Samhita, several citations); the pressing-stone is called "grāvā" and is referred to by that name in many contexts. Besides these, the stones are sometimes called "ulūkhala" (mortar) in some places.

The juice that flows over the cloth from the crushed creeper is described in the Rigveda in many ways: as tawny-brown (babhru), as reddish (aruṇa), as ruddy-hued (aruṣa), as golden-green (hariḍvarṇa), as red (śoṇa), and as white/bright (śukra).

On its taste and smell, it is described as sweet (svādiṣṭa, svādu, madhu, madhumat) and as fragrant. The Shatapatha Brahmana states that when this juice is left for some days it becomes foul-smelling through fermentation, and that, taken in excess, it can cause vomiting (Taittiriya Samhita and Shatapatha Brahmana, several citations).

Professor Max Müller, drawing on the Ayurvedic work "Dhūrtasvāmi-bhāṣya-ṭīkā," gives this account: the Soma creeper is somewhat blackish, leafless, its juice flows like milk, and the plant grows on a mountain, with many joints/nodes — which goats and other animals eat. Its juice, when freshly pressed, is sweet and fragrant, but after some days turns sour and foul-smelling.

original p. 675

This Soma creeper is no longer found in the lands of India today. The plant called Homa (Haoma), described in the Zend Avesta (the Persian scripture), must be the very same as this Soma. The German scientist Schindler, while travelling in Persia, reported that this plant had come to his notice. According to him, it grows especially on mountains; he saw it growing at about 2,000 feet elevation, reaching about four feet in height. Its stem is bare and soft, reddish-brown with a mixture of pink; it has a rough, thorny body; its leaves are very few, small, and of a pinkish, thin sort; leaves generally fall off, and at the tips of the stems there are clusters resembling millet-like seed-heads. Its juice is mixed with a greenish tint; in taste it is somewhat sweet, though to some people it becomes sour if kept; the colour of the juice is a reddish-brown (babhru) mixed with a yellowish tint. Growing near large trees, it climbs around the trunk like a creeper. It grows here and there in scattered fashion, and those familiar with it can find it readily. This German scholar's description closely agrees with the description Professor Max Müller drew from the Ayurvedic work.

This creeper grows in open ground, along riverbanks, and on mountains — but the mountain-grown plant yields the most juice. The more elevated its place of growth, the more juice it yields. For this reason, the Rigveda in many places speaks of Soma as "brought from the mountains" (several citations). A mountain called Mūjavat is famed as a Soma-growing peak (Rigveda 10.34.1; Atharva Veda; Vajasaneyi Samhita; Nirukta; Shatapatha Brahmana, etc.), and the Avesta likewise says Soma is carried down from the mountains.

The Rigveda says in several places that the Soma creeper is found in the lakes of a region called "Śaryaṇāvat" (Rigveda 8.6.39[?] and others); in a place called Ārjīka; in a country called Paśtyā, where five tribes of people dwell; and in the regions around the river Suṣomā (whose name — "su" + "soma," "rich in Soma" — probably reflects that the area yielded good Soma). From this we learn that in Vedic times, Soma grew freely on the open plains and along the riverbanks of what is now the Punjab. Since the creeper growing in the open yields less juice than the mountain-grown plant, people carefully soaked it in water and used it... The opening lines continue a string of Rigveda citations, whose exact chapter-verse numbers are not reproduced here.

original p. 676

...[the creeper was] moistened in this manner with water; this soaking is called "ābhyāyana" (swelling/refreshing). After the juice was pressed out of the creeper, it was purified by passing it through a filter called "pavitra" — a strainer of sheep's wool (Rigveda, several citations). For these strainers they used the tuft of hair at the tail-end of the sheep (called "aṇva"; the sheep's fleece is also called "avi"), which is why the word "pavitra" is said to arise from purifying with sheep's wool (Rigveda, several citations). The juice thus purified was collected in vessels made of cow-hide (called "kośa" or "pātra"; several Rigveda citations), and from there was poured into small vessels called "kalaśa" (pots). The freshly pressed Soma-juice was then mixed with milk (Rigveda, many citations) or curds (dadhi), or with barley (yava) — the mixed preparations bearing distinct names: gavāśira (mixed with milk), dadhyāśira (mixed with curds), yavāśira (mixed with barley); each mixture is called by its own name. The milk and other substances mixed with Soma are called "āśir." The vessel in which Soma-juice is offered to the deities is called "camū" (Rigveda, several citations); at times "camasa" is also used for such a vessel. The Soma-juice and the milk called "āśir" were mixed in a vessel called "kalaśa."

The word "Soma," when speaking of the Soma-juice, is customarily used both in the singular ("somaḥ") and in the plural ("somāḥ" or "somāsaḥ"). This is because — since milk and other different substances were added to the Soma-juice — the prepared Soma came in many kinds, so the plural "somāḥ" can properly be used. More detail about the Soma creeper and its juice will be given when the ninth Maṇḍala is explained.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ This section takes up the derivation of "darśate" [darśata], using the Uṇādi rule for roots such as "bhṛ, mṛ, dṛś, yaj, pari-…" with the affix "ataC," and then other words of the verse, in the established dense sutra-citation register; not reproduced in detail. This page continues the grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 in the established dense sutra-citation register. The specific numbered citations are not reproduced verbatim; the readable substance is summarized below.

original p. 677

"Darśata": the root "dṛś" takes the affix "ataC" (per the Uṇādi rule covering roots like "bhṛ, mṛ, dṛś, yaj…"); with the guṇa substitution this yields "darśata." Since the affix carries the marker "C," the final syllable takes the udātta accent; as a vocative, the word is accordingly treated as "āmantrita," and its accent is adjusted by the rule for vocatives.

"Somāḥ": the word derives from the root "su" (in the senses of pressing/extracting, giving birth, going, and others) with the affix "manin" [glossed in the source via a long list of roots beginning "ṣu, ṣū, ṣuñ…" for pressing, and others meaning "to go," "to sustain," "to shine," "to worship"]; the resulting form takes the initial-udātta accent.

"Araṅkṛtāḥ": here "alam" changes its "l" to "r" (a Vedic feature), giving "aram." Since "alam" (as an indeclinable particle, meaning "enough/adequately") is treated as a "gati" (preverb-like element), the compound with "kṛta" follows the rule that a word compounded after such an element keeps the accent of its first member — so that the initial syllable is udātta, the following syllables lose their accent (anudātta), and the accent is finally resolved in the Saṃhitā as svarita and pracaya, giving "araṅkṛtāḥ." The grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 concludes at the top of this page. Its readable substance: "pāhi" — the root "pā" (in the sense of drinking) in the second-person singular imperative takes the substitute "hi" for the personal ending; the Vedic accent-rules keep the verb unaccented after the vocative "vāyo," and, though the root would ordinarily take the substitute "piba" in later Sanskrit, the Vedic procedure means the substitution "piba" does not apply here. "Śrudhi" — from the root "śru" (to hear), imperative second person, with the affix "śnu"-class insertion and the substitution of "dhi" for "hi" in the Vedic language after such roots; the long "ī" seen in "śrudhī" of the Saṃhitā text arises by the rule of lengthening. "Havam" — from the root "hve" (to call), with contraction of the semi-vowel, giving "hava," accented on the final syllable as a root-derived noun. Specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced.

original p. 678

Sūkta 2, The Second Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायु॑ उ॒क्थेभि॑र्जरन्ते॒ त्वामच्छा॑ जरि॒तारः॑ । सु॒तसो॑मा अह॒र्विदः॑ ॥२॥

vā́yav ukthébhir jarante tvā́m áchā jaritā́raḥ | sutásomā aharvídaḥ ||2||

original p. 679

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो इति । उक्थेभिः । जरन्ते । त्वाम् । अच्छ । जरितारः । सुतऽसोमाः । अहःऽविदः ॥२॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे वायो जरितारः स्तोतार ऋत्विग्यजमानास्त्वामच्छ त्वामभिलक्ष्योक्थेभिराज्यप्रउगादिशस्त्ररूपैर्जरन्ते । स्तुवन्ति । कीदृशाः । सुतसोमा अभिषुतेन सोमेनोपेता अहर्विदः । अहःशब्द एकेनाह्ना निष्पाद्येऽग्निष्टोमादिक्रतौ वैदिकव्यवहारेण प्रसिद्धः । क्रत्वभिज्ञा इत्यर्थः ॥ अर्चति गायतीत्यादिषु चतुर्थत्वारिंशत्स्तुत्यर्चतिकर्मसु धातुषु जरते र्ह्वयतीति पठितम् । स्तुतेरप्यर्चनाविशेषत्वादौचित्येनात्र स्तुत्यर्थो जरतिधातुः । he vāyo jaritāraḥ stotāra ṛtvig-yajamānās tvām accha tvām abhilakṣyokthebhir ājya-praüga-ādi-śastra-rūpair jarante | stuvanti | kīdṛśāḥ | sutasomā abhiṣutena somenopetā aharvidaḥ | aḥ-śabda ekenāhnā niṣpādye'gniṣṭomādi-kratau vaidika-vyavahāreṇa prasiddhaḥ | kratv-abhijñā ity arthaḥ |

Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary: "O Vāyu! The praisers — the ritvijs and sacrificers — directing themselves toward you, praise you with the 'ukthas,' that is, with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya-shastra and Praüga-shastra. What kind of praisers? 'Sutasomāḥ' — those provided with pressed Soma; 'aharvidaḥ' — the word 'ahaḥ' (day) is known in Vedic usage to denote rites like the Agniṣṭoma that are completed within a single day; the sense is: those who know the rite (kratu). Among the roots listed in the sense of praising or worshipping, 'jarate' is read in the sense of 'praising'; the root 'jṛ' (jarati) is here used in the sense of praise."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | अहर्विदः (aharvidaḥ) — those who properly know the time for performing yajnas and the like | जरितारः (jaritāraḥ) — the ritvijs, sacrificers and others who offer praise | सुतसोमाः (sutasomāḥ) — those who have prepared Soma through the pressing and other rites | त्वामच्छ (tvām accha) — directed toward you | उक्थेभिः (ukthebhiḥ) — with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya and Praüga | जरन्ते (jarante) — offer praise.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Vāyu, the ritvijs, sacrificers and others know at what time and what work is to be done. Therefore they have now prepared the Soma-juice and are praising you with many hymns.

॥ English Translation ॥ A brief grammatical note follows in the source on "jaritāraḥ" from the root "jṛ" [to praise], on the accent of "sutasomāḥ" as a bahuvrīhi compound, and on "aharvidaḥ" as a compound, in the established dense register.

O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises.

original p. 680

Sūkta 2, The Third Mantra

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics on Rik 2.2) ॥

"Ukthebhiḥ" does not mean sung Stotras; it means the Shastra-mantras such as the Pṛhuga and others, which are recited rather than chanted. "Jarate" — of the four roots beginning "arcati" and "gāyati" [in the traditional list of praising-roots], the root "jṛ" is used in the sense of worshipping and singing, so "jarate" carries the sense of offering praise; likewise "jaritāraḥ" means "those who offer praise." "Aharvidaḥ" — in this word, "ahaḥ" means "day," referring to the Sutyā-day on which Soma-juice is pressed at the morning pressing and the others; this is a single day within the Agniṣṭoma. "Sutasomāḥ" — "those who have prepared the Soma-juice" — likewise makes clear that "ahaḥ" means the Sutyā-day specifically. Even so, one cannot say with certainty that the poet had precisely this sense in mind in using the word "aharvidaḥ."

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ Summarized. The particle "accha" takes a lengthened vowel in the Saṃhitā by the rule that particles in mantras take lengthening. "Sutasomāḥ" is a bahuvrīhi compound ("those by whom Soma is pressed"), with the accent of the first member retained by the rule for bahuvrīhi. "Aharvidaḥ" is a compound whose final member, being a verbal derivative, keeps the stem accent.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो॒ तव॑ प्रपृ॒ञ्चती॑ धे॒ना जि॑गाति दा॒शुषे॑ । उ॒रू॒ची सोम॑पीतये ॥३॥

vā́yo táva prapṛñcatī́ dhenā́ jigāti dāśúṣe | urūcī́ sómapītaye ||3||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो इति । तव । प्रऽपृञ्चती । धेना । जिगाति । दाशुषे । उरूची । सोमऽपीतये ॥३॥

original p. 681

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे वायो तव धेना वाक् सोमपीतये सोमपानार्थं दाशुषे दाश्वांसं दत्तवन्तं यजमानं जिगाति गच्छति । हे यजमान त्वयो दत्तं सोमं पास्यामीत्येवं वायुर्ब्रूते इत्यर्थः । कीदृशी धेना । प्रपृञ्चती प्रकर्षेण सोमसंपर्कं कुर्वती । सोमगुणं वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः । उरूची उरूनस्वभूजमानान् गच्छन्ती । ये ये सोमयोजिनस्तान् सर्वान् स्वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः । he vāyo tava dhenā vāk somapītaye soma-pānārthaṃ dāśuṣe dāśvāṃsaṃ dattavantaṃ yajamānaṃ jigāti gacchati | he yajamāna tvayā dattaṃ somaṃ pāsyāmīty evaṃ vāyur brūte ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśī dhenā | prapṛñcatī prakarṣeṇa soma-saṃparkaṃ kurvatī | soma-guṇaṃ varṇayantīty arthaḥ | urūcī urūn [bahūn] yajamānān gacchantī |

Translation: "O Vāyu! Your 'dhenā' — your speech — goes, for the drinking of Soma, to the sacrificer who has given the oblation (dāśuṣe). The sense is: 'O sacrificer, I shall drink the Soma you have offered' — thus says Vāyu. What kind of speech? 'Prapṛñcatī' — bringing about, in an excellent manner, association with the Soma, that is, describing the Soma's excellence. 'Urūcī' — going to the many sacrificers; that is, it reaches every one of those who have prepared Soma."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | प्रपृञ्चती (prapṛñcatī) — describing the qualities of the Soma | तव (tava) — your | धेना (dhenā) — speech | सोमपीतये (somapītaye) — for the drinking of Soma | दाशुषे (dāśuṣe) — to the sacrificer who offers Soma, and | उरूची (urūcī) — to the many other sacrificers who offer you Soma | जिगाति (jigāti) — goes.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Vāyu, the sacrificer who performs the yajna, and many others besides, call you for the drinking of Soma. Your speech, pleased by the hymns they offer and by their Soma-drinking, will gladden the sacrificer who calls you to drink the Soma, and many others as well.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver (of the oblation) and to many (others) who invite you for drinking Soma.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥

"Dhenā" — many scholars have held many opinions about this word's meaning. Yāska, in his Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta), placed this word "dhenā" among the fifty-seven words meaning "vāk" (speech). Some take "dhenā" to mean "tongue" (jihvā)...

original p. 682

...[Some take "dhenā" to mean] "tongue" (jihvā), and on their view this Rik's sense would run: "O Vāyu, your long (Udvāta) tongue reaches the sacrificer who calls you for the drinking of Soma." The German scholar Geldner, after many investigations into the word "dhenā," concluded that it means "tongue" (in the sense of "speech," vāk); the sacrificer's Stotra (vāk), he says, generates in the deity a desire for the Soma-drinking. A Rik of the Rigveda supports this view: "yaṃ te svadhāvan…" (Rigveda 8.?). But in a later study, this same scholar concluded that "dhenā" means "the milk-yielding cow's teat/milk-flow." According to Professor Max Müller, "dhenā" means "a stream of milk." Both scholars hold that "dhenā" means "a cow that yields milk" and, by extension, "the drinking of milk." In the Veda, the word "dhenā" is used in a variety of senses in different contexts:

  1. A Rik in which "dhenā" refers to a beloved woman — used in the sense of "wife": "striyo hi dāsa āyudhāni cakre kiṃ mā karann abalā asya senāḥ…" (Rigveda 5.30.9[?]) — where "dhenā" is used for women who are objects of affection.

  2. "ahan vyaṃsam uśadhag vaneṣv…" and "tvāvakro rathyo na dhenā rejante viśvā kṛtrimāṇi bhīṣā" — in these Riks "dhenā" is used in the sense of "sister/mother-cow" [i.e., a milch-cow].

  3. "viśvāḥ pinvathaḥ svasarasya dhenā anu vāmekaḥ pavir āvavarta" (Rigveda 5.?) — here "dhenā" is used for a female animal, a cow.

  4. "visṛṣṭadhenā bharate suvṛktir…" and "mādayasva haribhir ye ta indra viṣyasva śipre vi sṛjasva dhene" (Rigveda 1.101.10[?]) — here, from the root "dhe" (to drink), the word "dhenā" arises with the meaning "milk-cow," and this sense is still found in the later-literature word "stanandhaya" (a suckling child — "one who drinks milk"). Several of the Rigveda verse-locators above are too small to read reliably at this resolution and are given only in approximate form; the Kannada text's citations in this passage should be checked against the source if precision matters.

original p. 683

More Rigvedic uses of "dhenā" (continuing the numbered list from the previous page):

  1. In several Riks — among them "pitur…" (Rigveda 3.1.6[?]), "samyak sravanti saritro na dhenā…" (Rigveda 4.?), "yad īm upa hvarate sādhate matir ṛtasya dhenā anayanta sasrutaḥ" (Rigveda 1.141.1[?]), "dhiyo dhenā avasyavaḥ", "dhenā indrāvacākaśat", "viśaṃ-viśaṃ maghavā paryaśāyata janānāṃ dhenā avacākaśad vṛṣā", "indre dhenābhir iha mādayasva dhībhir viśvābhiḥ śacyā gṛṇānaḥ", and "vīreṇyaḥ kratur indraḥ suśastir utāpi dhenā puruhūtam ūtaye" — the word is used in the senses of speech, utterance, hymn of praise, and the act of praising.

M. Bloomfield, in translating the Rik (10.104.10) cited above, remarks that the Vedic word "dhenā" is related to the Lithuanian word "daina" and the Avestan "daena." These words generally carry the senses of speech, song, hymn and lay. Many scholars hold that in the Veda, "dhenā" chiefly and more often carries the sense of "speech, word."

"Prapṛñcatī" — means "touching, making contact." "Urūcī" — "broad, extended, plentiful." The Bhashyakara has glossed this as "sacrificers performing Soma-yajnas"; but "urūcī" may instead be taken simply as a qualifier of the word "dhenā." "Somapītaye" — the meaning of this word is clear; its use is especially frequent across many Riks.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ "Prapṛñcatī" — here, by the rule concerning words ending in the "śatṛ" affix and lacking the augment "num," the feminine-forming "ṅīp" affix (a "nadī"-class affix) is added, and the accent is treated accordingly: the word is accented on its final syllable, and the case-endings following it (such as "śas") likewise take the udātta accent. The grammar of "prapṛñcatī" concludes: the "ṅīp"-type affix's long "ī" takes udātta even though its marker would otherwise leave it unaccented.

original p. 684

Sūkta 2, The Fourth Mantra

"Dhenā" — listed in the Nirukta (Nighaṇṭu 1.11) among the fifty-seven words for "vāk" ("speech": ślokaḥ, dhārā, dhenā, gnāḥ, …); this is why "dhenā" is glossed as "speech." "Jigāti" — listed among the words expressing movement (Nighaṇṭu 2.14), where "jigāti" is glossed "gacchati" (goes).

Grammar (summarized): since "jigāti" is a verb of motion, the recipient noun takes the accusative/dative ("dāśvān" → "dāśuṣe") by the rule that verbs of going govern a fourth-case (dative) object of destination — hence the dative "dāśuṣe." "Urūcī" — the "ṣit"-marked class of words (with "gaurādi" nouns) takes the feminine affix "ṅīṣ," which brings its own accent. "Somapītaye" — though not a bahuvrīhi, the initial member's accent is retained by a special rule.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

इ॒न्द्र॒वा॒यू इ॒मे सु॒ता उप॒ प्रयो॑भि॒रा ग॑तम् । इन्द॑वो वामु॒शन्ति॒ हि ॥४॥

indravāyū imé sutā́ úpa práyobhir ā́ gatam | índavo vām uśánti hí ||4||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

इन्द्रवायू इति । इमे । सुताः । उप । प्रयःऽभिः । आ । गतम् ॥ इन्दवः । वाम् । उशन्ति । हि ॥४॥

original p. 685

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

एतस्या ऋचा ऐन्द्रवायवग्रहे द्वितीयपुरोनुवाक्यारूपेण विशेषविनियोगः पूर्वमेवोक्तः । हे इन्द्रवायू भवदर्थमिमे सोमाः सुताः अभिषुताः । तस्माद्युवां प्रयोभिरन्नैरस्मभ्यं दात्व्यैः सहोपसा गतं । अस्मत्समीपं प्रत्यागच्छतम् । हि यस्मादिन्दवः सोमा वां युवामुशन्ति कामयन्ते तस्मादागमनमुचितम् । इन्द्रवायूशब्दस्यामन्त्रितस्याद्युदात्तत्वम् । प्रीणयन्ति भोक्तॄनिति प्रयांस्यन्नानि । etasyā ṛcā aindravāyava-grahe dvitīya-puronuvākyā-rūpeṇa viśeṣa-viniyogaḥ pūrvam evoktaḥ | he indravāyū bhavad-artham ime somāḥ sutāḥ abhiṣutāḥ | tasmād yuvāṃ prayobhir annair asmabhyaṃ dātavyaiḥ sahopasā gataṃ | asmat-samīpaṃ pratyāgacchatam | hi yasmād indavaḥ somā vāṃ yuvām uśanti kāmayante tasmād āgamanam ucitam | indravāyū-śabdasyāmantritasyādyudāttatvam | prīṇayanti bhoktṝn iti prayāṃsy annāni |

Translation: "The specific application of this Rik — as the second Puronuvākyā in the Indra-Vāyu-graha offering — was stated earlier. O Indra and Vāyu! For your sake these Soma-juices have been pressed. Therefore, come to our side together with the foods (prayas) that are to be given to us, coming close to us. For, since the Soma-drops desire you two, your coming is fitting. [Grammar:] the vocative 'indravāyū' takes initial-syllable udātta. 'Prayas' means foods, 'those which please the eaters.'"

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) इन्द्रवायू ((he) indravāyū) — O Indra and Vāyu! (for your sake) | इमे (ime) — these Soma-juices | सुताः (sutāḥ) — pressed (prepared so as to be fit for drinking) | प्रयोभिः (prayobhiḥ) — together with foods and other things that please us | उपागतम् (upāgatam) — come to our side | हि (hi) — because | इन्दवः (indavaḥ) — these Soma-juices prepared for you | वाम् (vām) — you two | उशन्ति (uśanti) — desire.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra and Vāyu! These Soma-juices have been thoroughly pressed and made ready to be drunk. Come to our side to accept them, bringing food and other things that will please us. For these Soma-juices that we have prepared are awaiting you — that is, we watch for your arrival so that you may drink.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations (poured out for you). Come with food for us. For, the soma-drops are desiring You.

original p. 686

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

This Rik, as already stated, is applied as the second Puronuvākyā in the rite called the Aindravāyava-graha. In this Rik, and in the two Riks that follow, Indra and Vāyu are invoked together. The joint invocation or joint praise of two deities is often found in the Rigveda — for example: Indra-Vāyū, Indrāgnī, Agnīṣomau, Indrāsomau, Somārudrā, Indrāviṣṇū, Dyāvāpṛthivī, Uṣāsānaktā (or naktoṣāsā), and so on.

"Ime" — these (Soma-juices): that is, freshly pressed, made fit for drinking through the preparatory rites. "Sutāḥ" — this word, formed from the root "su" (to press), shows that Soma-creeper, crushed between stones and pressed out in the filter, has become fit for drinking. "Prayobhiḥ" — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "with foods" or "with meals." Since the word derives from the root "prī" (to please, to gladden), the sense "things that please, that bring joy to the mind" is entirely fitting. Moreover the Bhashyakara himself, in the Rik "pra yad vo yajñe…" — where "prayāṃsi" occurs (Rigveda 3.?.?) — glosses it as "dear things." In the Rigveda this word is used in many places in the sense of "food fit for sacrifice." "Indavaḥ" — Soma-juices mixed with various admixtures; the word derives from the root "und" (to wet/moisten): since Soma-juice is a liquid, "kledana" (moistening) is the sense; and "indu" is accordingly used in place of "soma" in many passages.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ "Indravāyū" — the vocative takes initial-udātta accent. "Prayāṃsi" — "those which please the eaters" — by analysis, "prayas" derives from the root "prī" (to please) with the affix "asun" (added after all roots, per the Uṇādi rule), giving "prī + as," with guṇa and substitution "prayas"; being formed with an accent-bearing affix, it is accented on the first syllable.

original p. 687

Sūkta 2, The Fifth Mantra

The grammar of "prayobhiḥ" concludes: the affix-final "s" becomes "ru" and then visarga, giving "prayobhiḥ." "Gatam" — the root "gam," in the second-person dual imperative, has its personal ending elided by the Vedic rule ("bahulaṃ chandasi"), and the nasal of the root is dropped when the following affix is marked as "kit" or "ṅit"; hence "gatam," not to be mistaken for a form ending in the "kta" affix. "Indavaḥ" — from the root "und" (to moisten), the affix "un" is added and the initial "u" becomes "i," giving "indu"; the affix marker makes the word accented on its first syllable. "Vām" — the dual pronoun "yuvām" is replaced by the enclitic "vām," which is therefore unaccented. "Uśanti" — a verb, hence normally unaccented; but here it is joined with "hi," which blocks the loss of accent, so the verb retains its own accent; "hi" itself, being a particle, takes initial accent.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायविन्द्र॑श्च चेतथः सु॒तानां॑ वाजिनीवसू । तावा या॑त॒मुप॑ द्र॒वत् ॥५॥

vāyav índraś ca cetathaḥ sutā́nāṃ vājinīvasū | tā́v ā́ yātam úpa dravát ||5||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । चेतथः । सुतानाम् । वाजिनीवसू इति वाजिनीऽवसू । तौ । आ । यातम् । उप । द्रवत् ॥५॥

original p. 688

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अत्र चकारेणास्यः समुच्चीयते । संनिहितत्वाद्वायुरेव । हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च युवामुभौ सुतानामभिषुतान्सोमान् चेतथः । जानीथः । यद्वा अभिषुतानां सोमानां विशेषणमित्यध्याहारः । कीदृशौ युवां । वाजिनीवसू । वाजिनीशब्दो यज्ञपुष्टोनामसु पठितस्तथास्य त्यासंभवात्रं गृह्यते । वाजोऽन्नं । तद्वत्यां हविःसंतत्तावस्ति सा वाजिनी । तस्यां वसतः इति तौ वाजिनीवसू । आमन्त्रितत्वादनुदात्तः । तौ तथाविधौ युवां द्रवत्क्षिप्रमुपसमीपे आ यातम् । आगच्छतम् । atra cakāreṇāsyaḥ samuccīyate | saṃnihitatvād vāyur eva | he vāyo tvam indraś ca yuvām ubhau sutānām abhiṣutān somān cetathaḥ | jānīthaḥ | … kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | vājinīvasū | vājinī-śabdo yajñapuṣṭo-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ … vājo'nnam | tadvatyāṃ haviḥ-saṃtatāv asti sā vājinī | tasyāṃ vasataḥ iti tau vājinīvasū | āmantritatvād anudāttaḥ | tau tathāvidhau yuvāṃ dravat kṣipram upa samīpe ā yātam | āgacchatam |

Translation: "Here the word 'ca' combines [Indra] with the other deity — by proximity, Vāyu. O Vāyu, and Indra — you two — know the pressed Soma-juices. Or, as a qualifier of the pressed Somas, [it may be supplied]. What kind of pair are you? 'Vājinīvasū' — the word 'vājinī' is read among the words for 'sacrifice-nourishing'; 'vāja' means food. That in which there is a continuous stream of oblation-food is 'vājinī'; 'those two who dwell in it' are 'vājinīvasū' — unaccented as a vocative. You two, being such, come here quickly (dravat), near us."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | (त्वम्) इन्द्रश्च ((tvam) indraś ca) — you, and Indra with you, both | वाजिनीवसू (vājinīvasū) — those who are foremost among the sacrificers, who are provided with oblation-food and the like | (अतः तौ यूयम्) — (you two, such as you) | सुतानाम् (sutānām) — of the pressed Soma-juices (that the Soma-juices are ready for drinking) | चेतथः (cetathaḥ) — know | तौ (tau) — you two, such | द्रवत् (dravat) — with alertness | उप (upa) — to our side | आ यातम् (ā yātam) — come.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra and Vāyu! In yajnas equipped with oblation-shares and the like, you are honoured as chief. You know full well that the Soma-juice has been made ready for your drinking. Therefore, for the sake of drinking the Soma, come quickly and attentively to our side.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Vayu and Indra dwellers in the sacrifices, You are aware of these Soma-libations. You both come hither quickly.

original p. 689

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Vājinīvasū" — many people have interpreted this word in many different ways. The Bhashyakara says that although "vājinī" is among the words that name Uṣas (the Dawn), that sense is impossible here and must be set aside; then "vāja" means food (the Vedic text says "annaṃ vai vājaḥ"), and "that in which there is oblation-food is 'vājinī'" — the sacrificial rite is thus called "vājinī" ("the yajna"). "Tasyāṃ vasataḥ" — "the two who dwell in it" are "vājinīvasū": the two who dwell in the yajna, hence so named.

Authors of the Vedārtha-yatna [a modern commentary] interpret the word thus: "vāji" means a horse, or a swift horse; "vasū" means those who possess them — that is, the two who possess swift horses. Or "vājinī" means "provided with horses" — a chariot; "vasū" means those who dwell or sit in it — those who sit in the chariot. Or "vājinī" may mean a mare, and "vasū" wealth — those who possess these. Or it may mean "givers." The German scholar Grassmann interprets "vājinīvasū" as "those who give abundant rewards."

The Bhashyakara glosses the word "vājinī" in some places as "food" (Rigveda 3.62.5[?] and many others); in some places as "sacrificial rite" (Rigveda 1.?; 3.?; and others); in some as "possessing food" (annavatī); in some as "strong" (balavatī); and "vasu" as "one who dwells" (Rigveda 1.?.?) and as "wealth, riches" (many citations).

"Vasu" is among the twenty-eight words for "wealth" in the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.10). Moreover, compounds ending in "vasu" are needed and found throughout the Rigveda, in which "vasu" generally means "wealth." A few examples follow:

Śacīvasū (Rigveda 1.139.[?]; 2.19.1[?]; 8.60.19); Sūryavasū (Rigveda 2.?.?); Vibhāvasuḥ (Rigveda 1.44.10; 3.2.?; 5.?; 8.?; and many others), and so on. This page continues the list of compounds ending in "-vasu" begun on the previous page, each followed in the source by a string of Rigveda chapter-verse references. Those numeric references are very small and were not read reliably, so only the compound names are given here; they should be checked against the source if the exact locations matter.

original p. 690

Further compounds ending in "vasu" in the Rigveda: Viśvāvasuḥ, Manāvasū, Viśvalāvasū, Snāvasuḥ, Tvāvasuḥ, Ṛtāvasū, Jenyāvasū, Divāvasū, Dhiyovasuḥ, Vṛṣaṇvasū, Puruvasū, Prabhūvasuḥ, Vibhūvasuḥ, Mahāvasū, Punarvasū, Aśvajivasū (?), Ābharadvasuḥ, Akṣitāvasuḥ, Kaitevasū (?), Gotrāvasuḥ, Pratevasū (?), Radāvasū, Vidadvasuḥ, Śatadvasuḥ, and so on.

In these words, "vasu" generally means "wealth." In the Shatapatha Brahmana as well, the word occurs in "Amāvasu" and in "Citravasu"...

original p. 691

"Vasu" — the word derives from the root "vas" (to dwell), and signifies "one who dwells." The Bhashyakara has followed this sense and explained accordingly here.

The word "vājinīvatī" — which is a derivative of "vājinī" — is used in the Rigveda as a qualifier of Uṣas (the Dawn) in several Riks (several citations). Yāska, in his Nirukta, when explaining one of these Riks, glosses "vājinīvatī" as "annavatī" (possessing food). There "vājinī" means "food"; and when explaining another Rik, he gives the same sense again.

Sāyaṇācārya has explained "vājinī" as "possessing oblation-food"; likewise Skandasvāmin, in his own Vedabhāṣya, glosses "vājinī" as "sacrifice." Veṅkaṭamādhava, in explaining this word, interprets "asmai vāsayitārau — vājinīvasū" — hence for "vājinī," the principal senses that may be entertained are: (1) food or nourishment, (2) strength, and (3) speed. "Vāji" is taken by some to mean "horse." Roth, the scholar, translates "vājinīvasū" as "possessing quick horses." Since this word "vājinīvasū" is used by many rishis when praising deities such as Indra and the Aśvins, no single fixed sense has been established for it; it was evidently in common use, and especially frequent in yajnas involving Soma-drinking, so it is reasonable to suppose that Soma-juice and foods of every sort were freely offered in such rites.

"Cetathaḥ" — "you both know." "Dravat" — in the Nirukta (2.15.?), this word is listed among the sixteen or so words expressing "quickly, swiftly."

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ "Vājinīvasū" — although Yāska lists "vājinī" among the names of Uṣas, that sense does not fit here and is not adopted. "Vājaḥ asyām asti" — food is present in this: the affix "ini" is added after "vāja," and the "a" is dropped, then the feminine affix "ṅīp" is added, giving "vājinī." Then "vājinyāṃ vasataḥ" gives the compound "vājinīvasū," a vocative dual; and by the rule for vocatives, its accent becomes fully unaccented (sarvānudātta).

original p. 692

Sūkta 2, The Sixth Mantra

"Dravat" — Yāska lists this among the sixteen words meaning "quickly" ("su kṣipraṃ makṣu dravat," Nirukta 2.15.?). Hence here, by the rule for such words, the final syllable takes the udātta accent.

॥ Iti prathamāṣṭake prathamādhyāye tṛtīyo vargaḥ ॥ Thus ends the third Varga of the first Adhyāya of the first Aṣṭaka.

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वा॒यवि॒न्द्र॑श्च सुन्व॒त आ या॑त॒मुप॑ निष्कृ॒तम् । म॒क्ष्वि१त्था धि॒या न॒रा ॥६॥

vāyav índraś ca sunvatá ā́ yātam úpa niṣkṛtám | makṣv ítthā dhiyā́ narā ||6||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । सुन्वतः । आ । यातम् । उप । निःऽकृतम् । मक्षु । इत्था । धिया । नरा ॥६॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च सुन्वतः सोमाभिषवं कुर्वतो यजमानस्य निष्कृतं संस्कृतं संस्कर्तारं वा सोममुपसा यातमागच्छतम् । नरा हे नरौ पुरुषौ पौरुषेण सामर्थ्येनोपेतौ युवयोरागतयोश्च सतोर्धियामुना कर्मणा मक्षु त्वरया संस्कारः संपत्स्यते । इत्था सत्यम् ॥ he vāyo tvam indraś ca sunvataḥ somābhiṣavaṃ kurvato yajamānasya niṣkṛtaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ saṃskartāraṃ vā somam upa yātam āgacchatam | narā he narau puruṣau pauruṣeṇa sāmarthyenopetau yuvayor āgatayoś ca satoḥ dhiyāmunā karmaṇā makṣu tvarayā saṃskāraḥ saṃpatsyate | itthā satyam ||

Translation: "O Vāyu, and Indra with you! Come to the prepared (niṣkṛta, refined) Soma of the sacrificer who is pressing Soma — or to him who prepares it. 'Narā' — O two men, endowed with manly strength! When you two have come, by this rite the preparation will quickly be completed. 'Itthā' — truly." The grammar that follows in the source — on the accent of "vāyo" as vocative, "indraḥ" as a word with the "ran" affix (final-syllable udātta), "ca" as a particle, "sunvataḥ" as a present participle in the class-5 conjugation, "niṣkṛtam" as a compound with the preverb "niḥ" taking the accent of its first member, "dhiyā" with an udātta case-ending, and "narā" as a dual vocative — is in the established dense register and is not reproduced in detail.

original p. 693

Application (viniyoga) of the next three Riks: "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam" and the following Riks — addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa — are applied in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha of the morning pressing, and (as Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra states, "mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam") likewise in the Ābhiplava-ṣaḍaha and related rites. The Kannada gives the citations in a compressed run; only the sense is given here.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca) — and Indra, both of you | सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ) — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam) — Soma purified by the preparatory rites (for drinking) — or to the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | उप आ यातम् (upa ā yātam) — come | (हे) नरा ((he) narā) — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength | धिया (dhiyā) — through this rite | मक्षु (makṣu) — quickly (the preparation will be accomplished) | इत्था (itthā) — this is true.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed out Soma-juice and made it pure through the preparatory rites, keeping it ready for you. O mighty ones, by your coming this rite — the yajna — is completed; that is, it is fully and correctly accomplished. Since you come and drink the Soma, the yajna will be carried through exactly as prescribed. This is true.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥

"Niṣkṛtam" — the Bhashyakara glosses this as "saṃskṛtam," that is, "refined, purified"; the authors of the Vedārtha-yatna simply say "Soma." Geldner takes it as "arranged in order," and Grassmann...

original p. 694

...[Grassmann] takes "niṣkṛta" as "a fixed [appointed] place" or "an enclosure/pen." But the right sense is "niṣkṛta" = "completely accomplished" (niḥśeṣeṇa saṃpāditam), as in "uta tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 1.20.6), where this same sense is found. And further:

  1. "ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varsaḥ … niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ" (Rigveda 3.58.9[?])
  2. "somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  3. "baḷitthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat" (Rigveda 5.?.?)
  4. "indra dṛhyasva pūrasi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 8.?.?)
  5. "vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  6. "ukthā minoti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  7. "kanikradad vṛṣā harir indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)

In these Riks, "niṣkṛta" is used for a place where work (that is, sacrificial work) goes on — "the appointed place where the work of sacrifice is performed" — or, more simply, "a suitable place." As on earlier pages, the exact Rigveda locators here were too small to read reliably and are not asserted.

"Itthā" — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "truly." Skandasvāmin — "itthā amutaḥ … asyā arthaḥ": from there, from the intermediate region, from their own station; Veṅkaṭamādhava takes "itthā" as "in this manner."

"Dhiyā" — "by this rite": the Bhashyakara, following the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?), explains "dhī" as "action, work" — "perform the sacrifice!" The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna take it as "by this our praise, made with heartfelt intent"; Geldner takes it as "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Veṅkaṭamādhava take "dhiyā" as "by this work." In the Nighaṇṭu, "dhīḥ" is a synonym of "prajñā" (wisdom); but that sense does not suit here. Since Madhucchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" meaning "by this rite" fits best.

original p. 693

Application (viniyoga) of this Rik: the Rik "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam" [the seventh Rik, next] and the two that follow are applied, in the Prātaḥ-savana, to the Maitrāvaruṇa Stotra — in the Ājya-śastra of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, and, as stated in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the Ṣaḍaha... The same is stated by Ashvalayana in the section beginning "caturviṃśe hotājaniṣṭ…": "mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam" (Ashvalayana 2.?), and in the section "pariśiṣṭā nāvāpānu…."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca) — and Indra along with you (both of you) | सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ) — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam) — Soma made pure through preparatory rites (for drinking), or [to the side of] the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | उप आ यातम् (upa ā yātam) — come | (हे) नरा ((he) narā) — O two Indra-Vāyu, endowed with manly strength and the like | धिया (dhiyā) — through this rite | मक्षु (makṣu) — with alertness (the preparation will be completed) | इत्था (itthā) — this is true.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra-Vāyu, come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and made it pure through preparatory rites, for your sake. O manly ones! With your arrival, this yajna-rite becomes complete and properly furnished. By your coming and drinking the Soma, the yajna will proceed as prescribed and reach its completion. This is true.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥

"Niṣkṛtam" — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam," i.e., "prepared, purified." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it simply means "Soma." Geldner says it means "arranged, set in order"; Grassmann...

original p. 694

...[Grassmann] takes "niṣkṛta" to mean "the appointed place" (the ritual ground). Both "niṣkṛtam = niḥśeṣeṇa saṃpāditam" ("completely accomplished") — this is the sound sense. The same sense appears in the Rik "uta tyaṃ cemasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 1.20.6). The word "niṣkṛta" is also used in the following Riks:

  1. "ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kerikratu-tāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ" (Rigveda 3.58.?)
  2. "somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?)
  3. "baḷittthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat" (Rigveda 8.?)
  4. "indra dṛhyasva pūrasi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 8.?)
  5. "vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?)
  6. "ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?)
  7. "kanikradad vṛṣā harir indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.100.?)

In these Riks, "niṣkṛtam" indicates a place where a rite (a yajna-rite) is performed — "the appointed place where the work of sacrifice is performed" — or a place made ready.

"Itthā" — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "true" (satya). Skandasvāmin: "amuta" — "from there"; from this it is explained as "from that heaven, from their own abode of the sky"; Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses it as "in this manner."

"Dhiyā" — the Bhashyakara takes it as "amunā karmaṇā" — "by this rite" — as in the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 3.?): "dhīḥ" is glossed as "action; perform the yajna." The authors of Vedārtha-yatna take it as "by this our mindful praise"; Geldner as "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Nārāyaṇa give "by this rite." In the Nighaṇṭu, "dhīḥ" is a synonym of "prajñā" (intelligence) — but that sense does not fit here. Since Madhuchandas and others were performing an Agniṣṭoma and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" — "in this rite," "by this rite," "by performing this rite" — is the most fitting sense. The next Ṛca, beginning "mitraṃ huve"... The page opens with the tail of the grammar for Rik 2.6, followed by a note on the application of the next three Riks, addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa.

original p. 693

मित्रं हुव इति मैत्रावरुणस्य स्तोत्रियः । ... तत्रैवाभिप्लवे षडहेऽपि विनियुक्तः । तथा चाश्वलायनेन चतुर्विंशे होताजानिष्ट्येत्यादिखण्डे मित्रं वयं हवामहे मित्रं हुवे पूतदक्षम् । (आश्व. ५-९) इत्यादि सूत्रितम् । mitraṃ huva iti maitrāvaruṇasya stotriyaḥ | … tatraivābhiplave ṣaḍahe'pi viniyuktaḥ | tathā cāśvalāyanena caturviṃśe hotā-jāniṣṭy-ety-ādi-khaṇḍe mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam (āśva. 5.9) ity-ādi sūtritam | (this compressed application-note is a best-effort reading; its sense is that the Mitra-Varuṇa Riks that follow are used in the Maitrāvaruṇa portion of the rite, and also in the Abhiplava Ṣaḍaha)

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (Rik 2.6) ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca) — and Indra with you (both of you) | सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ) — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam) — the Soma purified by consecrating rites (for drinking), or [the sacrificer's] presence, he who has got the Soma-juice ready | आ यातम् (ā yātam) — come | (हे) नरा ((he) narā) — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength | धियः (dhiyaḥ) — [through] this rite | मक्षु (makṣu) — with alertness (the preparation is completed) | इत्था (itthā) — this is true.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and, having purified it by consecrating rites, has kept it ready for you. O men of vigour! By your coming, this rite of yajna will be perfected — that is, made complete in all its parts. Since you come and drink the Soma, the yajna will proceed as prescribed and reach completion. This is true.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥

"Niṣkṛtam" — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam" — that is, consecrated, purified. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it simply means "Soma." The scholar Geldner takes it to mean "arranged/put in order," and Grassmann...

original p. 694

...[Geldner and Grassmann] take "niṣkṛta" to mean "the appointed place" or "the place of sacrifice." That is: "niṣkṛta" = "that which has been completely prepared" — this is the right sense. The same sense holds in the Rik "utā tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 1.20.6[?]). Other Riks where "niṣkṛta" occurs:

  1. ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kerikṛtsnā tāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭaḥ (Rigveda 3.58.9[?])
  2. somo no jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  3. baḷitthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat (Rigveda 8.?.?)
  4. indra dṛhyasva pūras ti bhadrā te iti niṣkṛtam (Rigveda 5.?.?)
  5. vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  6. ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam (Rigveda 9.69.4[?])
  7. kanikradad vṛṣā hariḥ indrasya abhy eti niṣkṛtam (Rigveda 9.100.?)

In these Riks, "niṣkṛta" suggests a fixed place where the work of sacrifice is performed (the appointed place), or an established, prepared place.

"Itthā" — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "true" ("satya"). Skandasvāmin explains it: "itthā amutaḥ" — "from there" — that is, "from your own place, from the sky" [where you dwell]; Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses "itthā" as "in this manner."

"Dhiyā" — the Bhashyakara glosses "amunā karmaṇā" — "by this rite." The Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?) lists "dhī" as meaning "action" (karma), which the commentators explain in the sense "perform, sacrifice." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say: "with our mindful (manaḥpūrvaka) stotra"; Geldner: "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Veṅkaṭamādhava also give "by this rite." In the Nighaṇṭu "dhī" is listed as a synonym of "prajñā" (understanding), but that sense does not suit the present context. Since Madhuchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma at this moment, offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" — "by this rite, or through this act, or by performing this act" — is the natural sense.

original p. 693

Application (viniyoga) note for the following Riks: the three Riks beginning "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam" [Riks 2.7–9, addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa] are applied in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha (the Mitra-Varuṇa offering) of the morning pressing — that is, they belong to the Maitrāvaruṇa Stotra-recitation; and this is also stated by Āśvalāyana in the section of his Shrauta-sutra beginning "caturviṃśe hotā" ("mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam…") — the sutra there giving these as the Puronuvākyā and Yājyā of the Mitra-Varuṇa offering, together with "mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo) — O Vāyu! | इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca) — and Indra with you (both of you) | सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ) — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam) — the Soma made pure by the preparatory rites (for drinking), or [approach] the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | आ यातम् (ā yātam) — come | (हे) नरा ((he) narā) — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength and the like! | धिया (dhiyā) — by this rite | मक्षु (makṣu) — quickly (the preparation will be completed) | इत्था (itthā) — this is true.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and, having purified it through the preparatory rites, has kept it ready for you. O manly ones! By your coming, this rite of sacrifice will be brought to completion — that is, will be made whole and complete. Since you will come and drink the Soma, the yajna will be concluded in accordance with the prescribed rules. This is true.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Niṣkṛtam" — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam," meaning "prepared, purified." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say that it here means simply "Soma." Geldner says it means "arranged/duly ordered," and Grassmann ...

original p. 694

...Grassmann takes "niṣkṛta" as "appointed, fixed," or a "prepared place" (a sacrificial ground). But "niṣkṛtam" — meaning "completed without remainder (niśśeṣeṇa), brought to fulfilment" — is the truly fitting sense. In the Rik "ute tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 1.20.6) this very sense appears. Further examples (numbering as in the source, locators approximate):

  1. "ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kariṣyat sutāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ" (Rigveda 3.?.?)
  2. "somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  3. "baliṭthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat" (Rigveda 5.?.?)
  4. "indra dṛhyasva pūr asi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 8.?.?)
  5. "vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  6. "ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
  7. "kanikradad dhvṛṣā hariṃ indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam" (Rigveda 9.100.?)
