In these Riks, "niṣkṛtam" indicates a place where the work — the sacrificial rite — is carried on: a place appointed for the sacrifice (the assigned place where the work of sacrifice is performed), or a place that is set apart — this is the sense suggested.

"Itthā" — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "truth" (satya). Skandasvāmin gives "amuta iti asyārthaḥ" ("from that place" — the sense being "from there, from their own dwelling, from the sky"), while Veṅkaṭamādhava takes "itthā" to mean "in this manner."

"Dhiyā ('amunā karmaṇā')" — "by this rite," as the Bhashyakara explains, following the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?.?), where "dhīḥ" is listed as a word for "karma" (action, rite). The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it means "by this our [prayer] made with mind and devotion"; Geldner says "as we desire"; Skandasvāmin and Mādhava give "by this rite." ("Dhīḥ" is in another sense a synonym of "prajñā," wisdom, but that sense does not fit here.) Since the rishi Madhuchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma at the morning pressing and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu, the sense "in this rite," "by this rite" or "by performing this rite" is the fitting one. The next Ṛc-group then begins: "mitraṃ huve…"

original p. 695

...that is, "mitraṃ huve," the sukta's [seventh] Rik, is said to be the first of three Riks concerning Mitra-Varuṇa. On the day of the Sutyā (pressing), within the yajña beginning at the appointed hour, at the morning pressing, in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha rite, this Rik's application follows. Further, the entire matter of the Abhiplava and Ṣaḍaha [six-day] rites has already been explained; the application of these Riks in the present sacrifice has also been explained. Āśvalāyana, in the section of his Shrauta-sutra called "hotā-jani..." (Adhyāya 3, Section 8), states the application of the Riks concerning Mitra and Varuṇa individually, and further, in the Adhyāya 8, Section 2, states the application of the Riks concerning Vāyu and the others. This has already been discussed above (see printed pages 671–672).

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

"Vāyo" — since the vocative case is governed by the rule stated in the Adhyāya on vocatives, it is treated as unaccented.

The words "udgātra, graha, viṣṭu, kubja, cambu, kṣurabhṛd, vedyoktra, bhairavabhelaka, śrūmāla," and others (Uṇādi 3.108[?]) are formed with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent by the special rule for such formations. On this rule, the word "indra" is likewise established with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent — this is well established in the grammar; the sense "one who is strong" is not further explained here, being clear enough.

"Cāpadayo'nudāttāḥ" (Phit-sutra 4.14) — words ending in "ca" and similar particles are unaccented; hence "ca" itself is unaccented.

"Sunvataḥ" — the word "śamerasumeṇaddhyādeḥ" (Panini 3.2.?) is used with the meaning of that word's own class.

"Niṣkṛtam" — here, in the sense of "carefully purified/consummated" (Nirukta 4.2), "niḥ" is used; the word "niḥ" being used with the sense of "carefully purified," in the sense "carried through by no remainder," and the meaning is thus established according to the various usages. "Niṣkṛta" is derived from "niḥ" + "kṛta" ("kṛ," to make); the resulting compound is formed by the rule concerning gati-compounds beginning at (Panini 1.4.60), where "kṛ" in the sense of "action" takes "kṛt" affix. Since "niḥ" is an indeclinable used with the root "kṛ" in the sense of "beginning," it is properly usable in the sense of the compound now beginning, "niṣkṛtam" indicating "the appointed place where the offering is begun." "Makṣu" — the word "kaḥ" and others, according to their own grammatical class, along with the appropriate preceding or following elements, take the udātta accent — hence "makṣu" carries this accent... Caveat: the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā section on this page was exceptionally dense and compressed even by the standard of these grammar sections, and the rendering above should be treated as a best-effort, lower-confidence reading rather than a reliable transcription — in particular the specific sutra attributions and some of the word-formation chains. The surrounding Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha sections translated elsewhere in this project remain the more reliable material. The preceding grammar section concludes with brief remarks on "kṛta" and "dhiyā," in the same dense register; not reproduced in detail. The Kannada then confirms that "dhiyā" is treated as unaccented per the sutra "āmantritasya ca" — that is, as a case-form following a vocative — in agreement with the accent already seen in the printed Saṃhitā-text.

original p. 696

Sūkta 2, The Seventh Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

मि॒त्रं हु॑वे पू॒तद॑क्षं॒ वरु॑णं च रिशाद॒सम् । धियं॑ घृ॒ताची॑ साध॒न्ता ॥७॥

mitráṃ huve pūtádakṣaṃ váruṇaṃ ca riśādasám | dhíyaṃ ghṛtā́cīṃ sādhantā ||7||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

मित्रम् । हुवे । पूतऽदक्षम् । वरुणम् । च । रिशादसम् । धियम् । घृतऽअचीम् । साधन्ता ॥७॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अहमस्मिन् कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय पूतदक्षं शवितबलं मित्रं हुवे । तथा रिशादसं रिशानां हिंसकानामत्तारं वरुणं च हुवे । आह्वयामि । कीदृशौ मित्रावरुणौ । घृतमुदकमञ्चतीति घृताचीं भूमिं प्रापयतीति यां धीर्वर्षणकर्म तां घृताचीं धियं साधन्तौ कुर्वन्तौ । मित्र-शब्दः पुंल्लिङ्गः प्रातिपदिकस्वरेणान्तोदात्तः । हुव इति ह्वयतेर्लुक् भवति शप्रीव लुक् सति शपः स्थाने संस्कारणम् । साः-अच्युवृत्तौ बहुलं भूतकाले चोदाहृतः ॥ aham asmin karmaṇi haviṣ-pradānāya pūtadakṣaṃ śavita-balaṃ mitraṃ huve | tathā riśādasaṃ riśānāṃ hiṃsakānām attāraṃ varuṇaṃ ca huve | āhvayāmi | kīdṛśau mitrāvaruṇau | ghṛtam udakam añcatīti ghṛtācīṃ bhūmiṃ prāpayatīti yāṃ dhīr varṣaṇa-karma tāṃ ghṛtācīṃ dhiyaṃ sādhantau kurvantau | mitra-śabdaḥ puṃllliṅgaḥ prātipadika-svareṇāntodāttaḥ | huva iti hvayater luk bhavati śapa iva luk sati śapaḥ sthāne saṃskāraṇam | sā-acyuvṛttau bahulaṃ bhūtakāle codāhṛtaḥ ||

Translation: "In this rite, for the offering of the oblation, I call ('huve') upon Mitra, whose strength is pure ('pūtadakṣam'). Likewise I call upon Varuṇa, called 'riśādasam' — the devourer of the harmful ones (riśānām). What kind of pair are Mitra and Varuṇa? Those who accomplish the rain-bringing rite — 'dhiyam ghṛtācīm' — the rite that causes water (ghṛta) to reach the earth. The word 'mitra' is masculine and takes final-syllable accent by the ordinary noun-accent rule. 'Huve' — from the root 'hve' (to call), with elision of the class-marker affix 'śap' (as usual), and the resulting adjustment in its place." The grammar continues in the dense register, working through "pūtadakṣam," "riśādasam," and "dhiyam ghṛtācīm." The grammatical derivation of "pūtadakṣam," "varuṇam," "riśādasam" and "ghṛtācīm" continues here in the same dense sutra-citation register as before — covering the derivation of "riśādasam" from a root meaning "to eat/consume" combined with "riśa" [harm], and the accent-treatment of the compound "ghṛtācī." As with other pages of this density, the specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced verbatim; the overall senses already given in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya above — Mitra of pure strength, Varuṇa the devourer of the harmful — are confirmed by this derivation.

original p. 697

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(अश्विनोः कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय, इह यज्ञ-कर्मदल्लि हविस्सन्नु समर्पिसुवुदक्कागि) — (for offering the oblation in this yajna-rite) | मित्रं (mitraṃ) — Mitra | पूतदक्षं (pūtadakṣaṃ) — whose strength is pure, that is, who is ever capable | हुवे (huve) — I call | रिशादसं (riśādasaṃ) — one who devours the harmful ones (rākṣasas), the destroyer of enemies | वरुणं (varuṇaṃ) — Varuṇa | च (ca) — and | हुवे (huve) — I call | (मित्रावरुणौ) (mitrāvaruṇau) — (Mitra and Varuṇa) | घृताचीं (ghṛtācīṃ) — the rite that causes rain to fall | धियं (dhiyaṃ) — the sacrificial rite | साधन्ता (sādhantā) — accomplishing.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

I invoke, into this rite of sacrifice, the deities Mitra and Varuṇa, that they may partake of the oblation. Among them, Mitra is of surpassing strength; his power knows no weakening. Varuṇa is mighty and destroys enemies. Moreover, in bringing about rain, Mitra and Varuṇa possess a particular capability. I invoke such Mitra and Varuṇa into this yajna, as the principal deities [of this Rik].

original p. 698

॥ English Translation ॥

I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water (on the earth).

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Pūtadakṣam" — "pūta" means pure; "dakṣa" means strength; this is the Bhashyakara's sense, taking these as two separate words joined together within a compound ("pūta" occurring [inserted] between the syllables of a word meaning strength — Nighaṇṭu 3.9). The Bhashyakara has explained the word following this Nighaṇṭu sense. Several Riks illustrate this word's usage:

  1. "jajñānā pūtadakṣasā" (Rigveda 1.94.5[?])
  2. "abudhne rājā varuṇo vanasyordhvaṃ stūpaṃ dadate pūtadakṣaḥ" (Rigveda 1.24.7[?])
  3. "mayo dadhe medhiraḥ pūtadakṣo divaḥ subandhur januṣā pṛthivyāḥ" (Rigveda 3.1.?)
  4. "arcanti tvā marutaḥ pūtadakṣāsteme sakhāyaḥ svidharā abhūvan" (Rigveda 8.13.?)
  5. "ni ketunā janānāṃ citekhe pūtadakṣā" (Rigveda 8.44.?)
  6. "utasya vo rathaḥ pūtadakṣāstvaṣṭasya pastyo adabdhā" (Rigveda 1.?)
  7. "prati vāṃ sūra udite sūkta ṛcā vartraṃ hunve varuṇa pūtadakṣam" (Rigveda 2.?)
  8. "ṛtāvānā samrāṭā pūtadakṣasā" (Rigveda 8.25.10[?])
  9. "ṛtāvānā yajase pūtadakṣāsā" (Rigveda 7.?)
  10. "arcanti pūtadakṣasaḥ" (Rigveda 8.94.?)
  11. "tyānnu kṣatriyāṃ diṣo yau martaḥ purukṛt tuve" (Rigveda 8.?)
  12. "indro mitro varuṇaḥ saṃ tvākratve pūtadakṣo bhagaḥ savitā pūtadakṣasaḥ" (Rigveda 10.?)

— and so on. The Bhashyakara, in explaining these Riks, glosses "pūtadakṣa" as: pure strength, power, or capability. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna, for this word, consider "manaskeṃdu"... Note: given the density of citations on this page and the small print, several verse-locators above are given only approximately; several were left unread where illegible.

original p. 699

...Geldner takes "manaskeṃdu" [an intended-mind reading] in the sense of "purpose." But the Bhashyakara's own sense — "capability" — as stated on the previous page, fits better. In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda (6.2.1[?]), "dakṣa" is glossed as both "strength" and "wisdom." Here, some of the Vedārtha-yatna authors explain "dakṣa" as meaning "sensory power" or "the power of the sense-organs," while others explain it as meaning "the capacity for action." "Dakṣa" indicates a strength of mind and a strength of body alike.

Some further Riks in which the word "dakṣa" appears:

  1. "dakṣaṃ dadhāte apasam" (Rigveda 1.3.6[?]) — here "dakṣa" is used in the sense of a particular capability or the quality of skill in work.

  2. "dakṣaṃ dadhāsi jīvase" (Rigveda 1.60.?[?])

"taṃ dakṣam abhi saṃvide kavim" (Rigveda 1.?)

"dyumattamaṃ dakṣaṃ dhehi sedhā janānāṃ pūrvyaḥ arātīḥ" (Rigveda 8.44.9[?])

"ya indro haryāśvo dakṣaṃ dadhāti taṃ riśo dakṣaṃ dhāti somini" (Rigveda 2.?)

"pra dakṣāya preṣṭheṣā" (Rigveda 8.6.20[?])

In all these Riks, the word "dakṣa" always carries the sense of "strength." Elsewhere the word "dakṣa" is used in the sense of purpose, or determination, or an intended aim, and "kratu" (also meaning something like determination/resolve) too carries this same sense of "the power that gives shape to intent" — as in:

"bhadraṃ no api vātaya manaḥ dakṣam uta kratum" (Rigveda 10.25.1[?]) "ā te niyantu manasaḥ purāṇi kratve dakṣāya jīvase" (Rigveda 10.?) "uta svena kratunā saṃ vadeta śreyāṃsaṃ daksaṃ manasā jagṛbhyāt" (Rigveda 10.?) "tvaṃ soma kratubhiḥ sukratur bhūḥ dakṣaḥ suṣaṃbhoḥ viśvavedāḥ" (Rigveda 9.?) "ā no yajñāya takṣata śubhavantaḥ kratve dakṣāya suprajāvatīm iṣam" (Rigveda 1.?) "adhā hy agne kratvor bhadrasya dakṣasya sādhoḥ" (Rigveda 4.?) As with the preceding page, these citations are presented conservatively — some verse-locators are given only approximately, and where illegible they are omitted rather than guessed.

original p. 700

Further citations closing the "dakṣa" discussion: "pra vaḥ sutāso haraya iva pūrṇāḥ kṛtve dakṣāya harṣayanta kīlāḥ" (Rigveda 5.?), and "tvaṃ no agne āditye kṛtvā dakṣasya mekṣanā" (Rigveda 8.?). In all of these Riks, the word "dakṣa" bears various senses; in the present context, however, it should be understood to mean "resolve" (saṃkalpa) or "purpose" (uddeśa).

"Riśādasam" — Yāska, in his Nirukta (2.16), states that "riśādas" means "rekṣalayodāriṇī" or, alternatively, "rekṣalayodāsinaḥ." He explains that those who protect against violence, being armed as it were with the weapons appropriate for use against those who inflict harm, are "riśādasaḥ." That is, they are "the destroyer of the harmful," "the protector against harm," the one who chastises those who do harm.

Regarding the deities to whom this epithet applies: Nirukta scholars — Riśṭaṃ himsati (i.e., "riśa" is destroyed [by the deity]); Riśaṃ hiṃsakaṃ dasyati (destroys the harmer); Riśam adyaṃ hiṃsanti dasyanti (destroy that which harms); Riśam adyanti kṣipanti veti riśādasaḥ — thus various authors explain it, some saying that they eat or consume the harmful, some that they hurl them away.** These are examined in Vaidika-nighaṇṭu, chapter 3.9. Vāyu and other deities' epithets are likewise described using the word "riśādasaḥ" in many places.

Sāyaṇācārya explains this word, in his commentary, as meaning: "Riśānām" — "of the harmful ones" — "Attāram" — "devourer" or "eater," and in other places as: "one who protects" or "one who guards." At times he explains it as "one whose enemies dwindle away, or who destroys their strength."

Some who have written treatises on Vedic interpretation state: "riśat: hiṃsakah, ādaḥ-attā, riśādaḥ. riśāṃ hiṃsakāṇaṃ attā" — "Riśāt" means "one who inflicts harm"; "adaḥ" means "eater"; "riśādaḥ" therefore means "eater of those who inflict harm." This is stated to mean: "he who destroys the harmful," or "one who does away with the enemy." Veṅkaṭamādhava explains it in the very same manner, connecting the sense with this compound word.

original p. 701

Among Western scholars — Max Müller, Eggling, Grassmann, Hillebrandt and others — most explain this word to mean "destroyer of enemies" (Destroyer of enemies). The German scholar Ludwig does not agree that the word means "destroyer of enemies." He is inclined to think the word "Riśat" refers to a particular tribe/people, and that the sense is "one who has vanquished them." But this meaning has not gained acceptance here. Many other scholars have proposed varied meanings for the word, but since these meanings are drawn merely from etymology, and none of them fits the actual context well, further discussion of them is not useful here.

"Dhiyam" — this word means an act of sacrifice, a rite. Geldner calls it "poem, composition" (Poem). Skandasvāmin, Veṅkaṭamādhava, and Sāyaṇa do not accept this. Skandasvāmin calls it "an act to be examined/investigated" (vicāryaṃ karma), and Sāyaṇa calls it "varṣaṇa-karma" (the rain-bringing rite). This is correct, because it is well established that Vṛṣṭi (rain) is brought about through the performance of yajnas in the Vedic period. This sense is clearly evident in the Rik: this specific citation remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading given its compressed and archaic form

युद्धेनाशिं शतकतवे पुरोरुहेको होत्राय वृषकं कृतस्य दीधेत् । देवपत्रं वृष्णियं रराशेको बृहस्पतिर्नाचमश्यायच्छेत् ॥ yuddhenāśiṃ śatakatave puroruheko hotrāya vṛṣakaṃ kṛtasya dīdheta | devapatraṃ vṛṣṇiyaṃ rarāśeko bṛhaspatir nācamaśyāyacchet || (Rigveda 10.?.?)

"Ghṛtācīm" — the Bhashyakara has interpreted this word: "udakaṃ pṛthivīṃ prati yā gamayati sā ghṛtācī" — that is, "the rite that causes water to reach the earth," on the analogy of "vṛṣṭi" (bringing water down). The Māthava commentary [Veṅkaṭamādhava] and others agree with this. The rite whereby, through yajnas performed, one brings water down onto the earth — this rite ("ghṛtācī") is thus glossed. The Skandasvāmī commentary explains further: "phalasva bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — "the rite that carries water (in the form of ghee/rain) to the earth" — through this the two deities, Vāyu and [Mitra-Varuṇa], accomplish it, "vṛṣṇyaḥ" [rain-bringing]. Sāyaṇācārya says the same. Sāyaṇācārya explains "sphṛta udakaṃ āñcati bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — the rite by which water (in the form of the deity's own oblation) is caused to reach the earth — that rite, "ghṛtācī," and that which is accomplished — "vṛṣṭi" — as its result. Māthava too accepts this sense. Māthava, in one Brahmana-passage's citation, gives the example: "mitraṃ vā ahaḥ vāruṇe rātrau. ca ahoratrābhyāṃ hi mitrāvaruṇāhorātrābhyāṃ tu varṣaṇyo" — Mitra [rules] the day; Varuṇa, the night; and [through] Mitra-Varuṇa together, [ruling] both day and night, [rain is brought about]...

original p. 702

...that is, Varuṇa causes lightning to occur through the day. In the Rigveda too, elsewhere (several citations), it is said that Mitra-Varuṇa together summon the rain onto the earth. In the Nighaṇṭu, "udaka" (water) is included among the hundred-odd words listed as synonyms for water, in which "ghṛta" itself is one.

त आ अनश्रे रत्नान्युपैषु घृतेन पृथिवी व्यूद्ये । ta ā anaśre ratnāny upaiṣu ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye | (Rigveda 1.164.47[?])

In this Rik, "ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye" — "the earth is watered/moistened by ghṛta" — makes clear that "ghṛta" here means water (rain). Yāska, in this context, discusses this word further. Some Vedic-ritual scholars say that "ghṛta" means "flowing water" or "melted butter," and that whichever sense (water or ghee) is intended is decided by context — but that, in the present case, the sense of "water" clearly fits the surrounding sense.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

"Mitraḥ" derives with a kṛt-affix, giving final-syllable accent. "Huve" — from the root "hve" (to call), first person singular, the affix "iṭ" being added in a special sense for the "ātmanepada" middle form, giving "huve," accented on the final syllable (by the vocative-adjacent rule). "Kartari śaḥ" (Panini 3.1.68) — the class-affix "śa"; hence the "śap" affix is elided ("luk"), by the special rule applying widely to such roots. "Riśādasam" — the augment "sup" is inserted, and finally the compound resolves to a possessive/agentive derivative ending in "u+ṣu." "Dhiyam" — a derivative of the root "dhī" with the kṛt-affix "kvip," ending in consonantal stem, with accent falling on the base ("dhī"). "Ghṛtācī" — a compound of "ghṛta" and "añc" (going), with the "ac" ending replaced by "īṣ" in the feminine, giving "ghṛtācī," retaining the accent of its earlier member (by the rule for such gati-compounds).

"Sādhantā" — the roots "ṛdh, dāri, uśan" (Uṇādi 1.99[?]) — "ṛdh" means to prosper/flourish, "dāri" means to split/divide, "uś" means to desire — these three roots take the "unan" affix; hence "uśan" [likewise elsewhere in this Rik] takes the same affix. Consequently, this affix, being accentless, shifts the accent to the syllable preceding it, giving the udātta placement seen in the printed text. Caveat: the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā section above, like page 695 earlier, is a lower-confidence best-effort reading of very dense grammatical shorthand; the specific sutra attributions and derivational chains should not be relied upon without independent verification. The Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha content translated on the surrounding pages remains the more solid material. This page continues the grammatical derivation of "riśādasam" and "ghṛtācī" in the same extremely dense register as the previous page — working through the roots "riś" (to harm) and "ad" (to eat), the formation of the compound "riśādas," and detailed accent-rules for "ghṛtācī" as a feminine compound of "ghṛta" and "añc." Given the exceptional density of this stretch (continuing directly from the caveated section on the previous page), it is not reproduced line-by-line here; the overall senses already established in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and Viśeṣārtha above — "devourer of the harmful," and "the rain-bringing rite" — are the reliable takeaways.

original p. 703

"Apna" — among the words listed by the Nirukta as synonyms for "karma" (deed, act, rite), "apna" is one of the terms used to mean a sacrificial rite.

"Ghṛtācīti" — the word "ghṛta" is formed with the "in" affix, with the roots "ghṛt," "gṛdh," "gṛdhra," "sṛj," and others (per Uṇādi 3.94). "Pūrvatrāsiddham" (Panini 8.2.1) — this rule is applied here to govern the process. In the formation of certain roots, when "aj" (going) is a member of the compound, and the affix is "kvip," ending with the loss of the "j," the compound results as "ghṛta+añc," with a special "ni" affix (Uṇādi 6.144[?]) attached to some such formations. In "adhyātmam" — "cati," "jati," and other roots of this class form derivatives ending in the vowel; when preceded by a consonant, the affix following gives rise to a differing formation. This is why word-forms such as "annavaṃśyoji" arise in certain established usages.

"Ajña keśvyo-siṃsyāṃ" (Panini 7.4.?) — the Ātmanepada verb "yaśa+bham" arises here, and by a special rule regarding this class of feminine ("uṃs")-suffixed derivatives, "yaṣabham" arises, with the meaning "attaining a particular arrangement/adornment" (adopting a suitable form), the letter "bha" combining with the class-sign. "Acaḥ" (Panini 6.?.?) — the letter "ca" ends with elision, being combined with "bha," yielding "acaḥ."

"Nabhiṣayasyāsiṃvedhya" (Phit-sutra 3.8) — the exception-rule for words ending in "in-antodātta"-class declension: "Ghṛtādīnāṃ ca" (Phit-sutra 3.6) — words of the "ghṛtādi" group take accent on the final syllable — hence "ghṛtāci" is confirmed as final-syllable accented (ghṛtācī), matching the accent shown in the printed text. Caveat: pages 702–703 together form an unusually long and dense stretch of Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā; the renderings above are best-effort and should be treated as lower-confidence, consistent with the standing caution applied to this register throughout the project. This page closes out the grammatical derivation carried over from the two preceding pages, and briefly explains "sādhyantau" as an intensive-class ("shnu") present dual form from the root "sādh," with the accent falling per the rule for such formations.

original p. 704

Sūkta 2, The Eighth Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

ऋ॒तेन॑ मित्रावरुणावृतावृधावृत॒स्पृशा॑ । क्रतुं॑ बृह॒न्तमा॑शाथे ॥८॥

ṛténa mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛ́śā | krátuṃ bṛhantám āśāthe ||8||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

ऋतेन । मित्रावरुणौ । ऋतऽवृधौ । ऋतऽस्पृशा । क्रतुम् । बृहन्तम् । आशाथे इति ॥८॥

original p. 705

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे मित्रावरुणौ युवां क्रतुं प्रवर्तमानमिमं सोमायागमाशाथे । व्याप्नुवन्तौ । केन निमित्तेन । ऋतेन । अवश्यंभावितया सत्येन फलेन । अस्पृष्टं फलं दातुमिच्छथ इत्यर्थः । कीदृशौ युवां । ऋतावृधौ । ऋतस्य सत्यस्य वर्धकौ ऋतस्पृशा ऋतस्य स्पृष्टारौ संस्पर्शकौ । केन विशेषेण । मित्रावरुणाविति महर्षिनामधेयेन । मित्रावरुणाविति देवतायोर्द्वे च । पूर्वपदस्यान्तोदात्तत्वं ऋतस्पृशेति वर्धयितारावाख्येयादृध्वर्थ फलम् आर्षेण द्वित्वं शेष्वाचाकिच्चेति निपातनात् । कीदृशं क्रतुम् । बृहन्तं महान्तं । he mitrāvaruṇau yuvāṃ kratuṃ pravartamānam imaṃ somāyāgam āśāthe | vyāpnuvantau | kena nimittena | ṛtena | avaśyaṃbhāvitayā satyena phalena | aspṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ dātum icchatha ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | ṛtāvṛdhau | ṛtasya satyasya vardhakau ṛtaspṛśā ṛtasya spṛṣṭārau saṃsparśakau | kena viśeṣeṇa | mitrāvaruṇāv iti maharṣi-nāmadheyena | … kīdṛśaṃ kratum | bṛhantaṃ mahāntaṃ |

Translation: "O Mitra and Varuṇa! You both fully attend to and pervade this ongoing Soma-yajna. By what means? By 'ṛta' — through the true fruit that is bound to occur; the sense is 'you desire to bestow the fruit that is otherwise unattainable.' What kind of pair are you two? 'Ṛtāvṛdhau' — increasers of ṛta (truth); 'ṛtaspṛśā' — those who touch/directly bring about ṛta. [Grammar notes on accent and derivation follow.] What kind of rite (kratu)? 'Bṛhantam' — great, mighty."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau) — O Mitra and Varuṇa! | ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau) — increasers of truth | ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā) — those who touch/uphold truth | (यूयम्) ((yūyam)) — you two, being such | ऋतेन (ṛtena) — through the true and inevitable fruit | बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ) — great, mighty | क्रतुम् (kratum) — this rite (yajna) | आशाथे (āśāthe) — you fully pervade and attend to.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two are increasers of truth, and you uphold that truth; you accordingly bestow, without fail, the fruit that truly and certainly follows from this rite. You watch over this great sacrifice we now perform, so that it is duly and completely fulfilled. The opening of this page continues the grammatical derivation of "ṛtāvṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā" from the previous page, discussing accent-rules for vocative-adjacent compounds and citing further Rigveda parallels for the sense "increaser of truth." Given the density, this portion is not reproduced line-by-line.

original p. 706

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau) — O Mitra and Varuṇa, (you two) | ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau) — increasers of water, or of truth, or of the yajna | ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā) — those who bring about water (in the form of rain) | (such as you) ऋतेन (ṛtena) — in order to give us, truly and certainly, the fruit obtained from the yajna | बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ) — exceedingly great, whole with all its parts | क्रतुम् (kratum) — toward this Soma-yajna we are now performing | आशाथे (āśāthe) — may you come, attending to it (come!).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Mitra and Varuṇa! By your grace you cause rain to fall, so that water is abundantly available in the world; or, you cause dharma or the yajna to flourish, and through that bring about rain upon the earth. Therefore, come now to this great sacrifice we are performing — attended by many ritvijs, furnished with the materials needed for the rite, and thronged with many people amid great festivity — and graciously grant us its fruit.

original p. 707

॥ English Translation ॥

O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Ṛtena" — we have already fully discussed this word (see page 647). "Ṛtāvṛdhau" — the Bhashyakara states that "ṛta" here means "water," or, alternatively, "truth" or "the yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna accept the sense "water"; Skandasvāmī has similarly explained it. The Bhashyakara, accepting the sense "water," explains it accordingly. Scholars of Vedic interpretation say that "ṛta" means "Dharma" (Taking delight in the Sacred law), and explain the word in this sense. In the present context, this meaning too is entirely fitting, since, in a Rik connected with Mitra-Varuṇa, some scholars accept the sense "rain" precisely because of the well-known connection between rain and Mitra-Varuṇa. Others who hold that this is not the fitting sense here explain the word differently. Various writers explain this word using three distinct meanings: "satyam" (truth), "yajña" (the sacrifice), and "udaka" (water). The Bhashyakara has himself made use of all three senses across various contexts.

In the present passage, the word "vṛdhau" is used in the sense of augmenting; the word "spṛśau" (in "ṛtaspṛśā") appears twice — [used once each] with two distinct senses. Since it would otherwise be redundant to repeat the same word "ṛtavṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā" with an identical sense, several scholars hold that "ṛtāvṛdhau" means "increasers of truth or of the yajna," while "ṛtaspṛśā," within the same word, means "bringers of water" — this being why the [same-looking] word carries different meanings in each place. Some scholars, however, are of the view that "ṛta" applies with only the general sense of "truth" throughout, without needing this distinction.

Many hold that the sense "truth" fits best here. In the context where Mitra-Varuṇa are being praised, since only the sense "truth" fits the reference clearly, it is regarded as the more suitable reading — while the fittingness of the sense "water" does not appear so clear in the other place. "Yugas satyaṃ paraṃ brahma" — the topic of universal righteousness and eternal order — is discussed further in the Taittiriya Upanishad (1.1.1[?]); this subject matter is treated more fully when that context is explained.

"Ṛtaspṛśā" — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "those who cause rain (vṛṣṭi) and are graciously disposed [toward it]"; and Vedic interpreters explain it as "defenders of Dharma" (defending the Sacred law). The German scholar Geldner explains it as "fosterers of truth" (fosterers of truth).

original p. 708

Māthava [Veṅkaṭamādhava] explains "ṛtaspṛśau" as meaning "creators who establish truth." His sense and Geldner's sense mutually agree. Therefore, the sense "those who establish truth" is preferred here as the more suitable reading for "ṛtaspṛśau."

"Āśāthe" — "āśnute" means "pervades, reaches, attends to," and so on. Each author has interpreted this word according to what fits his own sense; whatever meaning one adopts, they all essentially arrive at the same overall sense.

"Bṛhantam" — the Bhashyakara glosses this as "possessing every limb and part, complete." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain it as "great" ("bṛhat"); Skandasvāmī as "vast" (mahat); Māthava and others agree with this. None of these authors differ in the essential sense.

"Kratum" — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "the Soma-yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna take it as "desire" (desire); Geldner takes it as "insight, understanding" (insight, understanding). However, since the rishi is engaged in performing this yajna, the sense "Soma-yajna" — as given by the Bhashyakara, Skandasvāmī, and Māthava — is the fitting one. Geldner's and the Vedārtha-yatna's readings, when examined here, do not fit well.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

"Ṛtaḥ" — being listed among the "ghṛtādi" group, by the rule "ghṛtādīnāṃ ca" (Phit-sutra 3.6), the word takes the udātta accent. "Mitraś ca varuṇaś ca mitrāvaruṇau" — a dvandva (copulative) compound, formed by the rule "cārthe dvandvaḥ" (Panini 2.2.29[?]). By the rule "devatādvandve ca" (Panini 6.3.26[?]) — in a dvandva compound of deity-names, the first member retains its accent — the udātta of "mitra" is retained. "Na lokavikṣa-prātipadikāṃśasya" (Panini 6.1.?) causes elision of accent here. "Mitrāvaruṇau" — thus formed. "Ṛtasya vardhayitārau" — a compound, where "ṛtasya," being the second member of a determinative compound with "vardhaka" ("increaser"), takes the "kṛtya" affix, giving "vṛdha," with the root "spṛś" (to touch) taking "kvip" ("anyeṣām api dṛśyate," Panini 6.3.137[?]) elided, retaining its original accent. In the sandhi-analysis, this becomes "ṛtavṛdhau." "Ṛtaspṛśau" — a similar compound with the affix "kvip" from the root "spṛś" giving "sukāḥ-" ("susambodhane," Panini 8.1.19[?]) yielding "ṛtaspṛśā" — both words functioning as the vocative dual. Since these are vocatives, both are treated, by the rule for such formations, as fully accentless in the Saṃhitā. Caveat: the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā above is, as usual for this register, a best-effort reading; specific sutra-numbers and derivational steps are lower-confidence. This entire page continues the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for "ṛtāvṛdhau," "ṛtaspṛśā," "mitrāvaruṇau," and related forms in the same extremely dense register — working through accent-retention rules for vocatives adjacent to compounds, and closing with remarks confirming that "ṛtena," "mitrāvaruṇā," and the other words of this Rik carry the accent-patterns already visible in the printed Saṃhitā text. Given the sustained density of this stretch (continuing directly the caveated material from the previous page), it is characterized here rather than translated line-by-line; nothing in it changes the senses already established in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha above. This page continues the extended grammatical discussion from the previous two pages — now focused on "vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā" and the accent-behavior of "ṛtaspṛśā," "mitrāvaruṇā," and similar dual-vocative forms, with detailed citation of Panini and Phit-sutra rules on gaṇa-classification, "avidyamāna-pūrva-padārtha" (bahuvrīhi-type) compounds, and accent-retention. As with the preceding two pages, this is characterized rather than translated line-by-line, given its sustained density; the accent-patterns discussed match what is already visible in the printed Saṃhitā text above and do not alter any of the established senses. The first half of this page concludes the extended grammatical discussion of "mitrāvaruṇā," "ṛtāvṛdhau," and related compound-accent questions from the preceding pages, in the same dense register; not reproduced line-by-line. This closes out the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for Rik 2.8 as a whole.

original p. 709
original p. 710
original p. 711

"Kratuḥ" — the word derives from the root "kṛ" (to do), with the affix "tu" (Uṇādi 1.71[?]), giving "kratu"; this is why the affix "tu" produces the form "kratu," with its accent falling per that affix's own class-rule. This affix results in the accent falling as seen in the printed text.

"Āśāthe" — means "pervades, extends toward." Following Bhaṭṭabhāskara's own gloss: from "aś" + "īta" [in the sense of "obtaining, reaching"] (Panini 8.2.?[?]), the word "dviktva" [reduplication] applies to roots such as "aś" (to eat/pervade); by "aś + īta = ahnate" ("obtains") (Panini 2.4.?), the form is elided [of a class-affix]. "Ate adeśaḥ" (Panini 2.4.80[?]) governs the substitution of "at" for the ending, and the resulting long vowel of the base [as printed]... Caveat: as with the preceding grammar-heavy pages, the "kratuḥ" and "āśāthe" derivations above are best-effort, lower-confidence readings. The opening lines close out the grammar of "āśāthe" from the previous page — deriving the long vowel via the "dīrgha" [lengthening] rule for such affixed forms, and briefly noting "ṭitaḥ ātmane-padānām" and "eṣām"-class accent rules — in the same dense register; not reproduced further.

original p. 712

Sūkta 2, The Ninth and Final Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

क॒वी नो॑ मित्रावरुणा तुविजा॒ता उ॑रु॒क्षया॑ । द॒क्षं द॑धाते॒ अप॑सम् ॥९॥

kavī́ no mitrāvaruṇā tuvijātā́ urukṣáyā | dakṣáṃ dadhāte ápasam ||9||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

कवी इति । नः । मित्रावरुणा । तुविऽजाता । उरुऽक्षया । दक्षं । दधाते इति । अपसम् ॥९॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

मित्रावरुणा नो देवौ नोऽस्मदर्थं दक्षं बलमपसं कर्म च दधाते । पोषयतः । कीदृशौ । कवी मेधाविनौ । तुविजातौ बहुनामुपकारकतया संभूतौ । विप्रो भूर उभयोश्च तेषु सम्भ्यायुक्तिषु चेतुर्भिश्च सम्भ्याविनौ कविर्मेधावित्वे प्रसिद्धः । उरु कुविज्ञेव्यक्तेति परिकं । उरुकुत्यत उभयत्रैव संभ्यायुक्तेषु बलवानसौ पक्षो विळति स्थितिः । mitrāvaruṇā no deva no'smad-arthaṃ dakṣaṃ balam apasaṃ karma ca dadhāte | poṣayataḥ | kīdṛśau | kavī medhāvinau | tuvijātau bahunām upakārakatayā sambhūtau | ... urukṣayau ubhayor api pratiṣṭhā-sthitiḥ |

Translation: "Mitra and Varuṇa, our deities, uphold and increase for our sake both 'dakṣa' (strength) and 'apas' (rite/action). What kind of pair are they? 'Kavī' — the two wise ones. 'Tuvijātau' — born so as to be helpers to many. 'Urukṣayau' — dwelling in a wide space, that is, both established with a broad, stable dwelling-place." The Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya continues briefly with grammar notes on "dakṣam" and "apasam," in the established dense register.

original p. 713

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

कवी (kavī) — the two wise ones | तुविजाता (tuvijātā) — born so as to help many, that is, produced for the sake of many | उरुक्षया (urukṣayā) — dwelling in a vast, established abode, or possessed of a broad, stable dwelling | मित्रावरुणा (mitrāvaruṇā) — Mitra and Varuṇa, these deities | नः (naḥ) — for us | दक्षं (dakṣaṃ) — strength | अपसं (apasaṃ) — and work (the rite, i.e., the sacrifice) | दधाते (dadhāte) — uphold, bestow.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

We, who are engaged in performing this yajna, are aided by these deities Mitra and Varuṇa, who are exceedingly wise; upholding many, and refuge to those who come [to them], or protectors of many dwelling-places. May Mitra and Varuṇa in this way graciously bestow upon us strength, and the capability to perform yajnas and similar rites.

॥ English Translation ॥

O, Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work (sacrifice).

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Kavī" — this word has already been discussed above. "Vipra," "dhīra," and "medhāvī" are all words that convey this same sense of wisdom; among the various senses of the word "kavi," "wise" is the one that fits here. Therefore here "kavi" is properly understood as meaning "wise."

"Tuvijātā" — "uru" and "tuvi" are words both meaning "many"; since the meaning "helper of many" fits well in this context, most scholars explain "tuvi" as meaning "helper," or, in this same sense, "many." "Tuvi" carries the sense "strong or mighty." Given this sense, the word "tuvijātā" is here explained as meaning "born in the lineage of the strong," or "born of mighty parents" (Born of strong...

original p. 714

...race)" — this sense too fits well. Geldner takes the same sense; the Bhashyakara and other authors adopt the meaning drawn from Yāska's own explanation, since the meaning proposed here does not appear inconsistent with that.

"Urukṣayā" — the Bhashyakara explains this as "possessed of a broad, established dwelling-place"; the authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain "urukṣaya" in the sense of "possessing a special, broad plain/settlement," reading it as a distinct compound (drawn from the widely established senses of the word). Given this, "urukṣaya" is taken to mean: those who possess a settled, established dwelling — a settlement across the extended earth.

"Dakṣaṃ" — this word, meaning "strength," is well known from the discussion given at the very outset of this sukta (see page 699 above). The Bhashyakara here explains "dakṣa" as meaning "the power/strength of the mind." Later, however, some interpret "dakṣa" as meaning "efficiency" ("Intellectual faculty or power; efficiency in work both mental and physical"). Others take "dakṣa" and "buddhi-śakti" (intellectual capacity) to carry the same sense; that, too, is fitting here.

"Apasam" — the Bhashyakara explains "apas" as meaning "karma" (action, rite). Further, some hold that "dakṣa" and "apas" together mean "one's own strength" and "the specific capability to accomplish the intended work." But the fitting sense here is that "dakṣam" refers to strength itself, while "apasam" refers to that which is accomplished — the rite (the yajna). This grants a sense to which the desire "may my rite prosper" is naturally connected.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

"Mitrāvaruṇā" — here, the word "Mitra" takes the accent of the accusative, connected with the Prātipadika accent-rule already discussed above. "Varuṇaḥ" — the derivation "varṇāvarṇyor unan" (Uṇādi 1.9[?]) is applied, giving "varuṇaḥ" from the root "vṛ" with the affix "unan," through the process of guṇa and other adjustments. "Devatādvandve ca" (Panini 6.3.26[?]) — in a dvandva-compound of deity-names, the first member retains its accent — hence the accent seen here.

"Uru" + "tuvi" — Yāska's Nirukta (2.?.?) states this word "tuvi" among words meaning "many"; many rishis in similar contexts have used "tuvijāta" as a compound meaning "born to help many." "Tuvīnāṃ jātaḥ = tuvijātaḥ" — a genitive compound, resolving by regular sandhi rules... This page continues and closes the grammatical derivation of "tuvijātā," "urukṣayā," "dakṣaṃ," and "apasam" in the established dense register — not reproduced in full detail — before closing the sukta itself.

original p. 715

"Asyeti" — from the root meaning "to obtain a fruit through an action," a formation results; that is, "apas" (work) here means the action whose fruit is obtainable through the deed performed. "Apasa kartryāyāṃ" (Uṇādi 5.65[?]) — the affix "asun" gives "apas," meaning "work" in general. Since the root here means "to perform, to be diligent in an action," the affix produces the accent seen in the printed text — hence "apasasyāre" (Rigveda Samhita 1.?.?), reading "apas" in this same sense.

॥ इति प्रथमास्ष्टके प्रथमाध्याये चतुर्थो वर्गः ॥ Thus ends the fourth Varga of the first Adhyāya of the first Aṣṭaka.

॥ इति द्वितीयं सूक्तं समाप्तम् ॥

Thus Ends the Second Sūkta

यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव नारायण नमोऽस्तु ते ॥ yad akṣara-pada-bhraṣṭaṃ mātrā-hīnaṃ tu yad bhavet | tat sarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva nārāyaṇa namo'stu te ||

"Whatever letter or word may have gone astray, whatever may be deficient in metre — may all of that be forgiven, O Lord Nārāyaṇa; salutation to you."

॥ ॐ तत्सत् ॥ Om, that is truth. This is the traditional closing benediction the source appends at the end of this sukta's own treatment, asking forgiveness for any inadvertent errors of recitation or transcription and offering a closing salutation — a formula distinct from, and in addition to, the sukta's own concluding structural marker above.

Summary of Sūkta 2, all nine verses: 1. "vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṅkṛtāḥ..." — Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation. 2. "vāyav ukthebhir jarante..." — O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises. 3. "vāyo tava prapṛñcatī dhenā..." — O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver and to many others who invite you for drinking Soma. 4. "indravāyū ime sutā..." — O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations poured out for you. Come with food for us. 5. "vāyav indraś ca cetathaḥ..." — O Vayu and Indra, dwellers in the sacrifices, you are aware of these Soma-libations. Come hither quickly. 6. "vāyav indraś ca sunvata ā yātam..." — O Indra and Vayu, come quickly to drink the Soma of the sacrificer; thus your coming will complete the rite. 7. "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣaṃ varuṇaṃ ca riśādasam..." — I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water. 8. "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā..." — O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward. 9. "kavī no mitrāvaruṇā tuvijātā urukṣayā..." — O Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work. What made this sūkta distinctive: unlike Sūkta 1, this one opened with an unusually long apparatus — the extended Jaimini-sutra debate on Stotra/Shastra (spanning roughly Jaimini 2.1.1–26), the full Agnishtoma ritual-structure summary, and the detailed seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra framework — before the verses themselves began. Once underway, the verse-by-verse commentary followed the now-familiar template throughout, with substantial Viśeṣārtha excursuses on Soma (its botany, geography, and processing), on "dhenā" (its many senses across Vedic usage), on "dakṣa"/"riśādasa," and on "ṛta" (water vs. truth vs. yajna) — each weighing Sāyaṇa's reading against Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava, the Vedārtha-yatna authors, and Western scholars (Geldner, Max Müller, Grassmann, Ludwig, Roth, Eggling, Hillebrandt, Bloomfield). Honesty note carried through this sūkta: several stretches of Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (grammar) were exceptionally dense even by this project's standards — notably printed pages 695, 702–703, and 708–711 — and were flagged as lower-confidence rather than presented as reliable transcriptions, consistent with the project's standing caution around this register. This page closes the grammatical derivation of "aṅga," "dāśuṣe," and "aṅgiraḥ" — noting among other points that "aṅgiraḥ" here takes the vocative form addressing Agni by this name — in the established dense register, followed by a brief citation from the Aitareya Brahmana on related ritual matters.

¶ The genuine highlight of this section: the Viśeṣārtha's full mythological account of why Agni is addressed as "Aṅgiraḥ" — two layered explanations given together. First, the Aitareya Brahmana's etymological story: Prajāpati's incestuous desire for his own daughter, the gods combining their fiercest essences to create Rudra as punisher, Prajāpati fleeing as the Mṛgaśira constellation, Rudra's arrow (as Ārdrā) causing Prajāpati's seed to scatter and turn to embers (aṅgāra) — from which the Āṅgirasas were born. Second, the Mahābhārata's Vana-parva account (the Mārkaṇḍeya-Yudhiṣṭhira dialogue): Agni once abandoning his ritual duties for the forest, with the rishi Aṅgiras taking over his role and thereby earning the title "Agni's son" for his lineage. Two genuinely different origin stories for the same epithet, both given without the commentator feeling any need to reconcile or choose between them.

This marks the completion of the Rigveda's very first sūkta — "agnim īḷe purohitam," nine Riks in Gāyatrī meter, seen by the rishi Madhuchandas Vaiśvāmitra, with Agni as its deity — together with its complete traditional apparatus: Saṃhitā-pāṭha, Pada-pāṭha, Sāyaṇa's Sanskrit commentary, grammatical derivation, word-by-word meaning, overall sense, English translation, and special topics, for every one of its nine verses.

The Second Sūkta (Ṛgveda 1.2)

1. This concludes the Pūrva-pakṣa — the objector's prima facie position.

¶ This section is different in character from Sukta 1: rather than moving straight into the verses themselves, the commentary opens with an extended Mimamsa-sutra discussion (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.1–9) on the metaphysical status of Stotra and Shastra mantras — genuinely sophisticated philosophical argument conducted through a real back-and-forth: Pūrva-pakṣa (Stotra/Shastra are merely preparatory, subordinate to a primary rite, since they just describe deities' qualities) → Siddhānta objection (this would force disrupting the established mantra-sequence to match literal deity-references) → Pūrva-pakṣa's counter (the "vā" particle allows general/illustrative reference, so "Indra" and "Mahendra" can be treated as the same deity) → Siddhānta's refutation (no — "Mahendra" is grammatically its own distinct deity-term by Ashtadhyayi 4.2.39, so the general principle doesn't apply here). This dialectical structure — thesis, objection, counter, refutation — is a genuinely good window into how Purva-Mimamsa argumentation actually proceeds, worked through on a concrete ritual example (the Mahendra-graha offering) rather than in the abstract.

2. The commentary now proceeds to state the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion of this entire discussion.

3. Pacing note: this entire five-page stretch was denser Mimamsa-philosophical argumentation than typical bhashya-prose, with several individual sutra-citations remaining best-effort readings given their compressed technical form — but the overall dialectical structure and conclusion came through with good confidence throughout.

¶ This section completed the debate's remaining threads and closed it out properly: the "twelve Stotras/twelve Shastras" argument (a precise stated number proves twelve distinct rites, not one collective act); the resolution of an apparent redundancy between two scriptural statements about Agni (one establishes that Agni is the deity, the other establishes which specific mantras to use — genuinely different functions, not repetition); the demonstration that "Stotra" and "Shastra" carry genuinely distinct meanings (sung vs. recited-unsung), which only makes sense if both are primary rites rather than a single subordinate function; a grammatical proof via the accusative case construction (parallel to "agnihotraṃ juhoti"); and finally the decisive argument from fruit-bearing capacity — Stotra/Shastra mantras are shown, from direct Vedic statements, to yield their own fruit through recitation, which only a primary rite (not a subordinate part) could do. The whole argument is capped with summary verses from the Nyāyamālā-Vistara commentary, cleanly restating the final position.

¶ This section established: Sukta 2's full structure (nine Riks, rishi Madhuchandas continuing from Sukta 1, Gayatri meter, three deities across its three verses — Vayu, Indra-Vayu, Mitra-Varuna — plus its role as one Puronuvakya for the Indra-Vayu-graha offering); the detailed procedural sequence of the Agnishtoma's Pratar-anuvaka (the Adhvaryu's Praisha-command to the Hotr, the Ajya-oblations at the Agnidhra fire, entering the Havirdhana-hall); and a genuinely useful overview of the seven Soma-yaga types (Agnishtoma, Atyagnishtoma, Ukthya, Shodashi, Atiratra, Aptoryama, Vajapeya), with Agnishtoma identified as the foundational form from which the other six derive through modification. The commentary now opens a condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma's full ritual structure — explicitly flagged as abbreviated, since the full technical treatment lives in the Taittiriya Samhita's sixth Kanda (Adhyayas 1-8) and would otherwise make the commentary unwieldy.

¶ This page continues the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure begun on the previous page — roughly fifteen further couplets in a dense, technical, versified register, evidently walking through the ritual's major stages in sequence: the Dīkṣaṇīya rite (consecration of the sacrificer), the purchase and consecration of the Soma creeper (soma-kraya), the Pravargya rite, the Upasad days, and the various preparatory homas leading up to the Sutyā (pressing) day itself. Recognizable technical terms include "dīkṣaṇīyam," "somam," "pravargya"-related forms, and "upasad" — but the verses compress a great deal of ritual-procedural detail into terse poetic Sanskrit, using specialized vocabulary not always glossed in the surrounding prose. Rather than risk a fabricated word-by-word rendering of this densely versified technical summary, this page is characterized here at the level of its subject matter; a fully confident line-by-line translation would need careful cross-referencing against the Taittiriya Samhita passages (6th Kanda) that the verses are themselves summarizing — precisely the source Sayana names on the previous page as containing the full prescribed detail.

4. This page completes the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure, continuing through roughly fifteen further couplets in the same dense technical register — evidently covering the remaining ritual stages: the Soma-purchase sequence, further preparatory rites, the building of the sacrificial altar (vedi) and fire-pits, and the approach to the Sutyā day itself. As with the preceding two pages, this dense versified portion is characterized here at the subject-matter level rather than translated line-by-line, for the same reasons given above.

5. This confirms, directly from the source, the exact "twelve Stotras, twelve Shastras" structure already established through the ritual table on page 652 and the Mimamsa argument on page 661 — a satisfying cross-confirmation of the earlier discussion.

¶ This section completed: the dense versified Sanskrit summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's full procedure (honestly characterized rather than force-translated, given its compressed technical register); a genuinely valuable confirmation that Agnishtoma uses exactly twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras (cross-confirming the earlier structural table and Mimamsa argument); clear explanations of Sattra-yagas, the Abhiplava/Prishthya distinction, and the three Savanas (Prataḥ, Madhyandina, Tritiya); the complete structural breakdown of the seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra spanning Suktas 2 and 3 (Vayu, Indra-Vayu, Mitra-Varuna in Sukta 2; Ashvins, Indra, Vishvedevah, Sarasvati in Sukta 3, three Riks each); and finally — Sukta 2's formal header (rishi Madhuchandas continuing, Gayatri meter, deities by Rik-range) and the complete Samhita-patha, Pada-patha, and Sayana-bhashya for its first verse: "vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṅkṛtāḥ | teṣāṃ pāhi śrudhī havam" — "O Vayu, come, thou beautiful one: these Soma-drops are made ready. Drink of them; hear our call" — with a genuine Nirukta citation (10.2) confirming the same reading.

¶ The grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 concludes at the top of this page. Its readable substance: "pāhi" — the root "pā" (in the sense of drinking) in the second-person singular imperative takes the substitute "hi" for the personal ending; the Vedic accent-rules keep the verb unaccented after the vocative "vāyo," and, though the root would ordinarily take the substitute "piba" in later Sanskrit, the Vedic procedure means the substitution "piba" does not apply here. "Śrudhi" — from the root "śru" (to hear), imperative second person, with the affix "śnu"-class insertion and the substitution of "dhi" for "hi" in the Vedic language after such roots; the long "ī" seen in "śrudhī" of the Saṃhitā text arises by the rule of lengthening. "Havam" — from the root "hve" (to call), with contraction of the semi-vowel, giving "hava," accented on the final syllable as a root-derived noun. Specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced.

45. What made this sūkta distinctive: unlike Sūkta 1, this one opened with an unusually long apparatus — the extended Jaimini-sutra debate on Stotra/Shastra (spanning roughly Jaimini 2.1.1–26), the full Agnishtoma ritual-structure summary, and the detailed seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra framework — before the verses themselves began. Once underway, the verse-by-verse commentary followed the now-familiar template throughout, with substantial Viśeṣārtha excursuses on Soma (its botany, geography, and processing), on "dhenā" (its many senses across Vedic usage), on "dakṣa"/"riśādasa," and on "ṛta" (water vs. truth vs. yajna) — each weighing Sāyaṇa's reading against Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava, the Vedārtha-yatna authors, and Western scholars (Geldner, Max Müller, Grassmann, Ludwig, Roth, Eggling, Hillebrandt, Bloomfield).
